en: Preface to the Direct Explanation of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra:
Since my youth, I have had a penchant for the fourfold canon; beyond the texts of Confucius and Mencius, I have delighted in reading the various sūtras from the Western lands.

Yet, whenever I encountered points that seemed constant or perplexing, I would simply mark them with a stop—much like Tao Yuanming’s practice of not seeking an overly thorough understanding. Not long after this...
Setting aside all matters concerning Maitreya’s service to the Buddha, I have instead devoted myself to reading various sutras morning and evening.
Among those who have commented on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the ten or so families of Mount Gushan are the most prominent; yet I remain increasingly unable to dispel my doubts. Why is this?
The *Śūraṅgama* was translated by only one person, Paṇḍita Mitraśānti, and subsequently polished by the State Councilor Fang; its prose is concise, profound, and complexly interwoven.
Its meaning is so comprehensive, illuminating, and responsive that it seems beyond the reach of discursive thought and conceptual discrimination;
yet the interpretations of the ten or so schools ultimately remain merely ten or so versions of the *Laṅkāvatāra*.

In recent times, commentaries have proliferated in a chaotic clamor, where scholars compete for breadth while eating by the ears—looking at their fragmented and erroneous expositions, which entangle like creeping vines, they are not even comparable to the *Laṅkāvatāra* spoken by the Tathāgata; the difference is more than that between heaven and earth.
How remote was the Dharma Master Mo of Wuxing! During the summer retreat at Gānlù Ān, he frequently expounded the wondrous meanings of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* to others.
When I asked him from where he had obtained these teachings and what expedient means a student should employ to master the *Śūraṅgama*, the Master smiled but did not answer;
instead, he presented me with ten fascicles of his own handwritten *Direct Commentary*. The Master served as the *Yún*... [text fragment ends].

The Great Disciple of the Venerable Elder, whose power of wisdom and power of practice both reached their full development, was profoundly versed in the Sanskrit scriptures and skilled in composition.

Having participated in the collation of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and delivered lectures upon its commentaries, he now withdrew from the public eye to the green mountains. There, he composed this present exegesis;

its glosses and sequential order strictly follow the text of the sūtra itself. He has extracted its essential framework, set forth its topical outlines, and connected its underlying logic, having further edited and finalized it.

The eminent scholar excels where others fall short, delivering his insights with clarity and directness. He has completely swept away the habits of fragmented analysis, error, and the entanglement of over-elaborate digressions.
Upon reading it once, it was as if piercing through clouds to behold the heavens; the brilliance of his pen perfectly accords with the Buddha’s intent.
Rather than merely acting like those who pore over old papers for a dozen or so generations, this loyal subject has had my lingering doubts suddenly shattered.

The Prajñā of Words should not be kept hidden away; it is a supreme opportunity that members of this community—both monastics and laypeople, men and women alike—have contributed funds to carve into printing blocks and circulate it.
I lament that today in the world, while the craft of carving is flourishing daily, the study of the scriptures is declining.

The works of Confucius and Mencius have all been corrupted and thrown into disorder by vulgar scholars and the pursuit of the imperial examination system. If there are those capable of editing and establishing the texts of the renowned sages...

To clarify the direct and swift path and establish a complete school of thought—such as the person of Dharma Master Mo—is this not what the Master of the Zi-cha clan praised as being among the disciples of the Sage?
Having written this preface to the *Direct Explanation of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, I await [the Master’s work] with bated breath.
Preface to the Direct Explanation of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, inscribed by the Layman Xiangguang Li Taichong (also known as Moshengfu) on a summer day in the year Jiwu of the Wanli era.
To examine the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* in detail: although its text consists of ten fascicles, its meaning is subsumed under three categories—principle (*li*), practice (*xing*), and realization (*zheng*).
These refer to the wondrous significance of our own mind, which is termed "principle. The integration of the three contemplations (*sanguan*) to return to and follow one's nature is termed "practice.
To personally experience the states within that principle is termed "realization. From beginning to end, the entire sūtra culminates solely in this.
These three meanings are fully encompassed herein;

therefore, when our Bhagavān Kāśyapa first took Ānanda as his starting point to investigate the source of the manifestation of the mind, he directly traced it to its origin, whereby the triad of sense-faculties, objects, and consciousness was all transformed into unsurpassed Bodhi.
Where, then, could one find any further distinction between the real and the false?

The designations "true" and "false" both become superfluous terms. Therefore, know that one’s own mind is the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, and the empty *tathāgatagarbha* is the wondrous endowment of one’s own mind;
how could it ever be described as "empty" while being separate from "existence"?
For this reason, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena are, in their very substance, the *tathāgatagarbha*—inherently pure and the Middle Way.

The principle of the truths is the clear exposition for manifesting the ultimate reality. Next, by relying on this central principle, one practices true cultivation to realize perfect penetration within a single thought-moment:

the wondrous faculty of hearing is manifested, the six aspects dissolve and the one vanishes; the three contemplations merge into a single mind, residual defilements cease, and the wisdom of all modes becomes perfected.
These two texts and two statements exhaustively describe the realization of practice. To trace the origin of the sutra: [The remainder of the text follows as provided in the source.]

The meaning is fundamentally straightforward, yet those who interpret it tend toward circuitousness; this is what is meant by saying that it is not the Sūtra itself that is difficult, but rather the commentaries (*zhuanji*) that pose the difficulty.

Master An was well-versed in the Śūraṅgama-samādhi; he extracted the essential principles and grasped the core teachings with such profound clarity and perspicuity that even a few words would penetrate the entire scripture, causing one to suddenly find oneself within samādhi. This was possible because he possessed the True Eye (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*).

Who among those who have attained wondrous enlightenment could do as he did? Thereupon, the assembly of students requested that Master An provide a direct commentary on its meaning, and Master An consented.
After five years of cold and heat, the draft was finally completed. This commentary does not concern itself with names and forms, but directly dissects the profound mysteries;
every word accords with the truth, and every phrase reveals the ultimate reality. While I happened to be in my quarters at Yunqi, I...
Beholding it as if one had obtained a most precious treasure, they requested its return to the banks of the Yuer Creek. Hearing of this, fellow practitioners from afar arrived one after another;
each contributed gold to have it carved into woodblocks for publication. Alas! In this present age, when the Dharma stands at the end of its cycle, false stones and brass alloys confound the genuine.
Yet this commentary stands far apart from all other exegeses; truly, it is like gold from Jambudvīpa or jade from Mount Jing—those with discernment will surely recognize it.
This work is certainly not to be mentioned in the same breath as common stones or brass; it is my joy that its inception originated with me, yet its merit belongs to the multitude.
Although I am not clever, I know that the Great Way is without words and the highest goodness leaves no trace of achievement;
therefore, I venture to record this rough outline in all its crudity, merely to mark the time and month.
Written on the day of the Buddha’s birth in the fourth month of summer in the year Jiwu (47th year of the Ming Wanli era), at the Ganlu Chan Monastery,
by Ma Zhengchu, a disciple of the Bodhisattva Precepts from Yuxi, who has bathed himself in perfumed water and bows in reverence.
Direct Praise of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra (with Preface) Can a person within this world fail to hear of the Way?
If one hears not of the Way, one will be swept away along the turbid and deluded currents, thereby entering the path of suffering.
If one is able to hear of the Way, one may roam freely wherever one goes and thus enter the wondrously adorned land of bliss. Alas for me!... [text continues]
Wandering through the dust and toil of worldly afflictions and dwelling upon the path of thorns, every lift of foot and movement of step was beset by obstacles;

it was for this reason that I came to long for the Way with an intensity no greater than the thirst of one parched by hunger. Yet, what could have been intended by my past karma but this fortunate convergence, whereby I encountered the Great Master Ren'an at the Ganlu Chan Monastery?
He first produced his *Direct Commentary on the Śūraṃgama Sūtra* and showed it to me; upon my initial reading, I was utterly bewildered.

Reading it again, I attained a realization; reciting it a third time, I joyfully experienced its resonance with my own mind. I then sighed, saying: "The efforts I applied in the past were all merely reckless and superficial.
Now, by examining this compilation, my ignorance has been cleared away and I have been shown the pearl within my robes.

By means of this precious vessel, I shall ascend to the shore of enlightenment; having escaped the perils of the ocean of suffering, I can find self-comfort wherever I dwell—all of which is due to [this work]."
How could I dare forget the source of my teacher’s transformative power? Those who have benefited as I have are numerous throughout the world;
how much more so those who have benefited even more than I?

Thus I know that this compilation is a star-chariot on the path to enlightenment and a precious torch illuminating the dark alleys. Students must take it as their guide to ascend directly [to the goal].
Do not linger at the illusory city on the way to the treasure land, lest you abandon your journey midway; may you thus not fail the hopes of our Master.
For this reason, I have composed a eulogy for him, saying:
How great is the Kunpeng! Swooping and gliding in the Southern Abyss, Wuxing has emerged with his blade-sharp brilliance.
Yunqi Xuming: With a mind of broad learning and humble restraint, his Way fills the four quarters without being constrained;
he broadly propagates the Six Perfections, riding the White Ox Cart and upholding the Seal of True Reality.
Amidst the sea of birth and death, he serves as our reliance and our refuge.
Having completely eradicated all complications and overturned empty names and numbers, I know that this compilation will reach ever further and ever wider;
may those who wander aimlessly likewise ascend the path to enlightenment.
Furthermore, he offered this eulogy:
Were it not for those with prior awakening, who would open the way from ignorance and turbidity?
Were it not for the compassionate vessel, who would ferry those lost in their direction?
Therefore, the World-Honored Śākyamuni sent down his perfect radiance from Tuṣita and was born from the right side at Kapilavastu.
The teachings arose as sudden and gradual; the capacities were gathered through the partial and the perfect.
He rinsed his wondrous understanding in the perfect sound and articulated the profound meaning in refined discourse.
He secretly penetrated the five branches [of the Vinaya] and purified the three wheels [of giving, speech, and action] of the Mahāyāna, spreading and propagating the Way.
The True and Semblance Dharma alternate in their rise; now, in this final age, it is the benevolent one who upholds it.
Therefore, I, Upa, have engraved this record: with sincere devotion I take refuge in the Buddha and receive the Dharma from the Saṅgha;
I exert myself in the precepts and prohibitions, never exceeding them by even a fraction of an inch.
The instructions are already vast; let even the slightest trace of defilement be utterly exhausted.
Subdue the single mind to take root in the Pure Land, and eliminate the four marks of selfhood. When blessings are empty and wealth is discarded, the rites shall be successfully completed;
what obstacle could there be across kalpas? Grant amnesty for transgressions and rescue those from their faults.
Illuminating the mind to uproot suffering, pacifying the state and aiding the people, may you perpetually bestow your protection throughout all eternity upon the myriad species;
I do not seek this for myself alone, but offer these humble praises with reverence.
Written on the day of the Buddha’s birth in the fourth month of summer in the year Jǐwèi (1619), the forty-seventh year of the Great Ming Wànlì era,
by the lay practitioner Kōngkōng of [Làn]shuǐ, Lǐ Yúnlóng, while bathing his head and body in the Guībǎo Tower at Yǔxī.
A Brief Preface to the Direct Explanation of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra:
First, Establishing the Timing and Tonic.

Regarding the interpretation of this sūtra, Changshui [Zhuan'ao] distinguished it by means of ten gates; while these point to the distant [source], their meaning is comprehensive, yet beginners have not yet...

The *Yì* (Book of Changes) can provide illumination; however, that which is not detailed here—specifically the corruption of the flavor of the times that has remained unclarified for a thousand years—is now briefly set forth from its origins to be verified by the Great Masters.

Formerly, Master Xuán of Chángshuī pointed out that the events concerning King Ajātaśatru and Virūḍhaka did not occur at a single time, as the *Yēshǒuchí dì jì* (Record of Yaśodharā Holding the Earth) derives from the *Fǎhuá* (Lotus Sūtra).
Therefore, he judged this sūtra to follow after the *Fǎhuá* and precede the *Nìbàn* (Nirvāṇa Sūtra).
Before his seat on Mount Gu, Master Yi of Wuxing shared the same intent as Masters Changshui and Wenling Huan, who pointed out that the Dharma King’s preaching was systematic and orderly:
first, he taught the sudden vehicle of the One Vehicle to establish the foundation—this is the *Avataṃsaka*;

next, he taught the gradual vehicle of the Three Vehicles to accommodate various capacities—this refers to the *Āgama*, *Vaipulya*, and *Prajñā* sūtras; and finally, he taught the perfect vehicle of the One Vehicle.
This reveals that the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* is indeed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and the *Śūraṃgama* is indeed the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Within this context, the current Master Miaofeng Jue has examined the *Tiantai xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) and produced the "One Hundred Questions on the Śūraṃgama" to refute various interpretations;

thus, masters such as Changshui and Wenling would find it difficult to escape the "mirror that reflects the gall-bladder" [i.e., the penetrating scrutiny] of these questions. Upon careful examination, the intent of these One Hundred Questions certainly belongs to...

The Vaipulya (fangděng) is subsumed within the Vaipulya; this has been the established principle since antiquity. As for the fact that the "One Hundred Questions" does not provide explicit clarification, it is intended for people to investigate and seek the answer for themselves so that they may discover the thread of the teaching on their own.
Formerly, the two masters Shenzhi and Boting also judged this sutra to belong to the Vaipulya.
This is because the World-Honored One’s teachings throughout his entire life were generally categorized according to the five periods and five flavors. However...
At this time, the doctrine of the "Periods" (wǔshí) emerged from the *Avataṃsaka* and *Nirvāṇa* sūtras. Based on these, Tiantai established his system by arranging them into five periods:
the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Āgama*, the Vaipulya (*Fāngděng*), the *Prajñā*, and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Among these five periods, the Vaipulya is defined by its function of criticizing partiality and disparaging the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), while praising the Great and extolling the Perfect. However, within this [Vaipulya] period...
Is it not the case that the *Tanhā* (Vimalakīrti) Sūtra is likewise a Vaipulya? Yet, various masters, upon merely seeing the sequence of the sūtra’s text, offer inconsistent critiques;
they alone fail to realize that within these five periods there are both general and specific aspects. "General" means it encompasses the beginning and the end;
"specific" means it resides specifically in the Vaipulya. The meaning of their mutual pervasiveness is explained in detail in the *Fahua Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra) by Siming.

The *Guangming xuanji* states: "In the classification of teachings for ordinary beings, there is a division into 'prior' and 'subsequent. The prior division has a sequential order, while the subsequent division is indeterminate.

Although the subsequent is indeterminate, it must be subsumed within the prior. In this present sutra, the mutual references to various locations reflect the indeterminate nature of the subsequent division;

the texts concerning the seven inquiries, the eight refutations, and the three categories reflect the sequential nature of the prior division. Thus, the general is gathered into the specific, and the inclusive is subsumed."
Regarding the subsequent classification as belonging to the *Vaipulya* (fangděng), there are precedents available for examination; it is surely not a mere conjecture.

One should know that this sutra is subsumed within the Perfect Teaching (*yánjiào*) of the *Vaipulya*, yet people remain unaware of this and point only to its position relative to the preceding and following sections—what evidence is there for such a claim?

It is evident that its timing belongs to the *Vaipulya*, its flavor is determined to be "clarified butter" (*ghṛta*), and it is decisively judged that this sutra must have its own established source. As for those who point to specific illustrations without detailed investigation, their classifications remain incomplete.
I have not yet fully understood this; it would be fortunate if those who have attained mastery would deepen its current and swell its source.
Alas! This sutra arrived in our land of Zhendan at the latest of all times; thus, no definitive judgment from a single school has been heard, and errors spanning a thousand years have persisted.
Herein, I briefly set forth my humble views; may scholars who clarify the scriptures examine and critique them.

Next, the essential outline is clarified in accordance with the ancient path of Master Dao’an. Generally, the exegesis of a sūtra is divided into three major sections: first, the introductory section (nidāna); second, the main body (saddharma); and third, the dissemination section (pariṇāmanā).
In the present sūtra, the introductory and dissemination sections may be understood as they are. As for its main body, it is further divided into five parts, the first of which is the Principle (li).

This is divided into five sections: (1) the introductory section, (2) the causal conditions, (3) the main exposition, (4) the realization section, and (5) the conclusion of the sutra title followed by supplementary remarks.
In brief, the audience understands through the principles shown, practices through that understanding, and realizes through that practice.

Thus, the essential framework of this sutra consists solely of principle, practice, and realization; for this reason, Ānanda’s inquiry contains three essentials. First, the sutra says: Ānanda himself...
Regretting that although he has long been well-versed in the teachings, his power of the Way remains incomplete,

Ānanda earnestly entreats the Tathāgatas of the ten directions for the initial expedient means to achieve the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* that lead to Bodhi. Observing that this inquiry by Ānanda fully encompasses the three essentials of principle,
practice, and realization, and seeing how the World-Honored One follows it to sequentially reveal them, one knows the profound mystery of this entire scripture.
The profound [teachings] all emerge from this; for the purpose of answering the underlying intent, this section is established as the "Introduction to the Gate of Reasoning" (*Nyāyamukha*).

Therefore, the World-Honored One first sequentially refuted the seven bases of clinging, and subsequently revealed the two fundamental roots of birth-and-death and nirvana—namely, the distinct karma and the common lot—and the two kinds of false views.
He then demolished the four modes of being as having no master, clarifying the two moons.

Although he had already clearly understood that his own body and mind consist of both the real and the false, the substantial and the insubstantial, he still remained deluded regarding the fact that all illusory transformations arise and cease such that their very locus is the Truth itself.

Therefore, [the Buddha] further demonstrated that the five aggregates, the six sense bases, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and the seven great elements—all their natures and characteristics—are perfectly interfused and pervade the entire Dharma-realm; this is the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*.
The principles therein have been fully expounded; thus, Ānanda spoke verses of praise and aspiration to conclude the preceding text.
However, as the underlying principles were subtle and human understanding was becoming increasingly obscured, Ānanda’s power of inquiry reached its limit.
Consequently, Pūrṇa—whose eloquence was foremost and who surpassed Ānanda—seized upon the principle of the "pure and original nature" to initiate a series of questions.

Although this is difficult, the World-Honored One extensively relies on the three types of continuity to exhaust all profound dialectics, reaching such points as "neither identical nor different, neither the same nor not the same," all of which serve to progressively illuminate the perfect principle of wondrous *śamatha* and so forth.
Second, the Sūtra records: Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I am now like a traveler lodging for the night."
This person suddenly received from the Heavenly King the gift of a magnificent mansion; although he obtained a great residence, he must enter through a gate.
What is called "the Heavenly King’s gift of a magnificent mansion" is a metaphor for the principles previously shown, such as the wondrous *śamatha*.

Ānanda thought that although he had heard these principles, because he had not yet attained the gateway for cultivation and advancement, it was the same as not having heard them at all; thus he spoke these words.
For this reason, the World-Honored One, in response to my request, revealed the two definitive meanings for awakening the initial resolve.

Within that discourse, he clarified the five layers of turbidity, distinguished the relative superiority of the six sense faculties, tested the permanence of the auditory faculty by striking a bell, demonstrated the nature of knots by tying a cloth, and set forth the fundamental roots of perfect penetration of the twenty-five sages.
He then selected the faculty of hearing as the primary expedient means, thereby enabling one to enter deeply through a single door.

From the initial aspiration to realize the principle until the establishment of the *bodhimaṇḍa* and the manifestation of light to proclaim the mantra, every step is nothing other than the revelation of the perfect practice of wondrous *śamatha* and so forth.
Thirdly, although Ānanda understood the method of cultivation, he had not yet clarified the stages of realization;
just as one traveling a long distance first inquires about lodging, he therefore again requested the names for the beginning and end of the successive stages of cultivation and realization.

Therefore, the Sūtra says: Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, when one thus cultivates and realizes the Buddha’s samādhi, yet has not yet reached nirvāṇa, why is it called the stage of Dry Wisdom?
From what point among the forty-four minds does one gradually attain the vision for cultivation?
By reaching what state or locus is one said to have entered the stages? And why is one called an Equal Enlightenment Bodhisattva?"
However, as the World-Honored One was about to reveal the path to enlightenment, he first clarified the perversions; for one who eliminates perversion purifies the obstacles to the Path.

Because the elimination of perversion establishes the three gradual stages (*tri-krama*), the establishment of the fifty-five positions on the path to Bodhi through gradual cultivation therein is none other than the elucidation of the perfect positions realized through *śamatha* and the other [practices]. As above, these three...

The essential purport of this sutra is thus complete and exhaustive; therefore, there are no further profound doctrines beyond it, and Mañjuśrī merely requests that the name of the sutra be concluded.

Although the subsequent sections contain detailed accounts of the ten habitual practices, the six modes of mutual interaction, and the seven realms of existence—words that are both refined and rigorous—these were nonetheless elicited through Ānanda’s tireless dedication for the sake of others and the Buddha’s inexhaustible eloquence in joyful exposition, as he thoroughly investigated and revealed these matters.

Fulfilling this request, I wish to cause people to clearly understand the characteristics of good and evil and the causes for ascending or sinking, which follow one another as surely as a shadow follows a form;
this is the inevitable principle, intended only to ensure they do not become negligent.

Furthermore, as the Dharma assembly was about to conclude and the listeners had no further doubts, the World-Honored One returned once more to Mount Zijing, where he leaned against it again to discourse deeply on the five aggregates (*skandhas*) and demons, extensively refuting all errors.

Because of confusion regarding this, yet again, at the very end of this sutra, with profound compassion, [the compiler] has perfected the meaning from beginning to end, fearing that practitioners might not be familiar with the signs within meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), and thus provides a detailed clarification in advance.

However, these two instances are merely the remnants of the texts concerning practice (*caryā*) and realization (*siddhi*). In general, the compiler of the collection skillfully extracted these two passages and appended them to the conclusion of the sutra.
Thereafter, the intention was to provide a direct path between practice and realization, free from deviations, so that those who train might find it concise and easy to understand;
only then was the work entrusted for circulation and the scroll concluded.

Since the above has extracted the meaning of the sutra and grasped its principles to directly show the main outline—desiring that those who have not yet entered the heart of the text first clarify the essential tenets—I did not dare to offer divergent or far-fetched explanations that would create obstacles.

In his mind, it is sufficient that he attains a state of cool clarity without obstruction, that he masters both the words and their meanings, that he internalizes the text for himself, and that he realizes the principle while forgetting the words.
Therefore, there is no need to further entangle oneself in extraneous branches and vines; one simply provides a direct interpretation of the text.

**Preface to the Direct Explanation of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra:** The origins of this work stem from the fact that ancient commentaries have become overly ornate, leaving the students of the later generations bewildered at the crossroads.
Following the example of the Great Master Zhang Jiangling’s *Direct Explanation of the Four Books*, I was urged to compose this text; therefore, the entire work herein follows his format.
Because the direct instruction on the text allows for immediate understanding, it avoids the habit of trailing off into endless digressions;
thus, retaining its original title, it is titled *Zhijie* (Direct Explanation).
This compilation establishes its intent to reveal hidden mysteries, disclose the essential tenets of the school, and provide a balanced critique of the shortcomings and excesses of previous scholars.

I hope these corrections will cause the meaning of the scriptures to become clear, leaving no further obscurities; may readers not, because of their directness, treat them with neglect—this would be fortunate.
The phrasing of the scriptures is interwoven and their meanings are complexly arranged; their coherence, mutual inclusion, and resonance depend entirely upon the correct [text].
The eye may indeed follow the waves or drift with the current, rushing forward and forgetting its origin;
even if the flow spreads vast and wide like the floods of autumn, it is certain that it will dry up before long.
The compiled "Discussions on the Middle Path" follows the topical sections of the sutras and the principles of ancient commentaries to facilitate study and recitation during lectures;
as for any expressions that are迂僻 (perverse and obscure) or 舛謬 (erroneous and fallacious), they shall be set aside and not cited in discussion.
The textual meaning of this sutra originates from a distant source and flows in a long current; those with a beginner's mind cannot perceive its true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).

While a single reading may still leave one at a distance, a third repetition allows for comprehension. Nevertheless, one must investigate it with a vacant mind and a sincere heart; thus, the holy path may be expected.
What is most to be dreaded is the presence of thorns and brambles within the breast, for then there is no way to enter the gate of profound mystery (*gambhīra-guhya*).

The meaning and phrasing of this scripture are still quite concise; for instance, in the *Fifty Verses on the Path to Enlightenment*, one often advances through its stages by means of a single word—is this not too brief?
Were it not for those of lofty insight and vision, such brevity would likely be treated with negligence.
Please observe that the relative extensiveness and conciseness of scriptures such as the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* makes this clear. Generally speaking, [the teachings are] profound...
For those who study the principles, both the broad and the concise are equally convenient,
leaving no further doubts or obstructions.
[End of General Preface] *The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, the Definitive Meaning of All Bodhisattvas*...
In this first fascicle of the *Direct Explanation of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra of Myriad Practices*, only three of the five titles of the original scripture are included, while two are omitted;
furthermore, twenty-two characters from these three titles have been excised. Thus, the edited version is brilliantly formed into an elegant title that does not contradict [the original].
The "Original Meaning" (*Benyi*) is also titled "The Five Chapters Elucidating the Timely Appropriateness.

If one carefully contemplates the principles within these titles, one will have grasped more than half of the essential purport of the entire scripture. The five names of this scripture appear in the eighth fascicle;
however, according to the current title, there are three names, and the phrase "Great Buddha’s Crown" (*Dafoding*) corresponds to its first name in that [eighth] fascicle.

The Sūtra states: "This sūtra is titled *The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa-Sitātapatra Unsurpassed Jewel Seal, the Pure Ocean-Eye of the Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions.*" Now, in the present title, only the three characters "Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa" (*dà fó dǐng*) are retained, while the remaining eighteen characters have been deleted.
This is because these three characters constitute the essential substance of the Great Samādhi, whereas the other characters describe that samādhi.
Because the meaning resides within the substance, the meaning is deleted to preserve its substance. "The Tathāgata" and below constitutes the third name;
it is fully inclusive and does not delete [the title]. "All Bodhisattvas" and below constitutes the fifth name, from which the four characters "Anointment Chapter" (*guǎngdì zhāngjù*) are deleted.
This scripture originates from the *Guǎngdì* (Anointment) section; its essential meaning lies with the Bodhisattvas.

Because this work is among the myriad practices, I have deleted the redundant and extracted the essentials. The meaning clarified in the second title is merely the causal conditions for initiating the teaching;
the principles elucidated in the fourth title can now be subsumed under the headings "The Great Buddha-Topknot" and "The Secret Cause of the Tathāgata.
Since these three fundamental tenets are established, all others can be subsumed herein; therefore, this is the compilation of the sutra.

This person has skillfully arranged and compiled these words into a text. If one were to take all five names collectively as the title, the meaning would become redundant and cumbersome, lacking elegance;
therefore, I shall now follow the original title and provide a direct explanation.
"The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa" is the comprehensive name for the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. As the first sutra states: "There is a samādhi named 'Great'..."
The term *buddhāloka-samādhi* in Sanskrit is also called *samāpatti*, which is translated as "right concentration" (*zhèngdìng*).
This is the right concentration within the ultimate fruit. Originally, the *śūraṅgama-samādhi* contains the three meanings of *śamatha* and so forth;
since one must cultivate *śamatha* and the other two [methods] to realize this concentration, it is listed first here so that people may contemplate the name and thereby know its essence.
What is meant by "the Greatly Great"? It is so named because it is the essence of the fruit of the Samyak-saṃbodhi (Perfectly Correct Concentration).

It exhausts the three periods of time and pervades the ten directions; it is without beginning and without end, neither internal nor external. It transcends existence and non-existence, surpassing both the measurable and the immeasurable.

Its fundamental essence is inherently great; it is not called "great" in contrast to the "small," for there is nothing equal to it. Thus it is termed "Great. There were ancients who used the single character "Great" [to signify this].

The delusion of interpreting this as a real entity (*dravyadharma*) is incorrect. This is because "great" merely reveals the magnitude of the dharma-body; it simply indicates that its extent is so vast.
Furthermore, this word "great" is like the *Zhou Yi*, which says: "How great is the Great Primordial of Qian! All things derive their beginning from it.
Here, the word "how great" is a term of praise, while "the Great Primordial of Qian" is the real dharma, and "all things deriving their beginning" is what reveals its [nature].

The characters "Great" (Da) and "Meaning" (Yi) in the title are also words of praise. The two characters "Buddha-Usnīṣa" (Fo-ding) refer to the actual dharma, while the other two names are merely its meanings.
Those ancients who interpreted "Buddha-Usnīṣa" as a metaphor have utterly missed the intent of the sūtra.

Furthermore, the Awakening of Faith Treatise (Qixin lun) fully embodies the three meanings of essence, attributes, and function; these correspond to the meaning of "Great" here. The meaning of "Great" is difficult to fathom.
Thought cannot be exhausted by words. What is meant by "Buddha-peak"? In Sanskrit, "Buddha" is translated as "Awakening.
This Awakening is what the subsequent sutra refers to as "the nature of awakening. This nature of awakening is the numinous awareness inherently possessed by every person.

Because this numinous nature of awareness is profoundly still and unmoving, it is called "right concentration. It is quiescent yet constantly illuminating; it illuminates while remaining constantly quiescent.
Because quiescence and illumination are non-dual, it is called "nature-awareness" (*xingjue*).

Although this nature-awareness is one, there are differences between those who realize it in terms of partiality or fullness. What is revealed in this sutra is the perfect, ultimate, and unsurpassed fruition-awareness;
therefore, it is called the "Buddha-Crown" (*foding*), where "crown" signifies fullness and "Buddha" is the designation for the most supreme. Nevertheless, this does not depart from our own mind.
Yet it is called the Buddha-peak; the Buddha-peak is precisely the perfect enlightenment of our own mind. Therefore, the subsequent text designates it as the "ever-abiding true mind.
This is knowing that there is no scripture outside the mind—the entire scripture is the mind itself—and that there is nothing taught apart from the mind.
The above has been an explanation of the Great Buddha-peak according to the principle of the fundamental understanding of nature-enlightenment. Nature-enlightenment is precisely the ever-abiding.
Furthermore, based on the true intent, one should read the three characters "Great Buddha-Crown" (*Mahā-uṣṇīṣa*) as a heading that runs through the following two titles.

This indicates that the "Great Buddha-Crown" is the Tathāgata’s secret cause for cultivation and realization, the definitive meaning of the ultimate truth, and the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*—the foremost of all the myriad practices of the Bodhisattvas.

One must understand that the intention behind the ancients establishing this title was to clarify that ordinary beings and sages share the same source, and that the fruit and the cause are fundamentally one and the same.

Therefore, the three characters "Great Buddha-Crown" (Mahā-uṣṇīṣa) are placed above the two names [of the two Bodhisattvas]. △ Regarding the phrase "The Definitive Meaning of the Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, Cultivation, and Realization":
one should understand that the two characters "Tathāgata" (Rulai), when viewed in relation to the various Bodhisattvas below, refer to the person who has attained the fruit.
What is meant by "Tathāgata"? This is a name given according to principle; therefore, it points to and certifies the Sage who has realized the principle.

The name "Tathāgata" (Thus-Come) signifies that the meaning of emptiness thus comes, and the meaning of existence thus comes; because emptiness and existence are non-dual, they are joined as the name Tathāgata.
Furthermore, the meaning of quiescence thus comes, and the meaning of illumination thus comes; because quiescence and illumination are simultaneous, they are joined as the name Tathāgata.
One must know these two meanings of Tathāgata: since the Buddha-nature is originally present within my own mind, every person may be called a Tathāgata.

Because the Buddha has already realized this principle, he truly bears the title of Tathāgata; yet, although sentient beings possess this same principle, they have not personally realized it and thus do not dare to assume that title for themselves.
Furthermore, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "He comes by way of the path of reality (yathābhūta-mārga) to achieve perfect enlightenment.
This is also a designation of a person based on the principle. What is meant by the "secret cause" (*guhyahetu*)? The secret cause refers to two [aspects].
Regarding the interpretation of the meaning, there are two aspects: first, concerning the manifest; second, concerning the secret. As for the manifest, the first sutra states:

"The Buddhas of the ten directions attain the realization of Bodhi through the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*; Bodhi is the fruit, while the wondrous *śamatha* and so forth are the causes.
Regarding the secrecy of the cause, that is the "wondrous" (*miao*) of *śamatha*. Regarding the secrecy of the result, the seventh sutra states:
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, by means of this mantra-heart (*dharmacitta*), have attained unexcelled, perfect, and universal enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

This "mantra-heart" refers to the secret meaning; it also indicates that the mantra is the cause. All Buddhas of the three periods of time cultivated these two causes—the manifest and the secret—and thereby realized Bodhi.
Thus, regarding the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), this ten-fascicle work is explained in terms of the expressive vehicle (*vācaka*).

The "text" (*wen*) refers to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) rather than the non-definitive; the "clarity" (*liao*) refers to the ultimate meaning rather than the provisional vehicle’s non-ultimate meaning.
Therefore, within this single name, the teaching (*jiao*), principle (*li*), practice (*xing*), and realization (*zheng*) are clearly distinguished:

the Tathāgata is the principle, cultivation and realization are practice, and realization is the definitive teaching. If one carefully contemplates the meaning of the character "clarity" (*liao*), it implicitly extends upward to encompass all that precedes it.

Regarding the four meanings of teaching, principle, practice, and realization: once the expressive (the teaching) is understood, the expressed (principle, practice, and realization) is also understood;
and because the expressed is understood, the expressive is also understood. This is because the teaching is the expressive, while principle, practice, and realization are the expressed.

As for the "Shurangama" in the phrase "the Shurangama of the myriad practices of all Bodhisattvas," the word "all" (*zhū*) has two meanings. If one refers to the five [categories] of the subsequent sutra...

Regarding the statement that these fifteen ranks are "all [Bodhisattvas]," whether referring to those far [advanced] or to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), from the supreme state of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) down to ordinary beings, all who understand this principle—whether their realization is partial or complete—share the same path and are collectively termed "Bodhisattvas.

This is because the meaning of "Bodhisattva" is broad; thus, as stated above, when ordinary beings and sages share the same source and cause and fruition coincide in a single accord, they are called "Bodhisattvas."
Regarding the title "Bodhisattva," one should understand it by looking up at the perspective of the Tathāgata; a Bodhisattva is a person on the path of cultivation.
"Bodhisattva" is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term *bodhisattva*, which is translated as "Awakened Being" (*jue youqing*). "Bodhi" means awakening, and "sattva" means a sentient being (*youqing*).
"Sentient being" is a synonym for "living beings" (*zhongsheng*). One attains [the state of a Buddha] by awakening oneself and awakening others.

The name "Cloud of Vows" expresses the intention to awaken these people through this Way; yet, because awakening is not yet complete, they are called "Awakening Beings" (*bodhisattva*), which carries the sense of partial awakening.
"Beings" (*sattva*) refers to those who are deluded, for there is still delusion within their awakening.

"Ten thousand practices" is a general enumeration of all the practices cultivated by Bodhisattvas. These practices consist of both phenomena and principle, shallow and deep, conditioned and unconditioned.
Although the names for practices are numerous, they do not exceed the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) when categorized by their expansion and contraction;

thus, there are the designations of "eighty thousand" and "immeasurable. Here, we speak of the ten thousand practices (*daśa-sahasra-caryā*) according to the general path. "Practice" (*xing*) means to act;
because one acts according to this Way without ceasing, *Śūraṅgama* is a Sanskrit term. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Śūraṅgama..."

The meaning of the translation is as follows: "All matters ultimately adorned" is named "Firmly Established" (*Śūraṅgama*). This means that all matters are ultimately perfected and thus attain firmness;
hence it is called *Śūraṅgama*. "All matters" refers to the myriad practices (*saṃskāra*). "Ultimate" (*jiu*) has the sense of clear discernment; "ultimate" (*jing*) has the sense of completion;
and "firmly established" (*jiangu*) has the sense of being indestructible. It signifies that while clearly understanding all things, one is fundamentally rooted in the One.
The mind creates the ultimate single mind, which perfectly illumines all things such that they are all obtained as neither destructible nor mixed;
therefore, it is called the *Śūraṅgama* (Heroic March) of the myriad practices of all Bodhisattvas. Furthermore, if one carefully savors the meaning of *Śūraṅgama*, it encompasses two approaches:
first, speaking from the perspective of practice, it is called the *Śūraṅgama* of the myriad practices; second, speaking from the side of the true meaning of the single mind.

This means that if one does not realize that the One Mind is fully endowed with the myriad practices, then even though one performs the myriad practices, they are all merely matters of the provisional vehicles;
the six perfections are shallow and superficial, subject to destruction, and not ultimately firm or solid.

If one can clearly awaken to the fact that the One Mind is fully endowed with the myriad practices, then without departing from the realm of tranquil light (*sukhāvatī*), all manner of virtues will universally assemble. Therefore, the Sutra below says: "There is..."
The title *Samādhi*—the Great Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama King—is fully evidenced by its possession of ten thousand practices.
"Sūtra" is a Sanskrit term translated as "Kie-ching" (Scripture of Accordance).

Although various sūtras and śāstras refer to it simply by the character for "sūtra," what they indicate is always the "Scripture of Accordance," meaning it is called a Scripture of Accordance because it accords with principle and accords with the capacities of sentient beings; this was the understanding of the ancients.
To say that it accords with principle is to harmonize with the Two Truths; to say that it accords with capacity is to conform to the three levels of faculty.

Furthermore, the ancients used the character *jīng* (經) to gloss *fǎ* (法, Dharma) and *cháng* (常, eternal). This is truly because it is revered by both humans and devas and guided by both sages and worthies; thus it is glossed as "Dharma.
Because it spans from antiquity to the present without shifting or changing, it is glossed as "eternal. The first nineteen characters above correspond to the title.
That which is signified is the meaning (*artha*), while a single word of the sutra is the signifying expression (*vyañjana*).

Furthermore, according to Tiantai’s method of explaining titles through the fivefold profound meaning (*pañca-vidha-gambhīrārtha*), this present sutra corresponds to its title as follows: it is named after both person and dharma; its essence (*tattva*) is the permanently abiding true mind;

its thesis (*śāstra*) is the cause and fruit of right concentration; its function (*prayojana*) is to shatter delusion and reveal the true; and its pedagogical aspect (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*) is that of "fresh butter" (*navanīta*).
The introduction concludes.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramiti of India during the Tang Dynasty.
"Tang" is the dynastic name of China, while "India" (Tianzhu) is the general name for the Western Regions; this sutra originated from the Zhongzong era.
On the twenty-third day of the fifth month of the first year of the Shenlong era, the Tripitaka Master from Central India, Prajñā, translated this at the Zhizhi Daochang in Guangzhou.
It is titled according to the period to which it belongs, hence the designation "Tang.
Regarding "India" (Tianzhu), the *Xiyu ji* states that the appellation for India is subject to much dispute; ancient accounts refer to it as Shendu, while others call it Xian dou.
Now, according to the correct pronunciation, it should be called "Indu" (India) in the Sanskrit language; "Indu" is translated as "Moon" (*candra*), which is one of its many names.
This is truly because the sages and worthies of that land have succeeded one another in guiding ordinary people and governing all things, like the moon shining upon them;
for this reason, it is named "Indu. What is now called "Tianzhu" (India) is a corruption. Regarding the term "Tripiṭaka Dharma Master," the "Tripiṭaka" refers to—
These are the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras. Because this master was well-versed in the Dharma of the Tripiṭaka, he taught others through these very teachings and transformed them by his own practice;
thus he was called a Tripiṭaka Dharma Master. *Pramiti* is the name of the translator;

it is translated as "Extreme Measure" (*paramita*) or "Reached the Other Shore. Regarding the term "translator," the *Zhou Li* states that one who "presides over the languages of the four quarters" is a *tongshi* (interpreter).
It is called "Yi Li Ji" (Records of Translated Rites), also known as "The East is called Ji, the South is called Xiang, the West is called Di-di, and the North is called Yi";

these four were all official titles. That the West is now referred to as "Yi" (Translator/Interpreter) is because at that time the office for the West was vacant and the Northern Office took charge of it, so "Ji" was designated as "Yi. Later, the old practice was restored.
The Tripitaka Master from the country of Ujjayinī, Migaśaka, translated the terminology.
"Ujjayinī" (the country of Ujjayinī) was translated by Master Xuanzang as "Garden"; it refers to the royal park of King Aśoka and belongs to the region of Northern India.

"Migaśaka" (the translator) was translated as "Capable of Subduing. According to the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Song Dynasty), he is recorded as the translator of the terminology.
There were six official positions for the assembly: first, the Chief Translator; second, the Scribe; third, the Interpreter; fourth, the Certifier of the Sanskrit Text;
fifth, the Certifier of the Dhyāna and Meaning; and sixth, the Editor of the Text. Because he translated the language of the re-translation, he was called the "Interpreter."
The transcription was performed by Fang Rong of Qinghe, Minister of the Secretariat and Director of the Chancellery, during the Tang Dynasty.
"Zhongshu Menxia" refers to the two ministries of the Tang: the Secretariat and the Chancellery. "Pingzhang" means to harmonize and clarify the administration of the state.

"Qinghe" is the name of a commandery from the Han Dynasty, which is present-day En County in Dongchang Prefecture, Shandong Province. "Bishou" (transcription) refers to the act of recording the words as they were spoken.
This means that because the translation was received in writing according to the literary style of this region and subsequently refined, it is called "received in writing" (bishou).
Clarified by the junior monk Guangmo of Yunqi Temple in Ancient Hangzhou;
directly explained by the lay follower Chen Jiru of Yunchuan; proofread by [name omitted].
Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying [at such-and-such a place] together with twelve hundred and fifty people.
This section of the sūtra was placed by the compiler as the six introductory phrases (*ṣaḍ-vidha-nidāna*) in accordance with the Buddha’s final instructions.
Formerly, when the Buddha was approaching his parinirvāṇa, Ānanda was filled with longing and grief; overcome by sorrow and distress, he became bewildered and fainting. Then Anuruddha...
Ānanda said, "The Buddha is about to enter parinirvāṇa; you have been entrusted with the charge to collect and transmit the Dharma-piṭaka.

You should now inquire regarding future matters, lest you be entangled by the bonds of attachment and thus fail this supreme entrustment. Ānanda replied, "I am so clouded by grief and suffering that I am unable to find the words to speak.
Thereupon, Anuruddha instructed him to pose questions concerning four matters, the fourth of which was as follows:
Question: After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the various sūtras were compiled, what words were used at the beginning of each sūtra? Answer:
The Buddha replied that the beginning of a sūtra should place the words “Thus have I heard” (*evam mayā śrutam*), and so forth; therefore, these words are placed at the beginning of all sūtras.
First, “thus” (*evam*) is a term pointing to the Dharma. “I” (*mayā*) is Ānanda’s self-designation; although noble ones are without a self (*anātman*), he uses this term for his own sake.

For the sake of conforming to worldly convention, it is called "I"; this is merely a conventional expression. Because these sutras and teachings were heard by me from the Buddha, they are distinguished from mere speculative discourse.
Therefore, this interpretation is termed "straightforward," and thus it has not been recorded in the profound commentaries (*xuan-yi*); I hope you will not reproach me for this.
The term "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) is an indefinite expression, similar to how people today say "once upon a time" or "one day. This is truly because of the person...
The duration of time in the various heavens differs in its length and brevity;

for example, fifty years in the human realm constitute one day and night in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*), while fifty years in that heaven constitute one day and night in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

As one ascends from the lower realms upward through the four dhyāna heavens and the four formless (*ārūpya*) heavens, the higher the level, the longer the duration of time becomes. The sūtras spoken by the Buddha circulate throughout these upper and lower realms.
Because the specific date was determined, it is spoken of in general terms as "a certain time. "Buddha" refers to Śākyamuni Buddha. The character "Fo" (佛) is used for brevity;
fully stated, it is "Fotuó" (佛陀), translated as "The Awakened One. If one speaks only of "Fo," it carries the meaning of "that which is awakened";
by adding the character "Tuó" (陀), it refers to the person who awakens. Here, it refers to the person and is called "Buddha. Śrāvastī is a city.
It is the capital city of a kingdom; translated as "Abundant Virtue" (Fǒngdé) or "Renowned Things" (Wénwù).

Because it possesses four virtues—abundance of wealth, sensory objects of desire, extensive learning, and the path of liberation and moral reputation—it is called "Abundant Virtue" and "Renowned Things," as its fame is heard throughout the five regions of India.
The Jetavana Vihāra is the place where the Buddha preached the sūtras. The name "Jetavana" is... [text truncated]
The *Yijiji* (義集) translates this as "the name of the Crown Prince of the Victorious Kingdom," because at the time of his birth, King Prasenajit defeated foreign nations in battle;
thus, a magnificent name was established. Furthermore, the *Xiyuji* (西域記) states that *Jetavana* is translated as "Victorious Grove" (*Shenglín*);
the former [the *Yijiji*] highlights victory through battle, while the latter highlights victory through the grove. In total, these are names for the Crown Prince.

In Changshui’s commentary, *huan* (洹) is glossed as "forest" (*lin*), following the interpretation of the *Xiyuji* (Record of the Western Regions). However, this conflates the Indic and Chinese terms for "forest" (*vana* and *huan*), rendering them unclear.
Here, I have interpreted it directly as the name of the Prince, which seems more appropriate. As for *jing-she* (精舍), it refers to a dwelling for refined cultivation.
"The great assembly of *bhikṣus*" refers to the assembly listening to the Dharma; the Sanskrit term *bhikṣu* is translated as... [text truncated]
There are three meanings: first, destroying evil; second, terrifying Māras; and third, mendicants (*bhikṣu*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains:

"Bhik" means to destroy, referring to the destruction of the evil of afflictions (*kleśa*); furthermore, "bhik" means to terrify, referring to Māras, for through the practice of the Path one can terrify Māras;
furthermore, "bhik" means to beg, referring to the mendicant who can beg for pure livelihood (*pariśuddha-ājīva*) to sustain himself.
The term "Sangha" is a designation of excellence for the community; according to ancient precedent, it is often left untranslated and retains its Sanskrit name.

"Mahā" (Great) refers to those who have received full ordination and may thus be called the Great Sangha. "Assembly" (*gaṇa*) refers to the category of such a group. "One thousand two hundred and fifty persons" cites the number of those who constantly followed [the Buddha].
After the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he first ordained the five bhikṣus, including Ājñātakauṇḍinya. Subsequently...
He first converted the three brothers Kāśyapa along with their one thousand followers; next, he converted Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, each with their own hundred followers;
and finally, he converted Yaśas and others, numbering fifty people—though five are currently missing from this count, it is merely cited as a general figure.
All these bhikṣus had previously practiced under non-Buddhist teachers, yet they attained nothing at all.
As soon as Śāriputra met the World-Honored One, he realized the second fruit [of the path]. Moved by the profound grace of the Buddha, he constantly followed the Buddha’s transformation;

thus, he was called a member of the "Constantly Following Assembly" (*nitya-parivāra*). As for "together" (*sārdham*), it refers to the harmonious cohabitation of teacher and disciples through the transmission of the teachings.

From the words "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) to this point, Master Zao designates these as the "sixfold accomplishment" (*ṣaḍ-vidha-sampad*); only when these are present can the teaching arise. This refers to faith and hearing.
"Time, place, teacher, and assembly" refers to these very things.
All are untainted Great Arhats who rescue the future and transcend all worldly entanglements.
This section of the sūtra, following the preceding passage, praises their inner secret, true virtue and their outward manifestation of expedient means.

"All are" constitutes the first phrase, which is a general praise of the fruit-position realized, clarifying the provisional ritual. "O Son of the Buddha," and so forth, constitutes the specific praise, clarifying the actual virtues.

"Leakage" (*āsrava*) refers to seeping out; it is explained by way of analogy, for just as a vessel that leaks is unfit for use, so too are these bhikṣus now all without leakage, being vessels of the Path;
thus they are called "without leakage" (*anāsrava*). There are [two types of] leakage: [the leakage of the afflictions and the leakage of the objects of perception].

The three outflows (*āsrava*) are the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*). These are explained in detail in the *Fajie Cidian Chumen* (Introduction to the Sequence of the Dharma Realm).
An Arhat is the name for one who has attained the fourth fruit. This title contains three meanings: first, "slayer of thieves" (*arhan*);

second, "worthy of offerings" (*arhan*); and third, "one who does not arise [again]" (*arhan*). Compared to the three meanings of a *bhikṣu*, the *bhikṣu* cultivates the cause, whereas the Arhat realizes the fruit; thus, the latter is superior.

"Śrāvaka" (Arhat) means "one who kills. Because he has killed all the thieves of the afflictions (*kleśa*), because his outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted, and because he is worthy of receiving offerings from humans and devas, he is so called.
Furthermore, "A" signifies "no," and "Raha" signifies "birth";

because he will not be born again in future lives, and because his fetters (*saṃyojana*) are eternally severed, he is revered by both humans and devas. Thus, he is called a "Great Son of the Buddha. The following two [sections] are subordinate.
The preceding phrase is stated in reverse order because it follows the grammatical conventions of India; its wording should be rearranged to read:

"The Buddha-sons who maintain [the Dharma]. This is intended to clarify that while they manifest as Arhats through skillful means, their inner minds actually abide in the rank of Bodhisattvas, as "Buddha-son" is a general title for Bodhisattvas.
The subsequent phrase clarifies the meaning of the preceding one by showing how they are able to transcend.

All those who exist thereby abide in the rank of a Buddha’s son. "Existence" (you) carries the sense of attachment; the three realms possess twenty-five forms of existence (*bhava*), which are briefly summarized as three:
namely, the existence of desire (*kāmadhātu-bhava*), the existence of form (*rūpadhātu-bhava*), and the existence of the formless (*ārūpyadhātu-bhava*).

Since one is now able to transcend beyond these existences, it is called "internal reality" (*neishih*). This term "skillfully transcending" (*shan chao*) possesses two meanings: first, if "skillful" (*shan*) is directly glossed as "ability" (*neng*), then...

The phrase "able to transcend" (*śaknoti samatikramitum*) means that its meaning is shallow and lacks flavor [if taken literally]. According to the interpretation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one realizes that having a substantial body is itself the Middle Way;
because one flows into the center of this Middle Way, it is called "able to transcend. Regarding the following two phrases, they carry forward the meaning of the preceding sentence:
although one transcends all realms of existence (*bhava*), one does not depart from traveling and teaching within various lands, and yet those lands possess defilement (*saṃkleśa*).

There are those who are pure, those who are correct, and those who are inverted; as explained in the "Chapter on the World of Flower Adornment" (*Avataṃsaka-lokadhātu-parivarta*), there are immeasurable distinctions.
Thus, the sentient beings within those lands also possess immeasurable distinctions.

These bhikṣus manifest forms according to the various types [of beings], yet without arising from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), they display all manner of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*). The meaning of the two characters for "dignified conduct" (*īryāpatha*) is also broad, encompassing both the Vinaya and...

Among these, there are teachings concerning thirty thousand and eighty thousand [forms of conduct], all of which can be put into practice; they possess a majesty that inspires awe and a decorum that serves as a model.

Furthermore, while acting among different classes of beings, they engage in various conditions within, transforming others according to their capacities and gathering them perfectly in accordance with the Dharma-principle.
One must know that for a Bodhisattva there is no fixed code of deportment; that he now appears as a bhikṣu is but one such instance. From...
The two phrases following "the Buddha" also follow from what was stated above; that is to say, having already perfected their deportment, they are capable of being transformed by the Buddha.

The term "turning the wheel" (*cakravartin*) is explained metaphorically, signifying that through the teaching of the Dharma, one transforms consciousness into wisdom (*jñāna*), subdues the heterodox, and establishes the orthodox path.

Thus, the phrase "like turning the wheel" implies that they are not only capable of being transformed in the present life, but are also worthy of being entrusted with the teachings for future generations.
"Excellence of the matter" means that although one receives the final entrustment, one truly forgets the characteristics of self and other, subject and object;

because one preaches the Dharma as an illusion and delivers sentient beings in accordance with emptiness, it is called "excellent. This is synonymous with the meaning of "skillfully transcending," as the following sutra states:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "You should make a vow to enter the period of the Final Dharma to transmit and uphold the holy teachings, transforming and guiding all sentient beings."

To transcend the suffering of birth and death and attain *nirvāṇa* is precisely the matter of this final testament. The latter two phrases, "rigorously purifying" (*yánjìng*), also follow from what precedes them:
"rigorous" (*yán*) means steadfastness, and "purifying" (*jìng*) means non-attachment. *Vinaya* is the general name for the precepts;

it is translated as "skillful governance," because one governs oneself by subduing lust, anger, and ignorance, and likewise governs the evils of sentient beings. The following phrase, "expansively" (*hóng*), refers to...

"Great Model" refers to the standard of conduct; it means that in the final age, one who practices the Way must first firmly uphold the pure precepts before they can serve as a teacher and model for sentient beings within the three realms.
Since the teacher and model are solemn and strict, those who receive their transformation will surely be universal; thus, it is called "Vast.
The two phrases following "Response Body" (*nirmāṇakāya*) also follow from the above: meaning that since one is already able to provide a model for the three realms, [they then act] accordingly...
The term "universally responding" (*lei puying*) does not refer to the single characteristic of a *bhikṣu* as previously explained in the section on majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*).

Since there is no birth that is not saved and no bondage that is not liberated, it is said: "to deliver and liberate, to extract from suffering and rescue those who are submerged. The latter two phrases also follow from what was stated above;
the compassionate transformation is inexhaustible, reaching to the end of the future, extracting them from their afflictions and rescuing those who are drowning. This refers to the latter phrase.
The more one transcends the afflictions of *dṛṣṭi-heya* (delusions of view) and the entanglements of *bhāvanā-heya* (delusions of thought), the longer [the path]. Changshui’s Commentary states:

"This sutra is preached after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and before the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. Therefore, the praise of the *śrāvakas* in the introduction does not pertain to their limited practices (*hīnayāna*), as it refers to meanings such as the immeasurable *saṃbhogakāya* delivering sentient beings;
such praise did not exist prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Furthermore, it says 'voice'..."
It should be understood that prior to the *Śrāvakabhūmi* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, this [teaching] was not yet revealed;

however, according to the current text, it is taught after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. This passage praises the matter of the "inner secret great practice. It corresponds to the three types of arhats described in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*: the one who is real and the two who are provisional.
The two who are provisional refer to those manifested by Bodhisattvas and those manifested by Transformation Buddhas; the present meaning is the same as this.
If it is said that those bodhisattvas are emanations, then since emanated beings surely enter into reality, how can one claim that such praise does not exist prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*?
Other sūtras also contain it; how then can one say it is absent? It is merely that one has not investigated minutely.
To forcibly attribute what belongs to the earlier period to the later is certainly not correct doctrine. Furthermore, this praise of virtues was compiled after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Since these people have already heard the reality of the *Lotus Sūtra*’s revelation and clarification, they cite the meaning of the latter portion to offer praise;
this serves to show that the general is subsumed by the particular, and that the subsequent is brought back to the prior, which is why they offer this praise.
Their names were Mahāmati Śāriputra (up to) Upāliṣada, who served as the leaders.

This section of the sutra follows the preceding praise of virtues to specify the names of the twelve hundred leaders. In the standard practice of assembling the multitude in various sutras, three vehicles are clearly distinguished;
this is the assembly of śrāvakas. The phrase "their names were" is the terminology of the compiler of the sutra.
Below, the names of those of great wisdom are listed; they cannot be enumerated in full, but only the foremost among them are cited by way of example.
In the Sanskrit language, Śāriputra is translated as "Son of Śārī" or "Son of the Body. *Śārī* is the name of a bird belonging to the genus of storks;
*putra* means "son. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that Śāriputra’s mother was named Śārī, and he is so called because of his mother.
Because he established his name in this way, it is also said that this woman’s beautiful form was produced from his body; thus he is called Śāriputra.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Within my Buddha-dharma, there is no one whose wisdom is peerless for resolving all doubts;
therefore, Śāriputra is foremost. As for Mahāmaudgalyāyana, *mahā* is translated as "great," and *Maudgalyāyana* refers to Maudgalya.
Kauṇḍinya is translated as "radish root. Because his ancestors were fond of eating this, it became their family name;
he was named Kauṇḍinya after a tree of that name, for his parents prayed to this tree when he was born, and thus they gave him that name.
According to the *Ekottarika Āgama*, he was the foremost in supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Mahākauṣṭhila is translated as "Great Thigh"; he was a master of the treatises (*śāstrin*).
Because the kneecaps of the son born of Dhāra were coarse and large, he was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra.
According to the *Ekottarika Āgama*, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra is the foremost in debate;
"Pūrṇa" is translated as "Fulfilling Wishes," "Maitrāyaṇī" is translated as "Compassionate," and "Nī" is a feminine suffix. His father lived by the riverbank.

Because he prayed to Brahmā for his father’s wish to be fulfilled, he was called "Son of Pūrṇa" (Full-Wish); because his mother was named Maitrī (Loving-Kindness), he was also called "Son of Maitreyī.
Combining the names of both parents, he is known as Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, who is foremost among the Dharma-preachers taught by the Tathāgata.
As for Subhūti, it is translated as "Śubhamati" (Auspicious Intelligence); on the day of his birth, the household suddenly became empty.
His parents were astonished and marveled, requesting a master to perform a divination. The divination stated: "This is an auspicious sign. Consequently, he was named Shanji (Good Fortune).
Because his family’s wealth suddenly vanished, he was also called Kongsheng (Born of Emptiness). The *Ekottarika Āgama* states that he was foremost in understanding emptiness.

Regarding Upānisaṭa, it is translated as "the nature of dust is empty"; this refers to how he attained the Way by contemplating that the nature of sensory objects (*dharmas*) is empty, and so forth—this "and so forth" includes other similar cases.

The text of the *Bhikṣu-sūtra* is still somewhat brief; by encompassing it through its foremost leaders, it serves as the crown of the twelve hundred [disciples]—that is to say, it constitutes the essential framework.
To examine this sūtra in detail: since none can enter it without wisdom, the names are listed with Śāriputra first to resolve right from wrong and select the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
In concluding the title of the sūtra, all prioritize wisdom; therefore, Mañjuśrī is promoted to that position.
This is one point alone.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable *pratyekabuddhas* who had attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), along with those at their initial stages of resolve, who all came together to the Buddha’s presence.
This section of the scripture, following the previous gathering of the assembly, lists the multitude of *pratyekabuddhas*. This is because the *pratyekabuddhas*...

The *Śrīghanācārasaṃgraha* states that those who preceded the Śrāvakas constitute a separate category, which is called the Middle Vehicle (*madhyayāna*). Thus it says: "Furthermore, there are [others]...
In the original Sanskrit, they are called *Pratyekabuddha*, translated as "Solitary Realizer" (*yuanjue*) or "Self-Realizer.

Having followed the Buddha, they cultivate the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*), observing their arising and cessation, thereby attaining realization of the non-arising of phenomena; these are called Pratyekabuddhas. If they emerge from... [text truncated]
In the Buddha’s era, those who attained awakening to non-arising on their own were called *pratyekabuddhas*. Furthermore, there are two types of *pratyekabuddhas*:
first, those who dwell in seclusion in mountain forests, delighting in solitary tranquility, not relying on a retinue, and perfecting themselves alone;

second, those who train disciples and lead a following in groups. The present text refers to the latter type, known as the "group-practitioners" (*vargacārin*), who are designated as "those beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*).

This means that because they have already attained the realization of the fruit and have nothing further to learn, those who are beginners—meaning those whose principles of contemplation have not yet deeply penetrated—are those who belong to a specific group and have encountered the Buddha and turned toward him; they are called "those who realize through partial conditions" (*pratyekabuddha*) because what they realize is singular.
It is said that they do not constantly follow the Buddha, as they only go to him temporarily during the causal stage.

Regarding the phrase "Together they came to the Buddha's abode," the *Changshui Shu* (Long Water Commentary) states: "From this point upward, it is judged to be the General Introduction (*sūtra-nidāna*).
If one examines the assembly listings in various sūtras, they typically include the three vehicles; here, however, only two vehicles are present, omitting the bodhisattva assembly.

Yet, according to the later text, which mentions 'bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges gathering at the site of enlightenment with Mañjuśrī as their leader,' it seems to indeed constitute a general introduction."

If the names of the leading Bodhisattvas listed in the introduction correspond to the leading Śrāvakas mentioned previously, they ought to follow immediately after the introductory section on the *nidāna*;
this must therefore be a textual inversion resulting from an error during the translation process.

Furthermore, the subsequent passage concerning the end of the summer retreat and the *pravāraṇa* ceremony constitutes the specific introduction (*pratyuddeśa*) for the present sutra, as it was traditionally termed in contrast to the preceding [general] introduction.

Because they are universal, all sutras have their own specific origins; for example, the *Vajracchedikā* has its origin in the practice of begging for food, and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* in the emission of light.
This present sutra was initiated by the occasion of a mistake regarding the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, each arising according to its own particular conditions.

"At the time when the bhikṣus had concluded their summer retreat and were performing the *prātimokṣa* ceremony" (extending to "reverently attending the Compassionate and Venerable One, seeking the profound meaning").
This section of the sūtra, following the general introduction (*nidāna*), clarifies the specific origin (*nidāna*) of this particular scripture.
"At the time" (*shǔ*) means an assembly or an encounter. "The various bhikṣus" refers to the community of śrāvakas who have been gathered. Furthermore...
This refers to those who have received full ordination (*upasampadā*). "To suspend" means to dissolve [the retreat].

Regarding the summer retreat (*varṣa*), the Buddha ordained that bhikṣus observe the *anvāya* (rainy-season) retreat from the sixteenth day of the fourth month until the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
Each bhikṣu selects a pure location—whether with five or ten people—and formally establishes the retreat for three months; there is no other way.

Upon visiting the Buddha on the fifteenth day of the seventh month at the conclusion of the retreat, the bhikṣus who had observed the three-month *varṣā* retreat would each approach the Buddha’s presence.
Within their own minds, they might have experienced either gain or loss; thus, they would consult the Buddha to resolve their doubts and distinguish between right and wrong.
Alternatively, if they themselves possessed faults or transgressions, they would confess them before the Buddha within the assembly of the Sangha. Or, if they were unable to do so themselves...
"Pravāraṇā" (自恣) is so called because one invites the Saṃgha to admonish one’s transgressions so that one may be purified.

Regarding the three days permitted by the Vinaya for *pravāraṇā*—namely, the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth days of the seventh month—the commentary of Changshui (*Chang-shui shu*) states that if one were to take "the ten directions" (*śīpāng*) as referring to all locations where the summer retreat (*varṣā*) is observed, then the meaning would be too restrictive.
This [commentary] clarifies that "ten directions" refers to the Bodhisattvas who have gathered from other regions at that time.
The sutra text explicitly states that the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions were present at this assembly of the three vehicles;

how could there not have been a multitude gathered from the ten directions? It must be understood that the reference to those coming from other quarters is intended to include them all. Regarding the phrase "inquiring to resolve doubts":

"inquiring" (*tsi*) refers to the request made to the Bodhisattvas, while "resolving" (*chüeh*) refers to the definitive discernment provided by the Buddha. To reverently receive his compassionate [instruction]...

"Respectful" (*yan*) means to revere with awe; "to serve" (*feng*) means to offer up with devotion. These two characters, "revere" and "serve," fully encompass the three karmas of body, speech, and mind.
To revere with awe is to cease idle talk and restrain the mind; to serve by cupping one's hands and gazing upward is to bow the body in veneration.

This constitutes the ritual for those of the Three Vehicles who seek the Way. "Compassionate Respect" (*ciyan*) refers to the gathering of the two virtues of the Buddha: his familial kinship and his manifest enlightenment. It is gentle...

Ling’s commentary states: "Compassion" refers to benevolence, while "severity" refers to majesty. This is because the World-Honored One possesses benevolence upon which one can rely and majesty that inspires awe;
