benevolence is the virtue of gathering and sustaining, while majesty is the virtue of subduing.

Those who seek the profound meaning should follow the explanation in the relevant passage, for this is precisely the profound meaning of resolving doubts and seeking certainty. "Profound" (mi) refers to the wondrous intention.

Because he is able to resolve doubts and delusions, he is called the "Wondrous General. Although the ritual for requesting [the teaching] was complete, [the Buddha] did not yet dare to speak, hence it is said "about to seek.
At that moment, the Tathāgata spread his seat and sat in peaceful repose (until) his *kalaviṅka*-like immortal voice pervaded the ten directions.
This section of the sutra clarifies the Buddha’s intention to respond to the capacities of his audience and transform them according to their needs.

"At that time" refers to the moment when the assembly of those of the three vehicles had gathered. "Folding" (敷) means spreading out; "seat" (座) refers to a sitting mat, meaning to sit after having spread out the sitting mat.
"Tranquil rest" (宴安) refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*). It is the constant practice of the Buddha that he must first enter meditative concentration before preaching the Dharma.
"Ritual" (*yi*) refers to the various assemblies (*zhū huì*), meaning that the three vehicles and the eight classes of beings—both lay and ordained—gather together at the Buddha’s dwelling;

hence the term "various assemblies. "Proclaiming the profound and abstruse" (*xuānshì shēn'ào*) refers to the secret meaning sought [by those beings]; it is called "secret" because it is profound and abstruse.
The World-Honored One, in accordance with their respective quests, proclaims it. As the *Chángshuǐ Sū* states: "Just as in the *Lotus Sūtra*, first..."
The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* is the foundation of the One Vehicle; this present sūtra is likewise so.
There must certainly be a catalogue of these sūtras that is currently hidden and not yet seen. "Sūn" refers to a mat, meaning the mat upon which the Dharma is preached.

"Pure assembly" (*qingzhòng*) refers to the assembly listening to the Dharma, being pure and undefiled. Doubts and difficulties were naturally resolved because they were previously decided by the Buddha.
Because it has not been heard before, it is called "unprecedented" (*adbhuta*); because it is unprecedented, it is called "profound. *Kalinga* is an abbreviated form of a Sanskrit term;
its full name is *kalaviṅka*, which is the name of a bird translated as "bird of beautiful voice. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The kalaviṅka bird, while still within its eggshell and before it has even begun to cry out, produces a subtle and wondrous sound that surpasses that of all other birds."
This beautiful voice is such that neither gods, humans, nor *kiṃnaras* can equal it; only the Buddha’s voice is like it, and thus it is used as a metaphor.
Regarding the "voice of a seer" (*ṛṣi-svara*): "seer" (*ṛṣi*) means "wondrous intention.

Furthermore, those seers possess the power of transformation (*nirmāṇa*), just as the Buddha can preach with a single sound such that sentient beings each understand according to their own kind. Because it is like the transformations of a seer, it is so called.

The sounds of the sages and the sounds of the Buddhas pervade the worlds of the ten directions; thus, the voices of those birds are not even comparable to them, being cited merely as a metaphor for their clarity, elegance, and capacity to delight the mind.

As for these sounds that pervade all realms, even if Maudgalyāyana were to exert his supernatural powers to the utmost and listen to the Buddha’s voice across worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the western direction, it would still be as if he were face-to-face with the Buddha; the same is true for all other directions. Therefore...
"Proclaiming throughout the worlds of the ten directions," as explained in detail in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
"Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges came to assemble at the site of enlightenment, with Mañjuśrī as their leader.
This section of the sutra clarifies that the assembly gathered from other regions was as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
Although Bodhisattvas are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they must be headed by one of true wisdom; therefore, Mañjuśrī is established as the foremost leader.
"Ganges" (*gaṅgā*) is the name of a river in India; it is also called *kaṅgā*. It is translated as "Source of Heaven.
It originates from Lake Anavatapta; this merely clarifies that its source is high and remote in reality.
It does not come from the heavens. This river is forty *li* wide, and its sand is as fine as flour;
because the Buddha was near this river, he frequently used it as a metaphor. Mañjuśrī is translated as Miaojixiang (Wondrous Auspiciousness) or Miaode (Wondrous Virtue);
"Virtue" (*de*) carries the meaning of "auspiciousness" (*jixiang*). What was previously called the "Luminous One from the Ten Directions" is here called the "Ganges."

"Śā" signifies their number; Mañjuśrī represents ultimate wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), and as the master of the discernment of dharmas within this assembly, he occupies the position of the foremost leader.
At that time, King Prasenajit acted on behalf of his deceased father king [and others], as well as the arhats, serving as the host for the various offerings.
This section of the sutra, following the sequence, clarifies the occasion for the King and his ministers to provide offerings during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
"Time" refers to the time of the *pravāraṇā*. Regarding Prasenajit, he was the king of Śrāvastī; the Sanskrit term *Prasenajit* is translated as "Victorious Army.
Concerning the phrase "preparing a vegetarian feast on his [the king's] birthday," the *Changshui Shu* (Commentary by Changshui) states that this refers to a former king.
The "day of the demise" refers to the occasion of the taboo name; "taboo" means to avoid pronouncing the name when performing auspicious matters.
Xie of Wuxing cites the *Jiyi* (Meaning of Sacrifices): "On the anniversary of the day of death, one must feel sorrow; reciting the taboo name is as if seeing the parent.
"Ying" (to manage) conveys the sense of preparing and arranging; "zhai" (fasting) means one must fast with simple food and offer the sustenance with a purified mind.
Therefore, it is called the "Palace of the Fast" (*zhāigōng*). The term "掖" (*yè*) refers to a side chamber of the main palace, like the armpit (*yè*) of a person;

thus, by requesting the Buddha to the "palace of the armpit," the King expresses that he is welcoming him personally. This signifies the ultimate degree of reverence, for a king, being of supreme dignity, does not delegate such a task to his subordinates but welcomes him himself.
"Zhen" (*zhēn*) carries the sense of being precious and valuable; in antiquity, there were the "Eight Treasures" (*bāzhēn*) dishes prepared through boiling and roasting.
Slicing raw meat and roasted meat were esteemed by the world; the *Rites of Zhou* states that the Chief Cook (*shānfú*) presides over the delicacies of the King.

The *Fāngyán* says that "xiū" refers to cooked food. When it is said that there is no superior or wondrous flavor, it means that the excellence of the food is such that nothing can surpass it—the height of beauty.
Generally, India regards clarified butter (*ghṛta*, *típóhú*) as the supreme flavor; therefore, when a king invites the Buddha, he must invariably provide it alongside the *bodhi*.
"Sā" means that all [the people] personally invited him. Furthermore, among the wealthy householders and families of noble lineage within the city of Śrāvastī, there was a deep and reverent longing;
they believed that the merit would surely be double that of ordinary occasions, and for this reason, they provided meals for the Saṃgha simultaneously.
"Zhù" (佇) means to stand on tiptoe and gaze expectantly. The Buddha is the Great Compassionate Father of the world, and all people stood gazing toward him.
In response to their offerings to the Buddha and their reverence for the King, the King must surely grant their request;
therefore, he commanded Mañjuśrī to lead the assemblies of the Three Vehicles to attend the various patrons’ rites. "Command" (*chì*) refers to a superior’s order to those below.
One who is endowed with the ten virtues is called a *gṛhapati* (householder), and one who maintains himself in purity is called a *vaiśya* (lay devotee).
"Only Ānanda had previously accepted a separate invitation... (up to) "...on his way back alone, he had no offerings that day.
This section of the sutra, as compiled by the redactors, clarifies the circumstances of Ānanda’s mistaken fall.

It sequentially reveals the factual reality of how accepting a separate invitation and returning without provisions on the journey constituted the initial cause of his downfall, making the underlying truth clearly manifest.
The narrative herein follows a systematic method and may serve as a model for fine composition. In the Sanskrit language, he is called Ānanda; in the Great Treatise, it is translated as "Joy.

He was the son of King Droṇodana and the younger cousin of the Buddha. On the day the Buddha attained enlightenment, his father dispatched a messenger to inform King Śuddhodana that his noble younger brother had fathered a son.
The King’s heart was filled with joy, and he exclaimed, "Today is truly a great [day]..."

When the Auspicious Buddha attained enlightenment, his younger brother gave birth to a son. He spoke to the messenger, saying, "This child shall be named Ānanda. The entire nation rejoiced and celebrated.
It is further said that at the age of twenty, the Buddha ordained him and allowed him to leave the household life.

According to the *Ekottarika-āgama*, he was foremost in much learning (*bahuśruta*). Regarding those who are invited individually: this refers to being invited for specific matters or circumstances, which differs from [general invitations].

Because it was a separate invitation made prior to the *pravāraṇā*, and because Ānanda had originally made a vow not to accept separate invitations, one knows that this invitation must certainly not have been for a meal offering.
Furthermore, since this separate invitation was still far from being fulfilled, he could not find the leisure (*huáng*) to join the sequence of the Saṃgha at the time of the *pravāraṇā*.
"Leisure" means to have free time; thus, he lacked the opportunity within the order of the monks.
The Vinaya clarifies that when a bhikṣu travels afar, he must ensure that both others and himself follow the correct rules; this necessarily involves three parties: first, the *upādhyāya*;
second, the *ācārya*; and third, oneself. The *upādhyāya* refers to one of advanced seniority (*vassa*) and noble virtue who is worthy of being one's teacher;
such a person is called an *upādhyāya*. The *ācārya* is translated as "Master of Discipline" (*guifanshi*), so named because he is able to correct and guide his disciples.
Because he practices [the Way], he is called a "Model" (ācārya). Now, Ānanda happened to encounter other circumstances, and as the matter was necessarily urgent, he lacked his two teachers;
his statement that he would return alone on the road without provisions is precisely intended to give rise to the subsequent account of how he went begging for food and mistakenly fell.
"Immediately Ānanda took up his alms-bowl [and went]... to fully accomplish the immeasurable merit of all sentient beings.
This section of the scripture further clarifies the mental disposition with which Ānanda practices begging for food in the present.
Observe that the mind generated by Ānanda is precisely one of feeling shame for the small and aspiring toward the great; it is truly identical to the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) teachings.
Why do those who adhere to the characteristics of phenomena (*lakṣaṇavādin*) fail to discern this as being a forced and fragmented interpretation?
Where is the "eye" of the preceding and succeeding teachings to be found here? This section marks the beginning of the practitioner's practice and the occasion for the establishment of the teaching.

If scholars investigate and clarify this point, they will know that it undoubtedly belongs to the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtras). "Immediate" (*jishi*) refers to a time when there is no offering; it is the occasion for the *pātra* (alms bowl).
*Pātra* is the Sanskrit term; translated, it means "an appropriate vessel" (*yǐngliàngqì*).
To elaborate, it is called an "appropriate vessel" because its substance, color, and dimensions must all conform to the Dharma.

When Ānanda carried his bowl through the cities he traveled, he went on alms-rounds in successive order, making no distinction between the noble and the lowly, the honorable and the humble, or the wealthy and the poor.
The meaning of "pure" and "impure" follows the sense of "conforming to conditions. This is because the mendicant’s mind initially aspires to equality and feels ashamed of inequality;
thus, he wishes to beg from those who have not yet practiced giving so that they may plant seeds in the field of merit.
Since their act of giving is the very last, they are called "last donors" (*paścima-dānapati*). Regarding the term *dānapati*, it is explained in the *Mingyi ji* (Collection of Names and Meanings).
"Dāna" is translated as "dāna" (giving); it is called "generosity" because its meritorious retribution transcends the ocean of poverty.

However, those who practice giving at the very end are stingy and difficult to transform. Ānanda, feeling ashamed of his own minor [attainments] yet aspiring to the Great, and being capable of performing what is difficult to perform, sought out such individuals to serve as *zhāizhǔ* (hosters of the fast).

This explains that there is no distinction between the inferior and the correct [practitioners]. [Note: The phrase "無問下正明" (wú wèn xià zhèng míng) indicates that the following section provides the formal clarification.]
The characteristics of begging with equanimity involve the two terms "pure" and "impure," which serve as general designations. Below, the specific categories are revealed:
the *kṣatriya* (noble clan) family is "pure," while those such as the *caṇḍāla*, who engage in debauchery, liquor, and slaughter, are "impure.
*Kṣatriya* is fully termed *kṣatriya*, translated as "royal lineage. In India, there are four noble clans: first, the *brahmin*...
First, the Brāhmaṇas; second, the Kṣatriyas; third, the Vaiśyas; and fourth, the Śūdras—these four all consider themselves to have been born from Brahmā.

Therefore, this text mentions only one of them as a representative for the other three. Caṇḍāla is translated as "the one with the fierce banner" (*yánzhì*), because they adorn themselves with evil banners.
The *Faxian zhuan* (Record of Faxian) states: "Caṇḍāla is called 'evil person' (*èrén*); they are [distinguished] from others..."
When living apart and entering a city, he would strike a bamboo staff to distinguish himself; seeing him, people would avoid him.

Had he not done so, the King would surely have punished him. This is precisely the intent of encouraging good and signaling evil. As for "practicing impartial compassion" (*fang xing deng ci*), "method" (*fang*) refers to the method by which the Buddha practiced compassion with equality;
it means practicing compassion without selecting between right and wrong—this is the subtle essence of equality.
Regarding the phrase "begging without discriminating between noble and lowly": this means that he begs for alms regardless of whether the recipient is of high or low status.
The following sentence expresses the underlying intent: Ānanda has resolved to bring to full completion the immeasurable merit of all sentient beings;
thus, "all sentient beings" refers to the aforementioned categories of noble and lowly, pure and impure, and so forth. Question: How can a single act of giving immediately [accomplish this]?

The statement that "possessing immeasurable merit" contains a profound underlying meaning, as stated in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*: "Those who are equal regarding food are also equal regarding the Dharma.
If one practices giving with such equality, realizing the emptiness of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala-śūnyatā*), this is called the single true reality (*ekalakṣaṇa*).
Thus, one practice encompasses all practices; one practice is one merit, and within that one merit, immeasurable merits are fully contained.

Is it not likewise appropriate for merit? Now, this text is concise; one must understand that the word for "honored" (尊) implicitly contains the meaning of "lowly," while the word for "lowly" (賤) implicitly contains the meaning of "noble.
Within these terms of noble and lowly, there is further implicit inclusion of the meanings of "poor" and "rich.

Since it is called "equal compassion" (等慈), how could it discriminate between good and evil, or between those with whom one has a connection and those without, or between enemies and kin? One who reads this text will naturally be able to silently integrate and harmonize them as equal.
"It is acceptable.
This section of the scripture, from "Ānanda already knew that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One...

to "...expounded the unobstructed [teaching] to resolve all doubts and slanders," is the introduction composed by the compilers, wherein Ānanda cites the Buddha’s past reproach regarding unfairness as evidence.
Now, one should practice with equanimity. "Tathāgata, World-Honored One" is two of the ten epithets of a Buddha.
"World-Honored One" means that the Buddha’s great compassion universally covers all, and he is honored by the world;

since the nine dharma-realms are collectively called the "world" and collectively called "sentient beings," Subhūti saw before him Mahākāśyapa—whose full name is Mahākātyāyana—who had already attained liberation.

Ye-ba translates this as "Great Kāśyapa. The causal account of Kāśyapa appears in the fifth sūtra, the Chapter on Perfect Penetration (*Sūtra on the Perfect Penetration of the Dharma*), which distinguishes him from the three Kāśyapas by adding the prefix "Great.
This is because Subhūti, when begging for alms, would avoid the poor and follow the wealthy so as not to cause suffering to sentient beings;
whereas Kāśyapa would abandon the wealthy to follow the poor, so as to enable those who are poor to plant [the seeds of merit].
Because the cause is giving, both have good intentions; however, it is due to conceptual discrimination that they are rebuked for their unequal causes and conditions.

This passage from the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* was originally intended as a rebuke by a layman (*gṛhapati*). That in this sutra it is called a rebuke by the Tathāgata is to accord with the timing and adapt to the transformation [of beings], using a specific condition to provide exhortation and guidance.
Who knows that the Tathāgata might not also rebuke? This precisely clarifies the "rebuke" (*t'an*) characteristic of the Vaipulya (Vaipulya/Prativedha) teachings.
To praise exclusively the mind of greatness is to be partial; this is the censure of partiality. To open and reveal the unobstructed is to praise greatness;
"unobstructed" means being without limitation. Since the two venerable ones mentioned above both possessed limitations, they were rebuked.
Therefore, Ānanda resolved to open and reveal the impartial, unobstructed mind in order to cross over their doubts.
This refers to those who slander [the Buddha].

This passage from the scripture describes the manner in which Ānanda went on his almsround through the city gates with slow steps, maintaining dignified decorum and solemnly observing the rules of purification (*śīla*). The above two sections [explain this].
The first two lines clarify the etiquette of one’s movements; the latter two lines clarify the etiquette of the fasting ritual (*upavāsa*).

"Sūtra" means that which is traversed; "moat" refers to the defensive ditch of a city wall; "gate" refers to the city gate. "Stately pacing" refers to dignified deportment. Regarding the deportment of begging for alms:
it means wearing the robes and holding the bowl, proceeding with calm and stately steps without looking left or right; being neither elated when obtaining [alms] nor... [displeased when not].

To be free from anger while simultaneously using compassionate wisdom to discern the capacities of others, maintaining a correct countenance to awaken those around one—this is called the deportment of begging for alms (*piṇḍapāta*).

"Strict" (*yan*) means solemn; "orderly" (*zheng*) means disciplined; "reverent" (*su*) means upright and dignified; "respectful" (*gong*) means reverent and prudent—this is called the deportment of the *zhai* (fasting/observance) method.

Regarding the *zhai* method, the *Qing Guanshiyin Pusa Pumenpin Shu* (Commentary on the Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva’s Universal Gate Chapter) states: "The *zhai* is 'to align' (*qi*); it means to align [the mind]."
Furthermore, regarding the fast (*upavāsa*) performed through the actions of body and speech: it consists simply of eating only at midday.
The prohibition against eating after noon symbolizes that outside the Dharma-realm of the Middle Way, there is no other separate dharma.

The allowance to eat before noon means that although it is not the Middle Way itself, it represents the preparatory skillful means (*pūrvopāya*) prior to the Middle Way; thus, it possesses the sense of realization.
"Therefore, one obtains food; this is called the method for receiving the *upavāsa* (fasting) vows. Now Ānanda, with solemn reverence, practices this method while going on almsround.
At that time, as Ānanda was proceeding on his almsround, he arrived at [the house of] Yindu, who touched and stroked him, nearly causing him to destroy his precept-body.
This section of the scripture follows the previous theme of "not making distinctions" to clarify precisely the conditions for falling into error.
"At that time" refers to the time of sequential alms-rounding. Because he did not exercise discernment, he encountered [the woman] while passing by a brothel.
As for the "Great Illusionist," because it was transmitted by Brahmā, the *Mahāvaipulya* (Great Extensive) version identifies this as being of evil, heterodox, and deceptive nature.
Because it is a technique for transforming through delusion, it is called "illusion-technique" (*māyā-vidyā*); it is merely a single evil incantation, as the subsequent text states:
"the evil incantation is extinguished. Examining the intent of this technique, it does not merely involve the subjugation of lust;
rather, it can generally be employed for matters such as military arrays and acts of plunder and slaughter. Therefore, it is called a "great illusion-technique. [This refers to] Mātanga.

The *Changshui shu* states: "In meaning, it is translated as 'original nature' (*prakṛti*). Citing the passage from the sutra below regarding the 'bhikṣuṇī of nature' (*prakṛti-bhikṣuṇī*) as evidence, it is translated as 'nature.
This 'nature' refers to the nature of sexual habituation, not the true nature (*tathatā*).
Sāvikāla is translated as 'the Yellow-headed Rishi'; this rishi obtained a mantra transmitted by Brahmā in a previous life and taught it in turn."
The Mātanga girl, Denga, used this mantra to take Ānanda into the chamber of lust.

What is called the "seat of lust" refers to the fact that everything arranged within the room consists of erotic implements; because all such beautiful sights can stir up lustful thoughts, it is termed the "seat of lust.
As for "the body of lust stroking and caressing," "the body of lust" refers to Denga herself, whose every movement was full of lewdness.

Because this was an act of lewdness, it is called "lewdness of the person. As for "caressing and stroking," it refers to how Daṅga drew near to Ānanda, touching, caressing, and stroking him with the intent to destroy Ānanda’s *śīla-skandha* (the essence of the precepts).

Regarding the *śīla-skandha*, when viewed in contrast to the aforementioned "lewdness of the person," it refers to the fact that when the Venerable One received full ordination (*upasampadā*), all the precepts were maintained based upon his physical body;
therefore, they are called the "essence of the precepts" (*śīla-skandha*). Although the individual branches of the precepts may be obscured by the faculties of ignorance, [the essence remains].
Because the original Immovable One was in a state of extreme distress, it is said that he was on the verge of being destroyed;
this can be verified by the subsequent scripture which states, "Because his mind was pure, he had not yet sunk into ruin.
The Tathāgata knew that they were subjected to the arts of seduction (up to the point where) they all came to follow the Buddha and desired to hear the essentials of the Dharma.
This section of the sutra collection describes the Tathāgata’s protective compassion as he opens the path to the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*.

While the Tathāgata was in the palace of King Śrīgupta and Ānanda was wandering elsewhere, [Ānanda] inadvertently fell into [an error] without knowing how many stages of the journey had been traversed.
The Buddha’s eye can see this, and the Buddha’s wisdom can know it; now, through the reflection of that knowledge, he perceives it.
Indeed, the movements of the body, the utterances of speech, and the operations of the mind—the impurities of these three karmas—are all entirely within the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision;
there is nothing that is not clearly understood. Therefore, having finished the meal, he returns. "Returns" implies a swift return.
It is the constant custom for the Tathāgata, upon receiving a meal, to preach the Dharma and then return at his leisure; today, however, he returns with haste.
The kings and their ministers had doubts that there must be a specific reason for this, and so they all came to follow the Buddha, wishing to hear the essentials of the Dharma—
the "essentials of the Dharma" being the core principles of the Great Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a hundred jewels from the crown of his head (until) he sat cross-legged and proclaimed a divine mantra.
This section of the sutra collection describes the compassionate procedure by which the World-Honored One returned to the grove to recite mantras for protection.
"At that time" refers to the moment when the World-Honored One had returned, spread his seat, and the assembly was gathered.

Before the Buddha was about to proclaim the mantra, he emitted light from the crown of his head, possessing the colors of a hundred jewels. "Fearless" means that the light of the hundred-jewel colors is capable of destroying [all fears].
Because all dark, evil, and heterodox things are entirely extinguished upon encountering it, and because it can cause all that is feared to become fearless, it is called "Fearlessness.
As for "Hundred-Jewel Radiance": radiance is the essence of light; the colors of the hundred jewels are the characteristics of light;
and the manifestation of the Buddha within the lotus is the function of light. Thus, the essence, characteristics, and function are fully revealed.

Because the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa abides eternally within the heart, light emerges from the crown; this light manifests as a lotus flower, upon which transformation Buddhas appear adorned with the Lotus Sūtra.
This is the compassionate method for proclaiming the mantra. To examine this in detail: phenomena do not arise in isolation, and the mind relies on symbols to be clarified.
While the Original Buddha remains silent, the transformation Buddhas preach; this signifies that the Dharma-Buddha is fundamentally without speech.

Without demonstrating, there is the manifestation of signs through signlessness; without speaking, there is the revelation of discourse. The single truth is profound stillness, yet the myriad transformations are mysteriously interconnected.
Through the power of wisdom that is like an illusion, one remains unmoved while circulating through all things. The essential purport of this entire scripture is to be found herein.
"Command Mañjuśrī to take the mantra and go to protect [her], until the Mātanga woman returns to the Buddha’s presence.
This section of the scripture describes the benefit of the introductory sequence for establishing a karmic connection by explaining the act of going to protect and the exhortation to return.

The "Nidāna-parivarta" (Introductory Section on the Origin of the Teaching) concludes here. "Command" (*cājñā*) refers to an order issued from a superior to a subordinate; "taking" (*jānīya*) refers to the intent of upholding the mantra.
The instructions proclaimed by the emanation Buddha are the mission of the Original Buddha; they are transmitted solely through oral recitation and originally possess no written text.
If one upholds this, Mañjuśrī will uphold it in his heart and go to protect Ānanda. This true mantra, once uttered, causes illusory mantras to be dissolved;
the true can destroy the illusory, and the good can eliminate the evil. "Tí" (提) means to uplift; Mañjuśrī shall lift [the practitioner] out from the pit of craving and desire.
Ānanda rescued him; this rescue and exhortation caused Daṅga’s lustful desires to fail.
Ashamed, humiliated, and terrified, Mañjuśrī exhorted and admonished him with kind words, using skillful means to subdue his evil mind and expediently inspire his wholesome thoughts.

Furthermore, Daṅga relied upon the power of the divine mantra for secret assistance and benefit, whereby he immediately attained the fruit of realization; thus, he was able to become equal [to the others].

"Returning to the Buddha's Abode," as stated in the subsequent sutra: "That courtesan, though without the intent to practice, was secretly aided by spiritual power and swiftly realized the stage of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa).
This marks the beginning of the section on the Correct Teaching (samyak-siddhānta-bhāga).
"Ānanda saw the Buddha, prostrated himself, and wept with grief... (up to) "...the initial expedient for *samādhi* and *dhyāna*.
This section of the sutra precisely clarifies that Ānanda has emerged from the pit of desire and reached the shore of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

It describes his self-reproach and attribution of fault to his own excessive learning (*bahuśruta*), as he requests the meaning of the untainted path and meditative concentration (*anāsrava-mārga-samādhi*). The six phrases following "Ānanda" are still...
"This is the language of the compiler. From "In the ten directions, in the lower regions" onwards are the words of Ānanda as he poses his questions according to the occasion.
Everything from the beginning, "Thus have I heard," up to this point consists entirely of the compiler's own words.

Only from here on does the dialogue between teacher and disciple begin, where the capacity of the student and the teaching of the master strike one another like the first basketful of earth forming a mountain. From this point forward, students should understand that they are riding upon the initiative of Ānanda.
How truly marvelous! For what reason, upon seeing the Buddha for the first time, did he immediately reproach himself and, through his extensive learning, recognize the root source of his own ailment?
Upon opening his mouth, he requested the wondrous *śamatha* and so forth. Thus, extensive learning is the illness and wondrous concentration is the medicine;
the revelation of this very point through the critique in this sutra lies solely here. One should carefully contemplate the general purport of this sutra.

This is because suppressing wisdom (*prajñā*) and exalting concentration (*samādhi*) serves to ensure that practitioners are balanced and not partial. Generally speaking, if a practitioner is biased toward wisdom, they become狂 (mad);
if biased toward concentration, they become 癡 (deluded). To avoid madness and delusion, it is essential to cultivate both concentration and wisdom equally.
For this reason, the *nidāna* (introductory origin) of this sutra begins with Ānanda being partial toward extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), as extensive learning belongs to the category of wisdom.

Because his power of concentration was insufficient, he encountered this perverse defilement. Furthermore, if we speak from the perspective of beginningless time, it has not been accumulated over merely one or two lifetimes;
for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* also states that Ānanda has remembered and upheld the Dharma-treasuries of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas of the past.
Thus, it is said here to be "beginningless. Later in the sutra, the Buddha reprimands him, saying: "Although you..."
To recollect and uphold the Tathāgata’s secret and wondrous adornments throughout kalpas is not equal to cultivating untainted karma for even a single day;
this is merely the sense of "suppressing the former and elevating the latter. Furthermore, the ailment of excessive learning arises from the faculty of hearing;
thus, the selection of the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty as Ānanda’s initial expedient was for a very good reason, as it involves following sounds into the cycle of transmigration.
To cure this illness, one must cause it to turn back and restore its profound stillness by attuning to the underlying mechanism;
the mutual relationship between the medicine and the illness is as clear as the sun and stars, leaving no room for dispute. Yet, the illness of excessive learning is not unique to Ānanda;
all sentient beings in this Sahā world fall prey to this ailment. Therefore, it is said: "The true essence of the teaching in this region is pure."
"Purity resides in hearing. Now, Ānanda has accumulated the fault of excessive hearing; therefore, he requests the medicine of the Path of Samādhi to cure it.
"The ten directions" below refers to the formal request for the Path of Samādhi. Bodhi is this Path; śamatha and so forth are the Path of Samādhi.
Because it is accomplished through samādhi, the Sanskrit term *bodhi* is translated as "Awakening" (*jue*) and also as "Path" (*dao*). This is because the Path is itself Awakening.

This refers to the unsurpassed and ultimate path realized by the Tathāgata himself. *Śamatha* is translated as "stopping" (*zhi*). Ancient masters explained that it means "to restrain," and it is also called "quiescence. Furthermore, because the principle of the mind-nature is eternally unmoving, it is termed "stopping. Although there are many paths of meaning for "stopping," three points are briefly set forth here: first, the reality of the essence; second, the cessation of discursive thought; and third, the pacification of afflictions. (The second and third points follow. First, the reality of the essence: the nature of the mind is originally quiescent and non-arising. Since its nature is inherently tranquil, it is called "stopping. This is the meaning of "stopping" as the reality of the essence. Second, the cessation of discursive thought: all mental activities are fundamentally empty and non-existent. Since they are originally non-arising, they are called "stopping. This is the meaning of "stopping" as the cessation of discursive thought. Third, the pacification of afflictions: all afflictions are originally non-existent and have no place to abide. Since they are originally extinguished, they are called "stopping. This is the meaning of "stopping" as the pacification of afflictions. These three meanings are unified within the single essence of the mind-nature. Thus, the term "stopping" encompasses these three aspects. This is the meaning of "stopping" as the single essence of the body. First, "stopping" (śamatha) refers to the realization that the delusion of ignorance and perversion is itself the reality of the true mark; therefore, it is called "stopping through realizing the true" (tǐzhēn zhǐ).
Second, "stopping by following conditions through skillful means" (fāngbiàn suíyuán zhǐ) refers to the intent of skillfully and adaptively accomplishing [the goal];

that is, while following conditions and traversing various objects, one settles the mind so that it remains unmoving; therefore, it is called "stopping by following conditions through skillful means. Third, "stopping the two extremes" (xī èrbiān).
"Discriminating cessation" (*vibhāvanā-vipaśyanā*) refers to not discriminating between the two extremes of existence and non-existence regarding the ultimate and conventional truths.

Because this non-discrimination is itself a state of stillness, it is called "cessation of the discrimination of the two extremes. In Sanskrit, *samādhi* is fully expressed as *samāpatti*, which is translated as "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).
"Contemplation" carries the meaning of clear illumination; it means to clearly illuminate that within a single thought-moment, [all things] are already complete.

Regarding the meaning of the three contemplations, within each contemplation there are likewise three points. First is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). "Emptiness" refers to the intention to sweep away all marks;

it means contemplating that the present thought-moment does not exist in any of the three locations—inside, outside, or in between—and because ultimately no mind can be apprehended, it is called empty.
Because one contemplates the emptiness of a single thought-moment, when one is empty, all are empty.

There is no provisional, no middle, and nothing that is not empty; when these three characteristics are all swept away, this is ultimate emptiness, and thus it is called the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

Regarding the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*): "provisional" refers to the explanation of the extreme of existence. Although things exist, they are not real; being unreal, they are what is termed provisional existence.

This means observing that the single thought-moment of the present is fully endowed with the three thousand nature-and-characteristics (*tri-sahasra-svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*); therefore, it is called the provisional. By means of this observation...
Because a single thought is provisional, one is provisional and all are provisional; there is no emptiness, no middle, and nothing that is not provisional.

When these three characteristics are all immediately established as wondrous provisionality, it is called the contemplation of provisionality (*jia-guan*). Within these three, the contemplation of the Middle means that within the Middle itself, the Middle is precisely the severance of the meaning of dualistic opposition.
This refers to contemplating the present single thought-moment as being neither empty nor provisional, yet identical to emptiness and identical to provisionality.

Because the provisional and the non-provisional are not identical, they are called the "Middle. Since one contemplates the Middle within a single thought-moment, within that one Middle all things are the Middle.

There is no emptiness, no provisionality, and nothing that is not the Middle; these three aspects are mutually transcendent. This is the Perfect Middle, and thus it is called the "Middle Contemplation" (*madhyamā-pratyavekṣā*).

In the Sanskrit language, *dhyāna* is translated as "meditative concentration" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*); "concentration" (*śama*) is cessation (*śamatha*), and "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) is insight (*vipaśyanā*). Cessation and...
Because one contemplates them as neither identical nor different, neither the same nor distinct, they are joined in name as "dhyāna" (静虑).
This perfect fusion constitutes the abiding in equality; this is called the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of *dhyāna*. Someone may ask: "The two preceding meanings each possess three aspects.
Why, then, is it not said here that *dhyāna* possesses these three? The answer is found in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-ṭīkā*, which states: "Dhyāna also... [and so forth].

It is said that *samādhi* (equipoise), *vīrya* (the canopy), and *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) have no separate essence; rather, the latter two not allowing for partiality or leaning upon the basis of *samādhi* is precisely the meaning of *dhyāna*.

Therefore, they are not spoken of as three. Now, regarding these three—*śamatha*, [vipaśyanā], and [dhyāna]—to mention one is to mention all three, and to speak of three is to see their essence as one.
It is neither one nor three, yet it can be three and can be one; this is precisely the single thought-moment of the present.

Because such wondrous meanings are fully contained within the mind, it is called "wondrous" (*miao*). This single character "wondrous" permeates the two subsequent names—namely, "wondrous *śamatha*," "wondrous *samādhi*," and "wondrous *dhyāna*.
Since all three meanings are wondrous, they constitute the three contemplations in perfect fusion (*yuanrong*), rather than being separate or distinct meanings.
Someone may ask: "The meaning of the three types of cessation (*zhi*) and the three types of contemplation (*guan*) as being perfectly fused can be understood; however, regarding..."

Question: What does this sutra designate as the object of contemplation? Answer: In the subsequent text, the Buddha interrogates regarding the meaning of "mind" and "vision" (*citta* and *darśana*), taking these two meanings as the objects of contemplation.
Now, it is stated that the single thought-moment of the present is itself the object;
thus, although it is called a delusory object, it inherently possesses the three truths (*triratna*). Therefore, both the contemplating subject and the contemplated object are non-dual.
Because it is apart from the single mind, as explained in the sections on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the present text is extremely concise;

one should understand it through the Perfect Mind (*pariniṣpanna-citta*), for it cannot be fully exhausted by words. Nevertheless, these three meanings constitute the essential and subtle purport of the mental dharmas of this sutra;
therefore, they are explained in detail here. Readers should not weary themselves with their prolixity. Furthermore, these three meanings are the very means to attaining Buddhahood.
One must necessarily attain [enlightenment] through this, just as clouds must necessarily emerge through a doorway.

Among all the scriptures and treatises of the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions, there are none that do not elucidate the subtlety of these three contemplations; they are the most urgent of heart-teachings.

However, the *bodhi* realized by the Buddhas mentioned in the preceding text is the "subtlety of the fruit," while the three—such as *śūnyatā* (emptiness)—are the "subtleties of the cause. One realizes [the fruit] only by cultivating these causes.
The essence of the fruit of Bodhi is precisely what is referred to in the title as the "Secret Cause" (*guhyahetu*).
Furthermore, this essence of the fruit of Bodhi is itself the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, and this wondrous samādhi is the eternally abiding true mind;

it is simply one dharma with a thousand names, its titles being established in accordance with conditions. The twenty-five perfect penetrations (*āveśa*) in the subsequent sutra are the response to that initial request.
This request is indeed the primary skillful means, and it is also the initial skillful means for entering the wondrous Samādhi of Śrāvakas and others.

However, knowing that the twenty-five perfect penetrations (āveśa) are collectively termed the "primary skillful means," [the Buddha] specifically selected the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty because the auditory faculty is sharp in this land;
thus, he chose the ear-faculty’s perfect penetration to suit the capacities of those here and to respond to those who have heard much.
Regarding this illness, Ānanda’s single question contains within its intent the three essentials of principle (*li*), practice (*xing*), and realization (*zheng*).

The subtle and wondrous [teachings] such as the three [categories] are principle; the initial skillful means is practice. Since there is that which is practiced, there must be that which is realized; this is merely manifested within the context of practice.
The profound purport of the entire sutra emerges from this. For the sake of the sequential order of the response, I have provisionally set forth these points.
This section constitutes the primary essential of the *Nyāyamukha*.
At that time, there were again bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges [who] withdrew from their seats and remained silent, receiving the holy instruction.
This passage from the scripture describes how the assembled multitude, desiring to hear this request, sat in silence.
"He awaits the holy decree" means that after Ānanda has finished his questioning, he should himself receive the Buddha’s feet and pay his respects;

then the assembly follows the host as they rise to perform their salutations, and once the salutations are completed, they withdraw and sit upon their original seats—hence the phrase "retreats to his seat.

"Silent" signifies the state of stilling the mind in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). In the preceding text, it says that after the meal was finished, they returned, and there were various kings and ministers.
This is not cited here for the sake of brevity.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "You and I share the same vital breath" (extending to "...suddenly renouncing the deep and heavy affection of the world").
This section of the sutra shows the World-Honored One responding to the request; he follows the petitioner's initial resolve by using the point of his realization as a sign.
To examine their delusion: they expose the root cause of others' ailments and thereby break through [the barriers] to reveal the fundamental basis.
Ānanda was the son of King Droṇodana and the Buddha’s cousin; since they shared a single ancestral line, he is said to be "of the same breath. Parents constitute the natural order (*tionalun*);
this "natural order" refers to siblings, as Confucians call brothers the "natural order. Parents, wife, and children constitute... [the family].

The world possesses deep and heavy bonds of affection; yet, when one now interrogates the origin of these thoughts and examines their manifestations, one must scrutinize whether they are truly or falsely conceived, and whether they are real or unreal.
If they accord with *śamatha* and other such states, they are authentic; if they are subject to arising and ceasing, they do not so accord.
Since the causal mind does not accord with *śamatha* and the like, it is like casting a boat toward the north—no matter how far one proceeds, one only moves further away from the destination.
Because they merely exhaust themselves in vain, the Buddha interrogates them regarding the causes of their minds; this contains a profound meaning found in the following scripture:
"If one takes birth and extinction as the basis for cultivating the cause, yet seeks the Buddha-vehicle of non-birth and non-extinction, there is no such possibility.

This serves as proof. Furthermore, the two characters "this mind" (cixin) and "seeing" (jian) lead into the subsequent passages that investigate the mind and discern seeing, all of which proceed from these points.
"This arose.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha: "I saw the Tathāgata... [and so on] "...for this reason, out of thirsty longing, I followed the Buddha to shave my head and beard.
This section of the sutra is Ānanda’s response to the preceding inquiry, wherein he truthfully recounts the beginning of his realization of the mind to clarify its initial manifestation.
This is the origin of their discourse. Yet, observe Ānanda’s arousal of the mind upon seeing the physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*):

the mind and its objects, the self and the other, stand towering and sharply defined against one another—is this not the mind of arising and ceasing? It can be seen that the root of his ailment lies herein.
As for the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks, beginning from the level soles of the feet and ending with the high and rounded *uṣṇīṣa*, they are described in detail in the *Dharmapada*.

The initial gateway to the sequence of the *dhātus* arises precisely because the Tathāgata, through the cultivation of morality, concentration, and wisdom over many kalpas, has planted the seeds of a hundred merits;
thus he has elicited a state that is supremely wondrous, extraordinary, pure, and stainless, with inner and outer clarity like lapis lazuli.
"Lapis lazuli" (*vaiḍūrya*) is a term from the Sanskrit language; its full form is *vaiḍūrya*, which is translated as "the jewel not far [from the source]" (*bùyuǎnbǎo*). It is located at Vārāṇasī.
Not far from the city there was a mountain from which this jewel emerged; therefore, Ānanda habitually reflected that the marks of the Tathāgata do not arise from desire or attachment.
Why then does [the text] below cite and explain the meaning of what precedes? It means: how could such coarse and turbid vapors of desire produce something superior and wondrous?
How could something putrid, rank, foul, and rotten produce something extraordinary and sublime? Truly, it arises from the union of man and woman.
All the limbs produced from such purity are a chaotic mixture of pus and blood, unable to give rise to the supreme, pure, brilliant, and wondrous mass of purple-gold light.
"Purple-gold light" refers to the Tathāgata’s physical body, which is like a radiant cluster of purple-polished gold;
none can equal it. For this reason, Ānanda suddenly desired these marks and shaved his head following the Buddha.
[The text] ends.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, Ānanda! You all should know—[up to] 'because this perception is not true, there is cyclic existence.
This section of the sutra, in which the World-Honored One intends to shatter the delusions of mind and views, first establishes the true essence."
The opening words "Excellent! (*sādhu*) accord with the meaning of the sutra; they should be understood as the World-Honored One’s words of compassion.
He felt pity for those who are deluded by false conceptions and have lost their true essence.

When the Buddha speaks of "all sentient beings," he means that the entire world is deluded, not merely Ānanda alone; it is through the case of one person, Ānanda, that he encompasses the multitude. Thus it is.

Furthermore, delusion has persisted for a long time; from the beginningless past until now, the continuous succession of birth and death arises entirely from not knowing the eternally abiding essence of the mind.
This eternally abiding essence of the mind is precisely the nature of spiritual awakening inherently possessed by every person.
Since it has been quiescent and unmoving from the very beginning, it is called the "eternally abiding true mind. This is contrasted with the false views described below.
Yet this true mind is by nature luminous, pure, empty, wondrous, and all-encompassing; people themselves do not know it.
This ignorance is itself delusion, and delusion is itself ignorance. It obscures this fundamental luminosity, causing one to employ various false thoughts (*vikalpa*).
Since these false thoughts are easily perceived—vivid and alert within the very midst of our seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting—everyone employs them.
They consider this to be their own mind, unaware that it is but deluded thought (*vikalpa*) and not the true mind (*bhūta-citta*).

The true mind is fundamentally quiescent, leaving no trace to be perceived; thus, being deluded and ignorant of this, they mistake this "bright and alert" consciousness for their own experience and enjoyment.
This very word "use" refers to the use in daily life—that which corresponds to what must be done amidst the activities of daily life.
Those who encounter this all mistakenly take it to be real, yet the Buddha directly denounces it as false. Because it is false, there is arising and ceasing;

arising and ceasing constitute the cycle of saṃsāra. Since that which is false is not real, and saṃsāra is not permanent, is it not a great pity that people are deluded regarding this true permanence?
For this reason, the Buddha exclaimed, "Excellent! and instructed them to establish their foundation therein.
Furthermore,
this section of the sutra— “You now wish to investigate unsurpassed bodhi... until there is forever no sign of any crookedness in between”—
is where the World-Honored One refutes the delusions of mind and views in response to the subtle and wonderful request for bodhi.

Please further admonish him to respond with a straightforward mind. The phrase "unsurpassed bodhi" (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) refers back to what Ānanda asked regarding that which is realized by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
The term "investigate" (yan) means to thoroughly investigate; "truly illuminating the nature" (zhen faming xing) requires one to carefully contemplate the meaning of the text.
One must read from "unsurpassed bodhi" down to "illuminating" (faming) as a single, continuous breath. This is because...
What is the nature manifested within the true essence of bodhi? That which is manifested within bodhi refers precisely to wondrous śamatha and so forth.
These three meanings are inherently possessed by the principle; they are the wondrous functions manifested upon the essence of bodhi.
"Manifesting" (faming) means to manifest or reveal; there are those who [interpret it as] "to give rise to."
Those who mistakenly interpret this as "elucidating through speech" are incorrect. One must understand that the character *yan* (研) in the preceding phrase already carries the meaning of elucidation;
how could there be two instances of the word "elucidation" within a single sentence? Such a grammatical construction does not exist.

One should immediately admonish [the interlocutor] to answer the question with a straightforward mind. The section beginning with "The ten directions" below demonstrates the application of the straightforward mind.
The reason for employing a straightforward mind is that all Buddhas of the ten directions who have passed from birth to death share one and the same path;
this single path is none other than the unsurpassed bodhicitta. If one’s mind is not straightforward, one deceives the Buddhas.

"Under the words 'mind'" means that it is not only the mind that must be straightforward, but speech as well. For the mind is the root of the Way; if the mind is not straightforward, [the Way cannot be realized].
Thus, the path practiced consists of using crooked speech as a manifestation of the mind; if the mind is not upright, then speech will be deviant.

Therefore, it is necessary for both mind and speech to be straight. From the ordinary person to the sage, from the lowly to the high—from the initial stage of faith through to Equal Enlightenment—passing through all intermediate stages of abiding, practice, transference, and realization, one is forever free from all signs of crookedness, all resulting from an upright mind.
"Therefore, there is no crookedness.
Ānanda, I now ask you: when you first gave rise to the aspiration [until] what did you see, and who was it that you cherished?
This section of the sutra is the World-Honored One’s thorough investigation of from what the vision arises and who it is that cherishes it; this constitutes the seventh [point].
This serves as the foundation for the eightfold interrogation. Having first determined the source of delusion, one then proceeds through the stages of interrogation and debate.
These two terms, "this mind" and "seeing," are precisely the "mind and seeing" from the preceding passage concerning the manifestation of the mind and its objects;
they serve as the handle for the logical inquiry that refutes and reveals. Students must not lose sight of their origin.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, it is because of such love and delight [that I have resolved my mind to abandon birth and death].
This section of the sutra records Ānanda’s response to the aforementioned questions. In the preceding questions, "vision" (*darśana*) and "love and delight" (*ruci*) were explained separately;
now, in his answer, he first unifies them and subsequently analyzes them. He first points to the eye and mind as being one in their love and delight, and then...

To speak of the mind and the eyes as distinct means that because one perceives with the eyes, the mind gives rise to attachment and delight. Below, the Buddha concludes by explaining the reason for the aforementioned arousal of the bodhicitta.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As you have said... [up to] ...then one will not be able to subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*)."
In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One follows up on his previous response to make it known that the mind and eyes are thieves;
one must first examine their nest before they can be subdued. From the words "As you... onwards is the formal restatement of the response.
If he did not issue this command to know their nest, the Buddha’s intention was that all afflictions arise from the mind and eyes, because the mind and eyes...
The nature of the "thief" will be clarified in the subsequent text. Now, wishing to subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*), one must first investigate and know the hidden location of the mind and its eyes.
The location of the mind refers to the seven places mentioned below, which are its supports;
the location of seeing refers to the eight points of discernment mentioned below. One should use these seven places to exhaustively investigate [the thief] until it has no place to dwell.
By relying on this, one first destroys their nest; once the thief’s form is exposed, their stratagems are exhausted and they are easily subdued.

Thus, the afflictions of dust naturally cease. "Dust" refers to dusty conditions belonging to the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); "affliction" refers to weary deliberation belonging to the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*).
For example, it is like a king who has been invaded by bandits... (until) "...only the mind and the eyes; where are they now?
This section of the sutra uses a metaphor to clarify that the mind and the eyes must necessarily be eliminated; one must first know their location before they can be removed.
The king is a metaphor for the previously mentioned eternally abiding true mind, and the royal law and the nature-land serve as metaphors for the kingdom.
The analogy of the king and the thief refers to the mind and the six sense-faculties acting as thieves and intermediaries who plunder the family treasures; thus they are likened to thieves.

To mobilize troops to suppress and eliminate them is a metaphor for the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) such as *śamatha*; this "suppression" is what was mentioned above as "subduing. The location [of these thieves] can be known.

The phrase "causing you" and so forth applies the Dharma to the process of *saṃsāra* (flowing and turning) in contrast to the eternally abiding; that is to say, the True Mind is originally and fundamentally eternally abiding.
Because the True is transformed by delusion and invaded by thieves, it is identical to the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*);

since "transmigration" refers to the "wheeling and turning" mentioned in the preceding text, it is said that "the mind and eyes are the fault. Here, "mind" (*citta*) refers to the sixth consciousness, the攀緣心 (*pān-yuan-xin*, the grasping-consciousness), which encompasses the meaning of the first five consciousnesses;

"eyes" (*mù*) refers to the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), which encompasses the meaning of the remaining five faculties. The final three lines beginning with "I now" [refer to] the formal inquiry into where [this fault] resides.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, all worlds... [up to] ...thus the consciousness-mind truly dwells within the body.
This section of the sutra is Ānanda’s response to the previous question regarding the mind and eyes, clarifying the location upon which it relies.
“All worlds” refers to the dependent world of the ten types of birth; these ten kinds of ordinary beings are...

Because they differ in their primary retribution (*vipāka*), they are called "ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*); since both their primary bodies and their environments (*niśraya*) differ, there are ten types of ordinary beings.
These ten are: those born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; those with no feet, two feet, four feet, or many feet;
and those with perception, without perception, and neither with nor without perception. Other sutras and this current version of the scripture both refer to them as twelve categories. Now...
Excluding "empty," "scattered," "dissipated," and "sinking" because they lack the mind and eyes of existence, it is simply called "ten.

Ānanda replied that although the retributions of the ten types of birth differ, the mind is necessarily located below the face; while the eyes of ordinary beings differ by being above, the location of the mind and eyes of the Buddhas at their highest limit is identical.
Ordinary beings speak of the "mind" but do not mention the "eyes," whereas the Tathāgata speaks of the "eyes."

Furthermore, the text alternately clarifies that [the faculties] do not reach the mind. Because the Tathāgata’s eyes, physical marks, and radiance are like blue lotuses, they are called "blue-lotus eyes.

From the phrase "I now" onwards, the text follows the previous example to show that while the Buddha and ordinary beings differ, Ānanda’s own eyes are likewise on his face and his mind is likewise within.
As for the "floating roots of the four dusts," this refers generally to the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).

All are produced by the eight dharmas of the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and their objects; each faculty possesses two types of dharmas: the *pudgala-rūpa* (the coarse, phenomenal root) and the *paramārtha-rūpa* (the ultimate, subtle root).

That which has a visible form and appearance is called the *pudgala-indriya*. That which consists of the pure four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and is visible only to the divine eye is called the *paramārtha-indriya*.
Both are produced by the four great elements derived from the four subtle particles (*anu*), which are themselves composed of the eight dharmas. Now, regarding the term "coarse" (*pudgala*)...

"Roots" refers to the physical sense organs (*rūpa-kleśendriya*), while "four objects" (*catur-viṣaya*) refers to the four subtle elements (*catvāraḥ paramāṇavaḥ*) that constitute them; thus they are called "objects" (*viṣaya*).

The four gross elements (*mahābhūta*) produced by these are omitted, and only the four subtle elements that act as the constituents are mentioned. These four subtle elements are color, odor, taste, and tangibility.
As for the four gross elements produced by these, they are earth, water, fire, and wind; because they are not manifest, they are termed "subtle" (*paramāṇu*).
"It is called 'great' because its form and measure are all-pervasive.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "You are currently sitting here [until] this Jeta Grove is actually outside the hall.
In this section of the sutra, the Buddha takes up the mind that clings to the interior to verify the reality of the interior and exterior, and only then does he refute it.
This intention is to enable Ānanda to attain awakening easily. In the preceding text, both the mind and the eyes were interrogated; now, first the location of the mind is interrogated.
Once the location of the mind is refuted, the faculty of vision will then be refuted. Students should understand the sequence of the sūtra’s text.
Your current [statement], "one sentence," refers to Ānanda, implicitly likening him to the mind within; "the lecture hall" is implicitly likened to...
Regarding Ānanda’s body observing where the Jeta Grove is now located: one must clarify that from the internal to the external, one should first see the internal and subsequently see the external.
As for the mention of the Jeta Grove in the following text, it is called the "Jeta Grove" because the trees of the grove were bestowed by Jeta;
Jeta is the same as Jetavana, differing only in the sequence of their translations.

Therefore, the World-Honored One [asked], and Ānanda answered below. "The multi-storied pavilion" (chónggé) refers to a double-eaved structure with soaring galleries, like the so-called Āgē (Cloud Pavilion) with its three tiers of steps, which signifies loftiness.
The area beneath the pavilion is precisely the lecture hall;

since worldly dust does not reach it, those who gather there are all practitioners of refined cultivation, hence it is called "pure. In the preceding passage, the Buddha merely asked about the Jeta Grove.

Now Ānanda replied, "It was established at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden. "Anāthapiṇḍada" is the elegant title of the elder Sudatta, so called because he delighted in providing for the destitute and solitary;
it is called "Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden" because it was purchased by that elder with gold coins.
Thus, each name highlights the donor. In this present exchange of questions and answers, both donors are mutually manifested.
Regarding the phrase "the grove and garden," the two lines "The Jeta Grove is actually outside the hall" constitute the direct answer to the question. [The Buddha said:
"Ānanda, what do you first see within this hall now? ... [until] ... looking thus outward, one then beholds the grove and garden."

In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One proceeds from the internal to the external in successive order, examining and verifying each stage to establish their sequence and thereby break down [the misconception] so that awakening may be easily attained.

Why does the World-Honored One not directly clarify that the mind is not within, but instead poses questions regarding the internal and external, as well as priority and sequence? This is precisely to lead Ānanda from this...
Regarding the sequence of the internal and external bases for views (*āyatana*), he clarifies that if his mind were within, it should likewise perceive both the internal and the external;
since he does not see the internal but only sees the external, it is clear that this mind does not reside within.
The Buddha’s intention was to lead [the interlocutor] to self-realization; therefore, he poses the question by means of the sequential order of the internal and external. Now, the Buddha asks:
It is asked: "When you were in the hall, what did you see first—what was internal or external, what came before or after? This must be clarified here.

When the World-Honored One descended, Ānanda replied: "That I saw the Buddha first while in the hall was because the Buddha stood among the assembly, his physical marks and radiance eclipsing all others, like the moon among the stars; therefore, as soon as I raised my eyes, I saw him first."

The Buddha next sees the assembly. Although the Buddha and the assembly see one another within the hall, with the Buddha seeing first and the assembly seeing later, this sequence implies that they subsequently see what is outside.
By clarifying this point, it becomes evident that a mind existing within [the body] cannot be established.
"Ānanda, you gaze at the grove and garden; for what reason do you see them? [This passage continues until: "Therefore, while I am in the hall, I am able to see them from afar.
This section of the sutra is the World-Honored One’s inquiry into the preceding point—that seeing occurs by means of the eyes—whereby he re-examines the external causes of that seeing.
Throughout the preceding sections, the Buddha has interrogated Ānanda point by point, causing him to state his own position so as to lead him toward realization.

The errors are easy to see; the World-Honored One subsequently refutes them so that the phenomena may be gathered back into the mind for the sake of awakening—this is the meaning of the World-Honored One’s skillful and indirect accomplishment. "Zhu" (gaze) is simply "shi" (to look).
The World-Honored One, clearly knowing that Ānanda’s grasping at seeing arises from the eyes, asks, "By what cause does seeing exist? in order to elicit an answer, which will be addressed later.
The intent of this refutation lies in demonstrating that seeing does not proceed from the eyes, but is manifested by the mind. Therefore, the subsequent text interrogates:
"While you are inside a room, can the door see? Now Ānanda indeed answers that when the doors and windows are wide open, one can look far out;
the fact that the doors and windows are hidden serves as a metaphor for the eyes being opened and thus enabling vision. This still pertains to the immediate facts at hand.
The exposition is not yet clearly revealed.
At that time, the World-Honored One was amidst the great assembly... (until) Ānanda prostrated at his feet and humbly received his compassionate instructions.
This section of the sutra shows the World-Honored One following the preceding sections, verifying the internal and external matters according to the facts; now he will [proceed].
To shatter the internal mind, one first establishes the essence to set its foundation.

With the foundation established before us, the subsequent demonstration—whether it be a single realization, a single shattering, or a single manifestation—is entirely the essence of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi; let the student not lose sight of this fundamental principle.
"Extending" refers to the stretching forth of the Buddha’s golden body, which is why they are called "golden-armed. "Touching the crown of the head" means...
The Buddha, intending to comfort the minds of those present, first offers reassurance before speaking, fearing that they might experience shock or terror as he is about to shatter their attachments.
He addresses Ānanda first because he is the primary recipient of the teaching; by addressing Ānanda, he includes the entire assembly.
Next, he reveals the name of the Great Samādhi: Śūraṅgama, which carries the meaning of ultimate firmness and solidity, as explained in detail within the title itself.
Because this samādhi is the foundation of all virtues, it is called the "King.
For one who is fully endowed with the myriad practices, this Great Samādhi is the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of profound stillness.

Since this mind universally possesses all virtues and all practices proceed from it, it is said to be "fully endowed with the myriad practices. The following section clarifies that the Way of every Buddha is the same.

This reveals the profound efficacy of the Great Samādhi. It means that among the Buddhas of the ten directions, there are none who do not transcend through the single gate of the Great Buddha-Crown Samādhi onto the Path of Sublime Adornment.
This "Path of Sublime Adornment" refers to the fifty-five stages of the Bodhi-path elucidated in the subsequent sutra.
As for "Sublime Adornment," it means that the Great Way is without action; by virtue of this—
The adornment of concentration and wisdom: concentration and wisdom are precisely *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*.

As the *Lotus Sūtra* says, "Adorned by the power of concentration and wisdom," this is it. Now, the subsequent scripture states that the ocean of Great Nirvāṇa is the place of arrival, while the fifty-five stages are the path for entering Nirvāṇa.
What is called "sublime" (*miao*) means being adorned without the need for adornment.
To be adorned yet not adorned is as stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā*: "That which is non-adornment is called adornment; only then is it termed 'sublime'.
Furthermore, the term *samādhi* mentioned in the present text—also known as *samāpatti*—is a general designation for great meditative concentration (*mahāsamādhi*);

there is no need to cite the third meaning of *samā* from the previous threefold explanation, for that refers to the concentration of the cause, whereas this refers to the concentration of the fruit. However...
That which is pointed out there is also unimpeded, because one is three and three is one;
as it is said, the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the One Vehicle is both cause and fruit.

Furthermore, although the three meanings of *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* revealed below are perfect, their textual expressions are inclusive, as in the first case where *śamatha* is primarily expounded while the other two are [implied].
Next, it correctly expounds *samādhi* while simultaneously incorporating *śamatha* and *dhyāna*; next, it correctly expounds *dhyāna* while simultaneously incorporating *śamatha* and *samādhi*.
These are mutually inclusive and thoroughly interpenetrating; as primary and attendant factors, they blend into one another.
They are one without being conflated, and three without being separated. Both the phrasing and the meaning are exquisite, never losing their perfect harmony and practice.
The intent of this exposition is the subtle meaning of the present sutra.

Should there be those who, being mired in the principle of "perfect interfusion" (yuanrong), find it difficult to practice the "sequential unfolding" (xingbu), they will confuse their discourse and fail to bring forth any of the three expositions.

If this occurs, the Way of the unity and triad, and the triad within the unity, cannot be heard. May students reflect deeply upon this when encountering the text. Hereafter follows the formal exposition.
In the second fascicle of the *Śamatha-vyākhyāna*, following the section on darkness, penetration, and various obstructions,
it is likewise stated:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "As you have said— that one can see forests and springs— is impossible."
In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One takes up the words previously established by Ānanda as his own testimony to question him, thereby compelling him to confess his errors.
In the preceding passage, Ānanda replied, "The doors and windows were wide open, so that I could look far out and see the Buddha.
The Buddha seizes upon these two phrases as the handle for his refutation; indeed, there is a flaw in Ānanda’s statement which the Buddha grasps to expose him.
Because Ānanda explained the matter with the utmost clarity, stating that he first saw the interior and subsequently saw the exterior;
yet, if his mind was inside, why did he not first see the interior but only see the exterior?
Therefore, the Buddha immediately questioned him regarding this very matter, saying: "There are also sentient beings in a hall who do not see the interior but only see the exterior."
This is the World-Honored One drawing out Ānanda’s point of error.
Ānanda indeed claimed that because one must first see the interior and only then see the exterior, it is impossible not to see the interior.
The World-Honored One now uses the physical object to reveal the mind; the flaw in his argument will become evident when the mind is subsequently correlated with the object. Ānanda...
Is it not the case that you will surely submit to this and easily awaken? From here begins the first of the seven proofs, which first refutes [the mind] being within.
"Ānanda, you are also like this; that your conscious mind (up to) dwells within the body—there is no such possibility."
This section of the sutra is the World-Honored One’s first refutation of the attachment that the mind resides within.

The phrase "You are also like this" precisely expresses the meaning of unifying the mind with the object. This is analogous to the previous instance where one does not see the Tathāgata while inside the hall, but sees what is outside the hall;
the intent is the same as the notion that because the mind is within, one does not see the interior but only sees the exterior.
Because the meaning of your name refers to the mind, the following sentence proceeds to clarify it: "Your mind is spiritually lucid and all-knowing.
"Spiritually lucid" means that this mind is bright and alert; thus it is called the "spiritual mind.
It is "all-knowing" because, being spiritually lucid, it is clear and comprehending in every situation; hence it is said to be "all-knowing. "If you... [and so forth] is the actual inquiry.
"Internal" means that since this mind is already within, one should first know what is inside; perhaps that might still be possible.
The Buddha asked, "Is there anyone in the world who can first see within their own body and subsequently observe external objects?
This sentence corresponds to the previous statement: "There are also sentient beings in the hall who do not see the Tathāgata, yet see what is outside the hall."
The body is joined with the hall, and the mind is joined with sentient beings; since neither the dharma nor the analogy can be established, one knows that this mind certainly does not exist within.
"Even if" (*zòng*) is a concessive term. When it says "the heart, liver, spleen, and stomach," the character for "heart" (*xīn*) refers to the physical, fleshy heart.
Even if you cannot see the heart, liver, spleen, and stomach hidden deep within, you can still see your nails grow and your hair.
The long tendons, revolving vessels, and throbbing pulses are all within the skin and outside the membranes;
your mind is certainly inside, so you ought to be clearly aware of it—how is it that you do not know? This rebukes the notion that the mind resides within yet does not know what is within.

If it did not know what is within, you would surely not know what is inside the heart, liver, spleen, and stomach. Yet even though [the mind] is within, you do not know things such as your nails, hair, tendons, and vessels.
Regarding the two phrases, "How could one know it as being outside? and "Furthermore, how could one know it?", these are the Buddha’s definitive words [of negation].
If one asserts that another cannot definitively know it, then one knows that this mind does not reside within.
Therefore, the conclusion below—that it is not within—is stated: "Your conscious, cognizing mind is not seen within; thus, your position is untenable."
"There is no such possibility" means that there is no such principle; all subsequent instances are to be understood accordingly.
Ānanda bowed his head to the ground and addressed the Buddha, saying: [from "behind the door of his chamber" up to] "and throughout the courtyard."
In this section, because Ānanda heard the refutation of [the mind] being within, he shifted his calculation to the view that this mind resides outside the body.

"Such Dharma-sounds" refers to the Dharma-sounds of the preceding refutation of the interior; because [the mind] was thus refuted, he realized the mind was not within, and subsequently calculated it to be outside.
Therefore, the following provides analogies to investigate and clarify the location of the mind as being outside.
"How do we know that the mind is not outside? To provide an analogy, he said: "Suppose there is a lamp burning inside a room.
This lamp must first illuminate the interior; only after that can it shine out through the door of the room to reach the courtyard.
This analogy makes it clear that clinging to [the mind] as being internal is incorrect. These words represent his realization and understanding.
The preceding was an error; the following text merely sets forth the reason why the mind is directed outward.
