[From] "All sentient beings do not see within their own bodies" [up to] "attaining the definitive meaning equal to that of the Buddha," will they not then be free from delusion?
This section of the sutra follows the preceding analogy to clarify that the mind is external;

when it says "referring to all sentient beings," the meaning is that because all sentient beings can see what is outside but cannot see what is inside, they reckon this mind to be external, just as others are.
It is also like the second instance of the lamp analogy, where [the person] is outside the room.

The analogy that one can only illuminate what is outside but cannot illuminate the interior means that when the mind is directed outward, it likewise perceives only the external and cannot perceive the internal.
Regarding this meaning: "this meaning" refers to the meaning of being directed outward;

because there is no further doubt concerning this meaning of being outward, one feels loftily self-assured, claiming to have realized the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of a Buddha and to be free from delusion.
When I previously observed Ānanda’s statement that "the mind dwells outside the body," I noted his sophistry; yet now he says, "This meaning must be clear," and so forth.

His arguments are so stubborn and forced precisely because the Venerable One has already demonstrated that he shares the same delusions as others, and thus his rhetoric remains so persistent and dogmatic.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "These bhikṣus... (up to) "...how can one person cause the multitude to be satiated?
This section of the sutra represents the World-Honored One’s second refutation of the attachment that the mind resides in the external world.
Rather than refuting the doctrine directly at the point of their attachment, the World-Honored One separately cites a manifest event and questions them, thereby leading them to realization.
The self-explanations and digressions are categorized according to the specific matters so that they may be easily understood. The meaning of "bhikṣu" (monk) has already been explained previously.

The phrase "just now" (*shì*) refers to what was cited immediately below as a present instance; "just" (*shì*) means merely or recently, while "following" (*xún*) carries the sense of conforming to conditions.
"Grasping" (*bó*) refers to a physical segment that can be grasped. "Prepared for the fast" (*sùzhāi*) means receiving the fast in advance. The Buddha addressed these various bhikṣus...
"Kāśyapa, when I had just followed me from here to the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food according to my circumstances, and upon returning to the Jeta Grove, I accepted an offering of alms;
did you observe that because one bhikṣu received the food, the multitude were all satiated?
World-Honored One, the reason you cite this matter to question me is precisely to clarify that the mind outside [the body] is like another person, having no connection to me."
The example of one person eating while many people remain unsated clarifies the meaning of the separation between body and mind.
Ānanda replies with "No" (the character *wu* pronounced as *xià*). Ānanda’s intention is that there is not a single instance in the world where one person eating can satisfy many;
thus he says, "No. This sentence is a general response. What follows is a detailed inquiry and explanation of the reason why he said so.
Although the bhikṣus have attained the same fruits of realization, their physical bodies and lives are each distinct.
How could one person eating cause all the others to be satiated? One person may be compared to Ānanda’s body, while the multitude are compared to Ānanda’s mind remaining outside;
since the body and mind are separated from one another, they are not unified. The refutation of this argument follows below.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If your awareness [extends] from [the point mentioned previously] up to 'if they know one another,' why would it be external?

This section of the sutra uses the Lord’s implicit analogy—based on the previous reprimand that a single meal could not satisfy the multitude—to hold him accountable for the error of failing to realize that awareness is self-knowing. The Buddha said: "Your awareness is capable of knowing..."
If you perceive that the mind truly exists outside [the body], then your body and mind are separated from one another. Being external implies a barrier;
if the body and mind do not interact with each other, then that which the mind knows as being "outside" cannot be felt by the body.

Since the sensation resides at the boundary of the body, the mind cannot know it. Although this passage does not explicitly state the principle of "one eating and the many being satiated," [it implies it].

The meaning of the matter is that there is a silent resonance of intent. In the passage beginning with "I now," the Buddha again shows his hand to demonstrate the proof of the mutual correspondence between body and mind.
*Tūla* is translated as "fine fragrance"; because the Buddha’s hand is as soft and supple as cotton, it is called the "Tūla-cotton hand.
The two lines beginning with "Your eyes" are words of reprimand and inquiry; the intent of the reprimand is to say: "If you claim to have mutual correspondence, you are mistaken."
"Supposing it were outside"—Ānanda’s response of this kind indicates that he has understood and recognized [the truth].
As for the two subsequent lines, the World-Honored One rebukes him for the error of thinking the mind is not outside.
Therefore, you should know that your claim that the awakened, cognizing mind dwells outside the body is impossible.
This section of the sutra concludes that the mind grasping at external objects is untenable.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One... [up to] the Buddha asked, “Where, then, does it reside?”
This section of the sutra records how Ānanda, having heard the refutation of the externalist's error, again shifts his calculation. The passage beginning with "As the Buddha...

below provides a dual account of the errors regarding both the internal and the external, which is clear enough to understand from the text. The passage beginning with "I now... marks the point where he again shifts his calculation.
Regarding the phrase "a single location of seeing," the subsequent text, "The Buddha says... and so forth, interrogates the claim of that single location.
Ānanda said: "This cognizing mind... [up to] ...that faculty follows the seeing and immediately discriminates.
This section of the sutra begins with Ānanda responding to the inquiry by setting forth a metaphor; it is a false synthesis regarding the location, not the actual location.
The three phrases beginning with "this cognizing" represent Ānanda’s preliminary statement of that location, first describing how the mind is dark within and luminous without.
Regarding the ability [of the mind] to be as it is within me, I shall now correctly explain its location. As for "the root being hidden within," the "root" refers to the eye-faculty.
This is because Ānanda, wishing to avoid both faults—being either internal or external—proposed that the root is hidden.
Now, since this mind has no substance, how could there be the principle of a hidden root? To illustrate this hidden root seeing the external, the following analogy is set forth.

Therefore, when Lapis Lazuli is held before one as explained—taking a bowl made of Lapis Lazuli and placing it over both eyes—the nature of Lapis Lazuli is inherently clear and pure, with its interior and exterior mutually transparent.
Although it is placed over the eyes, it does not act as an obstruction or a hindrance;
this is the meaning of "obstruction. Lapis Lazuli is a metaphor for the eye, and the eye is a metaphor for the mind-eye (*citta-cakṣus*). The mind-eye is likewise clear and pure.
Lapis lazuli is used as a metaphor for the mind because, although the eye is situated within it, the eye is not obstructed by it even when closed over the heart.

Below that root, there is further explanation by way of analogy: just as the eye-organ follows what is reflected by the lapis lazuli and perceives it, so too the eye follows the distinctions made by others;
this is used as a metaphor for how the mind follows what is seen and follows its own discernment regarding the forms reflected by the eye.
This is indeed so; however, when one closes the eyes, the eyes see the lapis lazuli, yet when the two eyes are closed, the mind does not see the eyes.
Thus, the hidden implication reveals the fault that the dharma and the analogy are inconsistent, which will be refuted in the following text.
"However, as for this mind of mine that awakens and is capable of knowing—up to its being unobstructed—it dwells hidden within the sense organs.
This section of the sutra reiterates the meaning of "dwelling hidden within the organs," intended to escape the fault of [the mind] being either internal or external.

Previously, when Ānanda first proposed that the mind dwelt hidden within the organs, he had already described the faults of both the internal and external positions; now, he again refutes the internal position.

As for the "external" [critique], whereas previously he directly described the faults of both the internal and external [schools], he now debates the latent root (*mūla*) to explain why the internal and external views are respectively seen and unseen, thereby clarifying that the strategy of the latent root succeeds. The text is explicit and easily understood.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As you have said... [up to] 'the lapis lazuli cage covers the eyes, yet one truly sees the lapis lazuli.

This section of the sutra is the World-Honored One’s third refutation of the hidden location of the sense organs. First, he examines the meaning of the analogy to bring out the fault of inconsistency:
it is because the lapis lazuli is so clear and pure that although it covers the exterior of the eyes, one can still see."
Mountains, rivers, and lapis lazuli are objects external to the eye; they too should be seen. This question and answer can be understood as follows:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "If your mind were identical [to the eye]... [it would be] hidden within the faculties like lapis lazuli joined with them."

This section of the sutra follows up on the preceding metaphorical meaning to directly clarify that the analogy is not perfectly consistent and that the calculation regarding the latent faculty is untenable.
"Your mind" refers to the lower part of the preceding metaphorical meaning;

it means that while your mind corresponds to the two eyes in the metaphor—which are like lapis lazuli—the mind, which is compared to seeing through the lapis lazuli, does not see the eyes themselves. Therefore, the text rebukes: "Why do you not see the eyes?"

If one sees that the two [theories] are refuted by the lower [position], it means that if the eye were identical to the object of perception, one could not say that there is "conformity" (anuvṛtti) between the seeing and the conceptualization.
For it is only when the eye serves as the locus upon which the mind relies—being intimately proximate to the mind—that one can allow for such conformity.

If the eye were identical to the external object, it would have the status of a guest rather than a host; it would not be the primary agent nor its companion. Therefore, it is said that conformity cannot be established. If not...

Since the strategy of concealing the sense-faculty (*indriya*) fails when the eye is seen, [the text] rebukes [you] with these words. The two instances of the character "sui" (隨) should be viewed as identical.
Therefore, you should know that your claim—that from the point of "awakened awareness" up to "like crystal"—is untenable.
This section concludes that the World-Honored One’s strategy regarding the concealment of the faculties has failed.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... [up to] ...is called 'seeing internally'; what is the meaning of this?"
In this section of the sutra, Ānanda, having heard that the sense organs were refuted as being hidden within, again shifts his calculation.

This conceptual attachment holds that the mind still resides within the body; altering the previous distinction between the internal and external, he asserts that both light and darkness can serve as objects of cognition, and thus constitute the locus upon which the mind depends.
He claims that in the bodies of sentient beings, the viscera and organs reside within while the orifices and cavities are arrayed without.

The seven locations, such as the eyes and so forth, are these [openings]. "Hollow" (xué) refers to an aperture; because the viscera and organs are within and thus obscure and indistinguishable, they are called "dark.
This is intended to avoid the error of [the mind] seeing what is internal. Since the apertures and hollows reside on the exterior, they are bright and can be distinguished;
thus they are called "bright. This is intended to avoid the error of [the mind] departing from the body to dwell outside. However, now, internally...
That external objects can be seen while the mind does not leave the body is intended to avoid the error of [the mind] hiding within the sense organs.

Now, in my current correct assembly, I clarify that both the internal and external—light and darkness—are the fourth basis for reliance. Seeing light when opening the eyes is "external seeing," which flows outward from the outside;
this is easily understood, so let it be set aside for now. However, seeing darkness when closing the eyes alone is "internal seeing," which does not turn back.
The reason for the subsequent section’s exclusive refutation of the internal [position] is that once the internal has been refuted, the external follows suit.
To understand the meaning of this—reflecting carefully on even a single phrase—one will find it significant; students should know this.
For when Ānanda previously maintained that the mind was external, he said: "This principle must be clear, so that I may not be deluded, being the same as the Buddha."
"Has he attained the definitive meaning so as to be free from delusion? Observe his words; how firm and resolute they are!
This was Ānanda’s first encounter with one who excels in debate, and his mind was still coarse. Now, regarding the words he has deliberated upon, he does not dare to claim them as his own;
he merely asks, 'How is this? Observe his words; how harmonious and gentle they are! This is the point where Ānanda’s mind gradually becomes subtle. Hereafter..."
"Entering the subtle, one becomes increasingly proficient; entering the wondrous, one becomes increasingly sublime.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "You should close your eyes... [if] there is no correspondence, how can seeing be established?
This section of the sutra is the World-Honored One’s fourth investigation and refutation regarding the mind's basis upon internal and external light and darkness.
In the *Madhyama Āgama*, when Ānanda reckoned both the internal and external, the World-Honored One refuted it by focusing solely on the internal darkness.
The intention behind this refutation was to reveal that although Ānanda reckoned both internal and external light and darkness, the mind upon which he relied actually remained within;
therefore, the World-Honored One refuted it by focusing solely on the internal darkness. You should now cite the aforementioned reckoning of internal darkness.

The following two points are set forth in secret to refute [the opponent's position]. If [the opponent claims] "it is with [the eye]," this can be understood as refuting the preceding passage on "confronting the eye.

If [they claim] "it is not with [the eye]," this is the subsequent refutation of "not confronting the eye. Generally, for an objective field such as light or darkness to be called "seeing," it must confront the eye.
Since it does not confront the eye, how can it constitute seeing?
"If one were to claim that [the internal object] is established by departing from external vision and facing inward, then your single body would have to become two Buddhas.
This section of the sutra is the World-Honored One’s direct refutation of the darkness perceived when closing the eyes while facing inward;
it demonstrates that such an internal facing cannot establish clarity. In the preceding passage, Ānanda had calculated that seeing darkness when closing the eyes is what is called "within the body."
Regarding the calculation of the two types of "internal confrontation" (*nèiduì*) within the "before-the-eyes" (*qián-yǎn") [category], the first type has already been refuted above;
now we shall specifically refute the initial passage concerning internal confrontation. It states: "To be separated from external seeing" means to be separated from the darkness before one's eyes.

"Internal confrontation of what is established" means that "internal confrontation" refers to closing the eyes and looking inward toward the darkness confronted within. This is done by closing the eyes.

The last four lines use the analogy of opening one’s eyes to refute internal correspondence: you claim that the darkness seen through internal correspondence when the eyes are closed is what is called "within the body.
If this were so, then just as you can internally correspond [to see] when the eyes are closed, you should also be able to internally correspond [to see] when the eyes are open.

Furthermore, if you see within the body through internal correspondence with eyes closed, why do you not see your own face when you internally correspond with eyes open? If you do not [see it], then [your premise is false].
The second line directly refutes the internal correspondence as being unestablished:

if you claim that when the eyes are open there is no internal correspondence because one does not see the face, then when the eyes are closed there should likewise be no internal correspondence because one sees the body within.

If seeing the face were established [as proof], the World-Honored One, fearing you might resort to such a shifting argument, has explained in full detail that there is absolutely no principle of internal correspondence. If you maintain this calculation...

If the eye were directed inward and able to see the face, then this cognizing mind and the eye-faculty would have to be in empty space—just as when the mind and eye are on that side, one can see the face on this side.
Since they would be in empty space, how could they be "inside"? Thus, your claim that seeing darkness when directed inward is what is called being "within the body" is untenable.
Furthermore, if the visual faculty were located in empty space and were not your own body, it would be like something belonging to another person;
thus, it is said that the Tathāgata’s current vision of your face would [be his vision of himself].
If your visual faculty were on another's body, then that other person's body would be your own body. Moreover, if your eye were outside [yourself],...
That which is known by the eye, your body ought not to perceive; yet now you insist that both body and eye perceive one another.
If both body and eye were to perceive, there would have to be two cognitions. If the eye were your body, then your single body would possess two cognitions and would thus become two Buddhas.
Although such a detailed and thorough analysis was made, in the end, it proved to be untenable.
This is the principle of turning the gaze inward to observe the internal.
Therefore, you should know that your claim—that seeing darkness is called "seeing the internal"—is untenable.
This section of the sūtra concludes that the assertion that seeing darkness when the eyes are closed constitutes "seeing within the body" is not established.
Ānanda said, "I have often heard the Buddha instruct the fourfold assembly... (up to) "...nor does it exist in the three locations of internal, external, or in between.
This section of the sutra records Ānanda’s further conceptualization after hearing the refutation of the "internal correspondence" [of consciousness].
All the four locations previously examined were established by Ānanda based on his own views; now he cites the Buddha’s past words.
Because it serves as the basis for devising schemes for others, it is said: "I have always heard the Buddha say... and so forth. "When the mind arises, phenomena arise;
when phenomena arise, the mind arises" means that the mind and phenomena arise in mutual dependence. The mind is the sixth consciousness, which grasps at objects;
phenomena are the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). It is due to the sixth consciousness grasping at external objects that those objects arise in accordance with the mind.

This means that because the mind arises, phenomena arise; furthermore, when the six external objects strike and stimulate the six internal consciousnesses, this means that because phenomena arise, the mind arises.
Thus it is said, "by means of the mind" and "by means of phenomena.

As for the term "various," it refers to the fact that both the mind and phenomena each possess immeasurable names and characteristics. From "I now" onwards, he correctly sets forth his calculation based on the preceding contemplation.

The term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers specifically to the sixth *pravṛtti-vijñāna* (active consciousness), because the sixth consciousness is preeminent in its function of deliberation (*manana*). Thus, what is here called "deliberation" (*cintā*) is essentially the act of deliberating.

Generally speaking, although the seventh and sixth consciousnesses differ in their respective supports—the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) for the former and the mental faculty (*manas*) for the latter—they both arise based upon the function of deliberation.
Therefore, when Ānanda identifies the essence of this deliberation as his own mind-nature, he is [identifying] the sixth...

The sixth [point] is that the mind which takes objects as its conditions is the mind itself. Following the place where it conjoins, it emerges from below; this refers to the locus upon which the mental factors depend.

It means that the mind has no fixed location, and it manifests whenever it encounters a conjunction. "Conjunction" means the mind conjoining with dharmas. Because it does not abide in one fixed place, it is said to "follow conjunction.
Because it follows conjunction, it is not restricted to the three locations of internal, external, or intermediate. Furthermore, in the passage below, the Buddha...
This refutation targets the *manas* (the faculty of thought) but does not refute the mind itself; it refutes only the points of conjunction.
By examining and refuting the seven locations—past and present—it merely refutes the locus upon which the mind relies. As the preceding text states: "One must know where the thief resides.
Readers should not forget this source.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "As for what you have just said... [up to] 'if it comes from outside, one should first see the face'—this section of the sutra is the World-Honored One’s fifth investigation and refutation regarding the point of conformity. From "The Buddha told" onwards, he restates the opponent's calculation;
from "is this mind" onwards, he formally refutes the notion of conformity. As for "conformity," it is defined as two objects fitting together like a box and its lid.
However, there must be a substance for there to be a conjunction; if there is no substance, then there are no characteristics—how could there be a conjunction?

Therefore it is said that "without substance, there is no conjunction. These two sentences constitute the direct refutation. The phrase "If there were no... and so forth serves to prevent a counter-argument.

The Buddha anticipates Ānanda’s counter-argument, namely: "Even though the mind lacks substance, it is still capable of conjunction. Thus, this follows from the preceding [point] regarding the absence of substance.
The *Tǐfáng* says: "If there were no substance yet it could still unite, then the nineteen realms would unite with the seven objects;
the realms would be the uniter and the objects would be the united. Since both the subject and object are empty, one speaks of 'nothing that can be united.
In the world, there are only eighteen realms and six objects; the [notion of] nineteen and seven is merely an empty name, for it is an attempt to unite emptiness with emptiness."

Since "emptiness and emptiness" cannot be joined, it is said that this interpretation is incorrect. If there is [existence], [the text] further relies on the absence of essence to successively refute the presence of essence;
"zhí" (挃) is pronounced "zhǐ" and means "to touch. "Touching" is equivalent to "joining," as can be understood from the text.
Ānanda said, "Seeing is the function of the eye; knowing is not the function of the eye... (up to) if one sees objects, how can it be called death?

This section of the sutra records that upon hearing the preceding statement regarding seeing the face, Ānanda—doubting that the mind knows while the eye sees—reproached the notion that the mind itself sees, arguing that this was not consistent with reason.
Ānanda said, "Seeing is the work of the eye; knowing is the work of the mind."
"Since the nature of this mind is fundamentally not the eye, why does the World-Honored One reprimand the mind for seeing? The Buddha said:
"In the world below, people have long seen that the mind returns to the eye; they claim the eye is composed of flesh and blood, like two apertures on the face resembling gateways.
The mind is the master of the one mind, and seeing proceeds from this master. If the master departs, how can the gateways remain?"
It is capable of seeing; therefore it is asked: "Are you inside the room? Can the door see? You are the master, the door is the room’s entrance;
you are likened to the mind, the room to the body, and the door to the eye—thus the five subsequent lines can be understood.
"Ānanda, as for this mind of yours that is aware and capable of cognition—does it pervade the entire body, or does it not pervade the entire body?
This section of the sutra further refutes the existence of a substantial entity (*sattva*) and clarifies in detail that its association with the body is not real.

While the preceding passage merely refuted the logical sense of 'association' regarding a substantial entity, the present passage directly refutes the existence of a substantial entity. The Buddha refutes this by means of four points."

This serves as a general heading for the detailed refutations that follow. In this current text, the first two instances of the term "body" (*ti*) refer to the essence of the mind (*xin-ti*), while the latter two instances of "body" refer to the physical body (*shen-ti*).
The former, the essence of the mind, is discussed in terms of unity and multiplicity; the latter, the physical body, is discussed in terms of pervasiveness and non-pervasiveness.
This can be understood from the text itself.
"If it were a single entity, then your hand [and so forth] up to your feet should be devoid of cognition; yet this is not the case for you.

This section of the sutra represents the World-Honored One’s refutation of the notion that the mind has a substantial entity (*ātman*), following his initial characterization by demonstrating that it is not the case in any of the four locations.
If [the mind] were a single entity, then it would pervade your entire body, just as if one part were injured... [the whole would feel it].
If all four limbs must experience pain simultaneously to be called a single entity, then if all four limbs are simultaneously stimulated, the point of stimulation would lack a fixed location;

that is, there would be no certain place where the sensation of being struck occurs. If the point of stimulation were fixed, yet there were places where it was felt and places where it was not, then your mind could not constitute a single entity.
[In the second part, he refutes the notion of multiple entities. The Buddha said: "A single person... [The text continues with the refutation of a plurality of minds.]
First, regarding the nature of awakening: if this mind were to have multiple bodies, it would constitute multiple persons;

if there were multiple persons, each would have their own separate body—then which of these bodies would be "you"? Now, since you certainly do not have multiple bodies, the multiplicity of this mind is likewise untenable.

If [the mind] were to pervade [the body], then when the lower three [senses] are destroyed, the mind pervading the body would be the same as the aforementioned refutation of a single body. Thus, it is refuted.
It is also said that if the mind pervades your entire body, there would be no place it does not pervade; thus, touching the head and touching the feet should both be mutually perceived.
If the head and feet possess consciousness while other parts do not, then the mind is not all-pervasive. The following four points refute the notion that the mind does not pervade the body:
if this mind did not pervade your body, then only the head and feet would have the capacity for cognition and sensation, while other parts would not.
If you claim it is not all-pervasive, yet when you touch your head and touch your feet, the perception is the same;

how can you say it is not all-pervasive? If you say this is not so because both the head and the feet possess cognition, then as explained above—that it is neither one nor many, neither all-pervasive nor non-all-pervasive—you must believe that this mind fundamentally has no substance.
Therefore, one should know that wherever there is conjunction, the mind likewise exists; it is impossible for it not to exist.
This section of the sutra concludes that the aforementioned instances of conjunction do not establish [the existence of a self].
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One... [up to] "...furthermore, if there is no seeing within, it must exist in between.

This section of the sutra records Ānanda’s shifting argumentation; having heard the refutation based on the principle of "conformity with the object," he again cites the Buddha's words to formulate a new position.
The passage beginning with "Ānanda" cites the Buddha's words as evidence. Regarding the term "Dharmaputra" (法王子), the translation of the name by Wenshu (Mañjuśrī) is as previously explained.
The King is the Buddha; the Buddha is the king of all dharmas because he has attained mastery over them.

A Bodhisattva is a son of the Dharma-king—this is a general designation for a Mahāsattva—and the term "and so forth" includes the multitude. Regarding those who discourse on the *dharmatā* (true aspect):
"true aspect" refers to the quiescent aspect of all dharmas, which is designated as the *dharmatā*. Whatever possesses [conventional] marks is not [the true aspect].
Taking non-characteristic as the characteristic is what is called the "true characteristic" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This is constantly discussed during both the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā periods;
because Ānanda was able to hear it, [the Buddha says] "as I... and so forth, which correctly turns back his calculation.

"Internally there is nothing seen," etc., is a reiteration of the previous error to bring out the reason why the calculation falls into the center: it is because one thinks the mind is located in the middle, and thus [is able to...]
Externally they recognize one another, yet internally there is no vision.

The Buddha said: "As for what you say regarding the 'middle,' within that middle you must certainly not be deluded... (up to) since the external forms are already intermingled, the mind should likewise be in a state of confusion."
This section of the sutra belongs to the sixth refutation of misconceptions by the World-Honored One.

The Buddha’s words below interrogate the location of this "middle" position, establishing two points for the sake of refutation. The Buddha asks: "In what you call the 'middle,' there must be a fixed location.
To say it has a fixed location means that its location is within the body; this is the point established by the Buddha. That it is located within the body refers to the physical frame.

Furthermore, regarding the "middle" (*madhya*) and "extremes" (*anta*), if one refutes the extremes, there is no middle; if the middle is identical to the internal, then when seeking the middle within the body, the middle has no location.
As for "place," it refers to the external location where the body resides. Moreover, regarding the distinction between the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*):

if one refutes the manifest by means of a planted pole used as a marker for the middle, then if there is no unmanifest, there is likewise no middle; if there is a manifest, then [the middle is] the manifest.
It cannot be fixed; the reason why it cannot be fixed is illustrated by this: suppose a person plants a pole as a marker. If one looks at it from the east, the marker is in the west;
if one views it from the south, the marker is in the north. The four directions lose their alignment, and there is no fixed location for the center.
Nevertheless, that which stands in the center reveals the locus upon which your mind relies. Now, since the substance of the marker is already indeterminate, your mind should likewise be so.
Since there is no mind within the state of confusion, one sinks away with it.
Ānanda said: "The 'middle' I speak of is not these two kinds [of states]; when consciousness arises therein, that is what constitutes the mind being present."
In this section, Ānanda refutes the notion that the "intermediate state" is neither body nor location, citing the Buddha’s own words to establish its true nature.

Formerly, when the World-Honored One was teaching within the vehicles of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), he spoke of how consciousness arises conditioned by the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*).
Relying on this, Ānanda erroneously calculated this to be the intermediate state; yet he failed to realize that this mind has no substantial essence apart from the organs.

Dust is likewise illusory; since both the producer and the produced are unobtainable, what therein could be real? Therefore, the Buddha below refutes this by means of both the inclusive and the non-inclusive.
He says: "The eye has discrimination, while the dust of form is without cognition. These two phrases distinguish that which has cognition from that which lacks it.
This is Ānanda’s false calculation that the eye possesses cognition while the dust of form lacks it, taking this "knowing" and "not knowing" as the basis for production.

Consciousness takes the state within meditative concentration as its condition; even so, it is certain that the eye itself lacks cognition. As the Buddha previously refuted in the preceding passage, saying, "When you are inside a room, can the door see?
one should follow the Buddha’s intention and accept this as true.

The Buddha said: "If your mind were in between the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*)," [and so on, until: "...then, being without a substantial nature, what characteristic could there be?
This section of the sutra uses the concepts of "inclusion" and "non-inclusion" to refute the reality of a middle position. From "The Buddha said" onwards, he generally indicates two points;
from "If it includes" onwards, he first refutes the inclusion of both, showing that there is no middle. From "The substance of things would be confused" onwards...

"Object" (*wu*) refers to the substance of the sense organs and their objects; "substance" (*ti*) refers to the substance of the mind. The previous line stated, "This substance of the mind is the substance of the substance of objects.

This definitively points back to the statement regarding the substance of the mind. The Buddha’s intention is that "objects" are without cognition, whereas the "substance of the mind" possesses cognition.
If so, how can knowing and not-knowing be confused and stand as opposing dualities? How could this be the Middle Way? It is necessary [to understand] the three [aspects].
The Dharma only permits the existence of the Middle Way; now, if these two [extremes] are established and one is lacking, then there is no Middle Way.

Furthermore, the failure to encompass both is next refuted as being likewise devoid of a Middle Way. Regarding the sentence "the failure to encompass both," the phrasing should have been inverted to say, "if it does not encompass both";
yet here it says, "if it does not encompass both the faculties and their objects, this mind has no substance, like empty space. Thus, it is one [extreme].
Since it is neither knowing nor not-knowing, how could empty space possess the meaning of knowing or not-knowing?
This mind is likewise so. Therefore, both "knowing" and "not-knowing" are non-existent as characteristics. When separated from the sense organs and their objects, the mind has no substantial nature;
within this, what characteristic could there be? Thus, one does not embrace both, nor is there a middle between them. If one seeks a middle in these two places, no such middle is found.
The location where the mind can be apprehended has also vanished.
Therefore, one should know that it cannot exist in the middle;
this section of the sutra concludes that the location of the mind within the center is untenable.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One... [up to] ...is this that which I call the 'unattached mind'?
This section of the sutra records Ānanda’s further deliberation after hearing the words regarding the "shattering" [of the mind].

When it says "the Buddha and four disciples together turned the Wheel of Dharma," this refers to the occasion during the *Prajñāpāramitā* assembly when the Buddha commanded the four venerable ones to turn the wheel.
The teaching for bodhisattvas is as explained in the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. At that time, the World-Honored One also said:
"The mind does not abide within, nor without, nor in between; it has no fixed location. This passage clarifies that the mind has no substantial reality.

The two phrases, "that which is called 'mind' is the non-attachment to all things," represent Ānanda’s erroneous interpretation of the Buddha's words; the Buddha certainly would not have said that there is nothing.
To take "non-attachment" as the mind is already an attachment; therefore, one must not cling to non-attachment as the mind.

However, what is called "non-attachment" means that the mind manifests in accordance with objects, such that wherever it contacts things, it is transparently clear and unattached—this is what is meant by non-attachment.
If one does not properly understand the mind in this regard, there will be endless errors hereafter.
The point where the text is refuted can be seen here. The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"As for your statement that the faculty of cognition and discernment [exists]... if there are characteristics, they must exist; how then can you say it is unattached?
This section of the sutra is the World-Honored One’s seventh inquiry and refutation concerning the location of the unattached mind. Thus spoke the Buddha.
Ānanda said: "If you maintain that the mind-nature capable of awakening and capable of discernment is entirely non-existent, this restates what you hold to be true.
"Non-existence" means being without attachment.

As for the term "all," it refers to everything in this world, from the void above down to the water and land below—those who fly are birds, those who walk are humans, beasts, and so forth. All such things...
"Phenomenal objects" collectively refers to the myriad phenomena arrayed before us; this is what is meant by "all.
When you say you do not cling to them, does this "all" of phenomenal objects exist or not? If it were non-existent, it would be the same as a tortoise's hair or a rabbit's horns—merely empty names;
why then trouble yourself with "non-clinging"? If there is a mind that does not cling, then it cannot be called "all."
That which is called "non-existence" is not non-existence in the sense that there is a characteristic to which one can cling; only then is it named "non-existence.

If one says it is "not non-existent," then "not non-existent" is itself a characteristic of existence. Since a characteristic of existence exists, there is clinging wherever it is. How, then, can you say there is non-clinging?
Therefore, one should know that it is impossible for the mind of non-attachment to be a conscious, cognizing mind.
This section concludes the Buddha’s refutation of non-attachment as being the mind. Thus ends the World-Honored One’s investigation of the seven locations where the mind might reside.
It must be noted that prior to this investigation of the mind, it was stated: "If you do not recognize and know the mind..."
Wherever the eyes are directed, one cannot subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*). Furthermore, it is said: "Where do the mind and the eyes currently reside?
Therefore, the sevenfold inquiry merely refutes their location; once the location is refuted, the thief has nowhere to flee.
The subsequent refutation of the "mind that can infer" is precisely the capture of the thief itself. However, the preceding inquiries into the location of the mind did not reach [the ultimate point].
Regarding the eighth [point], why is it that the first six do not persist while the seventh alone does? The *Changshui Shu* states:

"Although the calculations of ordinary minds differ in ten thousand ways, the basis upon which they rely does not exceed these seven. To investigate the substance of delusion, one must first destroy its basis;
this is like the enemy perishing when the city falls, or the eggs being destroyed when the nest collapses. These are words of profound insight.
At that time, Ānanda was among the great assembly... [until] ...he was so thirsting and yearning that he waited expectantly, desiring to hear the instructions.

This section of the sutra describes how Ānanda, because he had heard the sevenfold refutations of the false essence but had not yet reached the true source which is without dependence, rose from his seat once more and reverently requested the path of *śamatha*.
"Baring one shoulder and kneeling on the ground" is as described in the Confucian tradition.
The *Book of Rites* states: "The ruler bows twice with his head to the ground and bares his upper body, personally performing the carving; this is the height of reverence. It further states:

"Baring the upper body is the ultimate expression of service. Although those texts do not explicitly mention kneeling on the ground, it is likewise a ritual of bowing and service intended to demonstrate the sincerity of one's humility.
In all cases, the right side is specified because in antiquity, the right was considered the direction of order (*shun*), while the left was considered the direction of opposition (*ni*).
Therefore, "left" is used for demotion and "leftward paths" (left-deviant ways), as both signify a contrary intention; thus, "right" is employed.

Joining the palms is the ritual of reverent devotion in Zhugan (India), intended to convey the meaning of binding and collecting the body and mind. At that time, [the text] proceeds to address the Buddha, stating:
"This is the discourse of the assembled family," which describes the protocol of Ānanda’s request for the Dharma. From "I am... onwards, this is Ānanda’s own narration. Thus...
Regarding the phrase "relying on pride and affection," Ānanda, having withdrawn from his worldly sentiments, spoke thus out of a spontaneous emotional response.

As for the "youngest brother," because Ānanda was the youngest among the eight royal brothers, he was moved by the Buddha’s compassionate love in delivering him and causing him to leave the household life.
"Pride and affection" refers to what the Buddha said; "pride" (*jiao*) here carries the sense of "affection" (*lian*), meaning that [the Buddha] both took pride in and felt affection for him.
The Buddha’s compassionate love for him was such that, though he had now left the household life, he still relied upon that compassion;

thus, he long indulged in extensive learning without yet attaining the outflows-free state (*anāsrava*). Consequently, he could not subdue the evil incantation and was turned by it, falling into a house of prostitution.
This must have been due to the final phrase [of his question]: "Ānanda has emerged again to pursue the delusive. Therefore, that which is the True Limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) is...
This is the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the eternally abiding true mind. To proceed toward this is the meaning of "practice," while not knowing it is the meaning of "delusion.
Ānanda said to himself: "What fault caused me to initially drown in lust? It must have been because I was deluded regarding that true creation;
by pursuing the false and turning my back on awakening to unite with the dust of the senses, I invited such calamity as this. Now I seek to turn back from the false and return to the true."
This is why I previously requested the path of *śamatha*. I only pray that you will descend and truly seek it;

for the three meanings of *śamatha* and so forth constitute the path to the eternally abiding true mind. Now, I mention only *śamatha* because, in the sequential order, *śamatha* is taken as the beginning.
As for the previous explanation, it states that the practice begins from the initial "seven investigations," which is precisely *śamatha*. Now...
Question: Why does the text merely request the path? Answer: Although the sevenfold inquiry in the preceding section is called *śamatha*, it is actually a preliminary expedient for *śamatha*.
This is because the seven successive inquiries and refutations merely refute the location of the mind, which is like clearing a path at a fork in the road.
Only after the subsequent refutation of the "capable inferrer" (*nirūpaka*) does one enter the true path; the departure begins here.
Therefore, I now request the path for them. *Icchantika* is an abbreviated form of a Sanskrit term; in full it is called *icchantiko nirvāṇa*.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that *icchan* means "faith" and *tika* means "not possessing.
Thus, "not possessing" is a translated term referring to those who have severed their roots of goodness. *Huimiliche* (隳彌戾車): *huī* means "to destroy"; *mleccha* is a Sanskrit term translated as...
Sunk in evil views, they cling to existence or give rise to the sixty-two views; all these are termed "evil views.
Ānanda requested instruction on *śamatha* so that those clinging to evil views, upon hearing it, might destroy their evil and proceed toward the right path.
Thus, this "tilting downward" refers to tilting the mind downward; "thirst" is spoken of by way of metaphor, like one parched with thirst who longs for sweet water.

"Lù" (exposed) means to look up with the head raised; "zhù" (to stand) means to remain standing for a long time. This refers to looking upward while standing for a long duration, as if waiting for something, in the hope of receiving instruction.
At that time, the World-Honored One [from his face]... [until] all remained in their respective lands, joining their palms and listening attentively.

In this section of the sutra, the Buddha, intending to eradicate the thieves of the mind and unfold the correct orientation, first employs the metaphor of an elephant to indicate his fundamental clarity.
Regarding the "light from the face-gate," this refers to the simultaneous emission of light from the mouth, eyes, ears, nose, and the space between the eyebrows.

This signifies the breaking of the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) to reveal the six profound, perfect luminosities. As for the various kinds of light: [it represents the diverse manifestations of wisdom].
This means that because the light is not of a single substance but possesses the colors of a hundred jewels, it arises from within the pure *dharmakāya* and cannot be compared to worldly light;
thus, even the combined light of a hundred thousand suns only resembles a small fraction of it.
What was previously called "emitting light" is here followed by "shaking the earth," meaning that throughout the entire Buddha-world, the earth quakes in six ways. This refers to the totality.

Because all Buddha-fields throughout the entirety of space were shaken, there were six types of shaking: namely, moving (*calana*), surging (*prācalana*), trembling (*sampracalana*), rising (*kṣubhita*), roaring (*raṇita*), and crashing (*pra-raṇita*).
To sway and be unsettled is called "moving. To be undulating with convexities and concavities is called "surging. To have a deep, rumbling sound is called "trembling.
To rise from below upward is called "rising. To emit a crashing resonance is called "roaring. For various forms and characteristics to strike against one another is called "crashing. Universally...

"Movement is itself equality and pervasiveness," meaning that each possesses the three characteristics; this indicates that the six consciousnesses function simultaneously and all eighteen realms are entirely equal.
"Thus, below, the dust of the ten directions" refers to the aforementioned phrase "the worlds of all Buddhas";

therefore, it says "thus, at one time, they open and appear. This intends to clarify that when in a state of delusion, the six consciousnesses obstruct and conceal [the truth] regarding self and other.

Myself and others were obstructed by different regions and various hindrances, remaining stagnant and unable to pass through; now awakened, the six faculties have become vast and unobstructed, and the ten directions manifest all at once.

Regarding "the Buddha’s majesty unifying [all]": if explained according to the phenomenal aspect, the Buddha uses the Dharma-transformation and his majestic spiritual power to cause the lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, to merge into one; if explained according to the mental aspect, it is due to the wisdom of original enlightenment.
By means of power, the eighteen realms are fused into a single nature.

Within these worlds—referring downward from the above—the Bodhisattvas who are cause-conditions among the dust-motes of all Buddhas do not turn away from the false, but rely instead on the opening of true hearing.

Since all are subsumed within the cause of self-nature awakening, when one views and hears at the primordial limit (*koṭi*), how could there be any further change? Therefore, it is said: "Each abides in its own source."
The state depends on listening. In this sutra, every instance where light is emitted and signs are manifested constitutes a pivotal juncture.

While the preceding seven omens served to refute the mind, the present point is precisely for the decisive eradication of the enemy; as this marks the initial stage of the Three Contemplations, light is first emitted, followed by the presentation of the two sections.
Once these have been established, the subsequent refutation proceeds to push back the source of the opponent's arguments, tracing the rise and fall of their positions.
"You may not know this.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "All sentient beings... even if they were to pass through kalpas as numerous as atoms, they would ultimately never be able to attain it.
This section of the sutra, in which the World-Honored One responds to Śāma’s request, first clarifies that sentient beings are driven by karma.
To cultivate according to the categories into which one has fallen is not yet true. Various forms of perversion (*viparyāsa*) are like reversing head and tail;

they are called "perversion" because they are necessarily inverted. Because all sentient beings oppose the truth, pursue the delusive, abandon the root, and head toward the branches, they are termed "perverted.
However, these perversions have immeasurable names; to speak briefly, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) possess four of them.
Perversion (*viparyāsa*) refers to reckoning the impermanent as permanent, the unsatisfactory as satisfactory, the non-self as self, and the impure as pure.

The followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayānika*) likewise possess these four perversions, reckoning the impermanent as permanent, the unsatisfactory as satisfactory, the non-self as self, and the impure as pure.
Combined with the preceding [four], these are called the eight perversions of the ordinary and the small-vehicle practitioners. They are subsumed within both the mundane and the supramundane.
Because of the perversion of cognition, it is said that all various [phenomena] arise based on karmic seeds. There are three types of karmic seeds, namely:

afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering (*duḥkha*). All causes of karma and fruits of suffering arise from these; just as beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*) perfumes [the mind] to produce various [results], there must be seeds for the mutual production of cause and fruit.
Since the seeing of these seeds is not severed, they are called "karmic seeds. As it is said:
The "akṣa-cluster" (akṣa-puṭa) is a metaphor for a certain tree in the Western Regions that bears three fruits on each branch;

because these fruits must grow together on the same stalk, it is called an akṣa-cluster. This serves as a metaphor for the delusions, karma, and suffering of sentient beings, which must likewise coalesce.
"Delusion" refers to ignorance; based on delusion one creates karma, and through karma one experiences suffering. Because these arise in mutual dependence, they are said to be a "coalescence. This...
This refers to ordinary beings who do not practice; it means that even those practitioners who fail to attain the correct path cannot achieve unsurpassed *bodhi*.
Furthermore, "down to" (*zhì*) indicates the characteristics of those who practice but do not attain correctness;
"down to" is used here because it excludes the various humans, immortals, and spirits, and thus says "down to," which is equivalent to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Although such people are said to be compliant with the correct [path], they do not delight in superior progress but merely preserve minor fruits;
therefore, they are also disparaged as "separately accomplished" (bie cheng), which is precisely what is not correct.

All those among the various non-Buddhist paths (tīrthikas), the gods of the three realms, and even the Māra kings and their subjects, are entirely of false causes, false fruits, false karma, and false retributions. In Sanskrit, *māra* is translated as [the one who]...
They can snatch away life because they venerate the heterodox and loathe the orthodox, thereby creating the conditions for the snatching of life; thus they are called *māra*.
As for those called "non-Buddhists" (*bāhyaka*), it means their minds wander outside the Path and they do not practice with correct cultivation; thus they are called non-Buddhists.

All emerge from the lower realms; their calculations are based on heterodox delusion, meaning that practitioners fail to distinguish between the real and the false, resulting in confusion and wandering into divergent destinies.
All these arise from not knowing the two kinds of roots; failing to know them leads to delusion, and based on this delusive cause, one practices erroneously and in confusion.
As for the two roots, one is true and one is false, as will be clarified in the following text.

To illustrate the meaning of practicing erroneously and achieving no merit, the text employs metaphors: the metaphor of boiling sand illustrates erroneous practice, while the metaphor of a fine banquet illustrates the sublime.

The "wondrous fruit" refers to unsurpassed bodhi; that one does not obtain its nourishment even after passing through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is because sand is not rice by nature.
This serves as a metaphor for those who do not understand the two fundamental natures of truth and delusion, yet based on this, practice erroneously while hoping to attain unsurpassed bodhi;
even if they pass through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it will ultimately be unattainable.
"What are the two kinds, Ānanda? [The text continues] "...and thus, unaware of themselves, they enter erroneously into the various realms of existence.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding inquiry to explain the two roots, clarifying the delusion of abandoning the true and pursuing the false.
The phrase "What are... constitutes the inquiry; the passage beginning with "The first" is the explanation. Within the explanation, the root of delusion is clarified first.

"Then you [should know]"—this points to its characteristic, meaning that this deluded root is precisely what you now take to be the nature of the攀緣心 (pān-yuán-xīn, the攀缘心, the mind that grasps at objects).
The word "this" (者) refers to the root of birth and death; since it is in dependence upon this that beginningless birth and death exist, it is called the "root of birth and death.
Because everyone clings to this as being the mind, it is also referred to as "sentient beings" (眾生, zhòngshēng).

Regarding the statement that the "mind which grasps objects" refers to the sixth consciousness, this is because it grasps the six sense-objects moment by moment, taking the reflected images of those six objects as its own nature.
Second, the subsequent passage clarifies the true source;
the phrase "it is you" points to its characteristic, meaning that this true source is precisely the beginningless essence of Bodhi, Nirvana, and primordial purity.

However, this true essence does not exist elsewhere; it is precisely this fundamental clarity of the consciousness-essence (*vijñāna-sūkṣma-prakṛti*) within you now, which is capable of giving rise to all conditions.
Yet, all sentient beings mistake these conditions for reality and lose the truth; that which they thus neglect is exactly this.

"The fundamental clarity of the consciousness-essence" refers to the eighth consciousness as the essence of consciousness. "Essence" is spoken of in contrast to the "coarse," for the preceding six consciousnesses are coarse and superficial. Only...

The eighth fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is the quintessential source of all consciousnesses. This "original luminosity" (*yuanming*) refers to the state where the eighth consciousness is profoundly still and unshakable;

this is precisely that original luminosity. The various masters of Changshui, following the *Awakening of Faith*, interpret this original luminosity as referring to the meaning of "enlightenment and non-enlightenment.

However, according to my humble opinion, based on the second scripture, the "quintessential source of the seeing-clarity" (*jianjing mingyuan*), that "luminous quintessence" (*mingyuan*) is precisely [this original luminosity].
This is the primordial luminosity (*ādi-prakāśa*). Taken together, it is the single essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-ghana*); analyzed separately, it becomes the six profound, perfect luminosities.
Therefore, there is no need to treat this as the "Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha-satya*), as is seen in detail in the tenth section on the "aggregate of consciousness" (*vijñāna-skandha*).

Furthermore, according to the tenth fascicle of the Sūtra: "Because this profound state is not true, it is perfumed moment by moment; therefore, it is said to be able to give rise to all [phenomena]."

The meaning of "conditioned by these conditions" refers to the preceding seven consciousnesses; because they recognize conditions and thereby lose the truth, it is said that "that which is lost due to conditions.
The character "that" (者) points to the fundamentally pure essence of Bodhi and Nirvana.

To take the seven consciousnesses as conditions means, according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, the sense of "relying on those and taking those as objects": externally, they condition sensory objects (*viṣaya*); internally, they condition...

Because it is the mind, it is called the "condition. As for all sentient beings, they have neglected this original luminosity. This "original luminosity" refers to what is spoken of as bodhi and nirvana;
it means the luminosity inherently possessed by every person. Although everyone neglects this original luminosity, even while speaking of such neglect, in reality it has not been lost.
One carries it all day long while walking about, yet the deluded do not perceive it; therefore, it is said that "although [they carry it] until the end..."
The sun moves on without one’s own awareness, yet one exhausts oneself in vain; entering and exiting the various realms of existence (*gati*) is merely this very state.
The term "vainly" (*wang*) means that one enters what one ought not to enter. The underlying intent is this:

if one were to awaken to fundamental luminosity, one would attain Buddhahood immediately—why then do you humiliate yourself by vainly entering the various realms? Furthermore, regarding *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*: *bodhi* is original enlightenment (*benjue*). *Nirvāṇa*... [text fragment ends]

Non-abiding is movement. The Buddha said, "It is so. World-Honored One, seeing that he did not yet realize this, [the Bodhisattva] for the time being granted him permission, because the meaning of his discrimination regarding movement and non-movement was not in error; thus he said, "It is so," in general.
The reprimand for his subsequent delusion can be seen in the following passage.
From the phrase "The Tathāgata, thereupon, from the wheel-marked palms... up to "...who is it that causes the shaking?"—the Buddha said, "It is thus.
This section of the sutra describes how the World-Honored One again sent forth light from both his left and right sides to examine whether Ānanda was moving or not.
From the outside toward the inside: the "wheels and palms" refers to the five wheels and palms; the flying light reaching its left and right is precisely for Ānanda to move his head.
Then the Buddha asks: "For what reason did you move your head? Ānanda also answers truthfully. The Buddha says:
"Ānanda, look down [at your own head] to carefully examine the meaning of movement and non-movement. Ānanda also...

Answer: When the head moves, the vision does not move. The Buddha said: "Even if one were to temporarily grant this [distinction], it confirms that the meaning of the movement and non-movement of discrimination is not in error.
Thus, he generally rebukes his delusion; this is also seen in the following passage.
Regarding the first of these two sections, the Buddha’s hand opening and closing constitutes Ānanda’s external object (*bāhyaviṣaya*), because it is an external object.

By comparing the seeing with the movement—or lack thereof—of the body, we shall now test whether the flying light is moving. Head after head, Ānanda’s own internal body is the object of this comparison.
Furthermore, by comparing the seeing with the movement—or lack thereof—of the external objects and the internal body, we shall proceed from the distant to the intimate;
from the external to the internal, we shall examine the meaning of movement and non-movement, ensuring that Ānanda clearly understands which is actually moving.
"Who is it that is immovable?"—only after posing this question does he then reprimand him for his error. In this way, Ānanda will easily understand and submit his mind with conviction.
Although Ānanda has now awakened to the fact that the nature of seeing is immovable, he still clings to a location as being real;
this is truly because he has mistakenly identified the discerning vision of conditioned objects as the immovable nature. Indeed, this discernment of conditioned objects is...
It is not that one does not know the quiescence of the faculties and their objects because they are unmoving;
rather, movement and stillness arise from the mind, such that this very discrimination is entirely adventitious dust (*āgantuka-rajas*). This is the point intended by the subsequent criticism.
Furthermore, the statement in the second fascicle regarding "delusion within awakening" specifically refers to those who mistakenly identify with this [state]. Students must not forget this source.
"Then the Tathāgata addressed the great assembly... [until] 'within this cycle of rebirth, they themselves undergo transmigration.

This section of the sutra records the World-Honored One’s summary of the two preceding meanings regarding adventitious dust and Ānanda’s observations on the movement or stillness of the faculties and objects, collectively censuring him for the errors of his discriminative mind.
The words "Then" (*yúshì*) below introduce the Buddha’s narration.
Regarding the two meanings of "guest-dust," observe the following: you have described the meaning of Ānanda’s head moving, and you have also described the meaning of your hand opening and closing;
yet you speak of neither contracting nor expanding, and thus neither movement nor stillness. The passage beginning with "How can it be...
is precisely the general reprimand, stating that Ānanda follows external objects to give rise to the mind, and as guest-dust arises and ceases, he loses the true nature. He takes movement as...

"The body" refers to the head; since the movement of the head is itself the body, to take movement as the object is to take the opening and closing of the hands—the external objects of Ānanda—as such.

The intent of these two sentences is to rebuke Ānanda for failing to understand that it is the mind’s own discrimination that constitutes movement, yet instead taking movement to be the objective realm of the body.
From "From the beginning... onwards, [the text] directly reproaches him for [this error] arising from adventitious dust.
The Master’s intention in saying "extinguish" was to address your attachment to the body and objects as being in motion.
Even if the internal mind does not arise and external objects are tranquil, what movement or stillness could there be? For movement and stillness exist only through the mind's discrimination.
As the Sixth Patriarch said: "It is not the wind or the banner that moves; it is your own mind that moves. This is precisely what he meant. He then pointed his hand and opened [his palm].
From the joining of the fingers to the movement of the fingertips, all are thoughts of arising and ceasing; how could these be anything other than adventitious afflictions?
The passage below, beginning with "to lose," rebukes this for abandoning the True and pursuing the False.

Since the True Nature is precisely that which is non-arising and non-ceasing, to now discard the non-arising and non-ceasing while pursuing various states of arising and ceasing—how could this be anything other than perversion? Therefore, it is said: "One's actions are perverted, yet one seeks the nature of the mind."
The last two phrases mean: because you are deluded, you have lost the true essence of the nature-mind;
you instead take the objects manifested within the wondrous mind to be yourself, chasing after various states of arising and ceasing and transmigrating within this illusory self.
It is neither given by Heaven nor given by humans, but is taken up through your own volition as you flow and turn. The word "objects" (物) refers to the second fascicle.
All intermediate forms, mind, various conditions, and the mental factors that drive them are precisely the objects manifested by the wondrous mind.

*The Direct Explanation of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas*, Scroll One.

Direct Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra: The Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization by the Tathāgata of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas. Fascicle Two.
Written by the junior monk Guangmo of Yunqi Monastery in Ancient Hangzhou. Direct Commentary.
Verified by the lay follower Tongxi Yan Xueyi.
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly [up to] attained the two natures of luminosity: the non-arising and the non-ceasing.
This section concludes the compiler’s summary of what Ānanda and the others contemplated and aspired for within their mental ground (*manobhūmi*).
Regarding the phrase "At that time" and below, which describes Ānanda and the others receiving benefits from hearing the Dharma and being instructed, there are two interpretations:

if taken in a broad sense, it refers generally back to the first fascicle and all preceding passages that elucidated the meaning of mind and vision, collectively termed "instruction"; if taken in a narrow sense...
This refers to what was previously heard regarding the two meanings of "guest" and "dust," as well as the general reproaches and other words used as instructions.

By hearing the meaning of whether the faculties and objects are moving or unmoving, one attains liberation from the bonds of mind and views; because of this liberation from bondage, body and mind become peaceful and secure.
The passage beginning with "I reflect upon the beginningless... describes the thoughts within the mental ground of Ānanda and others; these thoughts belong to the domain of the mind.
"Regretful reflection" means regretting that from time immemorial one has lost the true and followed the delusory, thereby losing the single phrase of the original mind;

this directly follows the previous meaning of having lost the true nature. Because one attains awakening through the Buddha’s comprehensive reprimand, [the text says] "discriminating reflections based on objects":
discriminating based on objects is precisely the meaning previously explained as discriminating between the faculties and their objects, whether they are active or inactive.
All these are merely the mental ground vainly receiving the shadows of conditions from the six sense objects, taking conceptual discrimination as their actual substance.
Because they have lost the true nature that is neither arising nor ceasing, and instead pursue various states of arising and ceasing as their own mind, they are called "vain recognition.
Today's word should be read in conjunction with the preceding word "beginningless," meaning that one has been mired in delusion from the beginningless past until this very day.
Having finally attained awakening, he established a metaphor to clarify his sense of self-congratulation, saying:
"It is like an infant who has lost its mother's milk and whose hunger is nearly fatal, yet suddenly encounters a compassionate mother and immediately attains fullness and satiety.

The phrase "losing the milk, hunger nearly fatal" is a metaphor for how, from time immemorial, one was mired in delusion and nearly lost one's life of wisdom (*jñāna-jīvita*). The phrase "encountering the compassionate mother and attaining fullness and satiety" is a metaphor for [the attainment of awakening].

Today, having heard these instructions and thereby attained awakening and increased benefit in the factors of the Path, I join my palms below to describe the aspirations in the minds of Ānanda and the others.
As for those who join their palms and prostrate to the Buddha:
when Ānanda formed this thought, he rejoiced within himself and, with sincere devotion, touched his feet; in his heart, he further made this vow: "May the Tathāgata now..."
This reveals to us which aspects of body and mind are illusory and which are real;

it reveals that the illusory aspect is characterized by arising and ceasing, while the real aspect is characterized by non-arising and non-ceasing. Second, regarding the phrase "manifesting the nature":

one should carefully contemplate these two characters, "manifesting" (fāngxiàn), as having the meaning of bringing forth and revealing from the standpoint of principle (*li*). This refers to the True [Nature].
Within the nature and principle (*xingli*), there is inherently that which is neither born nor extinguished; what is manifested and revealed from this is the nature itself.

This refers to such phenomena as "the one becoming the immeasurable and the immeasurable becoming the one," and "the small appearing within the large and the large appearing within the small. Furthermore, regarding the nature manifested and revealed from the principle of deluded luminosity:
it is as when the dull darkness becomes emptiness, and within that dark emptiness, the coagulation of darkness forms matter (*rūpa*).
"Form is a mixture of deluded thoughts; the characteristics of thought constitute the body," and so forth—this is what some people say.

If one examines this by taking the two characters "reveal" (fāngmíng) as the primary meaning, then these two characters are merely words; the textual principle [of the passage] would become superficial.

One must know that the two characters "manifest" (xiǎnchū) carry the sense of "revealing. They should be read as a single breath [with the following text]; how could there be two separate meanings of "revealing"?
Those who lack knowledge of these grammatical conventions may discern this further; moreover, this section consists of the words of the compiler and is not the speech of Ānanda.
At that time, King Prasenajit rose and addressed the Buddha, [saying] down to: "All those with outflows (āsrava) all wish to hear it."
In this section of the sutra, King Ajātaśatru, upon hearing such words as "moment by moment arising and ceasing," realized that there exists a nature of non-arising and non-ceasing;
he thus understood his former errors and requested the truth of the present. In the passage beginning with "I formerly," he first recounts his past mistakes.

"Commands" (敕) refers to teachings; "not having yet received the instructions" means before he had taken refuge in the Buddha, when he previously encountered the doctrines taught by non-Buddhist teachers. All [of these]...
To claim that the name "annihilation" (uccheda) refers to *nirvāṇa* was incorrect from the outset.
Kātyāyana and Pūraṇa Kāśyapa were two heterodox teachers; among the six heterodox masters, the names appearing here are those of the third and fifth.
Kātyāyana is fully called Kālakauṭya-Kātyāyana; "Kālakauṭya" is...
The name is translated as "Ox-Neck" (Gośṛṅga) and the clan name as "Kātyāyana. In the customs of Western India, the personal name comes first followed by the clan name;

therefore, they are combined as "Ox-Neck Kātyāyana. This likely refers to him because he was among the class of ascetic non-Buddhists who practiced such austerities as plucking out their hair and fumigating their noses.
His doctrine that all phenomena possess both characteristics and lack characteristics constitutes the sixth [view].
The sixth teacher among those [six] is Pūraṇa Kāśyapa. "Kāśyapa" is a name-translation meaning "Rightly Victorious" (Saṃjaya);
"Pūraṇa" is the mother's name, translated as "Not-Making" (Akaraṇa). He is named after his mother, and thus the name refers to himself.
His doctrine maintains that the Path does not require seeking completeness; rather, one must undergo the suffering of kalpas of birth and death.
One who exhausts [all things] naturally attains the Way; this is the third of the six teachers.

Although the current text mentions only two names, the Buddha’s response further cites Makkhali Gosāla; thus, we know that the account provided by King Ajātaśatru encompasses the teachings of all six teachers.
When it says, "They all say that after death there is annihilation," the meaning of the word "all" (咸) refers comprehensively to the six teachers; therefore, they are referred to as "all."
Since both [views] belong to the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), they designate "nirvāṇa" by means of the term "annihilation. The terminology has been explained previously.

Generally speaking, in India (Zhugan), any claim of having attained the Way—without distinguishing between heterodox and orthodox—is termed "nirvāṇa. However, among those who practice the paths of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), there are actually none who attain nirvāṇa;
they each merely falsely conceptualize it as such. King Bimbisāra himself recounted his previous encounters with the six teachers.
What has been explained is as follows: although one now encounters the Buddha, the mind still harbors doubt regarding this encounter.

This is because external appearances have not been fully exhausted and one has not yet attained the Buddha’s mind; thus, one remains in a state of doubt. "Doubt" (*huxi*) is so called because *hu* is the name of a beast whose nature is to be full of suspicion;
since human doubt resembles that of the fox, it is termed "fox-doubt. How is it that [the following] constitutes the formal request for the present meaning? Previously, already...
"It is not that this is necessarily so now. King Pāyāsi asked: "Even though one has heard the teaching on non-arising and non-ceasing, how can it be manifested and its reality realized?

Furthermore, he pointed out that all those among the great assembly who are still subject to outflows (sāsrava) were included in the request, while those who are free from outflows (anāsrava) were excluded from the count.
The King’s intention was that he knew those who had realized the state of being free from outflows had already attained non-arising and non-ceasing.
Because those who possess outflows (*sāsrava*) still abide within birth and death and have not yet realized the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing, [the Buddha] addressed them as well.
The Buddha said to the Great King: "Your body exists now... (until) my present body will ultimately undergo transformation and perish."

In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One, intending to explain to King Ajātaśatru the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing, first poses a counter-question regarding the body subject to arising and ceasing.
The Buddha’s intention is to lead the king to discern for himself that it is easier to realize the non-arising and non-ceasing within the very process of arising and ceasing.
For how could a body of flesh and blood—like a wick being consumed by fire—possibly endure for long?
"Vajra is eternally abiding and indestructible" refers to the *dharmakāya*. "Vajra" is a metaphor for the most firm and sharp jewel in the world;
because it is firm and enduring, it does not shift, and is thus called "eternally abiding. This metaphor illustrates that the *dharmakāya* is eternally abiding and indestructible.
Now, the World-Honored One points directly to his own physical body and asks whether it is destructible or indestructible, thereby causing [the audience] to discern for themselves.
This is because it is easy to realize that the body is impermanent. When the World-Honored One [asked this], King Ajātaśatru replied, "This body must inevitably perish.
The Buddha said, "Great King, you have never before brought about its extinction; yet you know for certain that this body shall eventually reach total destruction."
This section of the sutra follows upon the Blessed One’s previous statement that the physical body must inevitably perish, thereby clarifying that cessation occurs through a gradual process.
The words "The Buddha asked" are for reference; "The World-Honored One" introduces the King’s response.
