The first two phrases follow the Buddha’s question, while from "I observe" onwards, the King answers by explaining the reason for arising and ceasing. The phrase "moment by moment, ever new" means that for a person—
The thoughts that arise in the present do not cease for even a moment; every thought manifests in contrast with its successor.

To speak of "new" in contrast to "old," it is said that when a thought first arises, it is new, and as it is about to perish, it becomes old. This means that the preceding thought has already become old and gives rise to the succeeding thought, which becomes new.
Subsequently, this [new] thought in turn becomes the predecessor and the former becomes old. Thus, the succeeding thought impels the preceding thought toward cessation.
The preceding thought draws forth the succeeding thought, causing it to arise; yet while each thought remains as it was, every moment is renewed.
Like waves that follow one another without overstepping their sequence and without interruption, the arising and ceasing of thoughts cause the body to pass away.
Just as a burning fire gradually turns to ash, this process of decay and dissolution continues without rest until it reaches total extinction; the physical body is likewise so.
"There is nothing that can be retained; 'perishing' means the physical form has passed away.
The Buddha said, "It is thus, Great King: how can your present age be compared to the time of your full vigor?"
In this section of the sutra, the Buddha poses questions based on the categories of old and young, while King Nimi answers according to the three stages of youth, middle age, and old age.
First, the two characters "thus" (*evam*) serve as a seal of confirmation that the preceding meaning—that every moment is ever-new—is indeed true.
Since the term "age of birth" (*jāti-vaya*) refers to the year of one's birth, the Buddha addresses the king, asking: "Your Majesty, you are in the stage of decline."
"Comparing his age and appearance now with those of his time as a youth, how are they? This question concerns the two periods of youth and old age;

it was answered by the World-Honored One through King Ajātaśatru. "A child" (*hai-ru*) is a general term for the very young; one whose seven emotions have not yet been stirred is called a "child," meaning a toddler.
Because it refers collectively to the period of youth, "child" and "toddler" are used in conjunction. "Skin" (*fū*) refers to the integument.
"Qì" (腠) refers to the same meaning as "moisture and glossiness" in the skin's texture (*fànlǐ*).
The answer states that during childhood, the skin and texture are nourished, moist, and glossy, and the flesh and blood are tender; this describes the physical characteristics of youth.

Regarding the two subsequent lines, "growing" (*zhǎng*) means becoming tall and large, and "establishing" (*chéng*) means reaching maturity; this answers the description of the physique during adulthood. Blood... [text fragment].

Because the vital energy (*qi*) is full and substantial, one is capable of accomplishing various affairs; thus it is called "long fingers," which refers to the physical characteristics of the prime of life.
Now, the following six phrases answer [the question regarding] old age. "Tailing" (*tuílíng*): *tuí* means to decline or collapse;

as the sun sets behind the mulberry trees, the physical form and years gradually incline—this general term for old age is called "tailing. "Pacing" (*pò*) means to be pressed or constrained, referring to the vital energy... [text fragmentary].

When the pulse is feeble and rapid without a state of relaxation, it is called "oppressed" (*pò*). Furthermore, the *Liji* states: "At fifty, one begins to decline; at eighty and ninety, one is called 'demented' (*mào*).
King Anathapiṇḍika was already sixty-two years old, which is extremely close to the time of such decline and senility.

Regarding his appearance, it is said to be withered and emaciated; regarding his spirit, it is said to be dark and obscured. This "withered and emaciated" refers, in essence, to the depletion of his blood and vital energy (*qi*).
"Kū" (withered) means parched; "cuì" (haggard) means emaciated. This refers to how when the blood and qi are parched, the physical appearance becomes haggard.

"Jīng" (essence) refers to the refined essence, and "shén" (spirit) refers to the spiritual intelligence. Because both the refined essence and spiritual intelligence have completely vanished, it is called "obscure and dim.
Furthermore, "kū" (withered) and "cuì" (refined) are contrasted with the preceding "rùnzé" (moist and lustrous) to show that the states of old age and youth differ in this way.
When the blood and qi decline, the hair turns white; when the pores and skin-folds become sparse, the face wrinkles—these are all signs of old age.

"Dai jiang bu jiu zhe" (reaching that which will not be long) means "dai" (to reach) refers to "jiang" (approaching); it signifies that his physical form is close to death and will not endure for long.

The final sentence summarizes the meaning of the preceding questions. The character "jian" (see/observe) in this context refers to the Buddha’s own state; that is, the Buddha [perceived] King Lao [as being near death].
Because he was compared to [the Buddha] when young, it is said: "How can one compare them? As for the saying, "Seeing him cherished and seeing him abandoned, the intent is the same," the Buddha said:
"Great King, from your physical appearance... (omitted)... therefore know that my body will ultimately undergo transformation and extinction."

In this section of the sutra, the Buddha questions King Nimi regarding the gradual transformation of the physical form, intending for the king to explain it himself so that he might easily attain awakening.
Since the body does not decay instantaneously, "not instantaneous" implies "gradual. Regarding this question on gradual decay, King Nimi’s response consists of five stages:
first, in terms of ten-year periods; second, in terms of annual changes; third, in terms of monthly transformations; fourth... [text continues].
"Approximately by the day, five [units] shift; approximately by the *kṣaṇa*, every thought-moment gradually decays"—this is the answer.

"The King said... and below is King Ajātaśatru’s reply. The first four lines first express humility and provide a general response. "Subtle transformation and secret shifting" generally encompasses the meaning of the five layers of gradual change that follow.
"Transformation" (*pariṇāma*) refers to the sense of passing away; "secret shifting" (*guhyasaṃcāra*) means that the shifting occurs within every thought-moment, remaining hidden.
Because it is difficult to perceive, it is called "esoteric. My statement that I do not truly realize this is indeed a humble expression.
Regarding "cold and heat," this refers to the beginning and end of a year; when cold comes, heat departs.

This is explained according to their broad characteristics, meaning that year after year and day after day, the flow does not cease and one gradually reaches old age—this term points specifically to the time of being old. Why?

The following serves as a corroborative explanation of the meaning of the preceding passage regarding the gradual progression of transmigration. First, the argument proceeds from the narrow to the broad, beginning with a period of ten years:
at the age of twenty, although one is called young, one’s countenance is already aged compared to that at the age of ten;
this is a comparison of old and young based on the contrast between twenty and ten years. Furthermore, by three... [text continues].
"Comparing ten times, twenty times, and even up to sixty times with King Nimi—since at that time [the Buddha] was already sixty-two years of age, it is said he stopped here.
This is based on a comparison made every ten years; by the time of the sixty-year mark, the decline of the fifty-year stage can be known.
'World-Honored One, I have seen' concludes the preceding discourse on the ten years."

Furthermore, next, one proceeds from the broad to the narrow: beginning with the breadth of the preceding ten years, it gradually narrows until reaching the extreme narrowness of every single thought-moment (*kṣaṇa*).
Twelve years constitute a *yuga* (a cycle); this refers to the periods of ten and twenty years.
Next, [the scale] narrows to annual changes, then to monthly transformations, and finally to daily shifts; the gradual progression of these meanings can be understood accordingly.
"Furthermore, contemplate deeply the final aspect of the subtle, secret shifting of every thought-moment. "Contemplate deeply" means profound reflection.
"Thoroughly observe" refers to observing its transformations with a hidden mind and through precise scrutiny. "Kṣaṇa" is a Sanskrit term;
the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* states that the smallest unit of time is called a *kṣaṇa*. One should view the *kṣaṇa* in contrast to the thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*). Regarding the *kṣaṇa*:
The *kṣaṇa* (instant) is spoken of in terms of time, while the *nānā-nāṇa* (moment-to-moment) is spoken of in terms of the mind; for indeed, each *kṣaṇa* is precisely the meaning of each moment.
Furthermore, according to the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, there are ninety *kṣaṇas* within one thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*), and each *kṣaṇa* undergoes nine hundred cycles of arising and ceasing.
Thus, compared to a single thought-moment, a *kṣaṇa* is subtle, whereas the thought-moment is coarse. Reflecting deeply upon this...
"My body shifts secretly in this manner without ceasing, until it finally undergoes transformation and extinction.
The Buddha told the Great King, "You have seen these transformations... (until) I now demonstrate to you the nature that is neither born nor extinguished."
This section of the sutra follows the Buddha’s transformations to clarify non-arising and non-ceasing in response to his question.

From "The Buddha told... onwards, the dialogue can be understood accordingly. From "The Buddha said... onwards, he grants permission to definitively demonstrate the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing.
"Great King, at what age did you first see the waters of the Ganges? [The King replied: "At that very moment, I knew it was the water of the Ganges.
This section of the sutra was taught by the World-Honored One to demonstrate that the perception of the river is of a nature that is neither born nor extinguished;
thus he asked this question. *Jīva* is translated as "life" or "longevity," referring to one who, having brought his son to visit him, sought long life for him.
Since life and lifespan are identical, the remainder of the text may be understood accordingly.
The Buddha said, "Great King, as you have said, [up until] the age of sixty-two, there has been no difference."

In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One intends to clarify that the nature of seeing is indestructible when observing the river, and he uses the water being seen to verify the nature of the seer.
This is because the nature of the reflected color while observing the river is profound and unchanging;
yet one must further understand that the discussion of its non-transience while the nature of seeing is temporarily within delusion does not refer to true non-transience.
Because it is like a second moon, the scriptural passage proceeds from the coarse to the subtle, from the shallow to the deep, gradually leading one into the minute;
therefore, the sequence is as follows.
The Buddha said: "Do you now see your own hair turning white and your face wrinkling... [up to] the King replied: "No, World-Honored One."

In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One, by citing the words regarding the transformation of wrinkles, seeks to verify whether the seeing-nature is subject to change or not—specifically, whether it undergoes the states of childhood or old age.
When the King heard these words, he realized that the seeing-nature is unchanging; therefore, he replied, "No, no.
By saying "no, no," he meant that there is neither childhood nor senility. This is because the nature capable of seeing remains identical from the age of three until old age.
By transforming the mutable objects of perception to cause the immutable mind to awaken, one may attain realization swiftly.
The Buddha said: "Great King, although your face has wrinkled... [and so on], until "...you leaped for joy and were filled with unprecedented delight."
In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One, following the preceding discussion, resolves the matter of the unwrinkled seeing-nature not undergoing birth and death.
Having heard this, the King [Ajātaśatru] releases his former doubts. Because the face is an illusory body, it wrinkles and changes;

because the nature of seeing is adjacent to the True and lacks substantiality, it does not wrinkle and does not change. What is termed the "essence of seeing" (*darśana-śuddhi*) is precisely the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).
The essence flowing into the eye-faculty is called the "seeing-essence," which is precisely the nature that reflects forms.
Regarding the wrinkled: this is now correctly determined and analyzed. That which has form and can wrinkle must undergo change; if there is no substance that can wrinkle, then it does not change.
As for shifting and transformation, these occur through natural extinction. That which lacks substance to transform is fundamentally without birth or death. Since... [it is thus].
Since there is neither birth nor death, how could you experience birth and death within it? "Within it" refers to within the physical body (*rūpakāya*).
Since one who does not die exists therein, how can you cite those non-Buddhists such as Makkhali Gosāla and others, who all claim that after this body dies, there is total annihilation?
"Makkhali" is the full name Makkhali Gosāla; "Makkhali" is... [the remainder of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
The name is translated as "Ajita" (Not-Seeing), which is an epithet for Kesa-kambalin; it is not translated [into Chinese] because it is the name of his mother, and he is named after her.
His doctrine holds that suffering and pleasure are not obtained through karmic formations (*saṃskāra*), but that suffering is natural and pleasure is natural.
To cling to these as being inherent is the position of the second teacher among the six. This name did not appear in the previous section on King Ajātaśatru’s questions.
Now, because the Buddha’s answer is manifested as a reflection, we know that King Bimbisāra is referring collectively to the six teachers; it is simply that the text is abbreviated.
From "When the king heard... onwards, it clarifies how King Bimbisāra resolves his previous doubt regarding annihilation:

having now heard of the nature of non-arising and non-extinction, he realizes that although the physical body perishes, the seeing-nature does not undergo birth and death; thus, he abandons this [view].
Born, they rush toward that birth, and again they calculate it as a continuous succession; this refers to the assembly of those with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Because the previous question included the assembly of those with outflows in its request, they attained what had never been experienced before by first awakening to the eternal mind.
As stated at the beginning of this fascicle, Ānanda’s wish was for the World-Honored One to reveal the true nature of body and mind.

Regarding the false and the real, as well as the two types of illumination, you have clarified that the nature of seeing does not change. This is consistent with the dialogue between the Buddha and King Bimbisāra, which selected the view that the nature of seeing is indestructible.
This precisely accords with your own wish; yet Ānanda, hearing this from the side, finds it no different from his own statement that the nature of seeing is immovable.
Why then, World-Honored One, do you suppress this and exalt that, rebuking me for the arising and ceasing of every thought-moment?
Because Ānanda harbored doubts regarding equality, he posed the following question.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated before the Buddha with palms joined, and [continued] until: "I pray that you will arouse compassion and wash away my defilements."
In this section, Ānanda, having heard the King of Videha taught that the nature of seeing is indestructible, raised this question because he suspected it was the same as his own experience.
From the words "World-Honored One" onwards is the actual inquiry. Previously, the text explained solely that the nature of seeing is unchanging;

now, by adding the single character "hearing," it is known that although the previous passage explained the immovability and indestructibility of the nature of seeing alone, [the present teaching extends this to hearing].
The nature of seeing is thus, and it is the same for all other faculties; because the reflection is manifested therein, the word "hearing" is added, while the others remain abbreviated.
Regarding the phrase "washing away my dust and grime," this is explained by way of metaphor: "dust" is floating and easily removed, which is a metaphor for the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*);

"grime" is oily and difficult to wash off, which is a metaphor for the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-āsrava*). "Washing" is a metaphor for the World-Honored One’s compassionate voice, which is like water capable of [cleansing].
Because it washes away the defilements of the minds of sentient beings, it is likened to washing.
As for why Ānanda harbored doubts, it was because at the end of the first fascicle, it was stated that although the hands open and close and the head moves, what is seen does not move;

yet the World-Honored One rebuked him, saying that his thoughts arise and perish moment by moment, causing him to lose the true nature and act in delusion. Furthermore, when he demonstrated to King Bimbisāra that the nature of seeing is indestructible, [Ānanda’s confusion arose].
"It is just as Ānanda has described the nature of seeing as being unmoving; why then, World-Honored One, is this not that [same nature]?

This question arose from the doubt initiated by Ānanda. His intention was to say that the World-Honored One’s reprimand was excessive, for he did not realize that the Buddha’s demonstration to King Bimbisāra that the nature of seeing is indestructible was precisely intended to give rise to Ānanda’s doubt, thereby providing a fitting response.

The second point of his vow was to point out the location of the perversion. One must understand that what the Buddha showed King Bimbisāra—the unchanging nature of seeing—is different from the locus identified by Ānanda. It is only because Ānanda was deluded that he claimed they were the same. Why?
Because what the Buddha pointed out is precisely the source of the clarity of seeing, the profoundly still nature; whereas what Ānanda described seems...
The points of identification are fundamentally different; this is because Ānanda mistakenly identifies the discerning vision that discriminates conditioned objects as being immovable.
It is for this reason that the Buddha rebukes him for his error. That which the Buddha points out is like a second moon, whereas Ānanda’s point of identification is like a reflection in water.
Furthermore, that which the Buddha points out is the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) within the eighth consciousness, while Ānanda’s is not.

That the locus of recognition is the arising and ceasing of reflected images within the sixth consciousness, while that which is not subject to arising and ceasing can be seen therein, is evident here.
Someone may ask: "The second moon should also be subject to arising and ceasing; why do you say it does not cease? The answer is:

"The eighth consciousness is the cause of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "The ocean of the ālayavijñāna is eternally abiding. Because it is eternally abiding, it is so described.

It is not extinguished because its flow continues without interruption; thus it is called "not extinguished. Since the preceding sixth consciousness perishes from moment to moment, compared to this [seventh consciousness], it is considered coarse.
In terms of coarseness and subtlety, one may discuss extinction and non-extinction. Did we not say previously that these are discussed based on the midst of delusion?
Students, please contemplate this with a refined mind; you will then understand it. If you merely take it as an object of the ear, you will fail to grasp it.
The words that issue from his mouth not only deceive others but also deceive his own mind.
At that moment, the Tathāgata extended his golden arm [and said]: "I do not know who is upright and who is inverted."
In this section of the sutra, the Buddha, in response to Ānanda’s inquiry, explains the origin of his doubt;

thus, he demonstrates the hanging down of the hand to distinguish and rectify the inversion. In the preceding text, Ānanda mistakenly identified the seeing that depends on objects as an unmoving nature;
this arose from a perversion, whereby he took motion to be non-motion. It is just like...
Because the inverted is taken as upright and the upright as inverted, he demonstrates it by extending his hand to provide a test, causing them to realize it for themselves.

*Mudrā* is translated as "seal. The Buddha’s hands, in their various movements—whether turned upward or downward, raised or lowered, like a lotus in bloom, or in the manner of bestowing or receiving, or in the gesture of joining palms or making an offering—are all capable of subduing demons and restraining external influences; there is nothing that is not a seal.
The meaning can be understood through the dialogue concerning the Hand-Seal (mudrā).
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If people in the world... [up to] ...your own bodies, you call their nature 'inverted'.

This section of the sutra shows that before the World-Honored One, he displayed his hand hanging down in its correct orientation, yet Ānanda reckoned it to be inverted. Therefore, [the Buddha spoke thus].
Re-examining worldly views, the Buddha rebukes their twofold inversion. The Buddha’s "lowering" refers back to the previous gesture of hanging down the hands;
the questions and answers therein are self-evident. The Buddha then "descends" to rebuke their inverted views. Taking up the previous response, he extends his arm upward and rebukes them, saying:
"This extended arm pointing upward is precisely an inversion; how can you call it correct? If this were the head..."
To say that reversing the head and tail is called "correct" is what people of the world call a "perverted view.

To reverse the head and tail means that the elbow is the head of the arm and the finger is the tail of the arm; if one holds the arm upright with the fingers pointing upward, then the head is below and the tail is above—is this not a reversal of head and tail?
Is it not indeed perverted? This is the same as the previous case of holding the hand downward versus upward.
Because what is considered inverted is now taken as upright when one raises one's arm, that inversion is further calculated as being correct; therefore, it is called "inverted view.

"Twofold gazing" means twofold with respect to both facing and turning away—that is, gazing by turning one's back is the meaning of inverted view. Thus, we know that what follows compares the correct and the inverted.
"Your body" refers to Ānanda’s body, encompassing the bodies of all people in the world; this is spoken in terms of the human bodies of the world.
If one examines and compares the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata with other categories to bring it forth, then the Buddha-body is the "correct" (zhèng) and your own bodies are the "inverted" (dào).
Purity is the meaning of the Middle Way; because the Middle is correct, what is partial is defiled, while the Middle is undefiled.
To be undefiled is precisely to be pure. However, that which is merely the "Middle" has not yet escaped defilement; it must necessarily be the Perfect Middle.
"Later, it is unstained. Regarding "Perfectly Complete Knowledge" (*samyak-saṃbuddha*), Changshui’s Commentary states: "To be free from inversion is called 'perfect' (*samyak*);
to exhaustively penetrate the Dharma-realm is called 'complete' (*saṃbuddha*). The Two Vehicles do not possess this title because they have not yet abandoned inversion.

As for 'inversion of nature,' 'nature' (*prakṛti*) has the sense of 'root,' meaning it is a fundamental inversion. Previously, what was correct was taken as inverted; now, what was inverted is taken as correct."
Thus, to be inverted and yet further inverted refers to those who are doubly deluded among the deluded.
As you carefully observe, where in the names of "your body" and "the Buddha's body"—both of which are called inverted—does the designation "inverted" actually reside?
In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One directly investigates the fundamental cause of inversion: from what does it arise, and where does that fundamental cause reside?
Following the instruction "according to you," the Buddha commands a thorough and truthful observation:

"What is the cause for the Buddha’s body being upright, and what is the cause for your own body being inverted? Since this contrasts the upright with the inverted, it is spoken in relation to the Buddha’s body; this must be understood.
"From where do these inverted names arise? This is truly an inquiry into their cause. Now, if the correct cause is set upside down, then when it is no longer inverted, even "correctness" has no name.
The Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is the inherent correctness that is free from both correctness and inversion.

In the preceding passage, Ānanda requested to clarify the true and the false, the real and the unreal, and the nature of arising and ceasing versus non-arising and non-ceasing regarding body and mind.
From this point on, it should be clear that King Bimbisāra [was enlightened].
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly [reached a state] where they did not know the location of their own bodies, minds, or inverted perceptions.
In this section, because Ānanda had heard the inquiry into the fundamental cause of inversion but did not understand its locus, he stared with wide-open eyes and failed to answer.
"Staring" (dèng) refers to the manner of gazing straight ahead; "blurred vision" (méng) refers to the lack of clarity in the eyes.

Because his mind was muddled and his thoughts were deep, his eyes could not open clearly; thus, he did not blink and remained motionless. In the preceding passage, the Buddha asked, "Where is it designated as 'inversion'?"
At present, Ānanda’s inverted mind has not yet been shattered; his state of inquiry is still muddled, which is why he stares blankly in silence, doubting and unable to respond.
The Buddha, arising in compassion and pitying Ānanda, [reveals that] the nature of precious clarity is realized within delusion.
In this section of the sutra, out of compassion for those who have not yet awakened, the World-Honored One directly clarifies the locus of their perversion and overturns their prior delusion.
Regarding the "Ocean Tide Sound," this is spoken by way of analogy: the rising and falling of the ocean tides do not miss their appointed time;

likewise, the Dharma-sound of the Tathāgata examines the capacities of beings and responds to them, adapting his transformation of others according to the time, without waiting to be requested. I always...

The following indicates the phenomena that are the objects of delusion; the two characters "matter" (rūpa) and "mind" (citta) are general terms for all conditions, while those below are specific, meaning that when expanded they refer to the eighteen *dhātus*, and when condensed they are merely the two phenomena of matter and mind. Matter refers to material phenomena;

the *Śata-dharma-śāstra* states there are eleven kinds, namely the five sense organs, the five sense objects, and the matter included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*). Mind refers to...

The *Cittadharmaparīkṣā* states: "There are eight, namely the eight consciousnesses. Regarding the term "conditions" (*pratyaya*), "condition" here refers to the subjective perceiver, specifically indicating the seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
This first clause addresses the mind-kings (*citta-rāja*) alone; it is only in the following clause that the mental concomitants (*caitta*) are clarified.
Thus, the word "and" (*ca*) is employed to denote those "employed by the mind-king," which is why they are called "mental concomitants" (*caitta*). This is from the treatise.
It is said that these are the fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*). As for "objects of cognition" (*ālambana*), this refers to the six sense-objects (*viṣaya*);
since the objects are what are cognized, the term "object of cognition" is viewed in contrast to the aforementioned "cognizing subjects.

Furthermore, in the passage beginning with "your body," the term "body" specifically indicates the present basis of support, referring to the physical form and the various sense-faculties (*indriya*). The term "mind" (*citta*) refers to the sovereign mind (*cittarāja*) and its associated mental states.
Regarding the various states of mind, these are subsumed under the two characters "body" and "mind," which encompass the three preceding phrases concerning the dharmas of form and mind;

this follows from the previous discussion to clarify that all such things are manifestations within the wondrous mind. The two characters "wondrously bright" (miao-ming) directly reveal the two meanings of stillness and illumination:
"wondrous" (miao) signifies stillness, while "bright" (ming) signifies illumination. Because stillness and illumination are non-dual, they are referred to together as "wondrously bright."
This is explained in detail within the fourth section. "True essence" (*zhēnjīng*) means that which is without falsehood is "true," and that which is unmixed is "essence.
Furthermore, the "subtlety" of the subtle mind below also comprehensively encompasses the meanings of "subtle brightness" and so forth mentioned above.

It is said that this subtle mind is fundamentally devoid of even a hair’s breadth of admixture with private desires; therefore, it is designated by these terms—subtle, true, and essence—and so on. Nevertheless, it is simply the one mind.
The phrases "the reality of its characters," "the supreme and wondrous clarity of the dharmas," and so forth, all manifest the virtues of this mind.
As for the passage beginning with "How could it be...," it directly rebukes the error of misrecognizing the objects of conditions while losing sight of this fundamentally perfect and wondrous mind;
this is precisely what is called the locus of inversion. The phrase "fundamentally wondrous" and so forth reiterates the praise of the virtues of this mind, praising it again and again.
This is because it clarifies that this mind is endowed with inexhaustible virtues. Thus, Changshui’s Commentary states: "It is 'round' (*yuan*) because its essence is all-pervasive;

it is 'luminous' (*ming*) because it is without obscuration. As a dharma that may be revered, it is called a 'jewel' (*bao*). Having been so from the very beginning, it is not merely so now; therefore, it is called 'fundamental' (*ben*).
Because the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished, it is called 'sublime' (*miao*). Furthermore, it speaks of the "mind" (*xin*).

Regarding "nature" (*xing*), it is the function (*yòng*) while being the essence (*tǐ*); thus it is called "mind. Regarding "mind," it is the essence while being the function; thus it is called "nature.

Although there are two names, "mind" and "nature," they refer to but a single dharma. To become deluded within awakening is precisely what is being overturned and demonstrated here, following the delusion at the end of the first scroll.

Based on the previous discussion regarding the meaning of "adventitious dust" (*āgantuka-rajas*), one awakens to the fact that adventitious dust is movement, while the fundamental space is non-movement.
Therefore, to point to the body and its objects as moving while the nature of seeing is unmoving is awakening;
yet, to mistakenly take the discerning vision that conditions sensory dust as unmoving—taking the moving for the unmoving—is delusion. Thus it is said:
"To mistake delusion within awakening. Among the various interpretations since antiquity, none have pointed this out with certainty, as they failed to investigate the source of the scriptural text.
When it comes to the passage "coming from a state of confusion," every time I reach this point, I have never failed to close the scroll and sigh deeply.

I hope that future generations will examine it closely; therein lies the point of entry for oneself. Furthermore, the word "thing" (*wu*) in the text refers to the end of the first fascicle, where it says, "recognizing things as one's own things.
This means that one mistakenly identifies the objects manifested within the wondrous mind as being one's own.
To lose the wondrous mind—how could this not be delusion?
"Obscured and darkened, it becomes emptiness; within that dark and obscured emptiness" (up to) "the Tathāgata calls them those who are to be pitied.
This section of the sutra, the World-Honored One, following the preceding passage, clarifies the characteristics of the inverted states and the fundamental causes of dependent origination.

To reprimand its delusion: this obscurity and darkness is precisely the fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), which is also what the *Awakening of Faith* refers to as the meaning of "non-enlightenment" (*abodha*).
Because of non-enlightenment, its characteristics arise; non-enlightenment is itself this obscurity and darkness.

Since one is deluded regarding the original luminosity, clarity transforms into darkness, and is thus termed "obscurity and darkness. Essentially, ignorance is the subject that undergoes transformation, while the insentient void is the object.
Transformation arises from the transformation of ignorance; because it gives rise to a stubborn void, it is said that "obscuration and gloom constitute emptiness. Someone may ask:
"If you say that the emptiness manifest before us is a transformation of ignorance, then what was present before ignorance existed?
The answer is: "Before ignorance existed, there was only the great, pervasive, perfectly enlightened true void. Once ignorance exists, [the void] is no longer so."
"Clarification" (*ming*) carries the meaning of being "obscured and dull"; thus, the Great Awakening of True Emptiness (*zhēnkōng*) transforms into an obscured, dull, and stubborn void.
This principle is inherently so—why then should one doubt it? Furthermore, the emptiness that is transformed and the obscuring darkness that performs the transformation interact and bind together;
this binding is a congealing, and from this congealing, form (*se*) is produced. Form is precisely the world. This arises because the internal mind is firm.
Grasping at external stimuli, they coalesce to form the colors of the world; the world takes the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—as its substance.
Furthermore, the colors of these four great elements intermingle with deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*), and the marks produced by such delusion constitute the bodies of sentient beings.
Indeed, the bodies of sentient beings arise from the three perceptions of the father, the mother, and oneself.

Since the semen and blood of the parents belong to the four great elements, the next four lines clarify the manner in which the deluded mind first comes into being through the aggregation of conditions.
"Conditions" refers to external conditions, namely the conditions of the six sense objects; when these aggregate within, they cause the mind to waver and move, leading it to rush outward in flight.
To "rush in flight" means that the eyes rush toward forms, the ears rush toward sounds, and so forth—this is called dissipation.

Because the mind cannot be gathered within, it is called "restless and runaway. Consequently, one takes this confused and turbulent state of the triad of sense organs (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) to be the nature of the mind; thus, the true mind is far removed.

Once deluded into taking this as the mind, one becomes certain that this mind resides within the physical body, failing to realize that the mind is not within the physical body, nor does it extend outward.
Mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth are all things within this wondrously luminous true mind; this is precisely a reprimand for their delusion.
It is like the following analogy used to clarify the meaning of how they have abandoned the truth to pursue the false, discarding the great while clinging to the small:
suppose there were hundreds of thousands of vast, clear, and pure oceans—the magnitude of even one ocean is infinite, let alone a hundred.

A thousand oceans are vast and even more vast; this serves as a metaphor for the wondrous mind inherently possessed by every person, which is so immense, yet people abandon it and instead recognize only the substance of a single bubble.
This single bubble precisely represents the deluded and agitated mind.
However, this deluded and agitated mind, within the wondrously luminous mind, is like a single bubble among hundreds of thousands of oceans. Thus, [it is insignificant].
To discard the ocean and recognize a bubble as small is already one delusion;

yet to further cling to that bubble as the ocean, claiming it to be the entirety of the tide and the full extent of the vast seas, is a delusion within delusion—what is this if not perversion? Therefore it is said:
"In delusion, they are twice as human. "The entire tide" refers to the tide of the whole ocean, and "the vast seas" (yíngbó) is another name for the ocean.
In the passage beginning with "As I," I cite the example of the downward-hanging hand to criticize its inversion.

When the Buddha first let his hand hang down for Ānanda, he took what was upright as inverted; this was one inversion. Then, when he raised his arm and pointed upward, he again took that which was inverted as upright;
this was an inversion upon an inversion. This is cited repeatedly to illustrate how those who are already deluded become doubly so. Thus, it is said: "As I... and so forth.
The Tathāgata says that those who hold such perverted views are to be pitied.

At the beginning of this fascicle, Ānanda’s vow was to reveal the nature of illumination within both the arising-and-ceasing and the non-arising-and-non-ceasing; the present text specifically reveals the nature of illumination within the mind of arising-and-ceasing.
"Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s compassionate rescue and profound instruction... [up to] 'you have uprooted my root of doubt and led me back to the Unsurpassed Way.

This section of the sutra describes how Ānanda, having been shown the teaching, first realized his wondrous mind; yet, because he again reckoned the perceiving faculty (*ālambana*) to be the fundamental basis, he requested a definitive resolution.
Regarding "compassionate rescue and profound instruction," Ānanda’s intention was to express his gratitude for the Buddha’s extraction of his inverted views.
To be mired in delusion is called "sorrow"; to rescue and instruct one with the perfect mind of the Right and Universal is called "profound instruction.
Because he felt sorrow for his past delusions and rejoiced in his present awakening, his heart was moved, and thus he shed tears. He joined his palms and addressed the Buddha;
this is the ritual of a solemn request. Although I, Ānanda, am of low station, I say that although I have awakened to the wondrous mind, which is perfect, eternal, and abiding, it is in truth...
I have not yet been able to personally realize this; I have merely attained an understanding of the Dharma currently taught by the World-Honored One.

Thus, I now rely on my conditioned mind to accept it with faith, gaze upon it with reverence, and look toward it with sincere devotion. Apart from this realization, faith, and reverent gazing, I have no other mind with which to conceive that "this is it.
Yet, I am left with the lingering doubt as to whether this realization is truly valid or not. My uncertainty has not been resolved.

I have not yet dared to claim that this "original mind-ground" (benyuan xindi) refers to the "mind-ground" (xindi). Here, "ground" (*di*) is used as a metaphor for the earth, which is capable of containing and developing;
my own mind is likewise so. Because the dharma and the metaphor are combined to reveal this truth, it is called the "mind-ground.

Other meanings, such as "perfectly complete" and "eternally abiding," are explained as before. In the passage beginning with "I pray that the Buddha," there is a formal request for definitive resolution, meaning to proclaim and demonstrate the perfect fusion (*yuanyong*).
The intent of these words is to uproot the very foundation of doubt and cause one to return to the Unsurpassed Way.

Yet, since Ānanda was already clearly instructed on the principle that [the mind] is not the thinking faculty when [the Master] refuted the "ability to infer" at the beginning of the first fascicle, why does he still propose the "conditioned mind" as the fundamental source here?
This is truly because while the state of alertness (*xingxing*) can be distinguished, the state of profound stillness (*jiji*) is difficult to know; therefore, he departed from it.
Because this mind, apart from its conditions, is vast, remote, and without trace, you still harbor doubts regarding it.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "You all [still] regard [it as such], because there is nothing to be discerned; you too are like this."

In this section of the sutra, the Buddha definitively eliminates the mind that clings to conditions (*pratyaya-citta*), using the analogy of pointing at the moon to urge one to recognize the moon and discard the finger.
"The Buddha said" and below, he provides the definitive elimination: if one hears the Dharma and contemplates its meaning, one should realize the meaning to clarify the mind.

If one listens to the Dharma with a mind that clings to conditions, then the Dharma itself becomes a condition; because it creates [clinging], it is not empty, and one will not attain the true meaning. — *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*
The Sūtra states: "Rely on the meaning, not on the words; rely on wisdom, not on consciousness. Now, to rely on the conditioned mind is to rely on consciousness rather than wisdom;
therefore, it is said that one does not attain the *dharmatā*. *Dharmatā* refers to the nature of the Dharma as it has been heard;

the nature of the Dharma is precisely the nature of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). As for the person mentioned below, an analogy is cited to clarify this: the person is a metaphor for the Tathāgata.

The finger is a metaphor for the taught dharma; the moon is a metaphor for the nature of reality (dharmatā). Showing [the moon] is a metaphor for the teacher, and showing [it] to the listeners is a metaphor for the text.

These three turnings are employed to reveal that both the finger and the moon may be misunderstood; thus it is said that "neither light nor darkness is recognized. Yet, the nature of that moon is inherently luminous, while the pointing finger is inherently dark.
When these two natures are not understood, they both vanish as realities. If these metaphors are applied to the Dharma: [The text continues with the application of the metaphors.]
One should say: "The Buddha used the sound of the Dharma to point to the mind and show it to people; those people, by means of that Dharma, ought to contemplate the mind.
If, however, one takes the sound of the Buddha’s Dharma as one's own mind, such a person not only loses their own mind but also loses the Dharma.
Why? Because they take the perceived characteristics of the sound of the Dharma as their own mind; thus, they lose not only the Dharma but also—
Furthermore, one does not recognize the wondrous clarity nor its conditioned marks. Why is this? Because one takes conditioned marks to be the nature of wondrous clarity;
since conditioned marks and wondrous clarity are mutually unapprehendable, the final phrase, "You are also like this," is a statement of formal application (*dharma-sādharmya*).
The subsequent passage constitutes the actual application of the dharma.

"If one discriminates that the sound of my Dharma-teachings [extends] from 'each has its own destination' to 'how can it be the master'—this section of the sutra is the Buddha’s refutation of the six sense objects as being the object of a mind that lacks a source; it corresponds to the previous metaphor of pointing at the moon.

The first phrase cites Ānanda’s speculative statement, and from 'this mind' onwards, the text properly employs the relationship between the subject that perceives and the object that is perceived to carry out the refutation."
"Breaking" refers to the analytical discrimination based on the sounds of the Dharma.

If one takes this discrimination as the mind, then this mind ought to exist separately from the sounds of the Dharma that are its objects of discrimination, possessing a nature of being a subject of discrimination; for you assert it to be the mind.

Therefore, he again cites analogies to clarify that this mind has no substantial reality: the traveler represents the discriminating mind, while the inn represents the six sense-objects such as sound.
Dusting off the pavilion attendant is used as a metaphor for the theory that the sound of separation possesses an inherent nature;
this is to clarify that while the host does not depart, the guest must necessarily depart. If it were indeed the host, it would be the true mind. Therefore, it says, "this is also like this.
This phrase applies the analogy: the word "this" refers to the speaker of the dharma-sound of discrimination, and it corresponds to the aforementioned word "guest," meaning—
"The fruit of your discrimination of the sound of the Dharma is your own true mind, which has nowhere to go.
Why, then, does the text below reprove it for lacking substance? It asks: "How can there be no capacity for your own discrimination apart from the sound of my preaching the Dharma?
Furthermore, it asks: "Is it only by relying on sound that the discriminating mind functions? Does it not also discriminate the physical appearance of the Tathāgata right now?"
If one were separated from the Tathāgata’s countenance and physical marks, you would likewise lack the capacity for discernment.
"And so on" means that it is impossible to describe in full [the discernment regarding] the six sense objects;

here, by bypassing the three categories of scent, taste, and touch, and stating that discernment is entirely absent, one completely severs the active discernment of external objects and internally maintains a state of profound stillness.
Regarding the phrase "a state that is neither form nor emptiness": it is not form because it lacks substantiality;
it is not emptiness because it possesses characteristics. The name *Kauśalī* refers to the latter half of the name of the aforementioned Makkhali Gosāla.

The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the other six teachers, all of whom were deluded regarding this state that is neither form nor emptiness, taking it to be the "Primal Darkness" (*tamas*). As for this "Primal Darkness": [it is as follows].

*Pradhāna* (Ming) means "darkness," and *tattva* (Di) means "truth. Because they cling to that which is neither form nor emptiness—a chaotic mass where light and shadow cannot be distinguished—they establish the name *pradhāna-tattva*.
These various non-Buddhist outsiders rely upon this "neither-form-nor-emptiness" to establish twenty-five *tattvas*:
the first being *pradhāna*, and the last being the *puruṣa* (Spirit-Self). This is seen in detail in the *Huayan jing shu chao* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) and other scriptures.
The treatise distinguishes from all inferior views to clarify the Buddha’s correct principle:

this profound and secluded state, which is neither form nor emptiness, is a mental object (*dharmāyatana*) within that is a reflected image based on conditions. If one is separated from this reflected image of the mental object, there is likewise no nature capable of discrimination.
Previously, one investigated the absence of discrimination amidst the movement of the five sensory objects; here, one investigates it amidst the stillness of internal mental objects.

Since there is no discrimination within this interval between movement and stillness, and ultimately no nature of yours that can discriminate, then the natures of your mind each have their own place to which they return.

How, then, can it be the master? As for what is meant by "returning," it means that all discriminations of movement and stillness each return to the sensory objects (*viṣaya*) from which they originally arose; they are like guests staying at an inn. How, then, can it be attained?
"O Lord, you who do not depart! These words of 'returning' precisely introduce the following passage on the eight returns that distinguish the seeing.
Ānanda said: 'If my mind-nature each has a place to which it returns'... (until) 'I shall now show you the ground where there is no returning.'"
In this section, because Ānanda heard that the "return" (*pratyāgama*) of the differentiated [elements] exists, he asked how the wondrous mind could be without return.
The Buddha first demonstrated that the visual essence (*darśana-vijñāna*) is without return. From "Ānanda... below, he follows up on the aforementioned existence of return by asking about non-return;
the text is clear and can be understood. From "The Buddha said... below, he answers; the World-Honored One did not directly point out that the wondrous mind is without return.

Furthermore, as for pointing out that which does not return among the refined essence of seeing: in general, the World-Honored One leads sentient beings into the Tathāgatagarbha by proceeding from the coarse to the subtle and from the shallow to the deep.
Thus, he first demonstrates the "second moon" to gradually approach the true moon;

this is the World-Honored One’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). It is truly because the wondrous mind is vast and boundless, making it difficult to demonstrate directly, that [he employs such methods].

For those who perceive the essence of seeing as shallow and superficial, this shows them that it does not return; if they awaken to the fact that the essence of seeing does not return, then the wondrous mind will be restored without being far away.
Furthermore, Ānanda’s doubt regarding the non-extinction of the nature of seeing before King Bimbisāra remains unresolved;
now, by showing that the essence of seeing does not return, I directly answer that previous point to clarify the reason for its non-extinction mentioned in the preceding text.
Furthermore, that which does not return now is precisely what did not cease previously; because it does not return, it does not cease. The "wondrously luminous original mind" is as explained before.
Regarding the phrase "the essence of seeing, the source of clarity": the "essence of seeing" is the nature of the eye that reflects objects.

"Essence" (*jing*) refers to a profound and tranquil qi, pure and bright without dregs; therefore, it is called the "source of the essence of seeing's clarity. This means the essence itself is luminous.
The "pure element" (*viśuddha-dhātu*) is the fundamental substance; this is the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness, which divides itself into six.
When it is in the eye, it is called the "essence of seeing" (*darśana-sāra*); when in the ear, it is called the "essence of hearing" (*śravaṇa-sāra*), and so forth.

Although it is divided into six, it does not depart from its profoundly tranquil fundamental substance; therefore, all six locations are termed "luminous elements. Nevertheless, although this essence of seeing is not the wondrously luminous mind, it nonetheless departs [from delusion].
This mind does not distinguish between the essence of the seeing-essence and the essence of the wondrous-essence;
yet the seeing-essence can be destroyed while the wondrous-essence cannot be destroyed, for it is the subtle and refined function of the eternally abiding substance of the mind.
Thus, although this seeing-essence is currently called "non-returning," once it later merges with the true mind, even this seeing-essence will perish.
Therefore, the subsequent passage says: "When seeing the seer, that seeing is not [true] seeing. These two sentences alone have already refuted the essence of seeing;
however, as this is currently a shallow demonstration, it says, "it does not return, like a second moon," which precisely clarifies that it is not real.
Now, the second moon is produced by pressing on the eyes; although the eye-pressing is false, it is not far from the true moon—this is used as a metaphor.
The seeing-essence is not far from the true mind, as the preceding text states: "The seeing that observes the river remains exactly as it was for the Tripitaka Master even at the age of sixty;
this lack of change is precisely what constitutes the stage of Non-returning.

That which is not the moon's reflection refers to the reflection in water, which possesses the characteristics of arising and ceasing, coming and going; it appears when there is water and vanishes when separated from the water—this is birth.
The extinction of phenomena is an analogy for the discerning views that depend on sensory objects (*ālambana*). When depending on objects they exist; when separated from objects they cease to exist.
This is what was previously described as the guest lodging in a roadside inn, who stays only briefly before departing. Therefore, it is like the reflection of the moon.

However, this present vision is clear and bright, reflecting forms in a manner that cannot be returned [to its source]; because it is adjacent to the true essence (*tattva*), it is not like a reflection in water.
"You should now lower your voice and listen attentively to demonstrate that there is no returning; the character 'ground' (di) refers to the locus of the original cause.
Ānanda, this great lecture hall opens wide toward the east... [until]... it is clear and cloudless; gather your breath and observe its purity."
This section of the sutra intends to demonstrate that which cannot be returned; it first clarifies the characteristics of that which can be returned.

"Opening wide toward the east" below indicates the cause of illumination. "Opening wide" means being hollow and empty; when the doors and windows open toward the east, there is a hollow void without obstruction.
As the sun rises, the light enters from the east, causing one to know that the cause of illumination is the sun. [End of middle section.]
"Night" below indicates the cause of darkness. During the "black fortnight," which lasts for sixteen days, the light gradually diminishes;

this entire period is called the black fortnight because the fifteen days prior [to the new moon] are called the white fortnight. "Doors and windows" indicate openness, while "walls and buildings" indicate obstruction.

Because they are obstructed, the two subsequent phrases are analyzed: "discrimination" belongs to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which takes "dharma-objects" (*dharmaviṣaya*) as its conditions.
When the discriminating mind arises, the object of dharma (dharmāyatana) manifests; the *Śata-śāstra* refers to this as "matter included within the sphere of dharma" (*dharmāyatanasaṃgṛhītarūpa*).
While the other seven characteristics are all explained in terms of external objects, this one alone is explained in terms of discrimination.

This is because it clarifies that the [other] eight characteristics all arise from discrimination; therefore, this phrase is placed among the eight characteristics. [The term] "stolid void" (*huánxū*)...
"Showing 'dark and turbid' (*yùpò*) refers to the miasmic, murky, and hazy vapors of wind; this demonstrates the sign of obscuration (*hūn-xiàng*). 'Winding' (*yú*) is like a barrier.
Regarding the two lines following 'clear and bright' (*chéng-jì*): 'clear' (*chéng*) means the sky is free from clouds, and 'bright' (*jì*) means the brilliance is open and radiant.

'Atmospheric vapors' (*fēn') refers to the mountain mists; because these vapors are withdrawn, it is 'clear and bright. This demonstrates the sign of purity (*jìng-xiàng*). These are the eight kinds."

The characteristics of light and darkness, etc., correctly demonstrate that which can be returned; the seeing-essence (*darśana-vijñāna*) among these eight characteristics is precisely what one intends to return.
This is what is being analyzed in the following passage:
"Ānanda, you all look at these various changing phenomena... (up to) everything that exists does not go beyond this category."
In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One again returns each of the eight marks to their original causes. First, there is a general summary of the returning causes;

next, under the heading "How so," there is an inquiry and explanation regarding how each cause specifically returns to its respective category. Within the detailed explanation of these returns, there are both headings and explanations.

Regarding "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*): that which was non-existent suddenly comes into being is called "transformation" (*nir-mā*), and that which exists returns to non-existence is called "transformation" (*mā*).
Because these various characteristics arise and perish and are not permanent, they are called "transformations. The first phrase generally refers to the eight characteristics;
the subsequent phrase first clarifies the cause for returning [to the source], and the following section explains this by clarifying what is returned to.

Since the "dark" and other aspects are all omitted, the characteristics of returning are collectively indicated without explaining the underlying reasons, using the "bright" as an analogy. Thus, the final section summarizes that all things can return to the ordinary.
Because nothing that exists in the world does not emerge from these eight characteristics.
You have perceived the essential nature of the clarity of the eight kinds of views; for this reason, the Tathāgata calls you "one who is worthy of compassion."
In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One directly points to the capacity for seeing as being without a point of return (*anivṛtti*) to awaken Ānanda from his self-delusion.
From the words "Your seeing... onwards, he specifically indicates that which has no return. Why? Because he subsequently investigates and explains the reason why it has no return. He says:
"If this nature of the capacity to see were to return to light and darkness, then when light ceases, the seeing would perish along with the light. Thus, there would be no [seeing] remaining.
If you can see darkness and that darkness is still visible now, then you know that while the light has ceased, the seeing itself does not cease;

thus it is known that seeing is non-returnable. The remaining seven cases follow this principle; therefore, one knows that external conditions are distinct from one another, yet the seeing itself is no different.

This concludes by identifying the wondrous mind within what is returnable, thereby alerting you to your own delusion: that which is returnable is merely the guest, whereas you yourself are non-returnable.
"This is your true master" is a paradoxical expression; it means that if this were not you, then for whom else would it be?
Viewed in this light, one knows that your mind is fundamentally wondrous, luminous, and pure, yet you have deluded yourself. "Stupefied" means the mind does not open;
"lost" means to lose the original luminosity and undergo the cycle of rebirth due to being deluded regarding the true nature.

Therefore, although the word "ocean" is not explicitly mentioned, it is understood from the words "drifting and drowning" that one is constantly being swept away and submerged within the ocean of birth and death;
the final two lines conclude by clarifying the Buddha’s compassion.
Ānanda said, "Although I recognize that this nature of seeing has nothing from which it can return, how can I know that it is my true nature?
This section of the sutra records Ānanda’s inquiry because, despite being shown that the nature of seeing has no point of return, he had not yet clarified the meaning of realizing the truth;
for although Ānanda knew that the nature of seeing has no return, he still...
One may doubt that the nature of seeing is dispersed throughout the myriad things, such that there is no seeing that is not a thing, and no thing that is not seeing.
Since the myriad things are manifold, the nature of seeing is likewise universal; how then can one know that this seeing is one’s own true nature?

For this reason, in the following passage, the World-Honored One repeatedly uses objects to refute [this doubt]. Now, the question regarding the true nature follows closely upon your [previous] words.

The phrase "the mind is fundamentally wondrously bright and pure" traces its origin to when the World-Honored One previously brought together [the teachings] by stating that seeing-nature is precisely your wondrous mind.
Therefore, Ānanda was not yet clear regarding this point of conjunction;

he reasoned that seeing-nature is external while the wondrous mind is internal, and since these two are entirely separate from one another, how could they be unified as my true nature? Thus, the Buddha [proceeds below].
He replied: "If you see, it is you and not me. Since the nature of seeing is all-pervasive, who else could it be but you?
Why do you doubt your own true nature? If you consider your nature to be unreal and seek the truth from me, this doubt will be resolved by what follows.
This doubt is naturally dispelled.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "I now ask you... (up to) "...the sentient beings' ability to see through objects does not exceed a few inches.
This section of the sutra answers the preceding inquiry regarding the realization of truth by developing the subject from the perspective of vision;

it demonstrates that when deluded vision is exhausted, the true mind naturally manifests. Therefore, I shall now explain in detail the meaning of the five stages of the measure of vision, clarifying the nature of seeing.
Although the distances of these measures vary, the nature of vision (*darśana-svabhāva*) is no different; thus, one may resolve them by directly examining the objects themselves.

Ānanda had not yet attained the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*). This means that although he had realized the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) and had severed the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), the afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) had not yet been eliminated;

therefore, it is said he "had not yet attained the outflow-free state. Because he had not attained the outflow-free state, his vision of the nature was obstructed, and thus he could not perceive [the Buddha’s] own vision from afar.
The Buddha’s supernormal power augmented his vision so that it reached the First Dhyāna.

Since the First Dhyāna is the foremost stage of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu), and because Ānanda—translated as "Free from Poverty"—had already attained the "half-head" divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) through the causes and conditions described in the *Āgamas* such as the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* and the *Udānavarga*, the extent of his vision surpassed that of those previously in Jambudvīpa.
The preceding explanation follows the response given by Ānanda in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*.
The Brahma King Śuddhāvāsa said, "I see the trichiliocosm as clearly as looking at a fruit in the palm of my hand. This refers specifically to Jambudvīpa;

the term used by the translator is an error. *Āmalaka* is translated as "difficult to distinguish"; it is the name of a fruit, a species of peach (*táo*) or jujube (*nài*), so called because it is difficult to distinguish [its ripeness].
The rest of the text is easily understood.
"Ānanda, furthermore, let us and you observe the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings... [until] 'who is my own substance and who are external objects?
This section of the sutra follows the previous inquiry into the realization of truth by the World-Honored One, wherein he examines objects to discern the distinction between self and other.
Regarding the palaces where the Four Heavens dwell, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-śāstra* states: 'Mount Sumeru...'"
From the ocean, it rises sixteen thousand eight hundred yojanas into the sky; the Four Heavenly Kings dwell upon the upper half of this mountain.
On each of its four sides resides one king: on the eastern golden terrace, the king is named Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
on the southern lapis lazuli terrace, the king is named Virūḍhaka; on the western silver terrace, the king is named Virūpākṣa; and on the northern crystal terrace, the king is named... [Vaiśravaṇa].

Regarding the passage "The many who are learned each survey from their respective palaces the spaces between their dwellings," this means that when looking out from the Jeta Grove toward the southern slope of Mount Sumeru, the intervening space consists of water as the great ocean and land as the plains, mountain valleys, and so forth;
the empty space refers to the vast void extending from the near to the far. The character *xing* (行) applies to both water and land.
The three locations of emptiness refer to such categories as birds, beasts, humans, spirits, fish, and dragons;
"darkness" refers to mountains, rivers, trees, clouds, mist, wind, and haze; and "light" refers to the sun, moon, and stars.
All such various forms of darkness and light belong to the objective realm (*viṣaya*) and are what the faculty of sight perceives and retains as obstructions. Regarding this, the Buddha said:
"You should distinguish between self and other among these myriad phenomena. Now, I shall descend as a Buddha and further assist you in this discernment:
"I will now take your seeing-nature and select from among all the objects you perceive who is my own substance.
Here, "my own substance" refers to the nature of the seer as my true essence; this is the "self," whereas all things are the "other."
Regarding the "I" and "me" that you address to objects, it is most excellent to understand these terms as being dynamic and alive.
Ānanda, that which reaches from the palace of the sun and moon to this very place—this subtle, wondrous, and luminous essence—is truly your seeing-nature.
In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One follows the preceding correct discernment of self and other to clarify that seeing must truly have its source.
"The source of seeing" refers to the origin of vision; explained through analogy, it is like the source of water. Seeing issues forth from the locus of the eye;

to reach its ultimate origin and exhaust the full measure of seeing is called "reaching the limit. That which lies between these points— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
Regarding the observation of those [deities] from the palaces of the sun and moon, the *Lokadhātunirdeśa-sūtra* states:

"The palace of the Sun Deity is exactly fifty-one *yojanas* in length and breadth, and likewise in height; the palace of the Moon Deity is exactly forty-nine *yojanas* in length and breadth, and likewise in height.
It is well known that these two spheres of radiant light in the sky are, in essence, their palaces.
From the palace, light radiates in the four directions; looking afar, it appears like a sphere.

The two deva-sons, Sūrya and Candra, who dwell there, naturally travel through the air in an unceasing cycle, revolving horizontally around Mount Sumeru. Because Mount Sumeru is high and acts as an obstruction, they create day and night.
The Buddha said: "What you see here is entirely external phenomena; it is not your own body. These are the seven golden mountains."

This refers to Mount Sumeru situated in the center, surrounded by seven tiers of Vajra Mountains, each separated from the next by a great ocean at a distance of several tens of thousands of millions of *li*; hence they are called the Seven Golden Mountains.

As for the "various lights," the mountains have their own mountainous radiance and the waters have their own colors; the sun, moon, stars, planets, clouds, and mists all manifest through transformation.
Because these are strange and marvelous, they are called "various"; all of these are objects, not the essence of your seeing.
Even those that fly or hide, whether large or small, human or animal—these too are objects and not the self. Ānanda, what follows below is precisely for the purpose of resolving this;
the preceding was a selection among objects, whereas now is a resolution regarding the nature of seeing itself. That is to say, if it were near...
If distant objects and forms differ in ten thousand ways, yet your seeing-essence remains pure and unobstructed as instructed—this is called "purity.
Thus, while objects and forms may vary, the nature of seeing is without distinction. This very essence, this wondrously luminous substance, is truly your seeing-nature;
why doubt that it is not real? This "wondrously luminous essence" refers precisely to the seeing-nature.
"If you see these objects, then you [must] also [be present]; since [the Self] is naturally not an object, how could it not be you?
This section of the sutra explains away Ānanda’s doubt that the faculty of seeing is an object, clarifying that while seeing is not an object, it is indeed the self (*ātman*).
In the preceding passage, Ānanda’s question was based on the doubt that the faculty of seeing is dispersed throughout the myriad objects, such that the seeing and the objects were inseparable.
To distinguish them: how can one discern objects through seeing, yet without objects there is no seeing? Thus, how easy is it to distinguish between seeing and objects?
Since they cannot be separated into two, one may doubt whether the object is identical to my seeing-nature.
Although the previous question was not explicit in its wording, its meaning actually contained this; by contemplating it, one will naturally gain realization. Therefore, the Buddha—
This refers to the phrase "If one sees this as an object" (*yadi dṛṣṭam idam vastu*). This section of the debate largely initiates its refutations based on this sentence.
"This as an object" means that if one sees this as an object, it must have a visible form and dimensions.
If that were so, then one could also see my seeing. Within the text, there are five instances of the word "I," all of which are the Buddha referring to himself. If...
Regarding the term "seeing" (jiàn) in the phrase "those with the same seeing" (tóngjiànzhě), if we interpret it as "viewing" (kàn), it becomes easy to understand.
The Buddha said: "I and you are viewing the same object together. You therefore know that my "seeing" resides within this one object; for this reason, it is called "my seeing.
If I were not viewing [it], then since "seeing" is itself an object, even without viewing the object, it should still be visible. Why is this?
If you do not see the place where I do not look, yet you claim you can see the place where I do not look, then the characteristic of my non-looking has not yet transcended objects.

This non-looking that does not transcend objects is naturally not the true characteristic of non-looking. If you truly do not see the ground where I do not look, then you will know that seeing is not [seeing].
"Things are manifest; why is this so? Because they have no form or segments that can be seen. Since they have no form, they are not 'things.
If they are not things, then how can you say, 'it is not you'? The phrase 'not you' is Ānanda’s expression of doubt, as stated in his previous question:
'How can I know that this is my true nature? This sentence appears to be a doubt regarding what is not the self."
Because of this intention, the Buddha rebuked him. In the text, the characters for "earth" (di) and "place" (chu) are viewed in the same way;
since ancient commentators used five layers of synthesis to return to their meaning, it seems obscure, and thus I have not employed them.
Furthermore, when you now see an object (up to) "your nature is not true; take my words to seek the reality."

In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One, building upon the previous discussion regarding the meaning of "seeing as an object," further argues that it is certainly not an object, thereby concluding with the true nature (*dharmatā*) to resolve the preceding inquiry. This is yet another argument:

the Buddha says that if seeing were an object, then seeing and the myriad things would both possess substantial form (*dravya*). When you see an object, since you have already seen the object, the object...
Furthermore, when you see [me], there is a confusion between the bodies of sentient beings and non-sentient things.

You and my finger are designated as "sentient," while the various worlds are designated as the "receptacle world" (the environment), which is "non-sentient. Thus, the intermingling of the sentient and the non-sentient prevents any stable establishment [of reality].
Ānanda, [the Buddha] concludes below by clarifying that the merit of seeing belongs to oneself; "How so? he asks below, pointing to the act of seeing.
Is this not truly to blame oneself for harboring doubts while instead seeking the truth from others?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if such is the nature of seeing... [as previously stated] ...I pray that you will bestow your great compassion and expound it for me."
This section of the sutra follows upon Ānanda’s previous observation that the nature of seeing is all-pervasive;

he now poses a question based on calculating the traces of its size, expansion and contraction, and continuity and interruption. "Victorious Treasury" (Śreṣṭha-kośa) refers to that palace being exceptionally adorned and containing a multitude of wonders.
"Dwelling in the palaces of the sun and moon"—the term "dwelling" (ju) has the sense of "facing" (dui)—refers to the Four Heavenly Kings.
The palace faces the palaces of the sun and moon. "Sahā" is translated as "Endurance," meaning it is capable of enduring all sufferings.
"Kālāma" is translated as "Garden of the Assembly," meaning a garden where the Saṃgha dwells.
This is Ānanda’s doubt: if this nature of seeing must belong to me and not to others, then at present, I—
When you look together with the Tathāgata from afar at the palaces of the four heavenly kings, which face those of the sun and moon, this vision encompasses the entire Sahā world-system.
This "Sahā world" is spoken of here merely in terms of a single realm consisting of the four continents;
it is intended to show that the nature of seeing is far-reaching and vast. If I were not looking at what is distant but instead returned to the vihāra, I would see only the monastery grounds.
If one sees what is near yet small, and if it is as if my mind were purified within the inner chamber so that when I raise my eyes I see only the eaves and corridors,
then what is seen is even smaller than small. Ānanda has raised the basis for his doubt based on these traces of seeing—
its distance and proximity, its largeness and smallness, and its expansion and contraction— and now the World-Honored One descends to directly address this doubt.

Question: The text may be understood; my present inquiry below is a concluding question. It is precisely because Ānanda clings to the view that [the self] exists externally that he harbors such doubts.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "In all the world... (omitted)... even excluding the location of the characteristics of empty space."

In this section of the sutra, the Buddha explains the previous doubt through a parable to clarify that the seeing of the large and small follows the objects and is not a matter of expansion or contraction.
"The Buddha said" below is the formal explanation of the previous doubt; "for example" below is the parable clarifying that seeing is neither expanded nor contracted.

Just as emptiness conforms to the squareness or roundness of its vessel, yet emptiness itself is neither fixed as square nor round—since it cannot be taken as a basis for determination, such is the nature of the primary truth (*paramārtha*).
You have come close to it. The metaphors of square and round vessels illustrate distant and near activities;

the emptiness of being neither square nor round illustrates that what is seen is neither expansion nor contraction, neither fixed nor unfixed, neither distant nor near—just as clarified by these metaphors. Your concluding statement below does not understand the intent of this question:
the meaning clarifies that there is no location and yet no non-location, because there is necessarily no fixed place. Therefore, the reprimand asks: "How [is this so]?"
Regarding the passage "If, Ānanda, one further enters below," the meaning of the term "enter" (ru) is understood as penetrating and realizing.
This means that if one wishes to penetrate the ground that is neither square nor round, one need only remove the squareness of the vessel; the essence of space itself has no fixed shape.

This single phrase refers only to the square while omitting the circular aspect because the scribe, in order to form a four-character line, omitted the word "circular" (yuan). Thus, the intended meaning of the circular aspect is implied.

This is like seeing a reflection; the latter two lines should be understood accordingly. Now, empty space has no characteristics of squareness or roundness, and likewise, the nature of seeing has no distance or proximity.

Distance, proximity, largeness, and smallness belong to the objective dusts (*viṣaya*), whereas the nature of seeing is like space—how could it possess characteristics of expansion or contraction, or of being fixed or unfixed? This is also as explained by the analogy.

Regarding the passage from "If, as you asked, when entering the room" up to "it can universally contain the lands of the ten directions," this section of the sutra is the World-Honored One’s direct explanation of the doubt concerning expansion and contraction, and his explicit rebuke of the fault of deluding oneself.

The phrase "If you" and so forth cites the words of the question: it refers to your question regarding how entering the room can contract [space] such that it appears small, and likewise, if one looks upward...
When observing the passage of time, how could one ever pull back the vision to make it equal to the face of the sun?
Since it is impossible to pull it back to make it distant, how could there be any contraction to make it small? Furthermore, you further doubt that walls and buildings can obstruct the vision;
yet if one were to pierce a small hole through them, would the vision from within the wall emerging through that aperture leave any trace of continuity? Certainly not.
