How could there be a severance of conditions when following in the footsteps [of the sages]? For the nature of seeing has no substance; it neither expands nor contracts.

Why then should one attempt to measure or reach it through the numerical quantities of ordinary sentiment? This interpretation is incorrect, as the following section correctly refutes the doubts of the common person.

The phrase "otherwise" (*bùrán*) means that the talk of expansion and contraction is not the correct doctrine. Thus, in the expression "deluding oneself into being an object," the character *jǐ* (self) refers to the person.
One speaks of one’s own mind as being distinct from others due to delusion; once it is grasped as a separate entity, it must possess spatial dimensions.
Possessing spatial dimensions, it is then obstructed by distance, proximity, magnitude, and minuteness.
Consequently, one loses the originally wondrous fundamental mind and becomes driven by external objects. Therefore, one should contemplate within the realm of the sense faculties and their objects.
To view the great as small is to expand and contract; that all sentient beings are deluded regarding themselves is a fault of this very nature.

If one can apply the merit of clear awakening, thinking, "If I can transform objects, then I am equal to the Tathāgata"—meaning that if objects such as the great and small, expansion and contraction, and so forth, follow the turning of my own mind, then I am equal to the Tathāgata—this is what the Tathāgata confronted.
The Superior Beings further state that if one says, "My mind can transform things," then the mind is identical to the Buddha-mind;
when the mind and things are both fused, one is able to achieve the perfect clarity of body and mind, such that self and others are both transformed.

To speak of the "unmoving site of enlightenment" means not to depart from one's current location while pervading the entire Dharma-realm. The two lines following "at the tip of a single hair" [refer to this].
This clarifies the meaning of the unimpeded nature of the one and the many, and the mutual containment of the small and the large:

that even the tip of a single hair, the most minute and smallest of things, can contain the lands of the ten directions. Thus, because all matters of the ultimate great and the ultimate many are transformed by me, they do not depart from me;

one should contemplate this with compassion. For while awakening and delusion differ in essence, and the functions of sentient beings and Buddhas differ, they depend upon whether there is transformation or non-transformation.
[The Buddha replied: "It is merely one interval.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if this essence of vision [extends] from here... please bestow your great compassion and reveal what has not yet been understood.
This section of the sutra shows that Ānanda still clings to the nature of vision as being external, arising in opposition to the internal body and mind.

Regarding my doubt: in the preceding passage, Ānanda raised a doubt based on the distance and magnitude of what is seen; in this present passage, he raises a doubt based on the internal and external, or the "other" and the "self.
The points of doubt are distinct, which students should understand. In the section beginning with "Ānanda," the doubt is that the seeing is located in external objects;
this can be understood through the contrast with the internal body and mind. In the section beginning with "If it were real," it refers to the exterior.
If it is because the visual faculty is truly my mind that it enables me to see, then external seeing would be my self and internal bodily sensation would not be my self.
How does this differ from observing the distinction between the internal and external, or the "other" and the "self"?
As for the Tathāgata’s previous objection that "an object can see me," this is another difficulty raised based on the Buddha’s words; the final two phrases are easily understood.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As for what you have just said... [down to] 'it can only have form, yet there is nothing that cannot be pointed out.

This section of the sutra represents the World-Honored One’s response to the question regarding external perception; he first interrogates him concerning the fact that there is a form which can be pointed out.

The passage beginning with "The Buddha told" first provides a general refutation of the irrationality of clinging to externals; the passage beginning with "If it were real" specifically challenges the notion that there is a form which can be pointed out.
"The grove" refers to a cluster of trees; "the channel" refers to a ditch or canal; the Ganges is before one's eyes. The rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
If you insist that it must be seen before you now, [then] like those various objects, it would be clearly manifest and free from doubt.
This section of the sutra follows from what the World-Honored One has previously listed among identifiable objects, instructing him to select and perceive the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*).

If [the Buddha] were to simply reiterate the previous question, you should now command him to point out the nature of seeing with certainty, speaking words that constitute a direct realization free from doubt.
"Ānanda," and so forth, distinguishes what is not seeing. First, he points to space to distinguish seeing; space is the object.
If seeing is the subject that perceives and the object perceived is empty, then once the perceiving subject—seeing—is established as empty, what further thing could be pointed out as being empty?
If one says it is space (*ākāśa*), space cannot be the subject; thus, that which is empty would not be seeing. Next, regarding the analysis of seeing by means of matter (*rūpa*):
matter is the object perceived and seeing is the subject that perceives. If matter is established as seeing, what further thing could be pointed out [as the object]?
Is this a material object? If you say it is a material object, then its essential nature cannot be altered; if that which is acted upon is immutable, then the object is not what is seen.
Although the myriad phenomena are diverse, they do not transcend the two aspects of form (*rūpa*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*); therefore, we distinguish them simply by means of form and emptiness.
You may now issue the correct command to select for yourself: examine this, investigate this, peel away this, and dissect this until the subtle, wondrous, and pure essence is revealed.
Unmixed, it is called "refined"; luminous, it is called "clear"; unstained, it is called "pure"; and where existence and non-existence are unfathomable, it is called "wondrous.
This nature of seeing possesses these four virtues; this is the fundamental Buddha.
You should, within these myriad phenomena, minutely peel away and analyze this seeing until you can clearly point it out, distinguishing it from material objects.
"If one clarifies that there is no doubt, it will be acceptable.
Ānanda said, "I now, in this multi-storied lecture hall... (up to) the Buddha saying, "So it is, so it is.
This section of the sutra records how Ānanda, having received this instruction, searched among the objects for such a seeing and yet returned with a negative answer.
"Ānanda, below [the text] says: 'Raising his hand and casting his gaze, he searched everywhere; everything was an object, but fundamentally it was not seeing.

Below this, the World-Honored One cites a superior case to illustrate an inferior one, clarifying that among the myriad phenomena there is necessarily no principle for analytically isolating 'seeing'—just as the Buddha has said.
This single phrase directly承接 (takes up) the preceding statement by the Buddha regarding the instruction to analytically isolate 'seeing.'"
This means that just as the Buddha commanded me to analyze and discern the "pure seeing" (*viśuddha-dṛṣṭi*) within objects, I lack the capacity to do so;
even those Bodhisattvas cannot extract the pure seeing from among the myriad phenomena, let alone those of us who are Śrāvakas still in training (*śaikṣa*).
Because their outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet exhausted, and because they are beginners who have only just realized the first fruit (*prathamaphala*), they are so designated.
A *śrāvaka* (voice-hearer) is so called because they realize the fruit by hearing the sound of the fourfold Dharma of realization;

since the present text explains "seeing" based on this, it says there is no such thing as "seeing. Below, however, it explains "seeing" based on "non-seeing," hence it says there is no such thing as "non-seeing.
That both the gates of "is" and "is not" cannot be definitively established—this is where the subtlety lies. The words "The Buddha said" below serve to verify his response.
"This is reasonable.
The Buddha again addressed Ānanda: "As you have said... [up to] among these various objects, which one is not seeing?
This section of the sutra shows the World-Honored One, based on the preceding discussion of "seeing," further interrogating what is "not seeing. The Buddha again addressed [Ānanda].
Regarding the passage beginning with "The aforementioned Ānanda, however, replied," and continuing with "Then you...

which relies on that reply to show that there is no such thing as a 'seeing' [independent of objects], he further interrogates: "Among all things, what else might not be seeing? The meaning of the text is clear and can be understood;
examine closely how seeing and objects are neither identical nor different, neither conjoined nor separated, and how the categories of "is" and "is not" find no counterpart therein.
One immediately perceives that this seeing and its objects possess a wondrous meaning difficult to conceive; their very substance is the Truth, and there is nothing therein that is not so.

For this reason, in the subsequent passage of the Sūtra, the Buddha answers Mañjuśrī by stating that this seeing and its conditions are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi.
Within this wondrously pure essence, the two meanings of "is" and "is not" have never existed from the beginning.
Ānanda said, "I truly see everywhere... (up to) the Buddha saying, "So it is, so it is.
This section of the sutra records Ānanda responding after having been instructed to investigate among objects that there is nothing that is not seeing.
The passage beginning with "Ānanda" summarizes his response to the question, meaning that even when investigating among objects, everything is still seeing.
Regarding the statement "there is nothing that is not seeing," why does the following passage verify and explain that not knowing [the tree] is not seeing?

It is because the tree belongs to the category of material forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), and it is also discussed in contrast to space; its intent is the same as the previous discussion on "seeing. Ānanda raises a doubt, saying: "If the tree is not seeing, how can one see the tree?
If so, then the tree itself must be seeing, and not 'not-seeing'. Furthermore, if the tree were identical to...
Furthermore, how can seeing itself be called a tree? Thus, the tree is not identical to seeing.
When one examines both meanings—that they are either identical or distinct—neither is tenable; therefore, within form, seeing is found to have no fixed location.
Moreover, if space were not seeing, how could one see space? Therefore, space is not non-seeing. Furthermore, if space were identical to seeing...

What is meant by "emptiness"? Thus, emptiness is not identical to seeing. When one examines this through the meaning of their non-duality, since neither [position] is tenable, it is established that within emptiness, the perception of seeing has no fixed locus. Furthermore, I conclude my response below:
I have further reflected that within this emptiness of form and the myriad phenomena, when minutely examined and elucidated, there is not a single thing that is not "neither-it-nor-not-it."
The one who perceives belongs, moreover, to this very perception. Now, the character "is" (shi) is not the "perception" (jian) that corresponds to what precedes it;
when analyzed, it constitutes the "negation of being" (fei-shi). Furthermore, by privately taking "negation" (fei) as its corresponding counterpart, it forms the "negation of negation" (fei-fei).
Thus, we know that "negation" (fei) encompasses two meanings, which can be understood by examining the text. Is an object ultimately "is," or is it ultimately "not"? Its...
"Is it that both are correct, or that both are incorrect? The paths of 'is' and 'is not' are thus muddled and confused.
Therefore, the Tathāgata does not rely on 'is' or 'is not,' but illuminates them with the Truth; thus, there is nothing that is not the Truth.
The Buddha’s words below seal the fact that [the Truth] cannot be attained through a perspective of 'is not.'
At this, the great assembly—those who were not yet those beyond training (up to the point of being learners)—were for a moment struck with terror and lost their composure.

This section of the sutra means that upon hearing these two meanings of "is" and "is not," they did not understand where to turn; they were startled and filled with doubt, thereby losing their steadfastness.
"Not yet those beyond training" refers specifically to those in training (śaikṣa), namely the practitioners of the three lower fruits and all ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).
"Is" ultimately points to the meaning of "non-is," while "is-not" initially points to the meaning of "is.
To be terrified and ashamed such that one loses their composure means that former views—those difficult to escape from within the dual meanings of "is" and "is-not"—are now suddenly swept away.
Consequently, the old foundation has no support and the new mind is not yet awakened; for a moment, the entire assembly feels ashamed and fearful, as if they have lost something.
"The Tathāgata knows that your spirits and anxieties have become agitated and terrified... (until) you should contemplate this with earnest attention so as not to disgrace your sorrowful longing.
This section of the sūtra was spoken by the Buddha out of compassion for the great assembly, who were startled, doubtful, and failed to awaken;

thus he admonished and comforted their hearts, declaring what is "as-it-is" according to the way things truly are. Regarding "the spirits and anxieties becoming agitated and terrified": when a person is first born, there is already a vital breath (*prāṇa*) upon which they depend.

Appendix: "Soul-consideration" (*hónlù*) refers to thought and deliberation. Now, when Ānanda and the others heard the Buddha refute their positions, they were struck with alarm and doubt, losing their composure;
their souls did not return to their dwellings, and their thoughts became frantic. "Change" (*biàn*) refers to transformation; "trembling" (*jié*) is the appearance of the heart being moved.

"Unsurpassed Dharma-King" is a title by which the Buddha refers to himself, meaning that the Buddha is skilled at understanding mundane and supramundane dharmas and has realized the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). There is none above him.
Because he can ascend to the pinnacle as the sovereign of all dharmas, he is called the Unsurpassed Dharma King. Because his speech is not false or deceptive, he is called the Truly Real.

This first phrase is the general statement; the following two phrases are the specific explanation of the meaning of "real. Regarding the phrase "speaking according to what is such" (*yathā-tathatvam*):

the upper character "such" (*tathā*) refers to the wisdom that accords with reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), while the lower character "what is such" (*tathatvam*) refers to the *tathatā* (suchness) that is the object of cognition.
Wisdom is the subjective faculty that takes principle as its object; because it accords with what has been taught, it is said to be "as it was spoken.
Because one’s upright mind is directed toward others, one does not deceive; because one knows and sees reality as it truly is, one does not lie.

Regarding the views of Makkhali previously explained, the four kinds of evasive equivocation concerning immortality—the term "immortal" (amata) refers to the intention that the mind remains active yet indecisive; this is called "evasive" (kuhana).
This refers to the "Evasive Eel-Wriggling" (*amarā-vikkhepa*), which is characterized by forceful, confused, and prolix speech.

Because one may sometimes say "it exists," sometimes say "it does not exist," sometimes say "it both exists and does not exist," or say "it neither exists nor does not exist"—answering in an indeterminate manner—it is called the fourfold evasive eel-wriggling.
Its varieties are not limited to one; as each person adheres to and speculates upon the four positions of existence and non-existence, there are thus four types. This should be understood in detail.
In the passage from the tenth section on the aggregates (*skandha*), "not disgracing" means not failing [one's duty].
Because the Tathāgata saw that the assembly was struck with alarm and doubt, he gave rise to compassion and comforted them with these skillful words; this can be understood according to the text.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, [proceeded] to the section concerning the meaning of seeing form as empty and what is or is not so.

This passage of the sutra records Mañjuśrī’s compassionate response to the alarm and doubt of the assembly, acting on their behalf to pose the inquiry; it first sets forth the thoughts of the assembly.
Ānanda, as the primary interlocutor, was unable to re-ask about the previous doubts because his wisdom was shallow while the principle was profound. Therefore—
Mañjuśrī acts as their advocate; yet this is not a mere repository of conventional reasoning, nor can it be understood without wisdom.
Now, Mañjuśrī manifests fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), and since realization of the truth must necessarily proceed from this wisdom, he advocates on their behalf to resolve the matter.

Upon examining Mañjuśrī’s words of inquiry, they are utterly different from those of the small-capacity practitioners (*hīnayāna*). Those of small capacity investigate within the realm of "is" and "is not," but...
Mañjuśrī had already directly investigated its root with two words, yet the World-Honored One’s response was likewise extraordinary;
he declared that this seeing and its conditions are fundamentally bodhi. Thus, the dualistic meanings of "is" and "is not" were completely resolved.
Therefore it is said: "It is not that wisdom does not illuminate. Zhuangzi also said: "To say 'it is' is one kind of infinity; to say 'it is not' is another kind of infinity."
If one wishes to grasp the pivot of this Way, there is nothing better than to clarify the intention in proximity to this.
World-Honored One, regarding these preceding conditions—the images of form, emptiness, and so forth—within them there is neither "is" nor "is not."
In this section of the sutra, Mañjuśrī requests a profound investigation into the root in order to transcend the threshold of right and wrong.
The World-Honored One subsequently describes the prior debate between right and wrong;
now he explains the reason for the great assembly’s shock and doubt, meaning that they do not know where right and wrong lead. Thus, their fear and trepidation are indeed not without cause.
In the past, my roots of goodness were slight and meager, and I did not believe the Buddha’s words;
how could I have known? "Meager" (*xian*) is synonymous with "scarce" (*xian*).

My sole wish is to clarify, on behalf of others, what these two things—the various phenomena and the essence of seeing—fundamentally are, and whether, between these two, there is neither right nor wrong. This is the direct investigation of the source.
Question: Previously, none of those of lesser capacity had ever asked such a question.

I humbly reflect that from the second fundamental section on "Discerning Views" onward, Mañjuśrī’s inquiry has merely contrasted the seeing-essence as the subject that perceives with form and emptiness as the objects perceived;
he has not yet revealed this to be the truly wondrous mind. It is only here that Mañjuśrī finally investigates its source, and as soon as the World-Honored One—

To present the whole matter at once in response means that the original essence is the wondrous, pure, and luminous substance of bodhi; this precisely points to the second fundamental meaning of the preceding text.

From here below, because Ānanda’s remaining doubts have not yet been severed, [the Buddha] again extensively refutes the four positions (*catuskoṭi*) to determine the sequence of the perfect substance, ensuring there is no confusion. How great is the World-Honored One in guiding sentient beings!
Entering the Tathāgatagarbha and skillfully expounding it is like a crescent moon gradually reaching fullness;

those of meager wisdom cannot fathom or admire it. Yet, do contemporary scholars not err by clinging to a bubble as the ocean, finding self-sufficiency in mere twigs, and instead mocking those who chart a course nine thousand li toward the south?
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī and the great assembly... [up to] "...how could there be 'is' or 'is not' within it?
This section of the sutra is the Buddha’s response to the aforementioned question, which also directly points to the ultimate source.
Whereas Mañjuśrī’s question was not discursive, the World-Honored One’s answer is likewise a direct shortcut. As for the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who abide in *samādhi*:
This samādhi is the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama Samādhi;

it is called "self-abiding" because Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are at no time outside of meditative concentration, never departing from this samādhi whether rising, sitting, moving, or staying—hence it is called "self-abiding.
This refers to what is known as "the nāga is always in concentration; there is no time when it is not in concentration. It is the seeing of the faculty and the seeing of the object.
These objects are the marks of mental conception; this consciousness, within this samādhi, consists of the three—sense organs, objects, and consciousness—which are like flowers in the sky.

How could there ever have been a "sky" [as a separate entity]? The "sky" is used as a metaphor for the substance of samādhi, while the "flowers" are metaphors for the sense organs, objects, and consciousness.

Since the sky is fundamentally without flowers, it is the sick person who falsely clings to them; yet the very nature of these flowers is originally empty space. Therefore, it is said: "This seeing and its conditions are originally..."
The phrase "the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi" refers distantly to the second fundamental name and phrase.
Mañjuśrī, I now ask you: [from here until] "this Mañjuśrī is no Mañjuśrī."
In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One cites an example to clarify that within the sublime mind of supreme enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), there is no characteristic of right or wrong.
When the Buddha addresses Mañjuśrī, he uses Mañjuśrī himself as the illustration, saying: "Mañjuśrī, you are but one; is there another who is Mañjuśrī, or is there no true Mañjuśrī other than you?

The intended meaning is as follows: [The Buddha asks whether, apart from the Mañjuśrī currently present, there exists a second, distinct Mañjuśrī, or if the true Mañjuśrī is none other than the one before him.]
If there were "is," then there would be "is not"; since "is" does not exist, "is not" likewise cannot be obtained.
This is very clear in the answer below the phrase "for the sake of non-existence" (wú wénshū yījù). Furthermore, the character "wénshū" appearing later is a redundant insertion.
"Thus, World-Honored One, in my true Mañjuśrī (up to: therein there is truly no duality of 'is' and 'is not.
This section of the sūtra is Mañjuśrī’s response that within his true Mañjuśrī there is no duality of "is" and "is not.
The two characters "thus" (*evam*) are words of assent; the first two phrases provide a general answer, while the subsequent portion explains why there is none.
This is why, in my previous response, I stated that there is no such thing as Mañjuśrī; the meaning is clear and can be understood.
The Buddha said: "This wondrous clarity of vision, along with all empty spaces and objects, [occupying] the space between them, is itself neither this moon nor not this moon."
This section of the sutra follows the World-Honored One’s pattern of using Mañjuśrī as an example to emphasize that the true moon is luminous and non-dual.
The passage beginning with "The Buddha said" correctly aligns with the preceding pattern; therefore, it states, "it is likewise.

Regarding the phrase "this seeing is wondrously luminous," the two characters "wondrously luminous" (miào-míng) refer directly to the function of the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*); there is no need to cite the "wondrous mind" (*miao-xin*) or explain them as being empty of dust and phenomena.
The meaning of "shadow" (*chāyā*) and "manifestation" (*prabhāsvara*) is that the seeing is the subject that perceives form, while emptiness is the object perceived;

however, the characteristics briefly conceived are also shadows and manifestations within the sense organs and their objects. Thus, by bringing together these various characters, one realizes that the root of all these delusions is the true essence of Bodhi.

It is only because sentient beings are deluded that they turn their backs on awakening and unite with the objects of dust, falsely creating the sense organs, objects, and so forth. This is the fundamental basis.
The term "wondrous clarity" (*miaoming*) precisely reveals that the wondrous mind can be separated from or joined with the aforementioned "wondrous clarity";

this should be viewed as such. Just as the preceding passage was called a "skillful explanation" by singling out the faculty of sight, the present passage adds the word "hearing" to shadowily reveal that all six sense faculties are illusory, and that there is only the single true mind without any other separate phenomena.
This is like the second moon appearing beneath the water, which uses a further metaphor to clarify the point. It says:
Just as the second moon is originally produced by pressing on the eyes, its entire substance is illusory; why then discuss whether it is a moon or not a moon?
The World-Honored One again called to Mañjuśrī and said to him: "There is only the single true moon; fundamentally, there is neither 'this moon' nor 'not this moon.
Although the second moon is fundamentally illusory, it does not depart from the truth. Apart from the truth, there is no illusion at all."
The false is itself the true; do not view it through the lens of nihilistic views (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), for the true mind is likewise so.

Therefore, as you now observe the seeing and the objects (up to "therefore able to cause you to emerge from 'this is a finger' or 'this is not a finger'"), it can lead you out of the distinction between "this is a finger" and "this is not a finger."
This section of the sutra concludes the Buddha’s response by clarifying the difference between the objects of delusion and awakening.

Specifically, it summarizes the observation of those who are deluded, stating: "If you, all of you, seek to manifest enlightenment based on the various distinctions of the sense organs, sense objects, consciousness, and their internal, external, or intermediate states, this is called false conceptualization; within such false conceptualization, it is difficult to escape."
This is not because one is submerged and unable to emerge; rather, it is from these two characters "from this" (*yóu shì*) that we discern the contemplation of those who have attained awakening.
One should view these two characters in contrast to the preceding two characters "for this reason" (*shì yǐ*). Each pair serves as a heading:
delusion and awakening diverge within these four characters. That is to say, if one can manifest [the truth] through this subtle, true, and wondrous mind, then there is no dharma.
Since it is not the true essence, how could there be "is" or "is not"? Therefore, it can cause you to emerge from [the duality of] "pointing" and "not pointing.
"Pointing is not pointing" is precisely "non-is. This is because the preceding passage contained the phrase "is and is-not-is"; thus, the phrasing is altered here to say "pointing is not pointing.
This is merely a discussion of the meaning of "is" and "is-not" as explained in the *Zhuangzi*, in the "Qi Wulun" (On the Equalization of Things). Indeed, this scripture...

Since this was transcribed by Fang Gong, it frequently employs characters from the Five Classics and the various philosophical treatises (*zhǐzǐ*). Although these characters are borrowed from those sources, their meanings here are actually different;
the discerning reader should examine this. Previously, Ānanda’s request spoke of manifesting the two natures—arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-non-ceasing—to clarify the nature that is revealed.
Now, from "thereby" (*yóushì*) onwards, the text correctly manifests the nature that is revealed as non-arising-and-non-ceasing.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, it is truly as the Dharma King has said... [omitted] ...pervading the ten directions; what difference is there?

This section of the sutra records Ānanda’s inquiry arising from hearing the principle that the nature of awakening pervades all. He poses this question to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox. "Truly as follows":
the character *yuan* (緣, condition) in "awakening conditions" (*jue yuan*) should be read as *yuan* (元, source/origin); otherwise, it is likely a scribal error from the translation site.
However, explaining it by means of the character "condition" (yuan) is itself a condition that is without conditions; this is the question posed by following the preceding text.
Ānanda takes up this meaning to raise an objection, asking how [this] is distinguished from the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) doctrine of a pervasive self (ātman).
"Brahmin" (brahmacārin) is a general designation for non-Buddhists; Sāṃkhyas and those with views regarding the obscure principle (avidyā-tattva) were mentioned previously.

Regarding those who practice self-immolation by throwing themselves into ashes and so forth, these are the ascetic non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), such as those who pluck out their hair, fumigate their noses, or lie upon beds of thorns.

Among these various non-Buddhist sects, there are those who conceive of a real self (*ātman*) that pervades the ten directions, as described in treatises such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
However, these non-Buddhists do not recognize the existence of the eighth consciousness; instead, they take this eighth consciousness and falsely grasp it as the divine self (*puruṣa*).
I, Ānanda, have cited that comparison of similarities and differences.
The World-Honored One also once, at Mount Laṅkā... [attained] the wondrously enlightened nature of the true mind.

This section of the sutra follows Ānanda’s reception of the aforementioned teaching on the "divine self" (*puruṣa*), wherein he further cites the Buddha’s words to pose a question regarding the comparison with *svabhāva* (nature).
Laṅkā is the name of a mountain located in the southern sea of India; in Sanskrit, Laṅkā is translated as "Inaccessible.
It is five hundred *yojanas* high, overlooking the great ocean, and lacks gates on its flanks; it cannot be reached except by those who have attained spiritual powers.
Because it is inaccessible to ordinary travel, the World-Honored One formerly expounded the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* on this mountain for Mahāmati and others, extensively refuting the non-Buddhists.
At the beginning of the second fascicle of that sūtra, Mahāmati asks the Buddha:
"The Tathāgatagarbha that you teach as pervading the ten directions—what is the difference between it and the 'Self' (*ātman*) taught by those non-Buddhists which also pervades the ten directions?"
The Buddha replied that the *tathāgatagarbha* is not the same as the "self" (*ātman*) imagined by non-Buddhists, and so forth.

In this sutra, it refers to the nature of awakening (*bodhi-svabhāva*), while in that sutra, it refers to the *tathāgatagarbha*; thus, the names differ but the essence is the same. Furthermore, in that sutra, the Buddha refutes the non-Buddhist reckoning of "spontaneity" (*svayambhū*) as *nirvāṇa*, saying:
"I teach dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), not the realm of spontaneity claimed by those non-Buddhists. I [the Buddha] say... [this is my teaching].
The Tathāgata himself declared this to refute spontaneity (*svabhāva*) by means of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
"Causes and conditions" refers to internal nature as the cause and external assistance as the condition. Regarding "spontaneity," the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"Who could create the variegated patterns of a peacock’s feathers or the sharpness of a thorn? There is no creator. Therefore, [these things] do not arise spontaneously.

Regarding the phrase "I now declare it to be spontaneous" (*svabhāva*): Ānanda is suggesting here that the essence of this awakened nature belongs to spontaneity and is not a phenomenon subject to arising, ceasing, or inversion;

therefore, he seems to imply that it is not the *hetu-pratyaya* (causes and conditions) taught by the Tathāgata. If that were so, it would be identical to the "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*) postulated by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
The final four lines are easy to understand.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "I now [explain] in this way... [down to] one must personally discern that there is a nature of spontaneity (*svabhāva*).

This section of the sutra records the World-Honored One reprimanding him for his failure to realize the truth and for again calculating a cause of spontaneity; he once more refutes and dismantles it. As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another; they do not arise from both, nor are they without cause."

For this reason, it is said that there is no arising; now Ānanda has drawn out the causes and conditions of spontaneity (*svabhāva*), which then fully encompasses the four modes of existence (*catur-koṭi*).
The Buddha told him [the following] to refute his objection: first, he rebuked him for not yet having awakened while still calculating spontaneity.
The Buddha said: "In the preceding text, I have repeatedly informed you with the truth; why have you not yet awakened, and why are you further deluded by taking it to be spontaneous?"
However, Ānanda, you must personally discern this for yourself: if there is indeed a substantial reality, then your calculation may be permitted;

if there is no such reality, then your delusion will naturally come to an end. Now, I shall first present the intent of the refutation, followed by the specific refutations of the objects, precisely because the nature of awakening pervades all phenomena;
thus, the refutation is conducted in relation to these objects.
"You should now observe this wondrously luminous seeing" (up to) "taking emptiness as self and taking obstruction as self.
This section of the sutra, in which the World-Honored One intends to refute intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), first sets forth four objects to demonstrate that intrinsic nature is unreal.
For although the various phenomena of form and emptiness differ in a thousand ways, they generally do not exceed these four categories; therefore [this is taught].
The general summary is followed by a specific refutation:
"Ānanda, if light were self-originated, you should not see darkness" [up to] "how could the nature of seeing be severed and extinguished so that it can see light?
This section of the sutra shows the World-Honored One following the preceding analysis of objects to specifically refute them, thereby clarifying that the nature of seeing is not spontaneous.

The substance [of this] is as follows: Ānanda, the preceding section on refuting [the perception of] light can be understood by following the text. Thus, the subsequent brief refutation of the obstructed object proceeds directly to the refutation of darkness;
therefore, it says "up to" (乃至). Regarding the third point, the refutation of darkness and all such things:

this means that the characteristics of darkness are not singular, each belonging to its respective sensory field (*viṣaya*). For instance, clouds, mist, gloom, mountains, rivers, rocks, and walls can all [serve as the basis for the perception of darkness].
Because "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*) is itself darkness, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) has been added; the rest is understandable.
However, since the term "breaking through obstructions" (*prabhedana*) is the opposite of emptiness, it has been omitted.
Ānanda said: "If this wondrous nature of vision is not self-arisen, how does its meaning accord with the nature of dependent origination?"
In this section of the sutra, Ānanda, upon hearing the refutation of the notion of "self," immediately shifts his calculation to the nature of cause and condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
As for the meaning of cause and condition: that which is the primary nature is the cause, and that which is the auxiliary nature is the condition.

If there were no auxiliary conditions, the cause would be unable to produce [the result]. This principle belongs to the commonality [of all things], just as the seed is the primary nature, while earth, water, and human labor are the auxiliary conditions.
When external auxiliary conditions assist its cause, the sprout arises; without them, it does not arise by its own nature. Therefore, it is called "co-arising.
Now, Ānanda, having heard the Buddha refute the doctrine of spontaneity (*svabhāva*), his inquiry was exhausted, and he next calculated based on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Although he shifted his calculation to this, his mind had not yet understood the meaning of causes and conditions. Thus, he inquired below, properly asking about causes and conditions, saying: "How is it so?"
"Can one obtain the nature of combined causes and conditions?

The Buddha said, "Regarding what you say about causes and conditions, I shall question you further. [The text continues] "...until: 'Is there seeing because of emptiness? Is there seeing because of obstruction?
This section of the sutra follows the opponent's calculations to refute them; first, it refutes the meaning of 'cause' by enumerating four objects."

As before, the character "seeing" (*jian*) in the phrase "seeing-nature" (*jian-xing*) refers to the perceived object, while the character "nature" (*xing*) in "seeing-nature" refers to the perceiving faculty.

Below, the four objects are listed in general; in this passage, the condition that gives rise to the self and serves as the primary cause for the manifestation of the self belongs to the meaning of the "conditioning cause" (*yuan-yin*).
This is because clarity and so forth belong to the other [the object], whereas seeing belongs to the self.
"Ānanda, if [the seeing] existed because of light, one should not see darkness... (up to) ...because of emptiness or because of obstruction, it would be the same as with light and darkness.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding discussion by specifically refuting each object to demonstrate that the nature of seeing is not produced by causes;
the text is easily understood. Thus, below, the two objects of emptiness and obstruction are briefly refuted in the same manner as light and darkness.
Furthermore, Ānanda, this vision [extends] from "furthermore" to "there is vision conditioned by space and there is vision conditioned by obstruction.
This section of the sutra follows the previous refutation of the meaning of conditions and likewise enumerates the four objects as before.
Why does the Buddha analyze them through causes and conditions? It is because if the notion of a self arises, then conditions cannot function.
Because birth merely assists me by means of birth, it is called a "proximate cause" (hetu) and a "distant condition" (pratyaya); thus, they are refuted through two distinct gates.
Following the meaning of the preceding section on causes, the word "furthermore" (fu-ci) is added to refute conditions as well.

"Ānanda, if [the seeing] were dependent upon space, it should not encounter obstruction... (up to) being dependent upon light or dependent upon darkness would be the same as encountering space or obstruction.
This section of the sutra follows from the preceding discussion by refuting the object-conditions individually, in order to clarify that the nature of seeing is not contingent upon conditions.
The text is easily understood. The subsequent sections on light and darkness are omitted here because their refutation is identical to the refutation of space and obstruction mentioned previously.

In the preceding passage, the refutation of the cause details light and darkness while omitting space and obstruction; in the present passage, the refutation of the conditions details space and obstruction while omitting light and darkness.
These texts complement one another; one should grasp their underlying meaning and harmonize them.

One should know that this section of the sutra—from "Thus, this refined awareness is wondrously luminous" to "detached from all marks, it is identical with all dharmas"—is the World-Honored One’s direct revelation of the true essence.
Having inherited the preceding arguments, he successively refutes various attachments and sweeps away all common misconceptions.
The two characters "thus" (*rúshì*) refer to the following phrase, "refined awareness is wondrously luminous. "Refined awareness" (*jīngjué*) refers to...

Because the essence of seeing (*jìng*) explains that the nature of seeing (*jiàn-xìng*) is far removed from all faults and is thus true awakening (*zhēn jué*), it does not speak of "seeing" but rather of "awakening.

The character *jìng* (essence) reflects the meaning of the essence of seeing; the two subsequent lines [of the verse] do not introduce new causes and conditions, but rather follow the preceding by dispelling the two views of cause-and-condition (*yīn-yuán*). The two following lines alternately dispel the notions of spontaneity (*zìrán*) and non-spontaneity (*bù zìrán*), as well as the notions of "is" and "is not," and "neither-is-nor-is-not. 1. [The first line: "The essence of seeing is explained as the nature of seeing being far removed from all faults, which is precisely true awakening; therefore, it is called 'awakening' rather than 'seeing. 2. [The second line: "The character 'essence' (*jìng*) reflects the meaning of the essence of seeing; the intent is not to establish further causes and conditions. 3. [The third line: "The two subsequent lines inherit the preceding by dispelling the two calculations of cause-and-condition. 4. [The fourth line:
"The two following lines alternately dispel spontaneity and non-spontaneity, 'is' and 'is not,' and 'neither-is-nor-is-not. 5. [The fifth line: "One. (This indicates the conclusion of the section.)

The phrase "generally dispelling" refers to the four negations of causes, conditions, spontaneity, and so forth. Furthermore, regarding "neither non-being nor not non-being," the character "wu" (無) runs through the latter half of the sentence.
"Not non-being" means there is no "non-being" and no "not non-being.

As for "not non-non-being," the four negations mentioned above were a single refutation of [the notions of] non-cause, non-condition, and so on; now, this is a further double refutation of [the notions of] non-cause-and-condition and non-spontaneity.
Therefore, it is said that there is nothing that is not non-; "non" refers to the absence of both the prior positions of "is" and "is not.
The word "non" also extends through the latter half of the sentence, meaning there is neither "is" nor "is not. When human sentiments are exhausted, sagely wisdom is revealed;
this very vision, free from error, is precisely the wondrously luminous true awakening. However, as for this wondrously luminous true...
Awakening pervades all places; it is neither localized nor non-localized. Simply by being free from all marks, all phenomena are the very essence of awakening.
Thus, the three—roots, objects, and consciousness—as well as the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, are not phenomena that are not true;
these so-called aggregates, bases, and elements are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness.
"How can you now apply your mind within this? [up to] "How can empty space be grasped by you?

This section of the sutra shows that within the Dharma that transcends faults, it is truly difficult to apply the mind; thus, the Buddha rebukes those who engage in frivolous proliferation as being merely a vain exertion.
Regarding the phrase "How can you now," "within this" refers to the Dharma that transcends faults. "Apply" (措) means to settle or place [the mind].

The mind is Ānanda’s mind seeking the Way; it is called the essence of wondrous enlightenment and clarity, far removed from all faults, like a great mass of fire that burns anything touched from any of its four sides.

How can you now, pointing at this [body], identify the mind by means of worldly causes and conditions or various frivolous conceptualizations (*prapañca*), and thereby differentiate these names of frivolous conceptualization?

"Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the aforementioned categories of cause, non-cause, conditions, spontaneity, and so forth, all of which are termed "worldly conceptual proliferation" (*prapañca*) and "names and characteristics" (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*).
"All worldly beings" refers to various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), devas, māras, spirits, nāgas, seers, and others, as they all possess such theories.
"Conceptual proliferation" is like the play of children; it lacks any real meaning. Thus, the following uses analogies to clarify this point.

Your frivolous arguments are merely a waste of effort; you say that space has no form and cannot be grasped by touch, yet even if you were to try to grasp it, you would only increase your own fatigue.
How can you seize that which has no form? This same principle applies to the wondrously luminous true awakening, which likewise cannot tolerate being scrutinized or conceptualized.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding the statement that the nature of wondrous enlightenment must [arise] from the mind or from the eyes—what is the meaning of this?
This section of the sutra has Ānanda taking up the previous points of negation and again citing the Buddha’s words to challenge the current point of negation.
From 'must be wondrous' onwards, he takes up the previous points of negation; from 'what is the meaning' onwards, he cites past teachings to prove the present negation."
These are the four conditions as follows: these four conditions are the conditions for the arising of vision, for if these four conditions are lacking, vision does not arise.
"Because of space" means that the eye perceives objects by being separated from them; it is because the field before it is empty and vast that vision becomes manifest.
"Because of light" means that although the field before it is empty, if there were no light from the sun, moon, or lamps, vision would not exist.
Regarding "because it depends on the mind": the mind is *manasikāra* (attention), which is termed "discrimination" within *vijñapti-mātra*. Discrimination is precisely attention;
this means that although one has attained the clarity of emptiness, if one does not attend [to it], the eyes are like those of a blind person.

If there were no attention, then even if black, yellow, red, and purple were displayed before one, there would be no discernment. Regarding "because it depends on the eye": although there is emptiness...
Regarding the clarification of mental attention (*manasikāra*): if there were no seeing by means of the eye, from what would the eye be manifested as the gateway to seeing?
Without a gateway, seeing is not manifested; therefore, it is necessary that all four conditions be present for seeing to arise, for it cannot occur if even one is lacking.

What is the meaning of this? The phrase "precisely" (*eva*) is a term of exclusion, implying: "Is it not the case that the Blessed One, who formerly relied upon causes and conditions, now suddenly abandons them?"
"Is there not a contradiction between what you have said before and now? Please explain the meaning of your refutation and establishment.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda, I have taught that the various characteristics of causes and conditions in the world are not the ultimate truth (paramārtha)."
In this section of the sutra, the Buddha demonstrates that the establishment or rejection of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), as well as their coarseness or subtlety, each has its own basis.
In the present text, "causes and conditions" carries the meaning of "conjunction. As previously seen, the realization of the nature of seeing must depend upon the four conditions to be accomplished;

therefore, the convergence of various conditions is termed "causes and conditions. All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) in the world exist through such conjunction and do not [exist otherwise].
This is the supreme ultimate truth of the world-transcending realm. Within this ultimate truth, the empty void is utterly beyond conceptual points, while wondrous existence is fully encompassed.
Previously, these were established by means of conventional truth; now, they are set aside because one has returned to the ultimate truth. The coarse and the wondrous are thus worlds apart;
one must not use the former coarseness to challenge the latter wondrousness. This is precisely the fundamental intent of the Buddha.
"Ānanda, I ask you again: among the people of the world... [they] cannot see the three kinds of light.
This section of the sutra, in which the World-Honored One follows the preceding discussion to refute the four conditions, first examines the actual meaning of seeing and not seeing.
First, "Ānanda," and so forth, is the Buddha’s question; the word "my" (*wo*) used by me refers to the people of the world. Next...
Ānanda’s response below, concerning the meaning of seeing and not seeing, can be understood from the text.
[The passage] from "If Ānanda, when there is no light, it is called 'not seeing'" up to "both are called 'seeing,' so how could it be 'not seeing'? [is explained therein].
In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One provides a detailed analysis of the meanings of "seeing" and "not seeing" to clarify the permanence of the nature of seeing.

The text contains three points: first, from "Ānanda," below, he refutes the meaning of not seeing; second, from "Ānanda," below, he cites darkness and compares it to light, showing that both are termed "not seeing";
third, from "If again," below, he uses a counter-argument to show that what was called "not seeing" is in fact transformed into "seeing. First, [the refutation of not seeing].
"Regarding the statement 'not seeing light,' this restates the meaning of Ānanda’s claim that he does not see. The words 'should not be so' are the Buddha’s refutation. The Buddha said:
'If you say that the absence of light is called "not seeing," then you should also not see darkness. This very vision that sees darkness is also called "seeing.
Why, then, do you say you do not see? Next, regarding the statement 'in the dark, not seeing light,' it is called 'not seeing.'"
"Regarding 'seeing' and so forth," this refers back to what was stated previously concerning "darkness. Now, by contrast, it concerns "light. The Buddha says:
"When you were in darkness, you did not see light, and you called that 'not seeing. Now, while in light, you do not see the characteristic of darkness, and yet you also call that 'not seeing.
Thus, in both cases there is non-seeing; why then do you claim that when you see light, you are 'seeing'? This repeats the previous argument three times.
To see both [light and darkness] is called "mutual encroachment" (*ling*). This "encroachment and usurpation" refers to the mutual encroachment and usurpation between light and darkness;
it does not mean that your seeing-nature momentarily exists or momentarily ceases in response to that light or darkness.
Thus, seeing darkness and seeing light are both called "seeing. Why, then, do you claim that you do not see? This first section clarifies that light and darkness exist.
In the second section, both [aspects] are negated; therefore, what is called "seeing" is termed "not seeing. In the third section, both [aspects] are affirmed;
therefore, what is termed "not seeing" is called "seeing.
For this reason, Ānanda, you should now know that when there is an obstruction, the seeing is not itself the obstruction.
This section of the sutra serves as the World-Honored One’s comprehensive summary of the preceding discourse on the analysis of views (*dṛṣṭi*).

Here, by separating the subjective and objective aspects, he directly shatters the essence of view (*dṛṣṭi-śarīra*) and returns to the meaning of *śamatha*. Within this passage, the four characteristics—light, darkness, emptiness, and obstruction—are the objective objects (*ālambana-viṣaya*);
the four instances of the word "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) are the subjective faculties (*indriya*). Although there are these four pairs of objects and faculties, the "views" themselves are the subject.
If it is now said that the single entity is seen but not perceived as light and so forth, then the perceiving faculty and the perceived object would be split apart.
First, the objects are dispatched below; then, the faculties are dispatched again. The meaning of the text is clearly understandable.

Furthermore, the concluding passage below—when considered broadly—comprehensively encompasses the entire argument regarding seeing; when considered narrowly, it concludes the preceding discussion on causes and conditions, spontaneity, and the four conditions.
The characteristics of their conjunction can be seen within the text;

however, although this seeing and its conditions were already identified in the preceding Mañjuśrī chapter as being fundamentally the true substance and true meaning of bodhi, Ānanda’s various doubts had not yet been fully resolved, so they were removed sequentially.
Furthermore, the previous text stated: "Although this seeing is not the wondrously pure and luminous mind..."
In the second month, one was only able to discern the "seeing-essence" (*darśana-vijñāna*) and had not yet eliminated it;
now, as the following text refutes it, the "second moon" finally vanishes.

The sequence of the sutra’s textual structure, its vital connections, and its source-currents cannot be fathomed through the inner sanctum unless one calms the mind, empties oneself, and investigates and studies them thoroughly; otherwise, one will often see those who cling to the "swallow."
There are many stones that become fine jade.
You should further understand that the four meanings are accomplished [until: "do not grow weary on the wondrous path to Bodhi.
This section of the sutra, the World-Honored One, following the preceding, concludes the refutation of the "ability to see," returns to the source, and deeply urges those who have not yet reached it.

This leads to the diligent advancement [of practice] through the accomplishment of the four meanings. One phrase承接 (links up) the above, where subject and object have already been severed, and initiates the following text that refutes the "subject" (the seer).
Therefore it says: "At the time of seeing the seer, the seer is not the seer. This is a statement that dispels the "seeing subject.
Previously it was said that "the faculty is not the object"; now it is said that "the seer is not the seer"—a single phrase suffices.
The second month has already broken it. Regarding the two characters "seeing-seeing" (*jian-jian*): the upper "seeing" is true seeing.

According to the subsequent example of the separate karmic activities (*bieye*), the text says: "The awareness of what is perceived is an eye-disease; the awareness itself is not within the eye-disease. This is truly "seeing-seeing.

Thus, one knows that the upper character "seeing" here is that same character "awareness" (*jue*) from the previous passage; awareness is true awareness. The lower character "seeing" is the former... [text fragment].

The ability to see while not being the seer is precisely the elimination of the "ability to see" (*nengjian*). This is the true [seeing] (*zhen*); the inferior is the seeing-substance (*jianjing*). "Not" (*fei*) is the meaning of elimination;
that is to say, true seeing is not the seeing-substance which is capable of objective cognition. The following two phrases, "the seeing is still...
and so forth, mean that the aforementioned true seeing is further removed from even the name and traces of "seeing. "Removed" (*li*) is also a sense of elimination; thus, it refers to that...
The ability to see [the truth] is such that it cannot be attained; how could the various false conceptualizations mentioned below ever reach it?

The "conditions" (hetu-pratyaya) and "spontaneity" (svabhāva) can be understood through the principle of conjunction (*sāmagrī*), which refers to the characteristic of the conjunction of the four conditions.

This briefly indicates the meaning of "is" and "is not" and so forth, stating that true vision is like this: how could those various false conceptualizations possibly reach it? You [should] now proceed with the lower strategy.
"Superior practice" means that you, as a śrāvaka, have narrow and inferior aspirations;

your knowledge is not extensive, and you are unable to penetrate the pure reality-mark (dharmatā) that is free from faults and transcends all deviations. This pure reality-mark is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya);
the ultimate truth is the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of wondrously enlightened clarity. Herein, the section on *śamatha* should be concluded.
What is meant by "meaning" (*artha*)? It refers to the "true aspect" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). The true aspect pertains to *dhyāna*, for the three [samādhis] are perfectly interfused.
Thus, the true aspect is also manifested within *śamatha*; it is precisely because they are "three while being one" that they are appropriately termed *śamatha*.

Now, because this is "one while being three," it points to the true aspect. The Buddha’s profound instruction says: "One should contemplate well; one should contemplate well. As for "contemplating well":
To immediately accord with the reality-mark (*dharmatā*), to penetrate deeply into its perfect fusion, and to hear and practice this—this is called "skillful reflection.
To not give rise to weariness or indolence regarding this is the path to the wondrous Bodhi; it specifically refers to *śamatha* and the other [meditative practices] as the path to unsurpassed Bodhi.
Because these three—one, three, and one—are perfectly fused, unimpeded, and inconceivable, they are termed "wondrous."
The fifty-five stages mentioned in the subsequent scripture constitute this path, for within each stage one practices based on these three contemplations.
Thus, the preceding section has completed the demonstration of the true meaning of śamatha—breaking through delusion to reveal the real.
In the following section, because Ānanda has not yet realized the meaning that "the seeing of seeing is not seeing," [the Buddha] further elucidates the subtle and esoteric principles within śamatha.

This contemplative observation clarifies that both the delusions of sameness and difference are utterly exhausted; it merely reveals the profound and hidden nuances within the meaning of "seeing the seeing.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha, World-Honored One... [said]... He wept with compassion, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, and received the holy instructions.
In this section, because Ānanda’s realization through hearing and seeing had penetrated deeply—far surpassing his previous state of delusion—he requested further instruction once more.
This passage contains three points of inquiry: two are primary questions and one is a secondary question.

First, he recounts the meanings of causality, spontaneity, and their combination or non-combination; yet his mind was still not fully opened. "Not opened" means that his understanding was not yet complete.
This is a secondary intention; examine it closely. Although Ānanda has not yet formally requested instruction, his underlying purpose is not unrelated to what follows.
After the Buddha answers the formal question, he immediately addresses the meaning of "harmony" and "disharmony.

One should know that while Ānanda’s current stated intention is indeed what he wishes to hear, the most vital point actually lies within the meaning of "seeing the seer and awakening to the mind. Therefore, the latter two intentions constitute the formal question.
Below this, the World-Honored One’s response first addresses the primary point and subsequently the secondary; the sequence is evident.

Now, when Ānanda asks why "seeing the seeing" is not "seeing," and his confusion and distress increase further, it is because since the beginning of the analysis of "seeing," the purpose has only been to discern the essence of the visual faculty (*darśana-viśuddhi*), while the meaning of breaking through the substance of seeing itself remains superficial.
This is what is meant by "like a second moon"; yet now he speaks of "seeing."
To see that which is not seeing is not merely to depart from the objects; it is also to shatter the faculty of seeing.

That which is shattered is the object of seeing, while the true seeing that performs the shattering is the subject. Yet even this true seeing that performs the shattering must have its name and traces dispensed with—is this not far more profound than what preceded it?
Thus, Ānanda’s confusion and distress will surely intensify. As for what follows in the text...
It is said that the subtle and profound contemplation truly lies herein.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "this seeing sees that which is not seeing," Ānanda previously combined the first two phrases into one; he spoke of it earlier as: "When this seeing sees, that seeing is not seeing.
There is no technique for the artful opening and closing of the phrasing more exquisite than this in the sutra. The above is what Ānanda described regarding his state of delusion; below—

I humbly pray that you remove this [obstruction] and correctly request the essence of awakening. Regarding the phrase "Great Wisdom" (*mahāmati*) in the second line, it should be viewed in contrast to the preceding "Vast Compassion" (*mahāmaitrī*).
Vast Compassion is the Buddha’s path-essence (*mārga-svabhāva*), while Great Wisdom is the Buddha’s illuminating function (*prabhāva-vṛtti*).

This is because Great Wisdom constitutes the essence of both the provisional and ultimate wisdoms of *mahāprajñā*: ultimate wisdom illuminates principle (*tattva*), while provisional wisdom discerns capacities (*indriya*). It is like a person with two... [eyes].

Because it is the eye, it is called the "Eye of Great Wisdom. Now, Ānanda requests the bestowal of the two wisdoms—the provisional and the ultimate—as eyes to mirror his own capacity and illuminate that True Principle;
thus, he harmonizes with both principle and capacity to reveal the awakened mind. The following three phrases may be understood accordingly.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda... [down to] ...those with outflows shall attain the fruit of Bodhi.
This section of the sutra represents the World-Honored One’s response to the request to see the Seer and awaken to the Mind;

first, he rebukes much learning, and subsequently, he provides instruction and benefit. From "At that time" onwards is the speech of the compiler; from "addressing Ānanda" onwards is the Buddha's own words.
Regarding the initial passage where he is about to expound the Great Dhāraṇī: the Sanskrit term *dhāraṇī* is translated as "total retention" (*zongchi*).
Ancient commentators explain that it means "to totalize all phenomena and to maintain immeasurable meanings.
However, since this meaning of "total retention" belongs to *samādhi*, it is indicated here in connection with *samāpatti*. The general purport of this passage follows from the preceding conclusion.
The exposition on the meaning of *śamatha* is now complete; hereafter, I shall proceed to expound upon *samādhi*. Therefore, the compiler records its title to manifest it.
Furthermore, because Ānanda had not yet clarified the profound meaning within *śamatha*, he requested further instruction.
The Buddha then demonstrated for him the two types of delusion—identity and difference—as well as the characteristics of their harmony and discordance, thereby perfecting the preceding doctrine.
From the passage "Below this, you yourself have not yet clarified" until the beginning of the *Samādhi-sūtra*, the sequence of the text's rise and fall is vast and far-reaching;
yet commentators have been muddled by it, each clinging to their own views and setting forth many divergent paths.

Consequently, the general course and systematic order of the original sūtra have become disordered, and its essential meaning is obscured and entangled. This is truly because the wise go too far while the ignorant do not reach it enough. Alas!
The threshold of the Sublime Adornment is truly not easy to enter. Next, he addresses Ānanda; the following passage contains two points.

First, he rebukes the strength of much learning and powerful memory. "Strong" (qiáng) should be read with a level tone. "Memory" (jì) refers to the diligent and unforgetting retention of what has been heard, which is called powerful memory.
However, in the world there are those who have heard much but possess little retention, and there are also those who do retain it.
To maintain [the teachings] while lacking extensive learning is a deficiency; now, because the Venerable One possesses both virtues, he is called foremost in extensive learning.

However, the Buddha here disparages mere retentive memory and instead emphasizes increasing extensive learning, for since extensive learning itself belongs to the outflows (*āsrava*), one cannot yet penetrate deeply into the path of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
"Subtle and secret contemplation" refers to that which is refined, minute, and hidden within *śamatha*.
The practice of "mysterious principle" is called contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*). "Observation" is itself "illumination. This is explained within the context of *śamatha* (calm abiding);
it does not refer to the meaning of contemplative observation within *samādhi*. Therefore, it is said: "Within *śamatha*, there is subtle and mysterious contemplative observation.

Ānanda had hitherto investigated only the external sense organs and their objects, which was still shallow; now, through the teaching on the meaning that "the seeing of seeing is not seeing," he has entered deeply into the principle.

To discuss this matter, one must first understand that the Buddha, having diagnosed the illness of excessive learning through his reprimands, subsequently administered the medicine of meditative concentration (*samādhi*);

this constitutes the sequential instruction and benefit. "You now," and so forth, is an admonition to listen and receive [the teaching], which provides equal benefit for both the present and the future.
"Ānanda, all sentient beings transmigrate through the world... (until) they arise in their respective places and revolve according to their karma.
This section of the sutra represents the Buddha’s response—using the "hidden illumination within cessation"—to the question regarding the seeing of seeing and the awakened mind;
it begins with the two inversions. "All sentient beings" refers to those in the six realms, and "the world" likewise refers to the six realms as the basis upon which they depend.
"Retribution arises from two inverted views and delusions" refers to the two delusions of the sense organ and its object within the eye-faculty;

these two delusions arise from the mind of inverted discrimination. Because these two delusions give rise to afflictions and the creation of karma, retribution is experienced—ascending through good and descending through evil.
This is the inevitable principle that cannot be altered. The final two lines of this section demonstrate affliction, karma, and suffering.

The "corresponding state" refers specifically to the present moment of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). If this present mindfulness gives rise to what is wholesome, one performs wholesome karma and transmigrates through the good realms;
if this present mindfulness gives rise to what is unwholesome, one performs unwholesome karma and transmigrates through the evil realms.

Wholesomeness consists of the human, celestial, and *asura* realms, while unwholesomeness consists of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals—this clarifies the relationship between delusion, karma, and suffering.

Third, regarding "following persons," one should contemplate how [delusion] arises from the two types of false discrimination within inversion. In the upper phrase, the character *chù* (place) pertains to affliction (*kleśa*);

in the lower phrase, the character *yè* (karma) pertains to karma. "Cyclic existence" (*saṃsāra*) refers to the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), which is the retribution of suffering. It may be asked:

In the previous section on "Explanation," it was stated that because this is a profound discourse entering into principle, it is called "subtle and secret contemplation. What is clarified in the present text is fundamentally only... [the same].

If you ask, "Is the preceding discussion regarding the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) not a profound discourse that penetrates the ultimate principle? I reply: Please examine the two examples—the common and the particular—as clarified in the text.
What kind of realm is expressed by such phrases as "the source of awareness is not a cataract"? Please investigate this carefully.

Furthermore, since the subtle principle of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) is also revealed solely upon the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), why speak only of the faculties and their objects?
Whether [the experience] is shallow or deep depends on the person alone.
What are these two types of views? First, the deluded vision resulting from the individual karma of sentient beings; second, the deluded vision resulting from the common karma of sentient beings.
This section of the sutra records the World-Honored One’s response to the preceding statement by enumerating their names. The phrase "What are... refers to the first question.
Regarding the first point, "Examining the Names": In the subsequent listing of names, there are two categories—individual karma (*bipākabhāga*) and common destiny (*sabhāgabhāga*).
Among those who offer false interpretations, there are no fewer than several dozen schools, yet not a single one has reached a thorough understanding.

Furthermore, what is the meaning of these four characters, "individual karma and common destiny"? Where does their intent lie? What is meant by "individual karma," and what is meant by "common destiny"? [They are] isolated...

Mount [Wenling] and [Tianru] both attempt to correlate true wisdom and true principle with the metaphors of the text, interpreting them as being esoteric in principle yet exoteric in their literary application;
however, this bears no relation whatsoever to what Ānanda asked and what the World-Honored One answered.
They labor to explain each metaphor through forced interpretation while forgetting the reason for their initial establishment. According to my own examination of the current edition of this sutra:

If one minutely examines the characteristics of the text, one will understand that "distinct karma" (*bipakṣa-karman*) destroys the faculty of seeing, while "common karma" (*sabhāga-karman*) destroys the object of seeing.

"Distinct karma" means that each is distinct; "karma" refers to functional activity. This signifies that the faculties of seeing each possess their own individual functional activity, which is also distinct.
Each respective faculty of seeing privately exercises its own functional activity, as it cannot be borrowed or substituted by another. Therefore, it is so called.

In the section on "Separate Karma," the initial example states: "Take your own eyes as an analogy: the mountains, rivers, lands, and so forth that you perceive are all produced by the eye-disease of beginningless time.
It further states: "Awareness and seeing are themselves the cataract; the objects perceived are not the cataract.

This is truly the seeing of seeing—is this not an answer to the question of whether 'seeing-seeing' is not seeing, by means of breaking through the faculty of seeing? This is identical [to the previous case].

"Shared" (sabhāga) means that although the sense organs are distinct and do not know one another, the objects they perceive are none other than external sensory data (*viṣaya*) such as form, space, and so forth;
because these objects are the common karma of sentient beings, they are called "shared. The subsequent passages follow this same principle.
At the beginning of the text, it says: "Taking Jambudvīpa as an example, the three thousand continents, along with the four great oceans, are all likewise [shared]."
Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are the conditions for illusory sickness; these conditions for sickness are precisely the objects of perception (*dṛśya-viṣaya*).
Furthermore, it is said: "Perfect Bodhi is the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing; the pure fundamental mind and original enlightenment are eternally abiding.

Is this not an answer that refutes the objects of perception in order to clarify the luminous purity of the awakened mind? One must understand that the textual meanings of these two passages on delusion alternate and interweave with one another.
I request that you set aside this mind of disparaging the ancients and exalting the present, and sit in stillness with a tranquil heart;
only then will you be able to comprehend each point of the preceding and succeeding matters and principles one by one, so that the meaning of the text will naturally penetrate through,
rather than mistakenly taking fish eyes for bright pearls.
"What is meant by 'delusive vision resulting from individual karma' (bīeyè wàngjiàn)? [From here until] 'seeing a complete reflection—what is this called?

This section of the sutra consists of the World-Honored One’s inquiry and explanation regarding the meaning of the term 'individual karma. First, he establishes a metaphor to skillfully demonstrate its principle.
'What is meant by... initiates the inquiry into the name and meaning; 'Ānanda... introduces the metaphor to provide the explanation. Within this explanation, there is further..."

Regarding the second meaning: first, a metaphor is presented; next, beneath the heading "in the mind," the seeing of the lamp is analyzed through contrast to reveal that the visual ailment constitutes the shadow.

Within the first part, it is said that one whose eyes have a red cataract (*rakta-paṭala*)—this red cataract being a disease in the eye characterized by a red film—sees, at night, a distinct circular shadow with five overlapping colors when looking at the light of a lamp, even though one knows that the lamp originally has no shadow.

That this [illusion] exists because of an eye disease is the metaphor; applying it to the Dharma, one should say that the eye disease represents the seeing-faculty (*darśana-indriya*), the lamp’s reflection represents the perceived object (*dṛśya-viṣaya*), and the five colors layered together represent the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) arising in succession.

The eye free from disease represents true wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*), and the lamp without reflection represents true reality (*tattva*). However, one knows that the lamp originally has no reflection, and it is due to the disease...

The analogy of the shadow illustrates that true reality is signless (*animitta*), yet becomes a delusory object through the faculty of delusion; the eye originally has no cataract, yet the cataract arises from an illness.
This illustrates that true wisdom is without conditions (*anālambana*), yet becomes the "delusory locus" through the power of delusion.
Next, in the middle section, the Buddha interrogates Ānanda with the example of a lamp's reflection, asking: "What do you think? Is the circular light upon the lamp the color of the lamp itself?"
Regarding this "seeing color," the Buddha again addressed Ānanda to distinguish between the two meanings of "lamp" and "seeing.
He argued that the circular reflection is neither the lamp nor the seeing, thereby declaring it to be illusory. He said:
"If this circular reflection were a color inherently present upon the lamp, why would those who do not have cataracts not see it as well? It is seen only by those with cataracts."

This demonstrates that it is not the color of the lamp. Furthermore, if this circular shadow were a color inherently present upon the visual faculty, then the faculty itself would have already become color;
yet what else could one call the circular shadow seen externally by that person with the cataract? This demonstrates that it is not the color of the visual faculty.
Furthermore, Ānanda, regarding this passage from "If this circular shadow... to "...therein is that which is neither lamp nor vision":

the World-Honored One, following the preceding meaning, continues by refuting the two positions of separation. Since both meanings are untenable, both the shadow and the visual aberration (*taimirika*) are false.
In the preceding text, where it says "it is the lamp" and "it is the vision," the character "is" (*shi*) should be read as "is precisely" (*ji*).
Regarding the phrase "immediately with separation": having already refuted "identity" above, one now refutes "separation. Furthermore, the following section correctly refutes separation.
This is followed by a summary of the refutation of both identity and separation. The initial passage states:

"If this circular reflection existed separately from the lamp, then when looking at objects such as a screen or a curtain from the side, a circular reflection should appear; yet if these objects truly lack [such a reflection], [then the reflection must not exist apart from the lamp]."
The circular reflection does not exist separately apart from the lamp.

Furthermore, if this circular reflection existed separately apart from the seeing, then hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching should all be able to grasp the circular reflection; why then would it depend upon the gaze of the eye?
Thus, for one with an eye disease who sees a circular reflection, it does not exist separately apart from the seeing. However, that which is neither separate nor identical—
