In the "Original Delusion of the Circular Shadow," it says: "As for 'the color actually resides in the lamp,' 'color' refers to the luminous color of the lamp and does not refer to the circular shadow.
This means that while this luminous color actually originally resides in the lamp, the circular shadow was originally absent within the lamp's light.

It is due to the affliction of the visual faculty that one perceives a shadow in the lamp. If one realizes that both the shadow and the vision are equally the result of cataracts, one can [attain liberation]."
One who perceives the optical aberration of the sense-organ and its object is not a person with diseased eyes;

yet, since that person with healthy eyes—who is not afflicted by disease—already knows that the circular shadow is produced by the aberration, they understand that the shadow has no real existence and will never again say it is the lamp or the vision.
This being so, how much less could one speak of "neither lamp nor vision" within this context?
"Just as the second moon is neither a substance nor a reflection" (extending to) "how much less can it be analyzed as being neither the lamp nor the seeing.
This section of the sutra uses a metaphor to clarify that because the circular reflection is produced by a cataract, its status as either a substance or a reflection cannot be determined.
There are two points in this passage: from "just as the second moon" onwards, the second moon serves as an analogy for the circular reflection.
This also [is explained] below by combining the circular reflection with the two moons; thus it says, "this is also like this.
In the first sense, it is said that the "second moon" is neither the substance of a true moon nor a shadow of the eye. Why is this?

The subsequent interrogation and explanation clarify the reason why it is neither substance nor shadow: the so-called "second moon" is produced by pressing upon the eye. Therefore, those who possess wisdom...
One should not say that this "pressing the root" is the shape of the moon or not the shape of the moon, nor is it seeing or not seeing.

Furthermore, regarding the two phrases following the word "shape": if they were contrasted with the preceding phrase "it is a lamp, it is seeing, it is neither lamp nor seeing," why is the word "separate" (*li*) used here once again?
This is because the preceding text uses "separateness" (*li*) as its point of contrast.

In this refutation of the "perfect shadow" (*paricchinna-chāyā*), the same characters are used with two distinct meanings: "separation" (*li*) corresponds to "belonging," while "non-belonging" (*fei-shu*) corresponds to "not belonging.

This is the refutation of the "two moons" passage; though the wording is concise, the meaning is skillful. Because the "shadow" carries over from that passage, the character "separation" (*li*) is used separately.

If one correlates this with the preceding text, it means that if these [distorted perceptions] were fundamentally separate from the moon and existed independently, then one would see them even when looking sideways.

Regarding the statement that "the grasses, trees, mountains, and rivers have two moons," this refers to the perception of something distinct upon emerging from [meditative] separation; it certainly cannot be what is seen by the eye.
How then can one see two moons by pressing on the eyes? By carefully examining the meaning of this passage, the principle becomes self-evident.

Furthermore, this distinction between identity and difference should fully encompass four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), for their meanings are entirely manifest: namely, being form and being vision, not being form and not being vision. This is as follows:

The meaning of "is" and "is not" is thus made manifest. Furthermore, when it is said that "this is form" and "this is seeing," yet one is "separate from form" and "separate from seeing," the meaning of "separation" and "immediacy" (*li-ji*) is thereby made manifest.
These details are set forth here so that students may know their source.
What is meant by "shared false vision" (sabhāga-mithyā-dṛṣṭi)? [This extends] up to thirty-four, thirty-five, or fifty [people].
This section of the sūtra, in which the World-Honored One intends to refute shared false vision, first establishes a metaphor to clearly indicate that the objective realm exists externally.
The passage beginning with "In this Jambudvīpa... takes two countries on a small continent as a metaphor; therefore, it refers collectively to the trichiliocosm. Jambudvīpa...

Regarding the translation of the term "Ti" (Jambudvīpa), as seen previously, among the four outer continents, excluding the great oceans, there are three thousand islands upon the level land in between.
That which surges forth is called Jambudvīpa; "level land" refers to dry ground, while that which can be inhabited within the waters is called an "island.
Of these three thousand islands, the central Great Continent is the sovereign, while the other small islands beyond the seas are its dependent satellite continents. However...
Thus, countries such as Lūlōu (Lauriyā), Japan, the Three Han, Lâm Yí (Lin-yi), Yuèshāng (Yue-chang), Sīzǐ (Sīhāzi/Siṃhala), and Bōsī (Persia) are all subordinate islands within Jambudvīpa.

The central great island is this very land; the five regions of India occupy the center of the island, with China as its eastern extremity, Persia as its western extremity, the territory of South India as its southern extremity, and [the northern extremity being] the North.

The regions of the Himālayas, Gandhamādana, and the Jambūvana forest, as well as the lands of the five Śāndunas and various Hu peoples beyond these passes, are situated within the northeastern borders of this continent.
The *Nīlābhaya-rāja-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:

"In this Jambudvīpa, there are sixteen great kingdoms, five hundred middle kingdoms, and one hundred thousand small kingdoms. Now, regarding the so-called "great kingdoms" mentioned in the present sutra:
Although the figures cited as "three thousand three hundred" differ between [the various sources], they all refer to this continent as the primary landmass.
The remaining minor islands surround it in every direction within the various oceans; therefore, it is called the "central" one.
When referring to the oceans, one speaks of the four seas of the east, west, south, and north. Among those minor islands, some may even have two or three [sub-islands].
Regarding "a hundred countries," this may refer to one hundred or two hundred countries; furthermore, there may be as few as ten countries, twenty countries, or thirty, forty, or fifty countries.
This clarifies the differences in the size of the three thousand continents (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*).
When the Buddha mentions many continents, his intention is to single out two small countries among them to demonstrate that [the former] does not [apply].
"It is merely due to the conditions of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness.
Ānanda, if within this there were even a small island (up to) that which one has never before seen or heard—
this section of the sutra uses various inauspicious phenomena as a metaphor to illustrate that the objects perceived are solely the mind, and not external forms."
"Because it is real, there are things seen and things not seen. Here, among the three thousand continents, we refer to the smallest of these, which contains only two nations.
When the people of these two nations alone collectively experience adverse conditions, the sentient beings of that specific land perceive various inauspicious phenomena.
This phrase "various inauspicious phenomena" is a general designation for misfortune; what follows below specifically clarifies the signs of evil.
"Xiang" (祥) signifies auspiciousness, while "buxiang" (不祥) signifies inauspiciousness; thus it is called "evil. To specifically clarify the two days within the month:

for example, during the time of Emperor Taizu of Song in the Later Zhou dynasty, when the military mutiny at Chenqiao occurred, he saw a second sun beneath the original sun, with black light swirling and clashing for a long time;
subsequently, the incident of the yellow robe being placed upon his person occurred—this is of that same category.
Regarding the "two months": this refers to the time of a lunar eclipse, when there appears to be a black veil or obstruction covering it;

generally speaking, such evil omens vary in a thousand ways and are difficult to define with certainty. As for "halos, rings, and jade pendants": a "halo" (*yun*) refers to an aura of baleful qi encircling the sun or moon;

what is commonly called a "moon-stallion" (*yuet-dun*) is close to this. "Shi" (適) is read as *shi* (式), meaning "to go toward"; in the present context, it refers to [the shapes] approaching [the celestial bodies].
The reading "zuò" (作) is incorrect. According to Du Yu, the sun moves slowly while the moon moves swiftly;

when the moon catches up to the sun and they meet at their conjunction (*yìjiāo*), and the sun and moon share the same path, an eclipse occurs. If the moon is either outside the sun's path or inside the sun's path, there is no eclipse.
The character "shì" (適) in the current text is that same "shì" from the phrase "pǐ yuè shì" (彼月適).
Regarding the term "pèi" (佩), the commentary of Xié of Wǔxīng states that "pèi" should be read as "bèi" (背). He cites Mèng Kāng’s annotation to the *Hànshū*, which says:
"The shape of 'bèi' is like the character for 'back' (bèi); the shape of 'jué' (玦) is like a jade pendant. All four of these signs are the baleful vapors of the sun and moon.

According to my own examination, the current scripture mentions "pèi" and "jué" together; the intended meaning is that the vapors take on the appearance of circular pendants or jade pendants, and it is not necessarily required [that they be shaped exactly like those objects].

The term "xuǎn bèi" (訓背) also encompasses the *huì* (彗), *bèi* (孛), *fēi* (飛), and *liú* (流). Regarding *huì*, Du Yu states: "The *huì* is a portentous star whose radiance points in a single direction like a broom.
Regarding *bèi*, it refers to the vapors of a star that emerge in a shimmering, spreading manner; such is called *bèi*. When the vapor resembles a broom, it is called *huì*.
Meng Kang states: "To depart without leaving a trace is called *fēi*; when the traces of light are connected, it is called *liú*."

It is said that the four phenomena above the "flowing" category are all the baleful vapors of the stars. Regarding the "bearing ears" (*fù'ěr*) and the "rainbow-aura" (*hóngní*), the commentary by Xuè of Wúxīng cites the *Tōngzhàn* (General Divination), which states:
"When the vapor appears like a half-halo upon the sun, it is called 'bearing' (*fù*); 'bearing' means leaning against. The *Wǔxíngzhì* (Annals of the Five Elements) reads "embrace" (*bào*).
Mèng Kāng says: "The 'embracing vapor' faces the sun. He further notes that "ears" (*ěr*) should be written as "pendants" (*èr*), and that the former is a phonetic error.
A pearl worn on the ear is called an *er*. Meng Kang stated that the form of an *er* is marked with black dots.

According to my humble analysis, the meaning of the scripture regarding "bearing the ears" (*fu-er*) likely refers to a single mark, or perhaps a vapor beside the sun and moon in the shape of an earring, which is named "bearing the ears.

Regarding the rainbow, the *Shi Jing* (Book of Poetry) calls it the *dizhong*; the commentary states that when the sun and rain vapors intersect, a substance suddenly forms, appearing as if it possessed blood and breath.
Such phenomena as these are the vapors of Yin and Yang that should not intersect yet do; they are the licentious vapors of Heaven and Earth.
It is further said: when two colors appear with brilliant intensity, it is called a *xióng* (male rainbow); when it is dark, it is called a *ní* (female rainbow).
When various such forms are formed below and tied above, appearing on the earth while being unseen or unheard in that country, this refers to two states on a small island.
"One sees and one does not see. This "one sees and one does not see" also contains a profound meaning.
"Sees" refers by analogy to sentient beings in the mundane world; "does not see" refers by analogy to the two vehicles of the supramundane realm; thus it is explained in terms of these two lands.
The masters Changshui and Gushan point to the two lands of the Buddha’s purity and the ordinary beings’ defilement as their explanation. I, however, maintain that the Buddhas' pure [land]...
The land is not as it exists for ordinary beings, nor is it as it is empty for those of the Two Vehicles;

therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* states that it is "not as" the three realms are perceived within the three realms—this "as-ness" (tathatā) being the meaning of emptiness. Furthermore, it says it is "neither as nor different," for the Buddhas transcend far beyond purity and impurity, existence and non-existence.
Thus, one cannot point to the Buddha’s Pure Land by referring to the mundane world. It is precisely because it points to the mundane... [that it is so described].
To briefly resolve the meaning of "seeing" and "not seeing" in these two cases seems appropriate; yet, if both are called sentient beings, how could they be anything other than Buddhas?
Ānanda, I shall now clarify this for you by advancing and retreating through these two matters.

In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One further clarifies the two dharmas of identity and difference by advancing and withdrawing upon the preceding two matters of identity and difference.
The two metaphors of identity and difference explained in the preceding text were originally established as provisional;

these "matters" (vastu) are so called because they are provisionally designated according to conventional sentiment, and are not ultimate truth. "Advancing and withdrawing" is a term for raising up and setting aside [the arguments].

Now, let us proceed by following the sequence of their advancement and retreat to evaluate them. This is because words cannot be fully manifested all at once; as before, we first distinguished [the individual] and then conjoined [them], whereas now we retreat from the conjoined to advance with the distinguished.
This serves to clarify the principle of distinct karma (*bhinnakarma*). The subsequent passage, "The following scripture illustrates for you," is the textual application of this principle.

Since the principle of distinct karma has been clarified, we again retreat from the distinct to advance with the conjoined, thereby clarifying the textual application of the principle of common karma (*sabhāgakarma*).

The subsequent passage beginning with "In Jambudvīpa" is the text that correlates this principle [to the analogy]. Therefore, it says: "By means of these two matters, they are advanced and compared to clarify the point.

Ānanda, it is like those sentient beings who, due to their individual karmic conditions, experience deluded vision (until: yet the one who perceives the optical aberration ultimately incurs no fault for seeing).
This section of the sutra follows the preceding discussion on the commonality of retreat and the distinctness of advance, once again citing a specific analogy to clarify a specific principle.
"Ānanda," [the Buddha said], "the previous analogy of what appears to be a present object suggests that it is not truly existent. A lamp actually casts no shadow;
it is produced by the visual disorder (*taimirya*) of the eyes. This disorder is the exhaustion of seeing; the fundamental cause of this disorder arises from seeing."
Because of toil, there arises what is called a "defect" (*śaṅga*). To see toil is to speak of seeing illness;

since toil is itself illness, the preceding text further states that "the shadow and the seer are both defects," meaning that both the subject who sees and the object seen are defects. In the present text, this is omitted and not explicitly stated.
However, regarding the two subsequent lines concerning "seeing": if a person of wisdom with keen eyes perceives this as a defect, then it is not mentioned.
Whether this shadow is a shadow or not, and whether this seeing is seeing or not—once one is free from both their separation and their identity, there is nothing left to distinguish.

Because one does not fall into delusion, it is said that ultimately there is no fault of seeing. The "seeing of the optical aberration" (the *mièng*) is precisely the "seeing of the seeing"; this refers to true seeing.
For example, the passage from "As for you today, with your eyes you observe" (up to) "the originally enlightened, luminous mind perceives conditions,
yet this is not a cataract," uses a specific teaching to correspond with a specific metaphor in order to clarify that deluded vision is not real.
This means that as you observe today those objects such as mountains, rivers, people, and animals with your eyes, all of these are the sickness of your vision.
The resulting illness is precisely what was previously called "perverted discrimination. These external objects correspond to the "round shadow" seen by one with an eye disease;
the "eye ailment" mentioned above corresponds to the "seeing" in the two subsequent lines.

This "seeing" is the faculty of sight (*darśana-indriya*), while the "conditions" are the conditions of the perceived objects, namely the mountains, rivers, and so forth. These faculties and these objects appear to have prior characteristics, yet in reality...
"It does not exist, yet it appears as if it were a present object"—this single phrase is as stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*:

"When the various consciousnesses arise, they transform and appear as if they were self and dharmas; these appearances of self and dharmas manifest as external objects due to discrimination. That text states that "discrimination" is precisely what is meant here.
The word "seemingly" (*si*) in this sutra is the same as in the aforementioned text; although it seems to be an external reality, its fundamental nature is solely [consciousness].
The phrase "consciousness" (vijñāna) combines with the preceding [passage] to show that the affliction of seeing is not produced by form;

it fundamentally refutes the root of seeing, and in doing so, it also simultaneously refutes the perceived object. Why? Because the object arises from the sense-root; once the root is refuted, the external object is likewise refuted.
Thus, "awakened clarity" (jue-ming) is true awakening (bhūta-pratyavekṣā); it means to illuminate that [object] with the true vision of awakened clarity.
The phrase "the object of perception is a cataract" refutes the dust; furthermore, the phrase "using enlightened clarity to perceive this perceiving vision is also a cataract" refutes the faculty.
Once both the faculty and the dust are refuted, the fundamental mind of enlightened clarity, though it perceives the preceding objects, is not itself a cataract.
This accords with the previous statement: "However, one who perceives the cataract ultimately incurs no fault of seeing."
"The awakening [to] that which is awakened to is a cataract; the awakening itself is not within the cataract" (up to) "because its nature is not a cataract, it is not called 'seeing'.

This section of the sutra takes up the meaning of fundamental awakening (*mūla-avabodha*) from above to clarify that true awakening is not a cataract, thereby concluding the answer to the question posed.

Regarding the two lines beginning with "The awakening to that which is awakened to": the first "awakening" refers back to the term "fundamental awakening" mentioned above, while "that which is awakened to" refers to...

This refers precisely to the defect of the faculties and their objects. It means that although the awareness of fundamental enlightenment (benjue) perceives the faculties and their objects, the essence of that awareness does not fall into the defect of the faculties and objects.
As the preceding sutra states: "This is like being apart from seeing; name and trace are both eliminated, and thus there is no falling [into defect].
This single phrase, "the reality of seeing seeing," is the concluding answer to the question, meaning that it does not fall into the midst of the defect.
"Awareness (jue) is precisely the seeing of the seeing; how can this seeing be further designated by means of the seeing of sight, hearing, awareness, and cognition?
The four characters 'awareness, hearing, cognition, and seeing' refer to the six sense organs (ṣaḍāyatana).

Among these six organs, 'awareness' refers to the awareness of touch, which is different from the 'awareness' mentioned in the preceding sentence; the rest may be understood accordingly. Therefore, the following concludes and clarifies [the point]."
The fault of seeing what is illusory is what I, the Tathāgata, am referring to when I say, "You point at Ānanda.
Looking down from this world upon the ten classes of sentient beings, this world is the common retribution (niśraya-vipāka) for these ten classes, and thus there are ten kinds of differences.
Myself, you, and the ten classes of living beings are all identical to Ānanda in terms of our faculties, objects, and dharmas.

The seeing of external objects is precisely the seeing of a cataract; however, it is not the seeing of the person who sees the cataract. The word "person" (*jén* 人) refers to one who possesses wisdom.
The phrase "that seeing" (*pǐ jiàn* 彼見) below explains the preceding "not the seeing" (*fēi jiàn* 非見).

The character "seeing" (*jiàn* 見) in "the seeing of that [person]" (*pǐ jiàn zhě* 彼見者) refers to the seeing of the true essence (*zhēn jīng* 真精), which is unmixed and non-delusory, fundamentally not being a cataract. Because it is not taught as [ordinary] seeing, it is not called "seeing. This concludes the answer.

The explanation of the analogy for individual karma is concluded. Furthermore, within the text of the "Example of Individual Karma," if one exerts effort upon the four characters "should with the eyes observe" (*yǐ mù guān jiàn*) by deleting them, and upon the two characters "eye-disease" (*mù zhēng*), then the meaning of destroying the root of seeing (*jiàn gēn*) will become clear.
Moreover, this concludes the response above to the question regarding whether the seeing of seeing is itself seeing.
"Ānanda, it is like the deluded vision of the commonality (*sabhāgatā*) of those sentient beings... all are produced by the beginningless delusion of seeing.

This section of the sutra follows upon the previous [analogy] and, having distinguished the individual cases, proceeds to the commonality; it again cites the common metaphor to clarify the common principle.
"Ānanda," and so forth, the Buddha recounts the preceding metaphor. Regarding the subsequent question: "In the metaphor of commonality, what..."

"Therefore, is there such an analogy? He replied, "The analogy is drawn because both the object and the faculty are equally illusory. Those five-colored circular shadows are produced by a cataract in the eye;
they reside in the eye and are not external objects. This inauspicious realm arises from the miasma of evil;

it resides in the object and is not within the body. Although there is a difference between the identity and distinctness of the faculty and the object, both are the perception of beginningless time."
Because they are produced from delusion, they fall under this category. In the past, the person of Wu-xing cited an example that erroneously confused the true with the false;
yet, whether advancing or retreating, the underlying meaning is clearly evident here. This is certainly not the intended meaning of the sutra. May those who possess the correct eye examine this.

In the first two phrases of the current text, the particular is illustrated by means of the general; in the subsequent two phrases, the general is illustrated by means of the particular. This can be seen in the following two [sections].

The first four lines clarify that the circular shadow arises from an eye disease; the following four lines clarify that these various inauspicious signs are induced by the evil of karmic obstacles in one's vision.
The final line summarizes this to show that both the sense organ and its objects are produced by the delusion of seeing.

Regarding the character *zhàng* (miasma/obstruction), its detailed meaning encompasses the "obstacle" (*zhàng*) of karmic obstacles; the current erroneous use of the character *zhàng* (miasma) can be understood through its contextual meaning.

For example, from "In Jambudvīpa, among the three thousand continents" up to "harmoniously falsely born and harmoniously falsely dead," this section of the sutra uses a common phenomenon to correspond with the preceding common metaphor in order to clarify that the perceived objects are not real. From "For example,
in Jambudvīpa" up to "the conditions for illusory illness," this directly indicates that external objects serve as the conditions for the illness of vision.
From the great oceans of Jambudvīpa to the dependencies of the lands and the sentient beings themselves—all are manifestations upon the true substance of enlightened awareness.
The three characters "root," "object," and "disease" refer to the conditions of seeing, hearing, and so forth;
the character "condition" (*yuan*) points to the external objects of Jambudvīpa. However, how could there be any disease of the six sense organs upon the true substance of enlightened awareness?

This is truly because sentient beings fail to awaken, whereby the real is transformed into the delusive; this delusion is precisely what constitutes the "sickness. This sickness should be understood as referring generally to both coarse and subtle ignorance.
If one knows that the essence of delusion is itself True Suchness—just as waves are themselves water—then for this reason, the text directly correlates them by way of the delusive phenomena.
The two subsequent lines regarding "conjunction" mean that when the mind and material phenomena are conjoined, then...
Birth, though it arises, is not real; therefore, it is called "false birth. If the mind and the dharma of emptiness were to unite, then death, though it occurs, is not real;
therefore, it is called "false death. Since the union of birth and death is manifested based on the locus of form and emptiness, both birth and death are termed "union.
Were it otherwise, one should have said that the gathering of causes and conditions is called birth, and the dispersal of causes and conditions is called death.
Separation is called death; one must know that union is the meaning of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Therefore, by clarifying the intent of birth and death through the union of form and emptiness, the meaning can be understood.
If one can distance oneself from all conditions of union, one will reach the pure fundamental mind, where original enlightenment is eternally abiding.
In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One instructs on returning to the original, constant mind through the integration of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
This integrates the contemplation of birth and death with the teaching on conditions; the explanations of conditions and causes are seen interchangeably.

This follows the preceding passage on the integration of birth and death, wherein he exhorts the cessation of those causes and conditions so that one may attain the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing.

This means that when the conditions of conjunction and non-conjunction cease, the cause of birth and death ceases. Conjunction belongs to the category of form-dharmas (*rūpa*), while non-conjunction is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Taking the emptiness of form as the condition for birth and death, the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) are the causal factors and the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) are the conditions.
If the causal conditions of the conjunction between the organs and the objects cease, one will be able to realize perfect Bodhi, which is beyond arising and ceasing.
When the deluded mind of birth-and-death by nature has ceased, the originally pure fundamental mind is restored;

because birth and death have been extinguished, one immediately attains the eternally abiding essence of original enlightenment. This concludes the answer to the question regarding the clarity and purity of the awakened mind.

Furthermore, this passage concerning the "commonality" (sabhāgatā) should be examined in light of the section on Jambudvīpa below, as it pertains to the afflictions of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
If one exerts effort upon a single phrase, the meaning of breaking through the duality of views and objects becomes clear.
Ānanda, although you previously realized that the wondrous clarity of original enlightenment (from "to" "neither produced by combination nor by non-combination").
In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One further answers a secondary question to clarify that the seeing-nature does not arise from either harmony or disharmony.

Although the preceding passage included both the meanings of harmony and disharmony while refuting [the notion of] causes and conditions, its primary intent was to answer the question regarding the luminous purity of the awakened mind;
the present text definitively answers the meaning of that secondary question. Previously, Ānanda had used three points as...
Question: There are two direct inquiries and one indirect inquiry. The Buddha answered the two direct inquiries regarding the identity or difference of the two delusions.
As for the one indirect inquiry, Ānanda initially stated his intention for questioning, saying that while the various harmonies and disharmonies exist, the mind has not yet been opened;
because the mind has not been opened, this constitutes an indirect inquiry. Now that the Buddha has finished answering the direct inquiries, he returns to answer the meaning of that indirect inquiry.
Although you have already attained an initial realization, as the World-Honored One has described, you still harbor doubts regarding that which has not yet been fully opened.

"The source of awareness" (*jueyuan*) refers precisely to the pure source of the clarity of seeing; since it was previously understood that seeing enters into awareness, it is called the "source of awareness.

In the phrase "not produced by combination," the two characters "not produced" (*fei sheng*) apply to the meaning of the subsequent clause, signifying that it is not produced through a combination [of causes].
"Neither produced through non-harmony"—this is the general heading, which is explained in detail below.
"Ānanda, I shall now again question you regarding the external objects: [do they arise] in harmony with what is open, or in harmony with what is obstructed?"

In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One follows up on the preceding discussion of neither-harmony-nor-disharmony; first he refutes the doubt and subsequently sets forth four objects to provide a definitive analysis.

Generally speaking, when one speaks of "harmony" (saṃyoga), it must be discussed in terms of the conjunction between the sense organ and its object; therefore, he refutes [the opponent's view] by means of these four objects.

In the passage beginning with "I shall now," the World-Honored One is about to pose a question; the section beginning with "first, he refutes the doubt" refers to the initial stage, while the section beginning with "then you" provides a general summary.
Regarding the four boundaries listed, the phrase "initially realizing the bodhicitta" refers to the aforementioned realization of the primordial source of awakening;
the translator has altered the phrasing to "bodhicitta," which may lead to confusion with the *bodhi* of the Buddha-fruit—readers must understand this distinction.
As for "synthesis and analysis," because the meanings of the two characters "synthesis" (*he*) and "analysis" (*po*) differ, it is like water and earth being combined to form [a single substance].
The term "harmony" (*he*) is like a box and its lid fitting together; because their meanings differ, they are analyzed separately, as was the case with the previous analysis of causes and conditions.
Furthermore, in the phrase "realizing the bodhicitta," the character "realize" (*zheng*) carries the sense of "corresponding realization" (*duizheng*), not the "realization" (*zheng*) of the Path.
"If 'luminosity' and 'harmony' are [to be analyzed], you should observe luminosity... and likewise for all the various obstructions.
This section of the sutra follows the previous general enumeration of the four objects and specifically explains the meaning of their deconstruction.

Regarding "If luminosity... and so forth, it first explains luminosity and harmony: luminosity does not manifest itself; it becomes luminous by means of seeing. Therefore, it says, "observe luminosity," because luminosity manifests through observation.
Observing this vision, it appears that there is a sense of blending between the vision and the light. However, since vision has no substantial essence, from what could it possibly blend?
Blending is precisely what constitutes union. Vision is without substance, while light possesses characteristics; these two natures can be distinguished.
How can that which exists and that which does not exist be blended? Never before have we heard of color and space being able to blend; now, the same applies to vision and light.
Since the meanings cannot be conflated, how can they be called "conflated"? As for the phrase "if it is not," this refers to the refutation by means of non-identity.
That is to say, if it is not the seeing, how could one see the light? This refutes the position that it is not [the seeing].

Furthermore, if it were identical to the seeing, then since the light is already the seeing, it would no longer be the seeing of light; instead, it would become the seeing of seeing. How, then, could it still be called "seeing the light"? This...
Regarding the refutation (*bhaṅga*), what is its meaning? "That" (*ji*) is a term of censure; "not-that" (*fei ji*) refers to both being untenable. The subtlety lies herein:

one must see that the following refutation is based on the meaning of the "half" and the "full. "Harmony" (*he*) is the meaning of "half," meaning that only when one half is seen and one half is clarified can harmony be permitted.
Now, if one sees [the truth] as necessarily complete and perfect, then harmony is impossible—just like half a bucket of water and half a bucket [of air].
The meaning of "blending" (andha) can only be established if the water is full; if the bucket were already full of water, no more mud could be added.

How, then, could they be blended? Therefore it is said: "Seeing must be complete. This clarifies the following sentence by explaining "completeness" as the opposite of the preceding statement. Next, regarding "seeing must...":

this means that the nature of seeing possesses the characteristic of cognitive clarity (*jñāna-prakāśa-lakṣaṇa*). Sentient beings and insentient things are distinct from one another; if they were mixed, then seeing [would be lost].

When both nature (*prakṛti*) and luminosity (*prakāśa*) lose their original names—such that "seeing" loses its name as seeing and "luminosity" loses its name as luminosity—it follows that the conjunction of luminosity is not logically tenable.
Since the subsequent section refutes [the opponent's view] by applying the three meanings of darkness (*tamas*) as analogies for luminosity, they are omitted here.
Furthermore, Ānanda, it is also thus for you now [up to] and for all the various obstructions.
This section of the sūtra follows the previous refutation of the "conjunction" (saṃyoga) and now further refutes the "union" (saṃghāta) to demonstrate that seeing does not arise from union.

First, the four objects are listed in general; second, the meaning of the refutation is explained in detail. Within the detailed explanation, the conjunction with light is first refuted; that is to say, if seeing...
If [the eye] were conjoined with light, then when it is dark, the seeing of light should cease accordingly; thus, it would not be conjoined with darkness.

If it is not conjoined with darkness, how could it see darkness? Furthermore, if it sees darkness without being conjoined with darkness, then by analogy, it should not see light when conjoined with light.
This is because the argument regarding darkness is stated as the reverse of the case for light; that is to say, although one sees darkness, it certainly does not [conjoin with it].
If it were conjoined, it would be conjoined with light; by analogy, it should not be seeing in the darkness above. "In the darkness" means that although there is seeing, there is no conjunction;

"in the light" means that although there is conjunction, there is no seeing. This reversal of the analogy is the same [as the previous case]. "Since it does not..."—the two lines below interrogate and explain why the conjunction with light and the failure to see are illogical.
That is to say, since one does not see the light, how can it be called "conjoined with light"? To understand this clearly is the point.
"Is light not the opposite of darkness? Since the refutation of darkness follows the same logic as that of light, it is omitted here.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, according to my contemplation... [up to] ...is it not the case that the mind and its thoughts are not in conjunction?"
In this section, Ānanda, having heard that neither "separation" nor "union" constitutes the true meaning, further proposes that it is not a matter of union;

he asserts that the primary faculty is the sense organ (*indriya*), the objects are the sensory fields (*viṣaya*), and the mental deliberations are consciousness (*vijñāna*). He refers generally to these three factors across the six bases, asking:
"Are these three and six not in union? Whereas the preceding text refuted [the notion of union] by contrasting only the sense organs and their objects, here...

Furthermore, regarding the addition of the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), one should refer to the preceding text where it is evident that [the refutation] should apply universally across the three categories (*triskandha*);
however, as the text is abbreviated and not explicitly stated, those who study the sūtras should synthesize the meaning and understand it accordingly.
The Buddha said: "You now further state that awakening is not a combination... (down to) it is neither a combination with the intangible nor a combination with the obstructive.
In this section of the sutra, the Buddha refutes the notion of non-combination; first, he restates the intent of the [opponent's] calculation as being "not," and next, he lists the four objects.
"If it were not through union with light that seeing would perceive light" (up to) "and so it is for all obstructed objects.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding analysis by specifically explaining the meaning of "destruction" (or "refutation") to clarify that the nature of seeing is not non-unified.
Regarding the discussion of boundaries: it is precisely because things are not unified that they each occupy their own domains; thus, one speaks of "boundaries. You should first... [text continues].

The Buddha commanded him to examine the reality of where the substance of seeing and light have their boundaries; for since they exist within seeing and within light, there must necessarily be a boundary.
Ānanda, [the Buddha] then proceeded to refute the concept of a boundary:

if there were truly no seeing within the limits of light, then light and seeing would be utterly separated and unable to reach one another; if seeing itself cannot even know the location of light, how could a boundary be established?
Thus, it is not that they are not in harmony; however, because the preceding section on "darkness" used the example of "light" to refute the notion of identity, this is omitted here.
Furthermore, from the statement that the essence of wondrous vision is not a product of combination, up to the various obstructive forms, it is likewise so.
This section of the sutra follows the previous refutation of non-union and now refutes union together to clarify that the nature of seeing is neither non-united nor united.
Furthermore, in the passage beginning with "Moreover, wondrous," first the intent of the [opponent's] calculation is cited as being incorrect; next, the four objects are enumerated.
Then, under the heading "If not," the refutation of non-union is presented first to clarify union: if seeing were not united with light, then the nature of seeing would be in opposition to light.
"Corner" (*jiao*) means to be at variance; it refers to contradiction. The following two lines cite an example of this contradictory nature:
for instance, the ear can only apprehend sound and does not grasp form; therefore, it contradicts light and does not come into contact with it.
Now, if seeing and light do not combine, it is likewise so. Furthermore, if they do not combine, then seeing—[and so forth].
Not knowing the location of the light, how can one discern the principle of conjunction and non-conjunction? "Discern" (*vibhāga*) means to clearly distinguish.
Since the subsequent examples concerning darkness serve as illustrations for the refutation of identity with light, they are omitted here.

Thus, the Buddha’s response to the incidental questions is complete, and the meaning of subtle, secret contemplation within *śamatha* is also clarified. The following text distantly inherits the previous heading.
The meaning of the *Mahādhāraṇī-samādhi* is elucidated through the four topical sections of the subsequent scripture, which clarify the first inquiry regarding the meaning of *samādhi*.
Above, because Ānanda had not clearly understood the subtle illumination within *śamatha*, [the Buddha] responded to him once more;
thus, although the preceding headings were established, the exposition of their meaning has only now begun. Students should understand that this marks the commencement of the textual meaning.
I submit that it may be so if one does not lose sight of its source.
Ānanda, you have still not yet understood that all floating dust [of phenomena]—up to and including delusion, awakening, birth, and death—is utterly unattainable.
In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One takes up the preceding heading to initiate the *samādhi* that fuses the four categories of delusive appearances into the single true nature.
This constitutes the general heading for the four categories, while the subsequent text provides the specific explanation. Regarding the phrase "You have not yet understood," etc.:
the World-Honored One has consistently refuted the delusive to reveal the true, thereby elucidating the principle of *śamatha*; thus, the delusive exists [only as a negation].
It can be broken down as follows: it was as if the delusion existed outside of the truth, unable to be fused into one;
now, that delusive appearance is fused such that it is itself the true nature, and outside of this true nature there is no delusion to be removed—this is the meaning of *samādhi*.
"Floating dust" and "illusory appearances" refer to the four categories mentioned below, which are unreal like illusions and subject to arising and ceasing.
Because they cease, they are like floating dust; though their illusory forms are unreal, their entire substance is the Truth. Arising is non-arising, and ceasing is non-ceasing.
Like flowers in the sky, they have no substance; arising and ceasing are themselves emptiness. The arising and ceasing of the four categories [of phenomena] are likewise thus.
Therefore it is said: "They arise in this very place and perish in that very place. "This very place" refers to the present moment of mindfulness.
This means that one should contemplate arising as it arises and contemplate cessation as it ceases. This is truly because, through delusion and lack of awakening, a single thought-moment flickers up;

yet the essence of this thought is fundamentally empty, such that its very arising is non-arising. A single thought-moment is thus like this: in the four sections below, arising and ceasing are identical to a single thought-moment.
Indeed, these two phrases contain the general outline and the subtle meaning of the four sections; they are all subsumed herein.
Because it can be disregarded, it is called a phantom and a falsehood designated as a "mark" (*lakṣaṇa*); yet its nature is truly the wondrously enlightened and luminous essence.
Furthermore, it is like water and waves: when sentient beings are deluded regarding the truth, they produce the false, which is just as the entirety of water becomes waves;

if one can awaken to the realization that the false is the true, it is just as the entirety of waves becomes water. Since waves and water are non-dual in principle, there is nothing outside of the truth.
Falsehood is entirely true within falsehood; thus, truth and falsehood are not two separate dharmas. Above, this directly clarifies that the four categories are fundamentally suchness.
Below, the names of the four categories are listed as causes and conditions, and below that, their characteristics are shown:

it is said that through the aggregation of the five aggregates, there is merely the arising of delusion; through the dispersal of the five aggregates, there is merely the cessation of delusion. This does not yet clarify what was stated above.
Arising and ceasing are themselves non-arising and non-ceasing; arising is coming and ceasing is going. Arising, ceasing, going, and coming are fundamentally empty.

At the very moment of their going and coming, this aspect of emptiness is the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha. "Tathāgatagarbha" is a general designation that reveals the essence of the fruition. It is eternally abiding and wondrously luminous;
in accordance with the principle of arising and ceasing mentioned above, it is said that arising and ceasing are themselves non-arising and non-ceasing. However...
Then arising and ceasing are themselves eternal abiding. Since arising and ceasing are coarse and obscure, they are precisely non-arising and non-ceasing;

thus, the coarse is itself the subtle, and the obscure is itself the luminous. "Immovable" means omnipresent. "Responding" refers to the meaning of going and coming. "Omnipresent" (zhu) has the meaning of being central;
it is called "central" in contrast to the extremes, and "omnipresent" (yuan) in contrast to partiality. This means that going is precisely not going, and coming is precisely not coming.

Coming is itself going; because coming and going are non-moving, they are extremes and partialities, yet because they are non-moving, these very extremes are the center, and this very partiality is the perfect.

This is because "permanently abiding, wondrously luminous, non-moving, and universally round" describes the inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*), while "wondrously luminous true nature" describes the essence of the nature (*prakṛti-svabhāva*).
The phrase "the true nature of the nature" below承接 (inherits) the meaning from above, manifesting the above by way of reverse exposition.
Since this meaning is presented in accordance with the truth, this inverse-and-direct explanation serves to clarify in detail that within the true nature there has never been any delusion.
Ānanda, how are the five aggregates originally the Tathāgata-garbha... (until) ...only a clear, open void, utterly devoid of anything at all?

In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One intends to clarify that the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) arises from false conditions; he first reveals that its true essence is without marks, using a metaphor to illustrate this.
The passage beginning with "How" is a general inquiry regarding the five aggregates and their convergence with truth.

The passage beginning with "Ānanda" provides a specific explanation of the false characteristics of the aggregate of form. Within this explanation, he first demonstrates the principle of truth to show how the aggregate of form is falsely established.

Generally speaking, when the World-Honored One preaches the Dharma, his fourfold eloquence is unimpeded. If he were to explain the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) directly, the ordinary mind would find it difficult to understand their emptiness.
Therefore, he relies on phenomena to illustrate principles and employs analogies and categories of dharmas to clarify that true emptiness is traceless;

yet the characteristics of the aggregates are merely constructed by the delusions of sentient beings. As an example, the following analogy is given: observing emptiness through the eyes within the metaphor.
The speaker’s intention is to clarify that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has characteristics because it is what is confronted by the eyes;

"pure eyes" refers to eyes free from cataracts, which are called "pure" precisely because they lack cataracts. "Clear and bright space" refers to space free from the flowers [of floating hairs]; thus it is called "clear and bright.
Because the eyes are free from cataracts, one perceives that space is without flowers; when both faculty and object are pure, there are no forms or colors whatsoever.
Therefore it is said: "Only a single clear sky, vast and remote, with nothing at all. "Remote" (*hōng*) signifies loftiness and distance. Master Jingmu compared this to Mount Gu;
Master Yuán compared it to the fundamental possession of true wisdom, which is like a clear sky. The "single clear sky" compares to the fundamental possession of true principle.
The "single clear sky" [further] compares to the oneness of wisdom and principle. "Vast and remote, with nothing at all" compares to the state of absolute transcendence.
The nine realms are illusory forms.
That person, for no reason, does not move his eyes (until the end of the passage). One should know that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is likewise so.
This section of the sutra shows the illusory nature of the aggregate of form, clarifying it by means of the preceding analogy. "That person" refers to...
The preceding passage used the analogy of a person to explain the matter;

therefore, the previous text stated that before that person’s eyes were fixed in a stare, the eyes originally had no fatigue and empty space fundamentally had no flowers, such that both the subject who perceives and the object perceived were pure.
Now, because that person stares with unblinking eyes for a long duration, fatigue arises; thus, the eyes become fatigued without any external cause.
Since space is empty and lacks causes, and flowers do not exist, the meaning of "causelessness" is used here to refer to the exhaustion of labor. Thus, one sees flowers in the void;
yet these floral forms arise and perish in a state of frantic confusion, rising and falling—this is precisely what is called "non-characteristic.
One must know that the void originally has no flowers, but because of one's own mental toil, chaotic flowers arise. When observed with the eye of wisdom, the flowers are entirely the void itself.

Arising is non-arising; the false and illusory nature of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is likewise so. Therefore, it is said that the aggregates themselves are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha.

The passage following "the aggregate of form" consists of words that correlate the Dharma with its analogies: "a person without illness staring fixedly until they develop eye-fatigue" is a metaphor for [ignorance] arising suddenly without cause due to the loss of mindfulness;
"empty visions of whirling flowers" is a metaphor for perceiving the true nature differently, resulting in the deluded confusion of the aggregate of form.
The "non-characteristic" (*a-lakṣaṇa*) illustrates the arising, ceasing, and continuous flux of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

Regarding the term "aggregate" (*skandha*), the *Dharmadhātu-krama* states that it takes the sense of "covering" (*āvaraṇa*); because it covers the true nature (*dharmatā*), it is also explained by way of analogy.
For example, when the sky is covered by clouds, its true azure color is lost; therefore, it is called an "aggregate. This merely demonstrates the delusive characteristics of the aggregate of form.
Thus, in the following text, the refutation of dharmas begins:
"Ānanda, these delusive flowers do not come from space... [up to] ...just as the substance of Ānanda cannot contain Ānanda."

This section of the sutra follows upon the preceding parable to clarify that the flowers do not emerge from two locations. First, Ānanda, the text provides a general enumeration; next, it proceeds to refute each point individually.
Within the refutation, it first addresses the notion of "coming from emptiness," which implies emerging. The meaning is this:
if these delusory flowers had emerged from within empty space, they would likewise have to return to empty space. Since there is indeed an emergence...
Entering is not called "emptiness of emptiness," for emptiness is fundamentally quiescent; how could there be entering or exiting? Because there is entering and exiting, it is not empty space.
If it were not empty, it would clearly be a substantial dharma. If it were a substantial dharma, it could not accommodate the arising and ceasing of manifested forms.
Furthermore, an example is cited to clarify the sense that arising and ceasing cannot be accommodated, such as in the case of Ānanda.
Since its substance is a real dharma, how could it possibly allow Ānanda to enter or exit? Now, that empty space allows the arising and ceasing of the illusory flower because its substance is void;
since its substance is void, there is no entering or exiting, and thus we know clearly that the flower does not come from space.
"If it emerges from the eye" refers to the passage from "since it emerges from the eye" up to "it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
This section of the sutra follows the previous refutation that the flower does not emerge from the eye, concluding the falsity of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

The first phrase restates the preceding argument; the phrase beginning with "since it emerges from" constitutes the actual refutation of its emergence from the eye, meaning: "since it has emerged from within the eye..."
Upon entering, one receives the sensory portion of the eye; logically, there should be seeing of this flower.

If there were seeing, then upon exiting and circling back through the empty space, one should see the eye. When this flower returns, if the eye is not seen, then the flower does not possess the faculty of seeing.
Furthermore, although the eyes emerge from the head, they are fundamentally without seeing. If they lack seeing, then upon exiting— [the same principle applies].
When it is able to obscure the sky and return to obscure the eye—should this flower not obscure the eye upon its return, then it would be clear that the delusory flowers do not emerge from the eyes.
Furthermore, the text below establishes a further refutation to clarify that the flowers do not emerge from the eyes:
when one sees the flowers in the sky, if the flowers were to emerge from the eyes, then [upon their return] they should [re-enter] the eyes.
If one were free from cataracts, then it should be said that the clear and bright eye sees flowers in space. Why, then, do you say that it is the cataract-afflicted eye that sees flowers in space?
If one sees the cloudless sky, then the flowers have returned to the void within the eyes; because there are no flowers, it is called "clear sky.
Thus, it should be said that the cataract-afflicted eye sees the clear sky. Why, then, do you instead say that it is the clear and bright eye that sees it?
The clear sky is thus described in such a detailed and circumstantial manner to show that the wild flowers do not emerge from the eyes.

The final phrase, "the clear sky is called the pure and bright eye," uses the metaphor of the finger to point toward the meaning; the initial words are therefore used below to conclude by revealing that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is as false and illusory as wild flowers.
If one knows that the aggregate of form is fundamentally illusory, why would one further calculate it to be caused by conditions?
The nature of spontaneity is neither of the two natures you have postulated; however, once the nature of delusion is exhausted, its very substance is the wondrous True Suchness-nature.
The preceding text explicitly reveals the truth, while the present concluding text dispels delusion;

since the introductory and concluding texts mutually clarify one another, all subsequent passages should be understood in this manner. The scriptural text is still concise, so students should grasp the meaning through their own insight.
[It is] so. Ānanda, it is like a person whose hands and feet are at ease... [until] suddenly, as if falsely arising, the nature has neither opposition nor compliance.

This section of the sutra, in which the World-Honored One is about to clarify the false characteristics of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), first reveals that the true essence is without opposition.
To "accord" means there is no opposition; to accord is itself to be without reception (*vedanā*), clarifying that the aggregate of reception (*vedanā-skandha*) is formed through delusion.

Now, the aggregate of reception is further elucidated by means of a metaphor. First, the true essence of being without reception is revealed by stating "tranquil, secure, and harmonious," which precisely clarifies the absence of all illusory contacts (*sparśa*).
Since reception is manifested through contact, if there is no contact, there is no reception. "The hundred bones" refers to the entire body.

"Harmony" refers to being well-adjusted; "composure" refers to being pleasantly at ease. This means that the entire body is tranquil and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are harmoniously pleased, such that it is as if they have suddenly arisen from delusion.
At the height of this composure, one seems unaware of having a body, and thus there is nothing of either the agreeable or the disagreeable to be experienced.

There are three aspects of experience: first, the agreeable; second, the disagreeable; and third, that which is neither disagreeable nor agreeable. Now, when it says "no disagreeable or agreeable," it refers to this third aspect.
The three feelings are both absent.
Because that person is non-existent, one should know that it is likewise with the two palms [of the hands] reaching up to the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).
This section of the sutra shows the false characteristics of the aggregate of feeling; it follows the preceding metaphor to clarify this. "That person" refers to...

Regarding those who were previously at ease: before their hands have even rubbed together, all tactile sensations (*spraṣṭavya*) are fundamentally non-existent. Now, due to delusion, they combine; due to delusion, there is contact; and due to delusion, there is reception.
To merely experience this within the mind is what is called "feeling" (*vedanā*). Although this is explained by way of analogy, it partially accords with the nature of phenomena.

In the section on the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), the following is the discourse that applies the analogy to the dharma: "The person" is a metaphor for sentient beings, and "the two hands" are non-existent [in themselves].

The rubbing together of two pieces of wood is a metaphor for the union of sensation (*vedanā*) and contact (*sparśa*); "empty" is a metaphor for true nature (*dharmatā*); "rubbing" is a metaphor for deluded reception;

"roughness" is a metaphor for the adverse; "smoothness" is a metaphor for the favorable; cold and heat are likewise [to be understood]. Herein, the sensations that are neither adverse nor favorable are omitted for brevity.

These sensations that are neither adverse nor favorable are also called "neutral" (*sama*) sensations. This is seen in detail throughout the various sūtras and śāstras. This passage demonstrates the falsity of the characteristics of sensation.
Thus, the following text begins the refutation of dharmas:
"Ānanda, these illusory contacts do not come from space... they should not be said to come and touch by selecting [a specific part] of empty space."

This section of the sutra follows up on the preceding metaphors to clarify that contact has no source from which it arises. "Ānanda" [is the address] below; "thus" (*evam*) and so forth below provide the general enumeration;
"individually refuting" [the positions] below provides the specific refutation. Within the refutation, one first refutes the notion of illusory contact arising from emptiness.

This refers to roughness, smoothness, cold, and heat, which are capable of giving rise to the nature of sensation; therefore, they are called "contact. Because they are fundamentally non-existent yet falsely appear to exist, they are termed "illusory contact. Thus, contact exists.
Because they possess the nature of being either contrary or compliant, they are called "all contacts" (*sparśa*); this passage is easy to understand. As for the final two lines:
since emptiness involves selection, it constitutes having a mind; yet emptiness is fundamentally insentient, and thus one should not select contact.
If the palm has contact while the body lacks contact, how could emptiness not be pervasive? One can thus know with certainty that contact does not come from emptiness.
"If [the touch] were to emerge from the palms, it would not depend upon their joining; [it would follow that] fundamentally it is neither a causal condition nor a spontaneous nature.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding metaphors to clarify that touch does not emerge from the palms, and concludes by demonstrating its falsity.
That is to say, if various illusory touches were to emerge from the palms, since the two palms themselves already possess the nature of touch, why would they need to wait for the moment of joining?
This phrase clearly refutes [the notion that light] does not emerge from the palm; the subsequent text, which refutes it by means of its separation and conjunction, can be understood accordingly.

Therefore, the concluding section clarifies that the nature of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is false and illusory, consistent with the meaning of the analogy. The two natures of causes and conditions are to be understood as explained previously.

Furthermore, within this text on the aggregate of sensation, although sensation itself is not explicitly defined, the refutation focuses on contact (*sparśa*); this is because contact— (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragmentary commentary on a Buddhist scholastic treatise, likely concerning the *Vibhāṣā* or similar Abhidharma-style analysis of the aggregates. The final sentence is incomplete.)
Since the capacity to initiate reception has been refuted, the reception that is initiated can likewise be understood as refuted; therefore, it is refuted by means of contact (*sparśa*).
Ānanda, for example, when someone speaks of tasting a sour plum—[you should know that] the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is also like this.

In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One clarifies the unreality of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) by means of present examples, while implicitly containing the principle that the void and the real are mutually integrated.

In the preceding text, regarding the first two aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and sensation (*vedanā*), he first elucidated the true essence and subsequently manifested the delusive characteristics of each respective aggregate.

From the aggregate of perception onward, for the remaining three aggregates, he omits the chapter on elucidating the true essence and instead proceeds directly [to the manifestation of their delusive characteristics].
This merely demonstrates the appearance of delusion; there must surely be a deeper intent preserved herein.

It is my humble opinion that, when compared as a whole, the first two *skandhas* (aggregates) are coarse, and thus it is relatively easy to clarify their true nature with just a few words. Consequently, the essence of reality is revealed.

However, because the latter three *skandhas* are subtle and their active characteristics are minute and hidden, explaining their true nature would require prolixity of expression; therefore, they have been set aside for now and not yet discussed.

This is simply to clarify the characteristics of movement within the aggregates (*skandha*) so that people may easily understand them. The present text explains that thinking of a precipice is a false conception, as there is no actual cliff;
yet, the thought of sour plums can cause saliva to flow and produce acidity, which is a real fact.
That the unreal can move the real precisely demonstrates the interpenetration of phenomena. One must know that this body is likewise composed of conceptualization.
Therefore, it follows that [the body] evolves according to perception (*saṃjñā*). Someone might ask: "How do we know that this body is formed by perception? The answer is:

The tenth sutra states that initially, based on the parents' desire and perceptions, they are brought together; furthermore, one's own *śukra* (semen) is cast into the midst of that perception to transmit life.
Thus, these three perceptions combine to form this body, and so we know it is produced by perception. "Acid" (*sukta*) has the meaning of sourness.
Because the character "suan" (sour) appears in the subsequent text, it is changed to "cuo" (vinegar). "Tuo" (treading) carries the meaning of stepping upon.

A "xuanyan" (precipice) is a dangerous cliff; because it hangs over [the abyss], it is called a "xuanyan. The World-Honored One cites these two examples to illustrate that all deluded thoughts are, when discussed in terms of both the real and the unreal, like this.
Below the section on the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), this analogy is applied to the plum, the thought, and the cliff.
These two matters are merely cited as examples and are not intended as metaphors; one need not view them as such. The final two lines are precisely the words of the example:
"Ānanda, this sourness you speak of does not arise from the plum... (until) it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature."
This section of the sutra follows the preceding examples to clarify that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) does not arise from two sources, and concludes by binding it as false.
"Ānanda" below provides a general enumeration; "in this way" (*evam*) below provides a specific refutation. Within the refutation, the first part refuting arising from the plum is easy to understand.

"If [it arises] from the mouth" below is the second part, refuting arising from the mouth and the entry [of the object], specifically addressing the claim regarding the sour plum. If it were from the mouth... [text ends].
If one enters [the water], the mouth should respond and hear it for itself; why wait for the ears?

If you grant that hearing occurs only through the ears, why does this water not flow out from within the ears? Such convoluted falsehoods cannot be believed as reality. This concludes the second matter, which was originally marked by the text as "Tāngxià" (踏下).
Now, because the explanation of *sīyá* (思崖) and vinegar (*zào*) are similar, its text has been abbreviated. This supplement is provided by Zhēnjiè (真際).
As for the feet, since they are of the same nature as speech, one should say that such thinking involves treading;
it does not come from a precipice, nor does the mind enter through the feet. If it were to come from a precipice, the precipice would naturally perceive it—why wait for human thought?

If it were to enter through the feet, the feet would naturally perceive it—why wait for mental perception? If it were perceived solely by the mind, why would the soles of the feet feel a sense of astringency and pain? This is [the objection].

Therefore, the following conclusion reveals that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is empty and false; this is explained by analogy with the vinegar, as previously understood regarding causes and conditions and spontaneity.
Ānanda, just as turbulent currents and waves succeed one another, you should know that the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is likewise.
In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One employs an analogy to clarify that the flux of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is similar to a torrential current.

In the text, the analogy precedes the application to the dharma. Within the analogy, "violent and contrary" refers to the waves; their uninterrupted succession from front to back is termed "continuity.

Because the subsequent does not intermingle with the preceding, and the preceding does not retreat to the subsequent, it is said they do not "transgress" one another. "Transgress" (*yú*) here means to overstep.

Because the characters are combined to form a compound meaning, they are referred to together as "xing" (行). In the section on the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), this is a term used in conjunction with the dharma;
the character "xing" is originally pronounced with a level tone (*píngshēng*), yet because it has been transmitted by scholars for so long, it is all recited with a departing tone (*qùshēng*).

Furthermore, influenced by Northern dialects, it is separately pronounced as "yìng" (硬), neither of which is the correct etymological definition. It is "xing" in the sense of "proceeding," taking up the notion of moment-to-moment flux and constant renewal.

The meaning of "abiding" is that the mind does not abide; this is the sense of "movement. The metaphor of a torrent represents the aspect of movement, while the metaphor of the continuous succession of waves represents the uninterrupted succession of moment-to-moment thoughts.
That preceding and succeeding moments do not overstep one another is like the arising and ceasing of deluded thoughts, which likewise do not transcend [this continuity].
Herein, the dharma and the metaphor are most closely related and easily understood.
"Ānanda, this nature of flowing does not arise because of space... (up to)... nor is it the nature of water, nor is it apart from space and water.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding analogy of flowing to list four refutations in total to clarify that the nature of flowing has no substantial essence.
Following this general listing, there follows a specific refutation.
Thus, Ānanda, [the passage from] "if it were produced by space" (up to) "fundamentally neither a causal condition nor a spontaneous nature.

This section of the sutra follows the previous general enumeration and now specifically refutes four points to clarify that the delusive characteristics of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations) have no source.

Within this text, there are four refutations; the first, which refutes [the idea of production] by means of space, is easily understood. The second, beginning with "if it were next... [refutes it] by means of...
If you claim that the cause of flow exists because of water, then this nature of flow ought not to be water. Why?
Because the nature of water is still and stable, whereas the nature of flow is shifting and moving; since stability and motion are incompatible, it is not water.
If it were not water, there would have to be some other distinct entity possessing the characteristic of flow. Yet, as it currently exists, how could there be flow apart from water? If...
First, the refutation based on identity: if the flow were identical to the water, then when the water is clear and still, where would the characteristic of flowing be?
It could not be the fixed essence of the water itself; yet if the essence of the water is not the flow, one must know that the nature of flowing does not exist apart from the water.
Second, the refutation based on the union of emptiness and water: this nature of flowing is separated from... [the text here is truncated].
Apart from space and water, there is no other flow. Why is this? All things exist within space, and space fundamentally has no exterior;
how could there be a flow outside of space? Since there is no flow apart from water, it is said that there is no flow outside of water.
When one investigates the flow through these four perspectives, the flow cannot be found; yet among these four perspectives, only the two locations of space and water are considered.
In reality, the lower two locations exist only within empty space and upon water; this is discussed in terms of their separation.

Therefore, the concluding summary below reveals that the falsity of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is identical in meaning to the analogy. "Conditioned causes and natural spontaneity" are to be understood as previously explained.
"Ānanda, it is as if there were a person who took a *piṅgala* bottle... [up to] "...you should know that the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) is likewise so.
This section of the sutra establishes a metaphor to clarify that the cycle of birth and death within the consciousness-aggregate is analogous to carrying empty space on a distant journey.
In the text, the simile precedes the application to the dharma. As for the metaphor set forth below: *piṅgala* is the name of a bird.
The translated term is as seen previously; because the shape of the jar resembles this bird, the body of the jar has two holes, just like the large and small openings of a jar in this region.
That person plugs both openings of the jar, fills it completely with empty space, and carries this jar of emptiness on a journey of a thousand *li* to present it to another country.
"To present" (*xiang*) means to offer food; it is called "presenting" because one gives food to a person. Now, [using] this...

The empty space is compared to people from other lands; the dharmas beneath the consciousness-aggregate (vijñānaskandha) are combined with the text, which is briefly supplemented to accord with the intended meaning.

It should be stated that "people" is a metaphor for deluded karma, while the "space within the jar" is a metaphor for the consciousness-aggregate, explained in terms of the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Since the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* clarifies that this *ālayavijñāna* is the cause of birth and death, the jar serves as a metaphor for the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*).
Because the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is able to sustain consciousness and select parents for conception, the body of this intermediate state is like that of a seven-year-old child.

When the death-aggregate (*mṛtyu-skandha*) has ceased at this place and the movement-aggregate (*gati-skandha*) has not yet arisen at that place, there exists this intermediate state between death and birth.
This body of the intermediate state cannot be seen by the physical eye; it is seen only by the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Now...
The *kaṅkama-puṭa* (the "falcon" or "cuckoo" vessel) serves as a direct metaphor for this body. Ancient commentators have taken the present physical body to be like a vessel;

yet, when examining the intent of the sutra closely, it means that [the body] carries emptiness on a long journey to provide sustenance to other lands. Can this body carry emptiness on a long journey?

Now that the body has died, how could it possibly carry emptiness far to provide sustenance? The *Dharmapada-sūtra* states: "Consciousness dwells within the form, just as a sparrow hides within its nest."
When the bottle is broken, the sparrow flies away; once the bottle is shattered, how can it hold space?
As stated in the *Dharmapada*, the "bottle" is a metaphor for the physical body (*rūpakāya*). There is no doubt that the "bottle" in this sutra refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Blocking its two holes is a metaphor for being deluded regarding the two gates of birth and death. When a person is born, they come riding upon delusion; when a person dies...
It also follows along with delusion; because "obstruction" is itself delusion, traveling a thousand li represents the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
The consciousness (*vijñāna*) is maintained as it travels far, selecting its conditions across thousands of miles—whether in this country or another—reaching everywhere without restriction.
Thus, it is said that the karma of traveling a thousand li causes the consciousness to run, just as a person carrying a jar to provide for another country represents the consciousness.
"Taking on a body in future lives in other lands" is a general metaphor for the six realms of existence (*ṣaḍgati*).

"The jar being empty is a metaphor for consciousness (*vijñāna*)" because the essence of consciousness is fundamentally empty. Consciousness is confined within the aggregates (*skandha*) like the space within a jar; since the dharma and the metaphor correspond perfectly, it is said, "it is likewise so."
"Ānanda, in this way, empty space does not come from that direction [to here]; it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor is it of spontaneous nature.
This section of the sutra takes up the preceding metaphorical explanation to clarify that space has no coming or going, thereby concluding the demonstration of the falsity of the *vijñāna-skandha*.

"Ānanda," and so forth, provides a general enumeration; "in this way," and so forth, specifically refutes [the notion of its origin]. Within the refutation, he first refutes the idea that it "comes from there," saying:

If that person comes from another direction carrying a vessel filled with space, then since they have come from that direction with a vessel filled with space, there ought to be less empty space at the location where that vessel now resides.
If the original location of the vessel did not lack any space, then one knows that space did not come from there.
"Filled" (zhù) means "contained" (chéng). The following passage refutes this entry [of space], meaning that the vessel came from that other place.
If empty space enters from this [opening], then since it can enter, it must also be able to exit. If one were to open the hole and overturn the jar, one should see the empty space exiting;

if no empty space exits, then one knows that no empty space entered. Therefore, the conclusion below clarifies that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is illusory, and that it neither comes nor goes, which is identical in meaning to the preceding analogy.
The causes and conditions and the spontaneous nature [of these phenomena] are to be understood as explained previously. This concludes the meaning of the three samādhis.
The section on the five aggregates ultimately converging into the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is hereby concluded.

Furthermore, Ānanda, what are the six entrances (*ṣaḍāyatana*)? ... [up to] ... they are all equally the appearance of fatigue produced by the fixed gaze of Bodhi.
