In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One follows the previous inquiry into the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). First, he sets forth the true essence, and subsequently, he analyzes and explains away deluded appearances.

Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Moreover" (fùcì) follows the previous general inquiry into the six sense bases in order to reveal their true essence. The passage beginning with "Ānanda" proceeds to specifically refute [delusions regarding] the first [sense base].

As for the term "moreover" (fùcì), it indicates that following the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the six sense bases are again raised for discussion; thus, they are brought into harmony [with the truth].
The meaning of "true" (*zhen*) is as explained in the opening passage of the *Pañcaskandhaka*. Regarding the refutation of the "entrances" (*āyatana*), the *Fajie Cidi* states:
"Entrance" (*ru*) takes the sense of "penetrating and entering. This is because there is a mutual relationship of entry between the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*).

As it is said: "When the object enters the faculty, the faculty is activated; when the faculty enters the object, the object is activated," for both the faculty and the object lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Because they exist in mutual dependence, the meaning clarified in this passage concerns the sense objects entering the sense faculties; the intent of the refutation lies in the sense faculties themselves.
Therefore, the other five [aggregates] follow this pattern. The current text corresponds to the two phrases from that [previous section], "the eyes staring until they become fatigued":

the first phrase cites the preceding statement regarding the aggregate of form, while simultaneously referring to the beginning of the present method. Here, "the eyes" refer to the sense faculty (*indriya*), and "fatigue" refers to what is produced within that faculty.
Because the delusive marks are subsumed within the mind which grasps objects, the subsequent passage speaks of both the objects and the mind.
Now, I say that including these faculties and objects, they are all equally the delusions manifested within the true nature of Bodhi. This clarifies the meaning of how delusion arises from the True.

However, the True is fundamentally without delusion; delusion arises through the entry [of consciousness]. Since there is no delusion outside of the True, one is able to realize that delusion is entirely [the True].
It is indeed so.
From "due to the two kinds of false objects, light and darkness" (up to) "the two objects of light and darkness ultimately have no substance.

This section of the sutra follows the preceding discussion on how the object of light enters the sense organ; since they are separated, they are fundamentally non-existent. From "due to" below... [text continues].
To demonstrate the principle of the objects entering the faculties: the term "arousing" (*fa*) is spoken in reference to the side of the objects.

"Arousing" means that external objects arouse the internal faculties, which then "suck in" and grasp them—referring to the two objects of light and darkness arousing that which dwells in the midst of seeing.

"Dwelling in the midst" refers to what is called the *bu-chen-gen* (the physical root); this is the form of the eye itself. For the other five [faculties], each points to the form of its own respective root as being that which dwells in the midst; it is the same for all.
This character "xi" (inhale) is spoken of in relation to the sense organs; the mutual arising of one exhalation and one inhalation is called "seeing-nature.
The following section clarifies that this seeing-nature is devoid of substance when separated from sensory objects; the text is easy to understand.
"Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this seeing—from its origin—is neither caused by conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding discussion on "entry" (*praveśa*) and establishes three refutations of dharmas to clarify the falsity of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-āyatana*).

"Thus" and below provide a general enumeration; "what" and below provide the specific refutation; "therefore" and below conclude by revealing the absence of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*). First, as for [the general enumeration]:
These characters are the terms used to introduce the subsequent section from the preceding one. Regarding the phrase "How so? (*kutaḥ*), this is a question (*paryanuyoga*).

From "If [one follows] the clarification" onwards, the text correctly reveals the intent of the refutation; the meaning of the passage can be understood directly. The section beginning with "Therefore" concludes by demonstrating that the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) is illusory.

Since its nature is illusory, it is neither produced through causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) nor is it spontaneous (*svabhāva*). This establishes the mutual manifestation of the real and the illusory.
As explained in the section on the five aggregates, all subsequent passages should be understood by analogy.
Ānanda, it is as if there were a person who, with two fingers—[up to]—these are likewise the signs of fatigue produced by the staring of Bodhi.

This section of the sutra follows the preceding [section] to specifically refute the ear-faculty (*śrotra-āyatana*). Here, it first clarifies that the sense-fields (*āyatana*) arise from delusion, thereby indicating that both the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are equally delusive.
The phrase "for example" (*tadyathā*) serves as an illustrative term; upon careful examination of the textual meaning, this is a principle (*dharma*), not a metaphor (*upamāna*).
Changshui’s interpretation as a metaphor is erroneous. Wuxing’s commentary states: "For example" here refers to the provisional (*prajñapti*).
Since these matters are established to clarify the instruction so that one may awaken to it, it is said: "For example, as the speaker from Wuxing [explains].

This is because the faculty of hearing has no time of movement or stillness; the faculty itself is inherently quiescent. This state of quiescence is the immediate proximity to the true essence (*tattva*), wherein not even a trace of delusion can be found.

Therefore, false and illusory phenomena are employed to clarify the characteristics of toil. As for the act of blocking the ears with one's fingers to produce sound, this precisely clarifies [the point].
The faculties and objects arise falsely; this constitutes the false characteristic of the ear-entrance (*śrotra-āyatana*).

Furthermore, the "ear" refers to the faculty, which is produced by the exhaustion of labor, while "sound" refers to the object. Both this faculty and its object are equally false characteristics arising within the true nature of Bodhi.

The manner in which falsity arises from the True is as explained previously. Furthermore, the character *deng* (staring) represents the false characteristic of the eye; the remaining five [entrances] all likewise speak of...
The term "staring" (deng) is intended to provide a single illustration to facilitate easy understanding for others.
This refers to the two kinds of delusive objects—motion and stillness—[up to] the point where these two objects of motion and stillness are ultimately found to have no inherent substance.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding passage to clarify the meaning of the objects entering the sense organs; it demonstrates that when separated, they are fundamentally non-existent.
The subsequent sections showing the objects entering the sense organs—namely "emitting" and "absorbing," as well as "this hearing"—are all to be interpreted as before.
"Thus, Ānanda, you should hear it thus... [up to] 'originally neither through causes and conditions nor by spontaneous nature.
This section of the sūtra follows the preceding entry into the meaning [of the sense bases] and establishes three refutations of dharmas to clarify the falsity of the ear-base (*śrotrāyatana*).

"Thus" and below provide a general enumeration; "what" and below provide the specific refutation; "therefore" and below conclude by revealing the non-nature [of the base]. Within this refutation of non-nature:

Why is this? The first phrase is an interrogative statement. From "If [it arises] from stillness" onwards, the text clearly elucidates the intent of the refutation, which can be understood through the words.
Therefore, the subsequent section concludes by manifesting that the ear enters into false causes and conditions, arising spontaneously, as explained previously.
Ānanda, it is like a person who suddenly pinches his nose... (until) "these are all manifestations of fatigue produced by staring at Bodhi.

This section of the sutra follows the previous [analysis] to specifically refute the entry through the nose. Here, it first clarifies that the entry arises from delusion, pointing out that both the sense-object and the sense-organ are equally delusory.
The word "like" (*pí-rú*) is explained as before. "Pinch" (*chù*) is read with an entering tone; it means to inhale and grasp external air.
It is called "possessing" because it possesses [the faculty], and because cold air enters the nose and remains there for a long time, the sensation of openness and obstruction arises.
When open, it is empty; when obstructed, it is solid. This precisely clarifies that the entry [of the object] arises from delusion.

Since the nose is a cognition through contact (*saṃsarga*), it is termed "contact" (*spraṣṭavya*); for contact is only manifested when the subject and object meet. Thus, although the objects of the nose are various fragrances...

The discussion of odors must be based on their penetration and obstruction; furthermore, it is explained previously that both the faculty (the nose) and its object (the odor) beneath it are equally false, arising from the True.
Due to these two kinds of false objects—penetration and obstruction—the two objects of penetration and obstruction ultimately possess no inherent substance.

This section of the sutra follows upon the preceding passage to clarify the meaning of the sense objects entering the faculties; since they are originally non-existent when separated, it proceeds below to demonstrate this meaning of the objects entering the faculties.
The terms "emitting" (*fa*) and "absorbing" (*xi*), as well as "this hearing" (*ci wen*) and what follows, are all to be interpreted as previously explained.
One should know that this hearing neither comes from being unobstructed nor from being obstructed; it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding discussion on the sense bases (*āyatana*) and establishes three refutations of phenomena to clarify the falsity of the olfactory base (*ghrāṇāyatana*).
"One should know" is the general enumeration; "what is it... begins the specific refutation; and "therefore" concludes by revealing its lack of intrinsic nature. This is the first part of the text.
Examining the various preceding and following passages concerning the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), each contains the phrase "Thus, Ānanda";

its omission here is an error resulting from the translation hall. In the section on "Refutation," the phrase "For what reason? (*tat kasya hetoḥ*) is an interrogative statement. If one follows the general principle below, it correctly clarifies the intent of the refutation.
The character for "trigger" (*jī*) in "auditory trigger" (*wén-jī*) is explained metaphorically; "trigger" refers to the bolt of a crossbow, taking it as that which initiates [the discharge].
The speed of an arrow serves as a metaphor for the nature of olfaction;

when the contact with a fragrance or a stench lies dormant within and is suddenly triggered, this olfactory faculty acts with the swiftness of a mechanical trigger, hence the analogy. The remainder of the text is easily understood.
Thus, the conclusion below clarifies that the sense base of the nose (*ghrāṇāyatana*) is false and arises through causes and conditions, occurring spontaneously as previously explained.
"Ānanda, it is as if there were a person who licks his lips with his tongue... [up to] 'these are all equally the appearance of fatigue produced by staring at the state of Bodhi.

This section of the sutra follows the previous [section] to specifically refute the tongue-entrance (*jihvā-āyatana*). Here, it first clarifies that the entrance arises from delusion, thereby indicating that both the faculties and their objects are delusive.
The word 'as if' (*pí-rú*) is explained as before. 'Lick' (*shì*) is pronounced *zhǐ* (with the radical for 'deity' and the phonetic *zhǐ*); it refers to using the tongue..."
To grasp a flavor is called "licking. What is now termed "licking the lips" refers to the lips; it is the tongue that performs a hollow licking of the lips.
"Mature licking" means licking for a long duration until the strength of the tongue is exhausted and fatigue ensues. As for "tasting," if one is ill, one perceives a bitter taste;
if one is not ill, one perceives a slight sweetness. This tasting and the experience of bitterness are manifested as flavors when the tongue moves.

When the sense organ is unmoving, the nature of neutrality (mādhurya) is ever-present; yet while those tastes of sweetness and bitterness have beginnings and endings, the taste of neutrality is ever-present.

This "ever-presence" is spoken of in contrast to "beginning and ending," and "unmoving" is spoken of as stillness. Neutrality is the taste of stillness, and stillness is spoken of in contrast to movement.
Sweetness and bitterness are the tastes of movement. These two tastes—movement and stillness—are manifested by licking and kissing; this is precisely so.

This clarifies that [the sense] arises from delusion; the tongue also perceives within contact, as its cognition is manifested through the conjunction with flavors. Therefore, it includes the tongue below [in the list], showing that both the faculties and their objects are false.
These falsehoods arise based on the True, as explained previously.
"Because of the two kinds of delusive objects—sweetness, bitterness, and blandness... [down to] ...and the bland object ultimately have no substance.
This section of the sutra follows upon the preceding to clarify the meaning of the objects entering the faculties; when separated, they are fundamentally non-existent. From "Because of sweetness...
onwards, it demonstrates the meaning of the objects entering the faculties. "Emitting and inhaling," as well as "this cognition," are all explained as before.
"Thus, Ānanda, you should know that [the tongue-faculty] is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature.

This section of the sūtra follows the preceding discussion on the sense-bases (*āyatana*) and establishes three refutations of phenomena to clarify the falsity of the tongue-faculty (*jihvā-āyatana*).

The phrase "Thus" and below provides a general enumeration; within this enumeration, following the previous text, each item should list three factors. Although four are listed here, they should be understood according to the same principle.

The three dharmas are the intention [of the teaching]. Why is it that what follows specifically refutes them? Therefore, the subsequent section concludes by revealing the refutation of their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Within this refutation, the phrase "Why is this so? (*tat kasya hetoḥ*) is the interrogative statement. From "If sweet... onwards, the actual intent of the refutation is clarified.

In the initial refutation, sweetness and bitterness are contrasted with the neutral (bland) flavor; these are the two flavors of movement and stillness. When movement is added to the bitter flavor, the speaker’s intention is to reveal this through metaphorical implication.
Because of the five flavors within movement as well as the flavors of innate transformation and so forth, the remaining text is understandable.
Therefore, the conclusion below clarifies that the tongue-base (*jihvā-āyatana*) is a false cause and condition arising spontaneously, as explained previously.
"Ānanda, it is like a person who, with one cold hand [and the other hot]... (up to) "...these are all equally the appearance of fatigue produced by staring at Bodhi.

This section of the sutra follows the previous passage to specifically refute the body and the sense-bases (*āyatana*). Here, it first clarifies that the sense-bases arise from delusion, pointing out that both the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are equally illusory.
The word "like" (*pī-yǔ*) is explained as before; the mutual interaction of the cold and heat illustrates precisely how the sense-bases arise from delusion.
The two lines beginning with "arising falsely as a perception of contact" mean that contact itself has no name; it is manifested through separation.

However, since the nature of touch is originally non-existent at the time of separation, one knows touch by means of contact; thus, it is said that the "perception of contact" manifests the knowledge of separation.

Because the body also knows [objects] within contact, this "function" (*gōng*) is merely a transformation of "force" (*shì*); the text is simply stating this. Now, regarding the mutual relation of cold and heat:
Once the conditions for involvement have formed, they arise from the contact of exertion; furthermore, as explained below regarding the faculties and objects, both are equally false.
These falsehoods arise based upon the True, as previously interpreted.
Due to the two kinds of false objects—separation and union—[and so forth] down to the two types of objects, the disagreeable and the agreeable, these ultimately possess no substantial essence.
This section of the sutra follows from the preceding to clarify the meaning of the objects entering the sense organs; they are fundamentally non-existent when separated.
Below, the text demonstrates the meaning of the objects entering the sense organs through four phases. Why, then, does it speak of only two objects?

It is because the states of opposition and compliance are manifested through conjunction and separation; although all four phases are indicated, they are subsumed under these two objects of conjunction and separation. Thus, there is "emission" and "inhalation."
The subsequent explanations regarding "knowing" and "below" are all as previously interpreted.
Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this faculty of cognition (the body-faculty) is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding discussion on the sense-bases (*āyatana*) and establishes three refutations of phenomena to clarify the illusory nature of the body-base.

Thus, the section below generally lists [the arguments], while the subsequent section specifically refutes them; therefore, the final section concludes by demonstrating that they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Within the initial general listing, if one follows the structure of the previous discussion on the sense-bases (*āyatana*), only three refutations are listed; however, here four dharmas are listed.

Nevertheless, the way these are categorized according to their conformity or opposition, and their reduction through separation or combination, should be understood as before in accordance with the three refutations. Within the refutation, the phrase "For what reason? (*tat kasya hetoḥ*)— [End of excerpt]
This is a summary statement; when combined with the following section, which clearly elucidates the meaning of the refutation, the text becomes intelligible.
Therefore, the subsequent conclusion demonstrates that the body and its sense bases (*āyatana*) are causes and conditions of false delusion, arising spontaneously as explained previously.
"Ānanda, it is like a person who, when exhausted, falls asleep... (up to) 'these are all equally the appearance of exhaustion produced by staring into the state of Bodhi.

This section of the sutra follows the previous [section] to specifically refute the mind entering through the sense organs. Here, it first clarifies that entry arises from delusion, thereby indicating that both the faculties and their objects are equally delusory.

[Note on the commentary]: The word "like" (*pí-rú*) is explained as before. The phrase "exhausted and then sleeping" (*láo-jù zé mián*) corresponds to what follows. "Sleeping" (*shuì*) is contrasted with what comes below.
The character "awake" (*wù*) is examined by taking the meaning of "sleeping" (*mèi*); this means that when a person is weary, they sleep, and sleeping is precisely slumbering.

Once the slumber has matured, one awakens. This clarifies the two meanings of awakening and sleeping. Regarding the two lines beginning with "surveying objects" (*lǎn chén*): "surveying" (*lǎn*) means to grasp;

"objects" (*chén*) refers to the five sense-objects, such as form and so forth. Here, the objects grasped by the mental faculty (*yì-gēn*) are the past five sense-objects that have already fallen away.
Because it is like a shadow, it is said that "perceiving objects is recollection. This means that thinking back upon past objects is called "recollection" (*smṛti*).

When such thought does not arise, it is called "loss of recollection" (*muṣitasmṛti*). Losing this state of mind is what is meant by "forgetting"; this clarifies the two meanings of recollection and forgetting.
Recollection and forgetting are precisely arising and ceasing: when awake, one has recollection, which is arising; when asleep, one forgets, which is ceasing. Although...
There are four characteristics—waking, sleeping, remembering, and forgetting—which are collectively subsumed within the two dharmas of arising and ceasing.

Arising further subsumes abiding, and ceasing further subsumes change; therefore, they are termed arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. These four characteristics of arising and so forth are dharmas contemplated through the inversions of the mental faculty (*manas*).
It is by means of these that the mental faculty is manifested; apart from this arising and ceasing, the mental faculty has no substantial entity.
Therefore it is said: "Inhalation and cultivation return to the center. "Inhalation" refers to the drawing in [of objects], while "cultivation" refers to perfuming.

Within the meaning of the character *xi* (cultivation), there is contained the phenomenon of successive arising and ceasing. This means that by inhaling and cultivating external objects, they return to the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), where thoughts arise and cease moment by moment;

the preceding ceases as the succeeding arises without any interval. This is precisely what is called the faculty of mental cognition (*manovijñānendriya*). This clarifies the entry [into the stage of non-conceptualization].
It arises from delusion; furthermore, the following clarifies that both the faculties and their objects are equally delusory. As explained previously, delusion arises based upon the True (the Real).
Because of these two kinds of delusory objects—arising and ceasing—[it follows that] these two objects of arising and ceasing ultimately have no substance.

This section of the sutra follows the preceding passage to clarify the meaning of the objects entering the faculties; since they are fundamentally non-existent when separated, it now demonstrates this meaning of the objects entering the faculties.
Above, the four phases of waking, sleeping, remembering, and forgetting were explained; here, we refer only to the two aspects of arising and ceasing.
This is because the previous four phases are subsumed within arising and ceasing, and thus only these two "objects" (dusts) are mentioned, while the others are omitted.

Regarding the two terms "intermediate" (*sthiti*) and "change" (*anyathātva*), "accumulation" (*cita*) refers to the accumulation of the aforementioned states of waking and sleeping, as well as the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), within the mental faculty (*manas*).
While the first five sense bases (*pañca-āyatana*) are all said to be "emerging," only the present mental base (*mana-āyatana*) is here termed "accumulating.

This is because one knows that the first five [bases] take the present substantial entities of the five sensory objects as their basis and are therefore called "emerging," whereas the present mind accumulates those of the past.

Because it falls away from the conditioned shadows of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), it is called "accumulation" (*saṃcita*); this differs from the previously mentioned "arousing of the intention.

Regarding the "internal objects": these are the objects manifested within the mental faculty (*manas*). In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, they are termed "objects with substance" (*sadravya*) or "solitary images" (*kevala-pratibimba*), which refers precisely to the mental object (*dharma-viṣaya*).
In the two lines beginning with "seeing and hearing," the terms "seeing and hearing" are abbreviated; they should include the [other] five faculties in reverse order.
"Flowing" refers to the first five faculties, which grasp present objects and can only flow outwards in accordance with the stream;

the sixth faculty, the mind-faculty (*manas*), only takes as its object the past shadows of the five sensory dusts that have already fallen away. Thus, the objects previously seen and heard return against the stream;
therefore, "flowing against the stream" in seeing and hearing is called the "stream of recollection. As for "not reaching," it means:
When thought-recollection cannot reach [the object], it is called "forgetting" (*wang*); because one forgets, there is no further flow, and thus it is called "flowing beyond" (*liu bu ji*).
The single character "beyond" (*ji*) penetrates the interval between recollection/forgetting and arising/ceasing. These two phrases originally form a single continuous sentence;
if read as such, their meaning will become clear of itself. Everyone reads them as two separate sentences, though some point out that "flowing beyond" (*liu bu ji*)...

It is an error to claim that the nature of awakening and cognition resides in the stages of the fields and lands. Why? Because in those inferior stages, [the mind] has already been completely extinguished; what, then, could constitute the nature of awakening and cognition?

As stated previously, regarding birth, abiding, change, and extinction, it is within the process of inhalation and exhalation that one returns to the locus named the faculty of mental cognition (*manas-vijñāna-indriya*).
It is precisely at the juncture between birth and extinction—where one birth and one extinction occur—that the nature of awakening and cognition is revealed. Therefore, as stated before...

The text further states: "To perceive objects and lose mindfulness, whether awake or asleep," and so forth; these words all clarify that arising and ceasing constitute the essential nature of cognitive awareness.

Those who seek to clarify this principle should reflect upon them carefully. The subsequent passage, beginning with "Apart from those," clarifies that this cognitive awareness lacks an intrinsic self-nature;
the meaning of the text is thus understandable.
"Thus, Ānanda, you should know that [from 'thus' to] 'neither caused by conditions nor spontaneous in nature.
This section of the sūtra follows the preceding discussion on the sense bases (*āyatana*) and establishes three refutations of phenomena to clarify the falsity of the mind-base (*manāyatana*).
'Thus' and below is the general enumeration; 'what' and below is the specific refutation; 'therefore' and below is the conclusion revealing the non-nature. First is the enumeration."

This also establishes four refutations. However, because waking and sleeping, as well as arising and ceasing, collectively belong to the objective realm (*viṣaya*), they are identical to the previous three refutations.

Within these refutations, the phrase "Why is this so? (*tat kasya hetoḥ*) is an interrogative statement. From the words "If from waking" (*yadi jāgarāt*) onwards, the intention of the refutation is clearly explained.

From the words "If from the sense-faculties" (*yadi indriyebhyaḥ*) onwards, the faculties are successively refuted. That is to say: if this cognitive awareness (*vijñāna*) were to emerge from the sense-faculties, then this faculty—
The "finger" and "intention" refer to the peripheral sense organs; what is called the "fleshly heart" (*māṃsa-guḍa-citta*) is precisely this. Regarding the two states of waking and sleeping:

this clearly explains recollection and forgetfulness, for recollection and forgetfulness are manifested through waking and sleeping. Furthermore, since waking and sleeping are manifested in dependence upon the body, it is said that they "follow the opening and closing of the body.
"Opening and closing of the body" means that when the physical form opens, it is called "waking. When a person is awake, all six sense faculties are present.
The opening of the form corresponds to the union of the names; when a person is asleep, the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are all closed.
*Liezi* says: "When they awaken, the form opens; when they sleep, the form joins. "Joins" means to close. However, this matter of memory and forgetting belongs to the faculty of mind (*manas*).

Furthermore, the memory and forgetting of the mental faculty follows the awakening and sleeping of the body: one can remember during the time of awakening, but forgets immediately upon falling asleep.
Therefore, it is now clarified by means of waking and sleeping. Apart from these states of waking and sleeping, which involve opening and closing, memory and forgetting would have no basis;
since memory and forgetting do not exist, cognitive awareness is not manifested, being like a flower in the sky—meaning it has no substance. The rest of the text is understandable.
Thus, the conclusion below clarifies the meaning: entering into false causes and conditions occurs naturally, as explained previously.
Furthermore, Ānanda, how are the twelve bases (āyatana) fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous true nature of Suchness?
This section of the sūtra, following the preceding discussion, again interrogates the twelve bases by first identifying their true essence.
The phrase "furthermore" initiates the renewed interrogation; "fundamentally" identifies the true essence. As for the "twelve bases," these consist of the six sense organs and the six sense objects.

The *Dhātusūtra* (Sūtra on Elements), also known as the *Dvādaśāyatanasūtra* (Sūtra on the Twelve Bases), is now renamed "Bases" (*āyatana*) because the preceding section was titled "Six Entrances" (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Previously, the term "entrance" (*āyatana*) was used in the sense of that which enters; here, it is named "base" in the sense of that which is entered.

Furthermore, while the former "entrances" carry the implication of mutual interaction, what is here entered refers to fixed bases that lack such interaction. Moreover, the previous six entrances were based upon...

By refuting the sense-faculties (*indriya*), one simultaneously refutes the objects (*viṣaya*); now, by relying on the refutation of the objects within the twelve bases (*āyatana*), one simultaneously refutes the sense-faculties.
Those who realize the Truth should know that although the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of these twelve bases are illusory, their nature (*svabhāva*) is fundamentally true.

It is precisely because sentient beings falsely cling to these phantom existences that the True follows along with the delusions; what was originally the single, wondrously enlightened True Void suddenly becomes the ten [bases].
Second, where the false exists entirely, the true becomes false. Now the Buddha points out that the locus of the false is fundamentally empty;
because it is empty, the false is entirely the true. Thus, within the wondrous enlightenment of true emptiness, one seeks the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and finds them utterly unobtainable.

Yet this is not a matter of discarding the false to separately manifest a true essence; rather, one must understand the deluded and chaotic appearances of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*).
This is precisely the principle of pure original nature. Why? Because form is identical to formlessness, and confusion is identical to non-confusion.
Therefore, the ancient masters said: "The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature; the illusory, empty body is itself Dharma-body. This is what is meant.
The meaning of realizing the truth is simply this. This is a general inquiry, which will be followed by specific refutations below.
"Ānanda, you should now observe this Jeta Grove... [up to] ...who clarifies the substance of emptiness? Emptiness is also like this.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding part by specifically refuting the two locations of the eye and form; here, it first refutes the production of form from the eye.

"You should now observe" marks the initial presentation of the two locations, the eye and form; "at the mind" lists the sequence of their mutual production, thereby establishing the method of refutation, Ānanda.

Below, first, regarding the refutation of the arising of the eye within the heading: the character "contemplation" (*guan*) refers to the sense-base of the eye; "Ji-lin" and so forth refer to the sense-base of form, which can be understood from the list.
Regarding the refutation: if it is said that the eye arises from form, then because form arises from the eye, when one perceives emptiness directly before oneself, it is no longer form.
Since one sees emptiness and emptiness can refute form, the nature of form should be dissolved. If...
When the nature of form (*rūpa*) dissolves, everything is revealed as being utterly non-existent;

since non-existence is itself emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the two following lines regarding the characteristics of form distinguish between form and emptiness. This is because emptiness is manifested through form;

now that the characteristics of form are absent, there is a total, unified emptiness—who then could manifest the substance of emptiness? This means that the eye is the producer and form is the produced.
"Since 'arising' has already been refuted to clarify that form does not arise from the eye, 'emptiness' is likewise treated in this way by reversing the characteristics of form and refuting them.
To avoid redundancy, the text says 'likewise' (*evam*); if the full meaning were supplied, it should read:
'If the characteristic of form arises from the eye, then seeing form is not emptiness, and the nature of emptiness should dissolve; if it dissolves, then all things are revealed.'"
Since emptiness exists and there is no one who clarifies material form, it is said that "emptiness is also thus. This is the teaching on the mutual sublation of form and emptiness;

its intent is to clarify that form and emptiness mutually cancel each other out, such that the eye-faculty which arises from them is neither unchanging nor changing, and neither constant nor transient.
Thus, the subject and object are dissimilar, and one can know with certainty that form is not produced by the eye. This makes clear that form does not arise from the eye.
"If, moreover, visual form (*rūpa*) were to produce the seeing of the eye" (up to) "it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding arguments to refute that visual form produces [seeing] and concludes that it is not of a different nature.
In the previous passage, the eye was the producer and visual form was the produced; in this passage, visual form is again treated as the producer and the eye as the produced.
That which is produced arises because form can produce seeing; thus, when one contemplates emptiness before one's eyes, form is usurped by emptiness and form perishes along with it.
Since the sensory object of form that produces [seeing] has been extinguished, the nature of seeing that was produced also ceases. Therefore, it is said that "seeing itself is dissolved.
If seeing ceases, then there is no seeing anywhere at all. Since that seeing is absent, what is it that illuminates?
Is it space or form? As now, space and form can be distinguished; one may know with certainty that form is not produced by seeing, for this is clear.
Since neither the sense organ nor the object can produce one another, we know that both locations are false. Therefore, the following conclusion reveals the falsity of these two locations:
seeing is the sense organ and space is the object; since both dharmas—the organ and the object—have no location, and having no location...

Who else would further debate whether [the world] arises from causes and conditions or spontaneously? Since both are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the preceding section indicated the Real, while this section concludes by revealing the False;
thus, the indication and the conclusion mutually clarify the Real and the False, as all subsequent sections follow this pattern.
"Ānanda, listen further to this passage from 'within this Jeta Grove' up to 'the sound comes to the side of the ear' and 'the ear goes to the place of the sound.
This section of the sutra follows the previous [analysis] to separately refute the two locations of the ear and the sound, thereby clarifying that both are false.

In the phrase 'Ānanda,' the first part designates the two locations of the ear and the sound; in the subsequent list, the term 'listening' (*ting*) within the refutation of coming and going serves as the heading for the analysis of the phenomenon."
Regarding the sense base of the ear: "beating the drum and striking the bell" refers to the sense base of sound. The final two lines clarify the protocol for the assembly at Jeta’s Grove:
once the food is prepared, the drum is beaten to gather the multitude, and the bell is struck when they are to receive their meal; the arrangement of the assembly can be understood from this.
"Ānanda, if this sound comes to the side of the ear... (up to) "...upon hearing the bell, they all come together to the place of eating.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding argument to first refute the idea that the sound comes to the location of the ear. "Ānanda," and so forth, restates the aforementioned points;
"as I," and so forth, provides an example; "this sound," and so forth, applies the analogy to the case at hand, thereby refuting the "I" within the cited example.

This is the Buddha’s own statement, following the previous analogy regarding sound. If the Buddha says, "Suppose I were begging for food in the city of Śrāvastī," then I would not be in the Jeta Grove.
The correspondence of the principles should be stated thus: "I" is like the sound; the city of Śrāvastī is like Ānanda;
and the Jeta Grove is like Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, and the others. The combined meaning is that this sound must reach Ānanda.
The ear-faculty is like me begging for alms in the city of Śrāvastī; Maudgalyāyana and Kāśyapa should not hear it simultaneously.

As with the aforementioned Jeta Grove, there is no "self" [as a fixed entity]. If that sound of the bell were to reach Ānanda’s ear, then Maudgalyāyana and the others should not hear the sound of the bell.
How much more so, then, does this refute the claim below that the sound comes from elsewhere to reach the ear? Thus, it is clarified that the sound does not come.
Since the ear is able to hear everywhere, the sphere of sound is illusory.
Furthermore, if your ear were to go to the location of that sound, then if there were no coming or going, there would likewise be no hearing.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding arguments to refute the notion that the ear travels to the location of the sound. The phrase "If again... restates the previous argument;
"As I... introduces the example; and "As you hear... applies the principle to refute the cited analogy. In the aforementioned example, "I" was likened to the sound;
here, "I" is likened to the ear. The point of the analogy is as follows: if the ear were to travel to the side of the sound, then the Buddha... [would not perceive it].
It is said that if I were to return and dwell in the city of Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, then "I" would no longer exist. According to the principle of the analogy, it should be stated as follows:
"I" is like the ear; the Jeta Grove is like the place where the drum is struck; and the city of Śrāvastī is like the sound of the bell. The combined meaning is:

when you hear the sound of the drum, your ear has already gone to the place where the drum is struck, just as "I" have returned to stay in the Jeta Grove, while the sound of the bell [remains behind].
If they were to emerge simultaneously, they should not be heard together; as in the case of Śrāvastī mentioned above, there would be no "self" [of hearing].
If one were to claim that the ear travels to the location of the drum, then the sounds of the bell and other instruments should likewise not be heard simultaneously.

How much more so when, at the end, we directly refute this to clarify that the ear does not travel, but rather hears universally; thus, the location of the ear is also false. The final two lines further serve as a precaution.
[The text] shifts its argument:
"Therefore, one should know that hearing and sound (up to) are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
This section of the sutra concludes by revealing the falsity of these two locations; as explained previously, there is no location that is not of the nature [of emptiness].
"Ānanda, you should again smell this sandalwood in the incense burner... does it arise in your nose, or does it arise in space?

This section of the sutra follows the previous passage to specifically refute the two locations—the nose and the fragrance—to demonstrate that both are illusory. In the phrase "Ānanda," the text first identifies the two locations, the nose and the fragrance;
in the subsequent section, it lists three possible locations for the arising of the fragrance and refutes them, beginning with the initial identification.
The character "smell" (*ghrāṇa*) refers to the locus of the sense organ; "sandalwood fragrance" refers to the locus of the sensory object. As for the "one *zhu*," the *zhu* is a unit of weight.
According to ancient reckoning, twenty-four *zhu* constitute one *liang*. One *zhu* is calculated to weigh four *fen*, one *li*, and seven *máo*, with a slight remainder.
Yet, despite its small quantity, its fragrance is perceived from forty *li* away, which demonstrates the excellence of this incense.
This refers to ten *li* on each of the four sides of the city, not forty *li* in total.
The Buddha’s intention likely took the sense of "pervasive penetration" to manifest the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), rather than regarding forty *li* as a superior measure.

The *Bowuzhi* states that there was once a person from the Western Regions who presented incense; according to Han regulations, anything weighing less than one *jin* would not be accepted, so the envoy stole it.
If one takes a piece of incense about the size of a bean and places it atop the palace gate, its fragrance can be smelled for ten li in all four directions of Chang’an;
this can be verified and known from the records.
Ānanda, if this fragrance were produced in your nose (and so forth), then to say that fragrance issues from within the nose and that you hear it would be illogical.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding arguments to first refute the notion that fragrance arises within the nose. It states:

if this fragrance were to arise within your nose—as you claim that fragrance is produced from within the nose—it would have to emerge from the nose itself. However, the nose is composed of flesh and blood; it is not sandalwood.
How, then, could there be the scent of sandalwood within the nose? Furthermore, when you say you "smell" the fragrance, you are actually inhaling and grasping it.

If external air is what is called "hearing," it should enter through the nose; if it were to exit the nose as fragrance while being called "hearing," then hearing would not be its true nature, and the nose would be a locus of delusion.

Furthermore, if [the sense of hearing] arises from space, and the nature of space is eternal and constant, how could it be that one hears only within a range of forty *li*? How could it be that one has already heard [only within that limit]?

This section of the sutra follows the preceding arguments to refute the arising of fragrance from emptiness and wood. If it were produced from emptiness, then next one must refute the arising from emptiness:
since the nature of emptiness is eternal, fragrance should be eternally present; why then would there be times when there is fragrance and times when there is not?
Furthermore, if fragrance arises spontaneously from emptiness, why rely on burning this withered wood in a brazier before it can produce fragrance?

Thus we know that fragrance does not arise from empty space. If it were produced beneath the wood, there would be three contradictions: first, if it arose from the wood, then when the wood is burned, it should be consumed;
second, since fragrance arises from the wood, the substance of this fragrance should turn into smoke upon burning;
third, if the nose perceives through contact, one should only perceive the fragrance after being enveloped by the smoke. Now, a single *zhu* of smoke rises into the air before it has traveled far.
How is it that one can already hear [the fragrance] within forty *li*? One knows with certainty that it does not arise from the wood;

thus, the notion that the fragrance resides [inherently] in its location is false. Furthermore, the fact that it can be smelled even where the smoke does not reach clearly demonstrates its hidden penetration, and its nature as emptiness (*śūnyatā*) can be seen therein.

Therefore, one should know that the nose and fragrance, and the act of smelling (up to the point of "the fundamental nature"), are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
This section of the sutra concludes by revealing the falsity of these two locations; that there is no location that is not of the nature [of reality] is as explained previously.
"Ānanda, when you constantly hold your bowl among the assembly during the two times [of meal], [the sense of taste] arises within the tongue or it arises within the food.
This section of the sutra follows the previous passage to specifically refute the two locations of the tongue and flavor, clarifying that both are false.

In the phrase "Ānanda," the text first designates the two locations of the tongue and flavor; in the subsequent list of the three locations where flavor might arise, the text refutes each one. Within this initial designation:
However, when clarifying the locations of the objects (*viṣaya*) and the sense organs (*indriya*), these are treated briefly.

Yet, since flavor does not perceive itself but is known as flavor by means of the tongue, the location of the sense organ is already implicitly contained within the term "flavor" and is therefore omitted. As for the "two times," these are the morning and the midday;

according to the monastic regulations (*vinaya*), monks are permitted to receive food during these two times, and eating after midday is not allowed. Thus, curd, clarified butter, and ghee [are all included].
From milk, there is one transformation called curd (*dadhi*); a second transformation is called fresh butter (*navanīta*); a third transformation is called clarified butter (*ghṛta*);
and a fourth transformation is called the finest essence (*sarpis*). In India, these are known as the "superior flavors," which can be understood from their enumeration here.
"Ānanda, if this taste were produced in your tongue... (up to) "...how could many tastes be known by a single tongue?
This section of the sutra follows the preceding argument to first refute that [taste] is produced in the tongue. The phrase "If, moreover," cites the aforementioned statement;
"in you" is the actual refutation. Regarding "black rock sugar," the *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "This is cane-sugar hardened [into a solid]."
Therefore, as with the stone, ancient tradition also holds that on the cliffs of a mountain in the sea, wild bees build hives and produce honey;
because it is situated beside the cliff, its color is black, and it is called "black stone-honey" (*kṛṣṇa-śilā-madhu*). The rest is easily understood.
"If [taste] arises from food, yet food is not possessed of consciousness (up to: it necessarily lacks cognition, how can it be called 'flavor'?
This section of the sūtra follows the preceding arguments and subsequently refutes the arising of flavor from food and its arising from space.
Regarding "If [taste] arises from food," the following further refutes the arising of flavor from food: if flavor arises from food, and food is not a sentient being, how could it know its own flavor?
The intent is to clarify that if the tongue knows and tastes when food is present, yet you yourself do not know the taste, then this would be identical to another person tasting the flavor;

how could it concern you? How then can it be called the nature of your own knowledge of taste? If [the opponent argues] it is like space, the refutation of the three [positions] below regarding the arising of space from the text can be understood.
Therefore, one should know that taste, the tongue, and the act of tasting (up to the point mentioned) are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
This section of the sutra concludes by revealing the falsity of these two bases; that there is no place where they are not of this [illusory] nature is to be understood as previously explained.
"Ānanda, when you regularly rub your head with your hand in the early morning... [is this sensation] in the hand, or is it in the head?
This section of the sutra follows the previous passage to separately refute the two locations—the body and the touch—in order to clarify that both are false. "Ānanda" marks the beginning;
first, the two locations (body and touch) are identified, and then, under the heading of "intention," the two refutations of subject and object are set forth. The identification is as follows:
As for the body being situated in the manifest locus of tangibility, why is it said that external objects lack sentience and thus do not constitute tangibility?
It must be through the cognition of the body that tangibility is established; this very point indicates that the locus of tangibility has no independent status.

When one rubs the head with the hand, this precisely clarifies the meaning of the contact between two entities. However, since the body and the hand are produced from the same substance, [the hand] is the agent...

If one examines which side constitutes the locus of the subject and object, it is clear that neither subject nor object has a fixed position; since neither subject nor object has a fixed position, both locations are equally illusory.
That which touches belongs to the sense organ, and that which is touched belongs to the object.

If [the touch] were located in the hand, then when the hand is absent, there would be no cognition; if it were located in the head, then when the head is absent, there would be no function. How, then, could this be called "touch"?
This section of the sutra follows the preceding arguments to refute both the subject and the object simultaneously.

As for the phrase "if it were in the hand," this follows from the previous point regarding the touching of the known; its purpose is to reveal the nature of that which is known. This nature of the known is precisely the capacity to touch.
If it resided in the hand, then the head would be devoid of cognition; being devoid of cognition, it would become an insentient object.
How could contact be established? Since insentient objects do not constitute contact, if this nature of the object of cognition were located in the head or the hand, it would be of no use;

and that which is of no use lacks cognition. Therefore, how could contact be established? Whether in the head or in the hand, since the object of cognition is not fixed, contact cannot be established.
"If each were distinct from the other, then, Ānanda... (up to) space should not come into contact with you.
This section of the sutra follows upon the previous discussion of the head and hands to demonstrate that the subject and object cannot be divided, and thus contact is unestablished.
While the preceding text merely used the hands and the head to show that the perceived object has no fixed location, this present passage [proceeds further].
Furthermore, to prevent Ānanda from devising a further argument—that because the hand and the head each possess a nature of cognition—he first refutes it:
if the hand and the head each possessed a nature of cognition, there would then be two cognitions;
if there were two cognitions, then the single person Ānanda would have to have two bodies. Why? Because a single person possesses only one nature of cognitive awareness. Now, as for the head...

If each hand has its own distinct principle, then two cognitions should arise, and the body would become twofold; this refutes the claim that each part possesses its own [cognition], for such a thing is not established.

Furthermore, regarding the head and hands, we shall examine them in terms of identity or difference: if the nature of tactile cognition produced by the head and the hands were one and the same, then the hands and the head should merge into a single entity.
If the head and hands merge and cannot be distinguished, then tactile cognition could not be established. Why? Because [the conditions] would be indistinguishable.
Therefore, it is necessary for two things to combine in order for contact to be established; thus, this [argument] refuting a single substance is not valid.
If one speaks of two as being distinct substances—such as the head and the hand—since these two are distinct, with respect to whom would contact exist?
If the nature of the "known" (the object) resides in the "knower" (the subject), then the "known" is not established; if it resides in the "known," then the "knower" is not established.

If that which is established is neither the subject nor the object, then contact itself is not established. If both subject and object are ultimately untenable, then it would follow that space and you would establish contact;
this refutes the impossibility of their being either identical or different. Nevertheless, the nature of contact cannot be entirely non-existent;
however, since its subject and object have no fixed status, both the body and the locus of contact are illusory.
Therefore, one should know that the perception of touch and the body (up to the point mentioned) are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
This section of the sutra concludes by revealing the falsity of these two bases; their lack of intrinsic nature is both as previously explained.
"Ānanda, as for that which you constantly take as an object within your mind—whether good or evil (up to the point where it is asked): 'Does it exist apart from the mind, having a separate location?
This section of the sutra follows the previous [analysis] to separately refute the two locations of the mind and mental objects (*dharmas*), thereby clarifying that both are false.

From 'Ānanda' onwards, he first designates the two locations of the mind and mental objects; in the subsequent list beginning with 'this dharma,' he refutes them by means of the two alternatives of being either conjoined or separate. Within the designation, 'mind' refers to..."

The dharmas that are wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate within the sense-base of the faculties (indriya-āyatana) constitute the sense-object-base of dharmas (dharma-āyatana). Among these, the dharmas that serve as objects for the mental faculty (manas-indriya) do not transcend the three natures:
those that are wholesome are the nature of humans and devas; those that are unwholesome are the nature of the three miserable realms;

and those that are indeterminate are neither wholesome nor unwholesome. Because they cannot be defined or characterized within the categories of wholesomeness or unwholesomeness, they are called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta). This refers to the fourth dhyāna.

From the heavens up to the four levels of the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu), the equanimity (*upekṣā*) shared by these beings is collectively termed "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*), because its nature is neither wholesome nor unwholesome;
thus it is called "equanimity. Regarding the principle of the arising of phenomena:

this means that even without being taught, one is naturally able to give rise to [understanding], for all conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*) are produced through the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). All dharmas are constructed in this manner.
Since these three natures function as principles, they are called "the principles of generation and formation. In the preceding sections of this list, the text consistently asks, "What do you think?
However, in the present passage, because it follows directly from the aforementioned principles, the phrasing is abbreviated by altering the wording.

"Ānanda, if these dharmas were identical to the mind, then they would not be objects (*viṣaya*) nor objects of the mind's cognition (*ālambana*). How, then, could they constitute sense bases (*āyatana*)?
This section of the sūtra follows the preceding argumentation to first refute the identity [of the three natures] with the mind;

it means that if the aforementioned three natures were identical to the mind, then although they might be called 'dharmas,' they would not be 'objects. Since they are not objects, they are not [the objects] of the mind."
Since that which is the object of cognition is not itself an object of cognition, how can these three natures be established as sense-fields (*āyatana*)?
If they must now be established as fields, then they are not identical to the mind.
If there were a separate location apart from the mind, from what could the mind’s non-objective field be established?
This section of the sutra follows the preceding intent and next refutes [the existence of dharmas] apart from the mind.
It means that if these dharmas were to exist separately from your mind in some other location, would the intrinsic nature of these dharmas be conscious or unconscious?
If these dharmas are conscious, then being conscious is precisely what is called "mind. Since these dharmas are named "mind," [they cannot be separate].

Because it is the mind, it is not an object; furthermore, since it is distinct from you, if it were to exist separately apart from your mind, it would be equivalent to the mental capacity of another person.
If you claim that although it is separate from your mind, this phenomenon is nonetheless your own mind—how could your mind be two-fold?
Therefore, it is said: "Furthermore, these two are distinct from you. This argument establishes that the phenomenon exists as a cognition independent of the mind.

This is not so. If it were not knowledge, then to further distinguish phenomena would be to depart from the mind; yet to say that these phenomena are devoid of knowledge implies they are of the nature of non-knowledge.
That which is non-knowing belongs to the sense objects (*viṣaya*).

However, since these objects are neither the five objects such as form and so forth, nor are they contact—which consists of the union and separation of cold and warmth—nor are they the characteristic of empty space, they are neither form nor emptiness.
And as for this principle, where should it reside? Now, within the emptiness of form (*rūpa-śūnyatā*), there is nothing to be indicated;
it should not be that apart from emptiness there is separately a "human realm" (*manuṣya-loka*). Here, "human realm" refers to the objects of the mind (*dharma-viṣaya*);

because the human realm possesses these dharma-objects, the phrasing here is slightly inverted, and I shall now explain it by rearranging the text. The two lines beginning with "The mind is not... refer to [the nature of] form.

If one seeks this dharma within emptiness, it cannot be found; furthermore, if one seeks it within the mind, since the mind belongs to the subject that perceives (*ālambaka*), it is said that the mind is not the object perceived (*ālambana*).
Thus, the mind is not an external object (*viṣaya*). Yet, if one seeks this dharma among both the internal mind and external objects, it cannot be found in either.
Ultimately, from what could the locus of an object be established? The above constitutes the refutation.

The reason why the principle [of emptiness] merely refutes the objects of the mind (*dharmāyatana*) but does not refute the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*) is precisely because the faculty of mind has no independent substance;
it is manifested only through that which is thought by it. Now that the objects of the mind being thought have been refuted, the faculty of mind naturally ceases to exist.

Moreover, since the current analysis of the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) is specifically refuting the objects, the preceding passages concerning all the bases were explained in terms of the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).

In the section on the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), all explanations are given in terms of the six faculties; in the subsequent section on the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), all explanations are given in terms of the six consciousnesses.
This constitutes the great principle for refuting the three categories [of aggregates, bases, and elements]. One may understand this by observing the various concluding passages before and after.
Therefore, one should know that dharmas and the mind (up to "are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature").
This section of the sūtra concludes by clarifying that both [the object and the subject] are illusory; that there is no place where they are not of the nature [of emptiness], as explained previously.
Furthermore, Ānanda, what are the eighteen realms (*dhātu*) as the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous true nature of *tathatā*?
This section of the sutra, following the previous discussion, again interrogates the eighteen realms;

first, it harmonizes them with the true essence, and subsequently, it provides a detailed explanation of their delusive characteristics. The phrase "Furthermore" initiates the renewed interrogation, while "as the fundamental" introduces the harmonization with the truth. Regarding this harmonization with the truth:

The meaning is as explained previously. Regarding the statement "the eighteen *dhātus*": this refers to the six sense organs (*indriya*), the six objects (*viṣaya*), and the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*).
*Dhātu* has the sense of a boundary or limit, and it carries the sense of being a cause. Furthermore, it carries the sense of a nature (*gotra*). As stated in the subsequent text:

that which arises from the sense organ takes the sense organ as its *dhātu*; that which arises from the object takes the object as its *dhātu*. Moreover, with respect to the sense organ, it belongs to the nature of the sense organ; with respect to the object, it belongs to the nature of the object.

Because they belong to the nature of the sense objects (*viṣaya*), they are called the eighteen *dhātus*. Although this section addresses the refutation [of the self] by means of the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), the primary refutation actually lies in consciousness (*vijñāna*);
therefore, the text refers specifically to consciousness. This can be understood by examining the text itself.
"Ānanda, as you have clearly understood, with the eye and forms as conditions... [up to] ...arising because of forms, taking forms as its realm.

This section of the sutra follows upon the previous inquiry to specifically refute the first three [bases], the eye and so forth. "Ānanda" marks the initial designation of the three factors—the eye and so on;
"this consciousness" next enumerates the causes and realms. Within the designation, the phrase "as you have clearly understood" refers to [the preceding discussion].

Just as you pointed out Ānanda according to the teachings of the Hīnayāna—stating that Ānanda was a follower of the Hīnayāna and saying, "As you understand it, the Hīnayāna holds that consciousness arises dependent on conditions"—the Buddha thus cited that [teaching] to prove the meaning of the present element (*dhātu*).

When it says "eye and form are the conditions," it means that the sense organ (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*) serve as the conditions for the arising of consciousness; all subsequent instances should be understood in this same manner.
The meaning of the "middle realm" (*madhyadhātu*) is as explained previously.
The passage, "Ānanda, if [consciousness] were produced because of the eye, since there would be neither form nor space...

(up to) nothing being indicated, from what could a realm be established?"—this section of the sutra follows upon the previous refutation of production from the eye; it means that if this consciousness were produced because of the eye, [the following would ensue].
Consciousness has "discernment" as its defining characteristic. If no forms were present in the void, there would be nothing to be discerned;
even if consciousness were to arise, for what purpose would it be? If it has no use, then the nature of consciousness itself does not exist.

This argument—that consciousness is without function and thus lacks an essence—is further refuted below by the demonstration that the definition of the sense-bases (*dhātu*) is untenable. As for your [position]:...
The visual faculty is seen to be without marks, unlike the five colors which can be represented; if there were no representation, from what could the sense-sphere be established?
First, if that which produces lacks an object, then that which is produced is useless. Next, if that which produces lacks marks, then that which is produced lacks a sense-sphere.
Thus, it is clear that what is produced by the eye cannot be established as "light."
"If space were produced from form, then when form is absent, one should not be able to perceive the location of space.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding refutation of space being produced from form and can be understood accordingly.
"If both types [of conditions] are combined, such that the eye and form arise together" (up to) "originally neither a causal condition nor a spontaneous nature.

This section of the sutra follows upon the preceding discussion on the meaning of arising; it further refutes the combination [of conditions] and concludes that the characteristics of the boundaries of existence are not established.
While the preceding passage refuted arising by means of the separation of the eye and form, this passage again clarifies the meaning of arising through the conjunction of these two, the eye and form.

Furthermore, the following two lines correctly refute the impossibility of co-arising through conjunction. "Conjunction" refers to the union of the three—faculty, object, and consciousness—as subject and object.
Thus, this consciousness would be half-conjoined with the eye and half-conjoined with the form, while remaining separated in the middle. The second line establishes the meaning of the first:
if consciousness were separated in the middle, it would follow that the faculty and the object are conjoined as a pair, and thus consciousness would possess cognition.
Form is devoid of cognition; how can that which is cognitive and that which is non-cognitive be intermingled in their essential natures to constitute a realm (*dhātu*)?
This argument refuting co-arising is likewise untenable. Therefore, the concluding summary below reveals the falsity of the three bases (*āyatana*).

The first two lines clarify the absence of a locus, while the latter two lines clarify the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The preceding inquiry reconciled the text with reality; now, this concluding summary reveals its falsity. Inquiry.
The mutual possession of the true and the false regarding the fetters follows this pattern below.
Ānanda, furthermore, that which you understand as the ear and sound acting as conditions—[extending] to "being produced by sound"—takes sound as its boundary.

This section of the sutra follows the previous inquiry to specifically refute the three locations, such as the ear and so forth. "Ānanda" begins the first part, which identifies the three dharmas such as the ear;
"this consciousness" introduces the second part, which enumerates the causes and realms.
Within the introductory heading, the word "furthermore" (又) inherits from above to re-introduce the subject, thus changing "easily" (易) to "furthermore" (又); the rest is explained as before.
"Ānanda, if the two characteristics of motion and stillness arise because of the ear... (up to)... then from whom would the sphere of ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna-dhātu*) be established?

This section of the sutra follows the previous refutation that [the consciousness] arises from the ear. Within this passage, there are two points: first, the refutation of the ultimate sense organ (*paramārtha-indriya*);
second, the refutation of the coarse, physical organ (*vibhava-indriya*). First, under the heading "Ānanda," the ultimate sense organ is refuted; that is to say, if this consciousness...
When the two characteristics of motion and stillness do not manifest before the ear, the auditory faculty does not constitute cognition;

if there is necessarily no object to be known, then your faculty capable of knowing likewise remains unestablished, and as for the nature of the consciousness produced from it, what form or appearance could it have?
This demonstrates that both the subject and object lack intrinsic substance. Since this is analyzed in terms of the essence of cognition, it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
If you take the latter [position], it refutes the faculty of the floating dust-sensory organ (*bucen-gen*). That is to say:

if you maintain that hearing occurs by means of the ear, there would be no characteristic of movement or stillness in the external objects; since hearing would not be established, the faculty itself could not be established.
Furthermore, how can this ear—shaped like a newly rolled leaf—be a material phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*) composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), possessing form and being tangible?

If neither the physical object nor the auditory consciousness can constitute an element (dhātu) according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)—since both the coarse sensory faculty and its objects are untenable as elements—then from what could the "auditory consciousness element" be established?
Therefore, it is clear that the auditory consciousness produced by the ear cannot be established.
"If consciousness arises from sound, it exists because of sound" (up to) "if there were no knower, it would ultimately be like grass and wood.
This section of the sutra follows the previous refutation of the arising of sound.

It means that if this consciousness arises from sound and exists because of sound, it would have nothing to do with the faculty of hearing; it would clearly follow that sound does not produce itself, but rather [exists] because of hearing.
If there is a characteristic of sound that does not depend on hearing, then in the absence of hearing, the locus of the characteristic of sound would vanish.

Now, if you claim that consciousness arises from sound, yet do not allow that sound exists independently of hearing, then in the absence of hearing, the sound would likewise vanish. Therefore, you must admit that sound exists because of hearing.
If this is so, then it is hearing that hears the consciousness, and it cannot be said that hearing hears the sound. If you argue that it is not the consciousness that is heard...
If this were not the case, then sound would not constitute a sense-field (*dhātu*). Furthermore, hearing and cognition are identical to the cognition of sound;

once hearing has been perceived, who else could then know the cognition of the hearer? If there were no one who knows, the following two lines connect to the meaning of "who knows," stating that if there were no knower, one would ultimately be like insentient objects such as grass and trees, and would not be called "cognition."
Investigating in this manner, one truly knows that this consciousness does not arise from sound.
It is not the case that sound and hearing combine to form the intermediate realm; [it is] fundamentally neither a causal condition nor of spontaneous nature.

This section of the sutra follows upon the meaning of "arising" (*utpāda*) and further refutes the conjunction [of object and subject], concluding that the characteristics of the sense-sphere (*dhātu*) are not established.
That is to say, it is also illogical for sound and hearing to intermingle to form the sphere of middle-consciousness (*madhyavijñāna-dhātu*).

"Intermingling" means that sound is insentient yet subject to arising and ceasing, whereas the faculty and consciousness are sentient and eternal; thus, their essential natures would be confused and blended together.
If birth is not established, there can be no realm; since there is no intermediate position, how could the characteristics of internal and external be established?

This means that in all three locations—internal, external, and intermediate—they are entirely non-existent. "Internal" refers to the sense organs (*indriya*), "external" to the sense objects (*viṣaya*), and "intermediate" to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Therefore, the following conclusion clarifies that these three locations are illusory and have no location that is not of the nature [of emptiness], as explained previously.
"Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand as the nose and fragrance acting as conditions... [omitted] ...arising because of fragrance and taking fragrance as its realm.

This section of the sūtra follows the previous inquiry to specifically refute the three locations—the nose and so forth. "Ānanda" marks the initial presentation of these three factors, namely the nose and so forth;
"this consciousness" subsequently enumerates the cause and the realm; the remainder is explained as before.
"Ānanda, if [the sense of smell] arises from the nose, then within your mind... (until) these two natures do not exist; from whom would the boundary be established?

This section of the sutra follows the previous refutation that [the sense of smell] arises from the nose. The text contains four points: first, "Ānanda... and so forth, which is a general inquiry; second, "If you take...
and so forth, which enumerates the two categories—the ultimate and the phenomenal—to be refuted; third, "If you take... and so forth.
Below, first the provisional [nose] is refuted; if one takes the latter, next the ultimate [nose] is refuted. Within the refutation of the ultimate, there are further three points:
namely, the knowledge of flesh, the knowledge of space, and the knowledge of fragrance. First, regarding the general inquiry: the inquiry asks, "What constitutes the nose?

This specifically inquires into the two types of faculties—the ultimate and the provisional. Within the listing of the two categories, both the physical form and the [sensory] shape are presented together.
Regarding the mark of the "nail-like" (nakha-lakṣaṇa): this precisely clarifies the *saṃvṛti-satya* (conventional truth), for the shape of the nose is like a pair of hanging nails.

Regarding the statement that "the nature of olfactory cognition is mobile and fluctuating": this precisely clarifies the *paramārtha-satya* (ultimate truth), because the nature of olfactory cognition itself constitutes the ultimate truth. In contrast to the conventional, the ultimate is explained;
the conventional is coarse and rough, whereas the ultimate is pure, composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and perceivable only by the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Because it is seen, it is superior to olfactory cognition. That which is called "vibrating" refers to its remaining latent within when sensory objects do not appear;
once an olfactory object arrives, the nature of smelling vibrates, and this vibration is precisely the mind of arising and ceasing.
Regarding the initial refutation of the physical form: first, the superficial form is refuted; that is, the shape of the two nostrils is merely a fleshy substance.

If the substance of the flesh constitutes the body, then it is not the nose. If the cognition belonging to the body were to belong to the sense-object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*), then it would be called "body" and not "nose";

if it were called "touch," then it would belong to the object-field (*viṣaya*). Since the substance of the nose itself lacks a name [as a distinct faculty], how could it serve as the basis for establishing the intermediate realm [of the nose-faculty]?
This refutes the notion that the physical root (*rūpa-prakṛti-indriya*) is fit to be the realm of consciousness. Furthermore...
If you take the latter [position], it further subverts the ultimate truth. Furthermore, your two subsequent lines collectively interrogate the nature of cognition.
First, regarding the phrase "with flesh," the initial argument refutes the notion that flesh constitutes cognition: if one were to take flesh as cognition, flesh is fundamentally the body;

the cognition belonging to the body is fundamentally the object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*), and not the nose. Next, regarding the phrase "with emptiness," the subsequent argument refutes the notion that emptiness constitutes cognition: if one were to take emptiness...
If it is the emptiness that knows and that emptiness itself possesses cognition, then your physical body ought to be devoid of sensation;

why then does your flesh also possess cognition? If the cognition of emptiness were your stench, then empty space would be your body, and your physical body itself would necessarily lack cognition. If emptiness were your body, then today, Ānanda, you should—
It has no fixed location, just as it may be taken as being like the sphere of infinite space. As for using fragrance to refute the notion that fragrance is known:
if you claim that fragrance is what is known, then since knowledge itself belongs to fragrance, it would be just like the knowledge of another; how could it concern you?
If you say that the two gases of fragrance and stench must arise in your nose, then these two gases of fragrance and stench do not arise in the *eranda* tree.
As for *candana* and *eranda*: the *eranda* is a foul-smelling wood. The *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhi-sūtra* states: "The *eranda* grows amidst *mallikā* flowers;
its stench is like that of a bloated corpse. If these two things were not present, you would simply smell your own nose—would it be fragrant or foul?
