Because this [space] is the *tathāgatagarbha*, movement is itself non-movement; for within the *tathāgatagarbha*, one cannot find any wavering, arising, or ceasing. Therefore, they are equal.
It is said that the six elements are all equally real, perfectly interfused, and are the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally free from birth and extinction.

Ānanda, you who are submerged in the depths: although you have emerged from the death and rebirth of the segmented realm (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*), you have not yet left behind the death and rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmi-maraṇa*);
therefore, you are called "submerged. The World-Honored One earnestly and repeatedly exhorted him, saying: "If you do not awaken to seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition..."
Regarding this nature of the treasury (*tathāgatagarbha*), one should observe whether the fruits such as seeing possess arising and ceasing, or whether these fruits are devoid of arising and ceasing;

whether these fruits are identical or different, or whether they are neither identical nor different. While the preceding introductory text refers only to the single faculty of seeing and awareness, the present text refers universally to all six faculties;
furthermore, within the detailed refutation, the nature of seeing alone is singled out for analysis, while the others are included by implication.
The remaining examples are cited for this reason: thus, arising and ceasing are not [truly] arising and ceasing; this can be understood by referring back to the meaning of the refutation above.
As for "sameness and difference," it means they are the same because they mutually recognize one another within their nature, yet different because they oppose one another within their functions.
If one realizes the *tathāgatagarbha* nature, both sameness and difference cannot be apprehended; the Buddha points to this so that one may examine it with thorough scrutiny.
"You have never known that within the Tathāgatagarbha (up to) it is perfectly complete throughout the ten voids—how could it have a specific location?
This section of the sutra directly reveals the principle of the perfect fusion of nature and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) within the Middle Way, while reproaching Ānanda for his delusion.
Regarding the two lines beginning with "The nature of seeing" (*xing jian*), following the method of abbreviated textual variation used previously, their meaning is the same as before.
In the first phrase, "seeing" (*jian*) refers to the faculty; "awakening" (*jue*) and "clarity" (*ming*) are synonymous with the term "nature" (*xing*).

"Clarity" (*ming*) here refers to the clarity of dust—that is, the clarity of light and darkness—and its meaning encompasses light, darkness, emptiness, and form. In the second phrase, "awakening" (*jue*) is precisely "nature" (*xing*).

Upon careful examination, the two characters "awakening" (*jue*) and "essence" (*jing*) share a single meaning; it refers to the essence of the awakening-nature (*xing-jue*). Below, the two characters "seeing" (*jian*) correspond to the preceding [phrase].
In the phrase "seeing clarity" (*jian ming*), look back at the previous line to see that it is "seeing and yet clear";
in the subsequent line, "clarity and yet seeing," the faculties and their objects are presented in reverse to show that neither departs from the nature of enlightened awareness (*xing jue*).

Thus, when the faculty of sight perceives the entire dharma-realm, the hearing of the ear, the smelling of the nose, the tasting of the tongue, and the touching of the body all function accordingly; because the tongue knows through contact with what is tasted, it is called "tasting-contact. As for the body—

The awareness of touch and the consciousness of the mind—the six sense faculties—when realized as being in accord with their true nature, are all the wondrous virtues inherently possessed by that nature.
They shine brilliantly and pervade the entire Dharma-realm. Not only do the six faculties pervade the Dharma-realm, but the six objects also pervade the Dharma-realm;
that is to say, every faculty and every object fills the Dharma-realm, perfectly encompassing the ten directions of space. How could they have any fixed location? The rest is as previously explained.
The preceding explanation:
"Following karma, they manifest; the world is ignorant... (until) there are only words, but no real meaning.
This section of the sutra is the World-Honored One’s dismissal of conceptual calculations to guide those lost, concluding that the *tathāgatagarbha* is fundamentally detached from verbal expression.
The details are as explained previously.

From "Ānanda, the nature of consciousness has no source" to "it arises suddenly without any cause," this section of the sutra follows the preceding metaphors to specifically demonstrate the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-mahābhūta*), clarifying the conditions for its sequential arising.

This section sets forth the refutations of the locus [of consciousness]. First, "Ānanda, below this, it clarifies that consciousness arises dependent on conditions. Next, "You, now, below this, clarify the sequential arising [of consciousness] to explicitly reveal the characteristics of consciousness arising dependent on conditions.
Regarding "this consciousness" and below, four refutations of the locus are set forth. The first states: "Consciousness has no source," meaning that consciousness lacks intrinsic nature;
it is triggered by the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*). If one were separated from the organs and objects, the nature of consciousness [would not exist].
Just as flowers in the sky fundamentally do not exist, it is said that there is no source (*yuan*).

This "source" is a metaphor for water: if water has a source, it flows continuously and is never exhausted. Now, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is like a flood without a source; when it rains, it flows, but when the sun shines, it dries up.

This refers generally to the six bases of consciousness and mind; therefore, it is said that they falsely arise due to the six kinds of sense organs (*indriya*) and sense objects (*viṣaya*), thus establishing the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

It is said that the first five consciousnesses possess only *anusmaraṇa-vikalpa* (recollection-based conceptualization) and lack *abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa* (investigative conceptualization), because the latter exists only in the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Next, regarding the passage "using the eyes to observe everywhere" and so forth in the *Zhuan Falun Zhong*:
this refers exclusively to the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*). "Circulating and traversing" means using the eyes to move around and survey the surroundings; it is merely like a mirror.
There is no separate analysis of the other faculties within this [section], as they are all likewise; the present text merely cites one example to represent the others.
Regarding the sequential designation of this consciousness therein, this clarifies that the simultaneous mental consciousness (*sahaja-manovijñāna*) establishes the *vijñaptimātratā*.

It is called "simultaneous" because it arises concurrently with the five preceding sense-faculties, and it is also called the "clearly manifesting mental consciousness" (*vyakta-manovijñāna*), meaning this...
This demonstrates that the simultaneous, clear, and deliberative discrimination (*vikalpa*) is precisely what falsely arises from the sense organs and their objects.
However, when the first five consciousnesses perceive their respective objects, they naturally possess a nature of one-pointed discernment;
for instance, when a single eye sees something, one clearly recognizes it as "this" or "that" within one's own cognition, yet this does not involve deliberative calculation.
These preceding five [consciousnesses] refer to the meaning of "recollection" (*anusmṛti*) and "discrimination" (*vikalpa*).

To say "this is Mañjuśrī and so forth" is a general reference to the six consciousnesses being fully endowed with both these meanings of recollection and deliberative discrimination (*abhinirūpaṇa-vikalpa*).

Within the enumeration, it asks whether the nature of these six consciousnesses that cognizes objects arises from the faculty of sight, or from the characteristics of the sensory objects, or from space?
Regarding the character *yū* (耶) in the term *yūtō* (耶突), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means a dog emerging from a hole;
thus, the character is composed of "hole" (*kutsu*) and "dog" (*ken*) to clarify the sense of something appearing suddenly without cause.
"Ānanda, if the nature of your consciousness were produced within the faculty of sight... (up to)... it would not be the case that consciousness arises from nothingness without a source.

This section of the sutra follows the preceding general enumeration to specifically refute the notion that the nature of consciousness exists through a combination [of causes]. The text consists of five parts.

First, following "Ānanda," he refutes the idea that [consciousness] is produced by the faculty of sight; that is, the productive nature of seeing has no substance, and thus that which is produced [cannot exist].
From what does consciousness arise? The rest may be understood. Next, the arising of characteristics (*nimitta*) is refuted:

if that characteristic of the object arises from the characteristic itself, it would not depend on the sense organ to manifest the characteristic; yet if the nature of seeing is absent, the characteristic of the object cannot exist of its own accord, and thus the characteristic that could give rise [to consciousness] is simply non-existent.
From what, then, could the consciousness produced by it arise? The rest may be understood. If [it arises] from space, below...
The passage on the "three refutations of emptiness" can also be interpreted; the passage on the "four refutations of causelessness" following "if there were not" can also be interpreted.

Regarding the passage beginning with "you further," the fifth section concludes by exhorting detailed examination: "consciousness moves while vision is clear. This means that consciousness is of the nature of discernment (*vijñapti*), and thus it moves;
vision merely reflects forms without separate analysis, and is therefore clear. "Clear" has the meaning of "quiescent"; thus, [the text addresses] movement and stillness.
The same applies to the other [senses]: smelling, hearing, touching, and cognition are likewise.
One must see that these six types of consciousness arise because of causes; they should not be thought to emerge spontaneously without a source.
Since their emergence must have a cause, the rest is easily understood.
"If this consciousness-mind originally has no point of origin... it is neither identical nor different, neither empty nor existent.

This section of the sutra indicates that the Buddha points to this consciousness, along with the six previously mentioned great elements, to urge Ānanda to apply his mind to their harmonious integration and awaken to the fundamental true essence.
The phrase "If this" and following refers to the fundamentally great, perfect essence, denoting the nature of this consciousness.
"Arising from nowhere" means that arising is itself non-arising; nor is there cessation, for it is fundamentally without a source from which it arises.
This clarifies non-arising, and non-arising is the perfect essence (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). One should know that the following section reverses the previous views.

"Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing" refers collectively to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*); it means that the inherent nature of each of these six faculties is perfectly complete and profoundly still. Since they are so described...

Since they are perfectly still and profound (*yuan-zhan*), their nature likewise does not emerge from anything else. Furthermore, the subsequent passage "including those below" reverses the previous five elements;
these are also perfectly still and profound, and are collectively termed the "Seven Great Elements. The text is readily intelligible. Regarding the phrase "coarse and floating" (*cu-fu*) below:

although Ānanda has severed the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) still remain. Even if he were to suppress the delusions of thought, his ignorance (*avidyā*) would still be far off; therefore, [the text] refers to them as such.

Because the Buddha is coarse and floating, he urges you, saying: "If you do not awaken to the aforementioned six fundamental Tathāgata-garbhas, you should observe these six consciousnesses of the cognitive mind:
what is their relationship regarding identity and difference, emptiness and existence?

If this consciousness is different, it does not depart from identity; if it is identical, it does not exist outside of difference. Thus, it is both different and identical, yet neither identical nor different; it is inconceivable."
They are identical in being unobtainable and distinct in being unobtainable; because the characteristics of the seeking mind cannot be found, one should say it is empty (*śūnya*);

yet because the subtle spirit is inexhaustible, one should say it exists. Existence does not obstruct emptiness, and emptiness does not exist outside existence; thus, existence is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself existence.
It is neither empty nor existent, for it cannot be found as empty nor can it be found as existent. When it exists, the myriad virtues are simultaneous.
When emptiness is manifested, not even a single speck of dust can be established; there is only the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Whether it be empty or existent, identical or different, neither identical nor different, nor neither empty nor existent—there is nothing that is not the Garbha.

Since the nature of the single consciousness is thus, the perception of the Great [Element] is likewise so, the Great Element of Space is likewise so, and the four great elements, such as earth and the rest, are likewise so.
"In this way, as it is, the act of expanding [the teaching]—where one corner is shown but the other three are not inferred—is the ultimate skillful means of the World-Honored One’s great compassion.
How could Ānanda not have realized this? It was merely a playful lead-in made for the sake of sentient beings."
"You originally did not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha... it contains and exhales the ten voids; how could there be any fixed location?

This section of the sutra is the World-Honored One’s direct revelation of the principle of the perfect fusion of nature and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) within the Middle Way, rebuking Ānanda for his delusion.

Regarding the two lines beginning with "nature-consciousness" (*xing-shi*): the first line clarifies that "characteristic" (*xiang*) is precisely the luminosity of the nature (*xing-ming*). It functions as...
The character "nature" (*xing*) should be understood as "wisdom" (*zhi*); this wisdom is spoken of in contrast to consciousness (*shi*), based on the distinction between the true and the deluded.

Therefore, the character "clarity" (*ming*) in the following phrase is also spoken of in contrast to consciousness, such that clarity likewise belongs to wisdom. "Awakening" (*jue*) is the awakening of nature; this too is treated as the character "nature.
Looking back at the preceding phrase, "consciousness yet wisdom" means that which is deluded yet true. In the following phrase, "clarity yet consciousness," [it means that which is true yet deluded].
It is precisely because it is real that it is delusory; since it has always been the nature of the treasury (tathatā-garbha), what reality or delusion could there be?
Therefore, all instances employ the character "nature" (xing) to encompass both, merely altering the phrasing to make it difficult for others to understand.

The interpretation by Wēnlíng—which treats "your original," "your yet," and "your once" as a sequential series of forced constructions—does not accord with the intent of the scripture when one examines the text closely; it is merely a matter of translation.
People merely change their phrasing and expressions, yet do not trouble themselves to realize that this method of obscuring the eyes is fundamentally a level path;
it needlessly increases the treacherous narrowness. Why is this so? The remaining meaning is as explained previously.
"Manifesting according to karma, the world is ignorant... (until) there are only words, entirely devoid of real meaning.

This section of the sutra shows that the World-Honored One has dispelled misconceptions to guide those lost in delusion, concluding that the *tathāgatagarbha* is fundamentally beyond verbal expression;

this is explained in detail as previously analyzed. Thus ends the first fascicle, wherein the *dhyāna* is revealed through the seven elements (*mahābhūta*). *Note: The text provided contains an ellipsis indicating a longer passage from the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra*. The translation reflects the specific portion provided.*
It was difficult to request from the Buddhas the attainment of Bodhi through the wondrous *śamatha* and so forth;

now the World-Honored One, relying upon the eighteen *dhātus*, has revealed the three meanings in their proper sequence and responded to them. Thus, the correct principle of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) is now complete.
Therefore, the compiler records in detail the realization attained by Ānanda and the others. Now, Ānanda and the others rejoice at having heard these three [meanings].
The profound realization of the meaning was first accomplished; therefore, a verse of praise was spoken to conclude the preceding text.

However, although these three meanings are complete, since the underlying principles are subtle and human understanding has become increasingly clouded, how could the deep and far-reaching intent of these hidden, subtle, and fluctuating truths be understood otherwise than through one endowed with great eloquence? Thus, in the fourth fascicle, Pūrṇa...
Relying on the principle that all phenomena are fundamentally pure and quiescent as established in the preceding text, Pūrṇa— the foremost in eloquence—
raised a series of inquiries. The World-Honored One extensively followed the causes of the threefold continuity to exhaust his profound eloquence,
until they reached the point of "neither identity nor difference, neither identical nor non-identical," thereby reaching the ultimate limit of the awakened mind beyond the kalpa of Vimalacitra.
This marks the beginning of the complete elucidation of the profound mysteries of the Great Buddha-Crown and the ultimate, eternal mind.

Thereafter, Ānanda’s emotional defilements were completely washed away within this treasury of principle, leaving nothing remaining; he then, relying on this perfect principle, requested instruction on the perfect practice.
However, he knew that at the very start of initiating practice, one must first find its gateway—this, then, was his request concerning the initial expedient means.
One who exhaustively investigates the subtle meanings of the sūtra should understand its great path; when the great path is not mistaken, one may enter the perfect exposition.
Thus concludes the beginning and end of the fourth sūtra.
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly [proceeded] before the Tathāgata and spoke verses in praise of the Buddha.

In this section, the compiler describes how Ānanda and the others, having attained great awakening upon hearing the three contemplations, found themselves to be even more minute when reflecting back upon themselves.
The "subtle and wondrous instruction" refers generally to the texts concerning the seven investigations, the eight arguments, the four categories, and the seven elements;
it means that the World-Honored One skillfully revealed the three contemplations within the midst of tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) based on the ten [principles].
The illusory manifestations of the eight realms reveal that the three sublime contemplations are but the mind alone; throughout the world there is no object, for the entire realm is mind.
In the one, the immeasurable is subsumed; the immeasurable converges into the one. Within the one, diversity is explained;
within diversity, unity is shown—this is all a subtle and profound revelation. Before Ānanda received this instruction, his body and mind were constricted and obstructed, as if he were dwelling in...
Having now heard the Dharma, the previous obstructions caused by the thorny thickets are all eliminated together; thus it is said that they are "vastly open and unimpeded.
Regarding each knowing that the mind pervades the ten directions: Tiantai explains the ten directions in terms of the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*).
This is because the mind is the master of the ten realms, and the emptiness of the ten directions is precisely the emptiness that arises in accordance with the ten realms.
Having realized that Great Enlightenment contains the ten voids, Ānanda and the others [understand] what the subsequent sutra says:
"The void arises within Great Enlightenment, like a single bubble emerging from the sea. The current text uses the metaphor of a leaf held in one's hand to express how exceedingly small it is.
This is truly because the void is a transformation produced by ignorance (*avidyā*); therefore, it should be said to be small when contrasted with Great Enlightenment.
It is like floating clouds appearing in the vast clarity of the great sky. The commentary by Wuxing explains: "Each knows itself" refers to the wisdom-mind that is capable of awakening;
"pervading the ten directions" refers to the principle that is awakened to—the eternally abiding true mind which universally permeates and fuses the ten realms.
Therefore, it says, "Throughout all worlds in the ten directions. If one follows the ten directions to explain them by means of the ten realms, then...

This world should likewise be correlated with the ten dharma-realms; however, all things—both the environment and its inhabitants—within these ten realms are nothing other than the bodhicitta, for there is no separate phenomenon apart from the mind.
This is because the wondrous mind is so pure and refined that it encompasses the ten realms in their entirety, complete and without omission.
In the preceding passage, the mind was contrasted with space to clarify the distinctions between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; now, in this passage, once again...

By means of the body and the land, he demonstrates through uprightness that there is only mind; furthermore, this essence of mind is pervasive and perfect, which is precisely the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Because one takes the dharma of mind as the body, Ānanda and the others, having already realized that the Dharma-body is as vast as space and the ocean, looked back upon their own physically born bodies—produced by their parents—as being as small as a single mote of dust within the great void.
"The ears are as if existing and as if non-existent" means this phrase precisely clarifies that the subtlety of the fine dust is like being both present and absent;
rising and falling without ceasing, it is like existence and non-existence with nothing to rely upon.

Furthermore, "it is like a single bubble on a vast, clear ocean, arising and perishing without trace" means this phrase also clarifies that the smallness of the bubble is such that it suddenly arises and suddenly vanishes.

There is no way to determine which [interpretation] to follow. What was previously called "existence and non-existence" (saṃvarta-vivarta) is here called "arising and ceasing" (utpāda-nirodha); though the words differ, the meaning is no different.

This section generally clarifies that during the state of delusion, the body and mind are limited in this manner. Having made this clear, the following provides a summary showing that the body and mind entirely return to the eternally abiding.
Following the prostration to the Buddha, the subsequent section specifically describes Ānanda and the others reciting verses of praise and vows, expressing the sense of reverent admiration.
"Thus, the Wondrous, Profound, All-Holding, Immovable Honored One... [until] the śakara heart is without movement or change.
This section of the sutra concludes the preceding discourse with Ānanda and the assembly attaining realization and offering verses of praise and aspiration.
This verse consists of eighteen lines in total. The first four lines primarily praise the Triple Gem while clarifying the benefits obtained;
the next four lines express vows to seek enlightenment above and transform beings below; the following four lines request the witness of these great vows;
the subsequent four lines hope for further teaching of the Dharma; and the final two lines summarize the preceding vows. Regarding the first four lines, the initial line praises the Buddha.

Furthermore, "wondrously profound" (*miaozhan*) pertains to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); it refers to being hollow and signless, yet this profundity is not a state of withered stillness, hence it is called "wondrously profound.

True emptiness (*bhūta-śūnyatā*) extinguishes all phenomena; therefore, "wondrously profound" is attributed to the ultimate truth. "Total retention" (*zongchi*) pertains to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
total retention is *dhāraṇī*. The *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm) states: "In accordance with existence..."
Because it is able to maintain names, meanings, practices, stages, and merits, it is called *dhāraṇī*.

This is explained from the perspective of the door of establishment as referring to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). "Conventional" means worldly; because all phenomena are established therein, *dhāraṇī* is attributed to the conventional truth.
Yet, while being true, it appears as conventional; because it exists while being non-existent, it is termed "wondrous existence" (*prabhāsvara-bhāva*). However, by means of...
The wondrous existence corresponds to the sublime and profound clarity as if two halves of a tally joined;

its immovability belongs to the Middle Way, the First Noble Truth, for it cannot be tilted or shaken by the two extremes. It is pure, transparently penetrating, and perfectly interfused without obstruction;
it is three while being one, and one while being three—an inconceivable state called the Perfectly Interfused Middle Way, the First Noble Truth.
Furthermore, that which is immovable is the fundamental substance of Great Samādhi; because it is ultimately firm and solid, it is called the Honored One of Immovability (*Acalanātha*).
This title is one of the ten epithets of a Buddha, as he is honored by the nine realms of existence.

Of these, the preceding three meanings refer to the principle realized by the Buddha, while the single character "Honored" (*zun*) refers to the Buddha who is the realizer; this is cited to explain the reason [for the name].
This reveals their functional capacity. Furthermore, these three meanings correspond to *śamatha* and the other two [aspects] when situated in the cause;

they correspond to the three virtues of *dharmakāya*, *prajñā*, and *vimukti* when situated in the fruit; they correspond to the three truths (*trisatya*) when situated in the object; they correspond to the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) when situated in wisdom;

and they correspond to the three bodies (*trikāya*) when situated in the Buddha. If one were to precisely assign these three names to the three virtues, "immovability" (*acala*) belongs to the *dharmakāya*.

The *kāyadhāraṇī* (body-retention) belongs to liberation (*vimukti*); "wondrous stillness" (*miaozhan*) belongs to *prajñā*. This wondrous stillness is true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and true emptiness is the essence of *mahāprajñā*.
It was an error for Changshui to equate wondrous stillness with the *dharmakāya*;
this ancient tradition of equating immovability (*acala*) with the *dharmakāya* has been transmitted for a long time. How can the commentator of Wuxing be so lacking in reflection?
This is so. The second line praises the Dharma heard: "The Śūraṅgama King, which clarifies seeing the rare [teachings] of former lives.

This means that when a Buddha appears in the world, he skillfully preaches according to the capacities of beings, and while expedient teachings (*upāya*) are numerous, the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*) teachings are expounded only occasionally;

therefore, they are called "rare. Regarding the meaning of the following two lines, "To dissolve my... and so forth, the principles are profound and the meanings are abstruse, as noted by Changshui and Gushan.
The profound discourses of the various masters of Wuxing have appeared one after another, yet I have not yet dared to follow any of them exclusively. Why is this?
Because when ordinary minds attempt to gauge and measure the Sage’s mind, their explanations and proofs find it difficult to reach a definitive, one-sided judgment.

Therefore, nothing is better than direct realization for that which is known through inference; since such realization is currently difficult to attain, my intention must await further opportunity. For now, I shall merely provide a commentary following the text.
I truly dare not presume this [text] to be such; yet, reflecting deeply upon it, this sutra belongs to the period of the Vaipulya (fangděng) flavor and is categorized as "fresh butter" (sū).

While the Vaipulya generally discusses all four teachings, this specific sutra is subsumed within the Perfect Teaching (yánjiào) of the Vaipulya. The dharma and meaning revealed herein belong exclusively to the Perfect Vehicle (yuánchéng).
Although its timing falls within the gradual teaching (jiànjiào), in substance it is sudden (dùn); thus, one attains the Dharma without passing through the kalpas of a *śrāvaka*.

The meaning of the phrase regarding the body can be understood at once; yet, one must further consider that since the wisdom and decisive action appropriate to the occasion have not been fully exhausted, how could the Dharma-body have been attained beforehand?
Examining this in detail, we follow Ānanda’s understanding: although his understanding is perfect, his practical realization has not yet reached its full extent;
therefore, at the beginning of the fourth fascicle, Pūrṇa says that although the members of the assembly, such as Ānanda and the others, have opened [the way].

"Awakening to the practice, yet the outflows are not yet eliminated. Furthermore, the end of the tenth sutra states: "In principle, there is sudden awakening, and by means of this awakening, [the obstacles] are simultaneously dissolved;

in matters, they are not suddenly eliminated, but are exhausted through gradual stages. Based on these two passages, one can know with certainty that Ānanda currently belongs to the stage of intellectual understanding (*jiewu*), yet it is not as if he lacks realization entirely;
this is stated according to the majority of cases. Moreover, some may say that this is merely the teaching...

Since it is designated as "Perfect" (yuan), it must correspond to a Perfect capacity (ji). If Ānanda were not a recipient of this Perfect capacity, then, being gradual, the teaching would be established in vain.
This is what I mean by saying that [the teaching] awaits self-realization before its meaning can manifest; I do not yet dare to be certain of this point.
Nevertheless, I have privately conjectured that the *Awakening of Faith* (Yuánjué) was spoken for the sake of the twelve Bodhisattvas, and those twelve Bodhisattvas...
If one requests [the teaching] on behalf of sentient beings, then those twelve [sections] would not be appropriate for the specific capacity [of the audience];
that text merely states that "sentient beings of sudden capacity awaken from this," which seems as though the Buddha first established the teaching and waited for the capacity [to arise].

In the present sutra, although Ānanda is called the "appropriate capacity" (dangji), even if he spontaneously attains awakening, half of it arises from the request of the capacity, as in the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* (Yuánjué jīng), which says: "It is like, for example..."
The great ocean does not refuse even small streams; the present sutra is likewise, for there is no fault in its sudden teaching encompassing the gradual.
This must necessarily await those who have attained the Way to decide. Thus, the phrase "dissolving my [self]" in the preceding line also belongs to the category of explanatory teaching;

"dissolving" (xiao) carries the meaning of severance. If it were truly the severance of delusions, it would constitute a direct realization. [This is] in contrast to the inverted conceptions of billions of kalpas.
The meaning of the second phrase, "attaining the Dharma-body without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*," is explained as follows: "billions of kalpas" refers to what is not passed through.

This means that the profound ignorance of those billions of kalpas can now be severed by relying on this Perfect Teaching (*paripūrṇa-yāna*), without necessarily having to pass through such long eons.
"Perverted conceptions" refers to what is contrasted with the Dharma-body; it means that by dissolving those perverted conceptions, one attains this [Dharma-body].
The *dharmakāya* is the *samyaksaṃbuddha*. In the *Saṃghīti*, it is called *asaṃkhyeya*, translated as "innumerable.

Regarding the four lines [of the verse], the first two lines correctly clarify seeking enlightenment above and transforming beings below; the latter two lines represent repaying the Buddha's grace through this very deep resolve of seeking enlightenment above and transforming beings below.
The first line expresses a vow for the present, namely: [The text continues: ...the present, meaning... (Note: The provided source text fragment ends here).
I vow that in this very life I shall accomplish the task and attain the fruit of Buddhahood. As for the term "Jewel King" (*ratnarāja*) for the fruit of Buddhahood:
the Buddha is the king of the mind; because the Buddha is a *maṇi* jewel, he is the "Jewel. Because "king" signifies mastery, he is the sovereign of all sages.

Furthermore, his sovereign will is endowed with the eight forms of mastery (*aṣṭavaśitā*). The second phrase may be understood accordingly. Regarding the third phrase, it speaks of the "profound mind" (*gambhīracitta*).

This refers to seeking enlightenment above and transforming beings below, as these encompass the four universal vows. Since the followers of the Two Vehicles lack these, while only Bodhisattvas possess them, they are called the "profound mind" (*gambhīra-citta*).
It means that by taking these four vows with a profound mind and universally offering them to all Buddhas throughout the dust-motes and lands, one clarifies that one's practice must be vast.
Only by practicing extensively based on this profound mind can one truly be said to repay the Buddha’s grace.

Furthermore, regarding the next four lines that request the witness of the great vow: the first two lines specifically request the World-Honored One to bear witness—that is, Śākyamuni Buddha—to testify that the previous vows and pledges are not in vain.
The subsequent line concerns the "five turbidities" (pañca-kaṣāya), as explained in the fifth section;
because the five turbidities cause such chaotic agitation, it is called an "evil age," at which time sentient beings are stubborn and difficult to transform.
If one can practice what is difficult to practice in a degenerate age, how much more so in the various Pure Lands? Therefore, it is said: "I vow to enter [the path] first.

The latter two lines emphasize the heart of the vow: that as long as even a single sentient being has not yet attained Buddhahood, I shall never abandon this one being to enter *nirvāṇa* (mudie) first.
*Nirvāṇa* (niepan) is the same term; the difference lies in the new and old translations.

Therefore, it is translated as "extinction" (nirvāṇa) and "passing beyond" (parinirvāṇa). Furthermore, regarding the next four lines, the phrase "I pray that you will further preach the Dharma" consists of two preceding lines requesting the removal of delusions, because through the preaching of the Dharma one can eliminate delusions. The first line praises the Buddha with three great attributes:

"Hero" refers to the World-Honored One who, internally, is able to exhaust all obstacles to the Path and is thus fearless; externally, he is able to subdue Māra and is thus undaunted by external forces—this is fearlessness.
Because he is without fear and has no equal, he is called the Great Hero (Mahāvīra). As for the "Powerful One" (Bala), the Buddha possesses the ten powers (*daśabala*);

because he has attained knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūtajñāna*), he penetrates all things with thorough clarity and distinctness. Since nothing can destroy him and nothing can surpass him, these are called "powers.
These ten kinds of power are possessed exclusively by the Buddha; since Bodhisattvas only partially attain them, the Buddha is called "Great."
Powerful and Greatly Compassionate: "Compassion" (maitrī) is able to bestow happiness, while "pity" (karuṇā) is able to extract suffering.

The *Dharmadhātu-krama* states: "The Buddha abides in a mind of great compassion; by the power of the roots of goodness of great compassion, he is truly able to bestow upon all sentient beings both worldly and supramundane happiness.
Great pity is likewise the same. Therefore, only the Buddha is designated as possessing Great Compassion and Great Pity."
The next phrase, "I hope," expresses a longing for further investigation and exposition, which alone can eliminate my subtle delusions.

Regarding what are called "subtle delusions": if referring proximately to those to be abandoned within Ānanda’s own stage, they are the delusions abandoned through cultivation from the second fruit upward;
if looking further toward higher abandonment, they consist of the "dust-like" afflictions and ignorance beyond the realms.
Because the number of distinct categories is so vast, they are termed "subtle. The latter two lines reiterate the vow to ascend to Great Enlightenment and sit upon the Bodhimanda;
since "Unsurpassed Enlightenment" is the ultimate fruit-enlightenment, there is nothing further above it that can be attained.
The aspiration to seek Buddhahood was already clarified in the preceding verse; the reason for restating it here is precisely because the mind’s urgency to deliver sentient beings is paramount.

Because they seek [this state], they do not perceive its complexity. Those who "sit at the site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa) refer to sitting beneath the Bodhi tree to achieve equal and perfect awakening;

thus, this place of sitting is called the field for attaining the Way. However, the Buddha’s body—consisting of thousands, hundreds, and tens of millions—is such that when he sits once, he sits everywhere, and when he achieves it once, he achieves it everywhere.
As for these worlds of the ten directions, in their proximate sense, they are limited to the three thousandfold world system.
The "Dhātu" (Realm) refers distantly to the *dharmadhātu*. As in the *Avataṃsaka*, within every atom there appear lands, and within every land there appear atoms;
in every atom, Buddhas arise, and in every thought-moment, sentient beings attain enlightenment. Unity and multiplicity are without obstruction, and principle and phenomena are mutually fused.
It is like the bright moon suspended in the sky, its reflection appearing upon ten thousand waters; or like ten mirrors containing light, interlacing infinitely. And so it is.
Coming to respond to the world is likewise thus; hence it is said that [the Buddhas] sit at the site of enlightenment throughout the ten directions.
What was previously stated—that "as long as there is even one sentient being who has not yet attained Buddhahood, I vow not to enter *nirvāṇa*"—was a discussion of time from a vertical perspective.

What is now stated—that they "sit and realize [enlightenment] throughout the ten directions"—is a description of space from a horizontal perspective. This explains and completes the meaning of the previous verse regarding the intention to seek enlightenment above and transform beings below.
The final two lines summarize the entire verse. Regarding the first line, Śūnyatā (Śunyata) is explained as "emptiness";
regarding the second line, Śakara is translated as "solid" or "firm.
This refers to the mind of one's firm vow, meaning that while even emptiness might perhaps perish, my firm vow-mind shall never waver or shift. Thus it is cited.
The analogy of space is employed to conclude and manifest that the vow-mind transcends empty space and shall never undergo change or transformation.

At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra [attained] this stage where the meaning is ultimate and free from doubt.
This section of the sutra describes how Pūrṇa, having heard that the fundamental nature is pure, raised a multitude of doubts regarding that very purity and offered his request.
Before asking his questions, he first recounts the original circumstances.
"At that time" refers to the moment when Ānanda had finished his verse praise; "Pūrṇa" (whose name means "Fullness") has been translated previously, and in this text, he is referred to as Pūrṇa.

The reason the questioner posed this inquiry is that the fundamental principle is profoundly deep and subtle; were it not for one endowed with great eloquence, it would be extremely difficult to raise such a question.
Thus, while Ānanda was still in the stage of training (śaikṣa), his understanding was shallow and his words exhausted, preventing him from investigating deeply.
Now, Puṇṇa is one who has attained the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa) and was long renowned for his eloquence as the foremost in preaching the Dharma; therefore, he was able [to do so].

Having thoroughly investigated the profound and subtle mysteries, he requested that the dark and esoteric secrets be revealed. Regarding the ritual of baring one shoulder and so forth, it is detailed in the first fascicle of the *Commentary*.
As for "Great Majestic Virtue" (*Mahātejas*): the Buddha possesses both the gates of subduing (*nigraha*) and gathering (*saṃgraha*).

He subdues those who are stubborn, fierce, demonic, or heretical, causing them to humble their minds and return to the correct path; this is what is meant by "majesty. He gathers in those sentient beings who are gentle and good, causing them to...

The increase of the Path and the diminution of birth are what is called "virtue. Yet, the World-Honored One, by the power of the roots of goodness of his compassion, manifests these identically though under different names;
his mind is impartial, leaving no trace of enmity or kinship, nor of like or dislike. Therefore, he is called the Great Good.

To speak of him as "inferior" means that the Buddha is fully endowed with the two types of wisdom and, through skillful means, adapts to the capacities of sentient beings to expound the Dharma for them.
The "manifestation" refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) realized by the Tathāgata himself;
that which is "ultimate" is precisely the principle of the Middle Way, the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), which is inherently pure.

Below the words "World-Honored One," Pūrṇa recounts his own shallow capacity and the profundity of the Dharma as a request for instruction, stating that among those who transmit the teachings and expound the Dharma under the Tathāgata’s seat, he is commonly ranked [as foremost].
First, because the Dharma-sound now heard is subtle, profound, and far-reaching, it is truly difficult to realize and perceive;

therefore, a metaphor is employed to clarify the meaning that one's own faculties are shallow and the Dharma is subtle. The "deaf person" is a metaphor for oneself, whose faculties are shallow and who does not understand because they are like the deaf.

"More than a hundred paces away" is a metaphor for the shallowness and proximity of what one has realized; when compared to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), even one's own stage of realization is still... [incomplete source text].
At a distance of more than a hundred paces, even the *mǒnrài* (a type of mosquito) is as difficult to see as the subtle and elusive state of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Thus, the sound of the *mǒnrài* serves as a metaphor for the sound of the Dharma that expresses the ultimate truth.
The two subsequent lines mean that at a distance of a hundred paces, it is inherently impossible to perceive the physical form of the *mǒnrài*.
This is illustrated by the fact that their eye of wisdom is still shallow and unable to investigate the principles of truth in depth;
furthermore, because they are deaf, they do not hear its sound. The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is profoundly deep and subtle, like trying to see a mosquito from a hundred paces away;
thus, they cannot perceive the reality of the principle nor hear the Dharma-sound. Now, although the Buddha has proclaimed it—

"You have revealed and clarified our original intent so that we might eliminate our delusions; yet, we still do not fully understand how this meaning can be brought to ultimate completion and how one may reach the ground of non-doubt.
World-Honored One, even those such as Ānanda, though they have attained awakening, still find the sounds of the Dharma you have preached lingering with doubt and regret."

In this section of the sutra, Pūrṇa cites those still in training (*śaikṣa*) who, despite having already attained the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*), still harbor lingering doubts and regrets regarding what they have now heard.

Pūrṇa further cites Ānanda and his peers, suggesting that although they have been awakened by the preceding text, the meaning of the sudden and perfect (*yuan-dun*) path has not yet been fully realized through the incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
Furthermore, Pūrṇa states that their outflow-tainted habitual tendencies (*sāsrava-vāsanā*) have not yet been entirely eliminated. Pūrṇa then speaks for himself...
This refers to those such as myself who point to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Although these individuals beyond training are currently within the Dharma assembly of the Tathāgata and have exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) of the world, they still possess ignorance (*avidyā*) outside the [Noble] Realms;

therefore, even though the Dharma now taught by the Buddha is profound and subtle, they remain entangled in doubt and regret. "Entangled" (*yu*) means being bound or lingering; "regret" (*hui*) likewise [refers to remorse].
Having raised these doubts through the aforementioned narrative of Purna’s inquiry, he now begins the formal questioning:
"World-Honored One, if all the faculties and objects of the world... [they] yearn for the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed compassionate instruction."

This section of the sutra consists of Purna taking up the principle of "original suchness" (*benran*) mentioned previously and raising an objection by clinging to the distinction between the nature of phenomena and their characteristics.
The text contains two layers of meaning: first, he clings to the principle to challenge the phenomena, citing the "pure original suchness" to question how mountains and rivers could arise from it;
second, as shown below, he clings to the characteristics to challenge the nature, citing the earth [as an example].
Water, fire, and wind all pervade the Dharma-realm; "pervading" refers to their nature (*svabhāva*), while "mutually overcoming" refers to their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Yet, regarding these two questions posed by Pūrṇa, were it not for his possession of great eloquence (*mahāpratibhāna*), how could he have brought forth such words?

I privately rejoice that the subsequent text flows with vast waves, its world of meaning towering and majestic, its source of expression surging and pouring forth inexhaustibly—truly, this has its root.

Regarding the phrase "all these faculties, objects, and so forth arising from this very place within the aforementioned mind," this refers collectively to the four categories mentioned in the preceding text;

"and so forth" indicates the seven elements. That is to say, since all these phenomena are the principle of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is inherently pure and devoid of any objective reality, how could they suddenly give rise to the mountains, rivers, and other phenomena subject to birth and extinction?

Do conditioned phenomena successively migrate, ending and beginning again? Since they are called "pure and fundamental" (*viśuddha-mūla*), from where could mountains, rivers, and the great earth possibly arise?
This is because his wisdom-eye is not empty; when a single film remains in the eye, empty flowers arise in confusion. As the subsequent text says:
"Because of the manifestation of characteristics, they arise from deluded vision. When viewed with the True Eye (*samyag-cakṣus*), [this is seen as such].
Originally, there has never been a single thing; it is not that one must negate phenomena to see that they are thus by nature, for this is their fundamental reality.

That which undergoes successive flux, ending and beginning again—namely, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)—takes its initial arising as the beginning and its subsequent cessation as the end.
As it is said, "birth and death, death and birth," revolving without limit. Furthermore, regarding the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), it forms, abides, decays, and [is destroyed].
It is empty and yet again becomes manifest; because it does not perish instantaneously, it is said that it migrates in succession, ending and beginning again.
This is the fundamental principle (*li*), while conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) belong to the realm of events (*shi*). Pūrṇa clings to the principle and challenges the events.

The subsequent meaning—that earth, water, and so forth are pervasive—reveals that the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is inherently complete; although it possesses all characteristics, they have not yet [manifested].
How could their forms and signs possibly overcome one another? As the text below states: "The Tathāgatagarbha was originally neither water nor fire;
although the nature of fire is present within stone, the stone itself is not fire. If the stone were fire, the mountains would naturally be ablaze.
The nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is likewise. Furthermore, as discussed below in reference to the three of the seven great elements—water, fire, and wind:

"Greatly difficult," O World-Honored One. [The opponent] first takes up the nature of earth and opposes it with the nature of water; then, taking up the nature of water, he opposes it with the nature of fire.
In each case, he first sets forth their characteristics and then challenges them by demanding how their natures could be universally pervasive.

Furthermore, "O World-Honored One," he again takes up the nature of earth and opposes it with the nature of space, arguing that since they differ in being obstructed or unobstructed, they cannot be the same.

"Pervasive throughout" refers to the nature of the difficulty arising from grasping at characteristics; "yet I," and so forth, concludes the intent of the question and requests the Buddha to explain it.

That is to say, Pūrṇa meant: "Regarding the two meanings of principle and phenomena, as well as nature and characteristics, as mentioned above, I do not know where these meanings lead or what they are like.
I only wish," and so forth—these two lines express Pūrṇa’s thought that the Buddha’s greatness... [is such that he can resolve this]."
When Maitreya had not yet preached the Dharma, he remained hidden within; now he requests that it be proclaimed and spread abroad. For all the Dharma thus preached is the voice of Maitreya.
Therefore, by means of the meaning of awakening, he opens up my lack of awakening. This "lack of awakening" is precisely delusion. The clouds serve as a metaphor:
arising from non-awakening, various doubts cloud the fundamental nature and principle, just as clouds obscure the clear blue sky. I pray that you will grant this wish.
The Buddha, through great compassion, expounded the Dharma to dispel his delusions, like parting the clouds and mist to behold the sky of the nature;
hence it is said, "He opened the clouds of my delusion. As for the two subsequent lines, the phrasing and meaning are inverted;
for these two questions, Purna himself stated that he had finished asking, and the scribe’s narrative should have read: "Having spoken these words... and so forth.
Regarding the passage "The Great Assembly prostrates themselves on the ground," the original phrasing followed the current order;

however, if the phrase "the Great Assembly" is placed above and the words [of the question] are placed below, then these two questions would constitute a collective inquiry by the assembly. This is an error of the translation hall.

Examining the intent of the preceding questions, they were initiated by Pūrṇa himself; since the assembly, through their questioning, collectively desired to hear them, they all performed this salutation together.

When the rites were concluded, they withdrew from their seats; they revered and looked up to his compassionate instructions as one who, parched with thirst, longs for a drink—this is a metaphor for the intensity of their aspiration.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇa [and so forth], until: "Revere the Buddha’s voice of Dharma and listen silently."
In this section of the sutra, before the World-Honored One answers the question, he first enumerates the benefits of the Dharma and exhorts [the assembly] to listen well.
In the preceding sutra, when Ānanda requested the Dharma, his words included those with outflows (*sāsrava*); the Buddha’s response likewise addressed those with outflows.
Now, when Pūrṇa requests leave, his words include those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); the Buddha’s response likewise extends to those beyond training. Thus it is known:
The meaning elucidated here is even more superior than that which preceded it; therefore, it is called the "Ultimate Truth within the Ultimate Truth.

Regarding the two phrases following "Ultimate Truth": the former "Ultimate Truth" refers to the three meanings previously mentioned—wondrous, subtle, and so forth—which transcend the Three Vehicles by synthesizing the conventional and the ultimate to return to the Middle Way;
hence, it is termed "Ultimate Truth. Now, however, [this teaching] secretly turns back from the Middle Way to pervasively engage [all phenomena].

The ultimate and the conventional reveal the emptiness and non-emptiness of the *tathāgatagarbha*—what is called "pure and original," "neither identical nor different, neither the same nor distinct," and "transcending the real to enter the wondrous" such that nothing is impossible. Therefore, it is termed the "True Ultimate within the Ultimate.

That which is revealed in the following passage is this very nature of the True Ultimate. The section beginning with "To cause you... correctly clarifies the benefit of the Dharma for those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*).
Those who hear this say that the Arhats of dull faculties are addicted to the bliss of *nirvāṇa*, remaining in a stagnant, ignorant concentration like a fish trapped between ice;
because they do not turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle, they are called those of "fixed nature.

The latter two lines clarify those of "unfixed nature," meaning that although they do not abide in the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle, their meritorious practice has not yet reached its culmination, and they have only attained the emptiness of birth (*jātisūnyatā*).

Regarding the statement that one has attained the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) but has not yet attained the two emptinesses: this refers to the fact that the second [emptiness], the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), has not yet been attained.
Although their minds desire to turn toward the Supreme Vehicle (*anuttara-yāna*), they have not yet reached it;

"Supreme Vehicle" here refers to the Bodhisattva Vehicle, as the Bodhisattvas transcend the two vehicles and are thus called the Supreme Vehicle. The Buddha spoke of this true ultimate nature (*paramārtha-svabhāva*) to urge them forward.

Regarding the statement that "Arhats of both fixed and unfixed natures, and others, all cause others to attain the site of the single vehicle’s (ekayāna) quiescence (nirvāṇa), the locus of correct practice," the term "others" refers to other provisional and small-vehicle bodhisattvas. "Single vehicle" is the Buddha-vehicle;
"quiescence" is the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha. "Site" (kṣetra) refers to the ground for attaining the path to Great Nirvāṇa. (From the *Brahma-paripṛcchā-sūtra*)

"Āraṇya" is translated as "free from clamor and confusion. That which is cultivated by the followers of the Two Vehicles is also called *āraṇya*, but it refers only to the partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*).

Since this is the principle of the Middle Way realized by the World-Honored One, the character "true" (*zhen*) is added, and it is thus named "True Āraṇya," the place for the correct practice of cultivation.
"One Vehicle" (*ekayāna*) is the teaching; "quiescence" (*śānti*) is the principle; and "cultivation" is the practice.
This practice reflects upon the four meanings of realization, which fully encompass the Buddha’s teaching, principle, practice, and realization.
Before answering those who have not yet attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), he first clarifies the benefit of the Dharma in this way.
From "You now" onwards, he issues a warning to ensure that [the audience] listens well.
The Buddha said, "Pūrṇa, as you have said... (up to)... I have often heard the Buddha proclaim this meaning.

This section of the sutra represents the World-Honored One, at the very beginning of his response, interrogating the nature, awakening, essence, and function [of the mind] to test the extent of Pūrṇa’s delusion or understanding;
it serves as the foundation for the proclamation of the supreme truth. The phrase "The Buddha said" below reiterates the preceding question.
I say to you: you should immediately interrogate him regarding the essence and function of the nature-awakening.

Has the Buddha not already questioned you on the meaning of the "wondrous clarity of the nature-awakening" and its "mysterious brilliance"? It is simply because the World-Honored One preaches the Dharma based on the two truths, and this discourse on the essence and function of quiescent illumination is his constant teaching.
Although he speaks thus constantly, whether one understands or remains deluded depends on the person; now, Purna has understood.

Because delusion and awakening are still half-and-half, its profound depths have not yet been fully fathomed; therefore, the World-Honored One questioned him with commonplace talk to test whether his confusion had been resolved or not.

Regarding the phrase "the wondrous clarity of the nature-awakening" (*xing-jue-miao-ming*), the character "original" (*ben*) in the term "original awakening" (*ben-jue*) is also the character for "nature" (*xing*);
it is a stylistic variation of "nature," meaning that the essence of nature is inherently endowed with a spirit that is luminous and unclouded.
Because it is awakened, it is called the "awakened nature" (*prakṛti-vijñāna*); this awakened nature is precisely the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
This very awakened nature is the Middle Way, the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and is also the true ultimate nature within the supreme meaning.

"Subtle, luminous, subtle, and luminous" means that the awakened nature is the essence (*svabhāva*); "subtle, luminous, subtle, and luminous" is the function of that essence; and "subtle" is the True Truth.

Because all phenomena are extinguished and the true emptiness is beyond a single point, it is called the "Ultimate Truth" (Paramārtha-satya). Because existence is empty, it is termed "wondrously luminous";
this is the meaning of the "Conventional Truth" (Saṃvṛti-satya). Because all phenomena are established and the myriad existents are simultaneously manifested, it is called the "Conventional Truth.
Since "conventional" has the sense of existence, and because it illuminates everything without omission, it is termed "luminous. Because emptiness is existence, it is so called.
Because the wondrous existence is empty while being existent, it is called "True Emptiness"; because it is true while being conventional, it is called "Wondrous Clarity.

Because it is conventional while being true, it is called "Clear Wondrousness. Since both the wondrous and the clear, and the clear and the wondrous, all derive from the substance of the Middle Way, they are combined as "intrinsic awareness" (*xingjue*).
Furthermore, "wondrous" signifies quiescence and "clear" signifies illumination; thus, it is quiescent yet constantly illuminating.
It is said that because it is wondrously luminous and yet eternally quiescent, it is called "Luminous-Wondrous" (*ming-miao*); thus, its essence and function are combined as explained above.
Gu-shan says: "Quiescence means the three truths are all quiescent; illumination means the three truths are all illuminated.

Wu-xing further supplements this missing text, which is even more wondrous, stating that the three truths are neither quiescent nor illuminated. If this is so, what harm is there [to the original meaning]?
The three truths are simultaneously quiescent and illuminating; their non-dual, wondrous function adapts to conditions, and only then is the subtle meaning fully realized.
If one attains awakening through this realization, then the mountains, rivers, and the great earth are the wondrous existence of the fundamental nature of awareness (*prakṛti-vijñāna*).
How could Pūrṇa perceive this with his dusty eyes? The Great Sage merely asked such questions for the sake of sentient beings. Only—
However, below [this point], Purna accepts the questions posed to him.

The Buddha says: "Regarding what you call 'awakened clarity' (*jue-ming*), is it the nature itself that is luminous (*xing-ming*)... or is it because the awakening is not luminous that it is called 'luminous awakening'?"

In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One, building upon the preceding two meanings of essence and function, establishes the two poles of reality and delusion to investigate the nature of their respective confusion and awakening.
The two terms "awakened clarity" (*jue-ming*): "awakened" (*jue*) refers to the inherent nature of awakening, while "clarity" (*ming*) refers to wondrous clarity;

they constitute one essence and one function. When the function is singled out, the character "clarity" is used to represent the meaning of "wondrous. The following passage [beginning with] "Is it further... correctly uses the term "reality" (*zhen*)...
The two ends of the question concern delusion. Regarding the first phrase, "true nature" refers to the nature of enlightened awareness (*xing-jue*);
it is called "awareness" because enlightened awareness is inherently luminous by its very nature. Regarding the second phrase, "deluded awareness" is also the nature;
it is called "luminous awareness" because when enlightened awareness is not luminous, one must employ luminosity to illuminate it. Now, as for the Buddha...

The mind singularly fears this word "illumination" (ming). Therefore, the subsequent text says, "Based on illumination, one establishes objects," and further says, "By your awakening, you clearly know the nature of illumination," and again, "The fault lies in the awakening-illumination," and yet again, "Falsely taking it as awakening-illumination.
In every instance, it rebukes this word "illumination. This is because all mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena arise entirely from this illumination.

Because the Buddha had initiated this discussion by means of words, the World-Honored One raised the two types of awakening— the true and the false— to question Purna and examine how his own consciousness and vision were.
Purna said, "If this lack of clarity is what is called 'awakening,' then there would be nothing that is clarified."
In this section of the sutra, Purna takes the second question posed by the Buddha and, based on its latter clause, raises a doubt regarding its former clause.
Purna’s intention is as follows: although the nature of awareness is luminous, it has long been shrouded by ignorance; thus, clarity has turned into obscurity and truth has become delusion.
Consequently, the nature of awareness appears to be non-luminous because it is obscured by these two hindrances; it must therefore be realized through wisdom.
By illuminating it, one clearly perceives and removes the dust and defilements, thereby restoring its original luminosity.

From this, he doubts the meaning of the preceding sentence, thinking: "If this nature of non-luminosity were itself awakening, then the awakening that I currently perceive through cultivation would not exist."
The Buddha said: "If there is nothing that is illumined, then there is no awareness of illumination" (up to) "...and this lack of illumination is not the nature of the profound clarity of awareness.
This section of the sutra is the World-Honored One overturning [the opponent's view] by following their own doubts. The Buddha said: "You say that there is no object to be illumined;
if there truly is no object to be illumined, then that is precisely correct. Why? Because if there were no object to be illumined by you..."

There is no capacity for illumination; when both subject and object are forgotten, it is precisely as it should be. Within this fundamental nature of awakening (*prakṛti-bodhi*), the presence of something is not true awakening, and the absence of something is not true illumination.
The preceding phrase points to the essence (*tattva*), hence it says "awakening"; the following phrase points to the function (*vṛtti*), hence it says "illumination.
When viewed as a unity of essence and function, both existence and non-existence are simultaneously negated within the fundamental nature of awakening.
"It is not that there is something, nor is it that there is nothing. Regarding the following phrase, "ignorance" (*avidyā*), there are two interpretations.

The first is that these two characters, "ignorance," refer to the very "lack of clarity" that Pūrṇa clings to. The Buddha says, "The lack of clarity you cling to is also not the nature of the profoundly clear awakening.
The Buddha's intention is that fundamental awakening is profound and still; it is not a state in which there is a lack of clarity.

Your attachment to "non-illumination" actually negates the profound, true illumination of awakening. Second, this refers to the meaning expressed by the two preceding lines regarding existence and non-existence;

that is, since both existence and non-existence have been simultaneously discarded, if one proceeds spontaneously without exerting effort, it matters not whether there is illumination or non-illumination.
Thus, the two characters "non-illumination" (wú míng) carry the sense of spontaneity. The Buddha said:

"Spontaneous [arising] is not the nature of the profound awakening; therefore, this shares the same meaning as the refutation of the 'disease of spontaneity' in the *Complete Awakening Sūtra*. The first interpretation is correct.

'The nature of awakening is necessarily luminous; delusion constitutes the awareness of luminosity' (up to) 'Since that which is perceived has been falsely established, your false capacity [to perceive] arises.'"
This section of the sutra reiterates the preceding text regarding how the fundamental nature of awakening is inherently so, yet delusion creates the duality of subject and object.
The first sentence means that the Buddha says the fundamental nature of awakening is inherently self-luminous and does not require you to illuminate it;

if you insist on illuminating it, you have created the delusion of an "awakening" that acts as the subject of illumination. The middle two sentences mean that the fundamental nature of awakening is not you.

Regarding the statement "that which is illumined is the cause," you have taken that which is illumined to be the cause; thus, you falsely establish a "subject" (the illuminator). The latter two phrases follow from the preceding one:

since the "object" (the illumined) has been falsely established, it gives rise to your false "subject" (the illuminator). Because the subject and object are thus divided and separated, they are no longer based on the original nature.
This is why it was said previously that the character "illuminate" (ming) is most to be avoided; this can now be seen.
"Within the absence of identity and difference, they fiercely manifest as difference... (up to) based on this, one further establishes the absence of both identity and difference.
This section of the scripture follows upon the preceding discussion of subject and object to reveal the causes for the three continuities of sentient beings within the realm of emptiness.

The phrase "within the absence of identity and difference" refers back to the Innate Awareness (*prakṛti-bodha*); it means that the Innate Awareness is originally and fundamentally devoid of identity.

"Differentiation" means that through a single thought-moment of subject and object, differentiation is ignited within the nature-awareness (*prakṛti-vijñāna*) which is itself devoid of identity or difference.
"Ignited" (*citta*) refers to the initial intensity of a fire;

it signifies that while the nature-awareness is fundamentally pure, by means of that single thought-moment of subject and object, the smoke and flames of ignorance blaze forth like a fire, resulting in the differentiation of this intense ignition.
Regarding the subject and object mentioned above: since there is a distinction between subject and object, there arises that which transforms (the subject) and that which is transformed (the object).

The transformer is ignorance (*avidyā*), and that which is transformed is stubborn emptiness (*jaḍa-śūnyatā*). This transforms the fundamental nature of awareness (*prakṛti-bodha*) into a dull and insentient void;
this marks the beginning of the clarity of emptiness. As for "differing from what is different": it means differing from that difference, namely, differing from what was described above.
Regarding "the difference within the blazing": the difference within that which is different refers back to the aforementioned difference within the blazing;

it is used to indicate the difference of that [blazing] by referring to the world. Because the coarse and manifest characteristics of the world emerge externally, it is said to be "different from that" which is the object of differentiation.
As for "establishing identity based on difference," this means that based on the difference of the coarse and manifest world, one establishes emptiness.

Regarding the distinction between difference and sameness: that which takes the difference of emptiness as sameness means that although emptiness differs in nature, the awakened mind is called "the same" because it is without marks;
yet, because the worlds differ in a thousand ways, they must be said to be "different. This clarifies the beginning of the world.
The two subsequent lines, "The manifestation of sameness and difference," clarify the beginning of sentient beings; this refers to using empty space...
When the identity of these and the difference of the world are mutually illuminated, there arise therein sentient beings;
therefore it is said that based on this, "neither identity nor difference" is established.

The character "wu" (無) in "neither identity nor difference" should be understood as "fei" (非), indicating that sentient beings are neither identical nor different. This is because sentient beings consist of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Because that which is produced possesses the characteristics of form, it is not the same as empty space; because it possesses perception, it is not the same as the world;
and because it is distinct from them, it is said to be neither identical nor different when referring to sentient beings.
How do we know this is so? The subsequent text states: "Arising constitutes the world, while stillness accomplishes empty space; empty space is the same, and the world is different."

"Different from that" refers to the absence of identity or difference within true conditioned phenomena; "conditioned phenomena" here specifically points to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of sentient beings.

Furthermore, the character "different" (*yi*) in the phrase "blazingly forming differences" pertains to the three subtle [delusions], while the "difference from that" (*yi bi*) pertains to the six coarse [delusions].
Those who understand will naturally be able to grasp this meaning.
"Thus, through mutual disturbance and dependence, weariness arises... (until) there is no truly conditioned phenomenon that is either identical or different.
This section of the sutra concludes by clarifying the characteristics of the three continuities of sentient beings within the space-element mentioned above.
The first two phrases directly conclude and clarify the aforementioned three continuities of disturbance to demonstrate the causal conditions of karmic fruition. Thus.

The meaning of the two characters [“disturbance” and “confusion”] cited above is as follows: because sentient beings within the realm of space possess the triad of faculties, objects, and consciousness, they are said to be "disturbed and confused.
This nature of disturbance causes the fundamental stillness of awakened awareness to be lost.

It refers to "waiting"—that is, waiting for the forms of the world (both the similar and the different) which are the objects of waiting, and waiting for the sentient beings within that space who are the subjects of waiting.

When the insentient nature of form and emptiness is thus disturbed, how could weariness not arise? This weariness is the toil of deliberation, which is precisely the affliction of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *saṃyojana*).

When this weariness persists for a long time, it gives rise to "dust" (*rajas*); "dust" refers to karmic fruits, meaning that from the internal to the external, and from the subtle to the manifest, one becomes increasingly distant from the awakened nature.
Since one has already strayed far from the Way, one must not be separated from it even for a moment; to be separated from it is to fall into delusion.
After a long time, dust will inevitably arise, and from this, the three miserable realms and the five destinies are formed. This is because labor is stirred within and dust is manifested without;

the fivefold confusion and delusion become established, and their own characteristics become turbid. Therefore, the following line concludes by clarifying that from this, the toil of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) is induced.
This precisely explains the continuity of karmic results through the three periods of time in a cyclic rotation; hence, it is called "inducing" (*ākṣepa*).
"Arising" (*qi*) serves as the concluding term for the preceding section, clarifying the characteristics of sentient beings within the space-element (*ākāśa-dhātu*).

When viewed in contrast with the "stillness" (*jing*) that follows, "arising" carries the meaning of movement; since stillness and movement are opposites, the text here speaks of "arising" rather than "movement.

This is because "arising" refers to dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*): all worlds arise from conditions, and thus arising is itself movement. Therefore, it is used in opposition [to stillness].

Regarding "quiescence" (*śānta*) and "accomplished as quiescent" (*śānta-siddha*): space is called "quiescent" because its essence is fundamentally unmoving. Because it is quiescent and without marks (*animitta*), it is said to be "identical";
yet because it gives rise to the thousandfold differences of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it is said to be "different.

As for the two lines "neither identical nor different," they refer back to the preceding text; the final line "neither identical nor different" means that while it is neither identical nor different, it is truly existent.
This is because of the dharmas; for the internal mind and external forms of sentient beings are the dharmas of the five aggregates (*skandha*).
Thus, the aggregates, bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) all belong to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
From "the clarity of awareness and the darkness of space interact to produce agitation" (up to) "by these causes and conditions, the world continues in succession."
This section of the sutra follows upon the three preceding continuities to specifically clarify the characteristics of the world as produced through dependent origination.

Regarding the phrase "Awakened Clarity" (*jue-ming*) below, it first demonstrates the dependent origination of the wind-circle. This term "Awakened Clarity" refers to the aforementioned capacity for illumination within deluded awakening;
because the essence of awakening is itself without delusion and inherently possesses a nature of luminosity, it is termed "Awakened Clarity. Thus, it is called "Awakened Clarity."

The transforming subject (the capacity for transformation) is emptiness, and the transformed object (that which is transformed) is also emptiness; because it is fundamentally dull and insentient, it is called "empty-obscuration" (*śūnya-mūḍha*).
Since clarity and obscuration are mutually correlative, the internal mind wavers as clarity and obscuration contend with one another. This wavering nature belongs to wind (*vāyu*).
Due to this internal wavering of the mind, externally a wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) is manifested, which sustains the world-system. Therefore, beneath the world-system there exists a wind-circle.
The "wheel" (cakra) held [by the wind] is a metaphor for the sense of supporting and carrying, just as the wheel beneath a cart can support objects;
likewise, the wind-wheel supports the world. Beneath the wind-wheel, it rests upon space. Because it depends on space, the following explains the dependent origination of the golden wheel.
This golden wheel is the earth; the nature of the great earth is solidity and obstruction, and all gold is of this nature.
Because the nature of the gold produced from the ground of jewels is identical to the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*), it is designated by the name "earth" even when called the "golden wheel.
Due to the vacillation of false luminosity in space above, attachment becomes increasingly firm;

through this firm attachment, obstruction is formed, and this firm obstruction is the very nature of the earth element. That external gold and jewel arise from the attachment of the internal mind’s luminous awareness.
Because it establishes firmness, there is a golden wheel that maintains the land; this is discussed in terms of the upper world in general, while now it is explained in terms of specific lands.
