This is because each land has its own jurisdiction, just as the Hua, Yi, Rong, and Di peoples each have their own boundaries, which is what constitutes a "land.
Furthermore, all such lands necessarily abide upon the great earth; therefore, it is so called.
The golden wheel sustains the land through firm awareness; below this, three stages demonstrate the dependent origination of the fire element.
From the upper stage, the gold jewel is formed by firm grasping awareness. As its brilliance and dullness fluctuate, wind is produced.
When the wind and the gold rub against each other, warmth is generated within them; this serves as the cause of fire.
Because the movement of the mind clings to and rubs against forms, it externally induces the appearance of fire as its nature of transformation.

Fire is called the "nature of transformation" because fire can transform existence into non-existence and transform the raw into the cooked; its self-nature has no form, yet it manifests by relying on conditions, and is therefore called the "nature of transformation.
[The passage] from "Precious Clarity" downward indicates the dependent origination of the water-element. [The term] "solid clarity" refers to...

Because gold can produce moisture, it is held that gold can generate the moisture of water, which constitutes the nature of water. However, the moisture produced by that gold is still relatively weak;

it further relies on the power of fire to vaporize it upward. When water and fire vaporize one another, the force of the moisture becomes even more intense, much like the process of steaming in a rice steamer.
Consequently, this evokes the Water Wheel, which contains the worlds of the ten directions, just as the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha) does.

Because the world rests upon the fragrant-water ocean, it is called the "container-realm" (*dhātugarbha*). This demonstrates the five continents and the emergence of the vast waters and lands through the conditions of fire and water.
That is to say, the nature of fire ascends while the nature of water descends; thus, fire and water interact and manifest above and below.
If the force of the water prevails and the force of the fire is inferior, moisture becomes a vast ocean. If the force of the fire... [text truncated]
When the power of the water is weak and it dries up, it forms islands (*dzou-t'an*; *t'an* is pronounced *shàn*, with the second character *dú-hàn*);
these are sandbanks in the water. Based on this principle of the mutual interaction of water and fire, fires constantly arise within that great ocean.
Just as those traveling at sea often see fireballs like lamps in the middle of the night, which are called "divine lamps" (*shén-dēng*), they are in fact not divine.
A lamp is simply the manifestation of its own substance through the mutual friction of water and fire.

Furthermore, it is evidenced by the fact that within river channels and sandbars where great rivers flow constantly, there are often seen springs of water gushing forth from between the great mountains; this is the proof.
Water’s power is inferior to fire. [The following six sections] demonstrate the conditions for the arising of mountain rocks, grasses, and trees. If the water...
When the power of fire is superior to that of water, the force of the fire prevails, burning the water dry and solidifying it into high mountains.

Thus we know that mountain rocks are originally the differentiated energies of water and fire; therefore, when struck, they produce flames. During the fifth and sixth months, these stones melt within them and turn into water.
Furthermore, when the power of earth is inferior to that of water, the force of the water prevails, and the earth is drawn away by the water.

They become grasses and trees; therefore, grasses and trees are fundamentally the constituent vapors of water and earth. Thus, when they encounter fire, they return to ash and soil; when they encounter moisture, they become water again.
"Lín-sǒu" (林藪)—the character for *sǒu* being pronounced *sǒu*—refers to a category of vegetation; it denotes the dense growth of grasses, trees, and shrubs.
The final four lines summarize the meaning of the continuous succession of the world, stating that [it arises] from...
From the awakening of clarity and the vacuity of darkness, [the elements] arise and reach down to earth and water, from which they are drawn forth as grasses and trees;
therein, earth, water, fire, and wind each have their own causes and conditions, intersecting to produce the five [elements], which successively form various species.

The first two phrases summarize how delusion arises through intersection; the latter two phrases properly conclude that the world is continuous. For "world" is a general name for earth, water, fire, and wind.
Wind is a distinct characteristic; the world has no self-substance, for it is merely the continuity of the four great elements that is called the "world.
Furthermore, Pūrṇa, [you have explained] that delusion is not from another [source]... (up to)... by these causes and conditions, sentient beings continue in succession.
This section of the sutra follows the three preceding continuations to specifically clarify the characteristics of the dependent origination of sentient beings.

The four lines beginning with "Clarifying delusion" (*ming wang*) serve to conclude what precedes and introduce what follows. The first two lines conclude the preceding section, while the latter two lines introduce the subsequent part.

Regarding the initial phrase "clarifying delusion," it refers generally to the world as the locus of delusive clarity. As for "delusive clarity": (Note: This translation reflects the structure and intent of the provided Chinese commentary on the *Awakening of Faith*.)

Regarding the delusion of that which is perceived: because the world is formed by the delusion of what is perceived, the present intent is to clarify the preceding point by stating that those various perceived delusions do not arise from elsewhere, but are due to the fault of the perceiving consciousness.
Once the world of the perceived has been established, it is difficult to transcend the principle of the perceiver; this serves as the introduction to the subsequent text.
These following seven phrases correctly clarify the principle of not transgressing. That which is delusory refers to the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), which is easy to understand.

In the phrase "form, fragrance, taste, and touch," there is a redundant "form" (*rūpa*) at the beginning and a missing "phenomenon" (*dharma*) at the end; this collectively refers to the six sense-objects.

Therefore, the subsequent phrase says, "the six delusions are accomplished as the external six sense-objects. Once the external six sense-objects have been established, then the internal seeing [faculty]...
The phrase "the six sense organs are likewise separated" [refers to] the same karma; the following two lines indicate the causes and conditions for the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*).
The line "same karma" clarifies the two modes of birth from a womb or an egg:

that is to say, when the past karmic actions of those born from a womb or an egg are identical, they are summoned by the conditions of karma and become mutually entangled, never parting from one another life after life. This is their reliance.

These are drawn by the two delusions of emotion (*kāma*) and thought (*saṃjñā*). The phrase "union and separation" clarifies the two modes of birth from moisture and transformation. Regarding moisture-born birth:
if one is moved by union, one does not depend on parents, but merely relies on moisture and warmth as external aids. These aids trigger the fundamental nature of consciousness;

this is called the "harmony of the three conditions," through which the category of moisture-born beings is first formed. Regarding transformation-born birth: it should be understood as responding to separation.
"Leaving the old to take on the new" refers to birth through transformation (*upapāduka*), which has its cause in transformation.
This is like the transformation of a water-turtle, which leaves its former shell to metamorphose into a dragonfly; likewise, the various devas are also born by transformation.

While those [devas] represent the virtuous form of transformation, this phrase merely speaks of "forming through transformation" as an abbreviated expression for the meaning of moisture-birth, with the word "conjoining" implied.

Because it is "central," one sees clearly; the following eight phrases extensively clarify the characteristics of womb-birth (*jarāyuja*). The first two phrases clarify how the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) selects parents and takes rebirth in the womb.

The initial cause refers to the nature of vision of the intermediate state body, which is all-pervasive and penetrating, enabling one to perceive invisibly the moments when men and women engage in sexual union, even at distances of thousands of miles or tens of thousands of li in distant foreign lands. All such instances—
Because those with common karma and a shared affinity are all able to see it, it is said that "he sees light and colors appear.
Here, "colors" refers to the colors resulting from the parents' sexual union; because he sees the light, the colors of the parents' union manifest within his vision.
Since the intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) clearly perceives these colors, the thought of entering the womb (*garbhāvakrānti*) consequently arises.

Because it is accomplished, it is said that "clearly seeing the accomplishment of the perception. The next two phrases further clarify that within the accomplishment of this perception there are two intentions—aversion and attraction:
that which contradicts one's own feelings is called a "differentiated view," while that which accords with one's feelings is called a "concordant perception.

This means that if that intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) is female, she perceives her father as concordant and feels attraction toward him, while she perceives her mother as differentiated and feels aversion toward her.
If the intermediate state being is male, he perceives his mother as a woman of equal status whom he loves, and perceives his father as a rival whom he hates;
this arises from the jealousy born of lust. Furthermore, the next two lines clarify the actual process of entering the womb:
once the perception of sexual passion for that union has formed, the flow of passionate thought enters the mother’s womb.
Thus, the seed for birth from a womb is formed; once the mother’s womb has received that conception, the embryo begins to develop.
Furthermore, the next two phrases clarify the cause of birth from a womb, as this class of beings arises through sexual union.
By attracting those with similar karma from the past—where "similar karma" refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)—there are the following three phrases which provide the conclusion.
Regarding the names and characteristics of the stages through which conception develops, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that there are five stages within the womb: 1.
The first seven days are called *kalala*, translated as "congealed mucus" (*ning-hua*). This is the initial phase resulting from the union of the father’s semen and the mother’s blood.
2. The second seven days are called *arbuda*, translated as "bubble" (*pao*). This develops further from the *kalala*, and the five sense organs, such as the eyes, begin to form.
Because the sense organs form five blisters, the third week is called *peśī*, translated as "soft flesh," for it grows from the blisters into soft flesh.
Because it further grows from soft flesh into firm flesh, the fourth week is called *ghanā*, translated as "firm flesh.
Because it further grows from soft flesh into firm flesh, the fifth week is called *praśākhā*, translated as "the stage of formation"; thus, in the fifth week, there are three [features].
On the fifteenth day, the stage of formation is completed, and the head, feet, limbs, and body take shape such that male and female can be distinguished.

The current text mentions only the second week (the *dvādaśa-rātra*) regarding the names and characteristics, which encompasses the remaining three weeks as well. The six lines below concerning the womb and egg show the responses of the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*), each according to its own karma.
The first line states that among the four births—womb-born and so forth—whatever birth one receives is a retribution induced by the karma of that particular mode.
Because it responds accordingly, it is said that [birth] follows what is appropriate for each case. The following four lines demonstrate the reason for this response:

as for why "egg-birth" (*aṇḍaja*) arises solely from formative thought (*saṃjñā*), it is because eggs are produced from the binding of thought, or they are formed by attaching to the vital breath (*vāyu*) or riding upon sound;

since thought is light and buoyant, it brings about the class of egg-born beings who possess wings and are able to fly. Fetal birth (*jarāyuja*) arises from the emotion of craving and desire; however, as for that emotion...
Because they fall heavily back into the category of the womb, their movement is like that of earth and they cannot fly upward; they are moistened by the convergence of three conditions.

Because of separation, they transition toward a new transformation into a different substance. The four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*) receive retribution according to the resonance of karma; for the most part, it is like this.
The four lines below on "sentient thought" further clarify that the four modes of birth undergo further transformations and are not constant, such as the transformation of the nature of the womb.
Thus, from the union of eggs or moisture, there arises the perception of separation; from the state of separation, there arises emotion, which then changes back into union.

Or again, from the states of union and separation, there arise emotion and perception; emotion and perception are easily exchanged for union and separation. Following karma, beings ascend or sink, making it difficult to fix upon any certainty.
The final two phrases summarize the continuity of sentient beings.
"Pūrṇa, conceptual attachment (*saṃjñā-tṛṣṇā*) is identical to the bond of craving (*tṛṣṇā-bandhana*); one cannot be separated from it. (Up to:

By these causes and conditions, karma and its fruits continue in succession. This section of the sūtra follows the three preceding causes of continuity and specifically clarifies the characteristics of the dependent origination of karmic fruits.

The text consists of four parts; regarding "lust, killing, and stealing" as the bonds, first, under the heading of Pūrṇa, it initially clarifies that conceptual attachment is identical to greed and desire.

Regarding "knots" and so forth: conceptualization is the conceptualization of desire, and craving is the affection of the emotions. Since emotional craving is formed through the conceptualization of desire, then the conceptualization of desire is the cause and emotional craving is the effect.
As the *Awakening of Faith Sutra* states: "Lustful craving is the cause; attachment to life is the effect.

The present text concerns this relationship between subject and object, self and other, wherein conceptualization and craving bind one together across successive lifetimes, such that they cannot be untied.
Therefore, it is said that although they are bound together by the same fetters, craving cannot be severed. Thus, regarding the various lower worlds, there are generally only ten types of births;

these refer to the categories of the "ten births" based on the distinction between the primary body (the self) and the secondary environment (the world). Since the retribution experienced differs and the primary and secondary environments are distinct, they are all collectively termed "worlds," which is why the text says "various.
Furthermore, since all ten types of births possess parents, children, and grandchildren, one should not point exclusively to human relations when explaining them.
If one analyzes this through human relations as Wu-xing Xie does, the perspective becomes narrow.

Since the scriptural text clarifies within the context of "theft and greed" by specifically referring to the discourse on the ten births, the subsequent section concludes by naming these as "desire-greed," which is termed "greedy craving. Next, it clarifies "killing-greed";
that "craving and love nourish each other" means that craving and loving their flesh and blood nourishes one's own mouth and belly. Nourishing.

Since the mind of "self" and "other" is identical, it is said that they "nourish one another. Within this expression of mutual nourishment, there is already implied the sense of mutual devouring and retribution.
Because killing arises from greed and does not cease unless one kills, one must kill until the end;

therefore, it is said that "greed cannot be stopped. Regarding the phenomena of mutual killing and devouring in the various worlds as explained above, such things occur throughout the ten realms of existence.

All of these have their current texts which briefly indicate that the four modes of birth are explained by the strong deceiving the weak and devouring one another according to their respective capacities;
this is spoken from the perspective of mutual enmity. These [passages] below conclude the name of "killing-greed.
Since the preceding text spoke of the continuity of birth, the present text should speak of the continuity of killing. Next, the three sections below explain "theft-greed."
By citing the example of humans eating sheep and so forth to illustrate the retribution of a single being, it follows that this is the case for every being.
Thus, starting from the brief and moving toward the detailed, ten categories of birth-and-death are indicated.

Throughout successive lifetimes, beings come and devour one another; there is none who does not face retribution. While four types of birth were previously mentioned, the present passage encompasses all ten classes.
The texts refer to these matters interchangeably. Regarding "evil karma arising together": this refers to mutual killing and devouring, which constitute an extremely grave evil karma.
Because one is born together with it and dies together with it, it is called "arising together. For example, the current people of the world possess the intent to kill without being taught;
this is caused by past karma and is precisely what is meant by "evil karma arising together. This [refers to] mutual killing and devouring.
The karma of such acts cannot be exhausted even throughout kalpas reaching the limits of the future; this is an extreme expression of how profound the retribution for such enmity is.
This concludes the section on those who, out of greed for fame, kill and devour one another—these are called "thieves and greedy ones.
It is like when people at home raise livestock: they protect them from mosquitoes and gadflies by providing food and drink, initially cherishing them as if they were benefactors.

Once one applies the blade and the block, that which was initially called "love" or "non-love" is revealed to be merely the desire to steal their flesh and blood for the sake of their fatness and sweetness.
Furthermore, those animals have never consented to offer their bodies; to take what is not given—what is this if not theft?
Moreover, in the preceding passage, lust, killing, and theft were all designated by the name "greed"; for although greed is the same in all cases, [the distinctions remain].
Enmity and gratitude, as well as thieving intent, each follow their own root. You owe the four lower fetters;

this clarifies the preceding point that the kalpa of poverty is never-ending, for it is through the continuity of karmic results that this occurs. As for "you owe my life," "owing" means being in debt;
because in a previous life you once killed my body, you owe me my life, and thus I now seek what is owed.

"Having incurred [a debt], one must surely repay it. Regarding the second phrase, "I shall return your debt": the first phrase speaks of "life," while this phrase speaks of "debt. Debt refers to wealth;
that is to say, if during my life I stole another's wealth, I incurred a debt to them.

Furthermore, if one kills another for the sake of wealth, the terms "debt" and "life" appear interchangeably in the texts. For such causes and conditions, [one may suffer] for hundreds of thousands of lifetimes.
"Enmity between kalpas does not cease; one constantly dwells in birth and death"—this is spoken in reference to hostile opposition.
"If you love my mind, that mind is emotion (*qing*)," whereas the other [aspect] is the nature of affection (*qingxing*).

The second phrase, "I pity your form," refers to form as physical appearance and beauty; "pity" (*lian*) means to cherish, which also carries the sense of love. The preceding line spoke of "emotion," while this...

The commentary states: "The terms 'form' (*rūpa*) and 'sentiment' (*qing*) are also seen interchangeably; for what reason, then, does [the text] not speak of sentiment but rather of the mind (*citta*)?

It is because, in contrast to the term 'form' used below, sentiment belongs to the category of mental phenomena (*caitasika-dharma*), while physical appearance belongs to the category of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*). This is a skillful literary composition.
Only form and sentiment bind one through craving and attachment; by means of such causes and conditions, one remains constantly bound throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas."

This is explained in terms of affectionate attachment (*sneha*). Previously, it was explained in terms of hostile opposition (*pratigha*) regarding birth and death (*saṃsāra*); now, it is explained in terms of affectionate attachment.
When one is entangled by bonds and encounters hostility, not being separated from it life after life—is this not entanglement?

Now, when affectionate attachments follow one another through successive births without being abandoned—is this not birth and death? The terms "birth and death" and "entanglement" are also seen interchangeably in the texts. However, this...
The two meanings do not go beyond the three matters of stealing, killing, and sexual misconduct;

therefore, the concluding sentence below states that "only the three—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—constitute the roots," thereby encompassing all derivative actions (*aṅga-karma*). Such causes and conditions are called the "continuity of karmic results.
Furthermore, while in the preceding text sexual misconduct was mentioned before killing, in this concluding passage killing is mentioned before sexual misconduct. This is also [the case].
Each has its underlying intent. Those who prioritize sexual misconduct do so to warn that desire is the root of birth and death;
since one seeks to transcend birth and death, one must first sever the root of craving—hence sexual misconduct is highlighted first.

Those who prioritize killing do so because when encountering all manner of adversaries, killing is the ultimate [offense]; since one seeks to extinguish enmity, one must first sever killing—hence these two are presented alternately, one before the other.
"Pūrṇa, these three kinds of inverted continuities (leading to) this false delusion that ends and begins again.
This section of the sutra summarizes the characteristics of the three continuities and directly identifies the root of delusion, thereby concluding Pūrṇa’s first question.
"Thus" and below is the actual concluding text; "all of which" and below indicates the root of delusion.
Regarding "the nature of clear and luminous awareness": the clarity and luminosity of awareness is fundamentally the true substance of the awakened nature (*prakṛti*).
It is only through delusion that a "nature capable of luminous awareness" is falsely established; thus, the true is transformed into the delusive.

All conditioned phenomena of the environment and its inhabitants arise from this nature of clear and luminous awareness; therefore, this is specifically designated as the root of delusion. This nature of clear and luminous awareness...

This immediately pertains to the three subtleties within the eighth consciousness; through the transformation of this karma, the three subtleties evolve into the six coarsenesses, whereby the world, sentient beings, and karmic fruits are all fully present.
This very act of cognitive discernment is termed "inversion.
For the nature of awakening is profoundly still and fundamentally devoid of characteristics; it is because of this discernment that all phenomena arise. Fundamentally...
Originally non-arising, yet through delusion one perceives arising; because there is arising, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, the aggregates, bases, and elements successively flow on.
From non-existence they come into being, and having existed, they return to non-existence; therefore it is said that "the end is the beginning.
This restates the words of the original question. Furthermore, the two phrases "because of this realization, the characteristics manifest" and "arise from deluded vision" [refer to this].
Regarding this couplet, "yuan" (delusion) should not be read in conjunction with "jian" (view);
rather, one should read it as "because of awakening [to reality], appearances arise; following delusion, views are produced. Only in this way does the meaning of the text become flavorful.
Pūrṇa said: "If this wondrous awakening [is thus], how could the outflows of conditioned habituation ever arise again?

This section of the sutra represents Pūrṇa restating his objection based on the Buddha’s first answer, asserting that although the Buddha and sentient beings are fundamentally identical and not different, [if they were so, defilement would be impossible].
"Wondrous awakening" refers to the "awakening of nature"; as previously stated, in the term "nature-awakening," both characters [refer to the same reality].
This true dharma-nature is itself awakening; therefore, what is now called "wondrous awakening" (miaojue) means that awakening is the true dharma, while "wondrous" is a sublime epithet for awakening.
It is like calling a person a "wondrous person": the person is the true dharma, and "wondrous" is a sublime epithet for that person.
Calling it "wondrous awakening" is likewise so. This is truly because the nature of awakening is pure and fundamental, its spiritual luminosity penetrating and transparently clear.
It is neither existent nor non-existent; it is profound and hidden, difficult to fathom, without marks and without name.

Therefore, we forcibly name it "Sublime Enlightenment" (*miao-jue*). The subsequent phrase, "the fundamental sublime enlightened clarity" (*ben-miao-jue-ming*), is a restatement of the profound meaning of the preceding phrase.
One should not regard the two characters "enlightened clarity" (*jue-ming*) as referring to a substantial entity. Why? Because the preceding phrase...
The essence of awakening has already been defined. Now, regarding this "awakening-illumination" (*jue-ming*), let us briefly examine it:

"awakening" means the sense of being spiritually alert, and "illumination" means the sense of being non-obscured. This is fundamentally what is meant by "abiding in the wondrous," as stated in the preceding phrase.
These four characters serve to re-emphasize the "wondrous awakening" of the previous line, signifying that it possesses these four fundamental virtues.
However, this wondrous awakening—from the lowest level of sentient beings up to the highest level of the Tathāgatas—possesses this mind equally.
It does not increase in the Buddhas, nor does it decrease in sentient beings. Why, then, do sentient beings suddenly give rise to the appearances of mountains, rivers, and so forth, "without cause"?
"Without cause" means that there is no [external] reason; it signifies being without a starting point. Since sentient beings already possess this mind, they subsequently give rise to all things.

If the Tathāgata also possesses this mind characterized by the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*), then when will the conditioned outflows (*āsrava*) of the mountains, rivers, and the great earth ever arise again?
As for what is called "wondrous emptiness and luminous awareness" (*miao kong ming jue*): emptiness and awareness are real dharmas;

emptiness is the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), while wondrous luminosity is its function—that is, the aforementioned sublime awakening. [Pūrṇa], you have briefly altered the phrasing; this objection of yours arises from...

The preceding text raised this objection because it states that both sentient beings and Buddhas equally possess the *tathāgatagarbha* nature. To equally possess wondrous enlightenment (*myōkaku*) constitutes their fundamental identity;
however, that while the various characteristics of a Buddha arise subsequently, the Buddha does not undergo further birth constitutes their difference at the level of the derivative.

This is similar to the objection raised by Vajragarbha Bodhisattva in the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*), which asks how one who has attained Buddhahood through different births could subsequently give rise to ignorance.
The meaning of the question, "When will all Tathāgatas again give rise to all afflictions?
is the same as this. The Buddha told Pūrṇa: "It is like a person who is lost [and so forth]... would they become lost again? "No, World-Honored One."

In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One employs an analogy to clarify that one who has attained awakening does not become deluded, thereby answering the question regarding the non-arising after awakening.
For example, as the following analogy states: it is like a person lost on a road who arrives at a village.
As for what is called a "village," it refers to a place where houses are gathered together, such as a hamlet in the countryside today. Regarding that—
When a deluded person first arrives here, they mistake south for north. The Buddha asks this delusion that mistakes south for north:
does it arise because of delusion, or does it emerge from awakening? Pūrṇa answers that this delusion arises neither because of delusion nor because of awakening.
Below, he provides a fourfold analysis to explain the reason why it is not dependent on either delusion or awakening.

The commentary on the text can be understood as follows: Below the words "The Buddha said," there is a further question regarding whether one who has attained awakening might subsequently fall back into delusion.

This refers to the moment when that deluded person, while in the midst of mistaking south for north, is suddenly pointed out by someone else and brought to realization, being told, "This is south, not north.
The Buddha then calls Purna and asks, "What do you think of this? Regarding that delusion:
"Even if a person returns from another place, would they become lost again in this village? Purna replied, "No, no.
"No, no" means that once one has clarified north and south and attained awakening, one will not be deluded again.
"Pūrṇa, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are also like this" (up to) "awakening dispels delusion; once delusion is extinguished, awakening does not give rise to further delusion.
This section of the sūtra applies the Dharma to the preceding analogy to clarify that after awakening, one does not fall back into delusion.

In the preceding metaphor, the "deluded person" represents sentient beings; the "village" represents the aggregates, elements, and sense bases (*skandha-dhātu-āyatana*); and "delusion" refers to the afflictions. South represents the direction of delusion.
The metaphor of "true north" represents the True, while "false north" represents the delusory.

It means that because sentient beings are deluded, they mistake the True Nature of the Tathāgatagarbha for the delusory manifestations of mountains, rivers, and all phenomenal existence. Originally, what was perceived as "north" was in fact "south.

This metaphor indicates that the very substance of the delusory manifestations of mountains, rivers, and all phenomena is, in its essence, the True Nature of the Tathāgatagarbha; it instructs those who have awakened to realize this.
This refers to one who has attained awakening, which is analogous to the Buddha’s pointing out [the way] to bring about realization;

it is analogous to the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma so that all sentient beings may realize that the entirety of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) is the Tathāgatagarbha, whereby there will no longer be the delusion of mountains and rivers.

"Even if this person is deluded" means that even if this very person—who is directed toward realization—is deluded; "even if deluded" is a metaphor for being obscured by pervasive afflictions (*paryavasthāna*).
Although the objects of knowledge have been severed, they have not yet been destroyed; thus it is said, "even if one were deluded, one would no longer be deluded in this village.

This is a metaphor for how, after awakening to the emptiness of the aggregates (skandhas), sense bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus), one will never again be deluded regarding the "village" of the elements, bases, and aggregates.

Since other sutras frequently use the dharmas of the aggregates, elements, and bases as metaphors for a village, and since the subsequent section on the ten directions serves as the application of the analogy, it says "likewise."

In this way, the explanation through dharmas and the explanation through metaphors do not correspond to the dharmas themselves; rather, they merely combine the two meanings of delusion and awakening to clarify that delusion is exhausted and awakening is perfected.
One seeks to grasp the meaning through the intention, so there is no need for detailed correspondence. To examine this in detail:

grasping the meaning and forgetting the expression does not depend on words, whether they correspond or do not correspond. Therefore, the two lines following "this delusion" mean that the essence of delusion is originally...
Because it is delusory, it is said to be "without origin. "Without origin" means that there is no fundamental root.
"The nature is ultimately empty" explains the meaning of this lack of origin. The phrase "from the beginning" means that from the very outset, this delusion has never existed;
subsequently, due to delusion, it appears as if there were both delusion and awakening. Since it is called "appearing," what appears is not real; yet, though non-existent, it suddenly...

There are those who say it is like using the wisdom of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) to awaken from and shatter delusion; once the wondrous enlightenment is perfectly complete, delusion will not arise again.

It is also like a person with cataracts seeing flowers in the sky—once they have cleared away the cataracts, when would those flowers ever appear again? How much less could mountains, rivers, and the great earth ever re-emerge?
In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One employs a further analogy to clarify that after attaining Buddhahood, appearances no longer arise.
The person with cataracts represents sentient beings; emptiness represents the *tathāgatagarbha*; the flowers in the sky represent the mountains, rivers, and the great earth;

the removal of the disease of cataracts represents the destruction of the ignorance of sentient beings; and the disappearance of the flowers in the empty sky represents the state of sentient beings after awakening.

The various phenomena of mountains and rivers are extinguished within the Tathāgatagarbha; yet suddenly there is a foolish person who, upon that empty ground where the flowers of space have vanished, awaits the rebirth of those flowers.
This is like Pūrṇa’s question regarding when the phenomena of mountains and rivers might ever arise again after the attainment of Buddhahood.
Observe how, below this, the World-Honored One uses the meaning of the analogy to question Pūrṇa.
This means to distinguish between ignorance and wisdom, and to cause the mind to attain realization through causes and analogies;
this is the intent of the question. Below, when Pūrṇa speaks, his use of analogies can be understood: he says that to wait for emptiness to produce flowers again is ignorance, not wisdom.

Why? Because emptiness originally has no flowers; to see the extinction of flowers and then regard that as emptiness is already a perversion. How could one further wait for it to arise? Emptiness is fundamentally...
The metaphor of the absence of flowers illustrates that within the *tathāgatagarbha*, the appearances of mountains, rivers, and so forth are originally non-existent.

The metaphor of the extinction of flowers and the manifestation of emptiness illustrates that upon first awakening to the nature of the *garbha*, all conditioned habitual outflows are extinguished within it. Although this is termed "initial awakening" (*ādikṣaya*), it has not yet transcended inversion;
therefore, it is said: "Having seen the extinction of flowers and the manifestation of emptiness, one is still inverted. Why is this? Because of original awakening (*mūlapratibodha*).
Because within the nature there is fundamentally no characteristic of arising or ceasing, [the Buddha] commanded that they be produced again. This serves as a metaphor for Purna’s inquiry:
"After attaining Buddhahood, when will the appearances of mountains, rivers, and so forth arise again? This, too, is folly and not wisdom.
The passage beginning with "The Buddha said" below shows the Buddha rebuking Purna’s question as being contrary to principle.
Furthermore, it is like gold ore mixed with refined gold; (up to: "Bodhi and Nirvana are also like this.
This section of the sutra uses a further analogy to clarify that once one has severed the afflictions and emerged from birth and death, one will never again be subject to rebirth.
While gold is within the ore, it cannot serve the function of refined gold; yet once it has been extracted from the ore, its essential nature [remains].
Only then will it be pure and never again mixed. The ore is a metaphor for afflictions (*kleśa*), and the gold is a metaphor for *bodhi*.
If *bodhi* remains within the entanglements, it is mixed with and obscured by afflictions; thus its wondrous luminosity cannot function.
If *bodhi* emerges from the entanglements and afflictions are forever extinguished, the true essence of *bodhi* finally manifests, and its inherently existing radiance is revealed.
It shall never again be mixed with [the world]. Furthermore, wood is a metaphor for birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), and ash is a metaphor for *nirvāṇa*.
Wood becoming ash is a metaphor for transcending birth-and-death and realizing *nirvāṇa*. Once wood has become ash, it cannot become wood again;

once one has transcended birth-and-death and realized *nirvāṇa*, one shall never again revolve within birth-and-death. The application of these two metaphors to the Dharma of the Buddhas below can be understood accordingly.
The details are not fully set forth; it merely combines and clarifies the two names. The underlying meaning is as before, along with the four preceding metaphors.
Of these, the first two metaphors illustrate *mūla-awakening* (original enlightenment), while the latter two illustrate *ādi-awakening* (initial awakening).

Regarding the metaphor for *mūla-awakening*, the intended meaning is that although the directions of one who has lost their way are fundamentally correct, the person themselves is deluded and inverted, mistaking south for north, even though the location of south remains as it is.
The fundamental nature is immovable and inherently free; it is not the fault of direction, and thus serves as a metaphor for original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*).

Furthermore, regarding the previous metaphor of flowers in the sky: space originally has no flowers; it is the sick person who, through deluded attachment, perceives the arising and ceasing of flowers—it is the person’s own delusion, not the fault of empty space.
Therefore, this also serves as a metaphor for original enlightenment. The subsequent metaphor for initial enlightenment (*ādi-awakening*) is the nature of gold.
Although the metal is refined, it must still be extracted from the ore; only after being extracted does it fully realize its utility.
Thus, this is a metaphor for initial enlightenment (*ādikṣaya-jñāna*), which reveals the Tathāgata’s wisdom-virtue (*jñāna-guṇa*). Once wood has been turned to ash, it can never again become wood.

Thus, this is a metaphor for transcending birth and death so as never again to be subject to the transformations of birth and death, which reveals the Tathāgata’s cessation-virtue (*prahāṇa-guṇa*). Furthermore, these first two metaphors directly respond to [the objection] that there is no...

The question regarding the sudden arising of [defilements] means that while the wondrous enlightenment is fundamentally thus, it is people themselves who delusively perceive the existence of marks. The latter two metaphors directly answer the question of how conditioned outflows (*sāsrava*) could ever arise again; they mean that once all outflows are exhausted, even the nature of exhaustion no longer exists—so how could anything arise?

Yet, the reason the Buddha offers four metaphors to answer a single question is intended to convey this meaning: [The text continues with the metaphors: 1. A person who has been cured of a chronic illness and regains their health.

2. A person who has been released from prison and returns to their home. 3. A person who has crossed over a great river and reaches dry land. 4. A person who has escaped from a burning house and stands in a cool, open space. These four metaphors illustrate that although one may have severed the various outflows, because the very nature of severance is also non-existent, there is nothing that can arise again. This is why the Buddha employs these four analogies together to respond to the single inquiry.
If one were to explain only the first two metaphors, it would merely clarify the fundamental awakening (*mūla-awakening*) while lacking the meaning of cultivation and realization.

If one were to explain only the latter two metaphors, it would merely clarify the initial awakening (*ādi-awakening*) while forgetting its original nature. Therefore, the four metaphors are presented together to manifest the perfect principle of the mutual completion of the initial and fundamental awakenings;
thus, the truth of reality is fully prepared without partiality. The above serves as a response to Pūrṇa’s objection based on his attachment to abstract principle.
The first inquiry regarding phenomena is concluded; here begins the second response, which addresses the difficulty raised previously concerning the nature of characteristics.
Pūrṇa, as for what you asked: "Earth, water, fire, and wind [pervade] the entire dharma-realm, yet they cannot coexist within one another."

In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One prepares to explain the meaning of essence and characteristics; first, he recounts the words of the original question, which can be understood from the text.
Pūrṇa, it is like empty space: its substance is not the various phenomena [from "the accumulation of earth forms mist" to "the clarity of water forms reflection"].
This section of the sutra employs an analogy to answer Purna’s inquiry regarding the nature and characteristics [of phenomena]. As the following analogy states:
it is like the essence of empty space, which is a single dharma that cannot be apprehended; it is tranquil and eternally abiding.

Although it is not comprised of manifold characteristics, it does not obstruct the manifestation of those various characteristics. "Manifestation" means to bring forth; that is to say, the myriad phenomena.
All things in the universe exist within space, yet space is capable of containing them all without resistance.
Therefore, to explain why it does not resist, it is said that when the sun shines upon that space, it becomes bright, and so forth; this can be understood.
As for "thunder" (*tun*), it refers to a gathering; as for "wind," it moves when shaken. One asks: how can space move? It is the wind that moves it.
It can blow forth the myriad differences such that all things sway together, appearing as if the void itself were moving; when the sky first clears after rain it becomes a bright day,
while wind-blown sand becomes a haze— all these are easily understood precisely because empty space is not inherently identical to phenomena such as light and darkness,
yet does not obstruct the manifestation of light and so forth.

"What do you think? Thus, from 'different directions' (殊方) to 'neither sun nor space, yet not different from space and the sun'—this section of the sutra follows the preceding [discussion] to refute false appearances.
It shows that they are neither form (*rūpa*) nor space (*ākāśa*), yet they are not different from space and form.

The phrase "what do you think" (*yathā manyase*) interrogates and sets forth the intent of the refutation. "Different directions" (*śu fang*) refers to the ten directions (*daśadig*). By means of these various appearances...
Because arising and ceasing are not constant, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is designated as the cause. The following two lines explicitly set forth the intent of the refutation.
"That" refers collectively to the various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) from which things originally arise; "if that" and so forth constitutes the specific refutation.

The phrase "that which is produced by it" refers collectively to the seven entities. First, regarding the refutation based on light, starting with "as when the sun shines," it means that this space, by means of the sun...
Since the illumination is produced by the sun, if this light now pervades the ten directions, then the ten directions should collectively constitute a single solar disc.
If that were so, why would one still see a distinct, circular sun in the sky? If there were another circular sun, its light should likewise be circular;
yet this light is not circular. Furthermore, if the light pervades while the sun does not, then it is not [the sun's light].
This light is produced by the sun. Furthermore, if this light were produced from emptiness, then emptiness should be able to illuminate itself;
why would it depend on the sun? Moreover, since light is produced because of emptiness and emptiness is eternally abiding, light should be constantly illuminating.

Why then does it fail to emit radiance during the middle of the night or at midnight when shrouded in clouds and mist? Since light undergoes arising and ceasing, one can know with certainty that light is not [emptiness].
Śūnyatāputra, you should know that this illumination neither arises from the sun nor arises from space, yet it is not separate from space and the sun. Why is this?

Because if one were to depart from space and the sun, there would be no illumination. Of the seven characteristics previously listed, here we specifically refute only the characteristic of illumination;
the others are omitted for brevity. By analogy with illumination, the rest can be understood.
"Observing the fundamental falsity of these characteristics, there is nothing that can be pointed out or described" (up to) "...how could you again ask why they are not mutually compatible?

This section of the sutra uses the Buddha’s clarification of the seven kinds of natures and characteristics to distinguish between the real and the false, thereby rebuking the opponent’s objection as being unreasonable. First, regarding the "falsity of characteristics":

following the preceding [text], it means that observing these seven characteristics is fundamentally false. Thus, [the text] states: "Observing the fundamental falsity of these characteristics... and so forth.
This is precisely why it cannot be pointed out or explained as being free from difficulty.

It is like demanding that one refute and examine the irrationality [of the claim] that the various marks are fundamentally false, like flowers in the sky; once they are known to be false, how can one interrogate them regarding the meaning of their mutual suppression and extinction?
Your interrogation of their mutual suppression and extinction is like demanding that flowers in the sky further produce fruits in the sky, and then speaking of them...
To seek delusion upon delusion is what is meant here; the current text appears inverted, but by reversing its phrasing, the meaning becomes clear to the discerning reader.
"Observe the nature" (觀性) refers to the nature of the phenomena mentioned below—namely, observing that the nature of light and darkness is fundamentally the true substance (*tattva*).
This nature is precisely the true nature of all dharmas (*dharmatā*), for it is the very essence of the quiescence of all dharmas.

The nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is the Tathāgatagarbha; it is the wondrously enlightened, luminous mind. Since there is no phenomenon outside of this mind, it is said to be "only the wondrously enlightened, luminous mind.
This wondrously enlightened, luminous mind is fundamentally neither water nor fire. "Fundamentally" refers to its original meaning.

To say it is "fundamentally neither water nor fire" means that while the wondrously enlightened, luminous mind is profoundly still and without trace, the principle of its inherent nature is not non-existent.

Yet these are fundamentally not the delusive appearances of water or fire; although their nature is the true reality, they manifest according to conditions and appear according to karma, and are thus delusive rather than real.
Therefore, the wondrous mind is fundamentally not delusive. Since the fundamental mind is not delusive, why do you further ask how [delusion and reality] can be mutually exclusive?
The preceding analogy of space is extremely clear; there must be no doubt about this. However...

If one contemplates the intent of this section of the sutra, it immediately follows the preceding metaphor of emptiness by concluding with the wondrous mind and addressing Pūrṇa’s critical questioning;
however, it is not a word that directly applies the dharma-illustration. This is because the application of the dharma-illustration is naturally seen in the subsequent passage.
"The truly wondrous, sublime awakening and clarity are also like this" (up to) "revolving in delusion and falsehood, with nothing to rely upon.
This section of the sutra takes up the preceding analogy of the Dharma to the principle that space does not reject forms, thereby clarifying that delusive appearances have no basis.

From "The truly wondrous... onwards, the Dharma corresponds to "the truly wondrous, sublime awakening and clarity," which corresponds to the aforementioned "empty space"; from "you" onwards, it corresponds to [the subsequent text].
"The various characteristics are manifested, each one illuminating itself" refers to sentient beings each individually illuminating [their own nature].
This is equivalent to the meaning of the preceding sentence: "If you take emptiness as the illumination, then there is the vision of emptiness.

"Each one manifests" refers to the characteristics of earth, water, fire, and wind appearing individually within the state of wondrous enlightenment according to each person. The repetition of "each one" emphasizes their individuality.
"Each separately" means that when sentient beings each individually manifest the seven great elements, they appear respectively within the wondrous enlightenment;
this is precisely what was previously called "manifesting according to karma. "Together manifesting" means "together" is synonymous with "simultaneously";
for example, if all sentient beings in the entire earth were to simultaneously manifest various phenomena, they would [appear] simultaneously within wondrous enlightenment.

"Manifesting according to [conditions]"—how is this? Below, the meaning of simultaneous manifestation is investigated and explained through three analogies: first, the analogy of the sun and its reflection.

This means that although there is only one great sun, when it illuminates all sentient beings throughout the entire earth, it manifests many forms according to those many beings, just as the reflection of one sun follows two people; if there are many thousands of people, then the sun... [follows them all].
As the reflections follow the many thousands of people away from a single location, so it is with the earth-element; the water-element, fire-element, and others are all likewise.

This illustrates that between the "one" and the "many," nothing can be fixed as a standard. A single body of water serves as a metaphor for True Wondrous Enlightenment, while the sun’s reflections serve as a metaphor for the various elements.
Within the one, the many are seen; the many arise through the manifestation of the one. One cannot point to the many and call them the one, nor can one... [the sentence is incomplete in the source].
One can be divided into many, yet there is no basis for either one or many; thus, through their mutual transformation, they become empty.
Therefore it is said that "one to the east and one to the west" has no prior fixed standard, and that what manifests as one is simultaneously two—this is precisely the lack of basis for one and many.
If one can harmoniously integrate this with the *tathāgatagarbha* nature, then the wondrous functioning of the seven great elements and of one and many will likewise exist therein.

"Pūrṇa, because you use the characteristics of form and emptiness to overturn and supplant one another (up to this point), you give rise to the dust of affliction and the characteristics of the mundane world.
This section of the sutra is the Buddha’s reprimand of Pūrṇa for his mind of overturning and supplanting form and emptiness;

thus, the truth is truly obscured by the false, and the characteristics of the world become a source of toil. The Tathāgatagarbha is the true [nature of] form and emptiness, whereas overturning and supplanting them is false; it exists outside of the truth.
The non-delusory is entirely delusory; this is because, due to delusion, the true is obscured by the delusory.

Thus it is said that "the characteristics of form and emptiness contend with and usurp one another within the Tathāgatagarbha. As explained below, since the true is obscured by the delusory, the entirety of the true becomes delusory;
thus it is said that "the Tathāgatagarbha accordingly pervades as form and emptiness. Therefore, what follows below clarifies this contention.
The "fault of usurpation within" refers to the midst of the false pervasiveness of form and emptiness. Regarding wind and space, there is usurpation by means of movement and stillness;
regarding the sun and clouds, there is usurpation by means of light and darkness. The meaning of the text is still somewhat brief;

as for the phenomena of clarity and turbidity, or haze and reflection mentioned in the preceding passage, the world is bewildered and distressed by such usurpations, and thus turns its back on the wondrous enlightenment and conforms instead to [delusion].
The characteristics of dust arise from dust; when toil is provoked, there come to be the worldly phenomena of rising and falling, birth and death, and so forth.
This clarifies the fault of the deluded.
"By means of my wondrous clarity—neither extinguished nor born" (up to) "...therefore I give rise to the wondrously enlightened nature of True Suchness."

In this section of the sutra, the Buddha employs his fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) to accord with the fundamental principle; essence and function mutually encompass one another, and principle and wisdom are co-arising.

This builds upon the previous discussion of past delusion to reveal present awakening. The phrase "I am" is the Tathāgata’s self-designation, which should be read in contrast to the word "you" in the preceding passage.

The term "wondrously luminous" (*miaoming*) corresponds to the preceding terms "form and emptiness"; thus, "wondrously luminous" should be understood as the two truths: the ultimate (*paramārtha-satya*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Observe closely that "non-arising and non-ceasing" is contrasted with "inclining toward and usurping.

To say that "wondrous clarity" accords with the *tathāgatagarbha* means that the nature of the *garbha* is the Middle Way, which is the synthesis of the ultimate and conventional truths. Furthermore, this "wondrous clarity and non-arising/non-ceasing" is the wisdom that is identical to the principle;
its accord with the *tathāgatagarbha* is the principle that is identical to wisdom—meaning the oneness of principle and wisdom.
It is like the simultaneous illumination and simultaneous stillness of essence and function. Furthermore, from "I" onwards, wisdom accords with principle;
from "as follows" onwards, principle perfects wisdom. The Tathāgatagarbha is principle, while wondrous enlightened clarity is wisdom.

Because principle perfects wisdom, it is said that the Tathāgatagarbha is solely wondrous enlightened clarity. Riding upon this wisdom that is identical to principle, one achieves perfect illumination.
The Dharma-realm is itself the Tathāgatagarbha; this refers to the wisdom that takes the principle as its vehicle returning to illuminate the principle that is itself wisdom.
However, when contemplating the meaning of this "Dharma-realm," it corresponds to the four Dharma-realms of the *Avataṃsaka*.
Therefore, the following clarifies the function of the mutual perfection of wisdom and principle; therein, "the midst" refers to the center of the nature of the treasury (Tathāgatagarbha). First:
"Immeasurable" refers to the Immovable Place of Enlightenment (*acalā-bodhimanda*) pervading the worlds of the ten directions;

that "the immeasurable becomes one" is not explicitly revealed in the text, so I shall now supplement it: as in the *Unlimited Meanings Sūtra*, everything returns entirely to the One Samādhi—meaning that the One encompasses all, and all tends toward the One.
"The small manifests the large" refers to the three phrases following "the body contains... [in the verse].
This refers to the characteristic [of the container and the contained]. Within the text, the characteristic of the large containing the small is also omitted;

this is because the phenomenon of the large containing the small is easy to understand, and thus it is treated briefly. Furthermore, the two phrases following "the body contains" refer to the manifestation of the support within the primary [retribution]:

the body is the primary retribution (*pratyaya-vedanīya*), while the ten directions of empty space are the environmental retribution (*bhājana-loka*). Thus, this "body" refers to the manifest physical body (*rūpa-kāya*) that is capable of containing [all things].
The emptiness of the ten directions cannot be pointed out as being the Dharma-body; yet if the Dharma-body contains this void, why need it be so described?

It is simply because my six-foot body is itself capable of containing the ten voids—this constitutes an inconceivable realm, such as the single room of Vimalakīrti that accommodates many seats, or the lands manifested within a mote of dust in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

"The jeweled king realm appearing at the tip of a single hair" refers precisely to this meaning: "a single hair" is the primary realm (*sādhana-bhūta-kṣetra*), while "the jeweled king realm" is the supporting realm (*āśraya-bhūta-kṣetra*).
This indicates that the Buddha taught that at the tip of a single hair, the Buddha’s three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system appears;
it is like the small containing the large. The following line, "seated upon a mote of dust," refers to the primary realm appearing within the supporting realm.
"A single mote of dust" refers to the basis; "turning the wheel of Dharma" is spoken in reference to the Buddha and pertains to the correct [teaching].
A single mote of dust is the smallest, while the Great Wheel of Dharma is the greatest—this is precisely the meaning of "breaking open a single atom to reveal a great thousand-fold scripture.
The first four lines clarify the wondrous function inherent in the essence (*tattva*); the subsequent four lines demonstrate that wondrous function.

The mutual communication [of this teaching] states: "The World-Honored One is fully endowed with the inconceivable wondrous function of principle and wisdom that accords with the nature, which manifests before us;
yet all marks of phenomena—whether one or many, large or small, limited or measured—are simultaneously extinguished. They merge and harmonize within the awakened nature.
Therefore, each and every manifestation is termed the wondrously enlightened, luminous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). 'True Suchness' refers to profound stillness and tranquility."
Although it is said that wondrous functions arise in profusion, the essence of True Suchness (tathatā), which is profoundly still and tranquil, has never once moved;
this clarifies the achievement of the awakened one. From the beginning of the first fascicle, where the two kinds of fundamental natures were first set forth, we have now reached the second:
the fundamentally pure essence of Bodhi and Nirvana. Why is this? If the manifestation of principle were not yet exhaustive—
Thus, since Bodhi and Nirvana have not yet reached ultimate fulfillment, it is only upon reaching this point that the second fundamental meaning previously mentioned is completed.
Now, having manifested that the principle is perfect, I shall further summarize and indicate the essential pivot of the wondrous principle of the Three Truths by arranging them into three sections.
Furthermore, regarding the points where the text transitions, the underlying meaning cannot be separated; this is precisely what is called the "Three [Truths]."
Without departing from the one, they do not merge; thus, perfect interfusion does not obstruct sequential arrangement, and sequential arrangement does not obstruct perfect interfusion.

Since both the words and their meaning are wondrous, this is reiterated as a concluding clarification, for there is indeed a profound significance in the wondrous purport of the gate of perfect principle.
"Yet the Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally the wondrous, perfect, and complete mind... (up to) it is neither permanence, nor bliss, nor self, nor purity.

This section of the sutra concludes by using the meaning of "non-existence" (*na*) to reveal that the ultimate truth is not exhausted by mundane or supramundane phenomena, as all are without marks (*animitta*).
The reason for first designating the Tathāgatagarbha-mind is that this Garbha-mind is...

Because it is the essence of the Middle Way, its wondrous nature is the meaning of the True Truth (*satyārtha*). Since the True is so profound that it transcends all things, everything is said to be "not.

Because the two truths—the Middle and the Conventional—proceed from the True, when the True Truth is manifest, the other two truths are concealed; thus, they are swept away until not even a speck of dust remains.

Nevertheless, the True is not clarified apart from the Middle and the Conventional; it is simply because their concealment and manifestation are appropriate to the occasion that it is called the "Fundamental" (*mūla*).
The character "wondrous" (*miao*) belongs to the Middle [Truth] because it signifies the meaning of original permanence; thus, it can be understood that "wondrous" pertains to the True [Truth].

The meaning of the character "perfect" (*yuan*) corresponds to the conventional truth, as there is nothing not encompassed by it. Thus, this single phrase completely subsumes the Three Truths in their perfection;
since the True and the Wondrous are the fundamental reality, it is called the "fundamentally wondrous, perfect mind. As for the initial phrase "not mind," this refers to all mind-kings whatsoever.
The mental factors that belong to the mind are all non-existent; next, the five great elements that belong to form—indeed, all phenomena belonging to form—are non-existent.
Next, the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the eighteen realms are likewise non-existent.
The phrase "and so forth" merely cites the beginning and the end while skipping the middle; thus, what precedes this refers to worldly phenomena. Next, [the following] are non-existent...
Regarding the supramundane dharmas, from the beginning there are no twelve links of dependent origination; rather, there are two meanings: arising and cessation.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the first dharma of arising, and the exhaustion of ignorance is the first dharma of cessation. This applies likewise up to—and including—what lies beyond the middle:
old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are not the final dharma of arising, and the exhaustion of old age and death is not the final dharma of cessation.
Regarding the "arising and cessation of phenomena" (*dharmotpāda-nirodha*):

first, as for the phrase "clarity regarding ignorance and its exhaustion," the character "clarity" (*jñāna*) above refers to the wisdom that contemplates dependent origination, while the character "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*) signifies the meaning of cessation (*nirodha*). Above the meaning of "exhaustion," there is also the character "clarity," which refers to the wisdom of cessation.
Next, regarding the "Four Truths"—suffering, origin, cessation, and the path—their four meanings have been explained previously.

Next, "not attained through wisdom" means that wisdom refers to the wisdom of the śrāvakas capable of contemplating the Four Noble Truths, while attainment refers to the principle realized by the śrāvakas.
Next, "not [attained through] the six perfections": first, *dāna*, translated as "generosity";
second, *śīla*, translated as "the general name for the precepts that extinguish evil"; third, *vīrya*, translated as "diligence"; fourth, *kṣānti*...
"Kṣānti" is translated as "patience"; "dhyāna" is translated as "meditative concentration"; "prajñā" is translated as "wisdom";

and "pāramitā" is translated as "reaching the other shore. Although the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) and the pāramitās are listed separately, this is because the six perfections possess two aspects:
those that are ultimate and those that are not. However, it is only when they are ultimate that they are truly called "reaching the other shore."
Because it pertains to the other shore, it is explained in sections. "Thus, even unto" refers to the supramundane dharmas: the three vehicles and one vehicle;
the teachings, principles, practices, and fruits; the one hundred and eight samādhis; and the eighty thousand dhāraṇīs.

Since the number of names and categories is so vast that they cannot be fully recounted, [the text] leaps over them to speak of the Buddha’s ten titles and the Great Nirvāṇa—eternal, blissful, self, and pure.
How much less so for those below them? This refers to the period prior to the kalpa of emptiness (*śūnyakalpa*), when not even a single character existed.
It is not that "Tad" (怛) is inferior; rather, it is the designation used to exclude the Buddha’s capacity for realization.

*Tathāgata* (怛闥阿竭) is translated as "Tathāgata" (如來); *Arhat* (阿羅訶) is translated as "Worthy of Offerings" (應供); *Samyaksaṃbuddha* (三耶三菩), in its full form, is *Samyaksambuddha* (三藐三菩陀), which is translated as [Perfectly Enlightened One].
"Samyaksaṃbuddha" (the Perfectly Awakened One) is the third of the ten epithets of a Buddha; although three are cited here, they do not exhaustively represent all ten.
"Mahāparinirvāṇa" (Great Parinirvāṇa) refers to the dharma that is realized, as explained previously.

Here, it is designated as the Nirvāṇa specifically realized by the Tathāgata himself, distinguished from the Nirvāṇa of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; therefore, the prefix "Great" (*mahā*) is added. Nirvāṇa is the eternal essence.
Bliss, self, permanence, and purity are the four virtues of nirvāṇa. Immortality is called permanence; the absence of suffering is called bliss;
possessing the eight masteries is called self; and being untainted is called purity. These are explained in detail as set forth in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
"Because these are both neither mundane nor supramundane... (up to) they are simultaneously permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding discussion by concluding and manifesting the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) through the meaning of "simultaneous identity" (*ji*).

It does so because it can be both "neither" and "identical. The phrase "because these are both neither... serves to conclude the preceding argument while generating the intent for what follows; it refers precisely to this "because."
A "character" (*zi*) is a term that transcends the written word; it is by means of citing what is not [the literal] that one can then immediately realize the meaning within the text.
Although the text may seem to pass over, the meaning does not cease. From this, the two meanings appear distinct yet are not divided; they appear severed yet are not cut off.

Like interlocking rings, they encompass and integrate both text and meaning, both of which are wondrous. There is an air of silent realization and mental penetration; to divine and clarify this is to preserve it.
Regarding the phrase "the primordial luminosity and wondrous mind": when the preceding passage revealed the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it spoke of the "originally wondrous and perfect mind";
now, this passage reveals the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), thus speaking of the "primordial luminosity and wondrous mind. "Primordial" (*yuan*) is identical to "original" (*ben*);

however, because "wondrous" was paired with the ultimate in the previous section, it was first called "originally wondrous," whereas here, because "luminous" is paired with the conventional, it is first called "primordial luminosity. This is the natural sequence of the scripture; it is not a matter of personal preference.

The commentator’s forced correlation follows each term according to its original truth. As for the second half of the verse, which says "the mind is wondrous," the two characters "mind" (xīn) and "wondrous" (miào) encompass both the Middle Truth and the True Truth;
furthermore, the character "originally" (yuán) above also derives from the meaning of the Middle.
Since the three truths are mutually fused, the Middle and True truths here follow the Conventional; thus, when establishing all phenomena, it is the Conventional Truth.

Because the other two truths are manifested through the concealment [of the middle], all phenomena are simultaneously revealed; yet this revelation of the conventional does not depart from the Middle Truth.
It is simply that concealment and manifestation are applied as appropriate. This single phrase alone fully encompasses the three truths. Since the conventional is made manifest, it is said:
"The mind is fundamentally luminous and wondrous; what is one conventional is all conventional. This essential point likewise originates from the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Because it is the essence, its name is first set forth. "That which is" means that which is so by virtue of not being [anything else] yet being [this].
What is called "not all appearances" is precisely "all phenomena. Thus, every blade of grass and every thread is the Tathāgatagarbha, perfectly encompassed without exception;
therefore, it is termed the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). All other categories of phenomena are to be understood in detail as previously explained.
"Because these are both identical with the mundane and the supramundane" (up to) "separate from identity and separate from non-identity; they are neither identical nor non-identical.

This section of the sutra follows the preceding passage by doubly negating and doubly illuminating to perfectly return to the essence of the treasury, thereby concluding and manifesting the Middle Way, the First Noble Truth.
The phrase "because these are both identical with" also serves to conclude the previous discussion and introduce what follows.

Regarding the meaning of the characters, they are as explained previously. One should carefully contemplate the word "both" (*jù*) and understand that it encompasses both [aspects] together; it does not mean merely returning to a single middle way.

Though the text is concise, its meaning is complete, and through this intended meaning, one can realize the wondrously luminous source of the mind. Here, "wondrously luminous" refers to the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional;
the character "mind" (*xīn*) broadly indicates the two minds of the ultimate and the conventional; and "source" (*yuán*) refers to the fundamental basis, which takes the Middle Way as its essence.
Because it is the source of the two minds, it is called the "wondrously luminous fundamental mind.
"Dual departure" refers to dual negation (*śamatha*), and "dual affirmation" refers to dual illumination (*vipaśyanā*). Negation is the intent of withdrawal; illumination is the intent of bestowal.
This phrase, "is yet not," is concise and somewhat obscure, appearing as if it were explained entirely from the side of "is. Now, by refining the phrasing, it becomes clear. For the preceding text...
To say that "is" is precisely in contrast to "is not," the former phrase functions as a negation of correspondence, while this present phrase functions as an affirmation;

thus, "is" and "is not" together constitute the intended meaning. This is because the Middle Way is revealed through both simultaneous negation and simultaneous illumination—negation and illumination occurring at once, wherein the one is the all.
Thus, every single form and every single fragrance is nothing other than [the Middle Way].

The Middle Way is precisely this meaning. In manifesting the Middle, the various dharmas are not explicitly mentioned because, as previously stated, "non-being" (non-existence) already merges [into the Middle], and once merged, it naturally belongs to the Middle;
thus, there is no need to state it again, but rather its meaning of merging is simply indicated.
No other literary skill or expedient means surpasses that of this sutra.
"How can the sentient beings of the three realms of existence in the world (up to) use worldly language to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision?
This section of the sutra concludes the exposition of the perfect principle by the World-Honored One;

it is a reprimand directed at ordinary and Hinayana practitioners who, with their biased minds, desire to fathom the Buddha-vehicle, yet are unable to reach its depths. The two characters "how can" (*jiānhé*) serve as words of reproach. "The world, the three realms of existence... [End of excerpt].

"Existence" (*bhava*) carries the meaning of "attachment"; that is, the three realms—desire, form, and formlessness—each attach to their own respective realms and traces, and are thus called the "three existences.
The Śrāvaka is the noble one of the four fruits of the Lesser Vehicle; the Pratyekabuddha is the Middle Vehicle.

Having already severed the active afflictions (*kleśa*), they further invade the residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*); thus, they are superior to the Śrāvaka and inferior to the Bodhisattva, and are therefore called "middle."
Because these two types of practitioners have already transcended the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), they are called "world-transcending.

The World-Honored One, following the preceding excellence and perfection of the revealed principle, temporarily employs this to reprove those of the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha* vehicles, who each attempt to fathom the unsurpassed *bodhi* of the Tathāgata with their own narrow and inferior minds of knowledge—just as if one were to try to burn Mount Sumeru with a firefly’s glow; in the end, it is impossible.
To "adhere" means the unsurpassed *bodhi*, which is the perfectly realized principle (*pariniṣpanna-tattva*) revealed previously.
To "use worldly language" refers to the aforementioned discourses on causes and conditions, spontaneity, harmony and disharmony, and so forth;
to claim that by using such language one can enter the Buddha’s wisdom and vision is impossible. The Buddha’s knowledge and vision is the knowledge directed toward sentient beings.
To see and yet say that sentient beings lack knowledge is an attachment to non-knowledge; to have knowledge and yet lack seeing is an attachment to seeing.

Thus, all worldly language is the knowledge and vision of sentient beings. Even the knowledge and vision of the two vehicles—which, though superior to that of sentient beings, are still far from the Buddha—is an attachment to emptiness.
The knowledge and vision of Bodhisattvas likewise has not yet exhausted the ultimate principle of truth. When compared to the Buddha, those of the nine dharma-realms are all alike.
What is called the knowledge and vision of sentient beings is not the knowledge and vision of a Buddha. The knowledge and vision of a Buddha is that which is personally realized;

it is not shared with the three vehicles. Because it is knowledge, it is non-knowledge; because it is non-knowledge, it is knowledge-vision; because it is knowledge-vision, it is non-vision; because it is non-vision, it is vision.
Being non-knowing yet having nothing unknown, and non-seeing yet having nothing unseen, it is ultimately perfect and absolute—this is what is called a Buddha.
Regarding "knowledge and vision": as the Fifth Sūtra says, "To establish knowledge within knowledge and vision is the root of ignorance;
to see no seeing within knowledge and vision is precisely nirvāṇa, the untainted, true purity. This is the meaning of the present passage.

For example, [the passage from] "the *qin*, *se*, *konghou*, and *pipa*" (up to) "cherishing the Hīnayāna and being content with what is little" constitutes a section of the sutra where the World-Honored One, following the preceding metaphors, clarifies that while ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle are fully endowed with the wondrous mind, they alone lack wondrous wisdom;
thus, they are ultimately unable to manifest its function. The *qin*, *se*, and so forth serve as metaphors for ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle.

The subtle voice of the bodhisattvas of shallow practice is likened to a wondrous mind, and their subtle instruction is likened to wondrous wisdom—just as lutes and harps inherently possess the pure resonance of the *gong* and *shang* notes, yet if there are no skillful fingers to pluck them, those pure resonances of *gong* and *shang* can never be produced.
You and those of lower capacities are like the lutes and other instruments described above; it is as when I press my fingers [upon them].
Regarding the "Ocean-Seal Radiance," those who possess the subtle finger will, upon the slightest movement of mind, find worldly afflictions arising first;
those who lack the subtle finger, the Buddha says, possess the precious, awakened true mind, which is perfectly complete in every person, just as it is in me.
