Because I possess this subtle wisdom, I am able to bring wisdom into accord with principle so that its wondrous function manifests before us—just as previously described, where one becomes the immeasurable and the immeasurable becomes one.
This refers to such phenomena as the small appearing large within a measure of one *cun*, or the large appearing small within a measure of one *cun*.

Therefore, it is said that the "Ocean-Seal Emitting Light" (Haiyin faguang) upon pressing a finger refers to the "wondrous finger. The Ocean-Seal Emitting Light is a metaphor for the Buddha’s wondrous function (*miao-yong*).

This is a case of a metaphor within a metaphor; it means that when I press a single finger, the wondrous sounds all issue forth—the *gong* and *shang* notes, the clear and the turbid, the five [notes].
The resonance is perfectly complete, like that great ocean, serene and still, with all things arrayed therein in brilliant clarity.

Here, rather than speaking of "wondrous sound," it speaks of the "Emanation of Light from the Ocean-Seal" (Sāgaramudrā-prabhāsa) to clarify the meaning by emphasizing the analogy once more. The analogy of the Emanation of Light from the Ocean-Seal is explained in detail in such scriptures as the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Nirvāṇa*, and the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*.
The phrase "if you momentarily raise your mind" clarifies that there is no wondrous wisdom [inherent in the mind]; thus, it is said "momentarily."
At that time, when the mind is stirred, the four propositions and hundred negations cannot escape the threshold of right and wrong;
hence it is said, "Dust and toil arise first because one does not descend [into the source]," which is precisely a word of exhortation regarding one's own deficiencies.

The preceding section, in which the Buddha’s response to the second question—concerning the difficulty of grasping characteristics while seeking the nature—is concluded. Hereafter, Pūrṇa again proceeds from the second answer.

In the middle [section], he raises doubts and difficulties; the World-Honored One then clarifies them through the analogy of fearing one's own head, thereby fully resolving the false notion of a causeless beginning.
This completes the remaining points within the second question. The intent behind the *Vaipulya* (fangdeng) critiques and rebukes can now be understood throughout this sutra.
Pūrṇa said: "I and the Tathāgata... [until] ...we have obscured our own wondrous clarity and thus suffered this immersion.
This section of the sutra has Pūrṇa taking up the previous point regarding the perfection of the true mind to further inquire about the cause of delusion. The phrase "I and...
directly takes up the preceding meaning to set forth the basis of the difficulty; "while I... describes how he himself encountered delusion.
The ultimate limit of awakening can be understood through the text; "the Sage Vehicle" refers to the Buddha Vehicle.

This means that although one has now encountered the Buddha Vehicle, one has not yet reached the profound depths of the Buddha Way. The passage beginning with "World-Honored One" is precisely the phrasing used to raise this objection:
"If this true mind is perfectly complete in every person, why is it that only the World-Honored One has extinguished all delusions and uniquely realized wondrous permanence?"
"For what reason do all sentient beings have delusion? From where does this delusion arise, whereby they obscure their own wondrous clarity and undergo this drowning in samsara?
The Buddha told Pūrṇa: "Although you have removed your doubts... [up to] ...this person's mind is deranged, and there is no other cause."
This section of the sutra is the World-Honored One’s response to the preceding false claim of causelessness by means of a worldly analogy.
First, he rebukes Pūrṇa for his delusions not yet being exhausted and his understanding not yet being profound;
thus, he employs a shallow worldly matter as a metaphor for the deep truth, so that it may be easily understood. *Yajñadatta* is translated as "Sacrifice-Granted" (Cishou).
Because he prayed at a shrine for the sake of obtaining an heir, this man suddenly washed his hair and face at dawn and looked into a mirror;

mistaking the reflection for the true self, he blamed himself for not seeing his own head and face. Suspecting it was some monstrous *chimei* (mountain-demon), he suddenly ran about wildly without cause.
By analogy, such groundless delusions are called "mountain-monsters" (*shan-yi*). "Mountain" (*shan*) is translated as "monster" (*guai*).
The Buddha then examined Purna’s mind, instructing him to carefully investigate and realize that the mind and consciousness are known to be delusions without cause or origin.
Purna answered according to the facts, saying, "Madness has no other source. Once it was known that madness has no cause, he understood that delusion is likewise of this nature.
The Buddha said: "Wondrous enlightenment is perfectly luminous; it is fundamentally perfect, round, and wondrous" (up to) "...though the Buddhas may manifest it, they are still unable to turn back.

This section of the sutra shows that the World-Honored One, by joining the deluded with the mad, directly reveals that there is no cause [for this state], and that one merely passes through long kalpas in delusion without returning.
Regarding the words "The Buddha said," he first points to the True which is fundamentally without delusion, referring to this essence of wondrous enlightenment.
The primordial perfection of luminous wondrousness is like the original head of Daṛadatta; it is inherently so from the very beginning.
Since it is stated below that delusion is causeless, this means that the true mind has no delusion, and delusion arises spontaneously from itself—how could there be a cause?

If there were a cause, it would not be called "delusion arising spontaneously. From the phrase "From among all" onwards, it points to delusion arising spontaneously from itself, meaning it proceeds from all manner of delusions.
These states arise through successive mutual causation; this "causation by mutual dependence" is not the cause of a truly existent cause.

Rather, it is the arising of delusion based upon delusion, like a creeping vine trailing from one tendril to another, accumulating confusion from confusion as one passes through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust. It is like the case of Pūrṇa, who ran about in madness for no reason;
how could there be any causal conditions? Thus, the beginningless extension of delusion is just like this: through the prolongation of delusion, vast kalpas are traversed.

Up to the present day, although the Buddha has revealed that the true nature is fundamentally without delusion, sentient beings—because their defilement by delusion is so profound—are still unable to turn back.
Such causes of delusion arise from delusion itself; since there is not even a single thing born, what is there to be extinguished?

This section of the sutra follows upon the preceding to clarify that delusion arises from a false cause; if one realizes that the deluded consciousness has no true cause, then all delusions will naturally subside.
For the deluded, delusion exists because of further delusion, and this "delusion" is itself the state of being deluded.

This delusion follows from the accumulation of delusion upon delusion mentioned above. The first phrase, "the cause of such initial delusion," specifically refers to the delusion spanning kalpas of dust mentioned in the preceding text.

This means that if this cause of delusion is itself due to delusion, it has no connection with the true mind; if one realizes that delusion is without cause, then the false has nothing upon which to rely.
Since delusion serves as the basis for the false, once that basis—delusion—is absent, the false that depends upon it naturally subsides.
When both delusion and the false have subsided, the characteristic of arising cannot be found; what, then, would there be to extinguish? What is there to be extinguished?
Once extinction has been extinguished, quiescent extinction (nirvāṇa) manifests before one.
One who attains Bodhi is like a person who has awakened; since the nature of delusion is thus, by what cause could it remain?

In this section of the sutra, after the Buddha has revealed and awakened [the disciples], he shows that delusion is like a dream; once awakened, one immediately realizes that the false is causeless and the True is immovable.
This means that those who have attained awakening to Bodhi are like people who have already woken from sleep and are recounting the events of their dreams.
Although they clearly understand the dream-events as false, there is certainly no causal basis for taking the dream-objects as real.

Because the whole body is non-existent, it is like the previous example of the heavy burden; the subsequent lines regarding "running mad in a dream" are antithetical, stating that there is no cause for such madness.
Or, if one's madness should suddenly cease, the head remains where it was on the shoulder, never having shifted by even a hair’s breadth.
This demonstrates that what is not obtained from without is precisely the original head, which is inherently unmoving.
If the head does not move, one knows that madness and fear are merely delusions emerging from it; even if the madness has not yet ceased, how could the original head ever be lost?
It has never moved at all. One can thus know with certainty that the true mind is unmoving, while delusion arises spontaneously.
When delusion suddenly ceases, the true mind is likewise not obtained from without. Even if its delusions have not yet been extinguished, how could its true mind ever be lost?
The concluding response to the original question regarding the loss of the "wealth" (mofu) states that the nature of delusion has no cause;
why then seek its location? If it had a location, it would be real and not delusive. Because it has no location, one thereby knows it is delusive.
"This passage of scripture shows the Buddha the method for ceasing madness;
once madness has ceased, the true mind is attained. The Buddha said to Pūrṇa:
'You need only not follow along with the various discriminations that arise from the three continuities, and the three external conditions will be severed.'"
Because these three conditions are severed, the three internal causes within you do not arise.

The "three conditions" refer to the external objects—the sensory dust—that serve as the objective conditions for the world, sentient beings, and karmic results. The "three causes" are the three types of discerning minds within you that act as the subjective perceiving faculties.
When these causes and conditions of subject and object do not arise, you will attain realization within your own mind.

The many states of madness naturally subside; "Madman of the Heart" (*Cittada*) is a skillful metaphor used to explain that through this, the causes and conditions of subject and object do not arise, and thus the deluded consciousness does not emerge.
When the fundamental ignorance is suddenly emptied—when it ceases once, everything ceases;
when it is severed once, everything is severed—it follows that this cessation is itself *bodhi*. For this mad mind, with respect to its root...
Because ignorance is spoken of, it can be extinguished; this is precisely bodhi. Bodhi is awakening (*bodha*); it is spoken of in contrast to non-awakening.

Once non-awakening is awakened to, ignorance is immediately transformed into bodhi. In a single thought-moment one returns to the Truth, and the delusions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are severed.

This is what the Chan school means by "the sound of a single *kōan* at the threshold [of the gate]: the source has always been right here. Therefore, it is said that the supremely pure and luminous mind is not...
"It is obtained from others; this is the meaning of suddenness (*tun*), for it does not rely on the cultivation and realization of three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

Therefore, how could one rely on the laborious cultivation and realization of 'ken-king' (the tough sinews and joints)? The character *ken-king* is as described in the 'Nourishing the Lord of Life' chapter of the *Zhuangzi*, in the section on the butcher carving an ox:
'The blade has never encountered the *ken-king*—the tough sinews and joints—let alone the large bones. The commentary notes: 'Ken refers to the meat between the bones.'"
"Kěn-zhuó" (the first character pronounced *qǐ* or *qìng*) refers to a knotted place; "gū" refers to large bones.

The meaning of that passage is that when Cook Ding’s skill attained divine transformation, he never found it difficult to pass through the places where bone and flesh were knotted together, let alone the large, empty spaces between the great bones.
Here, the characters are borrowed for their form rather than their meaning; now we shall simply say:
Once one has rested, what need is there for arduous toil or to cultivate and realize through subtle and minute efforts?
The phrase "ken-ki" (肯綮)—meaning "difficulties" and "subtle efforts"—is used here as an analogy.
It is like a person who, within their own clothing (*to*...), finally realizes that the divine jewel was not obtained from without.
In this section of the sutra, the Buddha again employs a parable to clarify the preceding meaning: that while delusion and awakening are inherently distinct, the wondrous mind has never been lost.
"People" represent sentient beings; "one's own clothes" represent the dharmas of the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus).

This is intended to show that the aggregates and so forth obscure the wondrous mind, which is like one's own clothing. Furthermore, because the aggregates and so forth manifest from one's own mind, they are like one's own clothes.
The parable of the tied jewel represents the wondrous mind following along; "unaware" represents being deluded;

"exposed in another land" represents the Dharmakāya transmigrating through the five paths; "having no wealth" refers to poverty; "being exposed" refers to being bare; "begging for food" represents cultivating tainted merit and goodness;
and "running about" represents dying here and being born there due to the rapidity of impermanence. Although one is poor...
The fact that the jewel is not lost is a metaphor for the fact that although one may lack the wealth of the qualities of the Dharma, the wondrous mind has never been lost.

The "wise person showing the jewel" is a metaphor for the Buddha preaching the Dharma to cause one to awaken to that mind. "Becoming wealthy from the mind" is a metaphor for realizing that the jewel of the mind brings about all the wealth of the qualities of the Dharma.

"Awakening that the jewel is not external" is a metaphor for awakening to the fact that one’s own mind is inherently and spontaneously endowed [with these qualities]. It is not [something acquired from elsewhere].
Regarding those who newly attain [realization] from the outside:

since the remaining points concerning the second question in the preceding dialogue between the Buddha and Pūrṇa have already been concluded, Ānanda now revisits the meaning of the "three conditions and three causes" from the previous text to challenge the Buddha on the fault of internal contradiction in his own prior statements.
Therefore, the World-Honored One overturns the previous [position] to reach [the conclusion].
The extensive discourse on the fear of the head clarifies that both "causality" (*hetu-pratyaya*) and "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*) are mere conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*);

it serves as a general critique of the futility of mere erudition. Having thus fully encompassed the section on the principle, the text subsequently presents Ānanda’s renewed request for the gateway to the practice of arising.
This may be seen by entering the text itself.
At that moment, Ānanda was among the great assembly... (up to)... "I have attained awakening of mind through causes and conditions.

This section of the sutra records how Ānanda, having heard the meaning of the three conditions and three causes, again raised his previous doubts regarding the apparent contradiction between the Buddha’s earlier and later statements.
Previously, Ānanda had heard the teaching on the causes and conditions for casting away the whisk; now he again heard...

The Buddha’s own explanations regarding the three causes and three conditions are internally inconsistent; therefore, I cite these passages to form an objection, proving that the previous sutra’s attempt to dismiss and clear away [the contradiction] is erroneous.
However, you have cited the texts incompletely—how could one take killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct as the "three causes and conditions"?
Killing and the like are matters within the results of karma; one should rather take the karmic fruits of sentient beings in the world as the basis.
"Because of three causes and conditions, this must be an error of the translation site and not the intention of Ānanda.
Now, you say that because the causes and conditions cease and the wild mind is stilled, Buddhahood is achieved; thus, the causes and conditions are clear and manifest.

Why, then, did the Tathāgata previously state that one should suddenly abandon causes and conditions? Furthermore, Ānanda cited his own realization, saying: 'I [attained it] through causes and conditions.'"
That we have attained awakening is truly due to the fact that Ānanda first resolved to leave the household life upon seeing the Buddha’s physical marks and signs;
it is for this reason of causal connection (*hetu-pratyaya*) that he is cited as an example.
World-Honored One, why is this principle not shared by us youths alone? (Omitted) We pray only that you will bestow great compassion and dispel our confusion.
In this section, Ānanda cites him as a witness to prove that all who enter the Way through causes and conditions must necessarily regard the sudden abandonment [of afflictions] as incorrect.
Ānanda asks: "How can it be that those who enter the Way through causes and conditions are only those young ones still in training?
Even those in this assembly today, such as the elder Maudgalyāyana, who are beyond training, have also awakened to the mind through causes and conditions."
To suddenly discard this [position] is to cite the testimony of others to prove that one must necessarily accept causes and conditions as valid.
Ānanda referred to himself as young because he was born on the night the Buddha attained enlightenment; five years after the Buddha’s enlightenment, he traveled abroad;
twelve years later, he preached the *Āgama* sūtras; and only then did he leave the household life. He had been practicing the Vaipulya teachings for eight years when [the incident occurred]. Ānanda—
Since he was approximately twenty-two or twenty-three years old, he is called "young"; since he still remained at the first fruit [of the path], he is called "one in training" (*śaikṣa*).
As for the "old brahmin," according to other sūtras and the fifth sūtra below, this refers to Maudgalyāyana and others who encountered the three Kāśyapas on the road;
having heard the Buddha’s causal conditions, they attained awakening. He is now called the "old brahmin" because a *brahmin* is...
This is a general designation for non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), referring here to the three Kāśyapas before they had returned to the Buddha;
as they were originally non-Buddhists and moreover advanced in years, they are called "old brahmins" (*vṛddha-brāhmaṇa*).

Now, [the text] below explains that Ānanda further cites the principle of "sudden abandonment of causes and conditions" to challenge the claim that this is identical to non-Buddhist views, asserting that the Buddha now teaches that *bodhi* is not obtained through causes and conditions.
This, then, would be the ultimate truth of spontaneous Buddhahood as taught by the non-Buddhist Kūṣmāṇḍa outside the city of Rājagṛha.
How, then, can one distinguish between the false and the correct? I pray that you will bestow your great compassion and dispel my confusion.
Rājagṛha is the name of a city in the kingdom of Magadha; the causes and conditions for its name "City of the King's Abode" are detailed in the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra].
The discussion of the non-Buddhist teacher Kauśṛti is found in the second fascicle of the *Jiejing* (Exegesis).
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "Just as within the city... [and so forth], until: "...the principle of dependent origination and spontaneity is exhausted therein."
In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One refutes the objection raised and, out of consideration for Ānanda’s disposition, extracts the underlying principle from amidst the mundane.
He explains that the state of madness belongs to causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), whereas the state of non-madness belongs to spontaneity (*svabhāva*).

Upon hearing Ānanda’s words, the Buddha immediately cites the case of Daḍa’s madness as an analogy to clarify his point, stating that when the causes and conditions of madness are extinguished, it ceases to exist.
The nature of madness manifests spontaneously because the conditions for spontaneity appear in contrast to it; thus, the principle of deluded perception is exhausted only through such relativity.
"Exhausted" (*jin*) carries the meaning of "ended.
Ānanda, the head of the yakṣa Rāvaṇa was originally spontaneous; [yet] why did it not remain spontaneous? It was due to causes and conditions that it was lost.
This section of the sutra records the World-Honored One’s simultaneous refutation of two positions by building upon the preceding intent.
First, regarding the six phrases beginning with "Ānanda": the first phrase names the madman; the subsequent five phrases first refute the notion of causes and conditions.
The first three of these clarify that Mahādeva’s original head never possessed even a trace of artificiality or forcefulness; therefore, it is said to be "originally so."
The two lines "If it were thus, it would not be thus" directly refute the deluded cause from which the false notion arises;
thus, the calculation of causes and conditions is destroyed. The subsequent four lines then refute "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*):

the first two lines expose the intent of that calculation by stating that the head is originally spontaneous, yet one becomes deluded due to the causes and conditions of looking into a mirror; the latter two lines likewise directly refute and destroy it.
If you reckon that there is such a thing as spontaneity (*svabhāva*), why do you not accept it as spontaneous? By relying on causes and conditions, you lose sight of spontaneity;
thus, spontaneity itself is refuted.

Fundamentally, the original head is not lost; it is only through deluded fear that [the notion of] it being lost arises. Since there has never been any change, what need is there for causes and conditions?
In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One again traces back the causes and conditions to clarify that while the original head was not lost, the madness arose from delusion;
the text is easily understood.
From "The original madness is naturally and originally present" to "The head is originally without delusion—why run about in madness? [the meaning is clear].
In this section, the World-Honored One again takes up the concept of spontaneity (*svabhāva*) to clarify that both madness and non-madness are neither self-originated;

the text is straightforward to understand. Having thus repeatedly explained in the preceding two sections that both reckonings are false, the following passage directly reveals that the place where the mad mind ceases is precisely the *bodhicitta*.
"If one awakens to the original head and recognizes that the frantic running was delusion" (up to) "the mind of arising and ceasing ceases—this too is arising and ceasing.

In this section of the sutra, the Buddha reveals that the fundamental reality is without delusion; through successive eliminations of causes and conditions, even the attainment of the *bodhicitta* is treated as a subtle fault to be guarded against.
The Buddha says: "If one awakens to the original head, which is unmoving, one recognizes that the frantic running was merely consciousness."
To falsely assert "causes and conditions" or "spontaneity" is for both to be termed false; they are all merely frivolous conceptualization (*prapañca*).
Previously, I cited only the single instance of one who, having lost his head, runs about in a frenzy to illustrate how both causes and conditions and spontaneity are but deluded reckonings.
Thus, all phenomena and dharmas are of this same nature. One must understand that the fundamental head, which is free from falsehood, serves as an analogy for the true mind.
Within the wondrous awakening of the true mind, there is fundamentally no discourse of causes and conditions or spontaneity.
Therefore, it reiterates the previous objection: once causes and conditions are severed, that is the Bodhicitta; the Bodhicitta is precisely the true, wondrously awakened mind.
As for this mind, the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished; from another perspective, it is [beyond] a thousand... [thousand things].
Contemplating this with a hundred deliberations, there is no interference whatsoever. The Bodhicitta is born; the World-Honored One has sent it forth with great reverence and care.
Such solemnity regarding the profound and wondrous principle is intended so that people shall not recklessly attempt to measure it with the limited scope of their own intellectual understanding.
Thus it is said: "The single phrase 'the Bodhicitta is born' is the same as the two phrases at the beginning [of the verse]. If one were to speak of the three conditions..."
Because it is severed, it is the bodhicitta; if there is a bodhicitta, it means that the mind of arising and ceasing arises and the mind of arising and ceasing ceases.

This, however, is merely arising and ceasing and not the bodhicitta. When one has reached the state where both cessation and arising are exhausted, it belongs to the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*).
The two characters "cessation" and "arising" refer back to the two preceding instances of arising and ceasing. Thus it is explained.
This path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*) resembles spontaneity (*svabhāva*).

If one erroneously clings to the existence of a spontaneous mind, thinking that such a spontaneous mind arises and this arising-and-ceasing mind ceases, then this too is subject to arising and ceasing and is not truly effortless.
Compared to the previous arising and ceasing of the bodhicitta, this subsequent arising and ceasing is coarser at first and subtler later; it is not the true state of effortlessness.
"Practicing the Way" refers to the practice of stilling conditioned activity; this is called the "effortless way" (*anābhoga-mārga*).
Upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), one first attains the effortless way, and upon reaching the eighth stage, one truly attains the effortless way.
This is explained according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
"That which is without arising or ceasing is called *svayambhū* (the self-existent)" [up to] "it is not something you have attained through diligent cultivation over kalpas.

This section of the sutra takes up the aforementioned nature of reality to clarify that only by being free from faults and transcending all that is non-true can it be called the dharma beyond conceptual proliferation (*aprapañca*), thereby exhorting one toward profound practice.
The first two phrases indicate the characteristic of the self-existent, as will be further illustrated below.

The preceding section illustrates that the characteristics of combination are not [inherently] combined; the following section demonstrates that the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) is itself suchness, thereby clarifying the meaning of spontaneity (*svabhāva*) mentioned above.
The phrase "the fundamental nature is not such" and the subsequent five lines employ successive negations and eliminations to distance one from faults and sever all non-being;

only then can it be called a real dharma. The various meanings and characteristics of the aforementioned natures can thus be understood. Within these negations and eliminations, the characters "not" (*fei*) and "separate" (*li*) carry the sense of elimination, meaning:
"Original nature is neither a combination nor is it original nature; that which is above is spontaneity, and that which combines is the aforementioned causes and conditions.

Furthermore, he brushes this away, saying: "Both 'combination' and 'original nature' are abandoned; one abandons that very abandonment of combination and original nature, for there is no place from which anything can be removed.
Only this phrase is called the Dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*aprapañca*). That which is free from conceptual proliferation is the Truth.
If one has not yet reached the realm of reality, even Bodhi and Nirvana remain far away; how could they be easily attained?
Were it not for deep cultivation and actual realization, one would ultimately be unable to reach them. The final phrase is precisely a warning to enter deeply.
There is no missing text above the characters "not you" (非汝); the meaning can be understood through reflection.
"Even though you may retain in memory the teachings of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions... [up to] ...drying up the river of craving so that you may attain liberation.

This section of the sutra shows how the World-Honored One, following the previous discussion on the reality of dharmas, severely rebukes those who possess much learning (bahuśruta) yet lack efficacy, thereby clarifying that through the path of meditative concentration (samādhi), one quickly attains realization.
The phrase "even though" and below constitutes the formal rebuke for the ineffectiveness of mere learning; as for the twelve divisions of the scriptures, they are all... [the various teachings].
The Tathāgata established his teachings according to the various capacities of sentient beings; as illnesses are of ten thousand different types, there is no single standard for the medicine.
Thus, the teachings comprise twelve divisions, differing in their modes of expression:

prose (*sūtra*), verse (*geya*), prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*), isolated utterances (*udāna*), unasked discourses (*nidāna*), causal narratives (*itivṛttaka*), parables (*avadāna*), past events (*jātaka*), former lives (*vaipulya*), and marvelous occurrences (*adbhutadharma*).
The treatises collectively comprise twelve names, as detailed in the thirty-third fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

It is said here that Ānanda was able to memorize and uphold not only what was taught by the single Buddha Śākyamuni, but could also universally retain the teachings of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions;
furthermore, he did not merely preserve the present, but through his extensive learning accumulated over many kalpas, he mastered the teachings of the three periods of time and the ten directions.

The pure and wondrous principles expounded within the twelve divisions of the scriptures are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; thus, one may say that the merit of their extensive learning is profound and vast.

Yet, because they have not yet reached the untainted concentration of the Path (*anāsrava-mārga-samādhi*), they are criticized for being fruitless and merely increasing frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
Nevertheless, they are able to discuss the calculations of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) regarding what is contrary or compliant with the truth.

The meaning of "transcendence" is definitive and clear; among humans, you are renowned as the foremost in erudition (*bahuśruta*), yet regarding the untainted (*anāsrava*), you have achieved no merit and thus fail to save yourself from calamity.
This is why, despite your accumulated merit and the perfuming of hearing, you could not escape the disaster of Dhanagarga.
Why wait for my words? You should omit what is redundant and clarify what is missing: if mere erudition were sufficient—
To oppose the afflictions of birth and death, calamities, and transgressions—why wait? The efficacy of my Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Divine Mantra is swift and manifest. It is said:
"As soon as my divine mantra reaches [the senses], the fire of lust is instantly extinguished. The first phrase clarifies the extinction of evil;
the second phrase clarifies the attainment of the fruit. Such is the swiftness of its power. Regarding the term "fire of lust," "fire" applies both to the dharma and as a metaphor.

In the teaching on the Dharma, sexual desire is itself fire. When the mind of sexual desire arises, fire erupts throughout the entire body, just as when the fire of lust blazes from within Śuka’s body, it is able to burn him;
therefore, it is called the "fire of lust. Within this metaphor, the mind of lust is like fire because it can burn away all roots of goodness, and thus it is likened to fire.
Now, having heard the mantra, Tāṭakā is able to extinguish her evil and give rise to goodness.
Having attained the fruit of realization through virtue, one further establishes a "forest of diligence" within the Dharma of the Tathāgata. Regarding this "forest of diligence":

when Dengga clearly recognized her own transgressions, she was able to apply herself with diligence, free from any retreat or cowardice. The word "forest" (*vana*) is spoken as a metaphor for practice;
it is not of a single kind, but is a dense collection like a forest. Because each and every practice is characterized by diligence, even the craving of desire throughout kalpas [is overcome].
The source of the river is distant and its flow long; once it has dried up, that liberation allows one to see even more clearly the efficacy of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state.
Therefore, Ānanda, although you have passed through kalpas [as described], how can you still deceive yourself by remaining attached to sights and sounds?

This section of the sutra concludes the preceding discussion on the lack of merit in mere erudition, exhorting [the practitioner] toward the profound benefit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) so that there may be no further stagnation.
Therefore, the following portion formally concludes the point regarding the lack of merit; "not inferior" (*abhyadhika*) serves as the exhortation toward meditative concentration.

The four characters "Secret, Immaculate, Subtle, and Adorned" (*guhyaka-vimala-sūkṣma-alaṃkṛta*) praise the meaning of the Dharma heard: "Secret" (*guhya*) refers to its being unfathomable, and "Immaculate" (*vimala*) refers to its being unobstructed.
"Conceivable" refers to the wondrous; "firm and indestructible" refers to the majestic.

This means that although the Dharma heard throughout kalpas truly possesses such wondrousness, the mind capable of hearing it has not yet become empty and remains stuck in outflows (*āsrava*), unable to transcend birth and death.
Therefore, it is said: "Much learning throughout kalpas is not as good as practicing the outflow-free karma for a single day. (The term "a single day" refers to the present moment.)

The first section, "Traversing Kalpas," clarifies that while the merit of extensive learning is shallow, the depth of one's realization of the Way increases; this is what is meant by the saying that "a day and a kalpa are equal.
The second section, "Far Removed from the Lowly," clarifies the various beneficial signs: it refers to being free from the two sufferings of worldly hatred and love.

Hatred pertains to enemies, while love pertains to kin; though one constantly seeks to be separated from kin and to avoid meeting enemies, such desires for rejection and acquisition can never be attained.
Thus, the five aggregates burn intensely, and birth, old age, sickness, and death preside over them; the eight sufferings are fully contained within the two characters of "hatred" and "attachment.
Now, to cultivate the untainted path (anāsrava) and eliminate these all at once—is this not a great benefit and a profound advantage?
As for the section on "Rama," it cites manifest phenomena as evidence to verify this through actual experience. As for Rama...
Throughout her successive lives, Dengga was a courtesan;

though her feelings were not shallow, she was able to dissolve her deep-seated desires accumulated over many lifetimes through the power of a divine mantra, and the power of that mantra was indeed profound.
She has now gone forth within the Dharma of the Tathāgata and is named Bhikṣuṇī Śīla; "Śīla" (Nature) refers to her habituation to lust.
Her nature is designated by the name of her habituation; although she has now left the household life, she has not changed her original name, which is a translation of "Mātangī.
When the bhikṣu saw her, he explained that "Nī" is a Sanskrit word for "woman," and "Rāhula" translates as "obscuration.
The detailed circumstances are found in the *Āgama* and *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses*, etc. Is this not the son of the Buddha?

Śuddhā (Yashodharā), translated as "Flower-Color," was the consort of the Buddha; because both the Buddha’s wife and his son had left the household life, Yaśodharā and Gopikā together awakened to their past causes.
Knowing that craving and attachment are suffering, she was now able to sever attachment in a single thought.

Through cultivation by means of the untainted (*anāsrava*), she attained supramundane noble goodness, or, as one who has emerged from the entanglements, she ascended [to the stage of Arhat]. Thus ends the section on Yaśodharā.
This refers to the entanglement of craving, or perhaps to those who have received a prediction [of enlightenment].

Yaśodharā received her prediction from the Buddha at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, being named the Tathāgata of Ten Million Radiant Marks. This is because the Vaipulya scriptures follow the precedent of including subsequent matters;

therefore, the events of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* are likewise included herein. The final two phrases clarify that the World-Honored One has already explained the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state.
With such high merit as this, I therefore urge Ānanda not to deceive himself; do not remain stagnant in mere learning, nor linger in the pursuit of sights and sounds.
These two words, "sights and sounds," implicitly include all six sense faculties. From the opening fascicle until now, the elucidation of the realm of principle (*li-fen*) is complete.
In the following text, Ānanda requests the practice based on that principle, meaning that although his understanding is perfect, it cannot be realized without practice.

Because realization follows immediately after principle, one must next request the practice. Practice means action; it is only by practicing in accordance with principle that one realizes that principle.
When Ānanda and the great assembly heard the Buddha’s instruction, [it was] for the purpose of leading all those who were submerged in darkness out of the sea of suffering.
In this section, after Ānanda has heard the preceding exposition on the perfection of principle, he is now about to request instruction on practice;
first, however, he describes his own benefit and praises the Buddha’s skillful guidance.

From "Ānanda" down to "addressed the Buddha," these are the words of the sūtra compiler describing in detail how Ānanda heard the Dharma, eliminated his doubts, and realized the principle, as set forth in the text. As for "the true reality" (*dharmatā*), it refers to...

This refers to the preceding sutra’s teaching on the perfect principle of the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*), wherein every phenomenon (*dharma*) accords with reality and is devoid of falsehood; therefore, it is called the "true aspect" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Because one awakens to this true aspect, there are no longer the coarse and heavy shadow-phenomena of external objects (*viṣaya*).

Consequently, one attains physical pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). Pliancy is a factor of dhyāna within meditative concentration (*samādhi*). According to the *Śata-dharmaka-śāstra*, pliancy is categorized as a virtuous mental factor (*kuśala-caitta*); that treatise states: [text follows].
To be free from heaviness is called "lightness"; for body and mind to be harmonious and relaxed is called "tranquility.

"Obtaining what has never been obtained before" means that because one has attained great benefit—something rarely encountered in the world—it is said that one has obtained what was previously unattained. Furthermore, the following section correctly describes the circumstances of his request for practice.
As for "weeping with grief," Ānanda grieved for himself because he had remained mired in delusion throughout kalpas; thus, his emotions were stirred within him.
The phrase "and raining tears" and "prostrating," etc., describes the standard protocol for requesting the Dharma.
The words "unsurpassed great compassion" and so forth are Ānanda’s own words of self-avowal. The two lines beginning with "unsurpassed" praise the Buddha’s virtues;

because the Buddha has fully realized the jewel of the mind and attained great mastery, he is called the "Jewel King. Because he is able to employ skillful means according to the capacities of beings...
Because it unfolds and clarifies the human mind, it is said that "it skillfully opens my heart.
Phrases such as these refer to the various paths of the meanings and words of the Dharma previously heard; thus, it is said that there are "various causes and conditions.

"Exhortation" (*tī-jǎng*)—where *tí* means to lift up and support, and *jǎng* means to encourage and admonish—is precisely the method of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). By means of such manifold approaches, it leads forth those who are submerged...
"Darkness emerges from the ocean of suffering. Here, "those who are submerged in darkness" refers to sentient beings; "submerged" signifies falling into decline, while "darkness" signifies obscurity.
Because suffering has no shore or limit, it is metaphorically likened to an ocean.
"World-Honored One, although I have now received such sounds of the Dharma... although I have obtained the great mansion, one must enter it through the gate.

This passage from the sutra describes how Ānanda, because he requested [the Buddha] to act, subsequently set forth the characteristics of the Dharma he had realized, using a metaphor to clarify that action must necessarily involve a request.
"Receiving" (*cheng*) refers to receiving and accepting; "such sounds of the Dharma" (*rúshì fǎyīn*) generally points to the preceding section on the "Section on Principle" (*lǐfēn*).
The teaching of the expressive sounds and words serves as the cause for awakening to the expressed nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Speaking of its essence, it is called the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind; speaking of its function, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Therefore, both are presented together—this is the expression "the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind of the *tathāgatagarbha*," where essence and function are like a pair of linked jade discs, perfect in every way. As for "pervading the worlds of the ten directions":
This reveals the greatness of this mind. Although the meaning of the ten directions as a great void pervading all is vast, it does not yet exhaust its full magnitude.
As the subsequent scripture states: "The void arises within the Great Enlightenment, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean.

By comparing it to this, the extent of its pervasiveness may be understood. Regarding "containing and nurturing lands": "contain" means to encompass, and "nurture" means to give birth; this refers to...
The mind not only encompasses the Dharma-realm but can also give birth to it.
Since the lands of the ten directions are governed by the Tathāgata, they are called "the lands of the Tathāgata. Regarding "pure" and so forth:

because they are not defiled or impure, they are called "pure"; because they are adorned with the seven treasures, they are called "jewel-adorned"; and thus they are the buddha-field of the King of Sublime Enlightenment.
The term "Wondrously Awakened King" (Miaojue Wang) refers to the Buddha as spoken by the Buddha; it denotes a *buddhakṣetra*.

Because the Buddha has attained ultimate realization of wondrous awakening and possesses great sovereign mastery (*vaśitā*), he is called the Wondrously Awakened King. This is an example of refined literary artistry. *Kṣetra* is a Sanskrit term;
its full form is *kṣetra-ma*, which is translated as "land" or "field. What was previously called "kingdom" (*guotu*) is now termed *kṣetra*. Within this *kṣetra*, there is... [the land].

Because Ānanda has now, by hearing the principle of the perfect interfusion of the three truths, realized the meaning of the mutual interpenetration of body and land, the text above says "containing and nurturing.
The Tathāgata further rebukes him with the following two lines;

Ānanda’s intention is to say that although he has heard the principle of the awakened mind containing and nurturing the perfect interfusion of body and land, this remains merely a matter of extensive learning. However, now...

The Buddha rebuked [the monk] for having much learning without merit, stating that he had not attained the cultivation of practice—meaning that his errors in extensive learning fell short of the untainted (*anāsrava*) perfuming and cultivation as previously explained.
Below, I shall now provide a metaphor to clarify that one must certainly request [instruction] regarding practice.
Traveling by land is called "journeying" (*lu*); a "journey" (*lu*) refers to an inn. Traveling by boat is called "mooring" (*bo*); "mooring" (*bo*) means to stop.
Since they also come to rest upon the shore, they are collectively referred to as the "guests within. Ānanda said:
"I am now like that traveler who has taken temporary lodging on a journey, drifting alone and exposed, when suddenly the Heavenly King (*Tianwang*) bestows upon me a magnificent mansion.
The *Zhou Shu* refers to the Son of Heaven as the "Heavenly King" when speaking in relation to the feudal lords. "Magnificent" (*hua*) means beautiful; it signifies a beautiful and splendid dwelling.
The "great mansion" refers collectively to the magnificent house. Ānanda said that although one may obtain a great mansion, one must enter through its gate;
if one does not find the gate, it will be difficult to ascend to the hall and enter the inner chambers.

The Heavenly King is a metaphor for the Buddha, and the magnificent house is a metaphor for the principle of the three contemplations—Wonderful, Lofty, and so forth. The profound subtlety of this principle is like a flower.
Although one may obtain [the house], the following two lines serve as a metaphor: even if one obtains this principle, there is no entry without practice;

therefore, the "great mansion" (mahāgṛha) serves as a comprehensive metaphor for the principle of the perfectly integrated contemplation of truth (*satya*), for it encompasses all without exception and provides shelter for the eighteen realms (*dhātu*).
Thus it is called a "great mansion. That which is now called the "gate" refers to what is described in the text below as "entering deeply through a single gate"; the gate is precisely...
The gate of practice is that which enables penetration, while principle is that which is penetrated; because it is both the means of penetration and the object penetrated, it is called a "gate.
As stated in the initial question of the first fascicle, the "wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* are the primary expedient means.

Here, the "great dwelling" refers to the primary expedient means for the principle of these three contemplations; as it is precisely the gate for entering into principle, it is called the "initial expedient."
What we now request to practice is precisely the initial expedient means for providing an answer.
We only pray that the Tathāgata will not abandon his great compassion... [as requested] ...that those present in this assembly may with single-minded devotion await the Buddha’s compassionate decree.

In this section, Ānanda follows up on the preceding metaphor to present his formal inquiry, thereby reversing the threefold contemplation within the aforementioned principle and requesting the fundamental path for generating the aspiration for enlightenment.
"Those who are obscured" refers to those covered by veils;

"those who are dark" refers to those lacking clarity—this indicates those who have not yet exhausted their residual habitual outflows (*vāsanā*). "To discard" means to cast off without remainder, referring to *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

Regarding those with remainder versus those without remainder: it is said that those of the Two Vehicles who have severed only view-delusions and afflictions but have not yet exhausted ignorance, and who realize *nirvāṇa*, are called "those with remainder.
World-Honored One, when ignorance is completely severed and the mind, intellect, and consciousness are transformed into the wisdom of all-knowledge, this is called "Great *Nirvāṇa*";
therein, all subtle arising and ceasing are purified until nothing remains.
The "remainder" refers to that which is without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*). As for the "path of the original arousal of the mind," *nirvāṇa without remainder* is the destination reached;
from the initial arousal of the mind until reaching that destination, all are termed the "path. Without practice, one cannot reach it;
thus, the "path" here is precisely the path of practice, directly referring to what you have requested to be explained. The term "original" (*mūla*) indicates the source.
The origin of the mind’s basis refers to relying on the fundamental to initiate cultivation; thus, "fundamental" points to the awakened mind.

This is as stated in the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* regarding the "dharma-practice of the ground of initial awakening. The two characters "initiating the mind" (faxin) refer to the "initial awakening-mind" mentioned in the subsequent text.
This sentence summarizes the discussion in terms of practice, whereas the following section reverses this to address the preceding section on principle for those in training.

Regarding the meaning of the "Three Contemplations," the phrase "requesting the subduing of former objects of attachment" is used; here, "former" (*chou*) has the sense of "nature" (*svabhāva*), referring to what has been since beginningless time.
This means that from beginningless kalpas until now, objects of attachment have been uninterrupted.

These "objects of attachment" refer precisely to the mind that discriminates and clings to the six sense-objects. The term "subduing" (*she-fu*) is synonymous with *śamatha*; "subduing" is itself cessation (*śamatha*).
Cessation of discursive clinging and the return from delusion to reality is the meaning of *śamatha*. As for "attaining *dhāraṇī*," the translation of the term *dhāraṇī* was seen previously;
it is synonymous with *samādhi*. Because it upholds all phenomena and integrates delusion into reality, it belongs to the category of *samādhi*.
"Entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" means that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is the primary truth (*paramārtha*), wherein both the real and the delusory are unified.
The simultaneous cessation of both [subject and object] belongs to the meaning of *dhyāna*. Here, these three meanings are collectively subsumed;

because the initial expedient means is being requested, the phrase "from what" is spoken to indicate from where the practice is initiated and arises. The following section, beginning with "acts thus," can be understood accordingly.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for those gathered in the assembly... [up to] ...opened the path of sublime practice of the Unsurpassed Vehicle.
This section of the sūtra records the Buddha’s acceptance of the request and his intention to demonstrate all practices, first clarifying the purpose for which he acts.

"At that time" refers to the moment when Ānanda had finished his request; although the assembly consisted of those of the three vehicles gathered together, the World-Honored One felt compassion only for [the bodhisattvas].
What are the followers of the Two Vehicles? This is said in response to those for whom the teaching is intended; because they are urgent in what they must accomplish, it is so.
Furthermore, Ānanda’s previous question was also a self-admission that those still in training (*śaikṣa*) cannot equal other vehicles; this is merely phrased according to what is most urgent.
Moreover, since those of the Bodhisattva Vehicle encourage themselves by encompassing all, why must one speak exclusively [of the Two Vehicles]? Although not... [the text here is incomplete].

Furthermore, regarding those whose mental realization is not yet pervasive and whose bodhicitta is not yet sovereign—referring to śrāvakas who have only resolved upon the enlightenment of a śrāvaka and lack the mind to deliver sentient beings—they are obstructed and unrefined within the practice of self-awakening and awakening others toward the Buddha-enlightenment;

because their objects of knowledge have not been shattered, they are not yet sovereign. Furthermore, "and for the sake of the lower" means that it is not merely [for the sake of] the specific [higher ones].
This was written out of compassion for those of the present time and even for those of future ages;

by "the age of the final dharma" (mofa), it is meant that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, there will be a millennium of the True Dharma (saddharma), a millennium of the Semblance Dharma (pratirūpaka-dharma), and ten millennia of the Final Dharma.

Now, at the very beginning of this Final Dharma period, the Tathāgata’s great compassion reaches far into this world, causing all sentient beings to resolve upon Bodhicitta and to expound the Unsurpassed Vehicle (anuttara-yāna).
The "Exquisite Path of Practice" refers to the Unsurpassed Vehicle, which is the One Vehicle.

Since there is no vehicle to be mounted above the One Vehicle, it is called the Exquisite Path of Practice; this is precisely what is taught for the commencement of the journey, taking the previously explained Perfect Fusion of the Three Contemplations as the Exquisite Path of Practice.

This section of the sutra, from "The World-Honored One proclaimed to Ānanda and the great assembly" up to "the two definitive meanings for awakening the initial mind," represents the World-Honored One’s formal response regarding the aspects of practice; he first sets forth these two meanings as the governing framework for practice.
Previously, in the first fascicle, the Buddha was about to reveal the principle and first set forth two kinds of roots as the general categories for the gate of principle.

Now, at the beginning of the exposition on practice, two definitive meanings are also set forth as the guiding principles for practice; upon careful examination, the general purport of the texts on Principle and Practice does not differ.

The present statement regarding "definitively generating the bodhicitta" and so forth should be understood as corresponding to Ānanda’s earlier inquiry concerning the relinquishing of the Hīnayāna and other matters.
As for "wondrous samādhi," this refers to the *śamatha* within the context of Principle.
The three meanings of *ma* constitute *samādhi*. Taking one to encompass the other two—where one is three and three is one—it is therefore called "wondrous.
Regarding the phrase "awakening the beginner's mind," "awakening" (*jue*) refers to the aforementioned *bodhi*, meaning the initial mind that gives rise to *bodhicitta*.
This word "initial" (*chu*) applies throughout the beginning and end of the practice gate (*xingmen*), for everything is termed "initial" in relation to [the ultimate].

Because it is taught as *primal awakening* (*mūla-bodhi*), there is originally no beginning or end; yet, because the beginning is made to accord with the primal, it appears as if there were a beginning.

Regarding the "two definitive meanings" (*dvividha-niścaya-artha*), as clarified by the principles explained in the subsequent text, "definitive" (*niścita*) refers to decisive discernment—that is, one must decisively discern.
For if one does not engage in decisive discernment, it is difficult to accomplish practice. Within the first definitive meaning, [it is] decided...
Because one must select the causal mind, one carefully examines the five layers of turbidity to eliminate the root of birth and death;
taking the perfectly湛 (zhan) and profound nature as the mind for the causal ground— this is the second point of definitive meaning, wherein one definitively discerns the root of afflictions,
thereby carefully examining the six faculties of reception so that they may flow contrary to the current of birth and death and instead follow a path of perfect penetration.
Entering deeply through the gates up to Mañjuśrī’s selection of the various sages constitutes the second matter within the section on "Definitive Determination.
One should know that these two types of definitive determination serve as the general overview for the gate of practice; scholars must understand this in advance.
This marks the enumeration, which will be explained in detail below.
"How are the two meanings of the initial mind determined? (up to) "it is impossible that there is no birth and no extinction.

This section of the sutra follows the preceding inquiry and explanation of the two meanings to clarify that the causal mind and the resultant awakening must necessarily correspond to one another, serving as the foundation for practice.
"How" introduces the general inquiry; "Ānanda," introduces the specific explanation. Within the explanation, first—
Regarding the first meaning: the three subsequent phrases of your question [beginning with] "you all" refer back to the preceding inquiry.

"Those who cultivate the Bodhisattva vehicle can know the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" means that the knowledge and vision of the Śrāvakas is partial and deficient, sinking into emptiness and stagnating in quiescence.

The Buddha’s knowledge and vision, however, integrates the ultimate and conventional truths, being perfect, central, and balanced—the three truths of emptiness, provisionality, and the middle within a single mind.
Within this, one attains what is called the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; those śrāvakas who now wish to enter it should contemplate in this way.
They should immediately establish a correct resolution by carefully examining the similarities and differences between the causal mind and the resultant awakening.

Ānanda, if one were to distinguish between the directionality of cause and effect here below—specifically, if one takes the mind of birth-and-death as the causal mind—then it would be inconsistent with the resultant awakening.
Because the further one goes, the further one strays from the goal, one should therefore exercise discernment.
For this reason, you should illuminate [the path] until, by means of this, there is no destruction or cessation from beginning to end.

This section of the sutra follows upon the preceding [section] to resolve the distinction between the signs of decay and non-decay by turning away from them, thereby causing one to examine and clarify them.
For this reason, the phrase "by this principle" (*anena arthena*) restates the preceding discourse.

"You should now directly demonstrate the signs of decay and non-decay" means that the demonstration of the signs of decay and non-decay is intended to cause one to abandon conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*) and rely upon unconditioned non-action (*asaṃskāra*). This "non-action" is as follows: [text continues].
Because they arise and perish, one first clarifies the characteristic of disintegration:

you should use right wisdom to illuminate that all conditioned and constructed phenomena, such as the various receptacle worlds, proceed from transformation and extinction; where there is construction, there is arising and perishing.
Ānanda, look closely and discern clearly: what is it that does not disintegrate? Next, he shows what does not disintegrate: namely, those things which are not constructed.
Although all things are ultimately subject to destruction, one never hears of empty space being decomposed or ruined. Why? To clarify below that it is indestructible:
because that empty space is not a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). For this reason, from beginning to end, there is no destruction of space; space has neither beginning nor end.

When we speak of "beginning" and "end" in the context of analytical discernment (*pravicaya*), it is because there is no destruction, and thus no arising or ceasing. The intent is to lead [the practitioner] to rely upon non-arising.
By performing the ritual procedure as the causal mind, one brings it into correspondence with the resultant awakening.
Thus, within your body, the solid aspect constitutes earth (and so forth), until finally, through the five stages from beginning to end, all becomes turbid and integrated.
This section of the sutra follows upon the meaning of "perishing" and "non-perishing," determining what within the body is non-perishing.
The passage beginning with "Now you... refers to people taking the four great elements as the body; it points to these four characteristics to demonstrate this:
solidity and cohesiveness are earth, moisture is water, warmth and touch are fire, and movement is wind. The human body consists of...
All things composed of earth, water, fire, and wind are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing, characterized by obstruction and entanglement.
By means of these four entanglements, your profoundly still, perfect, wondrously enlightened, and luminous mind is divided into six: it is divided into the faculty of seeing in the eye;
it is divided into the faculty of hearing in the ear; and it is divided into the faculties of sensation in the nose, tongue, and body—this being the sensation of contact.
"Awakening" (*jue*) is divided according to the faculty of thought (*manas*); because it is a discerning awareness, it belongs to the mind.

Regarding "from the beginning to the end," this is explained in terms of entering from the outside into the inside, which is why the character "enter" (*ru*) is used. Furthermore, when discussing the beginning and end in terms of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the subsequent scripture correlates the five turbidities with the five aggregates;
thus, the beginning is the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and the end is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). This is precisely...
Because the five aggregates, such as form, turbidify the wondrous mind, they are called the "five layers. This indicates their number; the following section provides an inquiry and explanation.
It asks: "What constitutes turbidity? Ānanda, it is like clear water [up to] "your fivefold turbidity is also like this."
This section of the sutra follows the preceding metaphor to clarify the characteristics of turbidity. The phrase "What constitutes turbidity?
is a question that承接 (takes up) the previous inquiry; Ānanda, the subsequent passage explains the characteristics of turbidity.

It means that just as water is inherently pure and dust is inherently obstructive—this being the intended sense—the two substances of water and earth are by their very nature (*dharmatā*) clear and turbid respectively.
Those whose natures are identical do not necessarily follow one another. Herein, the text below correctly clarifies turbidity;

the preceding passage merely explained that the two essences—clarity and turbidity—are not manifest when they have not yet harmonized. It is only through the blending of clarity and turbidity that turbidity becomes visible;
therefore, it borrows the terminology of worldly people to describe this "harmony. That is to say, suppose someone were to take dust and soil and cast it into...
Within pure water, when earth is dissolved by it, the earth loses its quality of solidity and obstruction;
when water is turbidified by earth, the water loses its appearance of clarity. Thus, the appearances of both earth and water are submerged together;
for this reason, it is called "turbidity. This is explained by way of analogy; the final two lines apply the Dharma to the case at hand, which you have pointed out.
The meaning of the difficulty encompasses all things; that is to say, the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*) of human beings are like water and soil.

Water is a metaphor for the wondrous mind (*citta*), while dust, earth, ash, and sand are metaphors for the five aggregates (*pañca skandhāḥ*). The wondrous mind is fundamentally pure and serene, whereas the five aggregates have from the beginning been clouded and obstructed.

The preceding passage’s mention of seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing refers to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ āyatanāni*); since the six sense faculties are the five aggregates, [this refers to] the aggregates and the sense bases (*skandhāyatana*).
The three realms are all collectively turbid, yet they are designated as five layers within the wondrous mind; that which is explained in the following text is precisely this.
This is the general indication of the number of turbidities, followed by their specific explanation:
"Ānanda, you see empty space pervading the worlds of the ten directions... (up to) this is the fifth layer, called the turbidity of life."

In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One follows the preceding discussion by revealing the characteristics of the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*) to clarify that birth and death are subject to discernment.
The meaning of the text is arranged into five segments. First, he demonstrates the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). "Eon" (*kalpa*) is a Sanskrit term;

in its full form it is *kalpala*, translated as "time-period. This is because the Śākya-muni Buddha’s original vow was made during a period of decline (*apakarṣa-kalpa*), and during such a declining eon, sentient beings...

The sense organs (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) have reached the ultimate state of dullness and obscurity; thus, both the subjective mind and the objective environment are turbid.

Therefore, in this passage, the "kalpa-turbidity" (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) is revealed by means of the visual faculty and empty space. In the phrase "your seeing," "seeing" refers to the visual faculty and "empty space" refers to the object;

this is explained in terms of the faculty and its object. Since it is so for one faculty, the same applies to the others; therefore, this section deals exclusively with the visual faculty and empty space.

Because both the discerning faculty (*darśana*) and emptiness (*ākāśa*) are devoid of characteristics (*animitta*), they are chaotic and indivisible. Emptiness has no substance, and the faculty of sight has no cognition;
since the sight lacks cognition, it can only reflect forms without further analysis, and is thus called "non-cognitive.

Because the faculties, objects, and deluded consciousness are simultaneously dull and obscured, it is termed the "impurity of the eon" (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). Next, following the words "your body," the text demonstrates the "impurity of views" (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).

Regarding the explanation of the "dust of the kalpa" (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) in terms of "views" (*dṛṣṭi*), the intent is to demonstrate that while the dust of the kalpa is the general context, the present text specifically clarifies the "dust" by means of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
Thus, it refers to the "dust of views" (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*) to indicate that each individual organ serves as an example for how all six organs are equally turbid.

As for the initial reference to the body, it is because all six organs are manifested in dependence upon the body; therefore, the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) is clarified first. The "body" (*kāya*) is that which is a composite aggregate (*piṇḍībhūta*).

Taking the four great elements as its substance, the following four lines—beginning with "seeing" and "hearing"—individually clarify the meaning of how the six sense objects are interwoven with the four great elements.
This means that the fundamental nature of the six faculties, such as seeing and hearing, is perfectly pervasive and unobstructed;

it is only when they are constricted and hindered by the four great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind that they lose this quality of perfect pervasion. These four great elements are inherently insentient things, yet they become [the basis for obstruction].
The wondrous nature revolves, causing the insentient to become aware; thus, the six apertures are able to discern, and the body knows pain and itchiness.
The four great elements and the six sense organs interweave their delusive appearances to form the body of a sentient being; therefore, it is called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).

Furthermore, your subsequent passage [from "you" onwards] demonstrates the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*); "recalling, cognizing, and rehearsing" refers precisely to the activity of false conceptualization.

Taken collectively, these are explained according to the three periods of time: "recollection" (*smṛti*) belongs to the past; "cognition" (*vijñāna*) is the discernment of present objects and thus belongs to the present;

and "chanting" (*lo-sung*) refers to the continuous application of mindfulness. To chant means to bind the mind to the object; to "lo" (chant) means that the conditions and the object of cognition are uninterrupted.
Because one contemplates future objects while chanting, it is called "lo-sung. Furthermore, the character *xi* (practice) possesses two meanings, the first of which is...

Regarding the "habituation of habit-energies" (*vāsanā-vāsanā*): recollection, cognition, and recitation—all three are habit-energies. Second, regarding the "habituation of perfuming" (*bhāvanā-vāsanā*):

the term "recitation" (*sūn*) refers to the continuous recitation of syllables, which is the habituation toward future objects. The intent of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Cheng weishi lun) is also the same as this.
This deluded nature arises upon the six sense-faculties; the two characters "knowledge" (*zhi*) and "vision" (*jian*) encompass the explanation of all six sense-faculties. Separation [from them]...
Those six faculties are thus deluded thoughts (vikalpa) that lack intrinsic nature. The manifestations of the appearance of these deluded thoughts appear within the six sense-objects;
apart from those six sense-objects, the deluded thoughts have no self-characteristic. Therefore it is said: "Apart from objects there are no marks;

apart from cognition there is no nature. Here, "cognition" refers to the six faculties. However, these deluded thoughts collectively belong to affliction (kleśa), arising in dependence upon affliction.

Regarding the statement that "delusive thoughts" are called *kleśa* (afflictions), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Because they are turbid and vexing phenomena that disturb the mind and spirit, and defile the true nature, they are named the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
Furthermore, in the section beginning with "Moreover, morning and evening," the fourth [point] demonstrates the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).

What is meant by "sentient beings"? The *Fajie Cidi Chumen* (The Sequential Gate to the Order of the Dharma Realm) states: "Sentient beings refers to 'self,' 'person,' 'sentient being,' and 'life-span'."
These sixteen types of views are that upon which sentient beings rely; thus, "sentient beings" here refers precisely to these.

The meaning of the present text is that the distinct inclinations of every thought-moment constitute the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), for these distinct inclinations do not transcend the sixteen views.
The phrase "ceaselessly from morning until evening" means that all sentient beings give rise to [thoughts] in every *kṣaṇa* from dawn to dusk.
Even if one extinguishes discursive thoughts without ceasing, there is nothing known or seen by others that one does not constantly feel a lingering attachment for.
Yet, how can one contend with the karmic destiny of one's actions, which perpetually migrates to other realms and lands—referring here to the five destinies?
Thus, although the physical body has not yet transmigrated according to its deeds, the force of karma shifts secretly, leaving its traces upon humanity.
"Alas! If one acts thus, though the body remains unmoving, karma shifts in secret and leaves its traces in the three miserable realms.

If this tendency is expanded and fulfilled, one's future elevation or descent can be foretold. Because cognitive views and karmic movements entwine with one another, it is called the turbidity of sentient beings.
You five lower ones, next I shall show the turbidity of life: 'Life' refers to the conjunction of consciousness, breath, and warmth."
To maintain [the continuity of] life is to remain undivided; if these three matters are dispersed, then one dies.

"You all" refers collectively to everyone—that is, all sentient beings. It means that within the six sense organs, such as seeing and hearing, the internal consciousness is fundamentally without distinction.

Because they are separated by the six objects, such as form and color, they are turned by external conditions and thus give rise to various differentiations. "Without state" (wùzhuàng) means "without form" (wúzhàng), which is to say, "without [inherent] existence."
The nature of offenses is fundamentally of one substance, yet they become differentiated through distortion; therefore, it is said that there is no offense.

Within this nature, the characters "middle" and "lower" are read with the level tone (ping sheng), signifying that within the nature of the *ālayavijñāna*, they are originally of one substance and thus mutually cognizant.

Because the functions of the six sense organs differ, they are mutually opposed. Within the nature, all is great sameness; in their functioning, they suddenly diverge. This is the relationship between sameness and difference.
In the interim, one loses the constant standard; to lose the standard means that identity and difference have no fixed rule.
At times of stillness they are identical, but at times of movement they differ. Within a single day, movement and stillness lack a constant standard;

thus, these identities and differences are interwoven such that even over a hundred years, their identity rarely coincides. Since such delusions are formed within the Way, how could they truly exist? Therefore, it is called "fate" (ming).
"Turbidity.
Ānanda, you now desire that seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition (up to) all accord with the pure and wondrous virtue of Nirvāṇa.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding teaching on the five turbidities, instructing one to select the false and rely upon the true, investigating the cause and attaining [realization].

This is indeed a profound and wondrous realization. Below, Ānanda, you shall issue the correct command to discern delusion. While the preceding text merely indicated the deluded characteristics of arising and ceasing, this present text correctly clarifies the definitive discernment.

The Buddha said: "If you wish to cause these six faculties—such as the faculty of sight—to reach a distant accord with the Tathāgata’s four virtues of nirvāṇa, you should select and eliminate the root of birth and death. As for the phrase "to reach a distant accord":
When comparing sentient beings to the Buddha, how could it stop at being as different as heaven and earth? Thus, it is said they are "distant.

The six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) are ordinary delusions, while the four meanings beginning with "constancy" (*nitya*) are the virtues of the Buddha. Since there must be a path by which ordinary delusions may accord with the virtues of the Buddha, one should select this [path].
That which is the root of birth and death is precisely the six sense organs; as the beginning of the fifth sutra states: "birth and death..."
The root of bondage is none other than your own six sense faculties; this can be verified by nothing else.

Now the Buddha reveals the path that accords with the Buddha’s virtues, which means you should select and eliminate the root of birth and death, relying instead on the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing as the causal mind.
Only by means of a cause that is non-arising and non-ceasing can one accord with a fruit that is non-arising and non-ceasing; it is like water merging with water, which alone is called "merging."

To "realize this nature that is unborn and undying, perfectly still and profound" refers to turning back the six sense-faculties from the flow of birth-and-death and desire, so that they return to their original unity—what is called "the profound entering and merging with the profound.
By unifying these six into one, it is termed "using the profound to turn back the false and extinguish birth. This "false and extinguished birth" is precisely the flow of the six sense-faculties.
The mutual revolution of the six flows, which subside and return to the awakening of the same essence, is called primordial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*).

This primordial awakening is fundamentally without arising or ceasing; taking this primordial awakening, which possesses the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing, as the mind of the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*), one then perfectly achieves the cultivation and realization of the fruition stage (*phala-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, this primordial awakening is precisely the eighth storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) in its state of profound stillness where it does not waver.

It is precisely because this consciousness is taken as the cause of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa—that flowing with the current results in the cause of saṃsāra, while flowing against the current results in the cause of nirvāṇa—that it is designated as the "causal mind.
On the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*), one points directly to the fruit of nirvāṇa;
this is merely a provisional indication of the characteristics of cause and effect from beginning to end. As for the passage below, it is explained in terms of... [the clarification].

An analogy is used to clarify the meaning of subduing and severing [delusions]: turbid water represents the six sense faculties; the character for "clear" (*chéng*) represents the turning back [of the mind] to subdue them;
the still vessel represents primordial enlightenment (*yuanjué*); and the fact that the mind is deep, still, and unmoving represents the non-functioning of the six sensory operations.

The sand and silt naturally settling until clear water appears before one represents the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions (*kèchén fánǎo*). These adventitious afflictions are precisely the two delusions of views and thought (*jiàn-sī èhuò*).
The sand and soil are metaphors for fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*); "sinking by oneself" is a metaphor for its initial subduing.
