Regarding the intent of this "initial subduing," if viewed in contrast to the subsequent meaning of "permanent severance," then this [ignorance of] views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) should be severed; how could it be merely initially subdued? To speak briefly, one should understand this through the intended meaning:
the clear water is a metaphor for primordial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*), which arises from the mind as described in the preceding section on the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).

The practice is likened to turbid water; here, the clear water represents primordial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*). The removal of the mud and the attainment of pure water represent the severing of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the realization of the wondrous mind.

As for the phrase "the manifestation of clarity" (*mingxiang*): once ignorance is severed, the darkness is transformed into clarity, and consciousness (*vijñāna*) is transformed into wisdom (*jñāna*).
When consciousness is exhausted and wisdom is perfected, the originally inherent manifestation of clarity becomes pure and refined, relying upon this wisdom.
In practice, the eight phases of enlightenment and the three bodies manifest all at once as wondrous functions;

they do not become afflictions, for all such manifestations accord with the wondrous virtue of *nirvāṇa*. This wondrous virtue is precisely what was previously described as permanence, bliss, self, and purity—this is the path of remote realization.
Thus concludes the clarification of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Regarding the second meaning: "If you insist that [the self] must reach [rebirth], who creates the karma and moistens the birth, and who is it that receives [the fruit]?

This section of the sutra follows the previous inquiry and explanation to clarify the second meaning, which is to examine who the thief of afflictions, the go-between, the agent, and the recipient truly are.
The phrase "The second meaning" cites the preceding heading and addresses you.
The following also restates the intent of the question:

"If you all truly desire to give rise to the bodhicitta, and since you are already able to turn away from the Small Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle, you must generate great vigor within the Mahāyāna. This 'vigor' refers to the subsequent phrase:
the resolute abandonment of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). These 'conditioned phenomena' refer to those false roots."
"Dust" refers to this very [defilement]. If one wishes to abandon these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), one should carefully examine their root.

If the root is removed, then all afflictions (*kleśa*) will be extinguished. This is because afflictions differ in their nature as seeds, active manifestations (*samudācāra*), and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
It is by virtue of these that all various wholesome and unwholesome karmas are produced; and karma, in turn, provides the moisture for the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

Therefore, as for who acts and who receives [the retribution], it is precisely to examine this thoroughly that we clarify: the functioning of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) is itself the receiving of retribution by the six sense organs.
Furthermore, the meaning of "fundamental" refers to what is called "co-nascent ignorance" (*sahaja-avidyā*) at the beginning of the fifth sutra;
since "co-nascent" is the meaning of "fundamental," co-nascent ignorance is the root of the fetters of birth and death (*saṃsāra-bandhana*). It is the fetter of birth and death.
"The faculties are none other than your six sense organs; they are not some other thing. The thematic thread of this scripture proceeds from this point;
students should not forget its source.
Ānanda, if you cultivate bodhi without careful observation... [down to] ...how can you subdue [the mind] and attain the rank of Tathāgata?"
In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One, following upon the previous discussion of afflictions (*kleśa*), exhorts the practitioner to necessarily discern them clearly;
for if one does not discern them, it will be difficult to enter the Way. The phrase "you practice" below follows the intent of what was stated above:

if one wishes to cultivate the Path and abandon conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), one must carefully examine the root of afflictions. This is because false sense-bases and objects (*āyatana*) constitute active manifestations (*samudācāra*); these manifestations...
From where do actions arise through perversion? This locus of perversion points directly to co-emergent ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*).
Co-emergent ignorance is precisely the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), because co-emergent ignorance is manifested through the six sense faculties.
Therefore, the subsequent section determines that the six sense faculties are the locus of perversion. If even this locus of perversion...
If one does not know how to subdue those various delusive afflictions that manifest through the sense bases and objects, one must recognize these points of inversion;
only by subduing what manifests can one subsequently attain the fruit-stage of the Tathāgata.
"Ānanda, observe those in the world who untie knots... (up to) "...they cannot transcend the vessel-world.

This section of the sutra marks the beginning where the World-Honored One cites an analogy to further clarify that the six sense organs are the locus of the knots of affliction and the fundamental cause of perversion.
From "Ānanda" onwards, he formally introduces the analogy to explain the aforementioned intent of discerning the locus of perversion.
This means that if you wish to subdue active manifestations, you must first know the locus of inversion. It is like the worldly method of untying a knot:
if one does not even know where the knot is tied, how can it be untied? If one understands the analogy, the thing being illustrated will also become clear.

Just as untying a knot requires knowing the place where the knot was tied, so too, in order to subdue the sensory faculties through the aforementioned method, one must first know the locus of inversion; this is not something achieved by descending to a lower level.
Using the example of space being without knots to clarify that conditioned phenomena possess knots, the Buddha’s intention is this:
because people take the sense organs and objects as falsely existent, there are false knots; where there are knots, there is untying. Since space is unconditioned, it has no knots;
where there are no knots, there is no untying. Therefore, he says, "I have never heard of space [having knots]," and so forth. Now, you have knots, and they must be untied.
"Excluding them" refers directly to the locus of your inverted fetters. Regarding "the six as the thieves' intermediaries":

the six external sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) are the thieves, and the six internal sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) are the intermediaries for the thieves. The six thieves are outside, but they are led in by means of these intermediaries;
just as in the world, those who commit theft must have someone to lead and direct them, these people who lead and direct are precisely [the sense-faculties].

These six sense-faculties are now like thieves and intermediaries; they are the ministers who drive and employ the mind-king, yet they instead invite external thieves to plunder the treasures of their own house.

These "household treasures" refer to the fact that the mind-king originally possesses all merit and the wealth of the Dharma, as well as *asaṃkhyeya* (Ganges-sand) inherent virtues, most of which are consumed by the six kinds of faculties and their objects;
therefore, they are metaphorically likened to the plundering of household treasures. From this point downward...

This clearly explains why the "roots" (indriya) and "fetters" (saṃyojana) are mentioned here: it reveals that the aforementioned six sense organs are illusory and their entanglements cannot be untied.
Regarding the "sentient world" (sattva-loka), this is explained in terms of the primary retribution (vipāka-phala);

that is, within the bodies of sentient beings as primary retribution, there are inherently present the four directions of spatial segmentation as well as the interpenetrating phenomena of the three periods of time; therefore, it is called the "sentient world. By means of... [the text continues].

Because the six sense organs, the four great elements, and the various phenomena of the world interpenetrate and entangle one another, one is unable to transcend the external vessel-world and its six objects;
that is to say, hearing does not go beyond sound, seeing does not transcend form, and so forth.
That the organs and their objects do not exceed one another is precisely the locus of bondage.
Ānanda, what is meant by the "world of sentient beings" (yāvat... each with twelve hundred merits)?
This section of the sutra follows upon the previous inquiry to explain the world of sentient beings, thereby clarifying the number of the meritorious functions of the six sense faculties.
The passage beginning with "Ānanda" further explains the aforementioned meaning: "world" (*loka*) refers to the process of flux and transition, while "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to spatial orientation.
This is a brief explanation of the two meanings of "world" (*loka*). From the phrase "You now," below, there is a detailed explanation according to its breadth:

the number of realms (*dhātu*) is ten, and the number of flows (*srotas*) is three. From the phrase "All these," below, it clarifies that within the bodies of sentient beings, through this spatial world, appearances are woven together to falsely constitute a world;
thus, "world" refers to trade and flux, while "realm" refers to distinct segments that occupy their respective positions and interact with one another. This concludes the enumeration of the realms.

Although the ten directions are discussed by defining them through the four cardinal points, these constitute the fixed positions; the four intermediate directions (vidiś) are derived from the cardinal ones and need not be discussed separately.

As for the zenith and nadir, they have no fixed position, nor does the center have a fixed direction. This is because the zenith can become the nadir and the nadir can become the zenith—thus they are said to have "no fixed position.
Regarding the center having "no fixed direction," it is as when one says that the center is indicated by means of the center of the east.
If one observes that looking toward the southwest results in facing north, it cannot be fixed; therefore, the numbers of the four directions must be established so they may be clearly understood.

Their interpenetration with the three periods is as follows: the "four above and three" refers to the periods interpenetrating the directions, while the "four below and three" refers to the directions interpenetrating the periods.
Because these revolve through twelve permutations, the "threefold transformation of flux" refers to the shifting interpenetration of the periods and the directions.

The transformation of the flow reaches its ultimate limit at three layers. As for this "transformation of the flow": one transforms into ten, ten transforms into a hundred, and a hundred transforms into a thousand;
in total, these encompass the beginning and the end. The beginning is twelve, and the end is twelve hundred (one thousand two hundred).
This clarifies that within the six sense faculties, each possesses a specific virtue and function totaling one thousand two hundred. Regarding what is called "merit and virtue," according to...
The meaning of the following passage is as follows: if spoken from the perspective of the sages, the functions of the six sense organs are all meritorious virtues;
their mutual interpenetration is without superiority or inferiority, and each possesses twelve hundred capacities.

If spoken from the perspective of ordinary beings, they are merely called "karmic functions" and cannot be termed "meritorious virtues. Why? Because through the six sense organs, various kinds of karma are created, as [the text continues].
The subsequent scripture states that transformed sentient beings constitute the twelve categories; how could these be called "meritorious functions"?

Therefore, they should be referred to merely as "karmic activities. Furthermore, because there is still activity and they have not yet reached emptiness, the six faculties differ in being complete or deficient, resulting in the distinctions of superiority and inferiority—namely, the one thousand two hundred and one thousand eight hundred [permutations]. However, regarding the transformations of the three preceding layers, this refers to the three... [text ends]
When each of the four directions of the world is further divided into three periods, twelve directions are formed; this constitutes the first layer.

Furthermore, within the four directions of the past, taking the eastern direction as an example: the past period possesses both the present and future; the present period possesses both the past and future;
and the future period possesses both the past and present. These nine directions, added to the fundamental single direction of the east, complete the count.
Ten are formed; this is the first instance of one transforming into ten. The same applies to the south, west, and north, thus forming forty.
With forty each for the present and the future, this forms one hundred and twenty; this is the second layer.
Furthermore, from within the forty of the past, nine are formed from each direction, and adding the fundamental one makes ten.
Thus, the forty fundamental [categories] together constitute four hundred; this is the process by which ten transform into a hundred, and a hundred transforms into a thousand.
The same applies to the present and the future, thus totaling one thousand two hundred; this is the third layer.
"Ānanda, you shall further determine the relative superiority and inferiority therein... [until] they are fully perfected with one thousand two hundred merits.
This section of the sutra follows upon the preceding discussion to definitively establish the relative superiority and inferiority of the six sense faculties;

it pre-establishes the basis for selecting the perfect faculty of penetration, and through its decisive resolution regarding completeness and deficiency, it causes them to understand the difference between that which is subject to birth and extinction and that which is neither born nor extinguished. "Ānanda," and so forth, is the general summary.

"Let it be definitively determined. "Definitively" (*ke*) means "certainly" (*que*). This is because one thereby determines superiority and inferiority. For instance, beneath the eyes, one clearly distinguishes superiority and inferiority. Within this detailed explanation, there are six parts.
First, the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) is explained; that is, the functional activity of the eye:
what is behind is dark, while what is before, above, and to the left and right is entirely bright. When looking sideways to the left and right, [the field of vision] is divided into three parts.
The second refers to dividing the front, left, right, and rear into three parts; however, because the rear lacks virtue, it is treated as only two parts.
Someone may ask: "In the Mañjuśrī-gāthā of the subsequent scripture, the four intermediate directions (intercardinal points) are also included in the description of being 'deficient by half.
Since the front two intermediate directions are bright and the rear two are dark, they are said to be deficient by half. Why, then, in the present case, are the directions subsumed [into three]?"
For this reason, they are not explained together; one should know that the following concludes the enumeration of the fundamental faculties. Next, the ear faculty is clarified:
when sounds move and are heard, the faculty of hearing seems to have proximity and distance throughout the ten directions without exception;
yet when it is silent and there is no sound, what boundary of hearing can be found? Therefore, the subsequent sutra says: "Hearing..."
There are three kinds of reality: the reality of perfection (*pariniṣpanna-tattva*), the reality of penetration (*sāmānya-tattva*), and the reality of permanence (*nitya-tattva*).

A detailed explanation will be found later; one should understand that the following concludes the enumeration of the fundamental faculties (*mūla-indriya*). As with the nose below, there are three clarifications regarding the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*):

namely, the olfactory nature of the nose, its pervasion through inhalation and exhalation, and the clarification of the nose's function by means of the movement of breath. Now, regarding the passage of inhalation and exhalation—
Regarding "the intersection and the deficiency": the "intersection" refers to the point where the incoming and outgoing breaths meet and turn back;
it is called a "deficiency" because of this insufficiency. Thus, while the two phases of inhalation and exhalation possess efficacy, the midpoint lacks virtue.

Regarding the regulation of breath, one exhalation and one inhalation constitute a single *xi* (breath). In a single day and night, a person takes exactly 13,500 such breaths.
This refers to the cessation of the breath; there must be an inhalation following every exhalation. If one exhales without inhaling, or goes forth without returning, then it is not "cessation.
Thus, when heaven and earth experience fullness and emptiness, or waning and waxing, these are simply the [movements] of heaven and earth.
As for "resting," the nose of a person is like a bellows; one should know that the fundamental root of this function is the number of virtues [associated with it].
Regarding the four luminous points beneath the tongue—the so-called "tongue-root"—it means that the nature of the tongue-root can proclaim both mundane and supramundane wisdom.
While its verbal expressions may be limited, its principle is inexhaustible; thus, the function of the tongue is preeminent. This is based on its capacity for tasting flavors.
If one knows that there is union when meeting but no inherent nature when separated, that too is inferior. One should know that this concludes the fundamental root;

as for the number of virtues, it is like the body. Below, the five faculties are clarified. The body-faculty refers to the body’s perception of touch, which is manifest when in union and absent when separated.
When separated, there is only the single state of union; how could there ever be three? By using this to verify it, [one understands] the body.
Regarding the phrase "one faculty is deficient," it should be understood that this concludes the enumeration of the fundamental faculties' virtues.

As for the subsequent six points clarifying the mental faculty (*manas*), it means that the mind is able to silently encompass the phenomena of the ten directions and the three periods of time, both mundane and supramundane, whether sacred or ordinary, without anything not being contained within it;
thus, at the very limit of the mental faculty, one should understand that this concludes the enumeration of the fundamental faculties' virtues.
"Ānanda, you now wish to go against the current of the flow of birth and death... (up to) who has attained perfect penetration and who has not?

This section of the sutra follows the preceding teaching on the six sense faculties, instructing you to discern between the perfect and the deficient, so that you may return the flow [of consciousness] by means of the perfect faculty.
Regarding the first sentence beginning with "You now": the two instances of the character *yù* (欲) mean "to desire" in the former case and "to aspire to" in the latter.
The six sense-faculties craving and relishing the flavors of the six objects are called "desire" (*kāma*). The wild rushing of the six sense-faculties is called "flow" (*ogha*).
Since this very flow of desire is the root of birth and death, it is termed the "flow of desire for birth and death" (*bhava-kāma-ogha*).

While all sentient beings go forth with the current toward birth and death, the Buddha now teaches them to go against the current; entering [the path] by reversing [the flow], they exhaustively investigate the root that causes the flow.
As for those who flow against the current toward the ground of ultimate, awakened non-arising and non-ceasing, this does not mean they enter through the six sense faculties in a haphazard manner;
rather, they must return through one specific faculty. Therefore, one should examine these six faculties to see which are complete and which are deficient, and which are shallow and which are deep.
Those that are complete are deep, while those that are deficient are shallow; thus, the ears, tongue, and mind are complete and deep, whereas the eyes and nose are [deficient].
The deficiencies and shallowness of one's faculties can be discerned through their patterns of association and separation;

by selecting those with perfect faculties (*paripūrṇendriya*) and entering deeply through a single gateway, one is able to turn back the current of all desires and reach the state of non-arising and non-extinction—this constitutes the initial resolve for the commencement of practice.
As for the "sixfold enjoyment," it refers to the seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing of those six faculties, which constitute the enjoyment of one's own mind.
"If you can awaken to the faculty of perfect penetration herein" (up to) "I shall clarify it for you so that you may advance.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding meaning, specifically instructing one to carefully discern the faculty of perfect penetration as the gateway for flowing against the current.
The phrase "If you can" and following continues the intent of the previous verification, meaning that among these six faculties, one must attain awakening to the root of perfect penetration.

When the faculties rely on this perfect faculty to turn back the stream of birth and death—the deluded consciousness of sense objects and faculties that has flowed since beginningless kalpas—one attains a state of circular penetration.

Compared with those of imperfect faculties, the difference between following [the path] and turning away from it is such that a day’s work for one with a perfect faculty exceeds a kalpa’s effort for one with an imperfect faculty; this describes their relative speed.
Their mutual opposition is thus; furthermore, the character "doubling" (*bei*) may also be understood as "increasing by doubling.

Regarding the phrase "I now conclude the count as stated above": the "six profound, perfect, and luminous" refers to the fact that if the faculties, objects, and deluded consciousnesses remain in motion, they become increasingly obscured and, though pervasive, appear limited.
If one can turn back from this motion and enter into stillness (*zhan*), then they become luminous and again perfect; for the internal nature is fundamentally still.

The clarity is divided and reflected within the six sense bases; when they are still, all six bases become clear and tranquil, hence they are called the "Six Claritys. From the words "According to your...
onwards, the Buddha correctly commands a definitive discernment among the six faculties, selecting that which is most perfect, profound, and capable of being entered.
The Buddha says he will further clarify it for them so that they may advance. "Advancing" is as described at the beginning of the sixth fascicle: "Within hearing, thus... and so forth.
"Gradually increasing" and so forth mean "progressive advancement.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions [attain] the eighteen realms up to those six faculties of cognition, all becoming pure simultaneously.

This section of the sutra follows from the preceding Buddha’s indication that the nature of all realms is universally perfect; yet, because sentient beings have inferior capacities, he causes them to make a selection in order to enter.
The intent of the following passage on the ten directions clarifies that for those with perfect capacity, every gate may be entered, as they share the same Buddha-vehicle;

therefore, it refers to the teachings of all Buddhas. Furthermore, the nature of each and every realm accords with the Truth (*tathatā*), and fundamentally there is no superiority or inferiority among them.

This was spoken for the sake of those with perfect faculties; however, as explained below, because the wisdom of those with inferior faculties is limited, they have not yet attained the wisdom of perfect, sovereign penetration within the nature of the realms.

Therefore, the Tathāgata proclaimed the relative superiority and inferiority of the six sense-faculties in this manner, so that they might enter deeply through one single, perfected faculty as their gateway, and by entering into one, [attain all].
The faculties attain non-delusion; those six cognitive faculties are simultaneously pure.
That all six faculties are termed "knowing" means that although their external functions differ, their internal nature is fundamentally pervasive, sharing a single essence of cognition.
This is what is meant by "the one is true, and thus all are true. "At one time" refers precisely to simultaneity.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how does one flow against the current [until] the six sense faculties can all be purified simultaneously?

This section of the sutra represents Ānanda’s inquiry based on the preceding discussion of flowing against the current, requesting clarification on the meaning of "entering deeply through a single gate.
Because Ānanda did not yet understand that the six faculties are externally divided yet internally unified, he doubted how entering through one could result in the purification of all six.
"Both are pure.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "You have now attained [the realization] up to the number of divisions and measures of arising, abiding, change, and ceasing.
This section of the sūtra shows the World-Honored One first judging the depth or shallowness of delusion in order to answer the questions regarding the six and the one.
The power of clear understanding has not yet overcome [the defilements]. The Buddha first clarifies the realization of the fruit for those below;

in Sanskrit this is *srotāpanna*, translated as "one who flows against the current" or "one who has entered the stream. "Against the current" (*ni*) and "entering" (*āpanna*) share the same meaning. "Stream" (*srotas*) has two meanings: first, it refers to flowing against the current of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and desire;
second, it refers to having initially entered the path of the noble ones (*ārya*). Although the expressions differ, their essential intent is one. Thus it is said.

The section on "Extinction" clarifies the extent of the abandonment of delusions: it refers to the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), wherein all the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) belonging to sentient beings within the three realms have been extinguished.
"View" (*dṛṣṭi*) refers to speculative understanding; arising from the two views of existence and non-existence, these lead to successive false understandings that fully comprise the sixty-two views.

Such speculative understandings are not correct and are collectively termed "delusions of view. One who realizes the first fruit abandons these delusions and perceives the principle; this is called [the stage of] "seeing the principle."

Regarding the phrase "afflictions abandoned through seeing" (*darśana-heya*) in the context of the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*): this specifically refers to the "seeing" of the Path of Seeing as it stands in contrast to the "cultivation" of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

As for the term "sentient world" (*sattva-loka*), it is explained in terms of the primary retribution (*upapatti-bhava*) of sentient beings, as was analyzed previously in the section on flux and transformation;

however, it still serves to clarify the afflictions of thought (*karma-kleśa*) below. This means that those who have attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) have severed only the afflictions of seeing; these [latter] afflictions are coarse.

It is easy to sever that which is floating; however, if among the six sense faculties there is the beginningless, false habitual energy accumulated since birth, this refers to the delusions of thought (*sī-huo*).
Regarding "beginningless," there are two meanings: first, the essence of delusion is beginningless.
If it truly had a beginning, it would not be called "delusive," for because it is without cause and without beginning, arising suddenly and abruptly, it is termed "beginningless."
The first two refer to the past; the number of kalpas is the ultimate limit of distance, and because it exceeds the immeasurable, it is called "beginningless.
Regarding the "empty habitual tendencies within the faculties": these arise from the greedy defilement and attachment to sense objects through the faculties;

this lack of knowledge is termed "empty habitual tendencies," which are identical to the delusive habitual energies known as "afflictions of thought" (saṃyojana-kleśa). These tendencies must be severed primarily through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). As for "cultivation": [it refers to] the path of cultivation.

This concludes the two fruits of the stage of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) and introduces the third fruit, which is also designated as the stage of cultivation. This refers to the nine stages within the three realms;
each stage possesses nine grades of afflictions of thought (kleshas), totaling eighty-one grades (nine times nine). All these are abandoned through the fruit of cultivation.
When one has completely severed these afflictions and realizes the fourth fruit, one is called an Arhat and is designated as being in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa). Why is this so?
Moreover, the following passage clarifies the great number of categories of afflictions of thought (*saṃyojana*).
Here, "the arising, abiding, and so forth within the faculties" refers to the fact that the afflictions of thought possess the four characteristics of arising, abiding, change, and cessation.

Because they possess these four characteristics and because one analyzes them moment by moment, it is said that their divisions and enumerations are numerous. "Thought" (*saṃkalpa*) means conceptualization; that is, deluded mental conceptualization.

Regarding the delusions mentioned above: those arising from *dṛṣṭi* (viewing) are called "delusions of view" (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) because they are explained from the perspective of conceptual discrimination;
now, those arising from the side of *vicāra* (reflection) are called "delusions of thought" (*bhāvanā-kleśa*), as their coarseness or subtlety can be known through reflective investigation.
Since Ānanda has only realized the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), his severance of delusions is shallow and the power of his understanding is not yet sufficient.
"Now you should observe the six sense organs before you... although the six may be dissolved, one has not yet been extinguished.

This section of the sutra follows upon the previous inquiry regarding "one" and "six," clarifying that neither "one" nor "six" is fixed; when pursued to its ultimate limit, both "one" and "six" are non-existent.
The preceding passage was intended to respond to the meaning of "one" and "six," first clarifying the initial stage of the fruit.
Because their severance of delusions was not yet profound, they had not yet clarified the meaning of the unity and multiplicity, or their opening and closing.

Since this current passage precisely and in detail elucidates the beginning and end of the one and the six, [the Buddha] first poses a counter-question: "Is it one, or is it six? When Ānanda says "If one were to say...
and below, although the World-Honored One has already asked, he does not wait for an answer but himself refutes that it is not one. Why? If one were to say it is one, how...?
Therefore, the ear does not see, the eye does not hear, the head does not tread, and the feet do not speak;
they are perfectly distinct as six. How can they be fixed? What are they? Furthermore, below this, it is explained in detail why they are not six.
Why? If these six faculties were definitively six, the Buddha asked: "I am now proclaiming the wondrous Dharma-door for you; as for your six [faculties]..."
"Which faculty comes to receive my Dharma? Ānanda replied, "I hear it with my ears. The Buddha said, "This clearly demonstrates that it is not [received by] the six [faculties]. To explain:
when you say 'you hear with your ears,' what does this have to do with the body or the mouth? If the mouth asks about the meaning, how can the body respectfully receive it?
When one faculty first perceives an object, the other faculties respond accordingly; furthermore, they mutually communicate. It is certainly not fixed to only six [faculties]. Therefore..."
The concluding summary clarifies that the indeterminate mind is neither one nor six: it is not that six conclude in one, nor is it that one concludes in six.
Finally, by way of negation, it is shown that it is neither one nor six;

that which is originally one and originally six is a dualistic, speculative statement, for in the end, it is simply not so. Is your root-organ originally one or originally six? One and six cannot be fixed.
Thus, both "one" and "six" are non-existent. Ānanda, you should know that what follows clarifies why "one" and "six" are not established, and why they emerge from "one" and "six.
Within the perfectly湛 (zhàn) and profound nature, there is fundamentally neither one nor six.

Due to the inverted and submerged state of beginningless kalpas, and through gradual decline, one falsely gives rise to the conceptualization of "one" and "six" within this perfectly湛 and profound nature. This is truly because...
Because the *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) flows against the current, the six functions are simultaneously dissolved; yet although the six are dissolved, the "one" has not yet perished.
The preceding passage already analyzed this "one" within the context of the six; the meaning of the present text seems to suggest that the six are external while the one is internal.
According to treatises such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the eighth *ālayavijñāna* is taken as this "one. [The following text...]

It is also said that originally, based on one luminous intelligence, it is divided into six harmonious unities; thus, the meaning of the "one" and the "six," as well as their internal and external aspects, can be clarified.
However, this very "one" is the locus of perversion; because of this perversion and its subsequent decline, the locus where the meanings of "one" and "six" arise can be known.
"Just as the great void of space merges with various vessels" (up to) "the six faculties of reception are also like this.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding analogy to clarify that the awakened mind, when free from thought, how could there be a division into one or six? It merges [into oneness].

The great void is an analogy for the perfectly湛 (zhan—clear and still) awakened mind; the various vessels are an analogy for the six sense-faculties. Setting aside the vessels, the following two lines [explain further].
The first six lines of the verse illustrate that while the six [sense-objects] have dissolved, the one has not yet perished;

those final five lines illustrate that within the perfectly湛 (tranquil) and awakened mind, there is fundamentally neither sameness nor difference, let alone the existence of "one" or "not one. This serves as a general illustration of the delusions regarding "one" and "six" mentioned in the preceding text.
The subsequent three lines beginning with "Then you... apply this principle through analogy (*dharma-sādharmya*), the meaning of which is as explained above.
"By means of the two aspects of light and darkness, etc., [the mind] rushes toward form through the four objects of the floating faculties.
This section of the sutra takes up the meaning of the preceding analogy to clarify that the principles of the Dharma correspond exactly with one another. First, it correlates the meaning of the eye:
"by means of light and darkness, etc. refers to how, due to the prior sensory objects, the clarity of the *zhan* (stillness) adheres to and reflects upon form; this is what is called [the faculty].

The character "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "brightness, darkness, and color etc. is intended to manifest characteristics such as high and low, above and below, and the manifest colors blue and yellow, up to the most remote and distant.

The character "form" (*ākṛti*) is used to manifest the state of mutual overlapping among brightness, darkness, and so forth; thus, the character "adhere" (*saṃśleṣa*) is employed metaphorically to convey the sense of being stained or attached.
When the essential nature of seeing reflects upon and illuminates forms and appearances, it becomes bound by form and constitutes the sense organ (*indriya*).
This term "organ" refers to the *pārvata-indriya* (the physical, floating organ), while the "original source of the organ" refers to the *paramārtha-indriya* (the ultimate sense organ).

That which is called the "pure four great elements" (*viśuddha-mahābhūta*)—the word "original" (*yuan*) here is precisely the "original of clarity" (*ming-yuan*) mentioned in the preceding text; these are the pure four great elements.

In general, all six sense organs are composed of eight factors consisting of the "agent" and the "object": namely, the four subtle elements (*tanmātra*) which are the agents, and the four gross elements (*mahābhūta*) which are the objects.
The four subtle elements refer to color, odor, taste, and tangibility; the four gross elements refer to earth, water, fire, and wind.

In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the four gross elements are cited as the objects, while in the conventional sense (*saṃvṛti*), the four subtle elements are cited as the agents. Since the four gross elements are themselves the four subtle elements, they are combined.
In brief, this is constituted by the eight factors of subject and object. Regarding the "supreme sense-faculties" (paramārtha-indriya) as the "pure four great elements" (viśuddha-mahābhūta):
this refers to taking the quintessential essence of the four great elements; that which is capable of reflecting forms with clarity and purity is called the pure four great elements.
These pure four great elements can only be seen by the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); they are not visible to the fleshly eyes of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Because it is visible, it is called the "ultimate sense organ" (*paramārtha-indriya*); furthermore, its nature of reflecting forms is also termed "ultimate.
As for the characteristics of the eye-organ, because it possesses a visible form and color, it is called the "adventitious root" (*tuccha-indriya*).
To say that "the substance of the eye is like a cluster of grapes" means that "grapes" refers to the eyeball itself; it is similar to a purple grape in appearance.
Because they are coarse and buoyant, they are called "buoyant faculties" (*ūrdhvendriya*). The faculty of the eye flows toward and grasps visible forms;
the other five follow this pattern. Furthermore, "flowing" refers to the functional capacity of the faculties; here, the subsequent sections follow the same principle as the faculties.
"Due to the mutual impact of the two aspects of movement and stillness... [until] the floating faculties and the four objects flow and rush toward dharmas.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding enumeration of the various combinations to clarify the principle of the "dividing of the tranquil" (*fen-zhan*).
Together with the previous text, it is divided into six sections; the first section has already been explained in detail, and now the present case may be applied by analogy.
This clarifies that there is no separate explanation [for the other organs]. Regarding the specific meanings within the five faculties, they are explained according to the text.
As for "movement and stillness can be known within the ear," this refers to all sounds. "Striking" means that the faculty of hearing lies dormant within;
it is called "striking" because it arises when struck by the sense-object of sound. "The sound rolls to form the faculty" means that the nature of hearing is without... [text ends]
Because the substance [of the ear] takes up the sense-object of sound to form the faculty, the newly curled leaf illustrates the appearance of the ear’s peripheral root (*bu chen gen*);
like a leaf that has withered by frost but has not yet turned significantly yellow or fallen, it is thus called "newly curled. Regarding the nose, its being open or obstructed can be known.

As for "arousing," it means that the nature of smelling has no independent substance; it is aroused by the sense-object of fragrance. Thus, when it is obstructed, the air is suppressed and does not manifest.
The "pervasive concealment" (*tongyan*) likewise belongs to the faculty of smelling, for it is able to receive odors—both fragrant and foul—to constitute the sense organ;
thus, the two downward-hanging claws signify the appearance of the nose’s peripheral root (*bu chen gen*), as the two nostril tubes resemble the shape of double hanging claws.

Regarding the tongue, "quiescence" (*tian*) refers to the still, while "transformation" (*bian*) refers to the moving; this means that when the tongue-root is in a state of stillness, the flavor of blandness is ever-present, and is therefore termed "quiescent."

When in motion, the five flavors undergo transformation; therefore, it is called "change. Both [the organ and the object] are objects of the tongue. "Intermingling" (*san*) refers to their mutual intersection:
it means that the two flavors—tranquility and change—are intermingled with the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya*) to manifest the nature of tasting (*āsvādana*).

Regarding "the faculty being formed by the gathering of flavors," "gathering" (*jiao*) has the meaning of grasping or collecting; it means that the tongue-faculty and the nature of tasting have no self-substance (*svabhāva*), as they are gathered through grasping.

Since external flavors only constitute a sense-base (*indriya*) when they are present, the "initial crescent moon" refers to the fact that on the seventeenth or eighteenth night of the lunar month, the moon is initially deficient and not yet full;
thus it is called the "initial crescent moon. The shape of the tongue is like this. When the body parts are joined, there is contact (*spraṣṭavya*);

when they are separated, there is no cognition [of contact]. Now, you speak of "separation and joining rubbing against each other"—is it possible that separation also constitutes rubbing? For if they are separated...

The combination of characteristics and forms constitutes tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*); thus, "rubbing" (*mṛśana*) refers to stroking. Consequently, stroking is a conforming touch (*anugata-spraṣṭavya*), as it conforms to the shadow, whereas obstructive touch (*pratighāta-spraṣṭavya*) constitutes the sense faculty (*indriya*).
This is because the sense faculty has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); it is formed by grasping the objects of touch to constitute the faculty.
Regarding the "drum-head" (*muraja-śīrṣa*): the drum-head is large at both ends and narrow in the middle; the skull is called the "head" (*śīrṣa*), and the body is the trunk.
Its form is like that of a drum, a six-foot body from crown to heels with a slender waist; thus it serves as a metaphor, commonly referred to as a "zhang-drum" (丈鼓).

Within this, one should understand that the mental objects (*dharmas*) are called "arising and ceasing. The character *xù* (continuity) takes the sense of the continuous succession of every thought-moment.
Through the four characteristics such as arising and ceasing, the meaning within the character *xù*—that the mind-faculty (*manas*) is signless (*animitta*)—is revealed by implication.
Because one grasps the arising and ceasing of phenomena to form the root [of perception], the "one who sees within the dark chamber" refers to the fact that the dark chamber is simply a dark room;

the person's inch-long mind is hidden within the body, and though it faces the world for a thousand li, its benefits and harms, its levelness and peril, cannot suddenly be known—this refers to the physical heart-mass as the "dark chamber.
Since this physical heart-mass is that upon which the manas (the faculty of thought) relies, it is like a person...
Being within a dark room, one can see what is outside but cannot see what is inside; thus, one does not know that others may harm oneself.
Therefore, it is likened to being in a secluded chamber; other passages can be understood accordingly.
"Ānanda, thus these six faculties arise from that awakened clarity... until they lose their essential lucidity and, adhering to delusion, emit light.
This section of the sutra concludes the preceding discussion on how the six faculties falsely manifest, losing their originally inherent clarity, and assigns blame for this deluded capacity.
It means that as shown above, the six faculties exist as false constructs within the wondrously awakened clarity.
The "clarity" of "clarity-awakening" (ming-zhi jue) refers precisely to the fault of taking this initial delusion to be clarity-awakening.
As soon as there is a capacity for clarity, distinctions between sameness and difference blaze forth, causing one to lose that originally possessed nature of pure, refined illumination.

One becomes falsely attached to the original stillness, giving rise to the six sense faculties and the "lights" of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; the word "light" (guang) here is synonymous with seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
It is considered the light manifested by the nature of consciousness.
Therefore, when you are now free from darkness and free from light (up to) neither ceasing nor arising, where can your clear awareness find its resting place?

In this section of the sutra, the Buddha demonstrates that the six sense organs mentioned in the preceding text have no intrinsic substance; they arise in dependence upon their objects and are fundamentally non-existent when separated from them.
This is because the organs exist only because of the objects; since the objects themselves lack substantial characteristics, how could the organs possibly exist?
This passage directly clarifies what was shown previously: apart from those twelve conditioned phenomena, the six dependent organs are like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.
The names of the faculties for the other [senses] can be understood from the meaning of the text.
You need only refrain from following after movement and stillness, union and separation, until these six faculties function as one another's counterparts.
This section of the sutra is the World-Honored One’s direct response to the question regarding the "one hundred and eighty-six purities.
The phrase "you merely follow" refers generally to the principle of following [the sense organs] rather than following the twelve conditioned objects (*samskrta-dharma*).

Since "conditioned" refers to phenomena characterized by arising and ceasing, the subsequent phrase "specifically pointing to one root" indicates that, among the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), [it specifically refers to the organ of hearing].
To pull out one root according to its nature is the meaning of liberation. Once one root is detached, external attachments cease and internal tendencies subside;
these fluctuations return to the source, and one thoroughly investigates this primordial ground of truth. This is the eighth consciousness, the *ālayavijñāna*.

Because the *ālayavijñāna* encompasses both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), when these fluctuations return to the source and become true, the *ālayavijñāna* itself naturally becomes untainted.
Therefore, it is called the "Primal Truth" (yuan zhen). Regarding "the source of manifestation emits its fundamental radiance":

this means that once one has subdued [the mind] and returned to the Primal Truth, reaching the state where the *ālayavijñāna* (store-consciousness) is profound and unmoving, the "radiance" refers to the luminous brilliance of this profound nature within this single faculty.

Once this fundamental radiance is emitted from within, the external attachments of the other five faculties are also completely liberated. "Complete" (*yuan*) signifies the sense of pervasiveness; it means the pervasive liberation from the attachments of all five faculties.

When one faculty is liberated, all other faculties are likewise liberated; because the internal essence is one, once the six faculties are liberated, the resulting cognition and vision do not arise from external objects.
"Cognition and vision" refers generally to the six faculties, meaning that the faculties no longer follow after objects.
To clarify that they do not follow the faculties means that this very seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing of the six faculties is the fundamental source.
Because this clarity exists, it is called "clarity";

that is to say, when the clarity of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing does not follow the transformations of the six superficial sense organs (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya-indriya*), then seeing is no longer restricted to the eye, hearing is no longer restricted to the ear, and so forth.

Therefore, the subsequent line states that [the senses] merely "rely upon the organs to manifest the fundamental clarity. If this is so, then the ears can see, the eyes can hear, and one can smell and taste through them.
It pervades all five faculties; therefore, the final two lines conclude by stating: "By this, it can be known that the six faculties function as one another.
Ānanda, do you not know that within this assembly... [up to] "...the perfect and clear cognition does not depend on mental thought"?
In this section of the sutra, the Buddha cites and clarifies the verifiable reality that [cognition] does not follow the sense organs, but rather manifests by relying upon them.
Āniruddha—the translation of his name is as explained previously—was the son of Droṇodana and the Buddha’s cousin;
the circumstances of his life appear in the Āgamas and other scriptures. Pūraṇa (translated as "Worthy and Good") was the name of a dragon king, so called because he protected through *homā*.
In the kingdom of Keta, rain and sunshine occurred according to the seasons, and the harvests were abundant; because the people were joyful and virtuous, it received this name.
"The earless who can hear" refers to the dragon's ear, which does not hear with the ear but hears with its horn. Gaṅgā is the Ganges;
its alternative translation is found in the first explanation. The "divine maiden" is the presiding river goddess, referring generally to a river deity.
The female body is often like those of the Luo Goddess or the Consort of Xiang; it is not that the nose does not perceive fragrance, but the source of this [statement] is not yet clear.
*Kauṇḍinya* is translated as "the cow-chewer" (*go-mukha*); the account of this appears in the "Chapter on Perfect Penetration.

"Different tongue" refers specifically to the cow-chewer, as his tongue is not of the true nature of a tongue, hence he is called "different tongue. *Śūnyatā* is translated as "seeing"; see the second [chapter].
At the end of the three sūtras, there is also the goddess of space. Because she presides over space, the substance of her body is like wind;

since it has movement and stillness yet lacks visible characteristics, she is likened to wind. Although she has no physical body, she is capable of perceiving touch. When touched by the Buddha’s light, the radiance reflects upon her body, causing a temporary manifestation of form and appearance.
The *nirodhasamāpatti* (attainment of cessation) is the final stage among the nine successive meditative attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*); it is so named because of its cessation.

Because it involves the two aggregates of sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), it is also called the "Cessation of Perception and Sensation Samādhi" (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*). Śrāvakas who have attained tranquility abide in this samādhi;
Mahākāśyapa’s account of this is found in the "Chapter on Perfect Penetration" (*yuan-tong zhang*), where the circumstances are explained as previously mentioned.

Regarding the phrase "the mental faculty has long been extinguished," within the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the first six consciousnesses are all extinguished, while the latter half of the seventh manas-consciousness remains.
If even consciousness is extinguished, how much more so its root? That [consciousness] is pervasive, perfect, and luminous, requiring no mental ideation;

"mental ideation" here refers precisely to the faculty of the mind (*manas*), which is the very clarity that does not follow the sense organs but manifests by relying upon them—this is the meaning of "relying on the organs for the manifestation of clarity.

This citation of the six bases serves to corroborate the preceding discussion of the mutual functioning of the six faculties, clarifying that they truly exist as a matter of present realization and faith.
This is no empty talk.
"Ānanda, if your faculties were now to be completely uprooted... they should be transformed by mindfulness into supreme awareness.
This section of the sutra follows from the preceding discussion of the complete uprooting of the six faculties to clarify the efficacy of returning to the source.

"The faculties being fully developed" refers to the meaning established previously. "Internally radiant and emitting light" below clarifies the efficacy of returning to the source. "Internal" refers to the inner mind;
it means that the original awakening of the inner mind is fundamentally luminous and emits a brilliant radiance. "Radiant" (*yìng*) refers to the warm, smooth, and bright luster of jade;
this is used as a metaphor for the state of the inner mind being brilliantly clear. Once the internal light has been emitted, externally...

When delusion does not adhere, then the peripheral objects such as form (*rūpa*) and the various vessel-worlds of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) vanish into emptiness together, like ice melting in boiling water;
this uses a metaphor to clarify the power of the perfect uprooting.

The boiling water is a metaphor for the wisdom of perfect uprooting observation, while the ice is a metaphor for the peripheral objects and all corresponding thoughts that should be perfectly uprooted—meaning these thoughts are transformed.

When those ephemeral sensory organs and the realms of the physical world, subject to arising and ceasing, largely achieve supreme awakening—this is what is called the transformation of the cognitive vision of sentient beings into the cognitive vision of a Buddha; this very mindfulness is contemplative wisdom.
"Ānanda, it is like those worldly people who gather their sights before the eyes... (up to) why would the awakened clarity not be perfectly wondrous?
This section of the sutra follows the previous analogy to clarify how the inner luminosity emits light, transforming deluded vision into the true essence.
It takes as an example those worldly people who gather what they see before their eyes; if one were to cause the seer—
When a person suddenly closes both eyes, the signs of darkness appear before them, and all the gathered forms can no longer be distinguished.
If those gathered forms were people, then their six sense organs, heads, and feet would all be indistinctly similar;

because closing the eyes prevents one from discerning external forms, they are said to be "darkened" (*anran*). Although that person’s eyes are closed, they do not see [the objects], yet they can still follow [them] with their hands.

If one rubs the head and feet from the outside of the body and can clearly distinguish the eyes, ears, mouth, and nose of the person being rubbed, then the perception of the one with eyes closed is identical to that of the one with eyes open.
If it were claimed that seeing arises by depending on external light, then seeing would cease to exist in the dark; yet if it does not depend on external [conditions], [then it must be internal].
When clarity arises spontaneously and one perceives this as true seeing, then all dark phenomena can never again obscure it.
It is like a person at night feeling for a pillow or blanket and finding a louse; this occurs spontaneously without depending on external light.
How could those dark phenomena obscure me? Therefore, once the faculties and their objects have dissolved, how could the originally inherent enlightened clarity not be present?

How perfectly accomplished and wondrous! Having concluded the section above on the characteristics selected by the Buddha within the two definitive meanings of the practice, the following section details Ānanda’s re-examination of the cause-mind and fruit-enlightenment within the first meaning, as well as his investigation of permanence and annihilation.
The World-Honored One further commands the striking of a bell to verify that hearing is not annihilated, thereby completing the matters of the definitive first meaning.
The rise and fall of the scriptural text and its literary sources should be clarified by scholars.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has said [up to] 'desiring to obtain the seven fruits of the Tathāgata’s eternal abiding.'"
This section of the sutra has Ānanda retrace the first causal mind to examine the resulting awakening, thereby debating and establishing the meanings of annihilationism and eternalism.
Below, Ānanda follows upon the previous challenge;

he first cites the first causal mind of annihilationism and compares it with the result, which is termed "permanence," requiring that cause and effect correspond. "Correspondence" means to harmonize and accord. Worldly... [text fragment ends].
Next, following the Honored One, the names of the resultant stages—bodhi and nirvāṇa—are cited. The translation and meaning have been seen previously. Regarding *tathatā* (Suchness):

it is called "True" (*zhen*) because it is not false, and "As-It-Is" (*ru*) because it is unchanging. As for dharmas, they are originally so; they abide in their own nature and remain in their own position.

Because they are neither false nor changing, and because the substance itself is suchness, it is called *tathatā*. Regarding *buddha-nature*: "Buddha" has the meaning of awakening; this refers to sentient beings.
He further said: "Every person inherently possesses the nature of spiritual awakening, which is called *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature). *Amala* is the name for its fruition;
translated as 'difficult to distinguish,' this fruition resembles a peach yet is not a peach, and resembles a crabapple yet is not a crabapple; therefore, it is called 'difficult to distinguish.

This serves as a metaphor for the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which resembles that which is defiled yet is not defiled, and resembles that which is true yet is not true, because it is the locus where the true and the false intermingle."
Because it is difficult to differentiate, it is called the *amala-vijñāna*.
Since the nature of this consciousness is inconceivable, it is the very "pure white consciousness" (*śuddha-vijñāna*) referred to in such scriptures as the *Ghanavyūha* and the *Saṃdhinirmocana*.

Because it is pure and untainted yet capable of cognition, it is termed the "pure white consciousness," which is an alternative name for the wondrous mind of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*). It is the emptiness of the Tathāgata.
The "Tathāgatagarbha" (the Womb of the Tathāgata) is precisely what is elucidated in the present sutra. Now, the Tathāgatagarbha possesses three meanings:
the empty Tathāgatagarbha, the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha, and the empty-and-non-empty Tathāgatagarbha. Here, by citing one meaning, the other two are implied;
these three meanings are the perfectly interfused Three Truths. As for the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, it is the fourth...

The *Jñānaika-buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states: "Just as various images appear in dependence upon a perfect mirror, so too, in dependence upon the mirror of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, all categories of mind—the various sense bases, objects, and consciousnesses—are fully manifested.

Because this wisdom is revealed by means of this analogy, it is called the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). Regarding these seven [wisdoms], Ānanda’s *Vibhaṅga* states that although these designations...
There are seven names with distinct designations; yet, when their seven essences are examined, they are in total a single, pure, perfect, awakened nature—firm, solid, and immovable.
To further illustrate this through analogy: it is like a vajra-jewel, which can shatter all other things and possesses the sense of sovereign mastery, and is therefore called a "king.
It abides eternally and is indestructible. The seven names of the Buddha-fruit are likewise thus.
If, as stated below, one uses the nature of cessation through causal mind to prove the present permanence—
just as the following three lines use the mind of recollection as an example to prove that seeing, hearing, and so forth lack intrinsic substance, saying "it is like... and so on—
how can one take this cessation as a cause while desiring to obtain the seven fruits of the Tathāgata’s permanence?
This would result in a contradiction.
World-Honored One, if seeing is ultimately empty when separated from light and darkness... (up to)... I only pray that Your Great Compassion will dispel my ignorance and delusion.
This section of the sutra follows upon the previous argument regarding seeing and hearing being without substance apart from their objects, and challenges the Buddha with his own words.
"It is not real, World-Honored One. This passage below immediately follows upon the preceding statement that seeing and hearing are devoid of substance when separated from their objects;

it begins with "seeing" and concludes with "thought," omitting the intermediate senses. By thus advancing and retreating through these six faculties in a cyclical manner and investigating them minutely, they are found to be absolutely unobtainable.
To speak of "advancing and retreating" means: advancing is to proceed from the faculty of seeing into the faculty of thought; retreating is to proceed from thought...
To emerge and see [the object] is to regress; to investigate this within the six sense-faculties without ceasing is called "cycling.
Because it cannot be found, it is said that there is fundamentally no causal mind of self, nor any mental factors of the self.

Since the mind of self does not exist, by whom shall one establish the cause for seeking unsurpassed enlightenment? The Tathāgata follows the previous statement regarding the profound stillness and perfection to challenge this.

"Truly, before the Buddha you said that the six consciousnesses are profoundly still, perfectly luminous, eternally abiding, and imperishable; yet now, when I seek them, I cannot find them, and thus they would become annihilated.
How then can the Tathāgata say they are profoundly still, perfect, and eternally abiding?
Your words seem inconsistent with your previous truth; it must ultimately be understood as mere frivolous discourse. I only pray that you will explain this further."
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As for your learning through much hearing... you should eliminate your doubts regarding all worldly matters.
This section of the sutra shows the World-Honored One intending to resolve his doubts; first, he rebukes his extensive learning to warn against the traces of failing to recognize true inversion.
The phrase "in one's mind one merely knows the causes of inversion" refers to being widely learned and erudite.
One may be able to describe the illness, yet never have personally seen its true reality; therefore, a genuine delusion manifests before one, and one fails to recognize it.

What, Ānanda, is this genuine delusion? It refers to taking the six sense-faculties—which are profoundly tranquil, perfectly luminous, and by nature devoid of arising and ceasing—and erroneously regarding them as subject to annihilation.
To mistake the permanent for the impermanent is precisely what the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) means by "clinging to the permanent as impermanent. This is it.
Because this is a true inversion, the Buddha—the Tathāgata, who speaks words of truth—fears that your sincere mind may still not be submissive through faith.
I shall now test you with matters from the mundane and superficial world, so as to cause you to realize that these things are permanent and not subject to annihilation.
These mundane matters refer to the following descriptions of beating silk cloth, pounding rice, and so forth.
At that moment, the Tathāgata commanded Rāhula: [From "until" (至) to] "When both sound and resonance are cut off, it is called 'no-hearing'.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding passage by using mundane affairs as a verification to demonstrate, in sequence, that hearing is not severed, thereby leading one to realization.

[The phrase] "not sounding" (不音) is negative; the following sections are to be understood accordingly. When there is sound, there is hearing; when there is no sound, hearing is quiescent. Furthermore, if one strikes [a bell], etc.
Because hearing arises following sound, it is said that "both hear. The Buddha’s question below serves to interrogate the meaning of hearing and non-hearing;
this is precisely to cause [the interlocutor] to describe in sequence his own realization of the permanence of hearing. Regarding "sound and resonance both cease":

"sound" refers to the high, low, clear, or turbid qualities of a voice, while "resonance" refers to the direct sound itself; thus, both "sound" and "resonance" are mentioned together. The rest of the text is easily understood.
The translation of "Rāhula" is as seen previously.
The Tathāgata further commanded Rāhula to strike the bell; when both the sound and its resonance ceased, it was called "soundlessness.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding text by substituting "easy to hear" with "sound," thereby investigating whether Ānanda has resolved his delusion or not.

For instance, one hears that the faculty belongs to the subject and sound belongs to the object; yet now, Ānanda, you cannot distinguish between faculty and object, nor differentiate between subject and object.
However, this nature of hearing is fundamentally constant, while the dust of sound is inherently intermittent. This is simply because you mistake sound for hearing;
what wonder, then, that you doubt the constant to be intermittent? Shortly thereafter—meaning within a brief moment—during the three rounds of question and answer, he cites sound as an example.

I have examined the intent to cause awakening; having clearly understood which of hearing or sound is severed and which is permanent, I shall now provide a sequential analysis so that the meaning of the text may be understood.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and the great assembly... [up to] "...as for 'hearing,' in reality it is said to be non-existent; who knows this non-existence?"
In this section of the sutra, the Buddha rebukes Ānanda for taking sound as the act of hearing in order to demonstrate that while sound ceases, hearing is eternal.

From "The Buddha said" onwards, he directly rebukes the confusion between the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*). "Kiao" (矯) means forcefulness; it refers to a mind that does not abide in the center and is neither wholesome nor supple—this is called "kiao.
Now, since the responses between hearing and sound are not fixed, the faculties and objects, the subject and the object, are intermingled and confused.

Because [Ānanda] had divided [the concepts], he was called "one who speaks with evasive confusion. Since Ānanda and the assembly had still not attained awakening, the Buddha spoke again below to clarify the point for him.
Regarding the passage "The sound has dissolved": this is the formal analysis of how the cessation of sound proves that hearing is constant.

The Buddha said: "You know that the sound has dissolved; you should say there is no resonance. How can you say there is no hearing? If there were truly no hearing, then the nature of hearing would have already perished, becoming like a withered tree."
Since wood has no nature of arising, how can you further strike the bell and yet be able to hear it? Furthermore, regarding that which knows existence and non-existence:
existence and non-existence belong to the sound; how could they belong to your faculty of hearing? If the faculty of hearing were truly non-existent, who would know its non-existence?
Who is it that knows its non-existence? That is precisely your faculty of hearing. As for the sound and the hearing, [the notions of] annihilation and permanence may be applied.
This is clear.

Therefore, from the passage "Ānanda, sound within hearing" (extending to "whether obstructed or unobstructed, hearing is said to have no inherent nature"), this section of the sutra concludes by clarifying that while sound ceases, hearing is constant; it thus points out Ānanda’s fundamental error.

Therefore, the following conclusion clarifies that the nature of hearing is eternally abiding: it means that while sounds within the faculty of hearing may arise or perish, this does not cause your faculty of hearing to arise or perish along with those sounds, nor does it allow your nature of hearing to become existent or non-existent.
This is because sounds themselves arise and perish, whereas the nature of hearing is eternally abiding—neither existent nor non-existent. "You still," etc., below, rebukes him for his inversion.

To constantly take what is permanent to be impermanent—that you have mistakenly fallen into such inverted delusion as to hear sound—is not surprising; it is only that you are so confused as to mistake the permanent for the impermanent.
However, one can never say that hearing lacks an intrinsic nature simply because it is said to be apart from movement and stillness.
Furthermore, the preceding text repeatedly clarifies that the six sense organs have no substance apart from their objects; yet why is it now said that they exist apart from their objects?

Did you not say previously, "Prostrating to return to the primal truth and bringing forth the fundamental luminosity," up until, "Because this luminosity does not follow the sense organs, but rather relies upon them to manifest, it attains perfect penetration and the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing"? Thus it is.
"Just as a person in deep sleep rests upon their bedding and pillows—though their physical form is asleep, the nature of hearing does not become dull.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding analogy to clarify that although the physical form is asleep, the faculty of hearing is not extinguished.
That is to say, it is like a person in deep sleep lying between the bedding and pillows; while they are there, someone in the house may be pounding silk or threshing grain.
"Milled silk" refers to the general practice of pounding silk fabric; the sound of this pounding was heard by the person in a dream as something else entirely.
This is the "solitary mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*) within a dream;
although the object is not clearly perceived, the nature of hearing does not cease, which is indeed real. Below, the mundane circumstances are detailed at length.

The description distinguishes the beginning and end of the dream-event; "awakening" (*wù*) means to wake from sleep (the character is pronounced *shuì* [shuǐ] with the radical for "market," and *rán* [rán] with the radical for "fire," meaning swiftness).
A "pestle" (*chǔ*) is the mallet used for pounding grain; both are called "pestles. The following section on Ānanda concludes by illustrating the principle of the dream:

it means that the faculty of hearing does not become obscured. The four characters "obstructed" (*bìsè*) and "open" (*kāitōng*) are spoken of in terms of the physical body, while the underlying intent refers to waking and sleeping.
Regarding the matters of opening and closing: when the fingers are closed, the forms intersect; when the forms intersect, the six sense organs are all blocked, hence it is called "blocked.

When the fingers are opened, the forms separate; when the forms separate, the six sense organs are all unobstructed. Thus, by citing sleep and dreams to demonstrate this opening and closing, as well as this penetration and obstruction, the reality of the nature of hearing is revealed.
Furthermore, "stillness," "shaking," and so forth, refer to the twelve categories of existence mentioned in the preceding text.

This is to illustrate the characteristics [of the nature of hearing]. Even if your physical form dissolves and the radiance of your life-force passes away—[up to the point where it is asked] how could you not achieve unsurpassed perfect enlightenment?

This section of the sutra follows upon the previous [passage] to further advance the argument, clarifying that the faculty of hearing is not subject to extinction even through death, thereby providing encouragement.
By following the constant, do not pursue the various delusions. "Even if you... and so forth means that the nature of hearing within that dream is not obscured;
even if the physical form were to dissolve and the light of life were to pass away, the nature of hearing would not be extinguished for you.
Thus, although a person dies, the nature of hearing does not die. This is because all sentient beings, from beginningless time, have followed along with the six sense-objects.
Chasing after various deluded thoughts, one transmigrates through birth and death because of being deluded regarding the nature of birth and death;

such false sentiments have never led to the awakening to the true essence, which is pure, wondrous, and eternally constant. The very nature that should be constantly followed is instead abandoned and not pursued, while one erroneously chases after arising and ceasing.
Thus, life after life, one undergoes the transmigration of those defiled states. "If one abandons [delusion] below" is an exhortation to awaken to and follow the eternal.
He said, "If you all abandon arising and ceasing and maintain the true permanence, then the originally existing constant light will manifest before you.

This 'constant light' is the light of eternal, tranquil stillness. Once you maintain this true permanence, the triad of sense organs, objects, and consciousness should completely dissolve at the very moment you maintain it.
'Conceptual appearances' refer precisely to the reflected shadows of the six sense faculties."

Because the characteristics of *saṃjñā* (perception) are coarse and floating, it is likened to dust; this refers to the delusions of seeing (*darśana-heya*). As for "consciousness-affection" (*vijñāna-vedanā*), "affection" (*vedanā*) refers to the affection of craving and desire, which arises dependent upon consciousness;

thus, the character "affection" (*vedanā*) should be viewed in contrast to the preceding "perception" (*saṃjñā*). Perception is fundamentally light and upward-moving, belonging to the five sharp afflictions (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-kleśa*);

affection is fundamentally heavy and downward-falling, belonging to the five dull afflictions (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*). "Defilement" (*mala*) means being soiled and greasy, as it cuts deeply into the mind. Therefore...

It is like a finger stained with grime, where the grime represents the afflictions of thought. Since the constant light has now appeared and the nature of consciousness is empty, both the dust and grime of views and thoughts are removed;
thus, at the moment you sever the afflictions, your Dharma-eye attains clarity and purity.

This is truly because sentient beings’ wisdom is obscured by the barriers of delusion, giving rise to false thoughts in accordance with sensory objects and becoming defiled everywhere; now that the delusions are severed, wisdom [shines forth].
Because clear consciousness follows wisdom and becomes perfectly luminous in every respect, it is said that "delusion is severed and the Dharma-eye attains purity.
The phrase "purity of the Dharma-eye" refers to entering the stage of the sages (*ārya*). At this time, how could the nature of seeing, hearing, and so forth fail to become unsurpassed enlightenment?
This is as previously stated: transforming the knowledge and vision of sentient beings into the knowledge and vision of a Buddha.
The Direct Explanation of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas,
Volume Four.

Direct Explanation of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra: The Ultimate Meaning of the Cultivation and Realization of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Scroll Five.
Written by the junior monk Guangmo of Yunqi Temple in Ancient Hangzhou. Direct Explanation.
The Upāsaka Renhe (Wen Qixiang) proofread this.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, although the Tathāgata has spoken [up to] this point, I believe that such a person will ultimately be unable to understand.”
In this section, Ānanda again takes up the analogy of "untying the knot" from the second principle to inquire and seek instruction as to what constitutes the knot.
Previously, at the end of the fourth fascicle, Ānanda had already taken up the first principle to provide a detailed analysis of the views of causality, mind, permanence, and annihilation;
now he once more turns back to take up the analogy of untying the knot from the second principle.
The questioner must understand how this knot was originally tied and how it is now untied.
The passage beginning with "The Tathāgata" below reiterates the preceding meaning; the sense can be understood from the following text.

Regarding the "knot," as per the subsequent text, the metaphor of the knot represents the fundamental source of the knots of the six sense faculties. It is "one" because the six arise from one; that "one" is affliction.
The root of these fundamental afflictions is precisely what was previously termed the "locus of inversion.
This locus of inversion refers to the innate ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*) indicated in the subsequent text.

Furthermore, below that, it is stated that this innate ignorance is none other than the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), because the six faculties perform actions and the six faculties likewise receive retribution; thus, it is explained by way of indicating the six faculties.

If one investigates this to its ultimate conclusion, the very beginning of the arising of the six [sense-faculties] is precisely the root of birth and death, namely, co-nascent ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*).
