This beginning of the arising of the six is the eighth storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), which is called "the one.
Because this one, being without marks (*animitta*), manifests within the six sense-faculties.
“World-Honored One, I and those in this assembly who are śrāvakas still in training (up to ‘awaiting the unsurpassed instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata’).

This section of the sutra follows the preceding analogy of the dharma to conclude the metaphor and requests the method for untying the knots. The passage beginning with “World-Honored One” is precisely the application of the dharma;
therefore, it says, “it is likewise so. The person in the world who unties the knots is a metaphor for all [the practitioners].
The Śrāvaka Ānanda harbors a doubt: since innate ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*) is the fundamental cause of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), he first describes this [ignorance].
"Arising together" and "ceasing together" mean they are identical; that is, the ignorance accumulated since beginningless time arises together with the self and ceases together with the self.
Because its instances are numerous, it is called "various" (*sarva*). Ignorance has the meaning of non-awakening (*a-prabodha*).
Although he attained the lower [fruit], Ānanda himself described his own great learning and minor wisdom as being unable to ultimately sever that ignorance;
thus it is said that although he attained much learning, he was merely one who had left home in name.

As for those who praise much learning as a root of goodness, while such learning belongs to the outflows (*āsrava*), it upholds the treasury of the Dharma, continues the Buddha’s life-force of wisdom, and discerns the heterodox from the orthodox.
That he illuminates the darkness and delusion proves he possesses great roots of goodness; yet these "roots of goodness" refer to the extensive learning accumulated over many kalpas.
Because he has now attained renunciation through this merit of accumulated learning over many kalpas, Ānanda feels ashamed of his former mind that was addicted to mere erudition.
Those who renounce the world for the sake of extensive learning have not yet realized the true essence of renunciation; therefore, [the Buddha] addresses him by name.
Regarding the statement that "leaving the household life is like a tertian malaria," this means that because the outflows (*āsrava*) have not been exhausted, the root of illness still remains;
since one is well for a day and weak the next, it is likened to a tertian malaria. The two lines following "I only pray" are self-evident.

Regarding the lines beginning with "Today," he formally inquires about how the interval between body and mind is called a "knot" (*grantha*) and where it is called "liberation. Now, as for the knots of the body:
The following passage directly points to that which binds the six sense-faculties; "the knot of the mind" must refer to that single place where [delusion] has not yet been extinguished.
Therefore, both body and mind are raised together and termed the "knot. Now, Ānanda’s request is not for his own sake alone, but is also intended to benefit those of the future;
thus it says, "for the sake of the future," and so forth. Having made this request, he and the assembly [prostrated with their] five wheels...

Prostrating on the ground, he felt pity for his own sinking into the depths of suffering, and this grief moved his heart so that tears fell like rain. "Qiao-cheng" (翘诚) means to look up with sincerity;

"qiao" (翘) signifies looking upward, while "cheng" (诚) signifies a sincere heart. The intent is to unify one's mind and wait for [the Buddha’s response]; thus, the following line says, "I await the Buddha’s instruction."
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda (up to the point where his hand, radiant with purple-gold light, touched Ānanda’s crown).

This section of the sutra shows that because the World-Honored One took pity on the multitude who had made their request and wished to extend his grace to the末代 (final age), he first offered consolation and then gave instruction.
From "At that time" onwards, it should be understood as the source for the two subsequent lines: "The Buddha, pitying the final age, bestowed his teaching upon it."
Later, he caused him to plant the causes for transcending the world and to become an eye of guidance for future generations; it was for this reason that he touched his head and addressed him.
Immediately, [the worlds of] the Buddhas throughout the ten directions (extending to... are none other than your six sense faculties; they are not some other thing.

In this section of the sutra, the Buddha, having comforted [the assembly] based on the preceding passage and being about to deliver his teaching, emits light from the earth and causes extraordinary sounds to be uttered in unison;
these serve as a prior manifestation of what is to come. Why did the earth tremble throughout the ten directions when he touched their heads and was about to speak?

The intent is to clarify that the six sense-faculties of sentient beings are deeply bound by fetters, persisting through vast eons and long periods of time, and that [this teaching] cannot be heard elsewhere.
O you who possess understanding, I shall now declare the method for the dissolution [of this assembly]. This matter is no small cause;
therefore, the ten directions tremble and the light of all Buddhas flows forth. There is indeed a profound intention behind this:

it is to cause those present in this assembly and those yet to come, who have not heard the Great Dharma, to first behold these extraordinary signs so that they may silently comprehend the meaning within their hearts, making the profound words easy to enter. Thus it is now universally [manifested].

The six realms move; the mind manifests this, overturning and breaking the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). By analyzing ignorance (*avidyā*), universal penetration (*pariṣvaṅga*) is spontaneously pervasive.
Because one breaks everything, all is broken; thus, the entire realm moves. The characteristics of these six movements are detailed in the first explanation.
When the Buddha’s crown-light comes to pour upon one, the mind manifests that since the six faculties have been broken, universal penetration is unobstructed in all things.

The "six destinies" (ṣadgati) refer to the return to the source; that "crowning the crown" signifies that the fruit of perfect awakening is such that self and others are not separated, the one and the many are mutually inclusive, all myriad virtues are honored together, and the single mind governs all.
"With one voice and one sound" signifies that the single path is universally common and that all diverse words converge in awakening. Before the World-Honored One Śākyamuni had yet spoken...
The Buddha’s previous statement intended to signify that the One Reality transcends words, while the various vehicles are merely adapted to suit the capacities of beings.
"Bondage and liberation are the same" refers to the six sense faculties; as stated in the text below, "to establish knowledge within seeing-and-knowing is the very root of ignorance.
This "seeing-and-knowing" constitutes the six faculties, and this "root of ignorance" is bondage. When "seeing-and-knowing is devoid of seeing," this is precisely Nirvana—untainted, truly pure.
To forget the six sense-faculties by means of the six sense-faculties is itself non-knowing yet knowing, and non-seeing yet seeing;
this is true knowledge and true vision—is this not indeed an understanding? From the previous sutra up to this point, the Buddha has emitted light on four occasions;

however, that the present dust-like Buddha shares the same light and the same Dharma, dissecting and revealing ignorance and manifesting the untying of knots, is entirely different from the previous sutra.
It is precisely because the fetter of ignorance is heavy and the method for its treatment is profound that this is like having a formidable enemy before one while the king’s forces are numerous;
thus, the display of the elephant surpassing [the opponent] is intended to convey this meaning.
Although Ānanda heard such a Dharma-sound... [up to] "...are likewise these six faculties and are nothing other than this.

This section of the sutra records Ānanda’s request for further clarification because, despite the preceding Dharma-sound regarding the Buddha and the dusts, he had not yet realized the principle that the knots and their untying share the same root.
The aforementioned imagery of the dusts and the Buddha sharing the same light and the same Dharma was merely temporary.

At that time, because he manifested the present state and then returned to his original nature, Ānanda took up another teaching of the Dharma to question his own teacher regarding the meaning of the "common source" (*tonggen*). The text is easily understood.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "The faculties and their objects share the same source... how could there be room for any other thing within this?"

In this section of the sutra, the Buddha answers and resolves the question regarding the shared root [of the faculties], clarifying that the three—faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—originate from the same true source and become differentiated only due to delusion.
The four lines beginning with "The faculties and objects" mean that the six faculties, six objects, and six consciousnesses all flow forth from the same true source;
both bondage and liberation depend upon the six faculties. The reason for not mentioning the objects and consciousness is as follows: [the faculties are the primary locus].
Because the faculties are the precursor, the bonds and liberations of false views do not shift the true nature. The preceding phrase refers to the true nature as being of a single source;
the following phrase refers to the six faculties as being non-dual.

Furthermore, the preceding phrase shows the convergence of appearances back into the nature, while the following phrase indicates the characteristics upon which bondage and liberation depend—namely, that both bondage and liberation are identical within the six faculties, for there is no duality of dharmas.

The following two lines clarify the falsity of the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna-svabhāva*). Although the two characters "false" (*xūwàng*) are spoken in connection with the nature of consciousness, their meaning extends to both the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*).

"Falsity" refers to the dharmas; "flowers in the sky" is the metaphor. The nature of consciousness is like a reflection, while the faculties and objects are what it reflects, thereby manifesting the three sixes as metaphors for emptiness.
The flowers represent the three sixes; in the present text, it appears that the words refer to the nature of consciousness alone.

The metaphor of partiality versus universal penetration refers to the three and the six. This means that emptiness is fundamentally without flowers; it is through deluded vision that their arising and ceasing appear.

It is like how reality is fundamentally without delusion, yet because of confusion, birth occurs. The four lines following "Ānanda" clarify that the sense organs (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) exist in mutual dependence;
if they were solitary, they would not arise. Thus, the six internal cognitive faculties are triggered by the six external objects; it is from the objects that the faculties are produced.
Furthermore, it is because of the six internal faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) that the characteristics of the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) first arise; the objects exist in dependence upon the faculties.

The following two lines clarify that both faculties and objects lack inherent nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). The term "seeing" (*jian*) in reference to the six objects serves as a correlative to the term "knowing" (*zhi*) in the preceding line, thereby indicating the six faculties.

This means that both faculties and objects are devoid of self-nature and arise only by depending on conditions. The text subsequently employs the metaphor of the "mutually supporting reeds" (*naḍakalāpa*) to illustrate this.

Both are devoid of intrinsic nature. As for the reed, although it has an outward appearance, there is no substance within; thus, it serves as a metaphor for the lack of reality in the two natures of the sense faculties and their objects.
Furthermore, they are both empty of inherent nature internally despite having provisional appearances externally. "Intersecting" (jiao) is a metaphor for the meaning of mutual dependence:
it means that the sense faculties and their objects depend upon one another, just as two reeds must intersect to provide support for each other and stand upright.
When solitary, they collapse; the same applies to the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*). Therefore, this is used as a metaphor.

Thus, the following conclusion clarifies that bondage and liberation are non-dual, answering the question regarding the commonality of the roots in both binding and unbinding. "Establishing knowledge within knowledge and vision" refers to the six faculties;
it means that if one falsely establishes these six roots as being substantially real, they are in fact non-existent.
To clarify that fundamental ignorance is the root of bondage: if the six sense faculties do not cling to cognition, then there is no cognition;
if there is no seeing, then there is no vision. This is true knowledge and true vision. Because it is true, it is without outflows (*anāsrava*), non-delusory, and unstained.
Thus, while functioning as cognition and vision, it constitutes the merit of true purity and nirvana. Because bondage and liberation are non-dual, [it is thus].
"To allow other things within" refers here to the midst of the six sense organs.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses.
This section of the sutra is the scribe’s account of the Buddha restating the prose in verse to conclude and clarify the meaning of the preceding exposition. Someone may ask:

Question: Since the meaning of the prose (*gadya*) is already complete, why are there repeated verses (*geya*); would this not be redundant? Answer: The World-Honored One’s preaching of the Dharma was perfectly suited to the capacities of all beings.
Formerly, when the Buddha was preaching the Dharma, an elder arrived late and had not heard the preceding meaning;

he requested that it be explained again. Out of great compassion, the World-Honored One briefly indicated the previous teaching and subsequently established it as a precedent; thus, these [verses] exist.
The method of *geya* (verses) is one of the twelve divisions of the canon.
True nature is empty of conditioned phenomena because they arise dependently and are like illusions; unconditioned phenomena have no arising or ceasing and are unreal, like flowers in the sky.
This section of the sutra consists of the World-Honored One’s verse restatement of the meaning previously set forth in prose.
First, he establishes the true source to clarify that both existence and non-existence are illusory. The term "true nature" (zhenxing) versifies the preceding idea of a common source;

it establishes the true source by indicating that within true nature, both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are unreal. Thus, the first phrase states that the conditioned is empty.
The first three characters, "first shatter conditioned existence" (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), constitute the meaning of the refutation. The subsequent phrase reveals the specific object of this refutation:
because conditioned phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and arise dependent upon conditions. "Conditioned" refers here to the triad of sense organs, objects, and consciousness;
since their existence is not truly existent, they are said to be empty. Because they arise from conditions, they are like illusions; the nature of an illusion is not real.
It is not that illusory appearances do not exist, for they are not non-existent through annihilation; thus, the triad of sense organs, objects, and consciousness is likewise so.
Although they are not truly existent, because their provisional names are not destroyed, they are like illusions. The next two lines further refute the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*):

within true nature, although the conditioned is destroyed, one must not stagnate in the unconditioned. If, upon hearing the refutation of the conditioned, one again stagnates in the unconditioned, [this is an error].
Non-action (*asaṃskṛta*) is also a sickness; therefore, it is further refuted: even if non-action were without arising or ceasing, it would still not be real, being like a flower in the sky.
Since the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is neither existent nor non-existent, both are refuted together. How could it be that only existence and non-existence are so?
All hundred negations are equally sicknesses; existence and non-existence are the primary head of all these sicknesses. Therefore, [the text] first...
The refutation of the others should also be understood in this way: the first four lines constitute a general refutation, while the subsequent lines provide specific refutations.
By speaking of "delusion" (mṛṣā), it is revealed that both the delusive and the true are equally dualistic delusions... [up to] ...entering the stream to achieve perfect enlightenment.

This section of the sutra follows the preceding general refutation to specifically clarify the falsity of the mutual causality between the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), further demonstrating the meaning of the "disappearance of the one and the six.
The first four lines constitute the direct refutation of their mutual causality;

the first line is a reductio ad absurdum that points to the falsity of the organs and objects, stating that because they exist as if they were non-existent—like illusory flowers in the sky—they are termed "false. This is intended to...
"Because it reveals all that is real," where "all" (*zhū*) is an auxiliary particle. The second phrase further clarifies the meaning of the first:

namely, that reality is revealed in contrast to the false. Since this is not an absolute reality but still belongs to the realm of the false, it is said that "the false and the real are both equally false.
The preceding "false" refers to the six [sense-objects], while the following two phrases (lines 10–11) reiterate the meaning of the previous two.
This verse clarifies that both "one" and "six" are not [the truth]. It means that the "True" which was previously contrasted with the "delusory" is still not the ultimate True;
this [verse] precisely negates that "one. Since even "one" is not the True, how could one further speak of "the seer" and "the seen"?

"The seer" refers to the six sense organs, and "the seen" refers to the six sense objects; this precisely negates those "six. Now, the meaning of this verse regarding what is true and what is not true is as follows:
The prose section’s discussion of the nature of consciousness refers to the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*);

since the eighth consciousness constitutes a single entity, the subsequent four lines follow from the preceding verse’s discussion of the "seer" and the "seen" to clarify that there is no self-substantial nature between the sense faculties and their objects, thereby concluding the prose analogy of the "mutually supporting reeds.
The final two lines eulogize the non-duality of bondage and liberation, while simultaneously clarifying the process of fettering and release.
The "original cause" refers to the fact that both bondage and liberation share the same cause; this cause specifically points to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

The following phrase clarifies the meaning of their shared cause: namely, that bondage pertains to ordinary beings while liberation pertains to sages, yet there are no two separate paths for being fettered or released.
Next, another four phrases also rely on the preceding metaphor of the sheaves of reeds to clarify that both emptiness and existence are neither [independent].
The "intermediate nature" refers to the substance and desire existing between the two—the intersection of the sense organ and the object. If one speaks of its substantiality, it is immediately void;
if one speaks of its emptiness, its illusory marks are not non-existent. Therefore, it is said that it is neither empty nor existent.
If it is neither empty nor existent, then the wondrous nature is natural; what further cause for doubt could there be? The following two lines clarify bondage.
The verse on "liberation from other realms" (*niḥsaraṇa-gati*) states that when one establishes knowledge based on false views and attachments, ignorance (*avidyā*) is thereby produced.

If one clearly understands that there is no seeing within seeing, then regarding the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), one should contemplate liberation. Therefore, bondage and liberation are non-dual;

they differ only according to delusion and awakening. The final four lines respond to the initial question by separately demonstrating the distinction between binding and untying across the six [faculties].
This explains the meaning of "the dissolution of one, the disappearance of six, the arising of selection, and the perfecting of the faculties.

The first two phrases provide a sequential response to resolve the distinctions and demonstrate the meaning of the dissolution of one and the disappearance of six; the latter two phrases give rise to the selection of the perfect faculties, returning from their deluded extremities to establish the true foundation.
Regarding the sequence of the initial phrase: first the six are dissolved, then the one disappears; thus, three become one.

The six sense organs being simultaneously empty and non-arising constitutes the vertical entry into the three successive stages. As it says below: "When this faculty first becomes liberated, one first attains the emptiness of the person;
when the nature of emptiness is perfectly luminous, one achieves liberation from phenomena; having achieved liberation from phenomena, both are empty and non-arising.
This is precisely the meaning of the sequence. Whereas the preceding long prose section did not yet contain the principle of selecting the faculties, this [passage] does.
Because this is where the *udāna* (spontaneous) verses from within the *geya* (versified) section begin:
"The subtle consciousness of *dhātu* (appropriation), whose habitual tendencies form a torrential stream... [until] ...the single path to the gate of *nirvāṇa*."
This section of the sutra follows the preceding prose by restating it in verse to separately present sixteen isolated meanings that give rise to the subsequent text.
These sixteen isolated lines constitute a single verse in total.

While the preceding verses that restate the meaning of the prose are termed "repeated verses" (*geya*), those now presented separately from the prose to expound other meanings are termed "isolated verses" (*udāna*).

The "Verses" (gāthā) are also called "Recited Verses" (*bhāṣita*). Since the preceding section clarified the "six disappearances" (*ṣaḍ-vigama*), this section clarifies the "one disappearance" (*eka-vigama*); thus, these verses arise following the prose.
According to the Indian Sanskrit tradition, a single verse (*śloka*) is defined by its meaning regardless of its length;

therefore, the *ālayavijñāna* (here referred to as *dhana-vijñāna*) is specifically designated here as one verse. This is because, although the preceding prose referred to it by the name "one," it had not yet clarified the nature of that "one."
The reality is now revealed. In Sanskrit, *ādāna* is translated as "grasping" (*zhíchí*). It so-called because it grasps and maintains the seeds of beginningless good and evil;
furthermore, it grasps and maintains the physical body, preventing it from dispersing or decaying. This thus carries the meaning of "containing" or "storing.

The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* also calls this the "storehouse consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna*). This consciousness has three characteristics: its subtle and hidden seeds and manifestations are uninterrupted, flowing and pouring forth continuously.

Because it is extremely subtle, even the followers of the Two Vehicles do not know it, let alone ordinary people or non-Buddhists; thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states that its perfuming and transformation are inconceivable.
It is called "subtle" because the six sense faculties arise from this cause, and these six are named as "one" in relation to this consciousness.
Although a Srotāpanna has attained the dissolution of the six [faculties], they have not yet eliminated the "one"; this is precisely what is being referred to here. Next...
The phrase expresses the meaning of "flowing forth. "Habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*) refers to the seeds of beginningless good and evil;
through the perfuming of these seeds and their manifestation, their energy issues forth externally to form a torrential stream.

Regarding this metaphor of a torrential stream, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* likens the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) to the ocean and the preceding seven consciousnesses to the torrential streams. The streams arise because of the ocean, and the seven [consciousnesses] likewise arise from the storehouse.

The evolving consciousnesses arise through the transformation of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*); the first seven consciousnesses act as the perfumers (*vāsaka*) and the storehouse consciousness acts as the perfumed (*vāsya*).
Because the manifest activities perfume the various seeds—this being termed "habitual energy" (*vāsanā*)—it is said that they form a torrential stream.

The two lines beginning with "True is not" explain the meaning of "true is not true" from the preceding passage, clarifying that this was not taught within the teachings of the Hīnayāna; thus, it is said that "true is not."
"True" refers to this *ādāna-vijñāna*. If one were to say it is true, non-Buddhists would grasp it as being permanent;
if one were to say it is false, they might instead negate it as being subject to annihilation. Thus, it appears to be true but is not truly so, like a second moon.
Regarding the phrase "I do not constantly expound it," the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, Chapter Eight, states: "The *ādāna-vijñāna* is extremely subtle."
The subtle stream of all seeds is not revealed by me to the foolish and ignorant, for fear that they might conceptually grasp it as a self;
the meaning of this passage is identical to that of the present verse.

This is because those of the Two Vehicles do not believe in the existence of the eighth consciousness and thus identify this consciousness as *nirvāṇa*, while non-Buddhists grasp it as the divine self (*ātman*). Therefore, in the world...
The Honored One does not constantly reveal or expound [this teaching] among the ignorant and foolish, for fear they might become confused by it.

Therefore, the five lines beginning with "one's own mind" (*svacitta*) precisely demonstrate the reason why confusion regarding the single principle must be feared. Now, this *ālayavijñāna* is none other than one’s own true mind;
since there is no consciousness apart from the mind, although we speak of "one's own mind," it must not be grasped. If it is grasped, then oneness is not lost, yet oneness is not realized.
That which is truly non-existent is itself the root of delusion; it is fundamentally not an illusion, yet it gives rise to illusory phenomena—this is clear.
Fearing that you might be confused by this, I do not speak of it. If you do not grasp it as your own mind, then it is entirely the true mind, and even the name "non-illusory" cannot be found.
Since "non-illusory" is spoken of only in contrast to "illusion," and now that even the non-illusory does not exist, how could illusory phenomena exist? This is so.
When truth and falsehood are transcended and the numinous mind alone shines forth, this is the effect of the "perishing of the one.

When the "one" is said to be opposed to the "six," since the one has perished, how can the six exist? It is because neither the illusory nor the non-illusory is the one, yet the six are the one; thus, the "perishing of the one through the liberation of the six" is the explanation thereof.
This is called the "Wondrous Lotus. The following four phrases, concerning the teaching and practice, clarify the relationship between the one and the six.
The "perishing" refers to the victory of function; the "wondrous lotus flower" is a metaphor for the teaching in its abbreviated sense.

It means that through the dissolution of the six and the perishing of the one, the purely singular, perfect mind achieves supreme enlightenment. Because these words and explanations constitute the teaching, the wondrous lotus flower is used as a name for the teaching;
this is to praise the excellence of the teaching. Just as in Tiantai, the lotus flower symbolizes the simultaneity of cause and effect.

The clarification of the six meanings refers to the lotus: for the sake of the lotus, there is the flower; when the flower opens, the lotus appears; when the flower falls, the lotus is perfected. The teaching likewise possesses these six meanings:

for the sake of the ultimate (the lotus), one provisionally establishes the expedient (the flower); one opens the expedient to reveal the ultimate; and one discards the expedient to establish the ultimate.

To correspond to this, the flower should be taken as a metaphor for the expedient and the lotus as a metaphor for the ultimate. Thus, he explains the provisional and the ultimate of the *Lotus Sūtra* through these six meanings; indeed, it is the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Regarding the provisional and the real (*upāya* and *bhūta-artha*) as discussed in the teachings of a single lifetime, this present sutra discusses the provisional and the real within its own specific section (*buddha-kṣetra*), also employing the six meanings for its explanation;

however, it does so specifically to manifest the superiority of its own section. For instance, when it says that "one and six" are provisional and their "vanishing" is real, this is spoken in order to reveal the wondrous mind (*vimala-citta*).
Thus, "one and six" represent the establishment of the provisional based upon the real; by opening up these "one and six," [the ultimate truth is revealed].

This very wondrous mind is the "opening of the provisional to reveal the real. When both "one" and "six" are forgotten and the wondrous mind alone shines forth, this is the "abolishing of the provisional to establish the real.
That "one" and "six" are the wondrous mind, and the wondrous mind is the one mind—this constitutes the "wondrous provisional and the wondrous real.
Therefore, the teaching is praised by means of the "wondrous lotus flower. Of the middle two phrases, the first phrase further uses gold...
The diamond-like awakening (*vajropama-bodhi*) is the wondrous mind; this is the ultimate meaning.
That is to say, this wondrous awakening can shatter all illusory delusions, just as a vajra can destroy all that is hard while remaining sharp. The wondrous awakening is likewise so.
Because the vajra is the most supreme among all jewels, it is called the "Vajra King. The four characters "Jewel Supreme" (*baoshang*) serve as the metaphor for awakening.
The single character "this" (之) refers to the *dharmatā* as being like an illusion (*māyopama*). This phrase "samādhi" is spoken in terms of practice;

when joined with the preceding phrase, they share a single meaning. The "Precious Enlightenment" (*ratnabodhi*) above refers to the fruit of practice, while the "samādhi" below refers to the cause of practice.
This "samādhi" is precisely the third of the three meanings of "wonderful" (*miaoxi*), namely *samādhi*. To mention one is to encompass all three; thus it is called "like an illusion."
Above, the sublime lotus was used as a metaphor for the teaching; now, the illusion-like is used as an analogy for practice.

This means that within the state of sublime awakening, these three meanings cannot be found as one, nor can a single dharma be obtained; how then could there be three? Nevertheless, it is not without practice that realization is attained.

One relies on practice to realize the principle, just as one uses a raft to cross a river and discards it upon reaching the shore. Because what was non-existent suddenly appears, it is said to be "like" [an illusion].
The phrase "a phantom snaps its fingers and transcends the stage of no-more-learning" is a distinct praise of the excellence of practice.
"Snaps its fingers" is a metaphor for the sudden realization of practice, equivalent to what is called "not passing through the *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. "No-more-learning" refers to the fourth fruit;

it indicates that the transcendence of this practice is so swift and miraculous. Furthermore, these four lines below are explained according to the four meanings of teaching (*śāsana*), principle (*li*), practice (*xing*), and realization (*zheng*).

"Miao-lie" (Wondrous Lotus) refers to the provisional teachings; "Jingang-wang-jue" (Vajra-King Awakening) refers to the principle; "Samadhi" refers to practice; and "No-more-learning" (Aśaikṣa) refers to realization.

To say it "transcends those of no-more-learning" is spoken from the perspective of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), meaning these are the Bodhisattvas of the Four Reliances who transcend the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Thus, this verse summarizes the excellence of these four meanings; the final three lines can be understood accordingly. The Sanskrit term *Abhidharma* is translated as [the "Ultimate Dharma"].

"It is called the incomparable Dharma because there is nothing with which it can be compared. This is a praise of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) regarding the Bhagavān, the honorific title for the Buddha, who possesses the six supreme meanings;

thus, it is not translated [into Chinese] but is presented in detail according to the categories of dharmas. The "gate" refers to that which enables one to reach *nirvāṇa*, while the "path" is that by which one travels.
When explained in terms of practice, it is the gate; when explained in terms of teaching, it is the path. As stated in the first sutra: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions..."
The "wondrously adorned path for transcending through a single gate" is identical in meaning to the present context.
Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly (until) were bestowed with the sound of the Dharma to wash away their deep-seated defilements.

This section of the sutra records the author’s praise for the preceding verses and explains Ānanda’s request for clarification regarding the meaning of the "loss of one and six" and the sequence of untying the knots.
In Sanskrit, *geya* is translated as "repeated verse," while *gāthā* is translated as "recited verse," or alternatively, "independent verse.
Initially, the author praises both types of verse, referring to them as "repeated verse" and "independent verse."
Because it appears interspersed throughout the introductory sections, it is called "intermingled" (*mi-ran*); "intermingled" here carries the sense of being mixed together.

"Refined and brilliant" (*jing-ying*) is an expression of praise for the exquisite purity of the phrasing, meaning it is as smooth and lustrous as jade. "Subtle, elegant, and transparently clear" praises the clarity and thorough penetration of the meanings explained;
because both the phrasing and the meaning are beautiful, those who hear them— (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding the effect on the listeners.)

"The mind and eyes opened and became clear" refers to the realization of those who hear. "Exclaiming that it is unprecedented" indicates that the hearers marvel at the rare encounter with this perfect union of the signifier (the teaching) and the signified (the truth).
From "Ānanda" onwards, the Venerable One speaks of his own request.
"Unobstructed great compassion" means that the Buddha’s heart of great compassion has no limits; it reaches all beings universally, like the light of the sun and moon.
Whether facing the pure or the defiled, they are not separated; the phrase "nature-purity, wondrous-constancy, and reality" flows forth entirely from the heart of great compassion.
The single phrase "nature-purity, wondrous-constancy" praises the meaning expressed (*lakṣya-artha*), while the phrase "reality" praises the expressive text (*lakṣaṇa-vākya*).
Furthermore, from "nature-purity" onwards, he summarizes what was previously heard; with "the mind is still," he again opens up the subsequent meaning. Venerable Sir!

This means that although I have heard such true words of the Dharma, I have not yet mastered the principle of "the six dissolutions and the one disappearance," nor the sequence for unraveling the knots.

Since the meaning of "unraveling" (*śu*) was briefly clarified in the preceding verse regarding the sequence of unraveling the knots, but was not fully explained, I request that you again demonstrate this sequence; this refers back to the previous verse's explanation.
Regarding the phrase "the sequence of the causes of the bonds": "sequence" (*krama*) refers to the order of arrangement;

for the sake of literary elegance, "jie" (*jie*) is changed to "shu" (*shu*) and "di" (*di*) is changed to "lun" (*lun*). Please deign to provide the concluding words of the inquiry below. The single line "to wash away the deep-seated defilements" is explained through a metaphor:
it means that the Tathāgata once again bestows the sound of the Dharma, using the water of the virtue of *prajñā* to wash away my mind.
"Sinking, subtle, defiled, and filthy" refers here to the afflictions of thought in subsequent stages as well as the "dust-like" ignorance and ignorance like fine sand beyond the realms.
From "At that time, the Tathāgata, upon the lion throne... up to "...successively answered the Buddha," this is termed the "conclusion."
In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One, intending to explain the untying of the knots, first demonstrates how they were tied so that [the audience] may realize the sequence;
once that is understood, the method of untying can also be known. "Neatly adjusting the *nirvāṇa-saṅghāṭī*" (整涅下二句): *nirvāṇa-saṅghāṭī* is a Sanskrit term translated as "skirt" (*qún*).
"Adjusting" (*zhěng*) means to gather and align. *Saṅghāṭī* is a term whose meaning is explained at the end of the third fascicle. [He] took hold of a seven-jeweled table.
As for the small tables, how many are there? They are composed of the seven precious gems. Before the Dharma-seat, small tables are set up; their scale is roughly that used by the Tathāgata.
Since these were either provided by royal families or offered by the various devas, they are as rich and magnificent as this.
One grasps them and moves them close to the seat. *Karpūra* is also called *Suyāma*, which is translated as "Excellent Time" (*Śubhakāla*); it refers to the realm of desire.

The third heaven of the Realm of Desire is named "Flower-Arrayed" (Kusumatalagarbha), as seen in the following sutra passage. The "folded-flower cloth" (diéhuá jīn) is the cloth offered by this heaven;

because many flowers are woven into its upper surface, it is called "folded-flower. Furthermore, considering that the cloth is woven from threads—perhaps similar to cotton fabrics used here in this land—it is termed "folded-flower.
A single cloth is tied into knots; the questions and answers [regarding this] can be understood as demonstrating this point.
The sequence of forming knots is intended to illustrate the order of realization.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "When I first tied the cloth (up to) the second and third [knots], they were not called 'knots'."

This section of the sutra follows the preceding investigation to reach a conclusion, thereby implicitly demonstrating that while they are identical within the same substance, they become distinct due to the formation of knots.
The Buddha says, "This cloth was originally but a single strip," which clarifies their identity as one substance.
Furthermore, by examining each of the six knots in detail, his intention is to cause [the audience] to secretly realize the original cause of their being knotted. Now...
Ānanda’s response was likewise precise, yet he had not yet reflected upon the identity of the single substance;
therefore, the Buddha spoke the following words:
"The Buddha told Ānanda: 'This precious flowered cloth... ultimately identical within it, yet ultimately different.'"
This section of the sutra follows the Buddha’s previous teaching that the one is identical to the six; that names are confused and cannot correspond to reality is likewise so.

the substance of the headcloth is the root and thus identical, while the six knots are the branches and thus different. This is the meaning. Below this, [the text continues].

When the Buddha said, "I seal what you have said as being thus," the word "thus" (*evam*) is a term of certification. Regarding the three phrases following "the six knots": they reveal that the six differences are rooted in a single source, which is the basis of the six.

What do you think? The Buddha’s intention in asking this question was to lead [Ānanda] away from the previous six knots so as to bring about the realization of their unity, gradually guiding him toward the state where the six are liberated and the one is extinguished.
Thus, he posed the question of "leaving the six to become one" to cause others to awaken for themselves.
When Ānanda replied that by leaving the six one becomes one, he answered with the extinction of the one; this response surpassed the original question. This is why—
Because this is an awakening, it is summarized by distinguishing between existence and non-existence; this refers to the six knots. If they exist, then right and wrong arise like sharp blades;

Below, the Tathāgata provides the direct answer regarding the "extinction of one": if the knots are collectively untied and do not arise, then...
There is no "this" or "that," no right or wrong, for they can all be stilled. The final two phrases conclude by clarifying the meaning of "the six being resolved and the one vanishing.
This refers to the first [of the six] confronting the six; since even "one" cannot be apprehended, how could the "six" be established?
These are Ānanda’s own words of self-discernment and self-awakening.
The Buddha said: "The six being resolved and the one perishing is likewise thus" (up to) "all are immediately the deluded toil of inverted flower-like appearances.
This section of the scripture corresponds to the analogy of the six knots not arising and the single [knot] not being established.

The words beginning with "The Buddha said" constitute the application of the Dharma (*dharmasaṃgraha*); hence it says, "likewise thus. The passage beginning with "By you" serves as a warning to bring forth the six.
"Initially, the mind-nature becomes deranged" refers to the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*); "derangement" refers to the three subtle states.

In contrast to the profound stillness of original enlightenment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), although these three subtle states are minute, they are called "deranged" because they turn away from that fundamental stillness.

This is what is meant by "one false perception arises": this refers to the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*), as the manifestations of the three subtle states subsequently trigger activity toward external objects.

Thus, the six coarse [objects] are established. When the six sense-faculties give rise to delusion without ceasing, and their objects do not return to their source, then the six faculties produce weariness, and the heavy appearance of sensory dusts arises again.
This clarifies that because the six sense-faculties give rise to the six dusts, such as form and so forth.
Therefore, the four lines following "as if weary" employ a metaphor to clarify the meaning of the unremitting arising of delusion. "As if wearying the eyes" means, for example:
If someone stares with fixed eyes for a long time, their vision becomes fatigued;

because of this fatigue of the visual faculty, they perceive illusory flowers (*keśoṇḍuka*) in empty space, arising and ceasing in disorder without any cause. The visual faculty is a metaphor for the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*);

the illusory flowers are a metaphor for the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), which refers below to mountains, rivers, and so forth. "Fatigue" is a metaphor for delusion, while "lucid and brilliant clarity" is a metaphor for the fundamental [nature].

Within the profoundly still nature of awakening (*bodhi*), all inferior dharmas combine to manifest the appearance of dust; the mountains, rivers, and so forth of the mundane world are like the flowers seen by one with cataracts.
The two terms "birth-and-death" (*saṃsāra*) and "nirvāṇa" encompass the full meaning of karma and its fruit. When contrasted with birth-and-death, nirvāṇa likewise belongs to the category of dharmas.
This is because within the profound stillness of original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), not a single dharma can be found; it is devoid of all names, both mundane and supramundane.
These numbers are all like the delusive appearances of a weary mind in a dream;

the term "birth-and-death" (saṃsāra) encompasses all worldly karmic fruits without exception, and the term "nirvāṇa" encompasses all supramundane dharmas without exception, because this concise text subsumes extensive meanings.

This section of the sutra uses Ānanda’s comparison of toil to the knot to request instruction on the method of liberation; the Buddha confirms that by acting upon the center of the knot, it can be untied.
Ānanda’s comparison of toil to the knot refers to the preceding text where the metaphor of the knot represented co-nascent ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*); now, with this...
Regarding the example of binding: "binding" refers to co-nascent ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*), which is precisely the locus of the delusions regarding the false sense bases and objects.
It resides within the six sense faculties and is nothing other than that; therefore, when the Tathāgata of the Dharma-Resolution intends to untie it, he pulls it to the left and right.
This is precisely to demonstrate the method of resolution. "Pulling" means to tug or draw; as for pulling to the left and right, one need only—
Regarding worldly matters, if one attempts to untie the knot from its sides or its ends, it will certainly not come undone.
One must untie it at the very center of the knot; only then will it disperse. The center of the knot is the fundamental source.
As stated above, the mind-nature being deranged is precisely the center of the knot, for it is due to the mind that the knot is formed. Therefore, this is pointed out.

The deranged mind is the fundamental cause and locus of the fetters. In antiquity, by pairing the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism with emptiness and existence on the left and right, the "fettered mind" was used as a metaphor for the Middle Way;
it is said that by entering through the Middle Way, one can sever fundamental ignorance at its root.
This "deranged mind" specifically refers to fundamental ignorance. Therefore, the World-Honored One intentionally draws upon the left and right extremes to lead [beings] toward it.
Having personally realized this, Ānanda understood that the left and right could not be untied; thus he said, "No.

The Buddha then cross-examined him, leading him to explain the method for untying it himself, saying that one should untie it at the very center of the knot. The Buddha further confirmed his realization, restating and completing his understanding.
"Ānanda, I say that the Buddha-dharma arises from causes and conditions" (up to) "...the whiteness of the crane and the blackness of the crow all have their fundamental origins.

This section of the sutra shows the World-Honored One the causes and conditions for untying the knots; it serves as a preemptive response to potential objections, warning that the wondrous cause must produce its fruit rather than merely grasping at the coarse appearances of the world.
He fears there might be an objection stating that the World-Honored One has always taught sudden [enlightenment].
The sending of the causal conditions now serves to tie the heart-knot and untie the knots; since this is neither right nor wrong, it closely resembles causal conditions.

Why, then, do you speak of abandoning them all at once? This is to provide a preemptive clarification: although the Buddha-dharma arises from causal conditions, it is not the coarse phenomenon of worldly conjunction.
It is, rather, the "causal condition of no-causal-conditions" that transcends the world. The Tathāgata lowers his intention here to reveal the nature of the Buddha.

Because he possesses the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), he is able to illuminate both mundane and supramundane phenomena, knowing each one’s fundamental cause (*mūlahetu*) and how it emerges according to its respective conditions (*ālambana*).
The fundamental cause is the primary object, while the conditions are auxiliary; that is, the true cause is made manifest by relying upon conditions.
Just as in the present case of Perfect Penetration (*pariśuddha-avacara*), which serves as the true cause, it must rely upon the twenty-five methods [of practice] as the conditions to be manifested.
If it were not for the perfect and pervasive nature of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), there would be no place from which such things could be manifested.
Thus, extending downward, all phenomena of both the mundane and supramundane realms—without exception—rely upon conditions to manifest their causes.

"Thus, even unto" means from sentient beings down to insentient matter, from those of the same class to those of different classes, whether they be the environment (*bhājana-loka*) or its inhabitants (*sattva-loka*).
Whether great or small, all can be understood through their original source; "original source" here refers to the primary cause.

Since it is not possible to describe them exhaustively here, I speak of them by way of transcendence. Thus, when it says "even as far as worlds outside the sands of the Ganges," this refers to the extremely distant to indicate that the near is likewise knowable.
When it speaks of "a single drop of rain," this refers to the extremely small to indicate that the large is likewise knowable.
"To know" means to know the number of drops as well; that is, to fully and exhaustively know the exact number of raindrops that have fallen.
This is the World-Honored One’s own description of his primordial wisdom (mūla-jñāna), which is profoundly clear and free from error.

Being vast yet without exterior and minute yet without interior, there is nothing it does not comprehend; this describes how the wisdom of all modes (sarvākāra-jñatā) is naturally so, manifest before one.
The latter two phrases refer to insentient things; "various kinds" encompasses everything. This means:
for what reason are pines and cypresses straight, and for what reason are thorns and brambles crooked? The phrase "the crane is white" refers to sentient beings of different species;
for what reason is the crane white, and for what reason is the crow black? "Xuan" (玄) means black. Generally, all cranes are long.
The reasons for such things as the webbed feet of the duck, the height of mountains, and the lowliness of water are all fully understood;

however, the text is concise and mentions only three or four specific instances. This passage is specifically composed to select the perfect penetration (yuan-tong), thereby clarifying that the Tathāgata’s wisdom-mirror is unerring.

This section of the sutra concludes the preceding discussion on resolving causal conditions and instructs one to select from among the six sense faculties to clarify the efficacy of extinguishing delusion and manifesting the real.
The Buddha says: "According to your own mind, choose from among the six faculties whichever corresponds to your capacity."
If one cultivates this, the root-knots will be severed and external objects will naturally cease; once external objects have ceased, internal consciousness will not arise.
When all delusions are eliminated, the true mind will manifest of itself. If you say it is not yet true, what else could you possibly wait for?
"Ānanda, I now ask you: regarding this *karpāsa* cloth (up to the point where it says) 'then when the knots are untied, how is it that they are all removed simultaneously'?

First, from 'I now' onwards, the Buddha asks whether these knots can be removed simultaneously. Next, from 'No' onwards, Ānanda [answers] himself."

"Awakening to the sequence of knots leads to their sequential untying"—this is explained by way of analogy; the application of this principle to the Dharma in the following text can be understood accordingly.
In the initial question, the character *yīng* (縈) is explained: *yīng* means "entanglement," which is precisely the meaning of "knot."
The Buddha said: "The liberation of the six sense faculties is also like this" (up to) "from samādhi, one attains the patience of non-arising.
This section of the sutra applies the preceding metaphors to the Dharma to clarify the sequence of liberating the faculties and the initial realization of their ultimate limit.
The two phrases beginning with "The Buddha said" generally apply the Dharma to these faculties; the phrase "these faculties" corresponds to the sequence mentioned previously. These faculties...

To refer collectively to the six sense faculties means that when the six faculties and the six objects are first resolved, one immediately attains the realization of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*);
this constitutes the first level of emptiness. Why is it that resolving the faculties and objects at the outset leads to the attainment of the emptiness of persons?

"Person" is synonymous with the meaning of "self" (*ātman*). Fundamentally, the binding of the faculties and objects arises because the faculties belong to the self, while the objects are what the self possesses; thus, they are called "mine."
All sentient beings that I have encountered have maintained a firm attachment to "self" and "what belongs to self" from beginningless time until now, never having understood it.
Now that the flow has been reversed and returned to its original unity, the six external sense-objects have no presiding master;
one does not oppose the various objects, and the six knots are naturally untied. Because there is no master, it is called the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*).

"Emptiness" here refers to the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). The two phrases "the nature of emptiness is perfectly luminous" below clarify the meaning of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

The character for "emptiness" in "emptiness-nature" corresponds to the aforementioned emptiness of persons; this is because while the emptiness of persons merely empties the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), it does not empty the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).

If the emptiness-nature of the emptiness of persons also shines forth universally and without attachment, then the grasping at phenomena is likewise emptied; therefore, it is called the "emptiness of phenomena."
The liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa*) is another name for emptiness itself; this constitutes the second level of emptiness.

The two phrases concerning "having liberated the dharmas" clarify the third level of emptiness. This means that once the emptiness of dharmas has been attained as described above, even the emptiness of that dharma-emptiness does not arise.
Since both the person and the dharmas—along with their respective emptinesses—do not arise, it is said that they are "both empty and non-arising."

The title concludes by manifesting the efficacy of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). This practice of perfect penetration is precisely the aforementioned three—wondrous relaxation (*miao-xie*) and so forth—which constitute the essential substance of the samādhi of perfect penetration.
Because one does not investigate perfect penetration apart from these three, it is said that "one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) from samādhi.
"Attaining the patience of non-arising" refers to the meaning of realizing the fruit of fruition. As...
The previous explanation followed the sequence of the metaphors from top to bottom, which cannot be properly aligned here; it should instead be understood through the underlying intent.

According to the Dharma, however, there are three layers of sequential resolution: regarding the Dharma, when the six sense faculties are first resolved, they proceed from the outside toward the inside.
Regarding the reiteration of the sequence: this constitutes a vertical exposition, which differs from the horizontal and vertical sequences in the preceding analogies;
this is a partial analogy rather than a complete one. Scholars must not become fixated on the order within the analogy and attempt to force a correspondence.
Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the Buddha’s instruction [up to the point of] withdrawing into the secret mechanism, hoped for the Buddha’s silent transmission.

This section of the sutra, in which Ānanda follows the principle of the "extinction of the one and the six" to earnestly request a detailed exposition of the perfect faculty, clearly allows us to perceive the sincerity of his words.
That which is called "perfect penetration through wisdom-awakening" is precisely the meaning of the extinction of the one and the six; this is because the assembly...

Due to the arising of delusion, this originally inherent wisdom-awareness (*prajñā*) is transformed into the six sense-faculties; thus, their six functions oppose one another and cannot achieve perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*).
Now that the six knots have been untied, even "one" is no longer maintained. The former six faculties revert to wisdom-awareness, achieving perfect penetration.
What was previously discordant is now harmonized and fused. One must know that the six faculties and wisdom-awareness are fundamentally [identical].
The fault does not lie in the two dharmas themselves; rather, it is because the divergence between delusion and awakening causes their application to differ.

Therefore, immediately following the six modes of liberation, [the text] refers to them as "the perfect penetration of wisdom and awakening. The scribe skillfully narrates this intent so that the reader may awaken to the *kaṇabhuj* (the ear).
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "Below this is my own account of the signs of attaining awakening; my body and mind are now radiantly clear."
"Body" refers to the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*), and "mind" refers to the *ālayavijñāna*. Since both the "one" and the "six" have vanished, the constant light first shines forth;

thus it is said that body and mind are pure and bright, and one joyfully attains non-obstruction. Although [the text] below formally requests [an explanation], the meaning has not yet been fully understood;
that is to say, although one has realized the principle that the "one" and "six" have vanished, among the six sense organs, one has not yet reached clarity as to which one is [the true organ].

Because the fundamental root of perfect penetration was [not yet understood], he respectfully requested further instruction. The World-Honored One [responded]. Below, the Venerable One details his sense of personal joy;
this serves as a sincere expression of his petition for the Dharma. The two lines beginning with "We... first describe the delusion accumulated over kalpas:
"drifting" refers to being tossed about, and "falling" refers to being scattered. This describes wandering through birth and death, rushing about without refuge.
The meaning is that to have no one to rely upon is called "solitary," and to have no covering is called "exposed.

To be without support and without protection—such suffering has accumulated over many kalpas and is indeed profound. Nevertheless, since beginningless kalpas, I do not know with what intention or concern I was predestined to become a member of the Buddha’s celestial kin;
this is truly a cause for self-congratulation. The term "celestial kin" refers to brothers; as for the following two lines, they clarify the point through metaphor.
Regarding this encounter: having been orphaned and destitute for accumulated kalpas, like a child who has lost its mother’s milk, my hunger and exhaustion were nearly at an end.
What great fortune it was that I suddenly met the World-Honored One, who, like a compassionate mother, rescued me with the milk of the Dharma, allowing my life of wisdom to continue.
Furthermore, [the text] below correctly requests what is shown: since I rejoice in this personal cause, my meeting with him is no shallow matter; furthermore, because of...
If, at this juncture, one attains the wondrous Way, then the subtle and esoteric words obtained will lead to awakening through those very words;

since the Way is fundamentally one's own mind and is not obtained from without, it is said that one returns to what was originally awakened. Regarding the phrase "originally awakened," there is an omission in the subsequent text such that the preceding and following parts do not cohere;
it should be supplemented as follows: "If you do not show me the fundamental root of perfect penetration, I shall have no way [to proceed]."
If those who cultivate and advance through consciousness merely obtain the secret words (*mantra*), there is no difference between this and not having heard them at all;

it is only when the meaning of the text is fully established that [the purpose is realized]. May you deign to provide the concluding words of inquiry to bestow upon me the majestic secrecy. To give an object to an inferior is an act of grace (*anugraha*);

"secrecy" (*guhya*) refers to that which is hidden, the most extreme form of being hidden. "Majestic" (*vyūha*) means adornment (*alaṃkāra*). "Majestic Secrecy" (*guhyavyūha*) is an exclamation praising that which is requested.

Regarding the "final revelation of the Dharma," this refers to the selection of those with perfect faculties (*indriya*), which occurs only after the principles have been manifested; hence it is called the "final revelation.
As for "withdrawing and concealing the secret mechanism," it is like the phrase from the *Zhou Yi*, the "Shang Zhuan": "Withdrawing and concealing within the profound.
That text says: "The virtues of the *shī* (divining stalks), the hexagrams, and the lines—these three—are the virtues by which the Sage washes his mind and withdraws [from the world]."
This was concealed in secret and is now employed to clarify Ānanda’s intention of restraining his mind and awaiting the Dharma, hoping for the Buddha’s subtle transmission.

"Hoping" (jì) refers to this aspiration; the character "subtle" (míng) should be read in conjunction with the preceding character "secret" (mì). The meaning is that he hopes the Buddha will silently discern his secret capacity and skillfully bestow the wondrous Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the entire assembly... [omitted] ...by what means does one enter samādhi?
This section of the sutra records the Buddha’s acceptance of their request and his general address to the great assembly, commanding each to recount the initial cause for entering the Path.
Those "born within my Dharma" refers to the sentient beings among the listeners of the Three Vehicles who have been born within the Buddha-dharma of Śākyamuni.

The reason why only the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*) are mentioned therein, rather than the seven elements (*saptamahābhūta*), is that the intention is to show that the seven elements are themselves the eighteen realms.
Thus, while the general inquiry mentions only the eighteen realms, the subsequent detailed exposition further opens them into the seven elements.

This is done to correspond in advance to the threefold contemplation of the *Miaoshan* (Wondrous Contemplation) chapter, wherein the seven elements manifest the meaning of *dhyāna*. Furthermore, this demonstrates the principle of the mutual fusion of inclusion and exclusion.
Because all [methods] are encompassed without obstruction, one should know that the twenty-five sages all extol the skillful means of their initial attainment of the Way;
these dharmas of perfect penetration are such that there is no entry into the Path that is not suitable.

It is precisely because the sentient beings of this realm possess sharp faculties of hearing that the faculty of the ear was specifically selected to accord with the capacities of those in this region; among all the sages, there was originally no superiority or inferiority.
This inferior [teaching] is intended to show Ānanda the faults of excessive erudition, serving as a preliminary guide for the sentient beings of this realm.

Nevertheless, although these various sages intermingle the Great and Small vehicles and alternate between the Partial and Perfect teachings—differing though they may in their respective approaches and depths—their entry into the inner hall is one and the same.
Here, I shall speak only of the skillful means by which one may enter, without making distinctions based on the Partial or the Perfect.
This concerns the demotion and promotion [of the disciples].
The five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya, immediately rose from their seats... up to "...as I have realized, sound is supreme.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding [passage] to specifically recount the first skillful means (*upāya*) of the initial cause. It is a specific narrative.
This is divided into twenty-five sections. This first section concerns the arising of the eighteen *dhātus*. Among these, the six sense objects (*viṣaya*) are explained first.
Rather than listing form (*rūpa*) first, sound (*śabda*) is listed because Kauṇḍinya was among those whose years and age were highest and who were the very first to be ordained by the Buddha;
therefore, sound is mentioned first. In Sanskrit, Kauṇḍinya is translated as "Fire-Vessel" (*Kauṇḍinya*); he was previously an outsider who worshipped fire.
In later generations, the Daoist school continued to regard [the Buddha] as having been of the same clan as his maternal uncle. As for the five bhikṣus, including Cunda, there were five individuals:
(1) Aśvajit, translated as "Horse-Winner," who was of the Buddha’s own family; (2) Bhadrika, translated as "Little Wise One," also of the Buddha’s family;
(3) Kātyāyana, which has no direct equivalent, who was of the Buddha’s maternal uncle’s clan; and (5) Kauṇḍinya.
The Crown Prince [Mahānāman] was the son of King Droṇodana and likewise a member of the Buddha’s clan.

Regarding the circumstances at the Deer Park, as recorded in the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions), I fear that further detail would be too prolix and thus omit it. As for Kukkutārāma, the ninth sūtra of the *Saṃyukta Āgama* states that there was the Kukkutārāma in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra;
this is the place where those who first beheld the Buddha saw him when he had recently attained enlightenment. Formerly, the Buddha...
At midnight on the first night, he left the city to renounce the world and traveled into the Snowy Mountains.

His father the King, missing him deeply, commanded three members of his own clan and two from his maternal uncle’s family to search for him to serve as companions. Once they had joined him, before long each of them abandoned him and departed;
he dwelt alone in the Deer Park, practicing the methods of non-Buddhist ascetics. For six years he lived alone in the Snowy Mountains, consuming only hemp and wheat for his daily sustenance.
Having already attained the Way, [the Buddha] first fulfilled his vow to deliver these five men; he immediately went to the Deer Park and turned the Wheel of Dharma three times.
Thus it is said, "He saw the Buddha attain the Way. The two lines following "at the Buddha" retrospectively recount the causes for their awakening.

Those who heard the Buddha’s Four Truths—namely suffering (*duḥkha*), accumulation (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*)—[realized that] suffering is the fruit of suffering, while accumulation is the cause of suffering, having been accumulated since beginningless time.
Because it accumulates karmic formations, it is called "origination" (*samudaya*); since suffering as a fruit is summoned by karma as its cause, this is the worldly cause-and-effect.
Cessation (*nirodha*) is quiescence, meaning that one extinguishes the aforementioned origination of suffering and realizes *nirvāṇa*;
this is the supramundane cause-and-effect. As for the term "truth" (*satya*), "truth" means—
Because the four meanings of "reality" (satya) are all real, and because one perceives the true nature in all four, they are also called the Four Noble Truths (*catur-āryasatya*).
Dignāga first explained that the Buddha sealed this name as *ājñāta*; *ājñāta* is translated as "already understood.

"Sealing" (*mudrā*) has the meaning of "eliminating error. Now, by discerning whether confusion or understanding is permissible, it is termed "seal of verification" (*ājñātamudrā*), according to Ghoṣaka.

Regarding "mysterious and perfect" (*miyuan*): "sound" refers to the sound of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths; because these truths are coarse and shallow, yet from them true realization is produced, they are called "wondrously mysterious" (*miaomi*) and "perfect" (*yuan*).

In the following two lines, I clarify the attainment of the fruit through merit. After the Buddha asks about the various forms of perfect penetration (*yuantong*), he concludes by asking about their respective meanings.
Hereafter, the twenty-five sages each enter through their own gate, using that which they entered themselves as the basis for their explanation.
It is called "Supreme" because it is the Dharma realized by each of the Honored Ones; furthermore,

The phrase "the nature of awakening" (*prativedha-svabhāva*) establishes the designation of "self" (*ātman*) based on that which is awakened. Regarding the words "at that time," etc., this correctly describes the initial cause.

As for "Buddha and others": having received the Dharma-gate, he temporarily left his seat before the Buddha; "banqueting" (*yan*) refers to peaceful repose, and "concealment" (*hui*) refers to remaining hidden.
This means he rested peacefully in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) while concealing his traces, not dwelling among the multitude. "Pure chamber" (*qingzhai*) refers to a pure and clean room.

Regarding the two lines concerning fragrance: fragrance possesses the quality of permeating subtly; although one has not yet received the smoke, the subtle flavor of tranquility has already reached the nose.
"Smoke" is spoken of from the perspective of its coarse and manifest aspect, while the "flavor of tranquility" is spoken of from the perspective of its subtle permeation.
As the third sutra says: "When that smoke rises into the air and has not yet traveled far, how could it not reach within forty li?"
I have already heard the correct explanation of the profound, quiescent nature of emptiness—the meaning that it is neither identical to nor separate from [phenomena].

"I observe below" refers to relying on the realization of existence as non-existence. That "the fragrance is obtainable in four places" means it is non-existent in those four ways. As for "non-existent," it means:

We know that fragrance does not reside in the wood, for smoke is not aloeswood; since the nose has not encountered the smoke, how could it perceive the scent?
Thus we know by faith that fragrance does not exist within the smoke. Space is neither arising nor ceasing, so from where does the fragrance come?

Space has no inherent nature, so with what intent would it produce fragrance? Thus we know by faith that fragrance does not exist within space. If fragrance were produced because of fire, then it should have existed before the wood was ignited.

If fire does not possess fragrance, one can know with certainty that fragrance does not belong to fire. Since fragrance is absent in these four elements, the nature of fragrance is illusory; the illusory nature is fundamentally empty.
Therefore, when departing there is no attachment, and when arriving there is no source. Emptiness is originally without arising, yet through false perception, coming and going are seen.
Thus, the following two lines clarify the attainment of the fruit through spiritual practice. The word "thereby" (yousi) refers back to the aforementioned four absences.

As for the merit of this awakening: since the four locations are not the fragrance, the nature of smelling is also empty. From fragrance, the true principle of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) is revealed;

Having received the seal of approval from the Buddha, one truly earns the name "brother" (bhrātṛ), signifying a true sibling.
