In the preceding and following chapters, it is consistently stated that [the interlocutor] "immediately rose from his seat"; yet here, this Venerable One does not mention rising from his seat.
This is truly because the Venerable One manifested a vajra-body as a protector and attendant, and since no formal seat was established, he did not speak of "rising from my seat.
Below, in the section beginning with "I always," the cause for awakening is correctly clarified; those who possess much greed and desire are about to be described in their realization.
First, I shall set forth the cause of delusion; once one attains awakening through delusion, then delusion itself becomes the cause of awakening.
As for the Buddha named Śūnyarāja (King of Emptiness), it is largely unknown in which past kalpa he was called Śūnyarāja. "Emptiness" refers to the *tathāgatagarbha*;
because one who realizes this essence attains mastery over all phenomena, they are called the King of Emptiness. [This applies even to] those with much lust.
Regarding the phrase "becoming a mass of fierce fire": desire is fundamentally fire; when desire is excessive, it becomes a multitude of fires, hence the term "mass of fire.
The passage beginning with "teach me" refers to the practice of cultivation through the Dharma. The "hundred limbs and four members" refers to the body as a whole.

Within the body, there is the breath of cold and warmth; this warm breath belongs to the element of fire. Because the fire of desire is intense, one applies effort based upon that very fire. As for "he": [this refers to the practitioner].

The Buddha, by means of this, revealed the method of the Fire-Light Samādhi (*tejovatī-samādhi*), instructing him to contemplate fire. Within the text, the character for "cold" (*leng*) is mentioned alongside "warmth" (*nuan*);

by perceiving cold in contrast to warmth, one simultaneously grasps the nature of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). One should apply effort specifically to the element of warmth in order to contemplate fire.
Since fire is fundamentally without form, from what could it possibly arise? When one contemplates in this manner for a long time, the divine light will coalesce within.

The divine light (*śen-guang*) is precisely the light of the mind. Although one does not speak of "mind" but rather of "divine," this is because when one contemplates the fire of desire, it cannot be apprehended;
that which is purely still and yet unfathomable is termed "divine.
Since the divine is immovable and concentrated, it is said that the divine light is internally coagulated. This very state transforms the lustful mind into the fire of wisdom.
Once the fire of wisdom is perfected, the merit of the Samādhi of Fire-Light is fulfilled.
By virtue of this merit, beginning from the time of the Buddha King of Emptiness (*Śūnyarāja*), he has served all Buddhas; they have all called him by the name "Fire-Head" (*Jvālāmukha*).
He is called "Fire-Head" because a sign of flames must appear upon his head, manifesting the posture for subduing demons and making a vow to manifest as a Vajra-body.
The following two lines clarify the attainment of the fruit through merit: the first line clarifies the merit, and the second line clarifies the attainment of the fruit.

"By the power of samādhi" means that by virtue of the power of the Fire-Light Samādhi (*jvālā-pradīpa-samādhi*), one severs the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and realizes the fruit.
"The mind is aroused" refers to turning the mind of a *śrāvaka* toward the Bodhisattva path. "The Mighty One" (*bala*) is the original name of Vajra; he personally subdues Māra.
A single phrase of resentment is the actual manifestation of a great vow; by means of protecting the Dharma, one subdues demonic adversaries.
In the passage beginning with "The Buddha asked," the current meaning of the question is summarized. The following six phrases refer to the primary cause:

through true contemplation, one realizes that the sensation of warmth within the body and the fire-element of the external world are non-dual and indistinguishable, such that they do not obstruct one another. This signifies the mutual inclusion of the body and the land.

Therefore it is said that the phrases regarding the unimpeded circulation of all outflows (*āsrava*)—if viewed in light of the subsequent phrase concerning "unsurpassed enlightenment"—must necessarily encompass ignorance (*avidyā*).

It is only by destroying ignorance that the "jewel-flame" (*ratnajvālā*) arises. Regarding this metaphorical expression, "jewel" refers to the jewel of the mind, while "flame" refers to *prajñā* (wisdom).
This indicates that only through the realization of the true wisdom of the perfect mind does one attain unsurpassed [enlightenment].
Because it is an awakening, the final phrase expresses the effect within the cause.
The Bodhisattva Earth-Holder immediately rose from his seat... [until]... achieving the Unsurpassed Way; this is the foremost.
This section of the sutra follows the previous passage to specifically describe the nineteen skillful means of the initial cause; it concerns the causal ground within these seven great elements.
The Bodhisattva is named "Earth-Holder" (Dharaṇīdhara); according to the text, he received this name based on his virtue of using his strength to level uneven terrain and push heavy wheels.
From the words "I remember... onwards, the text properly clarifies the cause of awakening in the past, under the Universal Radiance Buddha (Samantaprabhāsa).
Is it not the case that the Tathāgata is none other than the first of the fifty-three buddhas whose names were revealed by the Buddha in the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-bhaiṣajyasamudgata-sūtra*?

If so, then although Śākyamuni Buddha went forth into homelessness during the final dharma period of the Buddha Prabhāsa countless kalpas ago, he merely heard the names of these fifty-three buddhas; thus, [the Tathāgata] is indeed the Buddha Prabhāsa.
Going further and further—this is the fundamental distance of a bodhisattva.
At that time, acting as a bhikṣu and practicing various austerities, he encountered improper and perilous places on main roads, ferry crossings, and fields;

these were called "perilous" because they consisted of high and low cliffs, precipices, slopes, and treacherous bends, or because the paths were narrow, situated on dangerous heights, or bordered by water, marshes, and embankments.
Where there were ditches that obstructed the passage of carts and horses, causing wheels and hooves to stumble and fall, the Bodhisattva leveled the high ground and filled in the depressions.
Where water eddied to form sheer cliffs, he constructed bridges;
where shifting terrain had turned into ditches and canals, he filled them with sand and earth. Thus did he labor with tireless diligence.
It was not merely for one or two lifetimes that he passed through immeasurable kalpas of dust-like eons during which countless Buddhas appeared;
nor did he manifest solely in the form of a bhikṣu according to his kind, but rather caused the vow to uphold the earth to remain unforgotten life after life as he cultivated the ground.
Or perhaps, to demonstrate his humility, he acted as a porter; yet being a porter is necessarily a worldly appearance—how could he have been a bhikṣu acting as a porter? Or...

When people in a bustling marketplace require someone to carry their goods, a Bodhisattva will carry them to their destination; once the goods have been set down, he departs without taking any payment for his labor.
This demonstrates that carrying others is the practice of a Bodhisattva. A "huan" (闤) refers to the market wall, and a "hai" (闠) refers to the market gate.
"Qing" (擎) means to carry or bear; "zhi" (直) refers to the price or value of the burden. [The Buddha] is immeasurable in such power.

One does not know how many *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas like the sands of the Ganges have passed. Although it is said that when the mind-ground is leveled, all things are leveled, one must not neglect either the principle (*li*) or the phenomena (*shi*).
If one realizes them within the mind, then length and brevity, toil and ease, are fundamentally non-dual.
Therefore, Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, manifesting the fruit while practicing the cause, return to the midst of worldly afflictions to perform various Buddha-works.
The body of the pure *dharmadhātu* is fundamentally without appearing or disappearing; it is like the moon in the sky, whose reflection appears simultaneously in a thousand rivers.

What division could there be in the moon? This can be generally verified. Regarding the citation of the events of the time of Viśvabhū below: *Viśvabhū* is translated as "Pervasive Sovereignty over All.
"All" refers to all phenomena (*dharma*), and "sovereignty" has the meaning of "king"; thus, it means that his Dharma is sovereign over all.
Because his body pervades all phenomena and he has attained mastery over them, he is the final Buddha of the thousand Buddhas of the past *Vyūha-kalpa*.

Whereas previously it was said that he would not accept what was owed to him, now, due to the famine of the world, regardless of whether the debt was incurred far or near, he accepted only a single coin to provide for his food.
At this time, the person to whom he owed the debt was not the same individual as the debtor mentioned in the preceding passage; it was someone else entirely.
In this world, because one takes birth as a burden upon others, one accepts or refuses payment according to the conditions of the world.
Although he was named "Earth-Holder" (Dharaṇīdhara), his carrying of objects and pushing the wheel were merely secondary acts of that Earth-Holder.
At that time, when King Aśoka was observing the fast for the Tathāgata Viśvabhū, the Bodhisattva leveled the ground to await the Buddha, even to the extent of using his own body.
This refers to such acts as spreading one's hair on the ground to cover the mud while walking.
That Buddha, pitying his ascetic practices, rubbed the crown of his head to comfort him and instructed him that if he were to level the mind of the ground, then all things would be leveled;
this means that the myriad dharmas are but the mind, and when the mind is level, the earth is level. As the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says: "When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. Therefore, I...
The following section correctly demonstrates the characteristics of awakening and clarifies that this awakening involves seeing the body and so forth as equal;
that is to say, the atoms within the body and the atoms of the vessel-world are equal and non-dual. As for "weapons and the like," these also belong to the number of atoms;

because one has realized emptiness, how could they possibly cause harm? From "I" onwards, the text clarifies the attainment of the fruit through merit. The first two lines clarify the merit, while the latter two... [the text here appears truncated].

The first two lines [of the verse] explain the attainment of the fruit of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) through seeing; the latter two lines further clarify the cause for turning back from the Lesser Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle.

Regarding the phrase "hearing all [Buddhas]," this proclaims the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. At the end of the "Universal Gate" chapter (*Samantamukha-parivarta*), the Bodhisattva Dharaṇīśvara spoke of the merit of hearing this chapter;
what is here called "hearing all Buddhas" means encountering immeasurable Buddhas and thereby hearing [the Dharma].
The *Liang* [Dynasty] Buddha proclaimed the wondrous meaning of the Lotus; this is an example of subsuming the latter back into the former, such as the case of the "Equal" (Samatā) [chapter].

"Buddha-knowledge and vision" refers to the intent of the "Expedient Means" chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra*, for therein lies the opening, showing, awakening, and entering into Buddha-knowledge and vision.
As for the "stages," these refer to the positions (*bhūmi*); Tiantai assigned the four stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering to the forty positions. This is roughly the general outline.
The Buddha taught that the three vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings contain both the provisional and the real; once these have been revealed, all are seen as real.
What was provisional in the past becomes real today—meaning there is no provisional outside of the real, for the provisional exists within the real.
One must understand this intent regarding the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to avoid error. This present sutra belongs to the Vaipulya (Vaipulya) class.
The "Middle Round" (Zhongyuan) and the "Middle Round" of the *Lotus Sūtra* are non-dual and without distinction; since there is no further need for revelation, this statement is made.
When I previously testified, it was precisely to testify to the *Universal Gate Chapter* (*Pumenpin*), which attains identity with the *Lotus Sūtra* through the manifestation of reality (*dharmatā*);
thus, it is called the "foremost. Regarding the Buddha’s question below, this concludes the meaning of the present inquiry. From "I" onwards, the four lines summarize the cause.

The phrase "practicing the realization of perfect penetration" means that by contemplating the two objects—the body and the sense-field—one attains awakening to the hidden nature (tathāgatagarbha) as being illusory.
The following three phrases mean that when deluded feelings are exhausted, true wisdom becomes perfect and the Way of Enlightenment is accomplished.
The youth Candraprabha immediately rose from his seat... [omitted] ...to perfect enlightenment; this is the foremost.
This section of the sutra separately recounts the twenty expedient means of the initial cause. Among these seven elements, this is the element of water.
As for the youth Candraprabha, he is so named because he was called "Moonlight" due to his initial practice of the contemplation of water (*āp-kṛtsnāyatana*).
The moon is the essence of yin and is able to produce water; however, there is a further meaning that transcends words:

it implies that when a pond is formed, the moon comes of its own accord. Furthermore, there is another sense: water represents the Bodhisattva’s contemplative mind (*citta-vipaśyanā*), while the moon represents *bodhi*.
As it is said, "When the water of the sentient beings' minds is pure, the reflection of *bodhi* appears therein"; thus it is called "moonlight. (Wenling)

This refers to the former master Jalambara (Water-Heaven), who practiced the contemplation of water (*jala-bhāvanā*) until the nature of water became perfectly luminous; thus he was named Candraprabha (Moonlight).

His intention is largely the same as yours, yet his clarification of the nature of water is incomplete, and his underlying intent regarding "moon" is not fully realized; therefore, he does not provide an excellent interpretation of the name Jalambara. The meaning of that name is likewise this:
"water" is the water of the mind, and "heaven" is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). When the water of the mind is purified, it is the Ultimate Heaven.
Reflected within it, I recall that this is precisely the cause for awakening through the instruction of the water-contemplation (*āpasmṛti*). Regarding those who practice water-contemplation:

this water-contemplation is one of the ten *kṛtsnāyatana* (totality) concentrations. What is manifested by these *kṛtsnāyatana* concentrations is "concentration-resultant form" (*samādhiniṣyandavarṇa*). It exists when one has entered concentration and does not exist when one has emerged from it.
That bystanders are now able to see it is due to the superior power of that concentration, much like the case of Master Cōngchán.
Entering the *tejodhātu-samādhi* (fire-light samādhi), the mountain valleys are as if incinerated;
this is identical in meaning to the present account of how the Śākya World-Honored One subdued the fire-dragon, causing the stone grotto to blaze forth.

Regarding the power of downward contemplation (*adhaḥ-pratyavekṣaṇā-bala*), it penetrates deeply to unify the "dependent" and the "primary"—that is, the water-element within the body and the water-element of the external vessel-world. First, the various waters within the body circulate and flow back and forth.
Since they do not obstruct one another, although the fluids, excretions, and impurities differ, their watery nature is inherently the same.

Next, one perceives that the water within one’s own body and the water of the external vessel-world are equal and without distinction; thus, there is no obstruction between the environment and its inhabitants.
Regarding the phrase "floating pavilions and fragrant waters," the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Formation of the World," states: "This Flower Treasury Adornment..."
In the most lower fragrant-water sea of the Arrayed World-Ocean, there is a great lotus named Calyx-Fragrance Banner (*Kesaragandhadhvaja*).
It now floats because it has emerged above the waters of the fragrant sea; thus, that which supports the world like the stalk of a lotus is called a "banner" (*dhvaja*).
Upon the platform of this banner, there is another fragrant-water sea, and within each of these seas, there are twenty-fold Flower-Treasury Worlds (*kusumagarbha-lokadhātu*).
Because it gives birth to all lands (*kṣetra*), it is called a "land-cluster" (*kṣetra-vaṃśa*); in the present text, "cluster" is rendered as "king," which likewise carries the meaning of "seed.
"At this time" refers to the period when the Buddha Jaladharagarbha [was present].

Regarding the phrase "first accomplishing this contemplation" and so forth, it means that when the contemplation of water is first accomplished but one has not yet attained the "bodiless state," the mark of self (*ātman*) has not yet been eliminated; thus, the statement "not yet forgetting the body" is precisely [to indicate this stage].
The following passage describes the omens of heart-pain; hereafter, the reasons for this heart-pain shall be clarified, the text of which is easily understood.
Indeed, the water of the mind is neither existent nor non-existent; it is the wondrous form (*rūpa*) of emptiness.

Since coarse substances such as tiles and pebbles do not accord with its nature, because the body has not yet perished, the omen of heart-pain arises. The two lines following "like a house" cite an analogy for this pain.

In the past, while Śāriputra was in meditative absorption within an araṇya on the banks of the Ganges, two kingly ghosts—who were his宿怨 (past enemies)—struck him with their hands, causing him sudden headaches.

Now, Candraprabha suspects that [the current situation] is the same as that, yet because he has not attained supernatural powers (abhijñā), his suspicions remain unresolved. The text following "At that time" can be understood as follows: the young boy...
The son reported what he had seen; "swift" (*jié*) refers to the meaning of rapidity, implying that not long after the doubt arose, the youth came quickly to report this.

"Turning away from life" (*zhuǎnmìng*) and "removing [it]" (*qūchú*) and so forth can be understood accordingly. "Encountering the Immeasurable... and below clarifies the difficulty of casting off the body.

Regarding the Buddha "Sovereign King of Unhindered Penetration through Mountains and Seas," those with the same name are no fewer than ten or more; it is unknown in which eon this "Sovereign King" lived. According to the text...
Among the fifty-three Buddhas, there are Water-Heaven Buddha (*Vāruṇa*) and Universal-King Buddha (*Samantārāja*); however, beneath "Mountain and Sea" there is a character for "wisdom" (*hui*).
This means that at the time of translation, this character for "wisdom" was omitted, and it was only after an exhaustive investigation that it could be recovered.

Below, the attainment of merit and the realization of the fruit are clarified, as well as the non-duality of the primary and secondary [retributions]. In the first section above, one simply contemplates that the nature of water, both internal and external, cannot be deprived.
Having not yet realized the Truth, one now understands that it is not merely that the "supported" (the environment) and the "supporter" (the body) are fused;

because the self is extinguished, the nature of water—both internal and external—cannot be apprehended, and all thus accords with true emptiness. Since the whole body is the Tathāgatagarbha, it is said to be "without duality and without distinction.
Furthermore, by turning back from the Small Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle and attaining the name of "Childlike Purity," one then understands the meaning of the following five phrases.
Furthermore, regarding the fruit obtained through the three subsequent phrases, the Buddha asks about them below to conclude the present inquiry into their meaning.

"The nature of water flows through as a single flavor" precisely clarifies that one attains perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*) by means of the contemplation of water. "Obtaining [the state] below" in the two subsequent phrases is a pre-emptive indication of the ultimate fruit.
Moreover, within this chapter there are two types of meaning: general and specific. From "Even if one contemplates" below, up to "equal and without," [the general meaning is established].
The preceding section is a general and brief summary; from "From me" (*wǒ yú*) down to the end of the chapter is the specific and detailed exposition, which can be understood through careful study.
The Dharma Prince Lapis Lazuli Light (*Lǚlíguāng Fǎwángzǐ*) immediately rose from his seat... (until) "transmitting this one wondrous mind is the foremost."
This section of the sutra continues from the preceding passage to specifically enumerate the twenty-one skillful means of the initial cause.

Among these seven great elements, this refers to the cause of wind. The Bodhisattva named Vaidūryaprabha (Lapis Lazuli Light) attained this name because he realized that the various signs of deluded conditions and collective movement are all set in motion by the power of wind;
when their movement ceases, wisdom becomes luminous and there is no obstruction between the internal and external, thus becoming like lapis lazuli.
Clarity is the essence and light is the function; apart from the lapis lazuli, there is no separate light-function.
This serves as a metaphor for the function that is identical to the essence and the essence that is identical to the function; because essence and function are non-dual, both are mentioned together.

Furthermore, the complete transparency of the lapis lazuli serves as a metaphor for the wind-essence being signless. "I remember" and below clarify the cause of awakening; the Buddha’s name is Immeasurable.
Regarding "sound" (*śabda*), it is also designated based on wind with two intended meanings: First, by observing that the great element of wind has no fixed support, all the apertures roar;
because these many apertures produce sounds according to immeasurable causes, and because the fruit accords with the cause, the Buddha is named "Immeasurable Sound.
Second, regarding the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma, it accords with the capacities of sentient beings; since those capacities vary, [the sound varies accordingly].

The distinction between sharp and dull faculties results in the sudden and gradual approaches; this is named according to the benefit of others. The section beginning with "Revealing and showing" clarifies the intent of transmitting the teaching:
for those of the Bodhisattva vehicle, it is taught that fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) is wondrously luminous.

This refers to the nature of all movement, wherein the fact that all movements are non-moving is precisely the wondrously luminous true essence. Therefore, the subsequent section provides a detailed explanation of all movements in order to clarify true awakening.
There is no duality. The world is the support, and sentient beings are the primary support; the movement of these primary supports is all driven by the power of wind.
I shall clarify below that the characteristics of these various movements differ from those of the world.

Because "world" (*loka*) refers to spatial orientation, it is said to be "established," meaning established as the cardinal directions. Because "age" (*kāla*) refers to temporal flux, it is said to be "moving"; "time" here refers to the past and present.

Since it has not yet been stated that the body functions through movement and stillness, it says "moving and stopping. Because the deluded mind lacks constancy and undergoes transformation moment by moment, it says "moving thoughts.
Although the manifestations of movement differ in a thousand ways, the nature of movement is one; thus it says "the manifold movements are non-dual.

When the Bodhisattva attains profound insight, he perceives that within all movements there is no movement; how, then, could there be coming or going? Thus it says "there is nowhere from which [they arise]. 10.
Consider the sentient beings within a single mote of dust as all equally subject to inverted delusion, ranging from the vast to the narrow;
even all sentient beings within a single great trichiliocosm are like hundreds of mosquitoes contained within a single vessel—“contained” meaning they are held therein.
The vessel is a metaphor for the world-system, and the hundreds of mosquitoes are a metaphor for sentient beings; their chirping and clamorous noise is a metaphor for various forms of speech.
To stir up wild clamor within a mere fraction [of the path] means that although one’s intention for awakening is great, what one perceives is small.
"Meeting a Buddha" below clarifies that those who attain the fruit after not much time have not yet encountered many Buddhas;

because they possess the Mahayana root, they immediately attain the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*). When the mind of patience opens and moves, it accords with the immovable; thus, one sees the Unmoving.
In the eastern direction of the Buddha-land, the position of the Earth-shaking (Zhèn), there is a Buddha named "Immovable" (Bùdòng), which signifies that movement is itself immovability.
His attainment of patience (*kṣānti*) clarifies his merit; his being seen by the Buddhas as a Dharma Prince signifies his attainment of the fruit.

By employing his own wisdom to act throughout the ten directions, his body and mind develop the light of Immovable Wisdom (*akṣobhya-jñāna*). This light penetrates all movements, such that movement itself is non-movement.
Because it moves, it is unimpeded. The Buddha’s question below concludes the preceding; the current inquiry concerns its meaning. Regarding the six phrases beginning with "I":
"The power of wind has no support" means that the power of wind is movement, and the characteristic of movement has no support. It comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
Because one realizes this lack of support, one awakens to the Bodhicitta and enters right concentration; thus, by means of this very mind, one unites with the minds of all Buddhas.
Because the Buddhas transmit to one another solely by means of the One Mind, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha rose from his seat... [until] ...this perfect clarity of wondrous power is the foremost.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding passage by specifically enumerating the twenty-two expedient means of the initial cause.

Among these seven great elements, this refers to the element of space. The Bodhisattva is named Ākāśagarbha because, by contemplating that the four great elements and form are themselves empty, he realized non-dual emptiness and attained an infinite body;
the name is established based on this merit, hence he is called Ākāśagarbha.
However, because it is not a nihilistic emptiness (*uccheda-śūnyatā*), it is able to accommodate all skillful means for benefiting beings.

By adding the character "Zang" (Treasury/Storehouse), it becomes identical to the realization attained by the World-Honored One under Dīpaṃkara Buddha regarding the emptiness of the nature of form (*rūpa-svabhāva-śūnyatā*). Thus, his realization of the merit of the Boundless Body (*anantakāya*) is equal and harmonious with the Way.
Now, as this also participates in the "Accomplishing through Resources" (*sambhāra-niṣpatti*), there is nothing that is not permissible. Dīpaṃkara is none other than the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.

At that time, the following section clearly elucidates the cause of awakening. As for "holding four precious jewels in his hands," the hand serves as a symbol to express the meaning, while the jewels serve as a symbol for form (*rūpa*).
Since form is precisely Prajñā, one contemplates the forms of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as being without support;
this lack of support is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and emptiness is the essence of Prajñā. Since form is the function of Prajñā, it is said that he "holds four jewels in his hands."

However, by means of the light of *prajñā*, the forms and transformations of all lands and atoms are illumined and transformed into emptiness; it is not that form is extinguished to become empty, but rather that form itself is emptiness.
Furthermore, below this, the mirror is used as a metaphor for the mind, because the mind integrates the ten realms; thus it is said:
"The Great Perfect Mirror manifests and emits ten kinds of light. The Great Perfect Mirror is the name for fundamental wisdom (*jñāna*), and this wisdom arises from the mind.
This is because the wisdom of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-jñāna*) is elucidated through metaphor; because it encompasses the realms of the ten directions, it is called "Great";

because it is not limited by form, it is called "Round"; and because there is no hidden darkness it does not illuminate, it is called the "Mirror. As for the manifestation of the ten lights within the mind:

this refers to the light of the wisdom of original enlightenment flowing and overflowing into the ten voids and all the *dhvajendra* (banner-king) lands, such that these *dhvajendra* lands, in turn, enter into my own body.

This clarifies the interaction between the body [of the Buddha] and the land. Regarding "the body being identical to space," it means that because the two—the environment (*niśraya*) and its inhabitants (*adhiṣṭhāna*)—are mutually fused, they do not obstruct one another.

Regarding the phrase "the body is able to... (referring to the passage from the *Long-shui shu*): the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states that the pure, wondrous Dharma-body is serene and responds to all things;
that which is "identical to space" is the Dharma-body, while "entering the lands within the dust" is the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Thus it is explained.
Because it encompasses the teachings of the Three Vehicles, it is called "Buddha-work" (*buddhakārya*). Because it accords with the capacities of the four *siddhāntas*, it is called "conformity.

The passage below clarifies that the attainment of the fruit arises from contemplating that the four great elements have no basis; being without basis is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wherein all marks of arising and ceasing are empty. Because they are empty, there is no duality;
because the Buddha-lands are empty, it is said that they are "originally identical," meaning they are identical with emptiness. Within this identity—
The final two lines explicitly clarify the attainment of *kṣānti* (patience); the preceding five lines clarify the preparatory merit; and the last two lines clarify the attainment of the fruit.

The Buddha’s question below concludes the meaning of the present inquiry. The four lines beginning with "I" [the speaker] explicitly establish that awakening through the contemplation of emptiness serves as the cause for perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
Maitreya Bodhisattva immediately rose from his seat... [omitted] ...to attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); this is the foremost.
This section of the sutra separately enumerates the twenty-three skillful means (*upāya*) of the initial cause, following the preceding passage.

Among these seven great elements, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the cause. The Sanskrit name Maitreya is translated as "The Compassionate One" (*Maitrīputra*). Ancient commentaries explain that it signifies the Middle Way.
Contemplation is precisely the power of the root of goodness of objectless great compassion, which causes all mental factors to enter into the dharma of great compassion of the same essence;
because it distances one from all that is unwholesome, he is called Maitreya. Furthermore, "Maitreya" is a personal name;
Ajita is translated as "Invincible. I recall that what follows correctly clarifies the cause of his awakening: the Buddha’s name was Candrasūryapradīpa (Moon-Sun-Lamp Brightness).

The meaning of this can be understood as follows: those whose minds value worldly fame and who delight in associating with noble families are precisely the "fame-seeking bodhisattvas" mentioned in the *Lotus Sūtra*.

This is truly because such bodhisattvas, at the outset, have not yet realized that all is mind-only; they remain attached to external objects, seeking them out and becoming distracted by many names and signs.
Therefore, that Buddha, as an antidote, taught them to cultivate the concentration on consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra-samādhi*), from which [the realization of] this mind [arises].
This refers to entering and realizing the wondrous samādhi. Regarding "mind-only consciousness": mind is itself consciousness, for the eighth consciousness is fundamentally named "mind.

From kalpa after kalpa until the present, one has taken this *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) samādhi to serve countless Buddhas. As for the term "consciousness-only," the first chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:

"The term 'only' excludes the existence of external objects; 'consciousness' distinguishes it from the emptiness of the mind; thus, both extremes of ordinary beings and Hinayana followers are simultaneously refuted."
The detailed explanation of "proclaiming consciousness-only" is as found in that treatise. Regarding the second of the two lines beginning with "seeking the world":

it means that by cultivating consciousness-only, one realizes that what is called the "world" outside the mind is merely a provisional designation; both the provisional self and provisional dharmas are empty in their very essence. How could they possibly persist?

From the point "until then" onwards, it correctly clarifies the successive stages of serving the Buddhas, reaching the stage of Dīpaṃkara, at which point one finally attains the ultimate perfection of consciousness-only (Vijñaptimātratā). III.

From the state of obscurity up to the lower degree of clarity, that which is manifested by consciousness—namely, all the Buddha-fields existing throughout space—is such that the Tathāgata is the true field.
Between the dependent and the true, there are those that are pure and those that are defiled, those that exist and those that do not;
all of these are manifestations of consciousness alone. Because the Bodhisattva has realized consciousness-only through direct realization, it is called "my mind."
That which is manifested is what is called "all phenomena are consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra). Below, the World-Honored One clarifies the attainment of the fruit through merit.
"I have attained" explains the merit; the following two lines explain the attainment of the fruit. "Thoroughly realized" means to realize that all is mind and consciousness;
thus, apart from consciousness there are no phenomena, as everything flows forth from the nature of consciousness, up to and including the Tathāgata.

Down to the most minute crawling insects, there is nothing that is not produced from the nature of consciousness. In this passage, the text merely points to what the Tathāgata has taught, using the superior to manifest the inferior.
Following the realization of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), one receives the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) and subsequently fills the seat of Buddhahood.

"Filling the seat of Buddhahood" means that once a Bodhisattva has ascended to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), they are adjacent to the ultimate sage; yet, at the point when the Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha is extinguished—

Thereafter, Maitreya will immediately attain equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) within this very realm to continue the transformative work of the Śākyamuni Buddha; thus he is called a "Buddha of the Successive Seat" (*kṣetra-parigraha*).

[The passage] beginning with "Question" concludes the meaning of the present inquiry. The four lines beginning with "I" clarify that the realization of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) is the fundamental cause for attaining universal penetration (*pariśuddha-mūla-hetu*).
Now, having already realized and entered the nature of perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and because this perfected reality is all-pervasive (*vyāpin*):

"Perfect" (*yuan*) means being without destruction; "accomplished" (*cheng*) means being not empty; "real" (*shi*) refers to the three virtues within the fruit (*phala*). "Perfect" is the *dharmakāya*, because it pervades all places;
"accomplished" is *prajñā*, because its awakening is untainted (*anāsrava*); "real" is the virtue of *vimukti*, because it is unimpeded.
The three subsequent phrases refer to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), for it arises from conditions; they point to that which is grasped.

Regarding the statement that the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the nature of universal imagination) is explained by way of its objects (*ālambana-dharma*): because it universally conceptualizes, this refers to the cognizing mind.
However, since these two natures—subject and object—are both false and fundamentally unreal, they are naturally and inherently distant from the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (the perfected nature).
Thus, by means of the three natures, one realizes and enters the three absences of nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*); hence the expression "distant," and so forth.
"Attaining the patience of non-arising" is spoken of in terms of the stage of fruition; "entering the perfected nature" is spoken of in terms of the virtues of fruition.
The Dharma Prince Mahāsthāmaprāpta and his peers [attained] samādhi, and he is the foremost among them.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding passage to specifically describe the twenty-four skillful means of the initial cause.
Among these seven great qualities, this refers to the cause of vision. Regarding why the Bodhisattva is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta (Great Power Attained), the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
"Because he universally illuminates all beings with the light of wisdom, causing them to leave the three miserable realms and attain supreme power, he is named 'Great'."
Furthermore, the details concerning Śrīkṣetra are found in the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. He is one of fifty-two who are his peers;
because the Great Śrīkṣetra represents the fifty-two stages of practice (*caryā*), they are of the same class and rank. "I recall" and the following lines clearly explain the cause of his awakening.
Regarding the statement that twelve Tathāgatas succeeded one another for the duration of one kalpa, this is according to the *Mahā-amitābha Sūtra*.
The *Thirteenth Chapter on the Names of the Buddhas* states:

"The Buddha Amitābha is named Immeasurable Life (*Amitāyus*), and is also named Immeasurable Light (*Amitābha*), Boundless Light, Unobstructed Light, Unrivaled Light, Flame-King Light, Pure Light, Joyful Light, Wisdom Light, Uninterrupted Light, Inconceivable Light, Ineffable Light, and Light Surpassing the Sun and Moon. Each light is itself one."
The name of the Buddha in that sutra refers specifically to Amitāyus Buddha, who possesses the latter twelve names;

the present sutra speaks of twelve Tathāgatas succeeding one another throughout a kalpa, which does not mean there is only one Buddha, but rather that the teachings emanated from the transformation of one Buddha have spread into twelve.
The section at the very end clarifies the source of the samādhi, while the subsequent section explains the methods for practicing this samādhi.

Question: Since it is stated that "recalling the Buddha" is spoken of from the perspective of sentient beings, why is it further said that there are two kinds of mindfulness, and that [the former] is profound? Answer:
This is because that Buddha’s original vow was to compassionately mind sentient beings without ceasing for even a moment.

Now, by citing the Buddha’s mindfulness, it serves to establish the sentient beings’ own mind of mindfulness. Just as with the Buddha’s mind, they will certainly attain Buddhahood. If the Buddha were solely... [text ends]
If one remembers sentient beings with single-minded devotion yet forgets them, one becomes estranged from oneself; how then can there be mutual intimacy? Therefore it is said:
"If one meets them, it is as if not meeting; if one sees them, it is as if not seeing. Since one has already forgotten, what principle could there be for meeting the Buddha or seeing the Buddha?

This passage generally clarifies that the fault of forgetting is indeed profound. Furthermore, the following six lines of the analogy do not yet constitute the essential body of the samādhi contemplation.
To establish mindfulness, one must first explain the fault of forgetfulness. When two people are mindful of one another, this is precisely what constitutes correct contemplation.
Thus, the two individuals inherit from the above the states of being exclusively mindful or exclusively forgetful.

This means that if they can remember without delusion and do so constantly, then their mutual mindfulness will become profound. Once their mutual mindfulness is profound, they will become close and intimate, like a form and its shadow.

The two lines beginning with "not mutually contradictory" [refer to] the ten directions; the lower two lines [concern] the Dharma. "Comes to accord with the Tathāgata" corresponds to those who are single-mindedly mindful;

"sentient beings" corresponds to those who are single-mindedly forgetful. If one is forgetful, there is no capacity [for the teaching]; only when one takes up mindfulness as the condition does the capacity meet the teaching, like a mother [reaching out].
Below, he again clarifies this through a metaphor: it is like a mother who remembers her child; even if the child turns his back on her meaning and flees to another land, the mother...
What is the use of merely recollecting? If you, my son, were to recollect your mother as your mother recollects you, then mother and child would not be separated throughout successive lives.
Regarding the "Samādhi of the Multitude of Lower Rebirths" and the "True Dharma": the former was explained through metaphors;
the present refers to the current life, while the future refers to subsequent lives. This means that even if one does not manage to see the Buddha in this present life, [the merit remains].
Remembering [the Buddha] without forgetting, one will certainly see the Buddha in the future;

or, even if the level of realization attained is not high, one will not be far from the Buddha, as there is no need for other expedient means. By this single practice of mindfulness of the Buddha alone, the mind is opened.
To illustrate the merit of mindfulness of the Buddha through a metaphor regarding deep dyeing: it is like a person who has been smeared with incense, whose body comes to possess its fragrance.
The analogy of "recalling the Buddha and seeing the Buddha" implies that one is not far from the Buddha; this is called "Adornment of Fragrant Light.
"Fragrance" refers to the meaning of the preceding analogy—namely, the recollection of the Buddha; "light" refers to the light of the wisdom of samādhi.

"Adornment" means adorning the *dharmakāya* Buddha with the light of the wisdom of samādhi. The section beginning with "I originally... clarifies the attainment of the fruit through the practice of recollecting the Buddha.
"Manifesting merit and entering the patience of non-arising" refers to attaining the fruit; this attainment of the fruit through manifesting merit constitutes one's own practice (*sva-caryā*).

The following three phrases concern the transformation of others (*para-caryā*): once the Bodhisattva’s own practice is perfected, they are further able to transform others, thereby gathering those who recite the Buddha’s name and returning them to the Pure Land.
Whereas the previous discussion of "reciting the Buddha’s name" referred generally to the Buddhas of the ten directions, it now—
Directly pointing to Amitābha, he brings [beings] back to the Pure Land; the Pure Land is none other than Sukhāvatī. While the Sahā world is called "defiled" (sai), Sukhāvatī is called "pure" (jing);
it is in contrast to this defilement that the latter is termed pure. Regarding the passage beginning with "The Buddha asked," it concludes the meaning of the present inquiry.

The four lines beginning with "I have no... mean that regarding the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*), one does not discriminate among them; these faculties thus belong to the three karmas of body, speech, and mind.
With sincere devotion, the six sense faculties turn toward [the Buddha] without thought of the five desires, for the mind is purely unified.

Thus it is said that "pure mindfulness succeeds one another. By means of this pure mindfulness, one enters right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*). This concludes the entire chapter, serving as the skillful means for the *nienfo samādhi* (Buddha-remembrance samādhi).
