Based on the Great Buddha-Crown Dharma-Door of the Tathāgata’s Secret Cause of Cultivation and Realization.
Direct Explanation, Fascicle Six.
Explained by the junior monk Guangmo of Yunqi Temple in Ancient Hangzhou;
proofread by the lay follower Zhudayou of Xiushui. Direct Explanation.
At that time, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva rose from his seat... [omitted] ...entering samādhi through hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
This section of the sūtra specifically details the twenty-five expedient means (*upāya*) of the initial cause, following the preceding passage.

Among these six sense faculties, it is the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) that is selected as the appropriate capacity; because its textual meaning is most complete and detailed, this name of the bodhisattva has been moved here.

The name "Avalokiteśvara" (Guanshiyin) is established based on its causal origins and encompasses two meanings: first, one's own practice (*sva-pratipatti*), and second, the transformation of others (*para-pariṇāmana*).
According to this present sutra, which recounts the original cause, it is explained from the perspective of self-practice.

Once self-practice has been perfected, the merit of that self-practice is further bestowed upon all sentient beings; this refers to the thirty-two manifestations and fourteen fearlessnesses described below.
Regarding this matter, the subsequent text states: "Because my hearing is perfectly clear and luminous, the name Avalokiteśvara pervades the worlds of the ten directions.

This explains the name in terms of one's own practice (*sva-caryā*). If explained according to the intent of the "Universal Gateway" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is spoken entirely from the perspective of transforming others (*parārtha*).
That sutra says: "If there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings who hear of this Avalokiteśvara..."
"Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, if one single-mindedly calls his name, Avalokiteśvara, he observes their voices and all obtain liberation," and so forth.
This is an explanation of the name from the perspective of transforming others (*parārtha*). Some may ask: "Observing (*avalokita*) is the function of the eye;
sounds are the speech of the ten realms and must be heard by the ear. For what reason is it called 'observing'? This is [an objection] based on...
The teaching on the purity of the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*) arises precisely because the six faculties of sentient beings are partitioned and do not function for one another.
Because the Bodhisattva practices "returning the hearing," he attains internal perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa-samudaya*). As stated in the preceding text:

"When clarity does not follow the faculties, yet clarity is manifested by means of the faculties, then the six faculties are appropriately able to function interchangeably. For this reason, he is called Avalokiteśvara. Furthermore, as previously stated: "Not..."

Because cognition and vision arise from preceding sensory objects, one is called "Entering the Stream" (*srotāpanna*); why then is one now also called "Avalokiteśvara" (Observer of the Sounds of the World)?
Does this not incur the fault of falling into the cycle of following sounds? This is said for those who have not yet attained perfect penetration (*pariniṣpanna*).

If one has attained perfect penetration, what harm is there in entering the marketplace to extend a helping hand, uprooting suffering and bestowing joy, rescuing beings from suffering by following their cries, in every single dust mote?
Because he is unimpeded, he is also called Avalokiteśvara. The Bodhisattva vehicle employs unconditional compassion (*nirālamba-maitrī*) toward all sentient beings;
preaching the Dharma as being like an illusion, he delivers beings while remaining identical to emptiness. Thus, he responds through this unconditional compassion. As an ancient master said:
"The power of unconditional compassion reaches all capacities, like the reflection of the bright moon appearing in a thousand streams; it never forgets sentient beings."
Therefore, he is named Avalokiteśvara. Furthermore, having received the prediction from the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara since ancient times, he attained the name "Avalokiteśvara";

thus cause and effect correspond, and he shares this name. In the passage beginning with "In my past," the text correctly clarifies the causes for awakening through hearing, reflection, and cultivation;

"hearing" refers to the ear-faculty, while "reflection" is— *Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on the *Lotus Sūtra*. The translation reflects the available portion.*

"Xunxun" (熏熏) refers to perfuming (*vāsanā*), meaning that through the process of perfuming from hearing the teachings, one gradually cultivates and achieves it, thereby first entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
*Samādhi* is translated as "the sphere of right mental activity" or "right concentration."
"First, within hearing, one enters the stream and loses the object" (extending to "once arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescent extinction manifests before one").

This section of the sutra follows upon the meanings of hearing, reflection, and cultivation to correctly bring forth the essence of contemplation. Regarding "first," it first demonstrates the practice of the emptiness of persons. "Within hearing" refers to the ear-faculty;

the word "first" carries the sense of the subsequent phrase "gradually increasing. *Note: The provided text contains a commentary on the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*. The bracketed portion indicates the full extent of the passage being analyzed.*

The three layers correspond to the meaning of the three voids mentioned in the preceding text. "Entering" refers to the reversal of the flow [of consciousness]; this is the functional capacity of the nature of hearing.

Because it flows outwardly to grasp the sensory object of sound, the character "object" (*suǒ*) points back to the character "flow" (*liú*) mentioned above. "Movement and stillness" refer to the objects that are heard;
it is precisely because sentient beings follow after sounds that they transmigrate, and thus the nature of hearing flows outward.
The Bodhisattva does not follow the flow arising from the sensory object of sound, but turns it back inward to exhaust the faculty that causes this flow.

Since the flowing faculty cannot be apprehended, that which enters [the flow] perishes. Once the nature of the flow is stilled, the two external characteristics of motion and stillness clearly cease to arise.
At this stage, hearing, contemplation, and cultivation have already been roughly established. Since the nature of the flow has...
When the sense organs and their objects are stilled, one then understands this realm of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Why is this?

It is because as long as the mark of self (*ātman*) is not empty, there exist the sense organs and objects, as well as "self" and "mine. Now that the sense organs and objects have been resolved, this is precisely the emptiness of self; and "self" is none other than the person.
As stated in the first section of the preceding general demonstration of the sequence for resolving the knots in the *Yuan-tong zhang* (Chapter on Perfect Penetration): "This..."
"The faculties are first understood; one first attains the emptiness of persons"—this can be cited as evidence for this very point, which constitutes the first layer of meaning.
"In this manner" and below refers to gradually entering from here and further increasing one's merit; this should be viewed in relation to the first character of the preceding passage.
Since the faculties and objects have already been resolved and the subject and object are both empty, yet the nature has not yet been exhausted, the text restates and then dispels them once more.
It is said that when what is heard and the hearing itself are both exhausted, the nature of hearing likewise does not abide.

The upper character "hearing" (聞) refers to the faculty of hearing, while the lower "what is heard" (所聞) refers to the objects; the character "exhausted" (盡) means that both this faculty of hearing and its objects are entirely spent.

When even this awareness of the exhaustion of hearing does not abide or cling, then the awareness and the object of awareness are also empty. The upper character "awareness" (覺) here serves to dispel the notion of exhaustion.
When one hears this and realizes that what is perceived below is itself the perceiver, then because the perceiving awareness does not abide, both the perceiver and the perceived are empty.
This is the realm of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). As stated in the second section of the aforementioned sutra:
"The perfect clarity of the nature of emptiness constitutes liberation through phenomena. Liberation is simply another name for emptiness, meaning the capacity to...
That which is exhausted along with its objects is itself empty by nature; therefore, it is called the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*). This constitutes the second level of meaning.
Regarding the two phrases "emptiness-awareness" (*kōkaku*) below, the term "emptiness" (*kū*) refers back to the "emptiness" (*kū*) at the top of the passage.

This means that when both the awareness of exhaustion and the subject-object duality are empty, then "emptiness-awareness" reaches ultimate fulfillment and the object of emptiness is extinguished. Thus ends the section on the character "emptiness" (*kū*).

Regarding the phrase "this dharma is empty," the characters for "empty" below refer to the emptiness of persons; that is to say, both the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of dharmas are extinguished.
This is the realm of the three kinds of emptiness. As stated in the third section of the aforementioned sutra: "Having liberated from dharmas, both are empty and do not arise.
"Both are empty" refers precisely to the two kinds of emptiness—of persons and of dharmas—whereby their traces are swept away; therefore, it is said they "do not arise. This is it.
The third point concerns the meaning of the two lines following "birth and cessation. These two lines serve as a conclusion to clarify *nirvāṇa*.

This means that when those subtle birth and cessation are extinguished, one realizes great *nirvāṇa* from this state; since *nirvāṇa* is synonymous with Great *Nirvāṇa*, it is said that "nirvāṇa is manifested before one."
"Suddenly transcending the mundane and supramundane... [until] sharing the same sorrow and longing as all sentient beings.
This section of the sutra follows upon the preceding description of "the manifestation of quiescent extinction" (*śānta-nirvāṇa*) to clarify the attainment of two kinds of sublime merit.

The two phrases beginning with "Suddenly" mean that the Bodhisattva attains the realization of the principle of Great Quiescent Extinction, and that the essence of this principle of quiescent extinction—
Since not a single dharma can be apprehended and all is profoundly still and pure, how could there be any distinction between the ten realms? Therefore it is said:

"Suddenly transcending the mundane and supramundane. One should carefully examine the flavor of these two characters, "suddenly" (*hu-ran*), which mean that this principle does not require long-term cultivation, protracted effort, or circuitous detours; rather, one should directly descend into the state of sudden, vast emptiness and perfect roundness.
Once understood, everything is resolved; simply letting go is as the Chan school describes:
with a single "clatter" (*lìdì shēng*), all fragments are shattered, and in that instant of resonance, there are no longer so many difficulties. Thus it is said, "suddenly.
"Suddenly" means that in an instant one can transcend the realms of the four sages and six classes of ordinary beings. Furthermore, these two phrases follow from what precedes them.
The phrase beginning with "arising from below" is further a restatement of the excellence of the efficacy of the perfect penetration of the ear-organ.
The section beginning with "the ten directions" refers to the merit obtained by receiving [the teaching] above and benefiting those below.

Regarding the meaning of the "ten directions," following the Tiantai school’s interpretation based on the ten dharma-realms (*daśa-dharmadhātu*), this corresponds to the phrase "the world" in the preceding line; since "the world" refers to the ten dharma-realms, it is because one is able to transcend them.

Because it transcends the ten realms, it is called "perfectly luminous" (*yuanming*). Since the wisdom of the Bodhisattva that accords with principle is both perfect and luminous, it is called "extraordinary and supreme" (*shusheng*).
To say "extraordinary and supreme" means it is the most supreme among the supreme; thus, the word "extraordinary" (*shu*) is added.

These two forms of supremacy arise precisely because the Bodhisattva has realized the fundamental, wondrously enlightened mind in which the living being and the Buddha are of one essence; therefore, it is superior.

It harmonizes with all Buddhas below and harmonizes with sentient beings; because this awakened mind is inherently endowed with the compassion of the same essence (*samatā-karuṇā*), when it harmonizes upward with the Buddhas' minds, the compassion of the Buddhas is itself the compassion of the Bodhisattvas. Since this compassion can reach downward to bestow happiness upon others, it is said that they share the "same power of compassion.
Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva’s mind harmonizes downward with sentient beings, then [the suffering of] sentient beings...
The "sorrowful longing" (*bi-àng*) of sentient beings is the very same as the "sorrowful longing" of the Bodhisattva. As for the sorrowful longing of sentient beings, it arises from suffering;

they feel sorrow and look up with reverence (*qīn-yǎng*) for the Bodhisattva to come and extract them from that suffering. The character "longing" (*yǎng*) contains the sense of being moved [by compassion].
Because the Bodhisattva responds by looking down upon them, it is said that their "sorrowful longing is one and the same."
"World-Honored One, because I have made offerings to the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara... up to "...the thirty-two manifestations entering all lands.

This section of the sutra follows from the preceding passage: because [Avalokiteśvara] accords with the Buddha-mind and shares in the power of compassion, he manifests response-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) to bestow happiness;

thus, he first indicates the number of these manifestations. The phrase "because I have made offerings to the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara" signifies that the cause inherits the fruit, as he has received [this capacity] through such offerings.
Samādhi is the fruit that hangs from the cause; it is the samādhi of hearing-permeation and hearing-cultivation.

That which is called "like an illusion" refers to the Great Quiescent Extinction, the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) in which not even a single speck of dust can be established. Even the single word "Buddha" is like a mote in the eye—how could such a samādhi tolerate its presence?
This is truly because sentient beings turn their backs on awakening and unite with the dust, becoming addicted to and stained by it everywhere.

Being able to penetrate the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), the Tathāgata, out of necessity, establishes hundreds of thousands of samādhis and immeasurable gates of deliverance, so that all sentient beings may rely upon them for cultivation, cleanse their minds, and leave behind defilement to realize that ultimate emptiness.
Once they have ascended to this wondrous emptiness, the samādhis they cultivated can no longer be apprehended; they were originally non-existent, yet now exist.
Therefore, it is called "like an illusion," which is spoken of by way of analogy. "Hearing and cultivating through hearing" is explained as in the preceding text.

"Vajra" is a metaphor used to illustrate contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*); because it is as firm and sharp as a vajra, it can shatter delusions. "And with the Buddhas" refers to the accomplishment of the merit of samādhi;
following the previous [passage], this joins with the Buddha’s compassion to initiate the subsequent various manifestations. This is the general heading for the manifestations.
The preceding two lines of the separate explanation are a continuation of what was previously stated, while the following two lines introduce what follows.

Regarding "entering the various lands," according to the subsequent section on the thirty-two manifestations, these completely encompass the ten realms; thus, they refer to the lands of the ten realms.
"World-Honored One, if Bodhisattvas enter samādhi... [and] preach the Dharma for them so that they may attain liberation.
This section of the sutra begins with the Bodhisattva’s wondrous and skillful preaching of the Dharma starting from the Three Vehicles.

The true essence of the Bodhisattva’s Dharmakāya is as profound and still as empty space; it appears square or round according to the vessel, yet each sees it differently. How can empty space be said to have [different forms]?
When you manifest forms in accordance with sentient beings through both sameness and difference, emptiness follows their movements, entering into them all without exception;

the Bodhisattva’s body of wondrous, effortless response is also found herein. As for the statement that it should stop at thirty-two [marks], it is because the number thirty-two roughly encompasses the ten realms;
even if one were to speak of numbers as vast as those of hundreds of thousands of billions of atoms, up to the infinite...
Their number is immeasurable and inconceivable; how could they have any limit?
Furthermore, these thirty-two [manifestations] are because, above, they harmonize with the Buddha-mind and share in the power of compassion;

since compassion can bestow happiness, the text states that "causing them to attain liberation" and "attaining accomplishment" are both matters of bestowing happiness. Now, first, the text lists the three vehicles that transcend the world.
The four noble ones, by means of the Middle Vehicle, open the conditions for the Solitary Realizers; thus, among the three vehicles, the samādhi of the Mahāyāna is explained first.
Regarding the terminology, as seen previously, the names apply to both the Great and Small Vehicles. Consequently, the term "untainted" (*anāsrava*) also applies to both;
within the Mahāyāna, that which is called "untainted" refers to the supreme, world-transcending untainted state of the Bodhisattvas, which is superior.

The phrase "the manifestation of resolute understanding" (*adhimukti-pratibhāsa*) applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; although they equally possess this terminology, there are differences in depth and subtlety of meaning.

Thus, "the manifestation of resolute understanding" refers to the fact that when the sentient beings who act as the responsive conditions (*pratītya-kāraka*) possess various forms of resolute understanding and the power of wisdom is fully present before them, the Bodhisattva accords with their specific inclinations and responds to them; therefore, the subsequent line states, "I appear before them."

The various phrases mentioned above apply to all three vehicles; each should understand them according to the depth or shallowness of their respective vehicle. Furthermore, regarding the subsequent section on the "Middle Vehicle":

first, one practices *pratyekabuddha-yāna* (solitary awakening), and next, one practices *yogācāra* (conditioned practice); these are called "those in training" because they train in solitude and train in conditions.
As for "quiescent, wondrous, and luminous," it is because [this vehicle] delights in solitary tranquility and rejoices in tending toward stillness; thus, "wondrous and luminous" refers to...
This meaning of tranquil illumination attained within stillness is explained as a single phrase of resolute understanding (*adhimukti*), as taught in the Mahāyāna;
however, there are differences in the analytical meanings according to the respective vehicles. As for the Pratyekabuddha who appears and teaches the Dharma:

because they appear in a world where no Buddha exists, they attain awakening through the contemplation of the arising and ceasing of all phenomena; since they awaken to non-arising without a teacher and realize it by themselves, they are called "Solitary" (*pratyeka*).
It is understood that the present Bodhisattvas manifest conduct similar to theirs and teach the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas so that they may easily awaken and attain liberation.

Furthermore, "next, the various [beings]" below clarifies the Pratyekabuddhas. A Pratyekabuddha is so called because, relying on the teaching of the World-Honored One, they contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) and awaken to non-arising;
thus they are named Pratyekabuddhas. As for the twelve links of dependent origination, beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*) and continuing through the [twelfth link]...
The twelve links of old age and death are as explained in detail in the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm).

Generally speaking, those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle contemplate the arising and cessation of these [links] to awaken to non-arising (*anutpāda*). Once they have awakened to non-arising, they sever all conditioned arising and ceasing;

hence it is said that they "sever the arising and ceasing of the twelve links of dependent origination. When conditions are severed and the nature of non-arising manifests, this is precisely that non-arising.

Regarding the phrase "named *paramātman*, the supreme and wondrous nature manifests in perfection": this refers to the fact that the supreme and wondrous nature of non-arising manifests and attains fulfillment.
However, it is because the Bodhisattva manifests that body and teaches that Dharma for them that they first achieve and attain liberation.
Furthermore, as for those in the three lower stages who are Śrāvakas still in training (*śaikṣa*), from the first fruit up to the third fruit:
All are called "those in training" (*śaikṣa*). Those who have attained the emptiness of the Four Truths are the four: suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.

These four are all termed "truths" (*satya*) because *satya* means "trustworthy" or "real"; they are so called because suffering is real, the origin is real, and so forth. Emptiness is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) that is realized.
Since those in training have not yet perfected the principle of emptiness, how can they be said to have "attained" it? This is spoken of from the perspective of the causal stage.
This refers to the "fruit" (result).

The passage from "If sentient beings desire to awaken their minds" up to "he preaches the Dharma for them so that they may achieve success" follows the previous section on wondrous response and enumerates the seekers within the celestial realms of the desire and form realms.
Regarding the first section: "If among the various lower [states], the first should be the form-realm devas' desire-mind. The first two phrases concern the desire-mind;

the single phrase "awakening to the desire-mind" is likely a textual inversion and should instead read "awakening to the desire-mind. Here, "desire" refers to the desires of the desire realm, namely the five sensual pleasures (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
This is because one awakens to the fact that these five desires are suffering, coarse, and distracted, and that they obstruct meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
Because of the Dharma, he feels weary of [the desire realm] and rejoices in the pure and wondrous seclusion of the higher realms; thus it is said that he does not transgress the dust of desire.
Because he does not transgress, he attains purity within his very body in the desire realm. This purity is the cause for birth among the Brahmā gods.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva manifests in the form of a Brahmā King and teaches the Dharma of detachment from desire so that beings may attain liberation—namely, liberation.

When one attains birth in the realm of desire and the first dhyāna, it is designated as the Brahma Heaven; "Brahma" is a Western (Sanskrit) term, fully called *brahmā*, which translates as "free from desire" (*vītarāga*) or "pure conduct.
Next, regarding the various [lower] heavens, the Lord of the Desire Heavens refers to the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, who dwells upon the summit of Mount Sumeru;
the summit of this mountain is eighty-four thousand *yojanas* in circumference.
As there are eight celestial kings in each of the four directions with Śakra residing in the center to govern them, he is called the Lord of the Thirty-three Heavens;
because he governs this heaven, it is said that he presides over all the heavens.

It is said that for those sentient beings who possess the aspiration to govern the heavens, the Bodhisattva manifests in the body of Śakra and preaches such teachings as the ten superior wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*) to bring them to fulfillment.
Regarding the title "Śakra," the Sanskrit term is Śakradevendra, translated as "Capable Heavenly Lord" (Neng Tian Di).
Here, "Di" (Heavenly) is the Chinese word, while "Shi" (Capable) is the Sanskrit term; it is abbreviated as "Dishi" (Śakra). The causal account for this appears in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.

Examining the meaning of the current text: previously, when the Brahmā King appeared to preach the Dharma, he was called "Liberation" (Jietuo); subsequently, when Śakra appeared, [he was called "Capable Heavenly Lord"].
Regarding the teaching on "attainment" (*siddhi*): previously, those referred to as "liberated" were intended to be liberated from the objects of desire and granted the bliss of purity;
because there are three levels of bliss in the dhyāna heavens, they were called "liberated.

Subsequently, those referred to as "attained" are so called because the desire heavens belong entirely to the realm of scattered goodness (*vikṣipta-kuśala*), and the Bodhisattva, in accordance with that, attains the bliss of rebirth in the heavens; thus it is called "attainment."
The following sections should all be modeled after this. Third, regarding the phrase "the gods at the summit of the desire realm" (*kāmadhātu-śikharastha-deva*):

the character "desire" (*yù*) in "desire-body" (*yùshēn*) refers to the desire of sensual craving; it carries the same meaning as the character "craving" (*ài*) in the subsequent phrase "craving governs" (*ài tǒng*).

As for the title "Masters of Others' Emanations" (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*), the *Bie xing shu* (Separate Commentary) states: "Because these gods achieve their own pleasure by means of the emanations produced by others, they are called 'Masters of Others' Emanations.'"
Since "mastery" (*vaśitā*) has the meaning of bliss, the phrase "wandering through the ten directions" is also spoken from the perspective of mastery.
If one were unable to wander, one would not possess mastery. The "ten directions" here merely refers to a single world-system; I shall explain this below as in the preceding passage.
Regarding the two [points] above, they should merely refer to the desire heavens (*kāmadhātu*). As for the second and sixth [points], it is because of the Emperor... [text fragment].
The resolve to protect the Dharma is superior to that of other devas because he constantly attends upon the Tathāgata;

furthermore, since Paranirmita-vaśavartin is the pinnacle of the Desire Realm, by mentioning these two—the highest and the lowest—he intends to include all the others in between. Fourth, as for "if there are those below," this refers to the peak heavens of the Form Realm.
Regarding those who "seek mastery over their bodies," although the phrasing is the same as before, their mastery is vastly different because they have transcended the lower realms.
Because the realms (*dhātu*) are characterized by suffering, coarseness, and obstruction, and because they represent the ultimate limit of form, he is distinguished by the title "Great" (*Mahā*).

Furthermore, the phrase "flying through the void" also surpasses the previous meanings; as this deity is the sovereign of the great trichiliocosm, possessing mastery and excelling others, and flies through the space of the great trichiliocosm, he is called Mahādeva, the "Great Sovereign.
Regarding the passage "I [am] below," it is as explained in the preceding text. However...
Now, why is it that at the Peak of Form (*rūpāgra*) one does not speak of "liberation" (*vimukti*) but rather says "attainment"?
It is precisely because they aspire to flight and seek mastery, rather than having the intention for liberation; from the perspective of what they aspire to, it is called "attainment.

If those gods were truly seeking liberation from the cage of form and were to maintain the perception of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), then one would certainly speak of "liberation. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "Beyond..."
The Śuddhāvāsa devas consist of bodhisattvas in the tenth stage known as Mahāmaheśvara; it is definitively not the case that Chang Shui (Long Water) erroneously identified them as others.
In the present text, the Brahma King is listed first and the summit of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) is presented thereafter, which includes these [Śuddhāvāsas] within its scope.
However, because the translators did not arrange the names in their proper order, they appear to emerge or disappear in various positions; this must have resulted from the translation process itself.
This is because it was caused by the congestion at that time. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"The one who manifests with eight arms, three eyes, riding a white ox and holding a white fly-whisk is Mahādeva. Fifth, regarding the phrase "next, the heavenly generals" and so forth, concerning those who command spirits and deities:
according to the *Xuanshi lüshi gantong zhuan*, the celestial being Fei spoke of four [categories].
Beneath each of the Four Heavenly Kings are eight generals, totaling thirty-two generals according to that teaching.
The "Great General Tian" mentioned in the present text is not a single individual; it refers generally to the thirty-two generals.
Thus, each commands their respective spirits and deities to protect the realm, ensuring that rain and sunshine occur in their proper seasons and that the harvests of grain are bountiful.
Abundant harvests prevent other ghosts and spirits from harassing sentient beings. Regarding "I, below," it is as explained in the preceding text.
As for "If the various [beings] below," this refers to those who, under the governance of the Four Heavenly Kings, have attained rebirth among sentient beings;
these are the outer ministers of Śakra who dwell on the four terraces halfway up Mount Sumeru. This is drawn from the second explanation. Regarding "I, below," it is as... [text ends].

The preceding text spoke of the seven; next, regarding the four kings’ princes who are born in celestial palaces as exorcists—these are the duties assigned to the princes of the Four Heavenly Kings, such as the Prince Nārāyaṇa (Nata).
That which appears in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* refers precisely to this matter. As for "I [at]... below, it is as follows:
The preceding text states that the above merely lists the two realms of desire and form while omitting the formless realm;

this is for three reasons: first, because the formless realm lacks a physical body; second, because citing the meaning of the lower [realms] serves to encompass the higher; and third, because they are collectively included within the various categories mentioned in the subsequent text.
As for the seven aforementioned [beings], they should first list the primary lineage and subsequently list the ministers and attendants, as is the textual convention.
Although the body of wondrous response does not follow the sequence of ordinary forms, it is equanimous and tranquil, manifesting in every land.
If there are sentient beings who delight in being rulers [and so forth], he preaches the Dharma for them to bring them to fulfillment.

This section of the sutra follows the previous passage on the wondrous response to those of noble name and virtuous reputation among humanity, thereby demonstrating what is esteemed according to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and complying with their requests.
First, regarding "those such as the kṣatriyas": this refers first to the response to the human ruler, namely the king who governs the myriad subjects.
However, there are differences in scale, such as the four wheels [of sovereignty] and the minor kings (粟散), as well as distinctions between the Central Kingdom (Madhyadeśa) and the frontier regions.
Dividing territories and establishing boundaries, each governing their own state, they are called lords of men.

The Bodhisattva, in accordance with their needs, manifests his body for them and teaches the principles of social order and human relations, as well as the laws for cultivating oneself, regulating the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to the world, so that they may achieve success.
Next, regarding those who are elders, masters of affection, or heads of clans: this refers to those of high virtue within their own lineage.
In his advanced years, he yielded the position of Five-Service Official; this was not only the practice cherished within his own clan, but throughout the human world, everyone admired him.
Figures such as Huang Shudu, Guo Youdao, Chen Taichou, and Xun Langling would have been honored to have him visit their homes.
When the Grand Historian divined and reported that a True Man was traveling eastward, the "Virtue Star" gathered within five hundred li, and sages assembled there like clouds.
This is precisely sufficient to describe what constitutes an "elder" (gṛhapati); thus it is said that the world honors and defers to them.
The *Lun* (Treatise) also states that an elder possesses ten virtues; therefore, as mentioned previously, one may understand the following points accordingly.

Third, as for those householders who delight in discussing names and phrases (*nāmāpadeśa*), these "names and phrases" refer to the language of the fundamental social order, ethics, filial piety, fraternal respect, loyalty, and trustworthiness.
In this context, one must necessarily take this as the definition of a *jushi* (lay practitioner). Therefore, those who call themselves *jushi* should abide in purity;

they should naturally maintain their integrity whether poor or wealthy—being joyful in poverty and fond of ritual in wealth. Such a person is truly worthy of the title *jushi*. Regarding the section below, it may be understood as before.
Fourth, as for the subsequent section concerning officials: those who love governing the state must cultivate themselves in order to govern the state.
What Qi Shi called "loyal ministers emerging from the gates of filial sons" means that when one governs a state with this principle, there is no state that cannot be well-governed;

governing a state is, indeed, the business of the Chancellor. To "divide and determine" (剖斷) refers to dividing the commanderies and counties: "dividing" is to partition them, and "determining" is to make final decisions.

The "fanzhen" (regional commands) constitute the commanderies, while the "xianzhi" (prefectural administrations) constitute the counties. From the high ministers at the court down to the governors and prefects, all are so designated.
When Bodhisattvas manifest as magistrates, they invariably preside over legal cases to ensure that no disputes arise; the Venerable Nīti was precisely such a person.

Fifth, regarding those of the next rank, they are the Śuklānvaya Brahmins—translated as "Pure Lineage" or "Pure Conduct"—who practice the arts of divination, the *I Ching*, astrology, and fortune-telling, as well as the recitation of incantations and the use of talismans and registers.
Regarding the two methods: since the method for being able to sustain life and protect one’s vitality is itself the Dharma, as mentioned previously below, this may be understood accordingly.
If there is a man who delights in study and leaves the household life (up to) preaching the Dharma for him so that he may achieve accomplishment.
This section of the sutra follows the previous theme of the Buddha’s wondrous response to the fourfold assembly, complying with their requests.
First, regarding the response to the bhikṣus: according to the ninety-five types of non-Buddhist paths in India (Zhū Qián), there were many who left the household life to become śramaṇas;
thus, those who have renounced the world are not of a single kind. Those listed here represent various lineages from which they emerged.
Those who enter the lineage of the Tathāgata are these very ones. As for "upholding the various precepts," it refers to a bhikṣu who is endowed with the two hundred and fifty precepts;
because he possesses these various precepts within his person, he is called a bhikṣu—the meaning of which is as explained previously.
This can be understood from what follows. Next, if there is a "ni" following [the word], it should refer to a bhikṣuṇī; "ni" is a feminine suffix in the language of India (Tianzhu). That is to say:

Regarding female bhikṣuṇīs who observe the precepts: "prohibit" (*jin*) is a term meaning to restrain. The five hundred rules of the *bhikṣuṇī* precepts are found in detail in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-piṭaka*;
their characteristics are twice as many as those of male bhikṣus. The above concerns the two assemblies of the ordained;
these Bodhisattvas all manifest their bodies and preach the Dharma to bring them to fulfillment. Third, if there are those below [the ordained], they should next approach.

The Five Precepts for Laymen are the preceptual characteristics observed by those who have taken refuge in the Buddha as householders; though they are superficial, they serve as the foundation for all other precepts.
If these five precepts are not firmly maintained, then all other precepts will be destroyed. It is like building a house: one first solidifies the foundation;
if the foundation is not solid, the house will inevitably collapse. *Upāsaka* is translated as "Layman" (*Jinsi Nan*).
Because one draws near to and serves the ordained bhikṣu as one’s teacher and model; fourth, if there is no [male], one should draw near to a female lay follower (*upāsikā*).
The five precepts are the same as above. "Dwelling by oneself" means maintaining the body with the five precepts and guarding one's integrity with firm constancy.
*Upāsikā* is translated as "female lay follower. Regarding those below, it may be understood as before. The above is concluded.
This is because the Bodhisattvas of the two assemblies—both householders and those who have gone forth to the Buddha—manifest their bodies and preach the Dharma to bring about accomplishment.
If there are women, they establish themselves in domestic governance and so forth, and [the Bodhisattvas] preach the Dharma for them to bring about their accomplishment.

This section of the sutra follows up on the preceding account of the Virtue of the Woman of Wondrous Response (*Miaoying nüde*) and accords with her request. First, regarding "If there were... and so forth:

first, it responds to the virtue of the various palace ladies within the inner court. As for "inner governance" (*neizheng*), those who manage the domestic affairs of the royal household and the instructions of the Empresses and Consorts are called "inner governance.
Regarding "establishing oneself," this means first rectifying one's own person and only then correcting others.
If rectitude is thus established, then with the self cultivated, the family will be harmonized, and the state can be governed.
Proceeding from the internal to the external is as described in the *Shijing* regarding the *Zhou Nan* and *Shao Nan*, which were permeated by the transformative influence of King Wen and his Queen.
When the women of the inner court possess such aspirations and joy, they look up to the Bodhisattva, who manifests in the form of a female ruler and—
Because the National Ladies (*guófūrén*) and others have accomplished the preaching of the Dharma, the "Female Ruler" (*nǚzhǔ*) refers to the consort of the Son of Heaven;

the "National Lady" refers to the wife of a ruler, as in the phrase "the wife of a lord of a state. As for the "Enfeoffed Ladies" (*mìngfù*), it means that wives receive the edicts and mandates of the Heavenly King through the glory of their husbands;
thus they are called "Enfeoffed Ladies. Regarding the "Great Ladies" (*dàjiā*), the *Jiājùn* says: "The term 'Great Lady' refers to the paternal aunt."
The female teacher is like Cao Shituo’s wife from Fufeng during the Later Han dynasty, the daughter of Ban Biao of the same commandery, named Zhao and styled Huiji.
Emperor Huan repeatedly summoned her into the palace and ordered the Empress and the noble ladies to take her as their teacher;
she had no official title and was merely called "Dajia" (the Great Lady). Next, if there is a junior [teacher], it should be a young man who has not yet undergone ritual transformation.
Regarding the male organ (*puruṣendriya*): it means that the true essence is not lost and desires and evils are not practiced;
therefore, one is called a "virgin" (*kumāra*). As for the following [categories], they may be understood as before. Third, regarding the "next," it refers to those who should be virgins (*kanyā*).

Among women, those who dwell in seclusion, remain steadfast and chaste, and do not desire men to violate their bodies, are called virgins. The character "chù" (處) is read with the third tone (*shǎngshēng*), and it is also [so used].

Because she maintains herself in a state of youthful innocence (*kumārabhūta*), the two characters "invasion" (*qīn*) and "violence" (*bào*) appear in the *Mao Shi* [Book of Poetry]. This refers to a woman who is not chaste or virtuous;
because her conduct is as exposed as the morning dew, she becomes subject to invasion and violence by others. My interpretation of the passage below is as previously explained.

Because they seek birth in the right destination, or because they loathe the suffering, coarseness, and impurity of the lower realms while rejoicing in the purity, subtlety, and excellence of the higher realms, the eight classes of beings and various other miscellaneous types all understand through their own minds;
their aspirations to seek liberation and transcend their respective categories can all be understood in this way.

Because Bodhisattvas are able to manifest bodies and preach the Dharma to bring them to accomplishment, the rest should be understood by analogy. *Yakṣa* is translated as "Drug-eater" (or "Flesh-eater").

*Kiṃnara* (Gandharva): Translated as "Seeker of Fragrance. These are the celestial song-spirits (*gandharva*) of the Heavenly Emperor (*Indra*). Because the Heavenly Emperor desires their singing, he summons them by burning incense;
they arrive immediately upon smelling the fragrance, hence they are called "Seekers of Fragrance. *Asura*:

Translated as "Lacking Handsomeness," because their males are ugly and their females are beautiful. It is also translated as "Non-Gods" (*a-deva*), because they resemble gods but are not gods. *Kiṃnara*: [The text here appears to be truncated.]
The *Luo* (羅) translation says: "A person who resembles a person but has horns on its head" refers to the celestial musician deity of the *Indra*.
*Mahoraga* is translated as "great python"; those who are "non-humans" (*amanuṣya*) are the various ghosts and spirits.

Regarding the four lower classes—those with form and those without form—the seventh sutra at its conclusion states that "form" (*ākṛti*) is rendered as "color" (*rūpa*), for color is indeed form; thus it says therein:
Those with form are the spirits of good and ill fortune; those without form are the empty, the dispersed, and the submerged;
those with perception are gods, ghosts, and numinous spirits; and those without perception are spirits whose essence has been transformed into earth, wood, metal, or stone.

In this present text, these are treated concisely and combined into a single category for the sake of brevity. However, among the eight classes of beings, the garuḍas are still missing; they are translated as [the "Golden-Winged Bird"].
Among the twelve categories of *garuḍas*, there are further omissions— such as those that are neither material nor immaterial,
neither percipient nor non-percipient— which are omitted by way of illustrating the brevity through the extensive. Nevertheless,

one should know that since Bodhisattvas manifest the same activities (*samānārthatā*) and preach the Dharma even while dissolving and vanishing within emptiness, how could they not pervade all categories of form and perception?

This is merely a brief summary; furthermore, according to the traditional designation of the thirty-two manifestations, all beings—saints and ordinary people alike, mundane and supramundane—are fully encompassed, such that there is no realm where his body does not appear.
This is called the "Sublime Purity" (Miao-jing), the thirty-two manifestations (ending with) the accomplishment of sovereign mastery through the power of non-action.
This section of the sutra summarizes the preceding account of the thirty-two manifestations, attributing them all to the sovereign power of the samādhi of hearing-perfuming (wen-xun).
"Sublime Purity" means that while remaining unmoved from one's essential nature, one universally manifests birth. As it says:
The single moon in the sky appears as reflections in a thousand rivers; the moon does not come, nor do the reflections go.

Sentient beings naturally receive the power of compassion to accomplish their work. This is what is meant by "responding to conditions and meeting with stimuli without exception, yet always remaining upon this seat of Bodhi.
It is the principle of mutual correspondence, wondrous purity, and the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena—truly inconceivable.
Regarding the discussion on why it is called "Sublime Purity" (Miao-jing): Someone asked, "When the moon sinks into ten thousand waters, it does not change its original form;
yet, if it lacks the capacity to manifest appearances according to conditions, would this not be the fault of the analogy being inconsistent with the Dharma? The answer is:

Did we not say previously that empty space is unmoving, yet it follows the squareness or roundness of the vessels? Each vessel perceives the space, which transforms according to the shape of the vessel. This is the same for the moon and...
One must view "emptiness" and "should" together to fully grasp the meaning; the moon is used to clarify the mind, while emptiness is used to manifest form—neither loses its essential intent.
Please contemplate this in stillness. All that follows is the complete dedication of merit, returning it to the power of the samādhi of hearing-perfuming.
It is called "the non-actor" because this wondrous response is rooted in non-action; through non-action there is action, and through action there is non-action. This is the third [section].
Because its wondrous function of moving that which is unmoving is subtle and its supernormal powers are unimpeded and unobstructed, it is called "sovereign.
World-Honored One, by means of this cultivation through hearing and cultivation through hearing, I have further attained fourteen kinds of meritorious qualities of fearlessness.

This section of the sutra follows from the preceding by harmonizing with the fact that sentient beings equally look up to [the Buddha] with compassion; thus, the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) extracts them from suffering, and first the number of these response bodies is indicated.
The word "furthermore" (*fù*) in the phrase "I furthermore" (*wǒ fù*) carries forward the meaning of bestowing happiness mentioned previously;

hence it is called "furthermore. The phrase "by means of this samādhi" indicates that the merit returns to its source. The passage beginning with "bestows upon all... reiterates the preceding point regarding the harmonization with compassion.
Looking upward toward the fourteen fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), one uproots all those sufferings so that nothing remains to cause fear; therefore, it is called the "merit of fearlessness.
Regarding the phrase "in my own body and mind": "I" refers to the Bodhisattva’s self-designation. This merit of uprooting suffering is attained entirely upon the body and mind of the Bodhisattva.
Alternatively, it may arise from contemplating the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and thereby generating wholesome roots, or it may follow whatever [object] is encountered.
Because one attains fearlessness within the *nirmāṇakāya*, or because one subdues evil through the power of the path of contemplation, or because one cultivates and perfects it within samādhi,
and because all evils are naturally eliminated through the skillful application of the four *siddhāntas*—

it is said that this is attained in body and mind. Furthermore, upon careful examination of the fourteen preceding sections, it is stated that "knowing, seeing, contemplating, and hearing" and so forth belong to the body, while "severing and extinguishing" belongs to the mind.
Delusive thoughts and the like belong to the mind; they can be discerned through subtle investigation.
First, because of the self, one does not contemplate the ear (up to) contemplating its sounds, whereby one immediately attains liberation.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding passage by combining compassion and yearning to extract one from suffering;

therefore, it presents the essence of contemplation (*guan*) as a whole, so that by invoking the name, one may be liberated from all sufferings. This text consists of fourteen sections. Now, the first is the general [section], while the following thirteen are the specific [sections].
The first clarifies that "turning the hearing back toward its own nature" is the essence of contemplation; the remainder concerns its functional efficacy, and thus they are not [treated here].

The two phrases, "From [the practice of] Guanyin, observe with the observer," clarify the essence of contemplation (*guan*). Regarding the three instances of the character *guan* (contemplation), various commentators have interpreted them differently:
some take the lower instances as departing tones (*qùshēng*), while others take the upper instance as a departing tone.

None of these, however, capture the intent of the sutra. Why is this? This is the principle of "reversing the hearing to return to one's own nature. Now, let us consider these three instances of the character *guan*.
If one explains the character "wen" (聞) as "to hear," its meaning becomes clear. As it is said: "Because I do not hear the sound myself, I hear by means of hearing.
Here, "the hearer" is precisely the self-nature of hearing; this is clear, precise, and beyond doubt.

However, since all three characters in the term "sanguan" (三觀) are now explained with the level tone (*píngshēng*), "guan" (觀) is identical to "wen" (聞). Therefore, what follows below is an added empowerment.
The function of benefiting others refers to the empowerment of sentient beings through the aforementioned merit of "returning the hearing.
When sentient beings are able to contemplate the voice of the Bodhisattva—that is, the name—then by reciting that name, all suffering and affliction shall be liberated.
This is because the name is precisely the designation for the true nature; the name is [the reality itself].
Because it is real, although its nature is quiescent, its responsiveness is unimpeded; it is like when sentient beings suffer and call upon Heaven, Heaven will surely grant them aid.
In this text, "suffering and distress" is a general summary, while the following thirteen sections specifically demonstrate the various manifestations of suffering.
Furthermore, where the intended meaning of the names can be combined, they have been merged; thus, the text is divided into six sections.
Second, through the reversal of cognition and vision, one causes all sentient beings (up to) to be swept away by great waters, yet the waters cannot drown them.

This section of the sutra follows the preceding "wondrous response" and continues with the shared themes of sorrow and longing; these two points clarify that water and fire cannot burn or drown [the practitioner].
Regarding "the reversal of cognition and vision": because of the practice of returning the hearing, the other faculties are likewise restored. This clarifies [the point].
The term "seeing" (*jian*) is used again here; although it encompasses both the function of knowing and the intent of the teaching, it specifically refers to the faculty of the eye.

Thus, "revolving back" (*xuan fu*)—where "revolving" (*xuan*) means returning and "back" (*fu*) means returning to the original enlightenment—signifies that the eye-faculty returns and reverts to the original enlightenment.
Since the nature of the eye belongs to fire, once it has revolved back, the fire of the eye is extinguished, because the nature of the internal fire and the external fire are identical.
Because the source has ceased internally, the external also vanishes. By bestowing these merits upon sentient beings, one enters fire without being burned.
Regarding "observing and hearing revolve back," although this combines both observation and speech, the meaning actually belongs to hearing revolving back, as explained above.
That which was previously combined with knowing is here combined with observing; the meaning clarifies that when the One returns to its origin, the six faculties are liberated.
It is simply because [the ear] was previously bound by the nature of water; now that the root has returned, hearing of water naturally ceases.

This is because the internal and external are of one body: when the internal ceases, the external also vanishes. By the power of this merit, it is bestowed upon sentient beings; therefore, one does not drown when entering water.
Thus, the question is asked: "The ears and eyes belong to water and fire; from which scripture does the mind arise? The answer is: "According to the Worldly Physicians..."

This is because the *Nan jing* (Difficult Classic of Medicine) states that the five viscera correspond to the five elements: the eyes connect to the heart-fire, and the ears connect to the kidney-water;
this may be verified in detail in that text.
Fourth, severing delusive thoughts so that the mind is free from killing and harming—up to—"is also like blowing upon light, whose nature is without movement."

This section of the sutra follows the preceding theme of wondrous response and shared compassion, demonstrating that these three types of enlightened beings cannot be harmed by ghosts, calamities, or weapons.
The two lines beginning with "eradication" (斷滅) are due to the six sense organs returning to their source and the six consciousnesses being simultaneously extinguished.
"Delusive thoughts" (妄想) refers here to the sixth consciousness; when the mind grasps at objects, the three poisons circulate and prevail, leading to an excess of killing and harm. Now...
Once they have been merged and extinguished, killing and harming cease. By means of this merit, one brings protection to sentient beings;

even if one enters a realm of ghosts, the ghosts cannot harm them. This is because ghosts are the meaning of deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*), and since the meaning of ghosts is deluded thought, once deluded thoughts are severed, ghosts cannot cause harm.
As for "perfuming hearing so as to become hearing": since the aforementioned hearing is false, one perfumes and cultivates that falsity to make it...
When one forgets conditions and returns to the source, true hearing is perfected; once this single hearing has returned, the six deluded faculties and their cognitive roots are likewise dissolved.

Thus, it becomes identical to the forgetting of sound and the perfection of true hearing. Because that which is to be dissolved has already been dissolved, external objects no longer obstruct the mind.

Since the internal faculties have perished, how could external objects exist? By the power of these merits, when bestowed upon sentient beings, their material forms will naturally disintegrate; how then could they possibly [persist]?

The two lines beginning with "Harming oneself when it arrives" explain, in terms of phenomena (*dharma*), that one cannot harm oneself and that external objects will naturally perish. The section beginning with "If one causes...
explains, in terms of principle (*tattva*), that the true nature (*dharmatā*) is immovable and thus how can illusory objects cause harm? The former [section] can be understood through phenomena;
the latter [section], concerning principle, further employs a metaphor to clarify that water and light are analogous to the true nature—just as the nature of water has no self, it cannot be cut.
Thus, what harm is there in cutting through water? Furthermore, the light of the sun and moon cannot be grasped by seizing it, nor can it be moved by blowing upon it.
As the *Huainanzi* says: "Light can be seen but cannot be held; water can be followed but cannot be destroyed.
One may infer from this that the true nature (*zhenxing*) is likewise. For the true nature alone is quiescent and without trace; how could it [be affected]?
Is it that by cutting it one causes injury, or by blowing upon it one causes movement? The character "only" (惟) in the current text refers precisely to the nature of water and light;
for the nature of water and light is none other than the wondrous True Suchness-nature.
Sixth: "The permeation by hearing is brilliant and clear, pervading the Dharma-realm" (up to) "...passing through perilous paths, thieves cannot plunder.

This section of the sutra follows from the preceding "wondrous response" and likewise expresses this fourfold manifestation of compassion and yearning. It clarifies that when pure darkness has subsided, the faculties are stilled and the objects of perception are severed;

thus one is not plundered by thieves, and both demonic prohibitions and obstacles are leveled. The two lines beginning with "permeation by hearing" [refer to... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a commentary on a Buddhist scripture. The bracketed portion indicates that the final two lines of the verse are incomplete in the source.)
Because his body is observed to be purely one and transparently clear toward the outside, it is said that "clarity pervades the Dharma-realm.
Because this clarity can destroy darkness, it is said that "the nature of darkness is not complete.

Through the empowerment of these merits upon sentient beings, even when various evil ghosts and spirits draw near him, the Bodhisattva’s samādhi is so brilliant and flashing like the sun that the eyes of these ghosts dare not look upon it.
*Yakṣa* is translated as "Rightly Beholding" (as seen previously); *rākṣasa* is translated as "Terrifying";
*kumbhāṇḍa* is translated as "Demonic Ghosts of Obscuration"; *piśāca* is translated as "Eaters of Vital Essence"; and *pūtana* is translated as "Ghosts of Fever.
Regarding the last two lines concerning the nature of sound: the external nature of sound is universally dissolved, and internal observation and hearing are turned back into [the source].
The merit and power of this grace enable sentient beings so that they are not bound by shackles and are free from the profane;
for even the confinement of shackles and locks belongs to external objects, and thus they are not attached to them. Regarding the two phrases following the word "extinguished" (*mie*):

since the objects of sound have been extinguished, true hearing is perfected. However, through the compassion inherently possessed by this true hearing, there is no place where its power does not arise.

It can extract suffering and bestow happiness; thus, even though those who seek [these things] may travel through perilous paths where bandits cannot plunder them, the power of the roots of goodness of true clarity, kindness, and compassion pervades their intent and secretly influences the bandits' minds, causing thoughts of robbery and killing not to arise.
Even if they should wish to plunder, or if they brandish blades, swords, spears, or lances, these shall all be shattered into pieces.

Ninth: "The cultivation of hearing leaves behind sensory dust, so that one is not plundered by forms" (extending to) "...all those in the state of *icchantika* forever leave behind the darkness of delusion.

This section of the sutra follows from the previous "wondrous response" and likewise expresses compassion for those who look up [to the Buddha]. It shows that these five [faculties] are entirely free from the three poisons of greed, anger, and delusion.
Since the meaning of "the cultivation of hearing leaves behind sensory dust" has already been clarified in the preceding text, why is it repeated here?

The emergence of the excellent serves to permeate the single practice, which is endowed with immeasurable virtues. What has been cited here—these fourteen matters—is but a small fraction of that immeasurability.
If one were to clarify its ultimate limit, it could not be exhausted by words; how then could one say that "form does not rob"? Form is the desire for form;
yet, because the six faculties are profoundly still and perfectly luminous, the six sense-objects are empty and false. Since the false cannot rob the true, [the essence remains].
Therefore it is said that "form does not rob. Because form does not rob, sentient beings with much lust look up to it, and its spiritual efficacy must surely bestow benefit upon them;
hence it is said: "Far removed from greedy desire, the sounds are pure and free from dust.
As for the previous passage which spoke only of perfuming the hearing so that the nature of hearing was pure, now the sounds being heard are also pure; this is truly because...

Since there are no phenomena external to the mind and even sounds accord with the nature (*dharmatā*), it is said that "there is only sound. Because sound accords with the nature, no objects can be apprehended;
thus both the sense faculties and their objects are transformed into the single True Mind. Consequently, there is neither a subject nor an object of perception.
When this merit is bestowed upon sentient beings whose faculties are dominated by anger, all their hatred and resentment are transformed into compassion.

Therefore, it is said: "Far removed from anger and resentment, one dissolves the dust. The following four lines mean that by dissolving external false objects (*bāhyavikalpa-rajas*) and turning back the internal true luminosity (*antar-tattva-prabhāsvara*), the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*)—the support—and the body—the supported—are both fused.

Because they are thus transparently clear and unimpeded, they are like lapis lazuli, pure and penetrating both inside and out. By means of this merit of the mutual fusion of body and land, one bestows empowerment upon the darkness of ignorance.

Because sentient beings can cause the icchantikas—who are dull and obtuse—to transform their darkness into clarity, it is said that they "distance themselves from the obstacles of the nature of dullness and darkness caused by delusion.
This means that icchantika sentient beings have dullness as their nature and are entirely devoid of correct wisdom;
therefore, they deny cause and effect and cling to the nihilistic view of emptiness, which obstructs the root of true prajñā within their nature. Thus, [it is said].
"Cloud-nature" (*yunxing*) translates as *ātyantika*, which means "without desire" because one does not delight in *nirvāṇa*;
it is simply another name for an *icchantika*. Twelfth, "Fusing Form" (*rongxing*):
he again heard that at the Immovable Site of Enlightenment (*acalā-maṇḍala*), there was a woman with physical marks whom the multitude loved and revered.

This section of the sutra follows from the preceding "wondrous response" and continues with "sorrowful longing. These six clarify the meaning of the "provisional sustenance" (*upabhoga*) that is capable of being inherited, enabling one to obtain the two kinds of seeking.
Regarding the phrase "fusing forms and again hearing," according to the meaning of the text, "forms" refers to the provisional and the fundamental (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*).
It means to harmonize and integrate the forms of both the provisional and the fundamental; thus it is said that "without moving, one is able to traverse [them]."

Furthermore, "hearing that which points to the Real" refers to hearing the teaching of the ultimate meaning; "hearing accompanied by delusion" refers to returning from deluded hearing back to true hearing.
The two lines beginning with "immovable" refer to the site of practice (*do-ch'ang*), as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:

"ascending to and preaching at the Immovable Bodhi-field" means that without leaving one's current location, one travels everywhere throughout the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*). It is "indestructible."
"World" (*loka*) refers to the fact that it does not destroy the characteristics of coming and going, self and other, near and far;
thus it can pervade the four lower phrases to clarify the vastness of making offerings and the meaning of inheriting [the lineage] as a son.

However, the upper [phrase] "fusing form" and the subsequent phrase "returning to hearing" belong to the unmoving principle (*li*), while the two lower phrases refer to engaging with phenomena (*shi*) without moving from the principle; the mundane world belongs to phenomena.
Therefore, because one follows the phenomenon through principle, it is said that "the world is not destroyed" and so forth;
this precisely clarifies that principle and phenomena are mutually fused and inherently possess both the provisional and the real meanings. Thus, there is the title of "Dharma Prince.

By the empowerment of these merits, those childless sentient beings who seek a son shall obtain a son. Regarding the passage on the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*), it means that once the six faculties have been restored...

The Perfectly Round Universal [Wisdom] is without superiority or inferiority; seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are all luminously illumined, equal, and mutually fused—therefore it is called "non-dual.
It accords with the nature and pervades everywhere—therefore it is said to "encompass the realms of the ten directions.

The Great Perfect Mirror is wisdom (*jñāna*), while the *tathāgatagarbha* is principle (*dharmatā*). This means that this wisdom and this principle are established based upon the ten dharma-realms; yet, this wisdom...
This principle is established through the perfect illumination of the six sense organs;

thus, one is able to receive and accord with the secret Dharma-gates of the Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions. It is not merely a matter of receiving and acceding, for one can also receive and comprehend them without loss.
This very meaning of receiving and acceding enables childless sentient beings who seek daughters to obtain daughters.
Master Min of Zhulin’s commentary states: "That which moves while remaining unmoved before is expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).

Expediency belongs to the provisional (*upāya*); because the provisional can manage affairs, it should be classified as male. The Great Perfect Mirror-like [Wisdom] and the *Tathāgatagarbha* belong to real wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*);

because real wisdom accords with principle (*li*), and principle can contain and nurture all things, it should be classified as female. As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* says regarding the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Is it not this very meaning that the Bodhisattva’s mother takes skillful means as her father?
Fourteenth: [From] this trichiliocosm... [he] bestows the power of fearlessness, providing all beings with complete merit.

This section of the sutra concludes the preceding account of the merit of uprooting suffering for those with the capacity [to receive the teaching], summarizing it within the nature of hearing and generally manifesting its various names and superior titles.
Now, the benefit of this samādhi of perfuming through hearing is inexhaustible in aiding others;

this is because the suffering to be uprooted has limits, whereas the correspondence between the capacity [of the recipient] and the response [of the teaching] is inexhaustible. Thus, within that which is inexhaustible, the exhaustion [of suffering] is proclaimed.
In this fourteenth [section], it is generally revealed that although names and so forth are many, their merits are non-dual.
Why is this? It is because within this single realm of Sahā, the faculty of hearing among sentient beings is sharp;

thus, it perfectly accords with the mark of perfect penetration cultivated by the Bodhisattva, and medicine and disease meet one another. For this reason, the one can overcome the many. However, regarding...
To accommodate the capacities of sentient beings, the excellence [of this land] is manifested; it is not that the path realized by the Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is inferior.
What is realized by both is identical, yet the scope of those to whom it is addressed differs slightly. Regarding the phrase "these three," the character "these" (此) refers to the Sahā world;
there are three thousand great chiliocosms in total, all of which are named Sahā, and these are the domain of the single Buddha Śākyamuni.
The realms to be converted consist of the small chiliocosm, the medium chiliocosm, and the great trichiliocosm, as each possesses three sets of thousands. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"One thousand sets of the four continents, the sun and moon, Mount Sumeru, the heavens of the desire realm, and the Brahma worlds—this is called a small chiliocosm.
One thousand times this small chiliocosm is called a medium chiliocosm. One thousand times this [medium chiliocosm] is the great trichiliocosm; all are identical in nature."
Because it undergoes formation and destruction, it is called a trichiliocosm. Formerly, Master Xuan asked the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa:

"I have heard that the realm transformed by a single Buddha consists of three thousand lands, with the number of days, months, and years sometimes said to be ten billion, and at other times said to be a hundred billion or a thousand billion;
why do these accounts differ in their breadth and brevity? He replied: "It is as your question regarding ten billion, a hundred billion, or a thousand billion."

Regarding the term "billion" (*koṭi*) in the sutra text: when one Buddha manifests a thousand billion transformation bodies and each transforms one sun and moon, this results in a thousand billion suns and moons.
To state the essential point: ten million billion suns and moons constitute one great trichiliocosm (*mahāsāhasralokadhātu*).

This is because in India there are both small and large units for the number "billion"; specifically, one hundred small billions must be taken as one large billion for it to be established [as a great trichiliocosm].
Because there are ten billion suns and moons, it is said that "ten billion [Buddhas] currently reside.

The following clarifies that within this world-system, there are such vast numbers of Bodhisattvas currently residing in the mundane world who manifest in various forms; their manifestations cannot be fathomed by ordinary minds.
In this very region, the sages and worthies of the three teachings have appeared throughout the ages, all of whom belong to these various numbers and have transmitted various methods of cultivation.
I employ various skillful means to gradually lead beings back to the place of treasure, yet no one recognizes it.
In accordance with the manifold minds of sentient beings, I teach and transform them through immeasurable Dharma-gates.

From my own inferior state as a Bodhisattva, I have traced back all prior merits to their fundamental root; thus, by means of me, the original root of perfect penetration has been revealed and its subtle essence awakened.
Because of the gateway of the wondrous ear, one is able to make the body and mind subtle and wondrous, containing and pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

Regarding the body and mind pervading the realm, as stated in the subsequent text: "Manifesting each individual form from the one to the immeasurable; with many heads and eyes, the many bodies are but a single body.
This constitutes the containment of the body. Furthermore, it says: "Reciting each individual mantra from the one to the immeasurable..."
The expression "measures speech and sound" means that one is able to bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings. To take fearlessness as a gift is as previously described:
being such that fire cannot burn and water cannot drown, thereby causing others to have no cause for alarm;
this constitutes the mind's capacity for inclusion. Because there is nothing too large that its body or mind cannot contain, and nothing too small that it cannot admit, it is so called.
"Containing and pervading" means that this *dharmadhātu* is explained in terms of the ten *dharmadhātus*. It enables one to equalize the "few" and the "many":

it means that the merit produced by a single sentient being within the *dharmadhātu* who holds the name of Avalokiteśvara is exactly equal and no different from the merit produced by another person who holds the names of many bodhisattvas.
Thus, the merit experienced by these two individuals who hold the names is precisely the same.
The reason why the Honored One’s manifestation of the one and the many is equal and without distinction is precisely because it is equality.
This is truly due to the Bodhisattva’s development of the wondrous gateway of the ear, which is true and perfectly penetrating; thus, he is able to realize the equality of the one and the many.

This is called the concluding summary of the fourteen fearlessnesses. As for "power," this refers to the wondrous power of perfect penetration and non-action, which is said to be fully endowed with merit.
This means that causing others not to fear hardships such as water and fire is itself merit; because there is no suffering left unextracted, it is called "complete.
Furthermore, merit is itself happiness; since suffering has been extracted, one transforms suffering into happiness, and thus it is said that "merit is complete.

Regarding the term "sixty-two" (*liùshí'èr*) in the *Zhòngshēng fāngběn* (The Source Text of Sentient Beings), the character "hundred million" (*yì*) appears below it; however, according to the Southern Canon (*Nánzàng*), this character "hundred million" is absent.
“World-Honored One, I have further attained this perfect penetration through cultivation and realization... (up to)... saving and delivering sentient beings so that they attain great sovereignty.

This section of the sutra follows the previous discussion on wondrous response to further clarify that the nature and substance of perfect penetration possess four kinds of inconceivable virtues to respond to sentient beings.
While the previous section spoke of “powers,” the current section speaks of “virtues”; “power” refers to the functional efficacy [of these virtues].

Regarding the external, one should speak of "virtue" (*guṇa*) as inherent nature; regarding the internal endowment, it is called "virtue" because it is that which is inherently possessed by one's own nature.
Furthermore, "virtue" means "attainment": it is attained within the mind and responded to within the objective realm. As the Commentary of Changshui states:
"If internal virtue is not fulfilled, external function will not arise"—this is precisely what is meant. [The section] beginning with "The World-Honored One" below provides a general summary.
The characteristics of the marks possess four virtues because they are realized through perfect penetration; that which is thus realized is the Unsurpassed Way.
Therefore, the word "therefore" (故) refers back to the arising of the four virtuous states from perfect penetration.
All four are termed "inconceivable," for "inconceivable" is the general designation for the "wondrous. First, it is because of the non-obstruction between one and many; next...

First, because there is no fear regarding the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings; second, because the three aggregates (skandhas) communicate through faith and mystery; third, because the field of compassion and reverence is fulfilled;

and fourth, because virtue is complete within and its response is pervasive without—acting without action and acting while being without action, such that it cannot be discussed by words nor conceived by the mind—it is called the "Inconceivable Sublime Virtue.
The following section provides a detailed explanation of each point.

Regarding the phrase "The Bodhisattva who has heard the wondrous and wondrous with a mind of virtue," this is the Bodhisattva’s self-praise of the three types of wisdom—listening, reflection, and cultivation.

"Listening" refers to the faculty of hearing; the term "mind" (*citta*) pertains in meaning to reflection and cultivation, which thus signifies the "hearing-permeation" (*śruta-vāsanā*) of listening and cultivation.
This is done by skillfully altering the grammatical phrasing. Furthermore, because the meanings of reflection and cultivation pertain to the sixth consciousness, they are termed "mind. However...
Because one relies on hearing to contemplate and cultivate, it is called the "hearing-mind" (*śruticitta*). The repetition of "wondrous" (*miaomiao*) is precisely a term of praise;

it refers to wondrous hearing, wondrous contemplation, and wondrous cultivation, pointing to the essence of the initial observation. Therefore, it is said that at the outset, one attains the three types of wisdom (*trividya*), all of which are wondrous.
To enhance the elegance of the text, the term "wondrous-wondrous" is used together. The character "mind" (*xin*) in "the mind refines what is heard" (*xinqing wenxin*) is the "summit" (*mūrdhan*).
The "upper" refers to the mind of contemplation and cultivation; once this mind is refined, its deluded hearing is cast aside.
Consequently, the six faculties—seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—can no longer be partitioned, but are fused into the one true mind. Thus it is said:

"One attains a perfectly interfused, pure, and precious awakening. The interpretations offered by various schools regarding such phrases as "the wondrously wondrous hearing-mind" are indeed eloquent and worthy of consideration.
If one’s contemplation of the principles is not thorough, one cannot point directly to the actual reality; this is merely a laborious embellishment.

Therefore, when it is said that "the marks and characteristics of the sublime brightness manifest as a multitude of wondrous forms," this refers to the entirety of the body, not merely the head, arms, and eyes.
