As for the "boundless secret mantras," these include such spells as those in the *Amoghapāśa Sūtra*, the *Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, and the *Bhaisajyaguru-rāja-pūrvapraṇidhāna-vaipulya-sūtra* (Yanmukha).
All of these are secret divine mantras spoken by this Bodhisattva; yet, although they have come here to China, they are but one or two out of ten million.

Because they are so numerous, they are said to be "boundless. Among them, the first chapter showing the signs is the fundamental [text], while the eighty-four thousand [subsequent chapters] represent inconceivable transformations.
They serve as remedies for the eighty-four thousand afflictions of sentient beings.
Because there are eighty-four thousand afflictions, the Bodhisattva is wondrously able to extend his body throughout his entire being and across the whole earth;
these are the hands and eyes of the Bodhisattva—how could they be limited to merely eighty-four thousand? There is indeed a profound reason for the teaching of their "antidotes" (*pratipakṣa*).
*Ślakṣṇa* (or *śakala*) is translated as "firm"; the two arms are the basis, extending even unto eighty-four thousand, which is inconceivable.

"Transformation" (*nirmāṇa*)—the meaning of *mudrā* as explained in the second [section]—refers to the two eyes being the basis, up to the eighty-four thousand [transformations], which are inconceivable transformations. Because they are untainted, they are called "pure";

because they are rare and inconceivable, they are worthy of honor and respect, and are thus termed "jewels. "Compassion, majesty, concentration, and wisdom" collectively refer to the head, arms, and eyes.
Furthermore, the characteristics manifested by the entire body—whether analyzed or subsumed according to these four intentions—are all termed "compassion that protects sentient beings.

"Gathering" (*saṃgraha*) refers to *anugraha* (favoring/assisting), while "breaking" (*bhañjana*) refers to *vidhūnana* (subduing). Through concentration (*samādhi*), one restrains madness; through wisdom (*prajñā*), one transforms delusion.
Although the root dispositions of all sentient beings are not uniform, they generally do not exceed these four. Externally, they manifest in perfect accordance; internally, [they are realized].

Their virtue is without blemish, like a mirror that reflects both the beautiful and the ugly without contention; because they accomplish things in accordance with conditions, it is said that they have attained great mastery (*mahāvaśitā*).
Second, from "by means of what I have heard and contemplated, I am liberated from the six sense-objects" up to "all name me as the one who bestows fearlessness."

This section of the sūtra follows the preceding [passage] on the wondrous response to further reveal the four virtues; here, it reveals how through the bestowal of form, sound, and speech, both manifest (*vyakta*) and secret (*guhya*), one grants fearlessness.
"Hearing and contemplating lead to liberation from the six objects" refers to the three types of wisdom (the omission of the word "cultivation" is for brevity);
because once a single faculty returns to its source, all six sense bases are liberated, this passage speaks of liberation in terms of the six objects, such as sound.

Regarding "crossing the wall," sound is used as a metaphor; since a wall cannot obstruct or block sound, this illustrates that seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition are not hindered by the six sense objects.
This precisely clarifies the meaning of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), whereby one is able to employ them interchangeably.
As for "wondrous ability," this refers to explaining it in terms of function; manifesting forms and reciting mantras are both functions, and thus each and every [faculty] is so.
Regarding the "single form" and "single mantra": each one is itself manifold; this explains the forms of the one and the many, and the boundless mantras.

Because these forms and these mantras accord with conditions to extract suffering and bestow fearlessness upon sentient beings in general, all sentient beings throughout the dust-like realms of the ten directions call the Bodhisattva the "Bestower of Fearlessness. This is by means of... [no fear].
The differentiation of differentiations clarifies the wondrous virtue of the inconceivable for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
Third, because I cultivated my original, wondrous, and perfect penetration (up to: sacrificing my body and precious treasures, I sought your compassionate pity).
This section of the sutra follows the preceding marvelous response to further manifest the four virtues;

it demonstrates how, through their divine efficacy and swift influence, sentient beings who behold them spontaneously give rise to a mind of generosity and develop feelings of compassion and yearning.

It means that as the Bodhisattvas traverse the ten directions through the wondrous gate of perfect penetration, by the power of their samādhi, all sentient beings who see or hear them produce [these virtuous responses].
With a heart of reverent longing, he secretly resolved to practice the giving of his body; this is the internal gift, while precious jewels constitute the external gift.
Since even his own life and body—what the world holds most dear—he was able to relinquish, how much more so external objects?

He who gives both internally and externally does so out of a desire for compassion and in the hope of being delivered from suffering; all of these are moved by the inconceivable virtues of a Bodhisattva.
Fourth: "I have attained the Buddha-mind and realized the ultimate" (up to) "seeking great nirvana and attaining great nirvana.

This section of the sutra follows the previous [section on] wondrous response to further clarify the four virtues (*catur-guṇa*). Here, through the two fields of compassion and reverence, both the upward offering and the downward benefit are fully perfected.
Regarding "attaining the Buddha-mind": because the causal mind accords with the fruit, my own mind is itself the Buddha.
Because of the mind, one attains the realization of the meaning; furthermore, the character "attain" (*de*) should be construed with the following character "realize" (*zheng*).
Since "attain" and "realize" are explained as distinct phrases, "realizing the ultimate" means realizing ultimate enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Because one can, through the giving of an impartial mind, provide offerings to the Buddhas above and benefit all living beings below—the Buddhas being equal—this [practice] extends laterally to those below and correctly [establishes] those above.
The "Illumination" (Ming) section below explains that each [being] fulfills its own seeking; therefore, the sentient beings of the six realms—what do the beings in hell seek?
They seek to escape being burned, pounded, and ground, so as to obtain a moment’s rest. The hungry ghosts seek to be freed from hunger and emptiness;
the animals seek to be freed from the blade and the block. The rest may be understood accordingly. Wife, children, and longevity are worldly dharmas; [true] longevity is the *samādhi*.
Nirvāṇa is a supramundane dharma; the phrase "longevity" (*āyuṣ-pada*) should be connected with "wife and children.

If it were inserted here below "samādhi," then the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) would become confused; this was an oversight by the translation team. Regarding the phrase "inferior to precious jewels" in the subsequent section, the text is merely abbreviated;
logically, it ought to be present there as well. Furthermore, because mundane and supramundane dharmas cannot be fully described, the word "then" (*nai*) is used.
The preceding detailed explanation of the efficacy and transformative power of the perfect penetration of the ear faculty is hereby concluded.
From the Buddha’s question regarding perfect penetration, “I have followed the gateway of the ear,” up until, “therefore the name Avalokiteśvara pervades the worlds of the ten directions.”
This section of the sutra concludes that the Buddha’s inquiry regarding the primary expedient means for entering the Way through perfect penetration originally proceeds from the gateway of the ear.
The first phrase cites the Buddha’s question; the words "I [have practiced] from... and below are the Bodhisattva’s own account of entering through the gateway of the ear.
As for the samādhi being termed "perfectly illuminating" (*yuanzhào*), this refers to the cultivation of hearing through the permeation of hearing; it is not discussed here.

Regarding cultivation through perfuming, "perfect illumination" (*yuanzhao*) is so called because perfect illumination consists of the three types of wisdom; since illumination is itself wisdom, and all three are simultaneously empty, it is termed "perfect illumination.
As for "mastery over the conditioned mind," "conditioning" is the conditioning of non-conditioning:

initially, one does not follow external objects but returns the flow to its source, becoming entirely unified. Once this total unity is attained, it is called "perfect penetration" (*yuantong*), as one rides upon non-conditioning.
Compassion follows the sound to save suffering; responding without a deliberate mind, the very act of responding is non-response, for there is no lingering or obstruction.
Thus it is called "Mastery. Entering below refers to the original cause for entering the stream;
attaining Bodhi is the fruit, which takes the faculty of hearing as the primary expedient. The above twenty-five sages each rely upon their own realized entry.
It is called "foremost" because its return to the source is non-dual; therefore, each gate is designated as foremost.
The World-Honored One concludes this section by clarifying the distant origin and demonstrating the intent of non-forgetfulness.

Furthermore, he reveals his own provenance, for that Buddha points to the ancient Avalokiteśvara-Buddha as the speaker, and praises that Bodhisattva for having perfectly attained *yuan-tong* (perfect penetration).
The initial dharma-gate bestows the title of Avalokiteśvara amidst the great assembly to manifest the correspondence between cause and effect.
The term "ten directions" (śī-fāng) is explained according to the meanings of horizontal and vertical:

vertically it refers to the ten realms of existence, and horizontally it refers to the ten spatial directions, because each of the ten dharma-realms pervades the ten directions. Following this, the twenty-five sages have been detailed.

Because Perfect Penetration responds distantly to the eighteen realms and the seven great elements, the passage below—wherein the World-Honored One and the Buddhas of the ten directions simultaneously emit light from their entire bodies—is intended to signify that the dharmas of the eighteen realms are fully manifested and all return to the summit of enlightenment as the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
This will be explained in detail below; for now, I shall briefly indicate the source and the rise and fall of the text.
At that time, the World-Honored One [sat] upon the lion throne... (until) "the intermingling lights crisscrossed like a net of precious threads.

This section of the sutra concludes the Buddha’s individual manifestation of the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). The mutual infusion of intermingled lights serves to symbolize that although there are diverse entries, they all return to the same source.
Regarding the "five limbs" (*wu-ti*): this refers to the head and the four limbs, indicating the body as a whole. Five limbs.
The emission of light serves to manifest universal penetration, as there is nowhere it does not shine;

therefore, in the initial passage where the light of Śākyamuni Buddha pours over those dust-mote Buddhas and the various assemblies, it mentions only Bodhisattvas and does not include the two vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas).

However, if one examines the subsequent text, where the light from the dust-mote Buddhas comes to pour over the Buddha, the Bodhisattvas, and the Arhats, then when Śākyamuni’s light goes forth, it should likewise encompass all three vehicles.

It is logically necessary that all [beings] receive this infusion; however, it may be that the compilers of the sutra were incomplete in their narration, or perhaps it was overlooked during the translation process.

This is intended to represent the meaning through metaphorical imagery. The mutual infusion of light between the Buddhas and those of the Three Vehicles signifies that the various methods of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) previously mentioned do not separate self and other, for cause and effect ultimately converge. In the preceding twenty-five sages, the Great and the Small were intermingled.
Now, the empowerment by the flowing light (*ābhiseka*) should likewise be shared equally among the three vehicles;

it serves to symbolize that the mind-dharma of perfect penetration can be entered everywhere and realized by every person. All are "empowered" because the "crown" (*mūrdhan*) represents the locus of ultimate, perfect consummation.
It symbolizes that the limit of ultimate awakening within the mind-dharma is inherently possessed by all people; once perfect penetration is attained, what [further remains]?
If people do not realize this Great Buddha-Crown, then how could these insentient things—the groves, the trees, the ponds, and the marshes—be able to proclaim the sound of the Dharma?
To manifest universal penetration (*yuantong*) before one’s eyes means that all forms are the forms of phenomena and all sounds are the sounds of the Buddha.
Since this is called universal penetration, there is no distinction made among the environment and its inhabitants, form and mind, objects and self, or others and oneself.
Only that which is not limited by circularity can truly be called "perfect penetration" (yuantong);
this can be understood through careful examination of how the various sages in the preceding text all speak of unimpeded circulation. The final two lines are easy to understand.
"This great assembly attained what they had never experienced before" (up to) "Brahmanic hymns and songs were spontaneously performed.

This section of the sutra explains that when the assembly gathered by the World-Honored One beheld the light and attained realization, celestial joy rained down flowers, and the realms of dust and the world were no longer separated;
both sentient and insentient beings alike offered praise and celebration. These various assemblies refer to the gatherings of the Original Teacher.
The various explanations also state that "never before encountered" refers to the sight of the upper lights mutually interpenetrating—a phenomenon never seen before.
Thus, when the assembly collectively attains the Vajra Samādhi, it is because each of the previous sages who realized their respective perfect penetrations all referred to it as "Vajra Samādhi";

this indicates that "Vajra" is used as a metaphor for meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Although the *Changshui* Commentary specifically identifies it as the hearing through the ears, [the broader sense applies here].
Yuan Guan was mistaken. This is because the Buddha’s light mutually irrigates one another; this universally seals all the sages—how could it ever manifest for only one?

Read the following text, which instructs on selecting those who are "appropriate to the occasion" (*dangji*); only then is the faculty of hearing designated as the "Dharma appropriate to the occasion.

What is presented here is a general principle applicable to all beings, not a restrictive intent. The passage beginning with "At that very moment" clarifies how the various devas, upon hearing the Dharma and beholding the light, give rise to the Dharma.
Because of joy, a rain of various lotus flowers falls; these flowers possess the colors of a hundred jewels.
Although there are a hundred jewel-colors, they do not exceed the five primary manifest colors—blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth—as these are the manifest colors.

As for the statement that "emptiness becomes the color of the seven jewels," this refers to the aforementioned hundred jewel-colors used to clarify the marvelous craftsmanship of the flowers; because there are a hundred kinds of many wonders, it is now said that the "colors of the seven jewels" reflect [upon them].
"Emptiness" clarifies that the substance of the precious jewels does not consist of gold, silver, pearls, jade, *śukti* (conch), or *musāragalva* (agate);
thus, this lower section clarifies the imagery of the combined realms to reveal the fundamental meaning of perfect penetration.
When deluded, there is no separation yet one separates oneself; after awakening, all ten thousand obstructions are simultaneously permeated and the six sense faculties are unimpeded. Therefore:
The realms of dust merge into one. The following section on *brahmā-gāna* clarifies the intent of praise and celebration.
*Brahmā-gāna* is the music of the various devas; its chanting and singing are the hymns of praise by devas and humans.

This means that the manifold instruments sound spontaneously without being struck, and devas and humans sing naturally without instruction—wherein the animate and inanimate are moved by the profound manifestation of the Dharma-gate of universal penetration.
The sounds they produce naturally resonate in harmony with what they have perceived.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed Mañjuśrī: "By what gate of skillful means can [this] be easily accomplished?"
In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One commands the selection of which among the various sages of Perfect Penetration is suited to the capacities of beings in this realm.
The reason he selects the Perfect Penetrations and addresses Mañjuśrī is that Mañjuśrī is foremost in ultimate wisdom;

since choosing the Dharma according to the capacities of beings requires wisdom that nothing else can match, he issues this command. Thereupon, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify their respective scopes, first demonstrates [the following]:
This penetration is spoken of from the perspective of the various sages as being truly without distinction of superiority or inferiority, or of priority or posteriority;

yet, when discussing the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, it must be adapted to their capacities. Therefore, Mañjuśrī was instructed to select [the appropriate teaching]. "Observe those below" can be understood accordingly.
As for each [sage] speaking of the initial expedient means for attaining the Way: "Way" refers to the path of Bodhi attained by all Buddhas of the ten directions.

Skillful means are the principles for entering the Way; when it is said that one cultivates "true and perfect penetration," it refers to how the various sages mentioned previously each entered through their own respective gates and all attained the Way.
Because they took what they themselves realized as the truth, although the gates differ, that which is realized is one and the same. These refer to the twenty-five sages whom I now—

Regarding the capacities of those in this land below, [the Buddha] set aside the universal for the particular, asking Mañjuśrī and the other holy ones which among their various means of perfect penetration was suited to the faculties of the listeners, so as to enable Ānanda to attain awakening.

Furthermore, the Buddha stated that this would not only benefit those present at that time, but would also extend to future generations of the Dharma-ending age, enabling them to enter the Path; by what expedient means could this be easily accomplished?
Thus it was said.

This section of the scripture describes how Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, having received the Buddha’s compassionate command and being sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, spoke in verse in response to the Buddha.
It is a passage in which Mañjuśrī, at the Buddha’s behest, selected the essential teachings and compiled them into *gāthās* to provide an answer.

"May you understand that 'to respond' (*duì*) means to answer immediately. Below, answering what was above is called 'responding' (*duì*); as in Confucian texts, when a subject answers his ruler, it is commonly referred to as 'I respond, saying' (*duì yuē*).

From 'The nature of the ocean of awakening is clear and perfect' (*jué hǎi xìng chéng yuán*) to 'the beginner’s entry into samādhi differs in speed and kind' (*chū xīn rù sānmèi chí sù bù tóng lún*)."

In this section of the scripture, Mañjuśrī first designates the fundamental basis of his selection of the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) and simultaneously reveals the meanings of the empty realm, dependent origination, awakening and delusion, and the speed or slowness of realization; he then proceeds to choose and reject [the other methods].

The two lines beginning with "The ocean of awareness" (*jue-hai*) first clarify the true basis of perfect penetration; these two lines alone encompass many meanings, with the upper line representing the arising from the essence (*ti*).
The lower phrase is used to subsume function back into essence; the upper phrase, "Awakening" (jue), is the essence, while "clarity and perfection" (chengyuan) is the function.

Furthermore, "Awakening" is the dharma, and "sea" is the metaphor for its nature (*xing*); the term "nature" applies to both the dharma and the metaphor. The function of "clarity and perfection" likewise applies to both the dharma and the metaphor.

Within the dharma, "clarity" signifies quiescence (*ji*) and "perfection" signifies illumination (*zhao*); these two meanings of quiescence and illumination arise based upon the nature-awakening (*xing-jue*).

The nature of the ocean likewise possesses the functions of clarity and roundness: because its color is profound and still, it is said to be "clear"; because all things in the universe appear within it, it is said to be "round.
Since the ocean and the nature of awakened awareness (xing-jue) correspond quite closely in these metaphors, the ocean is taken as an analogy.

In the latter phrase, "roundness" and "clarity" represent the function (yong), while "awareness" represents the essence (ti); thus, there is the sense of subsuming the function back into the essence. The former phrase describes "clarity" and "roundness."

The meaning of the former phrase is that [the nature] is quiescent yet constantly illuminating; thus, the latter phrase speaks of "perfect clarity. The meaning of this is that it is illuminating yet constantly quiescent.
Being quiescent yet illuminating, and illuminating yet quiescent, these are different names for the same reality; both are fundamentally wondrous.

The first six phrases following "original clarity" (*yuanming*) reveal the beginning of the arising of delusion. The first phrase, "original clarity illuminates its own nature," is precisely original enlightenment (*benjue*).
The essence of wisdom is fundamentally luminous; this is the original illumination. The "shining" is the functional manifestation that arises upon this luminosity.
Although all phenomena are contained within this shining, fundamentally there is no knowing, yet it knows; there is no shining, yet it shines.

If even a single thought of a "knower" and "known" arises, the True then transforms into the delusory. Once that which is known is established, the nature of True Illumination perishes. This is delusion.

Regarding the delusion of subject and object, the nature of awakening becomes a void of empty stillness, which turns into a stubborn vacuity; thus it is said, "Due to delusive confusion, there is space.
Based upon this space, the nature of rigid attachment arises as the cause of the world-system; thus it is said, "Based on space, the world is established.
The phrase "the thought becomes clear" clarifies the appearance of the initial formation of the world; it refers to the clarification of thought.
This "clarity" (*cheng*) is not the same as the "clarity" in the names Shang-cheng and Yuan-cheng; here, "clarity of thought" (*xiang-cheng*) refers to the sense of deluded thoughts coagulating.
It means that when deluded thoughts have reached the extreme of stagnation and dullness, sentient beings transform into insentient things;
thus it is said, "the clarity of thought forms the land. The phrase "cognition and awareness" clarifies the initial arising of the aggregate body of sentient beings.
They say that the physical aggregates of sentient beings are composed of earth, water, fire, and wind; yet these elements are originally insentient things.

Because the six sense faculties revolve, they cause them to be perceived through awareness. Originally, the six faculties were of one nature, perfectly luminous, but they have been obstructed by earth and the other elements, causing them to become stagnant and congealed.
Therefore, hearing does not transcend sound and seeing does not surpass form, whereby one becomes a "multitude" (a sentient being).

Because the five aggregates arise and form a body, it is said that "perception" constitutes a sentient being. The following six lines beginning with "emptiness arises" clarify the extreme subtlety of sentient beings within the realm of emptiness;
by contrast, they reveal the greatness of Great Awakening. Thus it is said:

"Emptiness arises within Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the sea. The sea is a metaphor for Great Awakening, and the bubble is a metaphor for empty space. Even empty space [is but a bubble].
How much less so for the contaminated realms of dust and the sentient beings who depend upon space to exist? It is clear that these are even smaller than the small;
they arise and perish without constancy. This clarifies that because of delusion regarding existence, one perceives the fundamental non-existence of space as being like bubbles.
When the bubbles subside, the space [within them] vanishes. This phrase reveals both the dharma and the metaphor simultaneously, signifying that even empty space itself does not exist.
How could there be any world or sentient beings that, by virtue of their capacity to be dispatched [to liberation], would not do so—let alone those within the three realms of existence?

The "three realms of existence" (*trai-dhātu*) are spoken of here in terms of both the environment and its inhabitants. Thus, the phrase "all things return to the source" and the following six lines precisely clarify the intent of selecting the Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*):
it means that while the various sages previously mentioned all return to the nature of the source of enlightenment, which is fundamentally without duality, their...
The phrase "expedient means for entering" indicates that there are many gateways, signifying that the expedient means by which one enters differ.
The single phrase "the nature of the sages" refers to the fact that the nature realized by all sages is universally penetrating and is reality itself;
therefore, both the compliant and the contrary are expedient means. The "compliant" refers to those whose faculties follow this [teaching], such as the ear-faculty; the "contrary" refers to...

What other sages have taught is called "contrary" because it does not accord with the individual's capacity. The final two lines conclude the preceding discussion, establish the fundamental principle, and introduce the main section of the formal analysis.
Now, this sagely nature permeates everywhere; yet, when a beginner first seeks entry, they must rely upon a perfect faculty (*indriya*) to swiftly realize primordial enlightenment.
If one erroneously relies on an imperfect faculty, it will be difficult to reach the ultimate goal. Therefore, one should...
The selection process is as previously described in the sutra, wherein days and kalpas are mutually multiplied; by means of this selection, those who are capable of entering are admitted.
"Not of the same class" means that their rates of progress—whether slow or fast—cannot be made equal. The following verse specifically begins the selection with the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*).
"The perception of form binds one to dust" (up to) "how can one attain perfect penetration?

This section of the scripture records Mañjuśrī receiving the command to formally select the perfect penetrations of the various sages, necessarily prioritizing those that accord with the capacities of practitioners;

thus, he first addresses the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). The first verse eliminates the sense object of form. "Perception" (*saṃjñā*) refers to contemplative visualization (*bhāvanā*), arising from such contemplation.
The impure white bones return to fine dust, and the fine dust returns to emptiness. Thus, form is formed by the knots of false conceptualization;
it is an obstructive coarse substance that causes the nature of subtle clarity to no longer be bright and penetrating. How, then, could there be perfect penetration?
The next verse distinguishes the sense-object of sound. It means that the nature of sound arises from chaotic speech, and speech...
Names, phrases, and syllables do not emerge as substantial entities apart from the three types of sound; rather, names, phrases, and syllables are provisional designations based upon sound.
Specifically, direct sound constitutes "sound" itself, while the sequential arrangement and modulation of clarity, turbidity, height, and depth within that sound constitute "tone.

Because these tones comprise five distinct varieties—*gong*, *shang*, *jiao*, *zhi*, and *yu*—they are termed "variegated" (*za*). The character *yi* means "that," referring here to names and phrases.
Regarding "names" (*nāman*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Names signify intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); phrases signify distinctions (*viśeṣa*).

Intrinsic nature refers to the essential self-nature of all phenomena, such as when one speaks of "mountains," "clouds," or "objects. Since these constitute names, it is said that "names signify intrinsic nature.
However, without knowing which specific mountain or which specific water is intended—requiring the manifestation of a particularized meaning—one must call it a "phrase" (*pada*).
For example, mountains are distinguished as "Mount Sumeru," "Himalaya," or "Gandhamādana," and waters as "river water" or "ocean water";

because they are manifested through the meaning of differentiation, they are called *pada* (phrases). As for *vyañjana* (syllables), syllables are merely letters (*akṣara*), so they are called *vyañjana* because they serve as the basis for names and phrases.
As for *artha* (meaning), it is the flavor of the sense; however, while language and letters are finite, the meaning is inexhaustible.
The principle that "the ultimate is inexhaustible" cannot encompass all meanings and flavors; since it would not be perfect, it is excluded by this verse.
The third verse excludes the object of fragrance: fragrance is known through contact; if separated, how could it exist?
That which is not constant is subject to arising and ceasing, and thus Perfect Enlightenment is not achieved. The fourth verse excludes the object of taste: taste belongs to the tongue.
If the nature of each taste is sometimes present and sometimes absent, it is not an inherently permanent flavor;

how then could one attain perfect penetration based on these shifting perceptions of discernment? (Verse 5) This verse distinguishes the sense-object of touch. Touch is an arousal that exists through the mutual dependence of subject and object;
since union and separation are not fixed, how can it be considered perfect penetration? (Verse 6) This verse distinguishes the sense-object of mental phenomena (*dharmas*).
Furthermore, these dharmas are objects of cognition within the mind that depend upon external sensory objects; they are not universally knowable and cannot be fully apprehended.
Thus, the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) have been excluded above. Below, the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) are excluded.
"Although the nature of seeing is transparently clear... [yet] thoughts and perceptions cannot be shed; how then can one attain perfect penetration?
This section of the sutra follows the previous selection of the perfect penetration, which must accord with the capacities of the practitioner, and proceeds through the six sense organs.
The first verse selects the organ of sight: it states that although the nature of seeing is called "transparently clear," there is no distinction between before and after.
"Mutual reaching is likewise not perfect penetration. Regarding the two lines concerning the four intermediate directions (*vidiś*):
while the preceding sutra text spoke only in terms of front, back, left, and right, the current verse cites the four intermediate directions to mutually clarify what was previously stated.
As for the "four corners" being "deficient by one half": because one cannot see the two corners of the rear side, one sees only the two corners of the front side.
Therefore, it is said that "half is deficient"; this deficiency means that because the faculty does not perceive universally, it cannot be considered a complete penetration (*yuan-tong*).
The next verse excludes the nose-faculty. Next, since the ear-faculty is more adaptable to the capacities of sentient beings, its discussion is deferred to the later text;
this is because nasal breath only passes through inhalation and exhalation, lacking the middle intersection, hence it is said: "In the present, there is no intersecting breath."
Furthermore, because the breath has inhalation and exhalation but lacks a central point of intersection, it is said to be "fragmented and incomplete.

Because it is not circular, it is said that it does not "penetrate universally"; thus, it is not the universal penetration (*yuan-tong*). The first verse of three lines excludes the tongue faculty (*jihvā-āyatana*).

In the first line, the character "not" (*fei*) is misplaced; it should be read as "the tongue-faculty is not without cause," which would be easier to understand. "Without cause" (*wu-duan*) refers to the tongue.
The sense organs and their objects do not arise without cause; they must depend upon the flavor-objects (*rasa-viṣaya*) to produce cognition.
If the flavor were absent, cognition would fundamentally not exist. How, then, could one attain perfect penetration? The character "亡" (wáng) should be read as "無" (wú).

This first verse excludes the body-faculty (*kāya-indriya*). The first line identifies the body as the subject that touches and external objects as the touched; yet, even this subject-object relationship is not [ultimately real].

The preceding sutra states: "Is the capacity [of sensation] in the hand, or is it in the head? If the capacity does not reside where the object resides, and the object does not reside where the capacity resides, then there is no fixed locus for either capacity or object;
thus, contact has no reality. Because capacity and object are mutually deficient, this is not the contemplation of Perfect Enlightenment.

Regarding "limits" (*yā-lǎng*): "limit" (*yá*) refers to a boundary, and "measure" (*liàng*) refers to a finite quantity. This points to the limits and measures of capacity and object, which do not merge or coincide.

Therefore, "dark convergence" (*minghui*) carries the meaning of "unification" (*yunhe*). The first verse distinguishes the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*): the faculty of knowing is precisely the faculty of mental cognition.

The faculty of mind has no independent substance, as it is manifested through confused deliberation. As the preceding sutra states: "There must be something upon which one reflects to bring forth your mind;
if there were no prior phenomena, the mind would have nothing from which to arise. Thus, it is said that the faculty of knowing is characterized by confusion.
The second phrase, "profoundly clear" (*zhan*), refers to a state of crystalline clarity; "thoroughly understood" (*liao*) means reaching a final conclusion.

This signifies that when the mind is profoundly clear and thoroughly understood such that there is no further conceptualization or deliberation, the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) ultimately has nothing to perceive. If one cannot detach from discursive thoughts, perfect penetration cannot be attained.
Thus, the five faculties have been eliminated; next, the six consciousnesses are eliminated.
"Consciousness and seeing are mixed with the three-fold harmony... (up to)... how can one attain perfect penetration through the conditions of mindfulness that are not separate from objects?

This section of the sutra follows the previous selection of the Perfect Penetration (yuan-tong), which must accord with the capacities of the practitioners; it follows next upon the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*).
The first verse selects the visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*): "Consciousness and seeing are mixed with the three-fold harmony. Here, "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to the subject.
The arising of views takes the sense objects as their cause; when the faculty, the object, and consciousness—these three—conjoin, the substance of things is manifested.
Because this is a chaotic confluence, it is called the "confused conjunction of the three. As the preceding sutra states, "With the eye and forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises.
If one investigates its root, all three are without marks and lack substantial reality. Here, "intrinsic nature" refers to the eye-consciousness, which is said to depend upon the eye.
Entering perfect penetration by means of consciousness: since the very nature of the visual consciousness is already indeterminate, how could one rely upon it to attain perfect penetration?
The next verse distinguishes the auditory consciousness. "The mind-hearing penetrates the ten directions" is explained as previously in the Chapter on Samantabhadra;
this is accomplished through the power of the great causes of a Bodhisattva in their final birth, and cannot be achieved by those at the initial stage of the path.

The practice upon which one relies for entry is already advanced, yet the capacity of the practitioner who relies upon it is insufficient; thus, when the capacity and the teaching do not accord, one follows the simplified precedent.
The single verse simplifies the nose-consciousness. Regarding "contemplating the white light at the tip of the nose":

this was originally established as a provisional means to accord with the practitioner's capacity, intended to arrest the distracted mind by causing it to abide in the white light—a method employed only temporarily.
This is not a matter for long-term cultivation; if one remains here without ceasing, the mind will become fixated, and how could perfect penetration be attained?
The fourth verse distinguishes the tongue-consciousness. The tongue excels at preaching the Dharma, yet it merely manipulates sounds and characters;
it can only awaken those who have already attained the Way, but it cannot accommodate those of the future degenerate age.
Furthermore, names, phrases, and meanings are not untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*); one cannot attain perfect penetration by relying upon them.
(5) The fifth verse distinguishes the body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*). "Observance and transgression" refers to the precepts; speaking of observance and transgression merely constrains the body.
If the Dharma-body is no body, there is nothing to constrain. Thus, this observance and transgression of deportment are fundamentally not pervasive.

Therefore, the six verses beginning with "How can one attain perfect penetration? distinguish the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). This is because followers of the Two Vehicles attain supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) through volitional application (*manasikāra*);

thus, they demonstrate supernatural power by means of the mental consciousness. However, since those supernatural powers are fundamentally accomplished through past causes, what connection do they have to volitional application?
Furthermore, as long as volitional application has not transcended objective phenomena, how can perfect penetration be attained?
Thus, the six consciousnesses have been eliminated above; now, below, the seven elements are eliminated.
If one contemplates the nature of earth [and so forth], up to the point where it says: "The causes and effects are now distinct; how can one attain perfect penetration?"

This section of the sutra follows the previous selection of the Perfect Penetration (yuan-tong), which must accord with the capacities of practitioners, and it follows next upon the Seven Elements (da).
The first verse selects the element of earth; the text is easily understood. The next verse selects the element of water.
"Thought and recollection are not real" refers to the Water-Contemplation of Candraprabha; because the contemplation of water is like an illusion, it is not real.

The reality of suchness (*tathatā*) is fundamentally beyond both vitarka and vicāra. Regarding the use of two instances of the character "such" (*ru*), traditional commentators have explained that the upper "such" refers to wisdom (*jñāna*) and the lower "such" refers to principle (*li*).
They hold that when such-like wisdom accords with such-like principle, the "four suches" are established.
However, I maintain that since it is the same single character "such," how can one differentiate between wisdom and principle? If we discuss this according to the ultimate truth, it is truly so.
Because it is not different [from its own nature], it is called "thus" (*tathā*) and "immovable mind. Furthermore, this does not mean being as motionless and fixed as empty space;
rather, it is said to be "immovable" precisely because all phenomena (*dharma*) arise in profusion. Since each phenomenon abides in its own fundamental position, it is called "thusness" (*tathatā*).
As the *Prajñāpāramitā* says: "Thusness is immovable," and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "This dharma abides in the position of dharmas."

The dharma of the permanence of the characteristics of the world: these are the characteristics of the world; because the characteristics of the world are themselves permanent, permanence is the meaning of immovability.
This is explained with reference to the ten dharma realms. To take the present human world as an illustration:
"like" (ru) means "relying upon" (yi); it means "correct" (zheng). It is like heaven, like earth, and like the sun, moon, mountains, and rivers.
Whether it be grasses, trees, insects, Buddhas, or Māras, they are all "thus" (tathatā).
Yet, because there is no dharma that is not thus, a single "thus" cannot exhaust its full meaning; therefore, the term "thus-like" (yīrú) is added again to clarify that all dharmas are thus.
Since the principle of thusness does not shift nor change, how could there be any abandoning of this or grasping for that? Therefore, it is not [a matter of] awakening.
To observe this is to say it is not the practice of perfect penetration. The first three verses simplify the element of fire.
Vajra Fire-Head initially felt aversion toward desire and existence; because he practiced the fire-light samādhi, he used that fire-samādhi to suppress desire.
Thus, his mind’s aversion toward existence did not forget [the reality of] truth. This is the equipment for the Mahāyāna, not a skillful means for the initial stage, because at the beginning—
The mind is difficult to enter; it is also simplified by following the four examples. One verse simplifies the element of wind (*vāyu-dhātu*).
The nature of wind is not constant; movement and stillness are relative phenomena. Since there is relativity, it is not true awakening (*bodhi*).

How, then, can this be used to attain perfect penetration? Five verses simplify the element of space (*ākāśa-dhātu*). Rigid emptiness lacks awareness; it is a state of dullness. To lack awareness is different from [true] awakening.

How could awakening (bodhi) possibly constitute perfect penetration? (Verse 61) This verse excludes the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-mahābhūta*). "Consciousness" takes discernment as its essential meaning;

since discernment belongs to the realm of arising and ceasing, it is not the path of permanence. To seek to abide by means of consciousness is fundamentally deluded; perfect penetration cannot be attained in this way.
(Verse 71) This verse excludes the element of sight (*darśana-mahābhūta*). As for the "seeing" mentioned in the preceding sutra...

The "Great" (Mahā) generally subsumes the six sense-faculties; by means of the single faculty of sight, it subsumes the remaining faculties. "All formations" (*saṃskāra*) refers to the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha, for mindfulness belongs to the category of formations.
Since each moment of mindfulness flows and shifts, it constitutes a formation. Because there is this shifting flow, it possesses the nature of impermanence;
thus, it is said to be "originally subject to arising and ceasing. Here, the cause refers to mindfulness of the Buddha, while the fruit refers to perfect penetration; mindfulness is the cause.
Since the fruits of awakening arise from the cessation of birth-and-death while the response of the Unborn is fundamentally different, how could perfect penetration be attained?
Thus, the preceding seven elements have been excluded; the following text specifically selects the faculty of hearing as the path most conducive to the capacities of sentient beings.
"I now address the World-Honored One" (up to) "the Savior of the World brings all peace; transcending the world, one attains eternal abiding.

This section of the sutra follows the previous distinctions and selections, wherein it is shown that for the capacities of those in this land, the Ear-organ is the most appropriate, and thus Avalokiteśvara is supreme.
The two lines beginning with "I now" are self-evident. The two lines beginning with "this land" specifically point to [Avalokiteśvara].
Because the faculty of hearing is sharp among the sentient beings of this Sahā world, the essence of the teaching is sound; names, phrases, and syllables depend upon this.
By means of this, one can turn back to contemplate the nature of hearing itself, so that it is no longer swayed by the dust of sound. Thus, one immediately attains purity. Therefore, it is said next:

"If you wish to attain samādhi, you must truly enter through the medium of hearing. As for "departing from suffering," this refers to what was previously explained regarding the attainment of the fourteen fearlessnesses.

"Deliverance" refers to the thirty-two manifestations described; this refers to the merit of uprooting suffering and bestowing joy, and thus its name is well-expressed as "Excellent One, Avalokiteśvara.
Here, "excellent" (liáng) means good or beautiful, capturing the sense of being utterly good and utterly beautiful.
Furthermore, it continues: "This Bodhisattva, from kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, has universally entered into every dust mote..."
The Buddha-land employs the unconditioned compassion that wondrously responds to all beings, attaining mastery of mind;
through this mastery and fearlessness, it bestows gifts upon all sentient beings. The phrase "Wondrous Sound" below praises the excellence of its name.
Because the name accords with its reality, the name "Avalokiteśvara" is said to be subtle and wondrous. Why is this? Because by reciting its name even once, one immediately attains [liberation].
Is it not marvelous that one can attain liberation from all suffering and distress? Furthermore, its name is "Pure Brahma" (*brahman*), which carries the meaning of purity.
This is truly because, by contemplating all beings equally with the thought of them as one's only child, one leaves no trace of enmity, hatred, or the distinction between self and other;
thus, the name Avalokiteśvara is a *brahma*-sound. Moreover, its name is like the tide of the ocean.
The sound follows the cry to rescue from suffering without missing its time; it arrives instantly upon thought, just as the tides rise and fall without failing their season.

Thus, the two lines concerning "rescuing the world" reveal his actual merit: "the world" refers to the six realms of ordinary beings, for he causes them to leave all sufferings behind and attain complete peace;
"transcending the world" refers to the four classes of noble ones, for he causes those of the three vehicles to all obtain the eternal.

"Dwelling in the eternally abiding" refers precisely to the Buddha-realm. These two lines of meaning comprehensively encompass the two kinds of sublime and wondrous powers mentioned in the preceding sutra.
This verse consists of sixteen lines divided into two stanzas;

the first stanza concludes with "Excellent, Avalokiteśvara," summarizing the praise of how he adapts his teachings to suit the capacities of sentient beings, using the faculty of hearing as the primary means to accord with the final age.
The title is joined [to the verse], and the following verse follows upon the preceding to clarify that the Bodhisattva’s merit is profound and his power is great;

it is a long eulogy of his name and reality as a benefactor and friend to the ten realms. Changshui’s commentary truncates the verse without careful regard for its sequence, causing the continuity of the meaning to be obstructed; this is not a virtuous method.
"I now address the Tathāgata" (up to) "discursive thought and observation transcend deliberation, such that body and mind cannot reach it.
This section of the scripture is Mañjuśrī’s exhaustive praise of the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-āyatana*), which perfectly possesses the three kinds of reality.
The first two phrases generally rely on what was previously stated in the *Avalokiteśvara* chapter; the following verse serves as an illustration of this initial section.
The first four lines of the verse first praise the perfection and reality [of hearing]. Because it is heard simultaneously throughout the ten directions, it is called "perfect" (*pariniṣpanna*);
because what is heard is not false or delusive, it is termed "real" (*tattva*). Because it is real, it can be universally perfect.

However, upon careful examination, the striking of the drum is not the actual metaphor; rather, it is used to verify the perfection and reality of hearing based on the immediate phenomenon before one. Thus, the next verse follows.
Chapter Eight: Praise of the Penetration of the Real. First, by comparing the other faculties with the ear, it reveals their inferiority and lack of parity.

Next, from "separated by a wall" onwards, it clarifies the superiority of the ear; that is to say, this faculty of hearing can listen across walls and perceive both near and far—is this not penetration?
Because it is real and because it can penetrate, it is called "penetrating the reality. This is also [explained] by means of the five faculties.
The superiority and inferiority of "not-hearing" and "hearing" can thus be seen. The subsequent chapter of one verse in twelve lines praises the permanence and reality [of hearing].

The first four lines clarify that while sound has movement and stillness, hearing is without arising or ceasing. The next four lines clarify that while sound arises and perishes of itself, hearing is fundamentally and eternally abiding;
it is perfectly free from arising and ceasing, and is therefore neither transitory nor unreal. Because it is able to be constant, [it is real].

The phrase "constantly true" refers to the final four lines; the remaining meaning is that this nature of hearing exists even within a dream, and though there may be nothing being thought of, the nature of hearing is not absent.
As the preceding sutra states: "In a dream, one hears the sound of pestles and mortars, yet the nature of hearing remains.
The final two lines clarify that the faculty of hearing and its functions of discernment and observation transcend the realm of discursive thought and the body-mind.
It is beyond their reach.
Now, this Sahā world—does this not mean that by following the whirlpool of delusion, one attains non-delusion?
This passage of the sutra points precisely to this: because the faculty of hearing is sharp, it reveals the process of returning to the source by following sound.
Both benefit and harm pertain to hearing. Now, these eleven lines of verse constitute a single chapter.

First, it clarifies that in this Sahā world, the truth is proclaimed through sound; yet if one is deluded regarding fundamental hearing and pursues sound to drown in delusion, no harm could be greater.
Subsequently, it specifically identifies Ānanda to verify the error of pursuing sound, so that the harm may be seen. It says:
Though his powerful memory and vast learning were ultimately subsumed within the outflows (*āsrava*), he could not avoid falling into the illusory arts of the depraved thoughts of Ḍombī;
was this not indeed a case of being submerged by following sounds?

If one can truly reverse the flow of desire and internally exhaust the nature of hearing to attain the true hearing that is free from delusion, would that not be beneficial? Indeed, as for such benefit, there is no benefit greater than this.
"Great indeed!
Ānanda, listen attentively... (until)... how can the Buddha not hear what is heard?
This section of the scripture, through Mañjuśrī’s instruction on the samādhi of hearing-perfuming (*śruta-vāsanā*), exhorts Ānanda to abandon mere rote memorization.
This verse of eleven lines is taken as a single stanza because its meaning is complete within it;

thus, the first five lines describe how Mañjuśrī, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, selected the teachings on *śrutavāsanā* (perfuming by hearing) to proclaim this meaning, so as to instruct Ānanda and cause him to listen attentively.
The term *śrutavāsanā* is called the "Vajra King," where *vajra* is used as a metaphor for comparison.
The wisdom of contemplation is as firm and sharp as a vajra, for it is able to sever delusions; furthermore, because the vajra is the most precious among jewels, it is called the "King.
The wisdom of hearing the熏 (xūn, permeating influence) is not equal to that of the five faculties, and thus it is compared to a king.
"Illusion" is as previously explained; the term "inconceivable" describes its wondrousness. By means of this samādhi, one is able to give birth [to all things].
The Buddhas therefore call her the Mother of Buddhas; because she possesses the Three Jewels, she is named "True.

Furthermore, although the three phrases following "Vajra" are divided into three, they collectively convey a single meaning. The final six phrases correctly clarify the admonition and exhortation. When you say "you," it refers to Ānanda;
it means that upon hearing the essential Dharma-gates of the Buddha’s teachings from others, you must first eliminate the outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*). If there are outflows of desire...
If you do not eliminate the fault of accumulating [mere] learning, it will mislead your true cultivation. You have received and upheld what the Buddha taught;

why did the Buddha not simply hear himself? Why not turn back to one's own true hearing? However, Ānanda, because you uphold the Dharma taught by the Buddha, and because the Dharma is itself the Buddha, it is said that you "uphold the Buddha-Buddha."
"Hearing is not produced spontaneously" (up to) "Mātanga was in a dream; who could have retained your form?

This section of the sutra, in which Mañjuśrī explains the meaning of "hearing," provides a detailed demonstration of the merit of returning to the source and attaining the essence, thereby warning against the initial error.
The first six lines constitute one verse that directly clarifies the explanation of the name and the return to the source; next is "seeing and hearing."
The first six lines constitute one verse that correctly elucidates the attainment of the essence of tranquil illumination;

the final four lines constitute another verse that correctly warns that initial erroneous perception and subsequent observation are like a dream. Within the first verse, it is said that hearing does not exist inherently;
it is established as "hearing" only because of sound. If one turns the faculty of hearing around, it becomes detached from sound; that which is capable of such detachment...
"Upon hearing, one further desires the names of others; yet even the name 'hearing' itself does not exist. The two lines following "one faculty" demonstrate the meaning of returning to the source.
Regarding "the six [faculties] being liberated upon the return of one": although their external functions are separate, their internal nature is fundamentally unified.

Therefore, when one faculty returns to the true source, all external separations are simultaneously liberated and the internal unity is realized. In the subsequent verse, it refers to seeing and hearing.

The phrase "the six faculties are like illusions and cataracts" states that they are not real. The six faculties are explained in terms of their primary nature, while the three realms are explained in terms of their basis;
"basis" here refers to the six sense objects. This means that the six sense objects are also like flowers in the sky;

because the six sense objects pervade the three realms, they are used to represent the three realms. The following two lines clarify that when the faculties and objects are eliminated, true awakening becomes perfect.
When pure true awakening is perfected to its ultimate limit, the primordially inherent radiance penetrates through all;
this light is itself tranquil illumination, and the essence of this tranquil illumination is so vast that it has no exterior, thus encompassing empty space.
The final verse states that while deluded, one was detained by Ḍākinī; now, having awakened, one returns to observe the world, seeing that the entire world is but a dream.
Within Great Awakening, how could Tantrā (Ḍākinī) remain in a dream and be able to leave an impression of her form upon you? Truly, such are the benefits and harms of delusion and enlightenment!
It is like a skillful worldly illusionist who, [having manifested forms] in one place, brings them to rest; once they have ceased, the six faculties no longer function.

This section of the sutra follows the preceding discussion of the six sense organs by employing analogies to clarify that while there is a single source of activity and cessation (*ekāśraya-pravṛtti-nivṛtti*), the six organs themselves lack inherent nature.
This section consists of two verses; the first verse, comprising one chapter of six lines, presents a metaphor to illustrate how the six organs are illusorily formed.
It states that they must be drawn out by a single mechanism; if this internal mechanism ceases and returns to quiescence, then all external objects...
All movements are devoid of intrinsic nature. The subsequent verse consists of one chapter and five lines; its dharma corresponds to the preceding metaphor.

The first line is merely an introductory phrase, while the latter four lines properly constitute the correspondence (*yoga*). The six sense faculties correspond to the various men and women, and the single lucid consciousness (*ekaprasāda*) corresponds to the single mechanism.

The analogy of the illusionist (*māyākāra*) does not fully align with the meaning of the Dharma; this is because the deluded mind corresponds to the illusionist, and thus it is called the "illusionist."
Regarding "the one refined spirit within the dharmas such as illusions": this refers to the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) of the eighth consciousness.
Because the *darśana-bhāga* is fundamentally tranquil, it is called "the one refined spirit.

Because it is struck by external objects and divided into the six faculties, objects, and consciousnesses—forming the threefold union—it is called "the sixfold union. Since the six arise from the one, it is called "original" (*yuan*).

"Resting in one place" corresponds to "the cessation of the faculties. "Returning to stillness" corresponds to "the cessation of the faculties returning to quiescence. "Resting" is the cessation of the faculties; "returning" is the return to quiescence.
"The six functions do not arise" corresponds to "all illusions have no nature. Through these dharmas and metaphors, the meaning is clear and evident.
It is an error for the commentary of Wu-xing to equate True Suchness with the illusionist; since it is called "True Suchness," it should not be termed an "illusionist."
"Dust and defilements vanish at the mere thought [of them]... the nature achieves the Unsurpassed Way; such is the true perfection of penetration.

This section of the sutra, in which Mañjuśrī concludes by returning to the preceding meaning, reaches the ultimate point of perfect purity and exhorts the assembly to practice in accordance with this.
The meaning of this section is divided into two verses; the first four lines constitute one verse, which summarizes the preceding six sense organs.

When cessation and restoration are perfected, one attains the essence of perfect luminosity, purity, and wondrous subtlety. This is because residual defilements have not yet been exhausted, and one still remains on the stage of learning (*śaikṣabhūmi*);

since this stage of learning is explained as common to the three vehicles, the word "all" (*sarva*) is added. If luminous purity reaches its ultimate limit, this is precisely the Tathāgata’s stage of culmination.
The five lines following "The great assembly... constitute a single verse, which is precisely an exhortation for the assembly to rely [upon this].
The phrase "cultivating by turning back from hearing" follows; the word "you" (汝) in the subsequent line is inverted and should be read as "turning back your faculty of hearing.
"Turning back" (旋倒) carries the meaning of returning. The faculty of hearing is explained as in the third fascicle of the sutra; the following two lines may be understood accordingly.
The final line summarizes that this perfect penetration is indeed as you have selected.
"This is the realization attained by countless Buddhas (up to) I, too, have realized it from within; it is not only Avalokiteśvara.

This section of the sutra is Mañjuśrī’s praise of the aforementioned "reversing the hearing" (*pratyāhāra*) as the perfect means of penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*), which constitutes the core principle of the path for masters and disciples throughout the three periods of time.
These ten lines form a single verse; the first eight lines collectively clarify the masters of the three periods.

Relying upon this, one cultivates [the practice]. The first two phrases offer a general praise: "reversing the hearing" (*pratyāśravaṇa*) is the essential gateway for the Buddhas of the past to enter the Path;
it is a single path, which is itself the One Way. Nirvāṇa is that which is to be reached (*prāpya*), and perfect penetration (*pari-vy-ava-dhāna*) is that by which one reaches it (*prāpaka*).
Because the means of reaching serves as the gateway through which one reaches what is to be reached, the past refers to the Tathāgata’s teaching, while the present refers to the Bodhisattva.
When [the Buddha] speaks of the future, he refers to those in training; that training necessarily pertains to the Two Vehicles.
This is because the texts of the three periods of time mutually illuminate one another. One may skillfully interpret the words to grasp their underlying intent through the mind.

Furthermore, while the past and present are both termed "already realized," the future is exhorted to practice, which should enter through hearing. Regarding the final two phrases, Mañjuśrī says, "I too..."
That one enters realization from this point is not unique to Avalokiteśvara; this is a further clarification of the intent behind this single path.

It is truly as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, said: [up to] "it is not that those who have practiced for a long time and those who have studied for a short time preach the Dharma at the same level of depth."
This section of the sūtra clarifies Mañjuśrī’s intent in receiving the command to summon Avalokiteśvara and depart with the various holy ones.
The meaning of this text is divided into two verses. The first verse consists of one chapter of six lines, clarifying the intent of receiving the command to summon Avalokiteśvara;
the latter verse consists of one chapter of five lines, clarifying the intent of departing with the various holy ones. Regarding the former, the first part is as follows:
The four lines clarify the reason for entrusting one’s life and receiving the mandate through careful selection.
Furthermore, as is truly the case with the latter two lines, they concern the entrustment of life and reception of the mandate for the sake of salvation;

the following two lines precisely state the reason, saying that the reason for commanding this selection is the desire to save those in the final kalpa who seek transcendence from the world. The final two lines set forth the selection of Avalokiteśvara.
The meaning is this: for those who seek to achieve the mind of *nirvāṇa* that transcends the world, Avalokiteśvara is supreme.
*Nirvāṇa* is spoken of in contrast to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*);

the moment-to-moment arising and ceasing of worldly sentient beings is the mind of birth-and-death, whereas the non-arising and non-ceasing of supramundane *nirvāṇa* is the mind of all Buddhas. Now, one shall bring such a person to fulfillment.
To liberate oneself from birth and death and aspire to realize nirvana, nothing is superior to Avalokiteśvara’s practice of "turning the hearing back.

Regarding the intermediate method, it refers to the skillful means practiced by the remaining twenty-four sages; all are manifestations of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, which adapts the teaching to the capacity of the practitioner.

By working directly upon those very phenomena, one causes them to abandon worldly toil (*rajas*). Once worldly toil is abandoned, one has already transcended it and need not undergo a long period of time.
Furthermore, the methods of cultivation and study vary in depth and shallowness, and differ in scale and approach;

yet, while this depth and shallowness depend upon the capacities of sentient beings, the World-Honored One’s single voice expounds the Dharma such that each according to their kind understands it differently. Although these teachings appear distinct as they adapt to individual capacities, their ultimate aim is identical;
therefore, it is said that "the teaching of the Dharma is the same, whether shallow or deep."
"Homage to the Tathāgatagarbha... [up to] 'the true mind that transcends others through perfect penetration'—thus it is.
This section of the scripture concludes Mañjuśrī’s thorough examination;

having paid homage to the Buddha and respectfully reported back on his selection, he now contrasts it with "listening inwardly" (*praty-śravaṇa*) to summarize the entire meaning. This passage constitutes one verse, with the first two lines as follows.
Mañjuśrī pays homage to the Buddha. The *tathāgatagarbha* (the womb/essence of the Tathāgata) is the perfectly realized principle realized by the Buddha;
its meaning as a "treasury" (*garbha*) has been explained in the preceding text. This is the supreme, untainted (*anāsrava*) Dharma, wondrous and inconceivable.
Now, the intent behind Mañjuśrī’s homage and praise lies truly in the fact that he has completed his task and returns his report; this is the homage of the principal and his retinue.
The next two lines express the vow that what has been selected shall be bestowed upon the future so that there may be no further delusions.
Furthermore, the subsequent six lines are easy to understand. As for the final line, "the true mind," it refers back to the previously mentioned perfect, universal, and constant threefold reality.
Changshui’s interpretation based on biased sentiment is incorrect.
"Then Ānanda and the great assembly [attained] the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This section of the scripture records that there were differences among the members of the assembly regarding their realization of the mind upon hearing the verses and the stages they attained.
The two characters "yú shì" (於是) are the narrative opening of the compiler, indicating "Ānanda and the assembly."

Having heard the meaning of the preceding verses on the selection of the Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*), he attained the joy of the Dharma and was awakened; thus his body and mind became clear and lucid.

"Body" refers to the six sense faculties and "mind" refers to the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). Because the preceding [distinctions between] the first and the sixth had both vanished, he attained the true meaning of perfect penetration and was free from all doubt and obstruction;
hence it is said that his body and mind were clear and lucid. "Attaining great instruction" means realizing the nature of the storehouse.

Because it is spoken thus, it is called "the great revelation. Because one has attained awakening, the two kinds of resultant virtues—Buddha-bodhi and nirvāṇa—are perceived with clarity and without doubt.
Bodhi belongs to the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), while nirvāṇa belongs to the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).

As will be shown below through metaphors, the intent of this clarity is self-evident; the text is intelligible on its own. If one were to align the meaning with the phenomena, these would serve as the analogies.
The metaphor of the five stages of delusion as a long journey illustrates how one transmigrates through the five realms of existence because one is detained by the delusions of these five stages.
The metaphor of not yet having returned home illustrates *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*. The metaphor of traveling far from home due to specific circumstances illustrates the confusion of the past;
the clear description of returning home illustrates the awakening of the present. The following section on the universal assembly describes three points.
The vehicles and various categories differ in their realization and attainment. "Ten Ganges-sands" refers to the vastness of their number.
Those who "attain the fundamental mind"—the word "attain" (de) indicates varying degrees of depth—because there are those who have not yet realized it in its ultimate reality.

Thus, "fundamental mind" refers to the *ālaya-vijñāna* (storehouse consciousness), which is what all people inherently possess. Those who "leave behind dust and defilement and attain the purity of the Dharma-eye" are at the initial stage.
From the stage of the fruit upward, all belong to the level of the purification of the Dharma-eye (*dharmanetra-viśuddhi*).

The Bhikṣuṇī, who was formerly the woman Mātangī (as explained in the preceding commentary), attained progress through four fruits by hearing these verses. Furthermore, immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon the Unsurpassed Way (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The above describes the characteristics of differences in understanding and realization. In the Sanskrit language, this is *Anuttara*.

*Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*: "Anuttara" is translated as "unsurpassed"; "samyak" is translated as "correct and equal"; and "saṃbodhi" is translated as "perfect enlightenment. Regarding "unequaled yet equal":

the *Fahua wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra) states that the minds of the nine realms of existence cannot equal this principle, whereas the mind of the Buddha-dharma realm can equal this principle;
thus it is called "unequaled yet equal. Furthermore, the ultimate principle is itself unequaled.

Because one initially takes the ultimate principle as the object and generates the resolve [for enlightenment], being able to equal that principle, it is called "unequaled with the unequaled" (*asamasama*).
Furthermore, since both the mind and the principle are both unobtainable, by what thing could one equalize what thing such that one speaks of "the unequaled with the unequaled"?
Since both the mind and the principle are both unspeakable, yet one speaks while speaking, it is said that this mind equals this [principle].

From the perspective of principle, it is called "unequaled with the unequaled. The first is an explanation by way of horizontal [classification], the second is an explanation by way of vertical [classification], and the third is an explanation that is neither horizontal nor vertical.
All three explanations are subtle; they are detailed herein, and students should carefully and deeply contemplate them to gain understanding.
At the beginning of the fourth scripture, following the request for practice, the Buddha spoke on the arousal of awakening.
Regarding the "Two Resolutions for the Beginner," the second resolution involves thoroughly examining the root of afflictions while simultaneously selecting those of superior faculties;
it is only upon reaching this point that the second resolution is fulfilled. One should understand that these two resolutions constitute the general outline for one's own practice.

The subsequent sections—such as the repeated request for instruction, the establishment of the site, the construction of the altar, and the recitation of mantras—are all intended for the sake of [others].
That beings of the末法 (mòfǎ) age put forth this request is for the sake of altruistic practice; self-benefit and benefiting others constitute the general purport of the gateway of practice.
For students who exhaustively study the scriptures and penetrate deeply, first recognizing the great path is a helpful aid.

Ānanda adjusted his robes amidst the great assembly... [up to] ...he attained non-retrogression in the mind of bodhi. This section of the sūtra, from "Ānanda" downwards to "prostrating and addressing the Buddha," constitutes the discourse on the gathering of the assembly;

it describes how Ānanda, having previously attained awakening through his own practice, further requested the establishment of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and other matters as an act for the benefit of others.
First, from "Ānanda" down to "prostrating and addressing the Buddha," is the speech of the assembled group.
From the Great Compassionate World-Honored One, the following are Ānanda’s own words of self-avowal: "Adjusting his robes" refers to solemnizing the etiquette of his request;
"the mind and traces being perfectly bright" means that while the mind abides within, its traces manifest without;

"perfect" (*yuan*) implies being without partiality, and "bright" (*ming*) implies being without limitation—because he has attained awakening, his virtuous countenance differs from what it was before. "A mixture of sorrow and joy" means...

Grieving over his former immersion in samsara and rejoicing at his present opportunity, these feelings converged in his mind; thus, wishing to benefit those below, he first recounted the origins of his request for the Dharma.
"The Dharma-gate for accomplishing Buddhahood" refers back to the previously mentioned Perfect Penetration of the Ear-organ; herein, it specifically points to the faculty of hearing.
This represents Ānanda’s desire to first explain his own self-benefit before requesting [the means] to benefit others. As it is said: "I have often heard..."
The following citation provides an example to clarify the basis for benefiting others: The Buddha once said, "To save others while one has not yet saved oneself is the mind of a bodhisattva;
to awaken others once one's own awakening is perfected is the path of a Tathāgata.
This is the source from which Ānanda turned his mind away from the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle toward the path of the Mahāyāna. Below, the World-Honored One [proceeds to] explain this directly.
In the conclusion of this preface, I shall describe the many hardships of the final age (*kalpa*) and set forth the way to provide protection and salvation.

As the distance from the Buddha gradually increases, one passes through two thousand years of the *saddharma* (True Dharma) and *pratirūpaka-dharma* (Semblance Dharma) periods; having entered the period of the *mappō* (Final Dharma), the distance grows even further.

At such a time of extreme decline, when Māra and heterodox teachings blaze fiercely and difficulties as numerous as the sands of the Ganges become especially severe, those who wish to uphold the True Dharma of the Tathāgata...
How does the Dharma gather and transform their minds so that they enter right concentration;

how does it cause them to be established in the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), remain far removed from the affairs of Māras and externalists, and never retreat from the Buddha’s bodhicitta, free from the hardship of being cowed or disheartened?
At that time, the World-Honored One [spoke] amidst the great assembly... Ānanda and the great assembly responded, "So be it," and respectfully accepted the instruction.
This section of the sutra shows the Buddha first praising the excellence of the request before responding to it, and then admonishing them to listen attentively.
When the Buddha praised him as "Excellent," he was specifically praising his turning back from self-benefit to transform others and practicing the Great [Vehicle].
Because it is the vehicle of practice, this mind is firmly good. The reason for repeating the word "good" is that the Way of the Mahāyāna is rarely practiced in the world;
furthermore, because even those of the Lesser Vehicle who turn their minds [toward the Great] become firm [in this], it is the "goodness of the good," and thus it is repeated.
"You now" is a command to listen. "Ānanda" is the recipient of the teaching. "Only" (wei) signifies a prompt and responsive assent.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "You have often heard me [up to] 'this is called the three trainings in the absence of outflows'.

This section of the sutra is where the World-Honored One, in response to the request regarding the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), first clarifies the foundation for constructing the altar and cultivating the mind.
The Sanskrit term *vinaya* is translated as "discipline" (*lǜfǎ*). The Buddha cites three meanings from the Vinaya to provide this title.
"Certainty" refers to the fact that practitioners will certainly attain [realization] through these three dharmas in their proper sequence.
This is what is meant by the "sequence of arising" for the three names designated below. First, regarding "precepts": collecting the mind is called precepts.

By preventing wrongdoing and ceasing evil, one does not allow oneself to be dissolute in the five desires and worldly afflictions; this is what is meant by "collecting the mind. It is because of the precepts [that this occurs].

Regarding the generation of concentration (*samādhi*): the gathering of the mind is the cause of concentration; therefore, the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla*) is able to generate concentration.
Regarding the arising of wisdom (*prajñā*) from concentration: when concentration reaches its peak, it is able to give rise to the true light of *prajñā*.

Thus, the Sūtra says, "Immeasurable, pure wisdom all arises in dependence upon meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*)," which refers to this very point. From the subtle to the manifest, one proceeds until reaching the ultimate fruit of awakening.
