Because one does not depart from these three, they are called the "Three Untainted Trainings" (*trīṇi śikṣāny anāsravāṇi*). This is the general heading; what follows is the specific explanation.
Ānanda, how does one restrain the mind? I call this "precept" (*śīla*)... [up to] ...if it were not explained in this way, it would be the teaching of Pāpīyan.

In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One provides a specific explanation of the Threefold Training (*tri-śikṣā*) to clarify the foundation for constructing the ritual altar and cultivating the mind.

Here, he first explains the training in ethical discipline (*śīla*), beginning with the prohibition of sexual misconduct. The four subsequent sections that follow all explain the training in ethical discipline;

the meanings of the two trainings in concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are manifested within the training in ethical discipline and are therefore not explained separately. For this reason, throughout the text, it is repeatedly stated that one possesses "abundant wisdom and meditative concentration."

These words are truly because concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) take precepts (*śīla*) as their foundation; if that foundation is not solid, then those two trainings will likewise not be accomplished.

The general purport of the present passage is that the precepts are a matter of urgent necessity, and thus they are explained in detail, for the trainings of concentration and wisdom are manifested in dependence upon the precepts;
hereafter, all [explanations] shall follow this pattern. Furthermore, upon careful examination of the Buddha’s intention, he first sets forth the three trainings, and subsequently...
If one were to provide a separate explanation for each, the meaning of the text’s headings and enumeration would be fully complete;

however, here we clarify only the four admonitions within the *śīla* (precepts), while setting aside and not discussing the two trainings of *samādhi* (concentration) and *prajñā* (wisdom). This is because the Mahāyāna precepts inherently encompass concentration and wisdom. As the ancient masters have said:
"When a person of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*) trains in the precepts, they are training in concentration and wisdom. Since this sutra belongs to the Perfect Teaching, training in one includes all.
"What is meant by 'learning'? This is the downward inquiry into the name. "If there are... and so forth, is the correct explanation. There are two intentions regarding the phrase "all worlds":
first, it refers specifically to this Sahā world-system of a great trichiliocosm, which is why the term "all" is used;

second, it refers generally to the ten directions, meaning that all sentient beings throughout them sustain their lives through sexual desire, whereby birth and death become endless. Therefore, its...
If the mind is free from lust, the root of birth and death is severed; how could there be any further continuity? This clearly explains that restraining the mind constitutes the precept.
Regarding the passage beginning with "If those [who practice] below," it first explains the precept against lust: lust belongs to craving, and craving is the root of birth and death;

therefore, continuity persists through long kalpas. Regarding the passage beginning with "You who cultivate" below, those who cultivate samādhi fundamentally desire to seek escape from the dust and toil of the mundane world.

Regarding the statement that afflictions are exhausted at the fifth stage of dwelling (*pañcama-vihāra*): if the mind of lust is not eliminated, one can certainly not transcend the dust and toil of worldly existence.
The phrase "even if" used here is concessive; in general, if the mind of lust is not eliminated, neither meditative concentration (*samādhi*) nor wisdom (*prajñā*) can be accomplished.
Even if concentration and wisdom were to arise, they would merely be perverse concentration and perverse wisdom; the Tathāgata’s true concentration and true wisdom could never be attained.
Thus, those who practice while not severing lust will inevitably fall into the path of Māra. Among them, those with deep power of cultivation are superior;
those with shallow power of cultivation are middling or inferior. Yet, even as subjects of Māra, they are still male in body and are therefore called "superior.
If they become female Māras, their lustful minds burn even more fiercely and their power of cultivation becomes even shallower; thus they become female Māras, like ascending [a mountain].
Those such as Gā, whose delusions are profound, do not realize they are themselves Māras;
each possesses their own disciples of magical arts, training them and claiming what they have attained to be the Unsurpassed Way.
At the end of my extinction, during the period of the decline of the Dharma, such demonic followers will abound in the world, and the True Dharma will hang like a thread.

The false teachings of the *śīla* (silk) flourish and burn with evil like fire; they harbor deceit and fraud, widely practicing greed and filth while claiming to be "good spiritual friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*).
They transmit their lewdness from one to another, causing all sentient beings to fall into the pit of craving and views.
To metaphorically describe craving as a pit means that the entrapment of greedy attachment is like a pit from which it is difficult to escape; thus, the true path to Bodhi is lost.
"Furthermore, you have been instructed by the Buddha to remain in the age of the final Dharma to teach those sentient beings who wish to cultivate right concentration;
first, they must sever the mind of lust—this is called the foremost, definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the former Buddhas.
The term 'former Buddhas' is used in reference to the end times, for since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa has long passed, they are referred to as 'former. [The text] repeats this tenfold."
The three titles [of this section] are used to show gravity and respect. "Decisive" refers to what was explained previously; "restraining lust and impurity" is called "purity";
and "the teaching that reaches the Way" is called "clear instruction. These summarize the names of the initial instructions.

Therefore, the subsequent summary clarifies that without the precepts (*śīla*), it is impossible to cultivate concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). The phrase "like steaming sand" is cited as a metaphor to illustrate this point.
To discipline an unsettled mind means that one who cultivates meditative concentration (*samādhi*) without severing sexual desire is mistaken, like steaming sand in search of rice.

Sand is not the source of rice; even if it were processed for kalpas, it would remain nothing but hot sand. Steaming sand to seek rice is a metaphor for seeking the fruit of Buddhahood with a body still engaged in lust.
This serves to condemn the lustful body as not being the foundation for seeking the Way, even if one passes through kalpas.
These words are extremely clear; [your] grave error is profound indeed. From "You" (*rǔ*) onwards, there is a deep warning against error.
The word "you" (*rǔ*) first refers to Ānanda; because Ānanda fell into a chamber of lust during the final kalpa, it refers to Ānanda and extends to the assembly.
The Buddha said: "If one does not sever lust while seeking the wondrous fruit of Buddhahood, even if one attains wondrous enlightenment, it shall all be..."
These two phrases regarding the "root of lust" (*kāma-mūla*) are likewise words of concession. Why? For if one does not sever lust, there will certainly be no sublime awakening (*prajñā*);
how could there be one who attains sublime awakening while still possessing the root of lust?

Nevertheless, even if one occasionally gives vent to intellectual understanding, this merely assists the mechanism of lust and is not sublime awakening—just as with the three classes of demons mentioned previously. As for the "three realms of suffering" (*tridurgati*), *tuó* (塗) means...
This "poisoned path" refers to the hell named *Huo-tu* (Fire-Coated), the hungry ghosts named *Ji-xu* (Starving-Emptiness), and the animals named *Dao-zhen* (Sword and Anvil).
Furthermore, "tu" (coated/path) is interchangeable with "tu" (path); thus, these paths are merely the three evil realms. To necessarily link this below to the "trigger for lust":
"ji" (trigger) refers to a mechanical catch; by way of metaphor, it describes the mind of lust which, upon encountering an object, is immediately activated.

It is as swift as the discharge of a mechanical device. Regarding "the body and mind are both severed": the followers of the Two Vehicles restrain the body, while Bodhisattvas restrain the mind; since both are severed, even the nature of severance is non-existent.
This means that by severing lust, one realizes the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); by severing the nature of severance, one realizes the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-niṣṭhā*).
One must ensure that the attachment to phenomena is also eliminated, so that both person and phenomenon are empty. Because one attains these two kinds of emptiness, one becomes a Buddha.
Enlightenment may be hoped for. The final four lines summarize the first chapter;
"Mahāpāpīyān" is the name of the Māra King, translated as "The Slayer," because both the physical body and the Dharma-body are slain by him.
"Ānanda, furthermore, regarding the sentient beings of the six realms in all worlds... (up to) 'if one does not speak thus, it is the teaching of Pāpīyān.

This section of the sutra follows the preceding passage to provide a specific explanation of the Three Studies (*tri-śikṣā*), clarifying the foundation for establishing the altar and cultivating the mind through the precepts;

following the discussion of the precept against stealing, it now explains the precept against killing. Furthermore, "moreover, next... introduces the explanation of the precept against killing, wherein killing consists of mutual slaughter and devouring.

Therefore, there is likewise the continuous succession of birth and death. Regarding "you practice as described in the preceding chapter," even if one falls into the realm of spirits, because ghosts and gods crave blood and flesh, they do not sever their murderous intent;

thus, those who cultivate meditative concentration while failing to sever their murderous intent will be reborn among that same class. The three grades of power derived from cultivation are also as explained previously: [the first grade is] powerful ghosts.

The *Changshui Shu* (Commentary by Changshui) states: "Those who are subject to sacrificial offerings include the Five Peaks and the Four Rivers, as they preside over the consumption of blood-offerings.

The flying *yakṣas* and the class of *rākṣasas*—whose translated terminology appears previously—and the various ghost-masters (*bhūta-ācārya*) and so forth, constitute the followers of the Great Power Division (*mahābala-kula*).
These are equivalent to the river deities and the ghosts of the five directions in this land; they are the earth-walking *rākṣasas*."
There are also those who, through the power of their cultivation, are reborn as ghosts by retribution;
these are like the tigers and wolves that rely on the power of ghosts to devour humans. These various classes of ghosts do not recognize the True Dharma, yet each has its own followers.
Leading their multitudes with ghostly arts, they each claim to possess the Way. Their extinction shall be as previously described.

Their claim that one attains the path to Bodhi by eating meat is of the same intent as the current world’s tradition of transmitting ghostly voices and offering blood sacrifices to obtain some merit or exorcise some malevolent spirit.
Ānanda, I shall now set forth the reasons why bhikṣus eat meat. The Buddha addressed those present, saying: "I have permitted bhikṣus to eat the five kinds of pure meat."

As for meat, it is because the land of India (Zhugan) abounds in sand and gravel, making cultivation difficult; furthermore, when the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) first established its precepts, bhikṣus were not yet able to renounce meat consumption all at once.
Therefore, through the power of great compassion, the Buddha manifested various meats that originally possessed no life-force, designating them merely as "meat.
Regarding the five kinds of pure meat, the Vinaya permits the three purities, namely: not seeing, [not hearing, and not suspecting].

That which has not been heard of nor suspected to have been killed for oneself is called "pure. Gu-shan’s interpretation adds "died of itself" and "left by a bird" to these, collectively termed the "five purities.
Regarding the reference to the "land of the Brahmins" and so forth: the five regions of the Western Regions are collectively referred to as the "Country of the Brahmins";
thus, it refers to the Brahmins when speaking. During the Buddha's lifetime, the bhikṣus, having obtained its flavor, transmitted it [to later generations].
"In the final age, when no Buddha is present to transform sentient beings, there will be no means [for them to find sustenance], and thus they shall eat the flesh of living beings.
How can such meat-eaters be called disciples of the Śākya? The passage beginning with 'You all' correctly clarifies that they are not disciples of the Śākya; the text is easy to understand.
The passage beginning with 'Your teaching' contains the Buddha’s admonition and his vow to enter the final dharma-age; this concludes the second section, which clarifies the meaning of the name."
The explanation is as previously stated; therefore, the following conclusion clarifies that without precepts, it is impossible to cultivate concentration and wisdom.
Regarding the analogy, such as "plugging one's ears and shouting loudly while seeking not to be heard," this merely serves to deceive oneself;

how could others fail to hear? If one were not to shout, those who might hear would still be few. Thus, [the text] uses this metaphor to clarify the principle that without precepts, there can be no concentration.

Because one shouts loudly, those who hear it become even more numerous; yet, by plugging one's ears, one wishes to remain hidden. To shout loudly while seeking not to be heard is to make oneself all the more exposed.

Plugging the ears is a metaphor for practicing meditative concentration (*samādhi*); shouting loudly while seeking not to be heard is a metaphor for failing to cease killing while seeking to transcend the mundane world.
Practicing meditative concentration is a desire for concealment, whereas failing to cease killing while seeking to transcend the mundane world is [the opposite].
This makes the point even more manifest and clearly revealed. By harmonizing the Dharma with this analogy, one grasps the intended meaning and thereby attains purity.
Below, the intent of the Mahāyāna precepts is presented: because one follows the precept against killing, one does not tread upon living grass.

Since the growth and emergence of grass is like human life, a person who is cautious regarding the precepts would not dare to step on it, much less pull it by hand. One should take heed of the story of the bhikṣu bound by the grass as a mirror for oneself.
"How can the sons of Great Compassion take the flesh and blood of sentient beings as their sustenance? This is a profound reproach regarding the fault of bhikṣus eating meat.

If one were to correctly point out the instruction for those in the East—where "West" refers to China and its various nations—the silk, cotton, and fine fabrics are products of China; [this teaching] emerges from the midst of slaughter by boiling in cauldrons.
"Come, monks, you should be cautious; these [items] must not be worn. This land refers to the Five Indias (Pañcāla).

Boots and sandals are produced there, for India has many mountains that are lofty and steep, stretching far and wide; consequently, it produces many beasts. The clothing worn by those people consists mostly of furs and wool.
"Fur" (*qiu*) refers to garments made from the fine wool of lambs; the fine hair of the *rǒu* sheep is called "wool" (*kuì*). Furthermore...
Among the foods consumed, those such as milk are many, with clarified butter (*ghṛta*) being the supreme flavor. Initially, when the first stage of grain is fermented, it is called milk (*kṣīra*);
the first stage after fermentation is called curd (*dadhi*); the next stage is called cream (*navanīta*); and the stage following that is called clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
These are the bodily constituents of animals; one who observes the precepts should not consume them. Thus, by neither taking nor eating these, one remains aloof from all worldly things.
Truly, it is for the sake of liberation; because of this liberation, there are no remaining debts. As for "repaying past debts and not wandering through the three realms":
because one does not consume [the fruits of karma] and has no past debts to repay, one does not wander through the three realms.
Generally speaking, "past debts" refers to what is expected in the future based on the present; it does not point to past grievances from former lives. This is as stated in the following chapter.
The initial statement also refers to the past; the detailed explanation follows in the subsequent text. How does the following three sentences explain the meaning of "not repaying"?
It means that consuming his body constitutes the very condition for him; conversely, it reveals that by not consuming or eating, the conditions for such [retribution] are severed from this point on.

The two lines beginning with "As a person" cite an example to illustrate the sense of being a condition: when a person eats the "earth-flavor" (*pṛthivī-rasa*), they immediately become one with the earth.
Because of this condition, his feet do not leave the ground. As for the "hundred grains," these are simply the five grains produced in their various forms;
when the many are categorized, there are twenty varieties each of *qǔ*, *jì*, *dào*, *shū*, and *mài*. These five groups transform to constitute the hundred.

The final seven phrases necessarily serve to conclude and clarify the meaning of true liberation. Regarding the "body and its parts": eating meat constitutes the body's food, while consuming milk serves as clothing.
Body hair constitutes a part of the body; furthermore, craving for flavors belongs to the mind, while clothing and hair belong to the body.

Thus, it is said that there are two paths: body and mind. "Neither wearing nor eating"—these two lines below correctly conclude the meaning of true liberation. The final four lines are as explained in the preceding chapter.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding the sentient beings of the six realms in the world... (up to) "if it is not spoken thus, it is the teaching of Pāpīyān.

This section of the sutra follows the preceding [passage] to provide a specific explanation of the Three Studies (*tri-śikṣā*), clarifying that the foundation for constructing the altar and cultivating the mind lies in the precepts;
next, it explains the precept against stealing. As for the phrases "the continuity of birth and death" and "your cultivation," etc., they are all as explained previously.
The statement that even if one were to fall into lower realms or stray onto wrong paths through such conduct means that theft is unrighteous;
because unrighteousness is wrong, it leads one to fall into wrong paths. Thus, one who does not abandon theft yet practices meditative concentration will inevitably fall into its corresponding class.

In this text, the term "stealing" (*tou*) is used instead of "theft" (*dao*); whereas "theft" refers to robbery committed openly with weapons or by breaking doors, "stealing" refers to taking what is not given in secret.
This is called a great thief; one who steals by climbing over walls or breaking through windows, taking things while fearing for his head and tail, is called a petty thief.

The intent of the present text lies in prohibiting petty thieves—those who take what is not given and those who pilfer the name of benevolence and righteousness like the "honest village sycophants" (xiangyuan).
Therefore, it denounces them as a "thieving mind. If even petty thieves are to be cautioned against, how much more so the great thieves! For this reason, it does not... [continue].
To speak of "stealing" is to speak of "thievery. Regarding the three grades of refined spirits, one should understand them according to the intent as explained previously.

As for the category of "spirits," it is as described in the ninth scripture within the section on the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*): those who, with a deviant mind, harbor *chimei* (goblins) and experience false awakenings to spiritual anomalies;
or those who appear in distant marketplaces and towns, preaching the Dharma without cause yet seemingly attaining mastery over subtle meanings—these are their kind. They are demons.
Regarding "the *māra*s and so forth": they are like foxes that have lived for many years without dying and can manifest the seductive charms of women;
all manner of malevolent spirits, strange anomalies, and those whom the world calls the "Sages of the Five Directions" who can bring about misfortune or fortune—these are their kind.
Since the various classes of such heterodox beings are numerous and difficult to enumerate exhaustively, they are referred to as a "host of heterodox ones. Each of these has its own faction.
Each claims for themselves that they have attained the state of a superior person; this is taking delusion to be liberation.

It can be understood from the passage "After my parinirvāṇa... that those who hide their wickedness and deceit while claiming to be "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra) are precisely those who pilfer benevolence and righteousness—those so-called "village-pleasers" (xiangyuan) who soak themselves in the reputation of virtue.
What the ancients called "thieves within virtue" refers exactly to these people, who falsely claim to have attained the higher stages.
People are deluded by the deceptive arts of those who lack wisdom; these ignorant fools are led astray by them, while the wise observer perceives their innermost intentions with complete clarity.

As for "fearing the loss of mind," this refers to being terrified or intimidated by predictions of future calamities and blessings, such as water and fire disasters or auspicious and inauspicious events, which strike at the heart so forcefully that one loses composure. Therefore, one must guard against passing through the company of such people.
There are many instances where people's household wealth is dissipated; this is not empty talk.
In our teaching, the four lines [of the verse] correctly demonstrate the reason for not stealing. "Following the direction" means following the local custom.

Wherever one may be, one should always beg for food. By begging for food, there is no accumulation. Because there is no accumulation, one abandons the greedy mind. Once the greedy mind is abandoned, then...
This is the gradual process for attaining Bodhi. The six lines following "O bhikṣus" demonstrate the method for nourishing life and cultivating one's nature:
they show that the bhikṣus do not cook their own food but beg for what has been cooked by others to sustain their remaining years;
like travelers lodging in a temporary inn, they dwell within the three realms as mere guests, never conceiving the thought of them as a permanent residence. This is what is being shown.
The practice of *buddhānusmṛti* (mindfulness of the Buddha) is such that once one has departed for the Pure Land, there is no returning; this is the established rule.

How is it that these thieves, appearing in the guise of bhikṣus and borrowing the Tathāgata’s uṣṇīṣa and saffron robes to fuel their thieving hearts, trade in the Buddha-Dharma and create all manner of karma?
They instead slander those who possess the full precepts as followers of the Hīnayāna path—this is the corruption of the Dharma in the age of the Final Dharma (*paścimadharma*).
To reach such an extreme would mislead those of later learning and cause them to fall into the Avīci Hell.

If I were to show them below how to practice internal giving by returning their thieving mind to their own body and mind—where even the body itself can be sacrificed when lighting lamps and burning incense—how much more so for that which is outside the body?
Regarding the statement that "the debts of beginningless time are repaid all at once," this is still [merely] a matter of principle.

One might wonder: "How can the internal giving practiced now, as well as the aforementioned practices of not wearing [fine clothing] and not eating [delicacies], merely exempt me from the fault of repaying debts in future lives?
How then can the karmic debts from beginningless time be settled? Generally speaking, this is because the merit of internal giving is profound and the service rendered to the Buddha is supreme;
furthermore, it is due to the fulfillment of the practice of true liberation described in the preceding chapter. It is by means of this merit that [the debts are cleared].
To repay that debt, or alternatively, to direct one's own merits toward one’s former enemies so as to enable them to transcend and be liberated—only then can the repayment be considered complete.
This text is concise and its meaning obscure; it must be understood through personal insight.

Furthermore, if one possesses the true contemplation of the Perfect Vehicle (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), where both seeds [of karma] are extinguished and self and others are no longer separated, such that things and self are of one essence (*yathaika-rasa*), then what debt remains to be repaid?

"To bow long to the world" means to bid eternal farewell and sever ties, never to return again. Although the following four lines have not yet been presented, they clarify that the path of awakening is profound and distant;

it does not mean one has immediately attained great penetration (*abhisambodhi*). The Buddha says that such a person has already attained decisive faith in the Tathāgata’s wondrous Way, meaning they shall not regress.
If the following six lines were not presented, it would merely describe internal giving to its ultimate extent.
A subtle cause must not fail to be practiced. A "subtle cause" refers to that wherein what is relinquished from one's person is not much, yet the accomplishment thereof is exceedingly great;
the ancient debts of beginningless time are fully repaid—is this not a great achievement?

Therefore, by way of contrast, it is clarified that internal giving has a subtle cause but a manifest fruit, and is something that practitioners ought to practice. If one does not practice this, even if [other merits] were to be accomplished...
Because past debts must necessarily be repaid, the example of the Buddha is cited as proof; the incident regarding the horse-barley can be verified in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

It is recorded that because the Buddha, in a previous life, had reviled a bhikṣu who was entitled to eat horse-barley, even though he has now attained Buddhahood, he could not yet escape this consequence.
Therefore it is said: "Though one has attained the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), past debts must inevitably be repaid. The World-Honored One [spoke] this with profound [insight].
Exhort the practitioner not to forget the practice of giving. You have taught this below; the Buddha’s admonition remains as a vow to enter the age of the final dharma (*mappō*).

Furthermore, the meaning of the third clear instruction is as previously stated. Therefore, the following concludes by clarifying that without precepts, it is impossible to cultivate concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
To illustrate the point that without precepts there is no concentration, the text provides an analogy using water.
The metaphor designates the "leaking cup," which is commonly called a funnel; it serves as a simile for the body and mind that do not cease stealing [virtue], thereby constantly leaking water.

The *Shushu* (Commentary on the *Sūtra*) states: "If one pours the water of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) into a cup of broken precepts, yet seeks a fruit free of leakage, who is to blame if it remains unlevel throughout kalpas?
"If there are those... and so forth, correctly demonstrates the teaching and the precepts: namely, that a bhikṣu, regarding even a single robe or a single alms bowl...
Furthermore, one must not store even a fraction of food beyond what is needed, and any surplus obtained through alms should be given to hungry sentient beings.

This clarifies that the practice of giving until one is completely exhausted serves as the remedial method for counteracting the mind of theft. In the section following "At the Great [Assembly]," it further clarifies the meaning of subduing the mind;
that is, within a great assembly, one subdues the arrogance of pride by striking—that is, beating—and reviling—that is, scolding.
"Praising is the same as reviling; 'striking' is a brief term for the meaning of beating. [Supplementary note: "Beating is the same as stroking.
This refers to the method of subduing the mind by remaining unmoved by defamation or praise. One should physically offer a lamp wick, relinquishing both body and mind.
Therefore, it says below: "One must cause both body and mind to be relinquished," and furthermore, "one does not regard the Tathāgata..."
Liaozhi’s explanation that [the teaching] was intended for himself is narrow-minded both regarding his own mind and regarding others; it misleads those who are beginners.
If one does not do this, one will neither mislead oneself nor others. Foyin was such a person who attained true samādhi;
the final four lines can be understood accordingly.
"Ānanda, regarding these sentient beings of the six realms in this world... (until) if it is not spoken thus, it is the teaching of Pāpīyān.

This section of the sutra follows the preceding text to separately explain the Threefold Training (*tri-śikṣā*), clarifying the foundation for establishing the ritual altar and cultivating the mind through the precepts;

furthermore, it subsequently explains the precept against false speech. While the three untainted trainings (*anāsrava-śikṣā*) were previously indicated, the four admonitions are now enumerated because—
Although the three trainings may be perfected, if one commits a great falsehood (*mahāmṛṣāvāda*), one will not attain purity within samādhi;

therefore, this instruction is added. While the aforementioned four precepts constitute the four fundamental precepts (*mūlāpatti*) of a bhikṣu—wherein the root is the same—their specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are more detailed here because this belongs to the Mahāyāna.
Thus, "great falsehood" is specified to distinguish it from the various secondary and derivative forms of lying, which is why "great" is added.

Regarding the statement that "forming the demon of craving (tṛṣṇā-māra) causes one to lose the seed of the Buddha": because one covets the prior possession of precepts, prides oneself on reputation, and cherishes one's own name and virtue, various delusions arise;
thus, through craving and views, one becomes a demon. Once fallen into the class of demons, it is inevitable that one loses the seed of the Buddha.
As for the so-called two lower lines, the former merely provides the names, while this [passage] correctly demonstrates their characteristics; this should be understood according to the principle.
Regarding the statement on realization: it refers to claiming a fruit that has not yet been attained as attained, and claiming a realization that has not yet been achieved as achieved.
These two phrases constitute the primary meaning of false speech. Alternatively, to seek lower [reputations] is to specifically demonstrate the characteristics of seeking honorable renown.
The term *srotāpanna* and so forth have translations seen previously; this refers to being honored by disciples and esteemed by the world.

Because they are revered, they are called "most honored and supreme. The first three refer to the fruit (*phala*), while the fourth refers to the path (*mārga*). The first three are explained in terms of the future fruit to be attained;
the fourth refers to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-bhūmi*), as it is endowed with the Eightfold Noble Path.

The *pratyekabuddha* is a person of the Middle Vehicle who is superior to the preceding ten stages (*bhūmi*); this refers to those on the grounds (*bhūmi-stha*). "Before the grounds" (*pūrva-bhūmi*) refers to the stage of the Three Virtuous Persons (*tri-śukla-pakṣa*). This is what is meant.
Because it is Mahāyāna, it surpasses the previous three; this refers to seeking fame and seeking offerings, which together are termed "great lying" (*mahāmṛṣāvāda*).
*Īdantika* is translated as explained previously. In the two lines beginning with "As if a person," the metaphor clarifies the severing of the Buddha-seed.
*Tāla* is a Sanskrit term; its full form is *patala*, translated as "shore-form tree. [With] a sword, one cuts it...

Because it will never arise again, the following two lines use the Dharma to illustrate the metaphor: "The Buddha prophesies that this person shall forever perish" refers to the severing of the roots of goodness;
the "severed wood" is a metaphor for the extinction of the Buddha-seed, and the "sword" is a metaphor for great false speech.

Just as a sword severs wood, so does false speech sever the Buddha-seed. "The Buddha's prophecy" (buddha-avyākaraṇa) means that the Buddha bestows a prediction; according to the certainty of karma, the retribution must inevitably follow.
"Because of delusion, they sink into the three seas of suffering" refers to the three realms of existence (the three paths), for these three paths consist purely of suffering without any limit.

"When I enter parinirvāṇa," and so forth, refers to the Buddha’s command that those of the Three Vehicles should manifest their response-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) within the Dharma-ending age (*mappō*) to assume various forms;

this means practicing the four methods of attraction (*catuḥ-saṃgraha-vastūni*). By manifesting identical forms and engaging in identical activities, they cause sentient beings to easily believe and accept the teaching.
Therefore, the first four lines below illustrate conduct that accords with the Dharma; likewise, the next four lines illustrate conduct that opposes it.

The final two lines praise both the preceding accordant and opposing modes, extolling the Buddha’s propagation of the Dharma so that sentient beings may, through faith and inclination of body and mind, enter into right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
Although he manifests various forms and engages in these same activities, he never speaks of himself as a holy trace or one who has attained mastery.

To leak the Buddha’s secret causes and conditions and lightly disclose them to those who are beginners or of inferior capacity, or for such persons to likewise believe them lightly—both parties commit the offense of negligence and irreverence.
This applies except in cases where, at the time of death, there is a hidden entrustment; even then, one must not speak explicitly, but only reveal it slightly and briefly.
This is as in the case of the Cold and the Gatherer (Hanshan and Shide), as well as those of the Southern Peak and Tiantai, and the categories of the copper wheel and iron wheel.

The phrase "carving, etc. cites a metaphor to clarify the meaning that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is not indeterminate with respect to morality (*śīla*).

Specifically, it means that one who cultivates concentration without severing delusion is like someone carving a dried dung-stick into the shape of sandalwood; although its form resembles [sandalwood], its nature is inherently foul-smelling, and it will never become fragrant.
The carving of dung serves as a metaphor for one who cultivates concentration without severing delusion, while the sandalwood serves as the metaphor for [true concentration].
Right concentration is right concentration because it inherently possesses the fragrance of all dharmas of merit;

therefore, how could one who speaks falsely—whose body and mind are like the stench of human excrement, incomparably foul—attain right concentration? To provide correct instruction and admonition according to my teaching, I say:

"A bhikṣu should practice the Path with a straightforward mind. As stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*: "The straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), for it is free from falsehood. Regarding this:

In all four modes of conduct—whether going or coming, bowing or looking up, speaking or remaining silent—in every action, one must be without flattery, without deceit, without arrogance, and without falsehood.
How could one deceive oneself by claiming to have attained the dharmas of a superior person?
To illustrate the sin of such false claims, the text provides an analogy which is easy to understand: seeking the Bodhi of a Buddha while trying to bite one's own navel.
To say that it is unattainable is like biting one's own heel; as the *Spring and Autumn Annals* (Chunqiu Zhuan) records: "When King Wen of Chu attacked Shen, he passed through Deng.

The Marquis of Deng, who was his nephew, said, 'He is my sister's son,' and stopped him to entertain him. Zhai Sheng, Nian Sheng, and Yang Sheng requested to kill the King of Chu, but the Marquis of Deng would not permit it.
The three nephews said, 'The one who will surely cause the state of Deng to perish is this very man. If...
"If one does not plan early, the ruler will bite his own navel later. The commentary states: "This means it is too late. *Shi* (噬) means to gnaw;

it is like a person trying to gnaw their own navel—it is impossible to reach. Thus, the metaphor used here in the scripture clarifies that for those who seek *bodhi*, because of their false speech, the fruit of Buddhahood is unattainable.
If the subsequent sections follow directly upon the teaching of the straightforward mind, they mean "straightforwardness."
The mind is like a string; because it treads upon reality and uprightness within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), there is no Māra. This may be understood from the Buddha-seal below.
The final four lines are as before.

"Ānanda, as for your question regarding the gathering of the mind, I shall first explain [the stages] up to how all demonic activities arise."
In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One cites the preceding inquiry and the four prior instructions to clarify that when the root is free from transgression, the branches do not arise.
"As you asked below" cites the previous question;
since Ānanda had previously asked about "wishing to collect the mind" and so forth, the Buddha cites this and answers the four instructions as the foundation for the three trainings. Thus:

These four admonitions constitute the sublime gateway for cultivation and study; the precepts serve as the means of passage. With these means of passage serving as the gateway, right concentration and the Path are that which are to be reached.
Therefore, if these four roots are as pure as ice or frost, then their branches and leaves will not grow of themselves.
"Branches and leaves" is a metaphor for the three types of mental conduct, the four types of verbal conduct, and the remaining minor precepts. As for the "three mental conducts": [text continues].

Greed, anger, and delusion; and as for the four [verbal offenses], they are false speech, frivolous speech, double-tongued speech, and harsh abuse—these four derivative verbal acts are not the same as the fundamental great falsehoods mentioned previously.
Ānanda, thus, following the preceding to clarify these four roots:

if these are not lost, the mind will not falsely move, and the objects of the six sense-fields will likewise not be falsely conditioned. How much less so, then, regarding the remaining demonic affairs?
And so it arises.
"If there are past habitual tendencies that cannot be extinguished... (up to) "...the heart-mantra spoken while seated upon the precious lotus.

This section of the sūtra precisely clarifies the conditions and teachings for gathering the mind and removing obstacles, instructing one to recite the mantra while simultaneously revealing the mantra itself.

This is the origin of its name and meaning. It is said that practitioners in the末法 (mofa) age, though they may uphold the four precepts, may be obstructed by their past habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

As Wēn-líng remarked: "Those who desire purity are stained; those who prefer correctness are firmly attached to evil. This is caused by past habitual tendencies and is therefore difficult to eliminate.

If there is any deficiency in the observance of the precepts, the teaching instructs one to recite the *Buddhōṣṇīṣa-tejorāja-dhāraṇī*. (Note: *Buddhōṣṇīṣa-tejorāja-dhāraṇī* is the Sanskrit reconstruction of 佛頂光神呪, referring to the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī* or related protective spells associated with the Buddha’s cranial protuberance.)
The term "Mahā" is the Sanskrit name; it is translated as "Great. "Sātata-pattra" is translated as "White Parasol.
It is called "Unsurpassed" because it is the most supreme, meaning there is nothing higher that can surpass it. It is called "Divine" because it is unfathomable.
This is the source from which the following secret mantra emerges. The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, refers to himself as "The Unseen."
Regarding the *uṣṇīṣa* (cranial protuberance), the *Huayan chao* states that it is one of the Buddha’s thirty-two marks, namely the mark of the *māṃsa-kośa* (fleshy protuberance).
The crown of the Buddha’s head has a fleshy elevation resembling a topknot; it is also called the "invisible crown" (*adṛśya-uṣṇīṣa*).
It is termed "invisible" because followers of the Three Vehicles cannot see its summit. The Bodhisattva Āryāvalokiteśvara served as the Buddha’s wet nurse.
If one wishes to behold these marks, looking upward gradually higher until reaching the limits of the *sāhasra-lokadhātu*, they cannot be seen;
therefore, the Buddha of the unconditioned mind (*asaṃskṛta-citta*) is the mind of the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Because this mind of ultimate truth has nothing to be done, light is emitted from within the unconditioned mind, and within that light, transformation Buddhas appear. Since they are called "unconditioned," yet they are still able to [manifest].
The emission of light and the manifestation of transformation-buddhas (nirmāṇakāya-buddhas) symbolize that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) acts as the conditioned;

thus, the unconditioned and the conditioned are both inseparable from the mind of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Therefore, it is said that the Buddha of the Unconditioned Mind emits radiance from his crown.
This refers to the fundamental Buddha emitting a hundred jewel-lustres from his crown, within which manifested buddhas sit upon precious lotus flowers and proclaim the Heart Mantra.
The "Chengxin" (Satisfying the Mind) Mantra flows forth from the mind of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*). Since the Buddha is also this mind, he is called the "Mind-Buddha";
since the mantra is also this mind, it is called the "Mind-Mantra. The Buddha is the Jewel of the Buddha, and the mantra is the Jewel of the Dharma.

To rely upon this mantra and to realize this Buddha is the meaning of "harmony and union" (*saṃgha*), which is precisely what is meant by the Three Jewels as a single essence; this can be seen herein.
However, when one uses the mind of right concentration of the supreme meaning of the Middle Way to break through past habitual tendencies, what habit will not be eliminated?
Therefore, I teach you to recite this mantra.
Moreover, when you were with Mātanga in your previous lives (up to the point where it was like raising a sail with a favorable wind), what difficulty or danger could there have been?

This section of the sutra follows upon the preceding meaning of reciting mantras to eliminate habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), citing this present instance to demonstrate the swiftness of its efficacy.
Furthermore, from the words "And you," the text specifically points to Ānanda’s extremely deep and thick habitual tendencies as proof.
As the *Anurādha-sūtra* states: "In five hundred past lives, Ānanda was the husband of Anurādha."

Now, as for the statement regarding the passage through kalpas, how could it stop at five hundred? Such profound and deep-seated habitual tendencies are forever severed from the very core of her heart once the Buddha proclaims [the Dharma];
it is not merely that she is liberated from her past habits, but she is further able to attain the fruit of sainthood.
Even she, who was formerly a courtesan, contrary to the Way and devoid of the intent to practice, suddenly attained [realization] entirely through the secret assistance of the power of the mantra.
The swiftness of the merit in severing the root of craving and realizing the state of no-more-learning can generally be verified. How so?
Below, by using the inverse of that [previous case] as an analogy for this [present one], the swiftness of its efficacy is twice that of the former. It is like dust being blown by a favorable wind;

it vanishes in an instant—what difficulty could there be? The "light dust" is a metaphor for past habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and the "favorable wind" is a metaphor for the heart-mantra (*cittamantra*).
The analogy of the heart-mantra being like a favorable wind is used because the mantra follows the mind; this reveals its power to turn back that which is adverse.
If there are those in the final age who wish to sit at the site of enlightenment (up to the point where) the light of great compassion is emitted to come and sprinkle their crowns with consecration.

This section of the sutra directly answers Ānanda’s question regarding the establishment of the *maṇḍala* (place of practice), clarifying the underlying intention behind the consecration of the altar.

Regarding the phrase "If there be one who... and so forth: "one who wishes to sit in the *maṇḍala*"—a *maṇḍala* is a place for attaining the Way, which is precisely the location where one recites mantras.
"To sit" refers to sitting in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); the intent is to sit within the altar because one is advancing along this Path. Therefore, it is so stated.

Regarding the act of sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*): one who is about to sit at the site of enlightenment takes the strict observance of pure precepts as the preliminary intention for entering the ritual circle (*maṇḍala*).
For a *bhikṣu*, the "precepts of restraint" (*saṃvara-śīla*) refers to the two hundred and fifty precepts; because these restraints prohibit deviance, they are called "precepts of restraint.
Among the [four] types of *śramaṇas*, the teaching points to the *arhat* as the foremost *śramaṇa* in the world, for he has completed what was to be done.
Furthermore, because it is difficult to find such a person, one may take as a teacher someone who is regarded as the foremost pure individual within a single realm or kingdom;

by doing so, my precepts can be perfected. My desire to uphold the precepts relies upon a superior teacher, for it is by relying on their Dharma-eye to discern the nuances of observance and violation, and of permission and prohibition, that error is first avoided. If one does not encounter a truly pure person...

If a monk has not yet mastered the details of subtle conduct—such as purity and defilement, observance and violation, action and cessation, or what is permitted and what is prohibited—it is like a jade stone with a flaw;
it cannot be considered a fine gem. Therefore, one must rely on a strict teacher for our Way to be perfected. One who is truly pure is one who confronts reality;
those who speak of a semblance of purity or a semblance of cleanliness are not truly pure. They are like the "honest villagers" (xiangyuan), whose own minds are first plundered by thieves.
The phrase "How can my precepts be perfected? includes the character "true" (*zhen*) to signify that the selection of a teacher must be rigorous.

According to the subsequent text concerning the four *pārājika* and eight *pārājika* offenses, as well as the Bodhisattva vows, although this passage specifically refers to *bhikṣus*, it also encompasses both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions.

The "four *pārājikas*" refer to the *bhikṣu* rules, while the "eight *pārājikas*" refer to the *bhikṣuṇī* rules; the underlying intent is that all four assemblies may cultivate these precepts. Regarding "the perfection of the precepts," below...
The intent is that although one intends to establish a *bodhimaṇḍa*, one fears that one's own power may not yet be sufficient;
thus, one must rely on the efficacy of mantras to initiate the consecration of the altar. "Holding the precepts" refers to internal purity; "changing one's clothes" refers to external purity;

and "dwelling in seclusion" means closing off all external conditions. Regarding the "one hundred and eight recitations," the *Zhenji* commentary states that this signifies the removal of the one hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśas*).
This concludes the preceding section. First, one purifies the mind both internally and externally, and only then does one establish the boundary (*sīmābandha*).

To "establish the boundary" means to demarcate the boundaries of the ritual arena (*maṇḍala*) in the four directions, above, and below. The detailed methods for this are found in the *Maudgalyāyana’s Five Hundred Questions*; fearing prolixity, they are not recorded here.

At the time of establishing the altar, one prays for the light of the Buddhas of the ten directions to come and confer empowerment; the intent of this is to clarify the principle of spiritual resonance.

This should be understood as the Way manifesting to express the sincerity of the practitioner. The Buddhas currently dwelling in the ten directions—namely, the Buddha of Good Virtue in the East and others—are invoked to pray for the descent of light and the conferral of empowerment;
this is the intent of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*. That text states:

"Whether one sees light or flowers, or a Buddha coming to rub the crown of one's head, these are signs that testify to the extinction of transgressions. In the present sutra, the purity of both teacher and disciple [is established].
Double your solemnity and pray for the Buddha’s light to descend; you must exhaust your sincerity so that the response may be verified.
Should the Buddha-light not arrive, it means the practitioner’s sincerity has not yet been fully realized;
therefore, exert even greater effort with pure devotion and perform repentance until you behold auspicious signs as proof of my presence.
"Ānanda, thus in the final age, pure bhikṣus... [the Buddha] touches their heads with his hand to comfort them and cause them to attain awakening.
This section of the sūtra follows the previous discussion on the purity of precepts for practitioners of the fourfold assembly;

the Buddha again instructs them to make vows and exert themselves with diligence, aiming to realize the fruit in their present bodies. The phrase "Ānanda, thus... at the beginning of this section承接 (continues from) the preceding section on purity.

The precepts constitute the community; the two groups of those who have left the household life may be understood accordingly. The single phrase "laypeople" (*baiyi*) clarifies the two groups of those remaining at home.

Laypeople are called "white-clad" because monastic robes are dyed with a ruined color (*huaisè*); this ruined color is termed "black" (*zī*), and since black distinguishes them from white, laypeople are designated as "white-clad.
Thus, the two colors—black and white—are used to differentiate the monastic and the secular. This is the meaning of *dāna*.

The previous translation has already explained this; the current text cites the fourfold assembly specifically to clarify that for the rite of binding the altar and reciting mantras, there is no distinction between the ordained and the laity—whosoever possesses a sincere and capable resolve may participate.
However, one must extinguish greed and lust within the heart and uphold the precepts of the aforementioned four admonitions.
Furthermore, within the *dharmadhātu* (place of practice), one must further give rise to the Bodhisattva vows in every thought-moment.
Regarding the vows: as stated in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, one bathes before entering and exiting [the ritual space] so that external impurities do not enter.

As for the "six periods," these are the three periods of the day and the three periods of the night—namely, the beginning, middle, and end. Regarding "practicing the Way" (*xingdao*), it means directing the mind toward the Path.
"Not sleeping" means remaining alert and awake without falling into dullness. The appearance of the Buddha after twenty-one days clarifies [this point].
The swiftness of this resonance is such that the World-Honored One Śākyamuni himself refers to his own manifestation before the practitioner to touch their head in comfort;
this is precisely the verification of the aforementioned signs for praying for light and seeking a response.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I have received [the teachings] from the Tathāgata... [until] conforming to the pure regulations of the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
This section of the sutra specifically inquires as to how the matters of binding the ritual altar (*maṇḍala*) accord with the ritual methods of the Buddha’s ultimate truth-mind (*paramārtha-citta*).
Previously, when Ānanda first asked about the method of binding the altar, the Buddha first clarified the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*) as the foundation.

Regarding the foundation for binding the altar and cultivating the mind: having reached this point, the preliminary intention for binding the altar is clarified, and one now proceeds to the formal inquiry into the ritual rules within the altar.

"Ānanda" and below refers to the question concerning benefiting others; the preceding presentation of one's own realization and the compassionate instructions refer to the four previous instructions as well as the text above, all of which constitute compassionate instruction. The three phrases beginning with "The mind" are Ānanda’s own [words].
It is because one awakens through instruction and, by relying on this for cultivation and realization, the Path of the Sages can be accomplished.

Therefore, at the end of the Dharma, the request for the proper procedures and rules for establishing the ritual altar is made. Regarding "purity": it means that phenomena and principle are fused, and the ultimate and conventional truths are in accord;
there is no partiality and one does not abide in the middle. Although various affairs may arise in abundance, they do not hinder the single mind from being unmoving—this is the "middle of middles."
This is the procedure for entering into purity.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If, in the final age of the world... [one should] take a square of sixteen feet and make it an octagonal altar.
This section of the sutra is where the World-Honored One correctly demonstrates the ritual procedures; this first clarifies the preliminary preparations before binding the altar.

Yeshen takes the dung of white snow-mountain oxen and mixes it with clay, desiring that it not crack—this is like the intention of common households who must use straw fibers when mixing clay to plaster walls.
Since oxen eat grass, their dung is essentially straw fibers;
thus, using ox dung mixed with clay to plaster walls and floors is practiced not only in Western India, but also in regions such as Yan and Jin in this land.

I have also seen this before; the reason why white bull dung from the Snowy Mountains must be used for coating the altar ground now is that by eating fragrant herbs, drinking clear springs, and consuming only what is pure, they are entirely fragrant.
Because they take in fragrance and are minute, they are like musk deer;
even when they eat *zhè* (mulberry) leaves, their entire bodies become fragrant, and the dung of these white bulls is likewise so. However, these white bulls do not belong to ordinary households.
The cattle kept here are wild mountain oxen produced in the Snowy Mountains; only this mountain possesses them, for this mountain abounds in fragrant herbs.
Therefore, those kept on other mountains or in private homes are unfit for use. Thus it is said:
"If they are not from the Snowy Mountains, the oxen are foul-smelling and unfit even to smear upon the ground. Furthermore, as for other lands far removed from the Snowy Mountains...
As for the absence of white ox dung, one digs into a clean, level area of ground to a depth exceeding five feet;

because the soil obtained is of its natural color, it is called "yellow earth. As stated above regarding sandalwood, if there were white ox dung, one would simply use the single flavor of sandalwood to form the mud;
however, since there is no ox dung, one uses the ten fragrances mixed with the earth to form it.
Clay is used to coat the ground so that it does not crack and remains fragrant and clean. In the center of the ground, earth is raised to form an altar;
its square and circular dimensions are sixteen feet, forming eight corners with each side measuring two feet, such that the eight corners constitute the measure of sixteen feet.
As for the ten kinds of incense, first, regarding *candana*, one must specifically take *gośīrṣa-candana*.
Although these are not commonly seen in this region, *gośīrṣa-candana* (ox-head sandalwood) is indeed difficult to obtain; therefore, even "constant fragrance" (*sadāgandha*) may be used.

As for *agaru* (aloewood), it is well known. Regarding *sūhaka* (suhak), the *Continued Book of the Later Han* states that various fragrant herbs are blended and boiled until they form a paste, hence it is called *sūhaka*.
The *Guangzhi* also says it originates from the country of Ta-ch'in, which is [Persia].

In this country, the people gather fragrant herbs and press their juice to boil it into an ointment. The *Nanzhou Yiwuzhi* (Record of Extraordinary Things from the Southern Regions) states that its appearance is like peach resin.
The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) notes that in the kingdom of Aṭali in South India, there is the *kunduruka* tree, whose leaves resemble those of the jujube and the *turmeric*.
According to the *Zhouli*, in the section on the Spring Official, the *Yuren* (Director of Incense) gathers [the fragrance].
"Taking [it] with fragrant wine (*chāngjiǔ*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The flower of the *yùjīn* grass, a fragrant substance offered from distant regions;
the *yùrén* (incense official) blends it to brew wine for descending the spirits. It is used in the ancestral temple. "White resin" refers to *fēngxiāng*.
The *Qīngmùxiāng Pǔ* says: "Regarding the five aromatics: one plant has five roots, one stem, five branches, and each branch has five leaves."
The five joints on each leaf, arranged in groups of five, give it the name "Five-Perfume Tree," which is the same as *agallochum* (qingmuxiang).

The *Nan Yue Zhi* (Record of Nan Yue) states that the local people identify it as *yancao* (swallow grass), *yuxiang* (artemisia), or *gansong* (calamint); it is the very substance commonly seen in medicinal preparations today.
*Kesheliang* (chicken-tongue) comes from Wuma Zhou; the *Yiwuzhi* (Record of Exotic Objects) states that when this herb withers, it can be blended into incense. [Note: *Jian*.

The Hu people say that when the various fragrances grow together on a single tree, their flowers are *jīshè* (chicken-beak) incense. Létán Biāo points out that *jīshè* is actually *dīngxiāng* (clove).
It is not yet known which is correct. Regarding the ritual formats for the altar above, both the Chángshuǐ Commentary and the Wēnlíng Essential Exegesis employ them as symbols of the Dharma;
however, the numerical correlations of the Chángshuǐ are inferior to those of the Wēnlíng, which are more appropriate. Now...
Regarding the commentary by Wēnlíng, I fear it may be too prolix and have not recorded it in full; its meaning can be grasped through reflection. Wēnlíng’s commentary states:
"The Dharma-king’s words on the Dharma" means that phenomena (dharma) and principles (li) are simultaneous; phenomena do not arise in isolation, nor are phenomena established in vain. It says:
"The mountain is high," representing the earth as pure and the summit as faith. The "powerful white ox" represents the pure and great root.
The fragrant herbs represent the pure water and the wondrous, virtuous, and pure wisdom. The *śu-tui* (cow dung) represents abundance and surplus;
it refers specifically to white cow dung. *Candana* (sandalwood) is the foremost of the ten perfumes, representing the ten *pāramitās* as the crown of all myriad practices.
Originally, it signifies level ground and represents faith and sincerity. Because the surface of the earth was not yet purified, one digs down to a depth of five units.
Within that, from among the yellow colors, one takes the "middle-of-the-middle," which signifies pure faith. The ten incenses represent the ten *pāramitās*;
the Dharma-fragrance altar represents the essence of tranquil extinction and straightforward reality. Because this essence is endowed with the Eightfold Path, it is eight-cornered;

because it can subsume the eight heterodoxies, it is square. It is sixteen *zhang* [in size], and so forth. What is now called the ritual site (*chǎngdì*) was in antiquity called a leveled ground (*shàn*), where earth was raised.
That which is octagonal is properly called a *maṇḍala*.
At the center of the *maṇḍala*, place one [vessel] made of gold, silver, copper, or wood... (up to) ...to offer to the Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding expedient means regarding the construction of the altar and the arrangement of ritual implements.
The text states: "A square and circle of sixteen feet [in circumference] form an octagonal altar; now, in the center of this altar, place a single lotus flower.

This flower may be made of gold, silver, copper, or wood, according to the convenience of one's means, whether abundant or modest. Regarding the placement of the alms bowl and other items within the flower:
'exposed' refers to being in the open air, while 'moist' refers to the autumn eighth month, when the white dew has already fallen and the dew is at its peak."
Nothing surpasses this time for its clarity, coolness, and purity; therefore, it is used here. Placing flower petals within the dew conveys a sense of crystalline brilliance and solemn adornment.

The eight mirrors are arranged according to the cardinal directions between the flowers and the incense burner; that which encircles the center of the altar represents the simultaneous presence of both fragrance and light.
Flowers and the burner must necessarily serve as mutual adornments; however, here we speak of adornment specifically in reference to the area around the burner.

The partial intention is for completeness. As for burning aloeswood incense so that the fire is not seen—the intention is that while the incense smoke curls upward and the fragrance swirls in abundance, one does not allow the fierce blaze to be seen. Foods such as milk products must be refined and pure;
they are fit for offering and are certainly not ordinary meals. Each of these sixteen types is offered to the Buddha, encircling him according to the directions.
Furthermore, according to the memorial submitted by the Bodhisattva Wenlu: the lotus flower at the center of the altar represents the wondrous practice of the Middle Way;
the alms bowl, as the appropriate vessel, represents responding to things according to their measure;

the dew falling in autumn—specifically in the eighth month, the midst of autumn—represents the practice of benevolent coverage, bestowed according to the reach of the moisture; and the circular mirror represents the Great Perfection.

The mirror-like wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna) is situated at each of the eight directions. The surrounding lotus bowls represent the mutual dependence of wisdom and practice, responding to the square and circular forms according to their respective orientations.
Outside the mirrors, sixteen lotus flowers and incense burners are arranged at intervals;

the flowers symbolize wondrous practice, and the incense symbolizes wondrous virtue. Those outside the mirrors represent the establishment of skillful means beyond correct wisdom. [They] are purely ablaze.
The fact that the incense sinks without being seen by fire symbolizes the reversal of the storehouse of non-virtue and the cessation of vitarka and vicāra at the site of quiescence.
As for the taking of white cow’s milk and so forth, this symbolizes offering the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna to the two Honored Ones.

While the provisional teachings permit the use of milk and curd, the ultimate teaching prohibits it; yet, the reason for taking them again to offer in worship is intended to signify their harmonious integration.
Because the provisional and the real, as well as the heterodox and the orthodox, are identical, each of the eight flavors is likewise surrounded by sixteen;
that which encircles the outside of the flower symbolizes the method of harmonizing the provisional and subsuming the heterodox, which is established according to the practice of joy.
"Whenever at mealtime or during the middle watch of the night (up until the point where one burns [incense] until the smoke is exhausted), one makes offerings to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
This section of the sutra shows that the practitioner within the maṇḍala, following mealtime, performs offerings to the two Honored Ones as a skillful means (*upāya*) for concluding the maṇḍala rite.
"Mealtime" refers to the times of the morning and midday meals. Furthermore, it is raised...

Regarding "midnight": this means that because one practices the path within the altar with such hardship, hunger easily arises; thus, [the rules] are temporarily relaxed. "A half-measure of honey and three *he* of clarified butter":
the measure (*sheng*) can be understood [as standard], and the three *he* are three-quarters of a *sheng*.
"To separately install a small brazier before the altar" means that in front of the altar, near the side chamber, one should separately place a small wind-brazier (*fenglu*). *Dou*.
Regarding the name of the *lūba* fragrant herb: according to Chen Zangqi’s *Bencao Shiyi* (Supplement to the Materia Medica) of the Tang dynasty, it is called *douna* incense;
furthermore, the *Wei lüe* (History of the Wei Dynasty) states that *douna* incense is produced in the kingdom of Daqin (Roman Empire).

Thus, the present *douloupo* may simply be *douna*, with the difference being between the Chinese and Sanskrit terms. It is uncertain which is correct, so we shall provisionally retain this [reading]. As for bathing the charcoal with this incense: this...
Incense is non-toxic and can eliminate foul odors; it is burned upon charred coals so that no lingering scent remains.

If one throws ghee and honey into a blazing furnace, there must necessarily be a cauldron. If the current text is incomplete and one were to claim that a blazing furnace lacks a cauldron such that both ghee and honey turn to ash, then what would the furnace offer to the Buddha?
To "burn until the smoke is exhausted" means to boil them until the smoke is completely gone.

Refining the essence so that it is devoid of vital breath; according to the commentary by Wēn-líng, because the Buddha receives food at midday, he always offers his oblations at midday, taking midnight as the counterpart to midday.
Honey is produced from flowers, representing the harmonious integration of the Dharma-practice;
ghee is produced from milk, representing the harmonious integration of the Dharma-flavor. "Half" is a number for the middle, and "three" is...

The small fire-pit representing the number "one" symbolizes the awakened mind (bodhicitta) within a square inch. The incense used for bathing the charcoal symbolizes the method for awakening that mind.

However, causing it to blaze fiercely and casting ghee and honey into the flaming furnace until the smoke is entirely consumed symbolizes that once the practice is perfected, one must not remain stagnant;
rather, one should courageously smelt the awakened mind to fuse away all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) together.
When both conditions and reflections have vanished, one becomes suddenly enlightened, like snow falling upon a red-hot furnace; only then is one enjoyed by the Buddhas.
Those who dwell in the field of cessation and partake of the flavor of dhyāna-joy should apply their whole hearts to this.
"Have banners and flowers hung everywhere on the four outer sides... (until) spread out at the side of the gate and placed to the left and right.
This section of the sutra follows the previous instructions for constructing the altar and arranging the furnishings;

it further directs that the honored images be suspended to manifest the principal and retinue of the *Jiǎochăng* (Vajrāsana), so that the practitioner may have an object of veneration and reliance. "The four directions" refers to the four exterior sides of the ritual chamber.
The hanging of banners and flowers everywhere symbolizes the adornment of external practice through the four benefits of the *Karunāpuṣpa* Sūtra.
The four rows within the chamber and so forth symbolize that the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) are of such a nature that there is nothing that is not the true sovereign.

As for the image of Vairocana spread across the center of the chamber facing the entrance: "Vairocana" is translated as "Pure and Full" (*viśuddha-pūrṇa*); this refers to the Reward Body Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya*).
"Ka" refers to the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha. Although a single Buddha possesses the three bodies (*trikāya*), he does not equal Vairocana here;
this is because Vairocana is the Dharmakāya, and since the Buddha’s Dharmakāya has no manifest form, [his image] is not suspended.

This [central figure] is the true Lord of the Site of Enlightenment (*Bodhimaṇḍa*), and thus occupies the central position. Maitreya is the one who will dwell in this world in the future. Akṣobhya is translated as... [text ends].

The Immovable One represents the wisdom of the Buddha of the East; Amitābha is the abbreviated Sanskrit term, which in full is *Amitāyus*, translated as "Immeasurable Life," representing the compassion of the Buddha of the West.

That these two Buddhas of the East and West also reside facing forward on the altar signifies that for the practitioner within this mandala, wisdom and compassion are the primary focus. These are the various visualization practices.

The placement of the Bodhisattva Ghoṣa and Vajragarbha on the left and right signifies that the practitioner, mounting the vow of great compassion, attains harmony with those above and below, delivering sentient beings through diverse skillful means;
thus, the various manifested Avalokiteśvaras refer to the thirty-two responses and so forth mentioned in the preceding sutra.
Vajragarbha presides over all the Vajras to protect and uphold the mantra-heart, signifying that the practitioner provides protection.

Because mindfulness is not empty, the aforementioned intention clarifies that the Dharma King and the Dharma Minister constitute the internal principal and companions, while Śakra, Brahmā, and others serve as external protectors.
The translation of Ucchuṣma is as seen previously. Regarding Lan-de-ka, the *Myiṅ-tshig-mishan-bśad* (The Collection of Names and Meanings) states:
"He is the blue-faced Vajrasena; Krodharāja is a synonym for Vajra, and refers to the ten great vidyārājas."
Regarding "the King's number": *Vikūṭī* is as described in the *Vairocana-vikurvāṇa-sūtra*:
"On the left side is Vikūṭī, three-eyed and holding her hair in a topknot. Regarding "the Four Heavenly Kings may be known," etc.: "etc.
refers to the number of Nalakuvara (Nata-tai) and the Celestial Great Generals (*devasena-pati*). *Bhīma* is the pig-headed one; *Nairṛta* is the elephant-nosed one—these two.
The names of the messengers are both unknown, as their translated meanings have not been clarified.

As for those stationed to the left and right of the door, while the high-ranking Dharma ministers and others are arranged within the chamber to the left and right, these [messengers] serve as external guardians; therefore, they are placed to the left and right outside the door.
Furthermore, eight mirrors are taken and suspended in the void (until) their forms and shadows interpenetrate one another in successive layers.

This section of the scripture follows the preceding arrangement; taking its meaning from the imagery, it clarifies the principle through the facts, so that they are interwoven and harmoniously integrated without obstruction.
The Wénlǐng commentary states that the mirrors within the altar represent the mixing of things with their supports.
The wisdom of the practitioner is like a mirror in space: detached from objects and without dependence, it represents the wisdom of all Buddhas.

Only that which is mixed with objects and possesses dependence can reflect external things but cannot yet reflect itself. One must attain a wisdom that is detached from objects and without dependence;

when these two modes of wisdom function in mutual interplay, then object and self mutually reflect one another, and mind and environment are simultaneously integrated. Thus do all Buddhas [attain this].
The bodies and lands of sentient beings interpenetrate without the labor of movement and without waiting for a thought to arise; phenomena encompass all things, and affairs are free from obstruction.
At every glance, a thousand sages appear together; at every touch, the myriad phenomena are clearly manifest.

A single flower or a single incense offering pervades and makes offerings to all lands within the dust motes; a single practice or a single characteristic expands infinitely. This does not rely on supernatural powers, nor does it involve the emotions.

This refers to the Dharma of the site of tranquility; such is the fundamental nature of all phenomena. The subtle perfection of the cultivation and realization of the secret cause reaches its ultimate point here.
However, the mirror within the previous altar was explained by Wenling as representing the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).

Now, this explanation [of the mirror] as being mixed with objects and having a basis may cause practitioners of shallow understanding whose comprehension has not yet been integrated to doubt that the preceding and succeeding parts are inconsistent. This is not something to be doubted; it is truly so.

Because the wisdom of the practitioner and the wisdom of all Buddhas are of one and the same essence, there is no fault in stating that both are inseparable from the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
Within the first seven days, one should pay homage with utmost sincerity until the body and mind become clear and pure like lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*).
This section of the sutra precisely demonstrates the ritual for entering the altar and practicing the Way;
it shows that within twenty-one days, one must discipline the mind and pray for the Buddha’s manifestation, with the intermingling of lights serving as its sign of efficacy.

What was previously stated—that within the site of practice (do-chang), one practices the Way during the six periods for twenty-one days until the Buddha appears before them and touches their crown to bring about awakening—corresponds exactly to this present sign of efficacy.

For the first seven days, one should recite the auspicious names of the Principal and Retinue during the six periods of the day while circumambulating the altar, chanting the mantra one hundred and eight times during each session.
Since the mantra text is extremely long, how could one possibly recite it one hundred and eight times in a single period?
One’s intention must simply be to recite the eight lines following the word *Oṃ*. Regarding the method of recitation, one must ensure that the mind remembers and the mouth chants.
Maintaining a harmonious voice and slow steps, their movements and mantras are all appropriate to the occasion; thus, the profound efficacy lies herein.
During the second seven-day period, one neither recites nor moves, sitting in silent dhyāna and single-mindedly making vows without interruption.
Regarding the term *vinaya* (毗奈耶), its translation has been seen previously. As for "the teaching of vows," it specifically refers to that which is elucidated in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*. First...
Regarding the middle and upper periods of the three seven-day intervals, while it was previously stated that there were only six sessions, twelve sessions are now added;

this indicates that the efficacy is most profound and the diligent application is even more intense. As for those who maintain the mantra with single-minded devotion in every thought, based on this, one knows that during the second seven-day interval they were not failing to recite;
it was simply that they did not count [the recitations] nor perform [the formal sessions]. Upon reaching the final day of the third seven-day interval, throughout the ten directions...
Regarding the Buddhas appearing at the intersection of the mirror-rays to bestow empowerment by touching the crown of the head: in the preceding text, the mirror was used to symbolize wisdom;

now, as the Buddha-wisdom and the practitioner’s wisdom mutually stimulate and inspire one another, cause and effect are seamlessly integrated—this is the meaning of the empowerment by touching the crown.

When phenomena and principle merge and mind and object meet in profound stillness, this is the manifestation of the Buddhas of the ten directions. Thus, this accords with the previous verification that [the practice] is not in vain.

The Buddha immediately said to those practitioners of the final age: "If you are able to practice with such intensity for twenty-one days until your cultivation reaches its peak, cause and effect will interact and respond;
from this, you shall enter samādhi, and your body and mind will become bright and pure, transparent both internally and externally like lapis lazuli."
"Ānanda, if this bhikṣu’s original preceptor [from] (until) such a place of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*) does not achieve success, [it is because of this].
This section of the sutra serves as the Buddha’s admonition regarding the aforementioned lack of purity of intention;
it urges profound prevention and practical application in order to strictly purify the mind. The text is intelligible.
"From the end of the three-week period, he sat in formal meditation during the summer retreat... until you asked about the establishment of the site of enlightenment.
This section of the sutra summarizes the ritual of the altar based on the meaning following the three-week period.
