After the merit was accomplished at the end of the aforementioned three weeks, there were no other arrangements; he simply required one to sit upright and rigidly, silently contemplating one's own fundamental inquiry. Thus it is said in the sutra.

For those of sharp faculties, within one hundred days they shall not rise from this seat in their original ordinary bodies, but will immediately enter the stage of the noble ones and attain the state of *srotāpanna*.

To accommodate those of shallow capacity, it is said that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, by reciting this mantra-heart, achieve supreme enlightenment, sit upon the Bodhi throne, and enter Great Nirvāṇa; how could this apply merely to the small [vehicle]?
If even Denga, who merely heard the dharani, attained the third fruit of the path—how much more so those with pure faculties?
Even for those of inferior capacity or dull roots who have not yet achieved this, they will attain decisive faith and know for themselves that their attainment of Buddhahood is unmistakable.
Ānanda prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying: [up to] “I await the hearing of the Tathāgata’s secret verses.
This section of the sutra indicates that although Ānanda had requested the ritual for the altar, he had not yet personally heard the mantra; therefore, he requests its proclamation once again.
From the words "Since I... onwards, Ānanda describes his own failings to clarify why he has not yet heard the Heart Mantra.

The preceding chapter was when Mañjuśrī, while upholding the mantra, went forth to provide protection; he merely recited it in secret to resolve the difficulty of lust, and thus it is called "not yet heard.
Now, [the request is made] for an explicit exposition, intending to transmit it to those of the future.
Having initiated this by personally receiving the sacred words, I pray that you will grant the formal request to repeat the text, so that its meaning may be understood.
At that time, the World-Honored One [from within his *uṣṇīṣa*]... until the Tathāgata Emitting Light (*Prabhāsa*) proclaimed the divine mantra.

This section of the sutra records that the World-Honored One, having accepted their earnest request to proclaim the mantra, first emitted light and manifested transformation-buddhas to signify the spiritual power of the heart-mantra.
As for the *uṣṇīṣa*, it refers to the invisible-mark *uṣṇīṣa*; this is the same as the "invisible mark" mentioned previously.
The subsequent mutual clarification that "a hundred jewel-lights surge from within the topknot" signifies seeing form within the formless.
That "thousand-petaled lotuses surge from within the light" signifies that the light represents the essence of *prajñā* (wisdom) and the flowers represent the causal practices;
that the flowers emerge from the light signifies that the flowers of the myriad causal practices arise from *prajñā*. That "Buddhas appear within the light sitting upon lotus flowers" signifies...

The cause receives the fruit, and the fruit penetrates the cause. As for the emanation-buddha emitting ten rays of light from his crown, this symbolizes that within the transformative manifestation there is further transformation;
the ten pāramitās are fully encompassed without departing from the essence of Prajñā.

Thus, each ray of light possesses the inexhaustible function of the perfect mind that protects the Dharma. "Ten Ganges-sands" refers to the meaning of inexhaustibility. "Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada" refers to...

Because of his mind that protects the Dharma, he is called Vajrapāṇi (Vajra Secret Trace). "Vajra" is spoken of by way of metaphor; it refers to the meaning of firmness, for his vow-mind is as solid as a vajra.
"Secret Trace" (*guhyapada*) means that within reality (*tattva*), he manifests expedient means (*upāya*);

this is an inconceivable station above the [bodhisattva] stages (*bhūmi*). Because he manifests the vajra as his trace, he is called "Secret Trace. However, this is fundamentally the non-obstruction of principle and phenomenon (*dharmatā-dharmas*).
His traces are eternally fused; he transforms without moving and accomplishes things without acting.

Therefore, each of these ten *sāhasra-cosmos* assemblies manifests their majestic spiritual power—some lifting mountains, others holding vajras—pervading the entire realm of space. The great assembly looks up and beholds their majestic power as if it were descending upon them, and thus they give rise to a heart of awe.
They manifest light and manifest signs such as they have never seen before, and thus they give rise to [a heart of reverence].
"Love and compassion are held within this embrace" means that both fear and love are simultaneously embraced. For this reason, each seeks compassionate protection;

it is precisely because they rely on the Buddha’s compassionate protection that they attain single-mindedness without distraction and hear the divine mantra proclaimed by the Tathāgata manifested from the light atop the Buddha’s crown.
Namo satvatha sugatāya (up to) yantunamaḥ svāhā. (Thirty-seven phrases.
When the reciter reaches this phrase, he shall call out: "The disciple [Name] receives and upholds [this mantra]."
O-ha-niu (38), Li-se-jiē-na (39) ... [up to] Yin-tu-na-mo-mo-xiē (78). From this point up to this phrase, follow the previous procedure by reciting the name;
if it is a layperson, they should say, "I, disciple [Name], receive and uphold [this]."
Rājavataye (79), Cūḍavataye (80) ... [up to] Indutanamaṃ me kṣāntam (72).
Up to this point, call out the names as before.
*Bhagavān* (73), *Sattvabhadra* (74) ... up to *mama svāhā* (32).
Here, as before, call out the name of the disciple.
*Tuṣṭa-citta* (33)... *svāhā*.
This section of the sūtra, totaling four hundred twenty-seven phrases, was spoken by the Buddha to reiterate a secret mantra.
That which he previously commanded Mañjuśrī to go and protect is this very text. Now, "mantra" (*dhāraṇī*) has the meaning of "secret. It is for this reason that...
When practitioners of the secret Śūraṅgama recite this, they are able to give rise to the good and extinguish evil, transforming from the mundane to the sacred.
They secretly obtain its benefits without needing intellectual comprehension;

just as the *guoluó* (sire-wasp) uses its incantation for the *mínglíng* (cicada larvae), or as a general’s command is silently understood by his soldiers while others remain ignorant—this is the meaning of "secret exposition," which differs from the aforementioned "explicit exposition."
The power and function are no different; it is only that the capacities of those to whom it is addressed vary. Thus, in the preceding section on the explicit exposition, it says:

"There is a samādhi called the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, which fully possesses the myriad practices and is the wondrously adorned path by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend through a single gate.
Later, at the conclusion of the proclamation of the mantra, in the section explaining the benefits, it says: "This Buddha..."
The *Cūḍāmaṇi-mahāsitātapatra-rahasya-gāthā-sūkṣma-pada* gives rise to all Buddhas of the ten directions;
it is further stated that this mantra is also called the "Tathāgata’s Crown.
Thus, we know that both the exoteric and esoteric explanations are identical in both name and meaning. Changshui’s Commentary states: "This mantra [consists of] four hundred and two..."
The seventeen preceding phrases merely constitute the act of taking refuge in the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and various worthy sages,
as well as the invocation of mantras and prayers for protection against all calamities such as malevolent spirits and diseases; this continues until the four hundred and nineteenth phrase,
which says *tadyathā*— this is translated as "Now the mantra is spoken"— and it is only from the syllable *oṃ* at the four hundred and twentieth phrase onward that [the actual mantra follows].
This is the true mantra as previously stated; one should recite it six times a day, one hundred and eight times for each session, reciting this very text.
However, while it would be most excellent to recite the entire [sūtra], I fear that the text is too long to complete.

Among the five reasons for not translating (wu bu fan) since antiquity, this falls under the category of "the secret" (*guimimi*). The Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai [expounded] by means of the four *siddhāntas*.
The detailed explanation of the meaning of the mantra is omitted here for fear of prolixity; it is set forth in full within the text itself.
Ānanda, from [the phrase] "this Buddha-Usnīṣa-Raśmi-Kūṭa" up to "the strictly pure precepts shall all be rendered pure."

In this section, after the Buddha has finished proclaiming the mantra and manifesting its perfected power, he concludes by gathering the meaning of the fulfillment of the three types of awakening of all Buddhas.
He then clarifies the excellence of the two benefits [self and others] through ten matters. From "Ānanda" down to "giving birth to all Buddhas" is a general manifestation of the fundamental benefit;
from "the ten directions" onwards, the ten meanings specifically clarify the two types of awakening—both self and other—and...
Regarding the meaning of the fulfillment of awakening and practice, "The Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa-Ratna-Ketu" refers to the Blessed One’s own reference to the hundred-jeweled light emitted from his crown;
because these lights shine upon one another in an uninterrupted succession of transformations, it is called a "mass of light.
*Siddhārthānām* is the name of this root mantra, as seen in the preceding translation. This indicates the meaning of the mantra, for it is capable of giving birth to the merits of all Buddhas.

Nothing is greater than this; "mystery" (*mi*) is insufficient to fully express its meaning. Because it is the ultimate form of mystery, it is termed *guhyakagāthā*, translated as "verse-poem" (*yingshi*).
The *Chuan* (Commentary) states that "verse" (*yong*) means "to contain"; it praises the outward manifestation of magnificent virtue.

Indeed, "verse" (*yong*) and "contain" (*rong*) were interchangeable characters in antiquity. That the *dhāraṇī* mantras are now referred to as *gāthā* is likewise because they are beautiful verses, as follows:
The *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) possesses inconceivable and wondrous functions. The text is divided into ten sections;
the first states that "by means of this mantra-heart, one attains unsurpassed enlightenment," which refers to self-awakening (*svabodhi*).

This "means" (*hetu*) refers to the "cause" (*hetu*) within the title [of the scripture], for by taking the secret mantra as the cause, one attains the fruition of enlightened awakening. The second section states, "grasping the mantra-heart, one subdues..."

The subduing of Māra and externalists is the meaning of "awakening oneself" (*ātma-bodha*); this refers to the act of maintaining [the mantra] as previously described, where Mañjuśrī, holding the mantra, goes forth to protect and thereby subdues the intent of Māra.
Third, "riding upon the mantra-heart and sitting on a lotus to go forth and respond to all lands" is the meaning of "awakening others" (*para-bodha*).

What was explained above regarding the attainment of perfect enlightenment belongs to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), because one realizes the truth through that fundamental wisdom; what is now being discussed is the responsive manifestation (*nirmāṇa*).

Regarding his "response," it belongs to subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) and constitutes the transformation into consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*); this is because, by means of subsequently attained wisdom, he manifests bodies and lands for the sake of all sentient beings and preaches the True Dharma.
Fourth, regarding the "turning of the wheel of Dharma": the previous section merely described the "responding" [to requests], whereas here it concerns the "responding while preaching the Dharma.
This first section on "responding" is divided into two parts; the second part, "containing" (*saṃgraha*), contains five sub-sections, of which the fifth has two further divisions.
First, one’s own realization is already perfected and one receives the empowerment of the Buddhas by having one’s head stroked from all ten directions;

second, even if one’s own realization is not yet perfected, one still receives the empowerment of the Buddhas by having one’s head stroked. This encompasses both the meaning of self-realization and the realization of others.

Sixth, it is said that by relying on the power of the mantra’s加持 (*adhiṣṭhāna*), one is rescued from the manifold sufferings; this is the meaning of the practice of awakening. In the text, the four *gatis* (destinies) are mentioned together.

The fact that the two destinies of devas and asuras are not mentioned here is merely due to an omission in the text. Regarding "the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks" among the eight sufferings:
this refers to those whose past karma has predetermined their poverty, yet they seek wealth; or those whose destiny is fixed for an early death, yet they seek longevity.

Unless one possesses extraordinary karmic power, it is impossible to turn back such fate; thus, all that is forcefully sought cannot be obtained. As for "the blazing intensity of the five aggregates," it means:
When form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness blaze like a fire, they burn the sprout of Bodhi.
When the five aggregates are not empty and are filled with such blazing intensity, then the cycle of birth and death will not cease. This is the most grievous of all;

"great or small transgressions" refers to wrongful and unjust treatment. To inflict harm through irrational means is called a "transgression"; if great, it results in the loss of life, and if small, one encounters calamity and ruin. Irrigation.
The *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī-sūtra* states: "There are nine great calamities and innumerable minor calamities. Regarding the specific explanation of various hardships (*durga*) that follows:

they are called "hardships" because they crush and afflict the body and mind, making them difficult to endure. The meaning of these hardships, as well as the descriptions of the sufferings of the hells and other realms mentioned above, can be understood from those texts;
they need not be explained here in detail. Seventh: "One who knows how to comply with the matters of mantra practice" means...
Regarding the two meanings of "self-awakening" and "awakening others" for the sake of seeking the Way, the *Huayan Chao* states:

"A 'good spiritual friend' (*kalyāṇamitra*) is one who causes all sentient beings—who do not know the various wholesome dharmas—to know them, and who causes those who do not recognize the various unwholesome dharmas to recognize them;
this is called a good spiritual friend. Furthermore, "good" is spoken in contrast to "evil"; by honoring the Right Path, one reaches the cessation of transgressions.
"Merit" refers to a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). One who wields the handle of the world and whose calculations leave no strategy unexhausted is called an "evil friend" (*pāpamitra*).
The remainder of the text is intelligible. The eighth [section] states, "Gathering and receiving through direct causes and so forth," which refers to the meaning of awakening others.

This means that by practicing the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*), one attains the fruit of the path; subsequently, one gathers those with whom one has a karmic affinity, leading them to ascend to the shore of enlightenment. Thus, it directly points to the past.
Regarding the retinue, it is because they formed karmic connections in past lives that they have now met [the Buddha] due to those former affinities.

However, should any among them fall into the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), he employs the power of mantras to ensure they hear [the teaching] without fear; "Secret Treasury" (*guhyagarbha*) refers to the *tathāgatagarbha*, the heart-essence.
As for the passage beginning with "unsurpassed awakening" (*anuttara-bodhi*) and so forth, although it was already explained in the initial text, it is presented again here.
The essential point is that the compilation of the events from the beginning to the end of the eight phases culminates in the ultimate return to *nirvāṇa*.
Sitting beneath the Bodhi tree is the beginning, and *nirvāṇa* is the end; this is the meaning of the fulfillment of the three types of awakening.

As for the matter of entrusting the Buddha-dharma after his passing into extinction, it is truly because the power of the mantra-mind is supreme, remaining undecaying across the three periods of time, thereby perfecting both the beginning and the end through the complete efficacy of the mantra.
As for "Dharma-activities," this refers to the aforementioned ten matters, as well as the three types of awakening, precepts, concentration, wisdom, and so forth—all of these are Dharma-activities.
Since the precepts serve as the vanguard for all Dharma-activities, they are set forth prominently here;
once the precepts are pure, all Dharma-activities will attain ultimate accomplishment. Indeed, these ten matters all take the mantra-heart as their vehicle.
This statement means that the mind is the mantra because it is the *tathāgatagarbha*, and the mantra is the mind because the mind is the mantra.
This is precisely the meaning of what is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā*: "The *prajñāpāramitā* is a great divine mantra, a great illuminating mantra, an unsurpassed mantra, and an unequaled mantra.
This is because [the mind] is fully endowed with nature-virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The Buddha’s dharma-work, from beginning to end, is fully contained herein; those who read these words should deeply awaken to the profound meaning.
If I were to speak of this *Buddhānuttara-śikhara-raśmi-saṃcaya* Sūtra for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges, I could never reach its end.
This section of the sutra re-emphasizes that this dhāraṇī possesses inexhaustible virtues, such that even kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges could not fully describe them.

The four lines beginning with "From morning to evening" (從旦暮) mean that it does not consist of merely ten matters. From "morning to evening" through "passing kalpas as numerous as the sands," although the characters do not repeat, their phonetic resonance continues;
while such kalpas may eventually come to an end, the merit of the dhāraṇī can never be exhausted.
It is also said that this mantra is named "The Tathāgata’s Crown" (Tathāgatamuṣṭi). [From] "it will be impossible for any demonic activities to remain far away.
This section of the sūtra reveals the name and meaning of the mantra as before, clearly explaining the cause and exhorting practitioners to uphold it in order to attain the fruit.
Previously, its name was revealed as "The Great Buddha-Crown" (Mahābuddhāuṣṇīṣa); now, it is secretly designated as "The Tathāgata’s Crown. This is the name.
The meaning is identical in both cases; therefore, one should exhort all those in training (*śaikṣa*) to exhaust saṃsāra and attain the supreme fruit.
One ought to apply oneself to this [mantra], for if one sits in the *bodhimaṇḍa* without holding this mantra, demonic activities will be powerful and it will be difficult to reach the ultimate goal.
Now, as for those who point to the small fruits of those in training, it is because even those with small fruits should still hold the mantra and cultivate unsurpassed *bodhi*.
"How could it not be maintained? This is said in the highest terms to show that this mantra is superior by contrast with what is inferior;
Ānanda, throughout all worlds and in whatever lands, [it shall be such that] no poisons whatsoever can cause harm."
In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One repeatedly exhorts its retention according to the various directions;
that it benefits both the wise and the foolish alike when written and worn as an amulet, such that poisons cannot cause harm—this is its proven efficacy. *Huár* is the name of a tree;
its bark is red, consisting of more than a few layers, thin, soft, and lovely. I once personally used it to create a scroll at Mount Wutai and sent it to you.
All people among humans delight in this. The *palm-leaf* (pattra) is the leaf of the *tāla* tree;
it resembles the sheath of the bitter bamboo in this region, yet it is softer, with a lustrous interior and a coarse exterior, being smooth, glossy, and pure white.

I have also seen it produced in Western India (*Sīnyizhu*), where it is cut into squares and written upon horizontally in Sanskrit characters, with five-colored threads threaded through the center and read horizontally. It is also made from white woolen cloth (*dukūla*) and bird feathers.
Produced in Western India, it is exquisitely fine; here in this land, it is like white swan’s down, pure and bright as silk, hence it is called *pāṇḍukambala*.
The rest of the text is understandable.
"Ānanda, I shall now further recite this mantra for you... (until) all shall acknowledge this profound kindness and constantly provide protection."
This section of the sutra further clarifies that the benefits of the mantra provide secret protection against worldly poisons and can bring about supramundane wisdom.
Whether practiced by oneself or taught to others, its merit is identical; however, water and fire cannot cause harm, for they cannot burn or drown those who recite it.
This is in accord with the meaning of the sixteenth of the "Fourteen Fearlessnesses" in the *Avalokiteśvara-parivarta* of the sixth sutra, where one does not lose their life.
Great poisons cause illness, while small poisons include the various malevolent incantations of devas, nāgas, and spirits, such as the *Svīkāra* Brahmā incantation and others.
By the power of this [protective] incantation, these evil spells do not take hold, and one thereby attains right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).
"Right concentration" is translated as *samādhi*. Because the body is sustained by *samādhi*, no curses or spells can cause harm.
Regarding "yàn" (disgust/aversion), it is pronounced in the third tone (*yàn*). As for "chóng" (insects): these are insect poisons;

such as are found in this manner throughout remote villages and small towns in the two provinces of Guangdong and Guangxi. Regarding mineral poisons, such as arsenic (*pí*) and aconite (*jìn*), when gold and silver first emerge from their ores, they possess toxicity, as described in detail in the *Yàolèi Běncǎo* (Pharmacopoeia by Category).
Vegetable poisons are precisely medicinal poisons, such as *bádòu* (castor oil plant) and *mùbié* (stink bug tree).

While insects and snakes may be known [to be harmful], when the poisonous vapors of all things enter the mouths of those who recite mantras, they are all transformed into the flavor of nectar (*amṛta*).

As for all malevolent stars—such as Rāhu, Ketu, comets, and *pūrvaphalgunī*—when these evil stars descend, pass through palaces, or enter their limits, they can bring about calamities and misfortunes.
As for ghosts, such as *rākṣasas*, *piśācas*, reanimated corpses, and drought-spirits...
Deities such as the Pāpīyas (the Drought Spirit) are like those in the world who possess the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) yet inflict harm through pestilence and the like;
they are like grit in one's food. This is a metaphorical explanation: the stubborn, obstructive, and vast evil intentions within the hearts of wicked people are like grit in food.
Piṇḍola-bharadvāja is explained in the preceding text. Each of these spirits has its own retinue, all of whom are sustained by the Buddha.
Even toward those who harbor malice toward us, we should still extend protection;
Ānanda, you should know that this mantra always [protects] against places of poverty, lowliness, and misery.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding passage which correctly elucidates how the majestic power of the deity provides protection so that worldly poisons cannot cause harm,
thereby accomplishing supramundane wisdom. The Sanskrit term *nayuta*— according to the "Chapter on Incalculable Numbers" (*Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*,
among its one hundred and twenty major numerical units— states that one hundred *lakṣas* constitute one *koṭi*, and one *koṭi* multiplied by one *koṭi* constitutes one *ayuta*.
Ten *ayuta* make one *nayuta*; in this system, this corresponds to a hundred thousand million billion trillion (*koṭi-niyuta-bhūta*).
Specifically, a *lakṣa* is a hundred million, a *koṭi* is a billion, an *ayuta* is ten billion, and a *nayuta* is a hundred billion.
Now, there are eighty-four thousand such *nayutas* of Ganges Rivers. Thus, by means of so many [Ganges Rivers]...
Furthermore, as many grains of sand as there are in all those many Ganges Rivers—
each grain of sand being a vajra, the term "vajra" signifying a great abundance, and "race" (*gotra*) signifying its kind—
so many Vajragarbha Kings of such races each have many retinues; all these various races are Bodhisattvas who are Vajragarbha Kings.
The Vajrasattvas who are governed by him attend him thus day and night, not daring to leave his side for even a moment.

Even for one who recites mantras with a distracted mind and without entering meditative absorption—where the benefit is but slight, as the mind merely recalls them while the mouth holds them indistinctly—the Vajra hosts still constantly attend such a person despite this distraction;
how much more so for one who maintains the practice with focused concentration?
It goes without saying that for one who has attained decisive faith in that Bodhi, the diligence of their retinue is likewise unsurpassed.
One who attains decisive faith in the Bodhicitta occupies the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).

As for those whose refined minds have secretly and swiftly awakened their spiritual consciousness—referring to the assembly of the *Gūḍharāja* Bodhisattvas—they abide in the profound mystery with a heart of sincere devotion.
Within, there is a latent impulse that accelerates one’s spiritual consciousness;
whether in the dreams of a practitioner or during meditative contemplation, there arises an awakening that causes their progress to be unhindered.

"This person" and "that person" refer to the practitioner—this clarifies that by virtue of the power of secret protection, the practitioner is able to develop their past lives and remember many [previous existences].
The *Kalpa-pūrvayoga* and *Jātaka* stories pervade horizontally throughout the ten directions, and the *Saṃsāra-kalpa* extends vertically through the three periods of time;
all are fully known. How could this pertain merely to the past? By manifesting the past as a reflection, it is precisely supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*).
From the very first kalpa, there was the ordinary body (*pṛthagjana-śarīra*); passing through subsequent bodies, the "final body" (*paścima-deha*) refers to the ultimate [state].

Subsequently, regarding those who dwell near the stage of the fruit of fulfillment (*phala-paripūri*) as those in their "one-life-to-enlightenment" (*ekajāti-pratibaddha*), it is said that among them are various classes of yakṣas and others, both those subject to rebirth and those not;
this refers to the various classes mentioned previously in the translated terminology.

The passage beginning with "This son of good family" clarifies that those who offer material gifts do not only avoid rebirth in evil realms, but furthermore will not be born into poverty or incapacity.
To delight in the absence of wealth is poverty; to lack understanding is destitution.
These sentient beings, even though they themselves [do not practice], shall naturally observe the precepts of the fast without maintaining them.
This section of the sutra highly extols the merit of upholding mantras, encompassing immeasurable virtues to clarify the meaning that a single mind possesses all practices.
The phrase "even though" (*zòng qí*) below is a high praise for the superior power of upholding mantras;

it means that even if sentient beings who uphold mantras do not perform meritorious deeds, the virtues of the Tathāgata are entirely bestowed upon these individuals—how could they ever be shifted away?
That merit is here [in this] samādhi and may likewise be bestowed.
This is because the mantra-mind is the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s Crown, and the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s Crown is the practitioner’s own inherently possessed store-consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).

Therefore, one who can uphold the mantra upholds their own store-consciousness; since the store-consciousness is replete with the myriad practices, what meritorious deeds would not be complete? This is so.
Therefore, without performing meritorious deeds, blessings are naturally complete; because they are self-contained, it is as if the Tathāgata has bestowed them.
Yet the Tathāgata is the Tathāgata of one’s own nature; the Tathāgata is one’s own mind, and one’s own mind is the Buddha.
Outside of mind there is no Buddha; the Buddha is entirely mind. Thus, if one can maintain the mantra within the mind, then for eternal kalpas [the Buddha] will be with one.
The Buddha and [the practitioner] are born together; this cannot be described as the final number within the great calculations of the *Avataṃsaka*.

It is said that one "inconceivable-inconceivable" kalpa constitutes one "unspeakable-unspeakable-unspeakable" kalpa, and when one reaches an "unspeakable-turn," the numerical limit is reached. Since he is born together with the Buddha, it is due to the Buddha’s merit.
Regarding the virtues that are my own basis, there are three meanings that share the same category, like a cluster of akṣa fruits. "Cluster of akṣa" is the name of a tree;
as explained in the commentary on the first fascicle, the self and the Tathāgata, together with all merits, are identical in their cultivation and are not dispersed.
Therefore, the conclusion below clarifies that what was originally complete is made precepted where it was not yet precepted, and made advanced where it was not yet advanced. No [omission].
Wisdom purifies that which is impure; when non-fasting becomes fasting, the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) are complete.

Although the sequence of the preceding text places merit as the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā), precepts as the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), progress as the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā), wisdom as the perfection of insight (prajñā-pāramitā), and purity as the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā), the ability to endure fasting and precepts constitutes the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
Thus, although the order is not sequential, the six meanings are fully present. This is what is called "upholding the mantra" (dhāraṇī).
With a single mind, all myriad practices are fully perfected.

Ānanda, when this good man upholds this mantra (until the point where it says) "all are completely extinguished and removed, without so much as a hair's breadth remaining," this section of the sutra clearly elucidates the power of the mantra to wash away all defilements; for the sun of wisdom can dissolve the frost and dew.
This is the fault of [past] karma. While the preceding text fully describes the cultivation of merit, the present text describes the purification of offenses.

This means that although one may have committed various transgressions prior to receiving the mantra, once the mantra is held, all previous offenses of breaking the precepts—regardless of their gravity—are extinguished at once.
Thus, one further perceives the supreme power of holding the mantra, which is like the sun easily dissolving frost and dew. Nevertheless, regarding the holding of the mantra...
In practicing this mind, one must also exhaustively cultivate sincerity, empty the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*), and penetrate the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*).

When the *prajñā* of the perfect mind eliminates all accumulated offenses, their substantial reality vanishes. If one merely practices superficially and habitually, as if the practice both exists and does not exist, it is like seeing many broken ships crossing the vast oceans;
though the winds may be favorable, there is still the peril of drowning. Do not claim that the scriptures lack efficacy.
Seeing that he has fallen, even though the subsequent section on "Holding the Mantra" explains that there may still be traces of impurity, the sages do not reprimand him;
this is an effort to encourage the profound practice of recitation. Regarding the five pungent vegetables, see the following text.

If the inner mind is pure, then although outer clothing may be tattered, one’s conduct and movements are entirely pure; it is precisely because the mind is pure that all things are identical with the Truth.

Because mindfulness itself is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), those who commit the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*)—first, killing one's father or mother; second, killing an Arhat; third, killing one's preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or teacher (*ācārya*);
fourth, causing a schism in the Saṃgha; and fifth, shedding the blood of a Buddha with malicious intent—are [to be understood thus].

Regarding the four abandonments (*catur-tyāga*) and eight abandonments (*aṣṭa-tyāga*), the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that *pārājika* is translated as "abandonment" (*tyāga*). If one commits sexual misconduct, killing, or stealing...
The four root offenses of falsehood result in being permanently cast outside the boundaries of the Buddha-dharma and not being permitted to dwell together with others;
like a person whose head has been severed, they cannot be restored to life. Because they do not enter the ranks of the Sangha, they are called "abandoned" (pārājika).

Regarding the eight abandoned offenses of a bhikṣuṇī, one adds a fifth to the aforementioned four: this is called "touching. "Touching" refers to physical contact with a male, initiating a mind of defilement.
Therefore, the sixth is named "the eight," because there are eight matters:

namely, grasping the hands of a man with a defiled mind, or grasping his clothing, or entering a secluded place together, or sitting together in a secluded place, or conversing together, or walking together, or leaning against one another, or making an appointment;
committing these eight matters leads to being abandoned by the community. Therefore, the seventh is named "concealment" (*paticchādana*); "concealment" means to obstruct.

"Concealment" (*paticchādanā*) refers to when a nun, upon hearing the formal procedure of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) by the Great Assembly of monks, conceals another's offense and refuses to confess it before the community;
thus, the eighth [category] is named "concealment. "Following along" (*anuvartanā*) means following along with the communal residence (*sahavāsa*);

that is, even though the nuns have not yet performed the ritual of communal residence (*sāṃvāsika-karman*) with the Great Assembly of monks, they nonetheless follow them in their communal residence. These eight types mentioned above constitute the fundamental rules for the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha.

Regarding the fundamental precepts, committing these offenses as previously described is termed "abandonment. However, through the high efficacy of reciting mantras, both light and heavy offenses are all extinguished.
This is like wind blowing sand: the fierce wind is a metaphor for the power of the mantra, while the heap of sand is a metaphor for the accumulation of light and heavy offenses.
It means that although the multitude of offenses gathered together is as vast as a mass of sand, they can be extinguished all at once by the power of reciting the mantra.
It is as easy as a fierce wind blowing apart a heap of sand until it is completely and utterly purified, leaving not even a hair’s breadth remaining.
Ānanda, if there were sentient beings who, from immeasurable and incalculable kalpas ago... [until] they all attained the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
This section of the sutra follows from the preceding [passage] on how the power of the mantra eliminates past karma and leads to the realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Above, it was stated that the merit of the mantra eliminates all present karma; the current text further states that it not only eliminates newly committed transgressions but can also wash away all old defilements.
If there are those who can uphold this mantra and perform various offerings, [the effects will extend] back through the accumulated kalpas of the past.
When defilements have not yet been repented, they are like snow melting under hot water; once the warmth has penetrated, they vanish in an instant.
The hot water is a metaphor for the power of the mantra, and the snow is a metaphor for past karma.

Furthermore, it does not merely dissolve karma, but through the power of the mantra, one can sustain the mind so as to soon attain the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). This explanation of the patience of non-arising is found in the first sutra.

Someone asked within [the text]: "The previous explanation stated that one must empty the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) and realize the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) before the efficacy of mantra-recitation can be attained;
yet this current passage says that merely wearing and placing [the mantra] can eliminate accumulated karma. How can you take what is easy to be as difficult? Answer:
Mantras possess inconceivable power, truly as the sutras state. However, this refers specifically to making offerings, wearing, and placing [the mantra].

Relying upon faith—as previously stated, one who possesses decisive faith can quickly achieve accord with the practice—yet if that faith is slight or superficial, it will not necessarily manifest its efficacy immediately.
Nowadays, where are incantations and mantras not found? Yet their power remains hidden and unmanifest.
I have once worn and carried a charm for driving away malaria, which responded immediately; this is sufficient proof that its manifestation arises from faith.

Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are women—[down to] those of the lowest status on the fringes of society, let alone those of mixed forms—this section explains that through the power of the vidyā-mantra, all their wishes are fulfilled.

In this passage, only men and women with long lives are mentioned, while others are omitted; however, they are fully encompassed within the phrase regarding "fruition and retribution" (vipāka). Fruition and retribution.
In terms of the mundane and supramundane, the tainted and the untainted, for the most part this present text corresponds to the *āveṇika-āyatana* (exclusive sphere) of Avalokiteśvara;
thus, its various forms are as previously explained, and the rest may be understood.
"Ānanda, if in all lands, prefectures, counties, villages, and hamlets... [until] all calamities and misfortunes shall be entirely extinguished."
This section explains how the power of the vidyā-mantra avoids all calamities. *Cetiya* is translated as "a place worthy of offerings.
*Deśa* is glossed as "tall water" in the *Shushu*, while the *Lectan Biaozhi* states that *deśa* means "city tower";
the rest is easily understood.
"Ānanda, wherever there are sentient beings in any land, they shall sleep peacefully day and night, always free from evil dreams.
This section explains that the function of the *vidyā-mantra* pacifies the heavens, enriches the earth, subdues malevolent stars, and brings peace to the populace.
Regarding "the winds and rains being timely," the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "Unseasonable winds and rains..."

That it does not rain when the season has passed is one of the nine calamities for sentient beings; now, to say that the seasons accord with their proper times is due to the power of the mantra harmonizing with the heavenly order.
That the five grains are abundant is due to the power of the mantra nourishing the benefits of the earth.
"Ten billion" refers to the myriad subjects; this speaks of the ten thousand people. That the myriad subjects are at peace and happy is due to the power of the mantra.
To bring peace to the myriad people, the twenty-eight great malevolent stars manifest strange portents according to their respective directions;
all calamities and auspicious signs arise from their transformations. This incantation can suppress them, ensuring that these disasters and obstructions do not enter the realm.
This is achieved through the power of the incantation to subdue the malevolent stars; consequently, people will suffer no untimely or accidental deaths.
The two lines following "桎梏" (handcuffs and fetters) refer to escaping royal peril; sleeping peacefully day and night means being at ease while lying down and at ease while awake.
That there are no evil deeds by day and no evil dreams by night is the efficacy of the mantra.
Ānanda, within this Sahā world-system, there are eighty thousand [types of phenomena]—up to all manner of evil omens and calamities—that can never enter.
This section explains that through the power of the *vidyā-mantra*, all malevolent stars are suppressed so that they cannot enter the realm.

When the "Sahā world-system" refers here to a single set of four continents (*cāturdvīpaka*), one observes from the perspective of these four continents that the celestial bodies dwelling in space are not limited [to those alone].
The eighty-four thousand [demons] mentioned now refer only to this number, excluding the case of the "Good Star" (Sunakṣatra);

alternatively, it may symbolize the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*) of human beings. The twenty-eight lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) serve as the leaders of these eighty-four thousand; the twenty-eight lunar mansions are:

Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Āśleṣā, Maghā, Pūrvaphalgunī, Uttaraphalgunī, Hastā, Citrā, Svātī, Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūlā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, Pūrvabhadrapadā, Uttarabhadrapadā, and Revatī.
These are the constellations of Bì, Kuí, Lóu, Wèi, Mào, Bì, Zuǐ, Shān, Jǐng, Guǐ, Liù, Xīng, Zhāng, Yì, and Zhěn.
Each of these stars is assigned to its respective quarter, with seven stars per quarter, each presiding over specific matters that manifest according to the goodness or evil of people's hearts:
if they are good, auspicious signs descend; if they are evil, calamities are inflicted. This is explained in detail in the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, fascicle forty.

Furthermore, regarding the eight great malevolent stars acting as primary influences, the *Changshui shu* (Long Water Commentary) states: "They are the planets of Metal, Wood, Water, Fire, Earth, Rāhu, Ketu, and the comet.

Although there may be auspicious constellations, if these [planets] undergo transformations, they immediately bring about calamity; the twenty-eight lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) are likewise affected.
This section below correctly reveals the power of the mantra: where this mantra exists, those malevolent stars remain hidden, undergo no transformations, and do not produce calamities.
Therefore, it spans twelve *yojanas*—a *yojana* being translated as a measure of distance or limit—one *yojana* being forty *li*, totaling four hundred and eighty *li*.
This constitutes the ground of the boundary (*sīmā*), such that all calamities and anomalies do not enter its domain;
this signifies auspiciousness and fortune. Furthermore, "auspicious signs" refers to favorable omens. When it is now said that "calamities and auspicious signs do not enter," it means:
Calamity and fortune do not enter [such a person]. If this is so, how then is fortune to be warded off? My view is that equanimity and compliance constitute true fortune;
as the common proverb says, "A blessing before the courtyard is better than having none at all"—this is precisely what is meant.
Therefore, the Tathāgata proclaims this mantra... [until] "old karmic debts come to harass and harm.
This section of the sūtra shows that the World-Honored One, concluding and revealing the reasons for proclaiming the mantra, establishes it as a profound protection to assist the Path.
From "Therefore" onwards, the Buddha proclaims this mantra because there are many demons in the末法 (mofa/declining dharma) age, in order to protect [beings] and cause all...
That adverse conditions cannot inflict harm upon you, but rather that you sit in serene composure and advance along this path—this is the reason for proclaiming the mantra.
The meaning of the text is clear and can be understood.
Furthermore, if among your assembly there were any who have not yet attained realization (those still in training), it would mean that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are speaking falsehoods.

This section of the sutra again cautions regarding the conditions for purity to clarify that the Buddha’s words are not empty and that practitioners will necessarily attain the verification of mental penetration.

"This goodness" and below, the Buddha states that if a practitioner is indeed able to practice cultivation according to the Dharma, they will immediately attain sudden, thorough penetration and awaken to the Buddha-enlightenment from this ordinary body;
the text here uses a reductio ad absurdum to manifest the Buddha's [truth].
"Since my words are not false, they shall certainly not deceive you.
Having spoken these words, immeasurable [beings] within the assembly attained the realization of Bodhi and were forever freed from demonic interference.
This section of the sutra records how various deities vowed to protect the practitioner, each presenting their oath to the Buddha as described in the preceding text.
This reveals the efficacy of the mantra; now follows the vow for protection and upholding. First is the Vajra [King];

second are the Lords of the Desire and Form Realms along with the Four Heavenly Kings, who emerge from the assembly to pay homage and make their vow; the Formless Realm deities were mistakenly listed last.
Third are the various miscellaneous deities who cause the bodhicitta to be swiftly perfected, as previously stated: "With a refined mind..."
The fifth [category] is the Yin that swiftly activates the intent of the divine consciousness; it is the Yin that presides over the seasonal timing of the sky-dwelling Yin and Yang.

Since Yin and Yang govern wind, rain, clouds, thunder, and so forth, each having its own presiding deity, the seasonal timing governs the years, seasons, spring and autumn, the Eight Kings' Days, the daytime and nighttime excursions, and so on.
The years consist of the sixty *jiǎ-zǐ* (trunk-branch) cycles, the Tai-sui (Year Lord), and the like.
The "Circuit Officials" (xúnguān) are those who roam day and night as divine spirits and record good and evil deeds;
thus they are called Circuit Officials. These all belong to the Four Heavenly Kings.

The six [categories] are the terrestrial deities (*dìqí*), such as those presiding over mountains, seas, and all lands, as well as the spirits of all things—the *jīngzhī*—such as deities presiding over trees, forests, crops, and medicinal herbs.
As for the Wind Deity King (Fēngshén Wáng), he is the aforementioned Wind Master (Fēngshī);

since there is a distinction between king and minister, and whereas previously he was a minister, he is now a king, he is mentioned twice. These various deities of the upper and lower realms each have their own dharma-protecting mantras, the meaning of which can all be understood and need not be further elaborated upon.
At that time, eighty-four thousand nayutas (up to) constantly cause this person’s actions to be fulfilled according to their wishes.
This section of the sutra follows the protective mantra-holders who, riding upon the mind of Great Enlightenment, recite the names and renew their vows to provide protection;
in the preceding text, the World-Honored One first raised the royal lineage of the treasure-guardians who constantly protect this [teaching].

Regarding the present text of the Dhāraṇī: because the assembly has aroused the resolve to protect the dhāraṇī, the names of the various deities have been listed again merely to complete the required number.

Generally speaking, while the various miscellaneous deities mentioned in the preceding text aroused their resolve only after the Buddha proclaimed the dhāraṇī due to its great merit, this Protector of the Dharma (Dharmapāla) has always possessed the intention to protect from the outset;
therefore, the previous Buddhas cited his name, whereas now it is the Protector himself who [speaks].
Chen Benyuan explains that according to the "Ten Stages" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the King of the Dharma Treasury occupies the rank of a Dharma King on the higher stages;

for this reason, he personally recounts his own long-established merit and realization of Bodhi. Because his resolve to deliver sentient beings is so urgent, he does not enter Nirvana, but manifests a Vajra body to constantly protect this mantra.
The passage from "World-Honored One" (*bhagavān*) onwards clarifies the urgency of his own resolve to protect [the teaching], following in succession.
While that practitioner may experience a hundred instances of distraction amidst concentration, this Bodhisattva’s guarded mind remains ever one-pointed.

Even if he should drive away external Māras— including Maheśvara, the deity at the summit of the Form Realm who rules over the world with a heart deeply addicted to and stubbornly attached to existence,
becoming a great conceited deity who is the most extreme of Māras— they cannot find an opportunity against him, let alone other minor spirits.

The deity shall naturally drive [the demons] ten *yojana* away; previously it was stated that twelve *yojana* constitute the ground of the boundary (*sīmā*), so how can this [present statement] be reconciled with that?
It is simply because the preceding and succeeding parts were not cross-referenced during the translation process.
The smashing of their heads with the precious vajra is an expression of a vow, not comparable to the worldly intent to kill. [This is] broken.

Because these two gates are subsumed and applied according to the capacities of beings, the remainder is easily understood. The section on Practice is hereby concluded; below begins the Section on Realization.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and waited for the Buddha’s compassionate voice, gazing up at him with fixed, reverent eyes.

In this section, Ānanda, because he wishes to know in advance the characteristics of the stages of realization—their sequence from beginning to end, their relative depth, and their names and meanings—due to his practice, requests proof.

Although Ānanda has already understood the details within the various formations (*saṃskāra*) as described in the preceding text, he still does not yet know the distinctions between the stages of realization, their sequence from beginning to end, the meaning of their names, or their relative depth;
thus, he must know these levels of realization in advance, just as one who has reached [a destination] must first know the way.
The King first visited the lodgings of the travelers to verify [the truth], which signifies the meaning of personal practice and direct contact;
because there are differences in the depth of realization and the degree of wisdom and severance, he requested that their characteristics first be shown.

We, led by Ānanda, followed this by inquiring about the meaning of verification, first reproaching ourselves for our mere learning and setting forth the root of our ailment as the starting point for our questions. [This concludes] the section beginning with "Receiving the Buddha's... [down to the end].
Celebrating the benefit of hearing the Dharma previously, the World-Honored One now proceeds to correctly inquire about the names and meanings of entry into realization.

Regarding "Buddha-samādhi," the word "Buddha" is added to distinguish it from worldly concentrations (*laukika-samādhi*) and to distinguish it from the concentrations of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Furthermore, because the essential substance of the fifty-five stages of concentration is cultivated and perfected as Buddhahood, it is called "Buddha-samādhi. Nirvāṇa is that which is reached.

Because it is the ultimate stage, prior to entering Nirvana, the path of awakening is layered and manifold; thus, it is called "not yet reaching dry wisdom" (*anāgamya-śuklavidarśana*). This refers to the very beginning of setting forth on the journey.

The names and meanings of the forty-four mental states are explained in the following section: these consist of the ten stages each of faith (*śraddhā*), abiding (*vihāra*), practice (*caryā*), and direction (*mukha*), as well as the four types of preparatory application (*prayoga*), namely:
Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*). The above constitutes [the preliminary stage].

The phrase "furthermore, he separately presents [the stages]" below serves as a general inquiry, while the subsequent reiteration of the "gradual sequence" refers specifically to the three gradual sequences.
The two lines beginning with "Where does one go... inquire about the beginning and end of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) within the state of sainthood;

for the three positions prior to the stages are called the "Three Worthies," the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*) are the "inner ordinary beings," and the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) is the "outer ordinary being. Thus, the following section concludes the assembly’s discourse.
Regarding the manner of questioning, the *Wēn-líng* commentary states: "Staring fixedly is called *dèng*; concentrating the mind is called *méng*.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda, [saying] (up to): "With palms joined and hearts emptied, he silently received the instruction."

In this section of the sutra, the Buddha accords with his request; first, he praises Ānanda for possessing the great mind that asks on behalf of sentient beings, then he exhorts him to listen and receive the teaching.
The words of praise can be understood from the passage beginning with "From... [the text continues].

Below this, the Buddha recounts the entirety of what was asked, beginning with the ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) of the inner and outer stages and concluding with the nirvāṇa of ordinary persons; thus, it should be understood that the intermediate stages are included therein.

Because one clarifies [the path] in advance before having yet realized it, it is called a "provisional indication" (*xuànshì*); this is because it is like describing the circumstances of lodging and travel before one has even set out on the journey.
Now, below, the instruction is given: "Listen attentively," and Ānanda responds: "I shall hollow out my heart. Regarding "hollowing out" (*kūxīn*): the pronunciation of *kū* is *gū*.
The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "to empty the intestines of an object. The *Yijing* says, "Hollow out wood to make a boat. Here, the term is taken in that sense.
The meaning is that by clearing away deluded thoughts and emptying the mind, one becomes capable of receiving the teachings; thus, "hollowing out the heart" refers to this.
Joining the palms signifies composing one's demeanor, while remaining silent signifies closing the mouth; with the three karmas fully sincere, one awaits compassionate instruction.

The Buddha said, "Ānanda, you should know that from 'the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous' up to 'and Great Nirvāṇa' are the two designations for the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

This section of the sutra, as the World-Honored One prepares to explain the stages of realization, first sets forth the non-arising of the wondrous nature to demonstrate the two designations for the transformation of the basis:
the cessation of delusion and the return to the True. Now, the wondrous nature is profoundly perfect and transcends all names and marks; how could there...
Are these the names and characteristics of the world’s sentient beings and the fifty-five stages?

It is because there exist the vessel-world and its sentient beings that these names and characteristics are established. If both the support of the world and the primary [beings] therein cannot be found, how can names and characteristics exist?
Thus, the ten realms and the ten suchnesses are all merely superfluous words. Therefore, one first indicates the true source.
This reveals that both names and marks are illusory. "Name" refers to designations, and "mark" refers to appearances;

all distinctions between the noble and the ordinary, as well as the environments and inhabitants of the world, are comprised within names and marks. Yet these names and marks arise because of delusion; what arises must perish, and this arising and perishing is itself delusion.
Only when one extinguishes this delusion of arising and perishing can it be called the True. To transform arising and perishing is to rely upon [the Unconditioned].

Nirvana is so called because within nirvana neither arising nor ceasing can be apprehended; thus, when deluded thoughts are overturned, one relies upon true awakening, and true awakening is itself bodhi.
This constitutes the two designations for the "twofold transformation of the basis" (āśraya-parāvṛtti) of the Buddha-fruit.

However, when observed through the perspective of the wondrous nature, there is fundamentally no arising or ceasing—how, then, could there be nirvana? Since there is originally no deluded thought, how could there be bodhi? Bodhi and nirvana...
"Even 'nirvana' is but a forced designation; if one clings to either extreme, one again forms names and appearances. One who penetrates this Way may understand it through silent communion.
Ānanda, if you now wish to cultivate the true samādhi... [until] this is the Tathāgata’s true samādhi."

In this section of the sutra, the Buddha shows that those who wish to cultivate right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) must first recognize the causes of perversion; when these causes of perversion do not arise, one attains right concentration.

Since *samādhi* is itself right concentration, it is further stated that the locus of the practice of the right mind is the very essence of the meditative states cultivated throughout the various stages.
*Nirvāṇa* is the name for the fruit-stage upon reaching home, while "sentient beings" refers to the primary retribution body (*vipākakāya*).

The world is the vessel-realm that serves as the basis; because both the primary and secondary phenomena (the *dharmas* of the supported and the support) exist due to all manner of inverted causes, it is called the "cause of inversion.
The Buddha causes one to recognize this cause of inversion; the non-arising of this cause of inversion is precisely right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).
Since "right" and "inverted" are mutually remedial dharmas, this constitutes the general heading, which will be explained in detail below.
Ānanda, what is meant by the "inversions of sentient beings" (up to) "establishing the world and its inhabitants"?

This section of the sutra provides a specific explanation of the causes of inversion. First, it clarifies the primary retribution (the *puruṣakāra-phala*) to demonstrate that the primary and secondary retributions share a single cause, yet through delusion, two inversions arise.
First, the primary retribution is questioned; next, from "Ānanda" onwards, the causes of inversion are formally explained. Indeed...

Because one cause gives rise to two inversions, its cause is thereby demonstrated. By the phrase "by nature" (*xing*) and the following two lines, the preceding true essence is traced back to show how it erroneously becomes the cause of inversion.
"The luminous mind of the nature" (*xìng míng xīn*) refers precisely to the wondrous nature’s perfect luminosity;
it is the inherently luminous mind of the *tathāgatagarbha*. The character "mind" (*xīn*) arises from the functional illumination upon the substance of the *garbha*-nature.
This is what is called "mind," which is the substance of function and the function of substance; therefore, it is termed the "mind enlightened by its own nature.
When this mind enlightened by nature is universally pervasive within a single thought-moment, through error, the true is transformed into the false and the correct becomes inverted.
Within this single phrase, the distinction between the true and the false is made; fundamentally, there is no subjective state that can illuminate or encompass.

That the mind remains unmoved is precisely because it mistakenly identifies with the perfect luminosity (*vimala-prabhāsvara*); thus, when a thought arises within the nature of perfect luminosity, it immediately becomes delusion.
As the preceding sutra states: "The self-mind grasps the self-mind; this is not illusion, yet it becomes illusory phenomena.
This is clearly understood. Therefore, it says: "Because the nature is luminous and perfect. The word "because" (*gu*) initiates the logical connection for the following phrase, "all delusions."
It says, "The nature is manifested due to conditions. This "nature" that is manifested differs from the word "nature" in the preceding phrase;

for this manifested nature is a deluded nature. Once it is understood that this nature is deluded, one then perceives the arising of existence, whereby ultimate existence is established out of absolute non-existence.
"Absolute non-existence" refers to the fact that not a single dharma can be found within the aforementioned wondrous nature. Therefore, it is investigated.

In the end, because one gives rise to the delusion of the nature [of reality] through the causal conditions of the fingers, and observes based on that delusion such that the primary and secondary worlds appear distinct, it is said that they "ultimately exist.
This nature thus produced is the substance of ignorance; the entire body, sense organs, and the physical world are established by means of it.
As the fourth fascicle of the Sutra says: "The nature of awakening is necessarily luminous, yet delusion acts as the 'awakening of luminosity. Once this has occurred...
To falsely establish that which gives rise to you is for your delusion to manifest as difference within non-difference; this is precisely the meaning [of the text].
The phrase "this exists" below承接 (links to) the preceding section on ultimate existence to clarify that [the establishment of subject and object] is false.

This means that the capacity to exist (*nengyou*) and that which exists (*suo-you*) are fundamentally not causes or effects. That which has the capacity to exist is ignorance (*avidyā*); that which is possessed is the root-body, the vessel-world, and so forth. However...
This ignorance is fundamentally without cause; to falsely posit a cause for it is itself the cause of perversion.

Since it is not a cause, the characteristics of that which dwells [the subject] and that in which it dwells [the object] are utterly devoid of any fundamental basis upon which to rely. "That which dwells" refers to sentient beings, while "that in which it dwells" refers to the world.
This concludes the section below by establishing the false establishment of the two causes: the dependent and the primary.
This means that based on this lack of intrinsic nature, one falsely establishes the two aspects of the environment and its inhabitants;

that which is non-abiding is itself false abiding, because there is no fundamental basis. Thus, from within this false abiding, one establishes the inversion of the two aspects of the environment and its inhabitants.
"Delusion of the fundamentally perfect luminosity gives rise to the false" (up to) "neither arising nor abiding, neither mind nor dharma.

This section of the sutra follows upon the previous discussion of how delusion of the truth gives rise to the false; it points to the fact that the false is itself devoid of characteristics by showing that it is neither arising nor abiding, neither mind nor dharma.
The phrase "delusion of the fundamental" and so forth refers back to the wondrous nature and true essence, stating that one has become deluded regarding the perfect luminosity of the wondrous nature.
"The essence arises from delusion, yet the nature of delusion has no substance" means that the nature established based on the aforementioned non-abiding is delusory and therefore lacks substance;
because it lacks substance, it is not the basis [of delusion].

These two phrases precisely dispel the root of delusion, meaning that the wondrous nature—the true essence—is fundamentally complete, luminous, without deficiency or obscuration, and beyond cultivation.
If realization is already complete and lacking nothing, why seek further? If one intends to abandon the false to return to the true, then that "true" is not truly true.
I consider that the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is wondrously profound, luminous, and perfect; what need is there to labor again over returning to false views?

That which has been returned to is already not the reality of the essence of Suchness. This implicit statement points to those of the Two Vehicles who practice in a partial manner; it is not [a general teaching].

"Truly seeking" again reiterates the above; "furthermore, revealing the non-characteristics" means that "arising and abiding" are two of the four characteristics—arising, abiding, change, and cessation—stated by way of abbreviation.

Likewise, "mind and dharmas" are two of the four foundations of mindfulness—body, sensation, mind, and dharmas—as practiced by those of the Two Vehicles, also stated by way of abbreviation as above. All of these are further instances of the delusory.
Characteristics are not the true nature of *tathatā*. The meaning of the four foundations of mindfulness is as explained in the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm).

Since the two vehicles are already excluded, it can be known that ordinary beings and those outside the teachings are likewise excluded; this refers to those of the three vehicles who practice in accordance with the truth.
The following text separately clarifies the "contrary practice" of sentient beings, thereby manifesting the characteristics of the delusions of sentient beings.
"Successively arising, the power of birth brings forth illumination" (up to) "for this reason there are inverted sentient beings.
This section of the sutra concludes the preceding discussion by clarifying that the inversions of sentient beings arise from delusion. Regarding the phrase "successively arising":
having already lost sight of true nature, they rely on delusion to produce further delusion, with these delusions successively giving rise to one another; from that delusion, karma is produced.
The power of these [afflictions] manifests all delusions; as delusion perfumes delusion, they accumulate and form karma. When the karmas of self and other are identical, there is resonance;
because of this resonance, self and other arise together. Through this mutual arising and mutual ceasing, birth and death are endless.
The final phrase concludes by naming this state "inversion" (*viparyāsa*).
Ānanda, what is meant by the "inversion of the world"? (Up to: "The transformation of sentient beings results in the twelve categories.
This section of the sutra separately explains the cause of inversion and subsequently clarifies the *pariṇāmanā-vipāka* (retributive environment).
It takes non-abiding as the cause that transforms into the retributive lands of the twelve categories. First, the inquiry into the name; below this, it again cites the preceding text.

The two phrases "all that exists" (*sarvam asti*) and "the cause of that which exists" (*tasya hetuḥ*) constitute the cause for the arising of the world. Regarding the three subsequent phrases, first the meaning of "realm" (*dhātu*) is explained:

because this [cause] has the capacity to produce all that exists, the deluded arising of fragmented segments occurs; once these fragmented segments are established, the boundaries of the realms naturally arise.
Because these boundaries exist, the four directions subsequently come into being. Therefore, the following four phrases explain [this] next as not being the [ultimate] cause.

The worldly meaning is that what is fundamentally not a true cause is falsely taken as a cause; this is because non-abiding (*apratiṣṭhā*) is taken as the cause, and non-abiding is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*).
As the preceding text states: "Based on this non-abiding, the world and sentient beings are established.
This ignorance has no substantial essence and is truly not a productive cause; it is only because it is established through delusion that it serves as a cause.

The cause is fundamentally non-abiding, yet it is falsely taken as a place of abiding; since it relies upon ignorance, it perfumes that which is taken as the abode and the abode itself from moment to moment.

This very abode consists of the two aspects of the support (āśraya) and the supported (āśrita). Because of this moment-to-moment perfuming, there is a ceaseless flux that does not abide, thereby forming the three periods of time.
These three times, in conjunction with the four directions, interpenetrate one another to form twelve divisions. These ten [divisions]...

The two [categories] are divided into twelve classes of beings. Regarding the "dependent retribution" (*niśraya-vipāka*) of the world, it is explained in terms of the mind because the mind shifts and flows from moment to moment;
it is also explained in terms of the objective realm because the boundaries of the realm constitute the object.

When the mind and the realm interact and transform, sentient beings likewise form twelve classes. These classes are explained in terms of sentient beings, while the twelve divisions are explained in terms of the world.
From this it can be seen that the twelve realms of birth are formed by the mind.
Therefore, the world arises from movement and produces sound; (this continues) until the exhaustion of the twelve transformations, which revert into a single cycle.

This section of the sutra concludes by demonstrating how the mutual interpenetration of mind and environment results in the twelvefold manifestation of the transformation of the primary and secondary realms (*śāsanāśraya-vinivṛtti*).
The word "movement" (*dong*) refers to the aforementioned mutual interpenetration of phenomena; since this interpenetration is movement, it is explained through two meanings.
First, regarding the initial movement of the internal mind: this is the transformation of the environment according to the mind. When there is movement, there is karma; as for karma...

There must necessarily be retribution for the twelve classes of beings, through which they revolve. In this passage, "sounds and so forth" refer to the objects (*viṣaya*), while "the six deluded false thoughts" refer to the mind.
Because words cannot be manifested all at once, they follow one another in succession; yet, in the mental faculty, they must be simultaneous.

This is what is meant by the "five-associating mental consciousness" (*pañca-sahaja-manovijñāna*) arising simultaneously. Although it is said that they are simultaneous, their differences exist within that very simultaneity.
It is not that there is no cause for these marks; they are silently understood within the mind and can be realized through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Second, regarding external objects:

first, movement arises due to the mutual interpenetration of spatial and temporal characteristics, and sounds and other phenomena arise accordingly. Thus, the six types of deluded conceptualization exist because of this;

this is how the mind undergoes transformation according to its objects. Because these six deluded thoughts constitute the nature of karma, karma must inevitably have retribution. As for retribution...
There must be a basis, namely the twelve divisions of the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) according to the nature of karma.

To speak in terms of the primary retribution (*pratyaya-phala*), it is called "cycling through rebirth" (*saṃsāra*); to speak in terms of the secondary environment (*adhiṣṭhāna-phala*), it is called "revolving.

This "revolving" refers to what the fourth scripture describes as "successive migration and flow, ending and beginning again. "Ending and beginning again" refers to the formation of the world-system (*loka-dhātu*).

Abiding in emptiness through the destruction of emptiness, it culminates in emptiness as the beginning of formation; thus it forms an endless cycle, which is precisely the meaning of "revolving and returning.

The final statement, that sound and the other [objects] exhaust the twelve transformations to become one revolving return, means that the six external objects of the world reach their limit in the twelve transformative faculties, leading to their dispersal, dissolution, and subsidence into emptiness.
This is the ultimate point; because it is the ultimate, there is a revolving return. Furthermore, within this passage there are two instances of "for this reason" (*shìgù*).
The first "for this reason" concludes that the delusion of sentient beings consists in the objective realm changing according to the mind.

The second "for this reason" concludes that the delusion of the world-system consists in the mind changing according to the objective realm. This is truly because the preceding two sections, which provide distinct explanations, have not yet reached a concluding summary.
Because the current text provides a dual summary of the two preceding inversions, the subsequent section elaborates upon the characteristics of the twelve modes of transformation.
It describes how one rides this wheel of revolving inversion, from [the realm] "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" down to [the realm] "neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
This section of the sutra follows upon the preceding by providing a detailed explanation of the names and characteristics of the twelve transformations (*vikāra*). First, the names are presented;

next, their characteristics are demonstrated. The phrase "riding upon this" (*cheng ci*) cites the aforementioned characteristics of the twelve revolving wheels (*cakra*), which serves as the basis for the formal presentation of the twelve names below.
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, and other treatises, it is said that [the process] proceeds from the shell (*kośa*).
Emerging [from an egg] is called birth from an egg (*aṇḍaja*); emerging from a womb is called birth from a placenta (*jarāyuja*);

emerging from moisture is called birth from moisture (*saṃsvedaja*); departing from the old to enter the new is called transformation-birth (*upapāduka*). That which has no physical substance but manifests through radiant color is called "having form" (*rūpin*);

that which is empty and lacks the marks of form is called "formless" (*arūpin*); that which forms a substance solely based on the conceptual mind is called "having perception" (*saṃjñin*); that which is dull and insentient is... [non-perception].

That which is known is called "non-conceptual" (asaṃjñika) because its own substance is not real, being established in dependence upon that [other]. Although it exists, it is as if non-existent; therefore it is called "non-existent.
If it were not a form-possessor (rūpin), its own substance would originally be non-existent, yet by relying on that incantation (mantra), it establishes its own substantial form;

therefore it is called "non-existent. If it were not a non-form-possessor (arūpin), one would originally have no conception; yet by means of that conception, one's own substance is established. Although it exists, it resembles non-existence; therefore—

It is said: "If it is not that they have the perception [of themselves], yet I have the perception that they are my children, and they lack the perception of having parents—although they lack such perceptions, because the perception that they are my children has already been established in me—it is therefore called 'not without perception' (na-asaṃjñin).

This refers to cases such as the *pulu* (wasp larvae) mentioned below, where different substances mutually transform one another. The two characters "established-perception" (*chengxiang*) appearing in the subsequent passages serve as proof that this category is definitively named thus.
Because of the characteristics [of these states], the two characters "addition" (jia) and "conception" (xiang) are appended.
Ānanda, due to the causes of the world's false and delusory saṃsāra... [down to] fish, birds, turtles, and snakes, their various species fill the realm.
This section of the sutra follows the previous exposition of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) and first clarifies birth from eggs (*aṇḍaja*).
Wēn-líng’s commentary states: "Eggs arise solely through thought (*saṃjñā*); this delusion is precisely thought itself. The essence of thought is buoyant and light, which is termed 'movement.

This inversion is called the 'conjunction of breaths' (*vāyu-saṃyoga*) in the egg. When the breaths form thought, the predominance of rising or sinking thoughts is termed 'flying' or 'sinking'—this is disordered thought."
Thus, they evoke the various classes of beings, such as fish and birds, whether flying or diving.

However, if one examines in detail how each of the twelve classes possesses eighty-four thousand distracted thoughts, it is because every sentient being individually possesses eighty-four thousand afflictions;
yet, as these afflictions transform according to their respective categories, those afflictions manifest predominantly within that specific class, as is the case with fish and birds.
When categories such as these are manifested through the partiality of either flying or sinking, all afflictions belong to the realms of flying and sinking;

thus it is said there are eighty-four thousand deluded thoughts of flying and sinking. In the following sections, each category is manifested according to its predominant thought, thereby forming the thought of its own specific class.
However, if one knows that within a single class the thoughts of all other classes are mutually contained, then there would be infinite deluded thoughts—how could they be limited to this alone?
Of the eighty-four thousand [dharmas], this passage speaks only by way of illustrating the partial [aspects]. Therefore, the subsequent text says:
"Each mutually possesses twelve inversions (*viparyāsa*). Since inversion is the fundamental cause of disordered thought (*vikalpa*), the term *kalala* has been translated previously.
Furthermore, "movement" and "inversion" refer to the conjunction of afflictions (*kleśa*), while "below" refers to karma (*karman*). Thus, "below" refers to...
All classes of suffering beings revolve through birth and death by means of the three wheels of afflictions, karma, and suffering; the following sections are all modeled after this.
