From "Due to the world of causes, there is the cycle of defiled transmigration" (up to) "humans, beasts, dragons, and seers—these classes fill [the world]."
This section of the sutra follows the previous exposition on the twelve links of dependent origination; it now clarifies birth from the womb (*jarāyu-ja*).
Birth from the womb arises because of the defilement of emotion (*kleśa*), which is precisely this "emotion. Emotion is born of craving and is termed "desire-inversion" (*kāma-viparyāsa*).

The union of emotions is termed "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), through which growth and completion occur. Because emotion possesses both partiality and correctness, there arise "transverse" and "vertical" confused thoughts; thus, one receives the retribution of being a human or an animal.
The categories of "horizontal" and "vertical" refer to the *arbuda* stage (as seen in the preceding glossary), which is the appearance of the gradual differentiation of the embryo and egg.

Sentient beings all possess these states of false delusion, defilement, attachment, and obstruction; however, they are born into specific types of existence according to whichever of these factors predominates.
While both the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages are present in both embryos and eggs, the sequential description is given because the former can give rise to the latter, whereas the latter cannot.

Because they possess the aforementioned [conditions], and because the realms of transmigration and so forth consist of twelve distinct divisions within a single vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), twelve differentiations are thus established;
for there are differences in the retributions experienced according to one's karma.

"Due to the world's attachment to saṃsāra... down to 'the wriggling and crawling insects, their species fill [the world]'—this section of the sūtra follows the previous indication of the twelve modes of birth;
here, these three clarify moisture-born beings (*saṃsvedaja*). 'Moisture' refers to what is produced through conjunction;
'attachment' is precisely this conjunction. Conjunction arises from the lingering of craving; as one moves toward and clings to sensory objects, it is called a 'destiny' (*gati*), which is inverted."

Inverting moisture through the influence of yang gives rise to what is called "harmonious union" (*saṃyoga*); because it is formed by warmth, its destination is not fixed, and it is named "inversion" (*viparyāsa*) due to its chaotic thoughts.

Thus, one experiences rebirth among the wriggling and crawling species that turn over and flip about. "Bhūta-śarīra" (蔽尸) is a transliterated term seen previously; it refers to the initial stage of moisture-born beings.
All twelve [types of birth] are rooted in lust and arise from emotional conceptions; as deluded passion increases, they become ever more false.

The principles of transformation become increasingly perverse, leading to the dissipation of all into emptiness and the hardening of all into wood and stone. Although the delusions at the periphery differ, the root of delusion is one and the same.

"Chun" (蠢) refers to the state of the mind; "ran" (蝡) refers to the state of the form. That is to say, a mind that is ignorant and dull is termed "chun," while a form that is weak and supple is termed "ran.
When one observes only its moving appearance and cannot distinguish its specific name, it is called "ran."
"From the world of causal transformation and saṃsāra... to those that shed their skins and fly, their species fill [the world].
This section of the sūtra follows the previous indication of the twelve modes of birth; these four clarify *upapāduka* (apparitional birth).

"Apparitional" (*upapāduka*) means to be free from responding to transformation; it is "leaving" (*li*). Leaving this and relying upon that is called a provisional inversion; by touching upon all categories, one [realizes] them.
Because the name "contact" changes as it transforms into "conjunction," and because it moves toward a new name and is subject to disordered ideation, the resulting retribution is likewise so.
Because it sheds its skin, it moves toward a new state; the shell left behind is called a "cast-off skin.

Just as when a water beetle transforms into a dragonfly, its movement shifts from crawling to flying, or when a sparrow becomes a clam, it sheds its flight for submergence—indeed, all transformations through differing characteristics are like this.
The term *kalala* (translated as "transformative metamorphosis") refers to the initial formation of a new physical substance; from this point downward, all stages are collectively termed *kalala*.
This is the limit of the general designation for these categories.

As for the fifth stage, *peśī* (translated as "the stage of form"), it is not included here because it is not a general term, but rather a specific name applied according to the manifestation of particular characteristics.
"From the causes of the world’s obstructions and the cycle of rebirth... down to the spirits of portents and omens, their kinds fill the space.
This section of the scripture follows the previous demonstration of the twelve modes of birth; these five [categories] clarify that they possess form.
In their true nature, they are fused and tranquil, fundamentally neither obstructive nor luminous. Due to delusion and stagnation, they become obstructive and enter the cycle of rebirth.
When the obstacles are turned back, the loss of fusion results in the false union of clarity with attachment; from this clinging to stillness, light is emitted to form a refined radiance (*jìngyào*).

To cease [this process] is the "Three Lights" (*sānguāng*); to err in it is the "Comets and Meteors. All spirits and numinous objects that possess refined brilliance are manifestations of this refined radiance.
Because their conceptualization has already formed into refined radiance, they possess only form. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "The eighty deities all arise because of lingering [attachment]."

The fundamental nature of obstructive perception is the manifestation of its own refined radiance; although this is extremely refined and spiritual, it has not yet transcended the deluded perceptions of riding upon the cycle of saṃsāra.
Due to the causes of the world’s dissolution and the cycle of rebirth, [beings] reach the state of empty dispersion and sinking into oblivion, filling the realms with their kind.
This section of the sutra follows the previous demonstration of the twelve links of dependent origination; these six clarify the formless realm.

To loathe existence and cling to emptiness, to extinguish the body and return to non-existence, is called "dissipation" (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*); to be deluded by outflows and lack learning is called "confusion" (*viparyāsa*).

To loathe existence and return to non-existence is to rely upon the dark and obscure emptiness; thus, through the conjunction with darkness, it becomes the "aggregate" (*skandha*), which is named for its hidden concealment.

"Chaos of thought" refers to those among the non-Buddhist practitioners of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Because they possess perception within the formless state yet do not lack the substance of karma, they are also called *kalala*.

Furthermore, they belong to the category of those whose delusions and karma are heavy and obscuring, whose physical forms have dissolved, whose bodies merge with the void and dullness, and whose consciousness clings to the aggregates in a hidden manner—beings who are empty, dispersed, and submerged.
"Due to the causes of the world’s phantom-like transmigration... (up to) "...spirits, ghosts, and essences fill every space.
This section of the sutra follows the previous demonstration of the twelve modes of birth; these seven clarify the existence of thought (*saṃjñā*).

"Phantom-like" (*wangxiang*) means losing the true reality and being erroneously attached to shadows and lights, having no place of reliance. The yin [aspect] arises from recollection and thought within this state of phantom-like unreality.
Latent and congealed, its form and appearance are indistinct; it is obscure as a ghost-spirit (*guijing*) yet not fully formed, dispersed as a numinous being (*ling*) yet not complete.

It possesses no actual color, existing only as conceptualized marks (*xiang*); appearing and disappearing at will, resembling clarity yet resembling obscurity, it is named the "Formless Phantom" (*wangxiang*).
From "Due to the causes of the world's delusion and dullness in saṃsāra" (up to) "earth, wood, metal, and stone, their kinds filling it all.
This section of the sūtra follows the previous indication of the twelve modes of birth; these eight clarify the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*).
Because they do not understand the principle of the Truths and stubbornly cling to extreme dullness, their ignorance and stupidity are such that their spirit and energy are transformed into earth.
When wood, metal, and stone no longer possess feeling or thought, they become withered and decayed. For instance, the Yellow Head turning into stone, the Wife-to-be-Waiting becoming a mountain,
the earthworm transforming into gold, the lamp-flame into a fungus, and the deluded monk metamorphosing into a wood-ear mushroom—
all these are cases where sentient spirits, being obscured and dull, transform into insentient matter.

"From 'due to the mutual dependence of the world' to 'using shrimp as eyes, their kind fills [the waters],' this section of the scripture follows the previous demonstration of the twelve modes of birth; these nine clarify that they do not possess form.
Species such as the *vampira* (water-jelly) take water-foam as their substance and use shrimp as their eyes; fundamentally, they lack form and depend upon other things."

The perfected form cannot function for itself; it awaits external objects to serve as its function. Thus, one loses the natural state of the True Suchness and becomes entangled in floating falsehoods.

Because these distinct natures combine through the conditions of defilement, they are called "causal dependence. All categories such as fish that share the same eye or birds that share the same wing are like this.
"Due to the mutual attraction of world-phenomena, one revolves in saṃsāra... (up to)... curses and incantations arise, and their kinds fill the space.
This section of the sutra follows the previous indication of the twelve modes of birth; these ten clarify that they are not formless.
Driven by perverse karma, their natures and dispositions become inverted, and they ride upon incantations to entrust their consciousness, departing from natural principles and relying on delusion.
When summoned by worldly sorcery, curses, spirits, or malevolent objects, they consequently come into being; yet this does not arise through the process of physiological birth.
Thus, while they are fundamentally formless, once they are moved to manifest a substance, they are not without form.
"From the world’s conjunction with delusion and saṃsāra... until 'different natures mutually constitute one another, their kinds filling all space.
This section of the sutra follows the previous demonstration of the twelve modes of birth; these eleven [points] clarify that they are not characterized by perception.

Second, the false appearances conjoin with the nature and sentiment, which are delusively obscured; different natures mutually constitute one another, and the principles of their arising revolve and intermingle as described therein.
The caterpillar is not the silkworm; though it lacks the perception of being a bee, it takes on the form of a bee.

This is because it originally lacked such a perception, yet through the perception of another, its own substance was formed. Therefore, it is said that "though lacking the perception of a form, one forms a perception."
"Due to the world’s causes of enmity and harm within saṃsāra... (up to) all are devoured by them, and their kind fill [the world].
This section of the sutra follows the previous indication of the twelve modes of birth; these twelve clarify that they are not without thought.

Because enmity and harm repay one another and killing and injury oppose one another, the processes of life become grotesque and perverse, and human ethics are abandoned and severed; thus, this retribution is felt.
The earth-owl species and its like take form due to clods of earth or poisonous fruits; it is not that they lack the perception of a bird, yet fundamentally they lack [the perception of] a parent.
Master Wenling’s commentary on these two names is muddled and not fully elucidated.

It is because I have the perception of a child that it is said "not without the mark of perception," whereas because those clods of earth and poisonous fruits fundamentally lack the perception of parents, it is said "without perception. These are the two meanings.

This is because they are combined into a single name. Gu-shan says: regarding the "earth-owl" (*tǔxiāo*) and the "broken mirror" (*pòjìng*), according to the *Shiji*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Xiaowu," it states that in the sacrifices to the Yellow Emperor, the earth-owl and the broken mirror were used.
Meng Kang said: "The earth-owl and the broken mirror are names of two birds;
the earth-owl eats its mother, and the broken mirror eats its father. The Yellow Emperor wished to exterminate their kind, and thus [he ordered] that in all sacrifices to various spirits..."
When used [in this context], it refers to the *pòjìng* (the "broken mirror" bird), which has the eyes of a *chú* (pronounced *chū*) and a tiger. The *chú* resembles a wildcat (*lí*);

it is an animal, not a bird. Although current texts state it is a bird and not an animal, judging by its eyes being like those of a tiger, the identification as the *zhūkūn* mentioned by people in Jiangdong is likely correct.
However, its habit of eating its father remains unknown. Furthermore, among the sections on birds in the *Běncao* (Pharmacopoeia), there is...
The term "yún-xùn" (云訓) is a transcription of its sound; it calls out its own name. Its two eyes resemble those of a cat, and when this bird makes a laughing sound, someone is destined to die;
it is the *zhǔkūn* (鸀鶤). I suspect it belongs to this same class. This is set forth here, awaiting those who recognize it to distinguish it further.
These are called the twelve types of sentient beings.

The names of their fetters (*saṃyojana*) may be known. Alternatively, one might ask: "In the preceding text, why did the World-Honored One explain in detail the twelve inversions (*viparyāsa*) when Ānanda was inquiring about the stages of the path to realization?
The answer is: It is precisely because inversions obstruct right and universal knowledge (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The path to awakening is not pure; now the Buddha wishes to clarify that before realizing the Way, one must first eliminate obstructive defilements. When obstructions are removed, inversion perishes;
by departing from inversion, one attains correctness. Thus we know that the removal of obstructions is the essential requirement for entering realization—is this not the intent of the Buddha?

The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause, Cultivation, and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas.
Direct Explanation, Volume Eight.
Clarified by the junior monk Guangmo of Yunqi Temple in Ancient Hangzhou.
Direct Explanation transcribed by the lay follower Luer. Proofread by Li Taichong.
"Ānanda, within each and every class of these sentient beings (up to) they are fully possessed of such false and delusive discursive thoughts.
This section of the sutra reiterates the preceding classes of beings to clarify the meaning of their mutual possession [of delusions], thereby introducing the subsequent passage.
The phrase "In this way" (*rúshì*) cites the aforementioned classes of beings to explain the intent of their mutual possession; however, based on this mutual possession of inverted states—
If one understands that each category possesses eighty-four thousand types of distracted thoughts (*vikalpa*), one should also realize that they are mutually inclusive;
this clarifies that the power of karma is inconceivable. This is because distracted thoughts arise from inversion (*viparyāsa*). To examine this in detail:
the wondrous, perfect true mind is inconceivable and is fully endowed with ocean-like inherent virtues (*guṇa*); it is by overturning these inherent virtues that distracted thoughts are formed.
Since such thoughts involve calculation and deliberation, they are likened to the metaphor of pressing one's eyes so that disordered flowers appear;
"pressing the eyes" represents inversion, while the "disordered flowers" represent disordered thoughts, which should be understood accordingly.
You are now cultivating and realizing the Buddha’s samādhi—[from here until] washing clean the vessel before filling it with nectar.
In this section of the sutra, the Buddha reveals the method for removing perversions in order to purify the vessel; once the vessel is purified, the wondrous Way can be expected and realized.
Since Ānanda originally asked the Buddha about *samādhi*, the Buddha takes up that which was asked and answers it.
This is fundamentally because of "confused thoughts"; he points to what each of the twelve classes of beings mentioned above possesses, wishing to eliminate these thoughts.
The establishment of the "three gradual dharmas" and the designation of them as "gradual" refers precisely to the fact that these three dharmas possess a sequential progression.

To clarify the meaning of these three gradual stages, the metaphor of a clean vessel is set forth below. The "clean vessel" symbolizes the causal mind of the practitioner; the two characters "removing" (*qu*) and "excluding" (*chu*) specifically illustrate the initial function of the first gradual stage.
The metaphors of "poison," "honey," and "hot water, ash, and incense" represent the twelve inversions (*dvādaśa-viparyāsa*). One should examine these in detail.
The analogy of hot water and ash is that of coarse cleansing, while incense represents fine cleansing;
hot water is a metaphor for the forty minds prior to the stages of the grounds, ash for the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*), and incense for the contemplative wisdom of the eleven grounds.

Nectar is that which descends from heaven; by consuming it, one attains longevity, which is a metaphor for the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) realized through realization—by realizing it, one attains non-arising and non-ceasing.

Furthermore, another interpretation is as follows: the metaphor of hot water and cold water illustrates the various stages of correct concentration (*samyak-samādhi*); the metaphor of ashes and incense illustrates the dharmas of merit possessed at those various stages;

and the metaphor of dharma-fragrance and nectar illustrates the Dharma-body. The two characters "subsequently stored" (*hou zhu*) should be connected to the preceding phrase "first purify the mind" (*xian jing yi*), meaning that one first purifies the causal mind and subsequently realizes the meritorious qualities of the fruit.
This metaphor applies universally to all stages. If it is argued that this refers specifically to ascending to the First Abode (*prathamā-bhūmi*)...
When one portion of ignorance is destroyed and one portion of the Dharmakāya is realized, there is the sense of gradual purification and gradual realization;
this is "graduality within non-graduality. Since the present text speaks according to the general path, it says that "later one stores the nectar of immortality."
"What are the three gradual stages? (up to) "Third, advancing and opposing one's current karma.
This section of the sūtra enumerates the names of the three gradual stages. This merely lists the names and numbers; the detailed explanation is found in the following text.
One interpretation states that regarding "cultivation," the Buddha instructs the practitioner to guard and cultivate the physical vessel and to permeate it with pure dharmas.
This is the primary gateway for entering into realization. Regarding the elimination of auxiliary causes: the five pungent vegetables serve as auxiliary causes for the fundamental nature;
therefore, they should be eliminated. Second, regarding "true cultivation": if one excises [the roots of] killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying, the cycle of birth and death will cease;
hence it is called true cultivation. Furthermore, while such practices constitute auxiliary cultivation, true cultivation is the primary practice; thus, one must excise the primary [afflictions].
"Nature" refers to the true nature (*dharmatā*), which means that killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct constitute the true nature of sentient beings;

thus, the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Ārya-bodhisattva-garbha-samādhi-sūtra*) states: "All sentient beings take sexual desire as their true life-nature (*jīvitendriya*)," which is precisely this meaning.
Third, regarding "progression": the former two [precepts] are one auxiliary and one primary; within the primary, one merely restrains the three matters of bodily action.

The meaning was not yet profound; now it is further advanced. Its practice is such that the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) no longer flow out toward external objects, but instead reverse their flow to become entirely unified, so that the six functions cease.
Because this is more profound than the previous stage, it is called "further advancement" (*viśeṣa*).

"Contrary to the karma of present activity" means to turn back and oppose the karma of the six sense-faculties as they currently function. In the subsequent explanation of the meaning, all three [stages] are concluded by being designated as "further advancement."
This is because these three meanings progress sequentially.
What is the auxiliary cause? Ānanda, such a world [is the first stage of] the gradual sequence of progressive cultivation.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding detailed explanation of the meanings of the three gradual stages; here, it first explains the auxiliary causes.

As for the phrase "the auxiliary causes have been explained as above," this refers to what was previously understood. The subsequent passage, beginning with "furthermore," sets forth the reasons for consuming pungent foods:

it states that the twelve classes of sentient beings each possess physical form and life, and since they cannot survive without food, they are unable to sustain themselves on their own. Regarding those who dwell in reliance upon the four kinds of nutriment (*āhāra*), "nutriment" (食) refers to—
The meaning is "to provide benefit. Because the retributive bodies of the twelve classes of beings differ, their food is likewise diverse;
thus, there are four kinds of nutriment (*āhāra*). These twelve classes encompass all sentient beings within the three realms.

Therefore, humans and animals who possess appropriated bodies (*upātta-kāya*) are sustained by edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), while ghosts and spirits, lacking appropriated bodies, are sustained by contact-nutriment (*sparśa-āhāra*). As for the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*)...

The four formless absorptions (ārūpya-dhyāna) benefit from the food of volition; as they lack a physical body and maintain only the eighth consciousness, they take that consciousness as their nutriment, and thus are sustained by the nutriment of consciousness.
Because the two realms above [the desire realm] lack the two objects of fragrance and taste, there is no solid food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra).

Since the remaining three nutriments are present throughout all three realms, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun), fascicle 4, citing a sūtra, states that there are four kinds of nutriment: first, [solid food].

This [first] kind of nutriment has transformation as its characteristic; that is to say, the three—odor, flavor, and tangibles—bound to the desire realm, when they undergo transformation, can perform the function of nutriment.
"Lump" (kavaḍīkāra) refers to nutriment in the form of lumps; because it consists of divisible portions, it exists only in the desire realm.

Second is the nutriment of contact, which has the contact with objects as its characteristic; that is to say, when tainted contact (*sāsrava-sparśa*) first apprehends an object, it is able to grasp and sustain joy and other [mental states].
First, the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*): it is defined as the arising of joy and pleasure through contact with various objects such as softness, smoothness, cold, warmth, and fragrances;
it is called "nutriment" in the sense that this joy and pleasure benefit the body. Third, the nutriment of volition (*manahsaṃcetanāhāra*): its characteristic is aspiration.
It refers to contaminated volition that operates in conjunction with desire, which is able to function as nutriment by longing for desirable objects. *Manahsaṃcetanā* means volition.
This "volition" (saṃkalpa) refers to maintaining and not forgetting through a mind of aspiration;

it is like the story of the suspended sand and the longing for plums, which can satisfy hunger and thirst because both involve the mental act of thinking about food. Furthermore, in the Form Realm (rūpadhātu), meditative reflection serves as sustenance.

However, what is termed "outflow-tainted volition" (sāsrava-saṃkalpa) encompasses both the wholesome and unwholesome paths, just as among the twelve categories of beings, there are those with form and those without form.

The perceptions of "perception" and "non-perception" are reported to be unwholesome; however, because their conceptualization of food is the same as that of the gods of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), they are included there.

Fourth is the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*), which has the characteristic of maintaining [the body]. This refers to contaminated consciousness (*sāsrava-vijñāna*) that increases by the power of edible food, contact, and volition, thereby acting as a nutriment.
By means of the power of the preceding three nutriments, it increases and maintains the sense of growth, providing nourishment and benefit.

The body and mind constitute the food of consciousness (*vijñāna-āhāra*). Although this consciousness permeates all [eight] consciousnesses, because the eighth consciousness is preeminent in its function of grasping and maintaining [the body], the meaning of "food" applies most significantly to it.
Therefore, the Buddha taught that [beings] "dwell by means of food. As for "dwelling," it means that the physical life is sustained through food;
hence, it is called dwelling. Ānanda, the following section clarifies that consuming pungent roots is not appropriate for a practitioner.

The first two lines clarify that food has both benefits and harms; these two aspects of benefit and harm can be understood as referring to the five pungent plants (*pañca-garaka*), which are categorized as poisons.
Although they do not cause death, they can incite lust and anger—how could they be anything other than poison?

Therefore, those who seek right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) must sever their consumption of these. Regarding the five pungent plants, according to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* (*Fanwang jing*), they are: first, garlic (*laśuna*); second, [scallion]... [text fragment ends].
1. Garlic (laśuna), 2. Onion (gṛñjana), 3. Leek (palāṇḍu), 4. *Cicong* (慈葱), 5. *Lancong* (蘭葱), 6. *Xingqu* (興渠). The *Tiantai Fanwang Jing Shu* (Commentary on the Brahma Net Sutra) states:
"Garlic is the 'Hu-cong' (foreign onion); *gecong* (茖葱) is the leek (*xiè*); *cicong* (慈葱) is the common onion; *lancong* (蘭葱) is the small garlic (*sùjiǎn*); and *xingqu* (興渠) is the *sìjí* (蒠蒺).
Master Yunqi’s *Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden) comments on *xingqu*: "Regarding *xingqu* being called *sìjí*: *sì* is the *wúqīng* (mustard turnip)."

Some call it *húsuī* (coriander), others call it *āwěi* (asafoetida). The *Míngyì jí* states that it is called *xīngqú*; because it does not exist in this land [of China], it is left untranslated. It originates from the kingdom of Khotan;
its leaves resemble those of the turnip, and its root is like a radish. It is foul-smelling both raw and cooked.

These five [types of pungent plants] are collectively termed "vegetables. When eaten cooked, their vapors are turbid and thus arouse lust; when eaten raw, their acrid stench is even more violent and thus increases [passion].
Regarding anger, this section below clearly explains why practitioners should not consume pungent foods, and why the twelve divisions of the scriptures were taught for this purpose.
Wisdom belongs to the cultivation of insight (*prajñā*), while the three samādhis belong to the cultivation of concentration (*samādhi*).

Although one may possess both concentration and wisdom to maintain the mind, if one does not abstain from pungent foods, the various noble sages will not come to provide protection; thus, the powerful Māra gains an opportunity. This is the meaning of the passage.
All these can be understood as concluding the first gradual stage, named "The Name.
What is right nature? Ānanda, for such sentient beings... [this constitutes] the second gradual stage of progressive cultivation.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding detailed explanation of the three gradual stages; it now explains the "right nature" (*samyaktva*). The right nature is as previously described.
Below, the text provides a detailed clarification of the reasons for cultivating this right nature. It is evident that one should abstain from sexual misconduct;
furthermore, one should not consume alcohol or meat. This is because alcohol can disturb the nature and incite desire, while meat can harm compassion and give rise to a murderous mind.
Therefore, one purifies with fire so as not to consume the raw; this prevents the foulness of pungent odors and curbs the increase of anger.

Thus, the lower [practice] is cultivated to admonish that one must first excise the perverse nature before there can be the capacity for world-transcendence. One should contemplate the following three phrases which demonstrate the methods of remediation:
desire is like a venomous snake whose bite destroys the Dharma-body and forfeits the life-force of wisdom; desire is like a hostile thief who plunders the Dharma.
Because wealth robs one of merit, there are the four *pārājika* and eight *naiḥsargika-pāyantika* rules; as explained previously, the Śrāvaka precepts are shallow because they address only the body.

The Bodhisattva practice is profound because it disciplines both body and mind. Thus, the precept against sexual misconduct achieves the meaning of non-arising, and the precept against killing achieves the meaning of non-arising killing.
Furthermore, by not engaging in theft or robbery, one incurs no debt to the world and transcends the three realms.

This is certainly so; because those of inferior purity cultivate their original nature and force their minds to attain a semblance of understanding through the purification of the six sense-faculties, it is said that they "use the physical eyes of their parents to see the worlds of the ten directions.

According to the *Fahua Wenju*, the Brahma King possesses the retributive celestial eye (*divyacakṣus*) within his own realm, seeing throughout the great trichiliocosm; yet beyond the great trichiliocosm, there exists...

The wind-circle obstructs the eyes so that one cannot see the outside; furthermore, the *Fa-hua lun* states that the eyes can see both the interior and exterior of the great trichiliocosm, which should therefore be the "heavenly eye" (*divyacakṣus*).
To this, Master Zhi (Zhiyi) argued: "This refers to the stage of semblance (*sādharmya-avasthā*) in the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*).
Due to the power of the sutra, there is a superior function of the faculties; however, since true reality has not yet been manifested, it cannot be called 'heavenly.'"
The eye is still called the "fleshly eye" because it is a body subject to segmentation; thus, it is said to be "born of one's parents.

Although it is termed the fleshly eye, it possesses the function of the five eyes to see the interior and exterior of the great trichiliocosm. Now, this sutra takes the fleshly eye born of one's parents as equivalent to what has been explained there.
Generally speaking, by excavating the mind of true nature and forcefully attaining this realization, one verifies the power of the sutra.

The excellence of these merits—even reaching such points as attaining great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and roaming through the worlds of the ten directions—all pertain to the principle of the stage of the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*).
However, since the three gradual stages have not yet entered that stage, how can they already possess these functions?
This is explained in the following text; thus, this concludes the second gradual stage.
"What is present karma? Ānanda, such purity [extends] through the third stage of progressive cultivation.
This section of the sūtra follows the preceding section by specifically explaining the names and meanings of the three stages of gradual progression; it now further explains 'present karma.
Present karma refers to the actions performed as the six sense faculties flow outward and engage with the six sense objects; these are called present karma."
Ānanda, I now issue this admonition regarding the violation of these present karmas:

such a person who maintains the precepts—as described above regarding the one who has "excised their true nature"—is able to maintain the precepts with a mind free from lust. This term "freedom from lust" does not limit the definition of lust solely to sexual intercourse between men and women;
rather, the eyes grasping at forms, the ears grasping at sounds, and even the mind grasping at mental objects (*dharmadhātu*) are all termed "lust."

Because of lust, it is said that one does not allow [the mind] to flow excessively toward the six external objects; by not flowing outwardly, the revolving flow of desire returns to the original awakening, which is "meeting in union.
This means that when the six objects are not perceived by the six faculties, there is no union.
Once the six are fully unified, external functioning ceases. The lands of the ten directions are precisely the realms of the six objects; if the faculties and objects meet in union...
When [the waters] were combined, they were chaotic and turbid; now that they have become entirely one, they return to their original clarity and wondrous stillness without ceasing.
External objects are naturally purified; therefore, although the mind does not flow out toward external lands, those lands remain exactly as they were, acting as no obstruction.
Thus it is said: "The lands of the ten directions are brilliantly pure. This is further illustrated by analogy.
This means that it is like a bright moon suspended within lapis lazuli: the lapis lazuli is a metaphor for the wholly unified mind, and the bright moon is a metaphor for external objects.
Because one does not cling to external objects, they are precisely suchness (*tathatā*); hence it is said below that "the pure and wondrous [qualities] of the Tathāgata all appear therein.
"Therein" refers to the wholly unified mind. Thus, by means of such a causal mind, one will necessarily attain the non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Regarding "Dharma-patience" (dharmakṣānti) and "the patience of the non-arising of dharmas" (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti): the latter refers to the realization of the fruit.

In the previous section on the second gradual stage, it was indicated that this [patience] extends through the stage of semblance across the six sense faculties. Now, the patience of the non-arising of dharmas belongs specifically to the first abode (prathamabhūmi) and above.

The two subsequent lines correctly judge the three gradual stages as the foundational basis for the noble stages; thus it says, "From this, one initiates practice and establishes oneself in the noble."
This section concludes the third gradual stage, titled "Ānanda’s Initial Inquiry.

From the point where Ānanda first asks about the sequence for attaining the eye of cultivation, the Buddha establishes three gradual stages in response. Furthermore, it is difficult to determine the relative hierarchy, depth, and subtlety of these three gradual stages both textually and in meaning.
Why is this? For instance, regarding the first gradual stage, which eliminates auxiliary causes: [The text continues with the specific details of the gradual stages.]
It should be understood that in the second gradual stage, "excising the fundamental nature" (*zhengxing*) refers to excising the minds of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct;
the textual passage extending to "theft and robbery no longer practiced" and so forth constitutes the primary meaning of excising the fundamental nature.

Furthermore, the expressions "becoming a pure person" up to "attaining great supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*) pertain to the efficacy of excising the fundamental nature, which is remarkably analogous to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).

The textual phrasing regarding the "similar stage" (*sabhāga-bhūmi*) does not constitute the fundamental meaning of the three gradual [stages]; rather, it is a pre-emptive indication of the merit of the subsequent stages.

Within this third gradual stage, the phrase "those who violate present karma are persons who uphold the precepts," extending even to "not being dissipated by the six external sense objects," restates the preceding meaning.
From the point "since one no longer relies on sense objects" up to "the Tathāgata’s pure and wondrous [nature]," [the text proceeds].

That all [stages] appear therein belongs to the efficacy of the karma of manifesting what was previously transgressed. The attainment of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is a provisional indication of what will be realized later.
However, if one discusses these three gradual stages according to their natural sequence of shallow and deep, then the various noble stages (*ārya-bhūmi*) will not be confused;
thus, those ancient masters who interpreted them as being the primary meaning of the three gradual stages themselves were incorrect.
To suppress it too low or to raise it too high results in an unstable state of meditative equipoise; may those who have attained [this stage] reflect deeply and examine this in detail.
Ānanda, this son of good family’s craving for sensual desire has dried up... [yet he has] not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s stream of Dharma.

This section of the sutra follows the preceding discussion on the arousal of the practice and the stabilization of the position; here, for the first time, it clarifies the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*).
The phrase "good son" (*kulaputra*) refers to the person mentioned above who has cultivated the three gradual stages;

subsequently, throughout the stages of faith, abiding, practice, direction, and ground, the text repeatedly addresses him as a "good son. This is because, fundamentally, he is this very same individual.

When people advance through the stages of cultivation, the ancient masters assigned these to the categories of "outer ordinary beings" and "inner ordinary beings. I fear this may obscure the eyes of those who study;
therefore, I shall not employ such designations here. Nevertheless, the discourse on inner and outer ordinary beings and sages exists inherently within the principle;
it is merely a designation for the shallow and deep levels and the sequential order of the practitioner’s stages. It is like a person in the world at the beginning...

Having passed the provincial examination, one subsequently proceeds from the jinshi degree through the posts of district magistrate and prefectural governor, eventually reaching the highest offices of state and attaining the rank of a high minister.
In total, those who first pass the provincial examination find that their subsequent status becomes vastly different from those who did not; the disparity in their future ranks is immense.
Now, the progression through the stages of the Holy Path is likewise so. The following four lines concerning "desire" (yù-ài) follow from this.

The superior meaning is explained as follows: because the functions of the preceding six [sense faculties] do not operate and there is a reversal into the total unity, all cravings and desires dry up.
This is because when the sense organs and their objects previously joined, the internal grasping mind was solidly obstructed;
now, since the organs and objects no longer join and further rebirths are not continued, the internal grasping is liberated and becomes empty and luminous—thus, the former entanglements are resolved.
Now one has attained liberation from the darkness and obstructions of the past; now one has attained emptiness and luminosity. The nature of this emptiness and luminosity is itself wisdom (*prajñā*).
Since the grasping mind is already empty, there is nothing further with which it can be mixed; therefore, it is said to be "purely wisdom.

Furthermore, this nature of wisdom is fundamentally luminous and perfectly illuminating, reflecting throughout the ten directions. *Ying* means golden color; when it reflects outwardly, it is called *ying*. This refers to the present wisdom.
The light shining outward is likewise so. Because desire and craving have been dried up, this wisdom is named "the Stage of Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*);
these concluding words clarify the name of the initial stage. The final two phrases reveal the meaning of this stage as being still shallow:

it means that while the habits of desire have begun to dry up, one has not yet connected with the flow of the Tathāgata’s Middle Way Dharma-water; therefore, this stage does not yet belong to the true position (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
According to the commentary by the Master of Wuxing, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* clarifies the ten stages (*bhūmi*), initially establishing the stage of "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-jñāna*).

Tiantai, in his classification of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), establishes the five grades of dwelling prior to the stage of faith (*xin*), stating that by inference of meaning, these correspond to the stage of dry wisdom in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Alas! Although this scripture had not yet arrived during the Sui dynasty when Zhiyi lived, the names he established coincided with the Buddha’s own intent as if by divine inspiration. Is this not so?

"Who among the sages could be such [a person]? I, the humble one, examine the textual characteristics of the Five Grades (*pañca-vidha*) in the *Tiantai* tradition and find them differ in intent from those of the present sutra;

their explanations must each be presented separately, though their underlying meaning may well be the same. Under the section "Drying up Desire," it clarifies the very beginning of setting forth on this stage:

because one has merely dried up the craving of desire and has just attained the first flame, it is called "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-vijñāna*). This is when compared to the wisdom produced in subsequent stages.
The wisdom of today still belongs to the realm of habitual tendencies; therefore, it has not yet come into contact with the water of the Middle Way.

As for the Tathāgata, he is a person of fruition. When the term "flowing water" (*dharmasrotas*) is used to refer specifically to the Middle Way, the two characters "flowing water" are employed as a metaphor.
This is because the source of the secret treasury of the three virtues within the Middle Way is remote and its current is long, surging forth inexhaustibly; thus, it is likened to flowing water.
Longshui says: "Now, those who have not yet attained contact [with the Dharma-stream] are still at the stage of the ten faiths, which is termed 'resemblance' (*xiangsi*).

This term 'resemblance' is spoken in contrast to 'true division' (*fenzhen*); it is because their practice has not yet trodden upon the truth, but merely borders upon it, that it is called 'resemblance.

Only upon ascending to the stage of true division does one truly encounter the Dharma-stream. Since resemblance cannot yet be said to involve contact, how much less so for the current stage of dry wisdom (*ganhui*)? Longshui.
The Commentary states: "To say that one attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) at the third stage of gradual progression in this present sutra is an error.
If one were to attain this patience at those three stages of gradual progression, why would it not yet have been conferred at this current stage?

It is clear that the patience of the non-arising of dharmas is precisely the Middle Way and the flow of the Dharma; thus, we know that Changshui’s [Zongjing’s] recklessness was the height of thoughtlessness."

"Immediately, with this mind, one flows into the center of the center (until) reaching the destination according to one's vow; this is called the dwelling of the mind of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-citta-vihāra*).

This section of the sūtra follows the previous [section on] 'setting forth and abiding in the position,' and now clarifies the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). 'Faith' refers to the principle within faith;
therefore, it is said that being purely true in the middle way is called the dwelling of the mind of faith (*śraddhā-citta-vihāra*), because it is the principle within faith."
Because the nine stages following "Exquisite Faith"—namely, "Diligence," "Wisdom," and so forth—are all sublime virtues of faith, "Faith" is placed at their head;
thus, they are collectively termed the "Stage of Faith.
This clarifies that the first stage of faith consists of the mind of Dry Wisdom flowing into the Middle Way, for this flowing mind rides upon the principle of the Middle.
One is able to develop the perfectly wondrous function of this mind; "fū" (敷) has the meaning of "to manifest.
Since this perfectly wondrous function is vividly present between one's heart and eyes, without even a trace of doubt or obstruction, it is called "perfectly wondrous.

From this point on, within the faith that is neither biased nor obstructed—wondrous and perfect—one further develops true wondrousness. Relying on faith to give rise to wondrousness, one progresses without end.
Because it is unimpeded and neither arising nor ceasing, it is called "wondrous"; because it is eternally abiding, all deluded thoughts of arising and ceasing are extinguished without remainder.
One who can believe this is a practitioner; that which is believed by the mind is the Middle Way.
Since the admixture of delusion has been exhausted, it is called "pure and true. Because the principle is fully realized through that which follows it, faith is established.
This is called the "Abiding in Faith. "Abiding" refers to the stage (*avasthā*). True faith is explained below as being twofold.
True faith clarifies a single point by reiterating the meaning of the initial "faith": because it arises again from the truly wondrous and perfect, it is called "true faith.
Furthermore, because it was previously stated that "wondrous faith is eternally abiding," and thus is clearly manifest and not obscured, it is called "clearly manifest" (*vibuddha*).

Because true faith penetrates through all things, it is said that "all is perfectly penetrating" (*yīqiè yuántōng*). "All" refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), which do not constitute obstructions.
Because of this perfect penetration, one is able to recollect the karmic habits of birth and death throughout countless eons across the three periods of time.
Through such recollection, all habitual tendencies manifest before one; there is no forgetting, for they are present within every thought-moment.

Therefore, it is called the "Exquisite Perfection of Mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*). Below, the three types of faith are clarified; this also inherits the "exquisite perfection" of the preceding faith because it accords with the principle within the center.

Being purely one and true, this very true and brilliant faith brings forth inexhaustible transformation, whereby the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of birth and death throughout countless eons are transformed into a single brilliant essence. By means of this brilliance...
To clarify: "faith" refers to advancing toward the principle of true purity within the Middle Way;

"clarity" (jing) refers to the mind of this stage, which advances with vigor and clarity—this is what is meant by the term "abiding in vigor. The phrase "the mind is clear" below explains the four kinds of faith.
The first clause also follows from what was stated above: because one advances toward true purity with a mind of clarity and vigor, it is said that "the mind is clear and manifests."
Previously, it was further explained that beginningless habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are permeated by a single, brilliant lucidity; this brilliant lucidity is itself wisdom (*prajñā*).
As prior habitual tendencies are transformed and all become wisdom, no further residual habits remain. Therefore, it is said to be "purely through wisdom.

Because it is designated by the name and position of "wisdom," it is called the "Abode of Wisdom" (*jñānasthiti*). Regarding the term "abode" (*sthiti*), it refers to its functional activity; that is to say, one employs wisdom to advance toward what follows.
"Position" refers to the maintenance [of the state]; the following clarifies the five levels of faith.

The first phrase also follows from what was stated above, meaning that one maintains the illumination of the aforementioned wisdom so that it pervades the tranquil and profound principle; thus, complete wisdom becomes the principle, and the tranquil principle is eternally coalescent.

Because this eternal coalescence is concentration, it is called "abiding in concentration. The section beginning with "the light of concentration" below clarifies the six levels of faith; the first phrase here also follows from what was stated above.

This means that the concentration attained above was achieved through the maintenance of the light of wisdom; now, as this concentration arises again, it emits light, and since this light is itself the nature of wisdom, concentration and wisdom are equally luminous.
Because this luminous nature penetrates deeply without obstruction, it is said that there is only progress and no regression;
thus, "non-regression" is used as the name for this stage. "The mind progresses downward" explains the seven stages of faith (*śraddhā*). The first phrase also follows from the preceding.
The "superior" mentioned above refers to the superior non-retrogressive mind; by protecting and upholding it so as not to let it be lost, one remains secure and free from peril.
This meaning of "security" (āśvasta) is defined as follows: through discerning observation, both quiescence and function are non-dual;

this non-dual progress—wherein diligence is uninterrupted—is what is called security. If, however, subject and object are not forgotten, and principle and wisdom remain in opposition, [there is no security].

"The enemy is not at ease. Thus, because the practitioner’s mind accords with the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*), it is said that they "interconnect with the breath of the Buddha" and are called a "protector of the Dharma" (*dharmapāla*).
Since the Dharma is the Middle Way, and because one is able to maintain it, one is termed a protector of the Dharma. The Wuxing commentary states:
"According to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanwei*), reaching this stage means that the afflictions of the three realms (*tridhātu-kleśa*) have been completely severed; this is the sixth [stage]."
The purity of the faculties (*indriya-viśuddhi*) is the stage of the correct position (*samyaktva-niyāma*). According to the *Ratnavyuha-sūtra* (瓔珞經), it corresponds to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*);

according to the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*, it corresponds to the Buddha-stage. Master Zhiyi says: "If one compares the stage of the Buddha as defined by the Tripiṭaka masters with the stage of the purity of the six faculties, there are points of equality and points of inferiority.

They are equal in that both have eliminated the four abidings (*catvāra āśrayāḥ*). However, regarding the suppression of ignorance (*avidyā*), the Tripiṭaka [Buddha] is inferior. Since this is the stage of initial awakening...

Because it is the great juncture for truly severing delusions, it is specifically indicated as such. The phrase "the breath-energy of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions interconnects" clarifies the eight stages of faith (*śraddhā*).
The first four lines also follow from what was stated above; "awakened clarity" (*jue-ming*) is identical to the "wisdom-clarity" (*hui-ming*) mentioned in the preceding text, restating that meaning.
"Able to employ wondrous power" refers to the power of maintaining [the state] from above being redirected through dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
The Buddha’s light and the practitioner’s light move in accordance with one another; because the light moves forward to enter [the Buddha], it is said that "one dwells facing the Buddha.
These two phrases clarify the meaning of the aforementioned "interconnection of the vital energy (*qi-fen*) with the Buddha.

However, this is not a literal meeting of physical energies; rather, it is simply the subtle resonance between the causal and resultant mental lights, and the profound harmony between the fundamental and initial awakenings. This is expressed through metaphorical language.
Regarding the "vapor" (*qi*) mentioned above, it is now called "light" (*guang*). What was previously termed vapor was subtle and not yet manifest;
what is now termed light is evident and without concealment. This is like the following analogy used to clarify the meaning of turning the light back toward its source:
when two mirrors face each other, their radiance mutually encompasses one another; first, this mirror encompasses that, thereby containing both mirrors within itself.
If one takes those mirrors and encompasses them, they contain four mirrors; these four then transform into eight, the eight transform into sixteen, and the sixteen transform into thirty-two.
In this way, they mutually encompass and mutually reflect one another, reaching a state of infinite layers upon layers.

The fool once attempted to test this personally with mirrors, but looking only toward the inner circular light, it was small and could not be seen; therefore, it is said that "the subtle images within it" are what appear.

Regarding the convergence of the principle of mutual interpenetration, the analogy of the two mirrors illustrates it: the luminous mind of the practitioner and the awakened realization of the Buddha’s fruition.

The practitioner’s causal mind is *ādikṣaya-bodhi* (initial awakening), while the Buddha is *mūla-bodhi* (fundamental awakening). Fundamental awakening enters into the contemplation and practice of initial awakening;
within this, wondrous reflections clearly manifest, their radiance containing the inconceivable—how could there be an end? This is what is called "wondrous."
"Shadow" refers to this true contemplation of the light of the mind, which is neither quiescent nor illuminating, yet both quiescent and illuminating;

it forgets subject and object, transcends absolute duality, and while being non-existent, leaves no trace; while being empty, it possesses spiritual efficacy; it is neither one nor different, neither joined nor separated.

It can only be realized through personal correspondence and cannot be explained through stagnant discourse; therefore, it is called "wondrous. This is precisely the turning of the light back toward its own abiding, which constitutes the conclusion.

This stage is called "The Heart-Light Shining Downward to the Nine Faiths. The first phrase also follows from what was said above, referring to the practitioner whose heart-light is termed "secret" (*mi*, *guhya*).
"Returning" (*hui*) means that within the practitioner's meditative concentration, the eye of the mind shines radiantly;

it cannot be known by bystanders, and is therefore called "secret. It is only through the power of this dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) that one attains the Buddha’s eternally abiding, concentrated [wisdom].
However, this wondrous samādhi is eternally concentrated; its essence is precisely the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and is thus called "unsurpassed.
Because it is free from the defilements of the two extremes, it is called "wondrously pure. Since even the nature of purity is non-existent, it is "wondrous.
When a practitioner is able to dwell securely within this wondrous, pure, and unconditioned state, this is the Path.

Because it is the shared precepts (*sādhāraṇa-śīla*), the name "Abiding in the Precepts" (*śīla-vihāra*) is established. To clarify the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) within the lower section on abiding in the precepts:

the first phrase also follows from what was stated above. Abiding in the precepts refers to being securely established in the path of the shared precepts; because one is without dependence or attachment therein, it is called "sovereignty.

Due to this sovereignty of the precepts, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and distraction (*vikṣepa*) become one, and going and staying are no different; therefore, wherever one goes is according to one's vow.

This is precisely what is meant by the name and rank of "vow. Having privately examined the textual meaning of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), I find that the first nine belong entirely to internal cultivation, while the tenth is able to extend the mind outward.
The first is the essence (*tattva*) of faith, and the latter nine are its wondrous virtues (*guṇa*);

as essence and virtue mutually complete one another, they are collectively termed the "stage of faith" (*śraddhā-bhūmi*). Nevertheless, when entering this stage vertically through successive stages, each subsequent level is progressively superior.
The preceding stages can be understood from the text itself. Furthermore, the "Middle Way" referred to within these ten levels of faith is still merely a semblance of the Middle Way;
it is only upon entering the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) that it becomes the true, wondrous Middle Way. The *Miaozongchao* states:

"A 'semblance' refers to two things being similar to one another, such as brass resembling gold, a melon compared to a gourd, or fire being warm before it blazes, or the initial crossing of the ocean."
Píng further states that four analogies are used to clarify the "similar" stage of the practitioner. The fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) is characterized by both quiescence and illumination;
when these two aspects manifest in a manner similar to each other, they constitute the three types of awakening of the "similar" stage. This awakening resembles the true awakening.

Of the four analogies, the first two illustrate the initial similarity to the fundamental, while the latter two illustrate the "similar" stage as being close to the "partially true" (*bhūta-tathatā*). Therefore, it is named "similar."
"Ānanda, these good sons, through true skillful means... [up to] the arrangement of the consecration, which is called the 'Abode of Consecration' (*abhiṣeka-vihāra*).
This section of the sūtra follows the preceding "Setting Forth and Establishing the Stages," and now clarifies the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*).

Regarding the meaning of the "Abode" (*vihāra*) according to Tiantai’s *Sijiàoyí* (Outline of the Four Teachings): it refers to the stage wherein contemplation becomes manifest and the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*) is opened.
To achieve all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*), from the first stage through the tenth, one successively severs one grade of ignorance and increases one portion of the Middle Way.
The commentary states that this refers to ten successive advancements of outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*) that equally perceive the Middle Way, the primary principle of Buddha-nature;
by means of non-abiding dharmas, one proceeds from the shallow to the deep and dwells in the three virtues of the Buddha and all Buddha-dharmas.
Therefore, it is called the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*). By "the true" (*tattva*), the first abode is clarified. Regarding "true skillful means" (*tattvopāya*):

because True Suchness (*tathatā*) is first manifested in this abode, it is termed "true. This very "true" skillful means develops the ten minds of the stage of faith (*adhimukti-caryā*) mentioned in the preceding text;
those previous ten minds become refined and pure, and their ten functions penetrate into the midst of true skillful means, becoming perfect.
The reason for achieving the "One-Mindedness" of the First Abode (*prathamā vihārā*) is precisely because the True Expedient Mind (*bhūta-upāya-citta*) develops the ten minds of faith;
therefore, it is called the "Abode of Resolving the Mind. Wēnlíng’s commentary states: "The True Expedient is wondrous wisdom (*prajñā*). These ten minds are the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).
Guāngshān’s claim that the ten faiths are opened up horizontally within the First Abode is incorrect. Below this, in the section on the mind, the Second Abode is explained.
The first phrase, "elucidating within the mind," refers to elucidating the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) realized at the First Abode.
The subsequent section clarifies this through metaphors: pure lapis lazuli represents the true skillful means-mind of the First Abode, and refined gold represents the ten minds of faith.
These three phrases recapitulate the meaning of the preceding text. What follows below constitutes the meritorious practice of the Second Abode, namely:
The initial dwelling of the preceding stage is the "Sublime Mind" (*miao-xin*); practicing the treatment for this constitutes the causal ground for the second dwelling, "Treading upon the Ground.

By applying the wisdom of the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*) to cultivate the previously mentioned Sublime Mind, one causes immeasurable virtuous functions to arise, just as the earth gives birth to all things.
Therefore, it is metaphorically called "Treading upon the Ground," and this mind is termed the "Dwelling of Treading upon the Ground" (*chizhu*). This is the "Ground-Mind."
The following clarifies the third dwelling (*vihāra*). The first two phrases carry forward the meaning of the preceding section:

the word "mind" (*citta*) in the first phrase refers to the mind-ground that serves as the antidote in the second dwelling, while the word "ground" (*bhūmi*) refers to the ground traversed in the preceding stage.

"Interpenetrating knowledge" (*shèzhī*) means that the aforementioned antidote and the object to be remedied mutually interpenetrate, such that both are clearly understood; however, this is a duality within non-duality and is not ultimately real.
Regarding the capacity for subject and object, it is roughly by means of the mind that one integrates the preceding ten functions;

as their practice becomes increasingly pure, it is said that "the mind and the ground interpenetrate and thus one knows. To "travel throughout the lower realms" refers to the meritorious practice of the third stage (*bhūmi*);

it means that by riding upon this power of interpenetrating knowledge, one travels everywhere without obstruction, spontaneously practicing the Four Great Vows and the Six Perfections, and is not hindered by external objects.
Because it is unimpeded, it is called "abiding in the practice. This refers to the four abodes (*catur-vihāra*) explained below. The first phrase also inherits from what was said above;
the word "practice" (*xing*) in that first phrase refers to the practice of the person who is the cause for the four abodes.

That this practice is identical to the practice of the Buddha means that the beginning and the fundamental source are in profound accord. Because the practice accords with the central principle, it is said that one "receives from the Buddha."

Regarding the "stage of affinity" (*qi-fen*) mentioned in the preceding text, where the seventh stage of faith (*shì-xìn*) interfaces with the affinity of the Buddha, how does this differ from the present case?

It is because what was previously called "interface" (*jiē*) is here called "reception" (*shòu*); though they appear similar, their relative depth may be known by comparing the true and the semblance. Although the true and the semblance differ, both ultimately constitute the practice of a Buddha;
therefore, both the preceding and the following passages refer to them as "affinity. This is like citing examples to illustrate the principle in the middle and lower sections.
To make it easy for people to understand, I have generally entered deeply into the principles; since these are difficult to describe, I borrow worldly events to clarify them.
When a person dies, the subsequent *antara-bhava* (intermediate state) has not yet arisen, while the preceding *pūrvakāla-bhava* (prior existence) has already ceased.

Within this intermediate body (*antarābhava-śarīra*), one seeks out those of similar karma to serve as parents, entrusting oneself to the subsequent birth-state to form an embryo. Therefore, the ordinary eye cannot see within the profound darkness of this state.
Because they are mutually permeated by a single faith, it is said that "faith permeates in the darkness.

Now, the causal practice of the fourth stage of abiding (caturthābhūmi) and the resultant awakening of the Buddha’s truth (satya) are darkly permeated with one another, similar to how an intermediate state being (antarābhava) enters the parents' union. Because such practice accords with the Buddha-mind, it is called "entering the lineage of the Tathāgata.
In the world, the royal lineage is held in high esteem; in the supramundane, the Buddha-lineage is held in high esteem. Therefore [it is so called].

The name "Abiding in Noble Birth" is spoken by way of analogy with the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Since it has already been explained that one dwells in the lower [stages], this clarifies the five abidings.
The first two phrases also follow from what was stated above: when one attains profound resonance through contemplation of the truths, one becomes a seed of the Buddha;

thus, the embryo of the Way is already formed, and one becomes a direct heir to the fruit of Buddhahood. Regarding the phrase "the human characteristics are not deficient," "human characteristics" refers to the Buddha.

This is explained through an analogy based on conventional designations. Just as one is called a "human" when the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*) are fully complete, this constitutes the "human characteristic" (*puruṣalakṣaṇa*);

likewise, the Buddha takes compassion (*karuṇā*), skillful means (*upāya*), and the provisional and ultimate truths (*saṃvṛti-paramārtha*) as his internal characteristics, while the thirty-two marks (*dvātriṃśanmahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*) and eighty minor marks (*aśītyanuvyañjana*) constitute his external characteristics.

Now, because the internal and external phenomena and principles of those at the stage of the five abidings (*pañcamavihāra*) are no different from those of the Buddha, it is called the "human characteristic."

The absence of deficiency in skillful means constitutes provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), while the illumination of reality constitutes ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*). Because provisional wisdom arises in reliance upon the ultimate, it is called "endowment with skillful means.
The subsequent section on "appearance" clarifies the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭha-bhūmi*); this also follows from what was stated above.

Since it was previously said that "human characteristics are not deficient," it now follows by stating that "the appearance is like that of a Buddha," meaning that the external features of the person at the sixth stage resemble those of a Buddha.
The inner mind is likewise so; because it is balanced both internally and externally, it is called the "Abiding in the Rectified Mind.

The following section clarifies the seventh stage (*saptamī-bhūmi*). The first phrase also follows from what was stated above: "body" refers to one's physical appearance, and "mind" refers to the aforementioned mental characteristics, with the same intent.
"Synthesized" means that through the synthesis of the internal and external factors of the person on the seventh stage, one becomes a Buddha.
When virtue gradually increases day by day, advancing only without retreating, it is called the "Abode of Non-retrogression. The section on the "Ten Bodies" below clarifies the eight abodes.

There are two types of Ten Bodies: first, the ten bodies categorized as the body of a śrāvaka, the body of a pratyekabuddha, the body of a bodhisattva, the body of a Tathāgata, the dharma-body, the wisdom-body, the space-body, the karmic-retribution body, the sentient-being body, and the land-body; second, [the other set of ten].
Within the body of the Tathāgata, there are naturally present ten bodies, namely:

the bodhisattva body, the vow body, the transformation body, the sustaining power body, the adornment body, the majestic power body, the mind-born body, the merit body, the dharma body, and the wisdom body.
Since the Tathāgata fully possesses these two types of ten bodies, this practitioner, by virtue of their characteristics resembling those of a Buddha, likewise becomes fully endowed with them.
Therefore, because each and every [aspect] is called the nature of numinous awakening (*ling-jue-xing*), it is said that the "numinous marks" (*ling-xiang*) are simultaneously and fully present.

This refers to the intent of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), wherein the realization of one constitutes the realization of all. It is like the autumn moon suspended in the sky, its light pervading everywhere in a perfect and boundless manner;

because from the very beginning this essence is already complete yet subtle, it is termed the "Abode of Youthful Truth" (*tongzhen-zhu*). The following section concerns the formation of the physical form.
This clarifies the ninth stage (*navama-vihāra*). The previous [text] spoke of the "perfection of the ten bodies" while still within the womb;

now, having received those ten bodies and formed them, one emerges at full term from the womb and becomes a direct child of the Buddha; therefore, it is called the "Stage of the Dharma Prince" (*dharmarāja-putra-vihāra*). The Wēn-líng commentary states:
"From the initial arousal of the mind until birth into nobility is called entering the holy embryo (*āryagarbha*); from the perfection of skillful means until the stage of the youth..."

The "True Name" (Zhēnmíng) states that from the stage of nurturing the holy embryo (*āryagarbha*) until this point, the function of nurturing is completed; therefore, it is called "emerging from the womb" (*niṣkrānta-garbha*).

Master Gūshān’s interpretation of the meaning of "emerging from the womb" is that it refers to the destruction of the ignorance (*avidyā*) of the ninth stage (*bhūmi*), as well as the arising of function from essence.

Furthermore, he interprets "foolishness like emerging from the womb" (*garbhaniṣkramaṇa-mūḍha*) [as referring to the eighth stage]. However, I consider this interpretation not to be precise. This is because the True Mind remains hidden within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), and the aspect of its awakening has not yet been manifested.
It is like being in the womb; only now, when one recognizes and breaks through [ignorance] and awakening becomes perfect, is it called "being born from the womb.

However, this must also be explained in correspondence with the subsequent stages so as not to confuse the distinctions of depth and shallowness. The following section clarifies the ten abodes (*bhūmi*).

Although one has emerged from the womb and is called a Dharma Prince (*dharmaputra*), because one's age is still very young, one is said not yet to be an adult. Now, however, one's years have finally reached maturity.
Because he was now capable of succeeding to the throne and delegating the administration of government, the analogy of the King’s ritual is cited to clarify this:

when a king sees that his crown prince has reached maturity, he assembles the various kings and the hundred officials, takes water from the four oceans, places it within a golden pitcher, and the king holds this pitcher to pour it over the crown prince’s head.
At that moment, he is said to have received the royal position; this signifies that he has become a full adult.
Once his intention was manifest, the adult prince went forth to the Eastern Palace, whereupon the King entrusted him with the affairs of state and divided the administration of the commands;
this clarifies the intent behind the entrustment of governance. The subsequent passage concerning the Kṣatriya explains the intent behind receiving office.
The commentator of Wuxing remarks that "crown prince" (*taizi*) and "heir apparent" (*shizǐ*) differ only in their phrasing. As the *Zuozhuan* states: "He met the crown prince at Shouzhi."
The *Liji* (Book of Rites) states that the "Heir Apparent" (*shizi*) in the "Wenwang" chapter refers to the sons of the Son of Heaven.

If one were to refer specifically to King Wen, he was the Lord of the West (*Xibei*) and was thus a feudal lord; therefore, we know that the son of a feudal lord is called the Heir Apparent, while the son of the Heavenly King is called the Crown Prince (*taizi*).
In the current text, the term "Crown Prince" is used above and "Heir Apparent" below, which is a general and broad explanation applicable to both cases.
Wu Xing still considers this not yet definitive. The Wenzhong commentary states: "If one delegates state affairs by entrusting them to others, it is not a formal transmission of the national throne;

it merely serves to manifest the completion of the person. This is because in this land, only when one reaches the culmination of the Ten Abodes or fulfills the Ten Grounds is one fit for formal transmission;
thus, the reception of the Buddha’s position by a Bodhisattva of the Ten Grounds in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is comparable to that of a Universal Monarch."
The son receives his office; once he has resolved his mind, he must first cultivate the ground (*bhūmi*). Having cultivated the ground, he then practices (*pratipatti*).

Through practice, he is subsequently born into the family of the Tathāgata, endowed with the marks of awakening (*bodhalakṣaṇa*), and his mind becomes identical to that of a Buddha. He extends the essence of the Path, perfects the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), and as a son of the Buddha, he undertakes the Buddha’s work.
This is the sequence from beginning to end of the Ten Abidings (*daśavihāra*). Furthermore, the present text clarifies these ten stages by means of illustrative examples.
Scholars must not attempt to understand the meaning of the beginning and end of the causal practices through literal facts alone.
Ānanda, once these good sons have become children of the Buddha (up to: because their nature is inherently so), they are called those who practice true reality.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding "Initiating Practice and Establishing the Stages" to clarify the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*). The *Fourfold Teaching Ritual Commentary* states:
"Following the Ten Abidings, the true illumination of the reality-mark (*dharmatā*) is inconceivable;

through ten further stages of wisdom and severance (*jñāna-prahāṇa*), one progressively breaks through the ten grades of ignorance. Each practice encompasses all practices, advancing in every thought-moment until flowing into equality."
In the ocean of the *dharmadhātu*, the various *pāramitās* grow spontaneously;

because the merit of one’s own practice and the transformation of others is equal to space, it is called the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*). In the present text, from "Now becoming a child of the Buddha" onwards, the first practice is clarified.

The first phrase follows the preceding example of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); since the previous section already manifested the completion of the person, one has now become a child of the Buddha and is fully endowed [with these qualities].
There is the Tathāgata’s immeasurable wondrous virtue; this "wondrous virtue" refers to the spiritual marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and signs (*vyañjana*) of the ten bodies.

By means of this wondrous virtue, one causes sentient beings of the ten directions to follow in accordance and not oppose; because they are endowed with the superior above and accord with the inferior below, they give rise to joy.

Thus, "joy" is designated as the practice (*caryā*). This corresponds to the name "Joyous" (*Pramuditā*) given to the first stage (*bhūmi*) in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* Sūtra, which shares the same name as the present [text].

Although the meanings are identical, there are distinctions of depth and the differences between the ordinary and the noble-sage, for which reason [the text] skillfully clarifies two modes of practice below.
The first two phrases follow the preceding intent: since the aforementioned [practice] accords with both self-cultivation and the transformation of others, it gave rise to joy;
now, however, because it pertains entirely to benefiting others, it is termed "beneficial. Nevertheless, it is not that self-benefit is absent.

"Beneficial" (*artha*) means abundant; because there is nothing that is not beneficial, it is called "beneficial conduct" (*arthacaryā*). "Self-awakening and awakening others" clarifies the three types of conduct:
this means that above, one does not reject any Buddha-dharma; through self-awakening, one is able to practice what is difficult to practice and thus does not reject them.
Below, one does not reject any sentient beings; through awakening others, one treats enemies and kin equally.
Observing and awakening to this, with the upper and lower [realms] not being in conflict, one is free from anger and resentment; thus it is called "conduct" (*caryā*).
The phrase "categories" (*jāti*) below clarifies the four types of conduct. The two characters "categories" (*jāti*) follow upon the aforementioned "conduct of self-awakening and awakening others.
The meaning is that because the conduct of the category of self-awakening gives rise to the inexhaustible, its awakening is able to penetrate to the Tathāgata; this is "awakening others."
Because the practice of various types gives rise to that which is inexhaustible, one is able to reach the end of the future limit in order to deliver sentient beings.
Second, because these practices are fulfilled equally throughout the three periods of time and pervade the ten directions, they are called "inexhaustible practices.
The phrase "all" below clarifies the five practices; "all" refers here to all the practices produced by the aforementioned various types. This is the first [point].
All categories of distinctions are immeasurable, yet their practice accords with the One; this "One" is pointed out as the Mind.
