It is said that although manifold practices arise profusely, they fundamentally do not stir from the One Mind; therefore, it is called "the identity of all.
When one practices manifold practices by means of the One Mind, there is no dharma-gate among the various kinds that contradicts the Mind.
Therefore, there is no error; because there is no error, one is free from delusion and confusion, and thus acts according to names.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "In a single thought-moment, this bodhisattva attains countless samādhis and realizes that these samādhis share a single essence, even unto the attainment of the true wisdom of all dharmas. This is identical in meaning to the present [text].
If one examines the stages of realization according to this present sutra in conjunction with the *Avataṃsaka*, there is much to be understood through sudden awakening.
Thus, the six practices are clarified below: that is to say, within the sameness of the one mind, various distinct dharma-gates are manifested;
this is "difference within sameness. Within the difference of each individual dharma-gate, the sameness of the one mind is individually perceived.

This is the identity within difference and the difference within identity. Identity is quiescence; difference is illumination. Because it is illuminating while being quiescent, it is different while being identical.
Because it is quiescent while being illuminating, it is identical while being different. Quiescence does not obstruct illumination, and illumination does not obstruct quiescence.
Quiescence and illumination are simultaneous, and the integration of the provisional and the real is never disordered; this is called "skillful manifestation. It is as follows:
This section below clarifies the seven practices. "Thus" refers back to the preceding meaning: what was manifested above as the various practices is the mind that acts as the perceiver (*ālambaka*);
what now appears throughout the empty space of the ten directions as all dust-motes and lands (*rajas-kṣetra*) is the objective realm (*ālambana*).

Within a single dust-mote, the worlds of the ten directions are manifested; this is the case for every dust-mote. Within each dust-mote, worlds are manifested; within each world, dust-motes are manifested.
The wondrous nature of this object is that one and many are unimpeded, and large and small are mutually inclusive, encompassing, and penetrating without obstruction or attachment.
Since the object of focus is thus wondrous, it clearly demonstrates that the cognizing mind is also wondrous.

Because both the object and the subject are wondrous, the name "unattached practice" (*asaṅga-caryā*) is given by designating the subject through the object. The phrase "various kinds" and below clarifies the eight practices. "Various... [and so forth].

This refers to what was stated above regarding the manifestation of the objects of perception (*viṣaya*) and the spheres of perception (*dhātu*), as well as the pervasive manifestation of subject and object.
It means that all various modes of appearance manifesting before one are entirely the *prajñāpāramitā*; when one practices all deeds by means of *prajñā*, then those deeds are themselves *prajñā*.
This is because the aforementioned manifold deeds do not transcend the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), and among these six, [they are subsumed] within *prajñā*.
If one takes the first [perfection] as primary and integrates it with the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), then all five perfections will tend toward the perfection of wisdom;

therefore, they are all *prajñā*. Just as when real cinnabar is applied to the hand, grasses, trees, tiles, and stones are all transformed into gold, so too, because *prajñā* is the most honored among the perfections, it is designated by the name "Perfection" (*pāramitā*) through its quality of being most venerable.
The frequent translation of *pāramitā* as "reaching the other shore" carries the meaning of ultimate perfection.
Thus, following this principle of perfect integration (*yuanrong*), the text below clarifies the nine practices. The first phrase also follows from what was stated above:

because all dharmic practices are honored, supreme, and wondrous through the perfect integration of the six perfections, they all accomplish the tracks and rules of the Buddhas, proceeding spontaneously and without obstruction.

Because each [practice] accords with the Middle Way, they are called "the practice of wholesome dharmas. Each item below clarifies the ten practices; each also follows from the aforementioned manifold practices.
That is to say, every single one of those manifold practices, in accordance with the Middle Way, is a practice that is pure, untainted, and quiescent.
Thus, although the manifold practices flourish profusely, their very substance is the One True Suchness Mind—unconditioned and without effort.
Because their nature is primordial, each is called "true" and constitutes "true practice. To examine the textual meaning of the preceding ten abodes (*bhūmis*):
they consist entirely of awakening to principle; thus, they are illustrated by the analogy of entering the womb of the long path and wandering among the lineage of enlightenment.
Now, the textual meaning of these ten practices consists entirely of emerging into the provisional to clarify the Middle Way; therefore, they are manifested through various forms of conduct.
It is true.

Ānanda, this section of the sūtra—from "this good man fulfills his supernormal powers" up to "named the Infinite Dedication of the Dharma-realm"—follows the previous sections on the practice of the stages (*caryā-pratisthā*) and now clarifies the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*). This explains the dedication.
The *Huayan shu* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) previously stated: "To 'dedicate' (*pariṇāmana*) means to transform; 'to direct' (*abhimukha*) means to incline toward.

Because one transforms the myriad practices to incline toward three destinations, it is called dedication. There are ten different types of dedication. As for the three destinations, they are: first, sentient beings; second, bodhi; and third, reality (*tattva*).
Second, there are the actualities according to characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the actuality apart from characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, there are three [other sets of three]."

Furthermore, eleven further turnings are opened: (1) turning from self toward others; (2) turning from the few toward the many; (3) turning from one's own causal practice toward the causal practice of others;
(4) turning from cause toward fruit; (5) turning from the inferior toward the superior; (6) turning from the comparative toward the realized; (7) turning from phenomena toward principle;
(8) turning from differentiated practice toward perfectly integrated practice; (9) turning from the mundane toward the supramundane.
The ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) accord with both principle and phenomena; they are directed toward the phenomena established by principle.

Furthermore, it is said that among the ten preceding meanings, the first three all dedicate toward sentient beings, the next three all dedicate toward Bodhi, the next two dedicate toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the final two meanings apply universally to both the fruition and the limit of reality.
Moreover, according to the entire section on the Ten Dedications in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, [it is as follows].
The title "Ten Directions" is used because it refers to the ten vows; here, the phrase "first, fulfilling [the practices]" and what follows below also rely on the preceding explanation.

Having fulfilled the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and become a child of the Buddha, this restates that the ten practices mentioned previously are all supernormal powers in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*).
Since all various practices—whether identical or different—do not transcend these ten, it is said that the supernormal powers are fulfilled. Such is the cultivation.
Because all are in accord with the Tathāgata’s pure regulations, it is said that "Buddha-works are pure. The following two lines explicitly clarify the initial orientation:
since each of the aforementioned ten types of Buddha-works accords with the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*), they are called "pure" and "sublime.
Being both pure and sublime, there are no lingering afflictions. The subsequent four lines dispel [delusions] by means of actual reality.

The traces [of practice] truly arise from the ten preceding practices; since provisional phenomena are largely cultivated through the salvation of sentient beings, one cultivates the myriad practices.
However, once these practices have merged with the Middle Way, how could there remain any trace of subject and object, or of that which is empty and that which is not?

This is because one deeply guards against subtle transgressions and is cautious regarding the four marks of self, person, sentient being, and life-span. Since one does not speak of "persons," by what means can one know [this]?

Therefore, it is reiterated: if a bodhisattva still possesses the traces of one who crosses over and that which is crossed over, such that these have not yet been emptied, then the four marks remain distinct and belong entirely to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Consequently, one must eliminate the mark of "crossing over" and turn toward the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

By means of this causal mind, one proceeds toward the path of nirvāṇa, which is free from arising and ceasing; hence, the title is concluded as "Saving and Protecting Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from Sentient Beings."
The mutual dedication for the sake of rescue and protection is the meaning of "crossing over" (tāraka); thus, that commentary further states:

"The two characters 'dedication' (pariṇāmanā) refer to the vow that performs the dedication, while terms such as 'rescue and protection' refer to the practice to which it is dedicated. All subsequent instances follow this pattern. The section below clarifies the two types of dedication.
The first sentence follows the preceding intent, stating that because there is a "capable of crossing" (the subject) and a "to be crossed" (the object), these are subject to destruction.
This [state] now eliminates and transcends the marks of cessation, destroying that which is destructible; furthermore, it sweeps away all traces. It is said:

"If the mind capable of destruction were not empty, it too would be destructible. Therefore, one must distance oneself from all [marks]; only when one is distant from all can it be called "indestructible.
These "all distances" (zhū lí) are not merely a single layer of distancing that can be exhausted; thus they are called "all distances," as the *Awakening of Faith* says: "Distancing oneself is..."
Illusion is likewise detached, and detachment is further detached from illusion. Once all illusions are detached, the awakened mind is unmoving; that which is unmoving is indestructible.
This is identical in meaning to the present context, though the current text is brief. When the capacity for detachment is exhausted, there is neither destruction nor non-destruction;
this is called the "indestructible dedication" (*akṣaya-pariṇāmanā*) to original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). Below, the three dedications are clarified. First:

The phrase "also following from what was said above" refers to the fact that non-destruction is identical to fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), and immovability is identical to the meaning of profound stillness.

That the Bodhisattva’s initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*) is equal to the Buddha’s fundamental enlightenment is called "Equalizing toward Buddhahood. "Equal" (*sama*) is the meaning of the character "equalized" (*samāna*).
The section beginning with "refined and true" clarifies the four types of dedication. The first phrase also follows from what was said above: "refined and true."
This refers to the meaning of the fundamental awakening being profoundly still (*zhanran*). Because it is profoundly still, it is pure and true (*jingzhen*).

This means that because the mind of this Bodhisattva on the ground of causes is equal to the Buddha’s awakening, he is able to manifest through its pure truth; thus, the ground of causes becomes identical to the ground of fruition.

What was previously called "awakening equal to the Buddha's awakening" is now stated as "the ground like the Buddha's ground. This is because what was initially "equal" has now reached a state where it is fully "equal."
Furthermore, by treading upon it, one completes the ground (*bhūmi*), which gives rise to all virtuous functions.

Because the virtuous functions of the causal ground and the virtuous functions of the resultant ground are non-dual, it is called "the ground. Since the virtuous functions of the Buddha-ground are all-pervasive and nowhere absent, it is named "reaching all places.
The subsequent section on the "Turning toward the World" clarifies the five directions; the first phrase also continues from the preceding.
The explanation of "world" (*loka*) signifies the meaning of the "basis" (*āśraya*), which pertains to the *dharmadhātu*, while "Tathāgata" pertains to the "supported" (*ādheya*).
This clarifies the mutual interpenetration of the basis and the supported, and the non-duality of body and land (*kāya-bhūmi-eka-rasa*), whereby one attains unimpededness.

Because this Bodhisattva vehicle arises from the inexhaustible treasury of merit within the "stages" (*bhūmi*) mentioned above, it is named the "Dedication of the Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit. The following section clarifies the six dedications.

The first phrase also follows from what was stated above; while the previous five directions were discussed in terms of the inexhaustible manifestation of the source, the present six directions correctly clarify the functioning of virtue.

Therefore, it reiterates the same mind as that of the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*), which is the cause within both the causal and resultant stages, each giving rise to the pure original cause; this cause is the "cause of reliance" (*āśraya-hetu*).
Because one cultivates the myriad practices based on these primary causes, there is thus a cause of causes and a cause of fruits.
That which is produced within the stage of the cause of causes is called the "cause-cause," and that which is produced within the stage of the cause of fruits is called the "fruit-cause.
Both of these two causes are termed the "basis" (*āśraya*); relying upon these two causes, one manifests various practices and attains the path to *nirvāṇa*.
These two causes are themselves the roots of goodness of equality; because they are pure, they are termed "equality," as all Bodhisattvas are able to accord with them.
Thus, they are collectively named the "Roots of Goodness of Accordance with Equality.
The subsequent phrase refers to the seven dedications. The first clause also follows from what was stated above: each of the aforementioned roots of goodness of equality accords with the Truth.

Because it is identical to the essence (*tattva*), it is called the True Root (*bhūtendriya*). Once the True Root is established, those above—the Buddhas—are as such, and those below—sentient beings—are likewise so.
Both Buddhas and sentient beings are the original self-nature (*prakṛti-svabhāva*) of the Bodhisattva;
this original self-nature is precisely the Wondrous Mind (*citta*). Thus, there is no difference among these three: mind, Buddha, and sentient beings. In the text, however, [it only mentions]...
The statement that sentient beings do not speak of the Buddha is merely an abbreviation. Regarding "the nature is perfectly accomplished," this follows from the preceding phrase;

it means that the birth of sentient beings and the Buddha are identical to the mind. My own mind is perfectly endowed [with all qualities], and now this perfectly endowed mind accomplishes this principle.

Because this principle does not lose its reality, it is said that "it is not lost. Thus, neither sentient beings nor the Buddha are lost. Sentient beings, the Buddha, and the mind—these three are all... [identical].
The name "conforming to the contemplation of equality" (隨順平等觀) and the concluding name "dedicating by conforming to the equal contemplation of all sentient beings" both refer only to sentient beings;
however, when the meaning encompasses both mind and Buddha, it is then called "equal contemplation.
This first section clarifies the eight dedications. The initial phrase also follows from what was stated above: "all dharmas" refers to the aforementioned mind, Buddha, and sentient beings.

To speak of "arising" means that the ten realms and the ten suchnesses are all fully present; this is the meaning of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), for there is no phenomenon not subsumed within it.
To be "detached from all marks" is the meaning of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), for it sweeps away all characteristics.

When one clings to neither "identity" nor "detachment," this is the meaning of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), for it simultaneously negates and illuminates. Since the Middle is itself *tathatā* (suchness), [the text] concludes.

The name "Dedication of the Aspect of True Suchness" (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa-pariṇāmanā*) is explained in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* primarily through analogies, whereas this present sutra explains it directly through the Dharma itself;
the meaning in both cases is identical. The section beginning with "truly attaining" (*zhendé*) clarifies the nine dedications. The first phrase also follows from what was stated above:

"that which is truly attained as suchness" (*zhendé suǒrú*) means to personally realize (*pratyakṣa-sākṣātkriyā*) true suchness, thereby distinguishing it from error. The character "truly" (*zhēn*) at the beginning of the preceding phrase is... [text fragment ends].
The "Tathatā (Suchness) as the object to be realized" refers to the Tathatā that is the objective support (*ālambana*).

If one can directly realize Tathatā, then there will be no obstruction regarding what is aimed at; all phenomena are Tathatā, and because one is not bound by phenomena, the absence of bondage is itself liberation.
Therefore, this dedication is named the "Dedication of Unbound Liberation. However, there is a slight distinction between "unbound" and "liberation."
The absence of bondage is the cause of liberation, and liberation is the fruit of the absence of bondage; therefore, the term "bondage" (saṃyojana) is used to express both.

Regarding the meaning of the phrase "the nature and virtues," the following clarifies the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*). The first phrase generally inherits from the preceding nine [dedications], meaning that all the dedications cultivated in the previous nine belong to the category of "nature and virtues.
"Nature and virtues" refers to the true nature (*tathatā*) and its inherent virtues. Since these nature and virtues are already perfected...
Once accomplished, it transcends all measures; since all measures and quantities are ultimately immeasurable, it is said that "the measure of the Dharma-realm is extinguished.

The *Huayan Shu* states: "By means of the great wisdom that accords with the Dharma-realm, one turns back the roots of goodness equal to the Dharma-realm toward the great function identical to the Dharma-realm, thereby accomplishing the essential body of practice within the Dharma-realm."

Because its position is fulfilled and its nature is perfected, it is designated by the name "Dharmadhātu. In that sutra, there is the character "equal" (等) above the word "Dharmadhātu," which has been omitted in this sutra.
The Commentary further asks: "What dharma is 'equal' to the Dharmadhātu? This encompasses four meanings: first, the Dharmadhātu of Principle (Li); second, the Dharmadhātu of Phenomena (Shi);
third, the Dharmadhātu of the Non-obstruction between Principle and Phenomena; and fourth, the Dharmadhātu of the Non-obstruction between Phenomenon and Phenomenon.
Each citation should be applied to this sutra as well; because it is extinguished by the measure of the *dharmadhātu*, it is named the "Infinite Dedication of the *Dharmadhātu*.
The commentary on the *Sūtra* explains that there are two kinds of "infinite": first, being without spatial dimensions, which refers to the principle-*dharmadhātu*;

second, being without numerical quantity, which refers to the phenomenon-*dharmadhātu*. While the previous nine dedications clarify arising function based on the essence, this [dedication] clarifies...

Because the non-obstruction between essence and function is perfectly consummate and sovereign, it accords with the meaning of the present [text]. Nevertheless, the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) of the current sutra also pervade three locations:

the first, second, and seventh meanings are directed toward sentient beings; the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth meanings are directed toward bodhi; and the eighth and ninth meanings are directed toward *tathatā*.
The tenth, which universally subsumes them, is directed toward the *dharmadhātu*. *Tathatā* is precisely the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
That commentary treats these three points identically:
"Ānanda, this son of good family is entirely pure" (extending to) "the two [aspects] without objective reference are called the Stage of the Supreme Worldly Dharma.
This section of the sutra follows the previous discussion on the practice of the path and the establishment of the stages; it now clarifies the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*). (40)

"One-mind" (*ekacitta*) refers to the preceding stages of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*), as well as the ten stages each of Faith (*adhimukti*), Abiding (*vihāra*), Practice (*caryā*), and Direction (*mukha*), totaling forty-one;

this constitutes the section on the arising of the preparatory practice (*prayoga*). As for "preparatory practice," it means that once one has penetrated the principle deeply, one's application becomes increasingly subtle and dense, as one discriminates in accordance with the principle to eliminate the subtle cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); generally speaking, this is the function of ascending to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*).
One who has not yet attained high realization cannot easily enter; one must first cultivate subtle and secret contemplation, purify the mind through *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, and practice *dhyāna*.

Only then may one preside over this sacred ground; therefore, it is called "preparatory application" (*prayoga*). According to the meaning of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekayāna*), the preceding three stages are termed the "Three Worthies" (*tri-puṇya-kṣetra*), while the ten stages are termed the "Ten Sages.
Because one looks toward sagehood from the state of worthiness, preparatory application is required to enter the present sutra.

Thus, the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) also possesses this stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*). Although the *Avataṃsaka* does not explicitly open up these four stages, it is unclear what its discussion intends;
only the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* opens up this preparatory application. Now, this present sutra is entirely identical to that treatise.

My humble opinion is that while that treatise represents the Separate Teaching (Biejiao), this present sutra belongs to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). Why? Because the textual passages, dharmas, and their sequential order are identical to those in that treatise.
One must cite that commentary. Regarding the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it says:

"To manifestly posit a slight object as being the nature of consciousness-only—because there is something apprehended—one does not truly abide in consciousness-only; therefore, one must apply the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) to sweep away its objective image.
The Wuxing commentary states that regarding the tangerine and the plum, according to scriptures such as the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (or *Avataṃsaka*), they are not listed separately.

Regarding the four stages of application (*prayoga*): according to treatises such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the forty minds prior to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*) constitute the outer ordinary beings (*bālapṛthagjana*), while the stages of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, which are explained separately following the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), constitute the inner ordinary beings of the stage of application.

My personal view is that the current four stages of application are exactly as described in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. As for those who divide the stages prior to the [first] stage into outer and inner ordinary beings: [The text continues: ...it is because they... [the passage ends here].

The doctrine of the single path of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) holds that the stages of the Grounds (*bhūmi*) constitute the holy rank of a Bodhisattva; because this holy rank is difficult to enter, it employs these preparatory practices (*prayoga*). One may now ask:
what purpose does the distinct ranking serve in the Perfect Teaching (*Yuan-jiao*) of the present sutra? Answer: It borrows the names of the Separate Teaching to illustrate the Perfect Teaching;

there are examples of this, such as the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (Ren-wang jing), which states: "The Three Worthies and the Ten Sages abide in the retribution of fruition. This is precisely how it is here.
The text describes it as "wondrous and perfect" (*miaoyuan*). Regarding the practitioner, the very first passage of the ten stages of faith (*shixin*) states:

"Flowing into the center from the center, the wondrous and perfect blossoms; from the truly wondrous and perfect, one again gives rise to the truly wondrous and perfect. Based on this, even at the beginning of the ten stages of faith, it is already described as "wondrous" and "perfect.
Thus, we know that this sutra is consistently described as "perfect" from beginning to end, and that the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) is indeed such. Furthermore, if...
By comparing the "wondrous perfection" (*miaoyuan*) of the present text with that of the preceding one, the vast difference between them—like that between clouds and mud—is clearly discernible.

"Perfecting the perfect" and "wondering the wonderful" indicate that each subsequent stage surpasses the previous; this is like the moon on the fourteenth night compared to the moon on the fifteenth night.
This very point clarifies the stages of warmth (*dāna*). The Buddha’s awakening is precisely the Buddha’s wisdom; it is the fruition within one's own mind.
This is because it takes the wisdom of the Buddha-fruit as its own causal mind. Regarding "emerging yet not yet emerged," "emerging" has the sense of manifestation;

since at this stage one has just attained the function of the Buddha-wisdom but it is not yet pure, being at the juncture between manifestation and non-manifestation, it is said to be "emerging yet not yet emerged.
This is clarified below by means of a metaphor: "It is like drilling fire from two pieces of wood. The two pieces of wood are likened to the Buddha-wisdom.
This corresponds to the causal mind. The analogy of fire is derived from the path illuminated by wisdom: before the fire has emerged, the sign of warmth (*ūṣmagata*) first arises;

because it occurs at the juncture between whether the fire has emerged or not, it is said that "one wishes to ignite the wood. This is what is called the Stage of Warmth (*uṣmagata-bhūmi*). "Stage" (*bhūmi*) carries the meaning of a position or level.
According to the textual meaning of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, this can be clearly understood in detail. By citing that [text] to explain this, one enables others to understand.

The *Yì* (Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra) clarifies this by stating that based on the attainment of the "light-obtaining" concentration (*ālokalabdha-samādhi*), one gives rise to inferior-grade investigative contemplation (*vitarka*) regarding the non-existence of the grasped object (*grāhya*), establishing this as the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).

This means that within this stage, one first contemplates that the four factors—the grasped objects of name (*nāman*), meaning (*artha*), intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and distinction (*viśeṣa*)—are all transformations of one's own mind, existing only as provisional designations (*prajñapti*), and that no real entity can be found therein.
It is established [as the stage of Heat] because it is the first attainment of the preliminary signs (*pūrvanimitta*) that precede the sun of wisdom.
The "attainment of clarity" (*ālokalabdha*) is so named because it is the precursor to the fire of the Path attained therein; it is also called "heat" (*uṣmagata*).

In the present text, the Buddha’s awakening is identified with the initial attainment of the light of the sun of wisdom; since this is a designation based on a conventional agreement, it is termed the "attainment of clarity.

Because the attainment of clarity has the same meaning as heat, the current text is overly concise; one should consult the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) for a comprehensive understanding.
Furthermore, by means of one’s own mind, one attains the stage of the "Bright Crown" (*prabhā-mauli*). The first two phrases invert the meaning previously stated:
whereas previously one turned the Buddha-wisdom into one's own causal mind, now one draws upon one's own causal mind to become Buddha-wisdom;

whereas previously one relied on the fruition to cultivate the cause, now one draws upon the cause to achieve the fruition. Regarding the terms "relying" and "not relying," this refers to the former [stage].

The characteristic of warmth has not yet reached its proper stage, but now it has exceeded that stage; therefore, it is said that "the body enters into empty space," yet there is a slight obstruction beneath.
Because the body enters into empty space, it is not a true support; because there is a slight obstruction beneath, it is called a support.
Since this resembles a support but is not a support and exceeds its proper stage, it is termed the "Summit Stage" (*mūrdhan*). Indeed, the "summit" refers to that which is about to...

This refers to that which has transcended what was not yet transcended. The three phrases regarding ascending and descending can be understood through their metaphorical explanation. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"Relying on the concentration of Increasing Clarity (*vṛddhāloka-samādhi*), one gives rise to superior investigation (*vitarka*). Observing that there is no apprehended object (*grāhya*), it is established as the Stage of the Summit (*mūrdhan-bhūmi*).

This means that in this stage, one repeatedly contemplates the four factors—name and so forth—as being transformations of one's own mind; they are merely provisionally established and lack substantial reality."

Because the characteristics of clarity (*āloka*) cannot be attained [as a distinct stage] and yet they increase in intensity, it is called the Stage of Increasing Clarity (*ālokavṛddhi*). Because it is the ultimate point of the "searching examination" (*vitarka*), it is further named the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*).
Previously it was called "Attainment of Clarity" (*ālokalabdha*) because one first attains the light of wisdom; now it is called "Increasing Clarity" because it is intense, hence "increasing.
The meaning of the text is clear and should be thoroughly contemplated until mastery is gained. The section beginning with "The mind and the Buddha" below clarifies the Stage of Patience (*kṣānti*).
The former two [stages] refer to the causal mind producing the resultant wisdom; now, however, because cause and effect are equal, it is said that "the mind and the Buddha are of one essence.

Here, the mind is the causal mind and the Buddha is the resultant wisdom. Since only the cause and the fruit are mutually integrated without partiality, it is said that one "skillfully attains the Middle Way.
The phrase "like patience" (*kṣānti*) below explains this by means of a metaphor: it is like a person exercising patience toward an event.

Because it involves the arousal of desire, yet because it does not involve internal harboring [of resentment], and because it has not yet reached the point where the mind turns away from existing phenomena due to a lack of decisive discernment, it is called "patience" (*kṣānti*).

This is used as a metaphor for the practitioner who, through the mind, accords with the equality of the resultant wisdom and remains silently receptive; yet, because they have not yet attained the state of mutual forgetting, it is termed "patience.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Based on the seal of conforming concentration, one gives rise to the lower grade of 'as-it-is' (*yathābhūta*)."

Wisdom is the definitive sealing and upholding of the absence of anything to be grasped; within this state where there is no grasper, it also accords with the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) of the object to be grasped.
Because the grasped and the grasper are established in mutual dependence, at the time of sealing and acceding to this acceptance, it is collectively designated as "acceptance" (*kṣānti*).

The name "acceptance" is established because both the object and the consciousness are empty. Specifically, regarding the first two meanings, one contemplates the grasped object. (Note: This passage describes the stage of *kṣānti* within the path of insight, emphasizing the realization that the subject and object are mutually dependent and ultimately empty.)

Regarding the objects of perception (*ālambana*), it is said that first one employs inferior-grade investigation (*vitarka*); because it is of an inferior grade, its power is weak. Next, one employs superior-grade investigation;
because it is of a superior grade, its power is strong. By means of these two grades—superior and inferior—one destroys the grasped object (*grāhya*).

Since the grasped object is thus empty, it is called "contemplating the absence of a grasped object. Investigation (*vitarka*) is synonymous with meditative reflection (*dhyāna-cintā*). Now, this is patience (*kṣānti*).

Within this stage, one employs real wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) to destroy the grasping consciousness (*grāhaka-vijñāna*), thereby sealing the emptiness of the preceding object and conforming to the subsequent emptiness of the consciousness itself;
thus it is called "sealing and conforming" (*mudrā-anuloma*). "Sealing and conforming" is synonymous with "patience" (*kṣānti*);

for patience is the precursor to wisdom, just as, for example, the eight patiences and eight knowledges (*aṣṭa-kṣānti-aṣṭa-jñāna*) are identical in the Lesser Vehicle. The following section clarifies the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*). The first phrase承接 (*chéngqián*) refers back to what preceded.
"Mind, Buddha, and consciousness" are dualistic expressions; the Middle Way lies between these two extremes.

These two extremes belong to the peripheries, and the middle and the periphery are merely worldly quantifications. Now, these quantifications are extinguished, and both the middle and the periphery are forgotten.
The following two lines follow from the preceding one: that delusion and awakening are dualistic and belong to the peripheries, as they are contrasted with the Middle Way.

Since these two quantities have been extinguished, the names "middle" and "extreme" can no longer be apprehended; thus it is said that the two have no referent. Quantities are worldly phenomena (*laukika-dharma*);
now that they have been dissolved, one transcends all worlds. Because it is the most supreme, it is called the "Supreme Worldly Stage" (*laukikāgra-dharmā*).
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Based on the immediate concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*), one gives rise to the superior grade of suchness."
The Seal of Wisdom (jñāna-mudrā) that establishes the emptiness of the two graspings constitutes the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgra-dharma).

This means that while in the preceding stage of Patience (kṣānti), one only sealed the emptiness of the grasper, now, at the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma, one seals the emptiness of both simultaneously. Because one will necessarily enter the Path of Seeing immediately thereafter, it is designated as "Immediate" (anantara).
Among the dharmas of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), this is the most supreme; therefore, it is called the Supreme Mundane Dharma. The details are found in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.

This indicates that [the stage] can be realized; however, because that [other system] regards the first bhūmi as the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it contains the expression "entering the path of seeing.
Now, in this Sūtra of the Perfect Teaching, having ascended to the first bhūmi, one has already destroyed thirty-one grades of ignorance—how could this stage merely be called the "path of seeing"?
Although the principles differ, the contemplation of the Dharma is not distinct; therefore, it is cited for explanation, borrowing a name from another system to describe the Perfect Teaching.
As explained by Wu Xing:
"The good man Ānanda, regarding great bodhi (up to) the point where he enters the intersection of the limit of awakening, is called Equal Awakening.
This section of the sūtra follows the preceding [sections on] the practice of the path and the establishment of the stages; it now clarifies the eleven grounds (*bhūmi*). As for "grounds" (*bhūmi*):

The *Huayan shu* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka-sūtra) states: "The reason they are called 'grounds' (*bhūmi*) is as stated in the *Benye jing* (Sūtra of Fundamental Karma): 'A ground is called such because it sustains (*dhāraṇa*);

it sustains millions of asaṃkhyeya merits, and it is also called the generator of all causes and effects; therefore, it is named a ground. Furthermore, the *Weishi lun* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) states:
'These ten grounds collectively encompass all conditioned and unconditioned merits, taking them as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*')."
Because it serves as the supreme support for the practices being cultivated, allowing them to grow and flourish, it is called a "ground" (*bhūmi*).
Here, the first ground is explained within the *Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra*. The characteristics of the first ground are elucidated through four points of meaning:

since the number and measure [of phenomena] have been repeatedly eliminated and swept away through the four preceding preparatory practices (*prayoga*), and both the center and the extremes have been extinguished, one is thus able to be well-established in great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
"Attaining penetration into great bodhi" refers to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; it is only at this stage that one is said to have attained penetration.
Thus, the stage of Consciousness-Only (*vijñapti-mātra*) is named the "Stage of Penetration" (*prativedha-avasthā*).

"Awakening penetrates the Tathāgata" means that awakening is the Bodhisattva’s initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*), while the Tathāgata is the original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*); because the initial penetrates the original, "exhausting the realm of the Buddha" means reaching its ultimate limit.

The principle of exhaustion is called the Buddha-realm of exhaustion; because this first stage initially penetrates the Buddha’s awakening and is the first instance of exhausting the Buddha-realm, one gives rise to joy.
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "Now, relying on the root treatise, I shall briefly explain the names of the stages. The treatise says:

"Having accomplished the unsurpassed practices for one's own benefit and the benefit of others, and having first ascended to the station of the noble ones, one experiences great joy; therefore, it is called the Stage of Joy (*Pramuditā-bhūmi*)."

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Because one first attains the nature of an ārya, fully realizes the two kinds of emptiness (*dvaya-śūnyatā*), and is able to benefit oneself and others while giving rise to great joy, it is named the 'Stage of Utmost Joy' (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
The characteristic of abundant joy is detailed in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. The phrase "differentiation of natures" (*visabhāga*) and those following clarify the second stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
The two lines beginning with "differentiation of natures" encompass all the modes of practice within the second stage; though the words are concise, their meaning is complete.

It is truly difficult for those with meager power of understanding to enter [this teaching]; therefore, I shall briefly supplement and explain it by consulting the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Regarding "those of different natures entering into the same": this is explained in detail within the second stage (*bhūmi*) of the *Avataṃsaka*, concerning the nature of the ten virtuous precepts.
It means that because this bodhisattva has realized the nature of *tathatā* (suchness), their very nature is non-killing, their nature is non-stealing, and their nature is non-sexual misconduct.
The nature of non-false speech and so forth—these ten virtuous precepts—are termed "different" when contrasted with the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*), yet they are termed "identical" [to it].
When that different nature of the ten virtues enters into the identical nature of True Suchness, difference cannot be found;
just as the hundred rivers flow into the sea and all lose their original names, so too does the different nature cease. It is through difference that identity is manifested.
If that which is identical perishes differently from the present, then even identity cannot be established; therefore, it is said that "identity also perishes.
Because one is free from the defilements of both identity and difference regarding the violation of precepts, it is called the "Stainless Ground" (*vimalā-bhūmi*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"Because the true and pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) is far removed from the defilements of afflictions that give rise to subtle transgressions, it is called the Stainless Ground. This explains the third ground, wherein purity is most profound.
Because it is free from defilement, there arises purity; when purity reaches its ultimate limit, luminosity (*āloka*) is born. This luminosity is the light of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Because luminosity is born, it is called the "Radiant Ground" (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*). As stated in the third ground of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*:

"The Bodhisattva of this ground perceives the immeasurable benefit of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and perceives the immeasurable faults of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*); thus, toward all sentient beings..."
In every birth, one gives rise to ten kinds of compassionate minds and desires to rely upon the Tathāgata’s wisdom to rescue and deliver sentient beings;

for this reason, one diligently seeks the Buddha-wisdom and delights in hearing the True Dharma. Because the light of wisdom shines forth, it is called the Ground of Radiant Light (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*).

According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it is named the Ground of Radiant Light because one achieves supreme meditative concentration and the great dhāraṇīs of the Great Dharma, thereby able to emit the boundless light of wondrous wisdom.

The "Ground of Ultimate Clarity" (Dharmameghā-bhūmi) indicates the fourth ground. Following the previous explanation of the arising of the intention, the former was the initial emergence of the clarity of wisdom;

now, the clarity has reached its ultimate limit. When clarity is ultimate, the nature-awakening (prakṛti-vijñāna) is perfected. Nature-awakening is the essence (svabhāva), while the clarity of wisdom is the function (vṛtti).
With essence and function fully complete, the flame of superior wisdom (adhiprajñā-jvālā) arises. This function destroys subtle objective shadows; thus it is called a "flame."
The *Huìdì yǎnshù* (Commentary on the Ground of Wisdom) states: "Regarding 'Blazing Wisdom' (*Arciṣmatī*), both the dharma and the metaphor are presented together;

it is because one has newly entered the wisdom of realization and can burn away the firewood of pride regarding the understanding of dharmas from the preceding ground. That sutra explains in detail the internal contemplation of the body as body and so forth, but this text omits such details for brevity.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: "Abiding securely in the most excellent factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), one burns away the afflictions."
Because the flames of the firewood of wisdom increase, it is named the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*). All the lower stages of illumination are the five stages [prior to this].
The *Huayan shu* (Avataṃsaka Commentary) quotes the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, which states:

In this passage, all that is identical is ultimate truth-wisdom, while all that is different is worldly wisdom.
The knowledge of the various crafts, the five vidyās, and the four Vedas—these two being mutually contradictory, neither can reach this stage.
"To reach" (prati) means to arrive at; because at this stage one is able to harmonize the aforementioned similarities and differences, it is called the Stage Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā bhūmi*).

Since none of the preceding four stages can surpass it, the meaning of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is likewise the same here. Below, the six unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) [dharmas] are explained.
This is truly because, having thoroughly exhausted all aspects of similarity and difference within the preceding five stages, one enters the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) Suchness;

As the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "It is called the Manifest Stage. Furthermore, the *Vyavasthāna-śāstra* says: "It is called the Non-abiding [in Saṃsāra] Stage."

First, it is called "Far-Going" (*dūraṅgama*) because, through the excellent cultivation of signlessness (*animitta*), one reaches the limit of signlessness. Second, it is called "Far-Going" because the stage of effortful application (*prayoga*) has reached its ultimate limit.

Third, it is called "Far-Going" because it transcends what preceded it. The present text states that reaching the limit of true suchness (*tathatā-paryanta*) is precisely reaching the limit of signlessness;
as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: "Reaching the abode of signlessness, one stands at the very end of effortful application and emerges beyond."
Because this stage is called "Far-Going" (*dūraṅgama*), it transcends the paths of the world and the two vehicles; for it reaches the ultimate limit of all conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*).
Yet, because one has not yet ascended to the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra states that no afflictions (*kleśa*) manifest.

Thus, it is not called "existent," as the mind seeking the wisdom of the Tathāgata is not yet fulfilled; nor is it called "non-existent. Therefore, even if one were to become a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), [one would still remain within this stage].

The analogy illustrates the seventh stage: it refers to the Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*), who is the most excellent among humans; though he has not yet entered the ranks of the devas, he is still called a human.
This is precisely that meaning. "One True" below clarifies the eighth stage.

Within the previous seven stages, although one reaches the limit of true thusness (*tathatā*), as soon as that limit is reached, the mark of exhaustion has not yet been forgotten. Now, what is termed "one true thusness" is purely uniform.
In True Suchness (*tathatā*), all functional activities are stilled; therefore, it is called "immovable.

Scriptures such as the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Laṅkāvatāra* both contain the metaphor of crossing a great river in a dream: while one has not yet crossed, one employs various skillful means and exerts great courage and vigor with the desire to cross the great river;
yet once the dream has awakened, both the active and inactive modes of practice are stilled.
Therefore, it is named "Immovable" (*acalā*). The current text is too concise; one should consult that [other source] for a full understanding. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"Because non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) flows on spontaneously and continuously, and its characteristics and functions cannot be moved by afflictions (*kleśa*), it is called the Immovable Stage.

A detailed explanation is as stated in the commentaries (*ṭīkā*). The passage beginning with "Manifesting the Truth" below clarifies the nine stages. Within the first eight stages, one is merely able to remain pure...
Although True Suchness has not yet been able to manifest its function, it is now able to do so within this stage;
therefore, it is named "Excellent Wisdom. In this stage, the Bodhisattva acts as a Great Dharma Master.

Suppose all sentient beings throughout the great trichiliocosm were each to pose difficult questions using immeasurable modes of speech and sound, each being different from the others—[the Bodhisattva would be able to respond to them all].
The Bodhisattva, moreover, uses a single voice to provide universal explanations for all, causing their minds to rejoice and each to attain the joy of the Dharma;

his eloquence is unyielding and its meaning unobstructed, as the four analytical knowledges flow like a cascading river, surging forth without exhaustion—this is precisely the functioning of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Since this functioning of True Suchness is itself "excellent wisdom" (*sādhumati*), it is so named. The Commentary states: "As for the word 'excellent'..."
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Because of attaining the most excellent unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*). The commentary by Bodhisattva Asvabhāva explains:
"This means attaining the most excellent fourfold unimpeded analytical knowledge (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*). Among all forms of knowledge, this is the most preeminent;
because it is wisdom (*prajñā*), it is called 'Excellent Wisdom' (*Suvijñapti*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "One achieves the subtle and wondrous fourfold unimpeded analytical knowledge."
Because one is able to preach the Dharma skillfully throughout the ten directions, it is called the Stage of Good Intelligence (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
The passage from "Ānanda" downward concludes by manifesting the perfection of the merit of cultivation to clarify the eleventh stage.

The section from "Ānanda" down to "the stage of cultivation" (*bhāvanā-avasthā*) should be connected with the subsequent phrase "Equal Enlightenment" (*samyag-avabodha*). The section from "the compassionate cloud" (*maitrī-chāyā*) down to "Equal Enlightenment" should be connected to what follows this point.

Why is this so? According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, the various stages from the preceding ones are specifically categorized into five positions: the first thirty minds prior to the [ten] bhūmis are called the Stage of Provisions (*sambhāra-avasthā*);

the stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, and the First Worldly Dharma are named the Stage of Application (*prayoga-avasthā*); ascending to the first bhūmi is the Stage of Thorough Penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*);
the stages from the second bhūmi upward are the Stage of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*); and continuing until the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is the [final] stage.

Regarding the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*), that treatise does not open a separate [stage] for Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) after the ten stages. At the end of the ninth fascicle, it states:

"In each stage, two kinds of delusion (*moha*) are abandoned. Regarding the period after the ten stages, it says: "There exist seeds of innate, subtle cognitive obstructions (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) as well as seeds of spontaneous afflictive obstructions (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*);
when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, these are all abandoned simultaneously, and one enters [the ultimate stage]."
The Tathāgata’s stage is established here to clarify precisely that which is severed by Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi)—namely, the final ignorance.
Thus, it is only upon reaching Equal Enlightenment that one is said to have completed the cultivation of practice and entered the ultimate stage of Subtle Enlightenment (sūkṣma-bodhi).

Therefore, it should be known that this passage concerning Ānanda and those following should have been placed under the section on Equal Enlightenment; its presence here is an error introduced during the translation process.

This is because the names of the stages listed in the present sutra correspond exactly to the sequence in the treatise; therefore, citing that [treatise] as proof should leave no room for further doubt.
Regarding the phrase "the compassionate shade and the wondrous cloud" (*maitrī-chāyā-megha*), which correctly elucidates the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*):

does it not seem too brief to encompass the entirety of the characteristics of practice (*lakṣaṇa*) of the tenth stage? "Compassion" (*maitrī*) is the dharma, and "shade" (*chāyā*) is a metaphor; this refers to the bodhi of this stage.
Because the Bodhisattva covers all sentient beings with a compassion that accords with the Dharma-realm, it is called the "Cloud of Wondrous Compassion" (*miao-yun*);
this "Cloud of Wondrous Compassion" clarifies the essence of practice and clarifies the wondrous finger of the teaching of the Dharma. To summarize the metaphor:

the Bodhisattva of this stage, like a great cloud of the Great Dharma and Great Wisdom, universally covers the inconceivable; therefore, it is called the "Cloud of Wondrous Compassion. *Nirvāṇa* is what is realized.
The essence of the Way covers all; because it is the realm of nirvāṇa, praised for the merit of the great Dharma and great wisdom of the Bodhisattvas, it is able to universally cover nirvāṇa.
This "Dharma-ocean" is a metaphor used to illustrate the greatness of nirvāṇa, which is like the sea.
However, this metaphor merely takes up the sense of containing the hundred rivers and reflecting immeasurable images; if one were to compare its actual magnitude, it would not suffice as a parallel.
The greatness of *nirvāṇa* and the virtues of the ocean are insufficient to fully describe it; these are merely partial metaphors.

In the *Śūtra* and the *Vyākhyā*, the meaning of "clouds" (*yún*) is explained in detail, though the meaning of "benevolent shade" (*cí yīn*) is not explicitly stated. Regarding "clouds," there are briefly three meanings:
first, the sense of containing water; second, the sense of covering the sky; and third, the sense of pouring down rain. Furthermore, it is said that clouds possess...

The four meanings and one analogy illustrate wisdom; the second analogy illustrates the *dharmakāya*; the third illustrates the *nirmāṇakāya*; and the fourth illustrates the cause of cultivation through extensive learning (*bahuśruta*).

In this sutra, "concealing *nirvāṇa*" corresponds to the meaning of "concealing space" [in the previous analogy]. While that [previous passage] clarifies the point by means of an analogy, this explains it by means of the Dharma;

thus, their intent is largely the same. Furthermore, the two meanings of "containing water" and "pouring rain" are both fully contained within the character for "cloud" (*megha*), as stated in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.

The thirteenth [verse] says: In the tenth stage, by means of the gateways of samādhi and dhāraṇī, all causes of the permeation of hearing are gathered and pervade the ālayavijñāna, just as floating clouds pervade the sky;
by means of these clouds of the permeation of hearing, in every single moment and in every single aspect, [it can...]
Each and every excellence rains down immeasurable and boundless Dharma-rain from each and every pore, sufficing all sentient beings who are to be converted;
because it is able to act like a cloud and rain, it is called the "Dharma-Cloud Ground" (*dharmameghā bhūmi*).

The general meaning of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* does not go beyond what has been cited. Below, the text clarifies the eleven grounds. Regarding the phrase "The Tathāgata flows against the current": as for the Tathāgata...

The coming [of the Tathāgata] is the fruit; when the Tathāgata’s own self-awakening is fulfilled, he again gives rise to subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) and flows against the current to respond to what is elicited by others.

Thus, at the final moment of mind in the tenth stage, the Bodhisattva’s fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) proceeds in accordance with the flow and reaches the Tathāgata’s original awakening (*prakṛti-awakening*).

When these two limits—the original awakening of the Tathāgata and the initial awakening of the Bodhisattva—enter into one another and merge in equality, it is called [the state of] "box-and-seal" union (*samaya-mudrā*).

The Perfectly Enlightened One has thus explained this according to the text; yet when one attempts to measure the realm of the sages with ordinary worldly intellect, the wondrous meaning cannot be fully expressed through language.
If one were to claim that there is a Tathāgata existing externally who is to be united with as a "self," it would be identical to heterodox teaching.

Rather, it is that today, by cultivating and realizing *ādikṣānti-bodhi* (initial enlightenment), I have accorded with my own originally inherent, natural, and wondrous *tathāgata-bodhi*. This is the Tathāgata’s reversal [of delusion].

The flow arises from the entirety of nature as practice; when the Bodhisattva proceeds in accordance with this until it becomes the entirety of practice that is itself nature, then practice and nature are initially brought into mutual integration.
Therefore, this is called Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). This "I" of one mind is not something existing externally and separately. Only in this way does it accord with the correct teaching.
"Proceeding until" (*shun-hsing er zhi*)—the word "until" (*zhi*) refers precisely to arriving at home. This is explained extensively in the *Shuchao*.

Citing sutras and śāstras to prove these points, it is briefly stated that in the single moment of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) following the tenth stage, it is called "Equal Enlightenment" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), while the second moment is called "Sublime Enlightenment" (*su-buddha*). Furthermore, it says:

"The wisdom of a Bodhisattva who has reached the ultimate stage is equal to the wisdom of a Tathāgata; because they are without distinction, yet distinguished [by their specific names], it is called 'Equal'."
The meaning of awakening is indeed wondrous and profound; the boundary of awakening can only be personally realized through direct realization—how could words ever reach it?
As with the preceding stages, I have merely followed the scriptural text to provide a brief, connected explanation.

Fearing that I might not yet be intimate with the Way and thus dare not confuse the truth with my own arbitrary opinions, I have cited other sutras and treatises, as the scriptural text is extremely concise and difficult for scholars to fathom its profound efficacy.
This completed statement supplements and explains its meaning; its ancestral lineage has a specific source and does not merely construct empty rhetoric to mislead future students.
From the previous stage of "threefold advancement" onwards, through the "initiation of practice" and "establishment in the position," one reaches this ultimate stage of the sages.

The following section separately clarifies the "mind of the final moment of Equal Enlightenment," concluding by manifesting that the realization of the fruit is what is certified by the holy path. It is the ultimate limit.

This is the concluding section; therefore, the subsequent text states: "In this way, through these three progressive stages, one is well able to accomplish the fifty-five levels of the true path to Bodhi.
This serves to clarify the beginning and end of the sacred positions, so that one may know where the meaning of the text ultimately leads and that its source and flow remain undisturbed.
"Ānanda, from the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), if one views it otherwise, it is called a false view.

This section of the sutra concludes by clarifying the beginning and end of the noble stages (*ārya-bhūmi*) to indicate the realization attained, so that one may know how the provisional stations reach their ultimate source.
That the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) are like a temporary lodging and all are within the single mind (*ekacitta*)—this is the correct entry. "Dry Wisdom" is...
The phrase "beginning with Equal Enlightenment" (*samyaksambodhi*) concludes the preceding section on the beginning and end of the stages of the sages.

Following this, from the words "already perfected as enlightenment," there is a separate indication of the initial stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*) within the Vajra-like Samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*) of the final mind of Equal Enlightenment.
Other masters, failing to understand this, mistakenly identify this Vajra Dry Wisdom as referring back to the "habitual tendencies of desire" mentioned in the preceding text.

The initial stage of "Drying" within the "Drying Wisdom" (Kanhui) leads to no small degree of self-delusion and deluding others. Why is this? Although the names are the same, their meanings are vastly different;
one marks the beginning and the other the end, which is perfectly clear and evident, yet people simply lack the power of understanding.

As for these words regarding the "Stage of Initial Drying Wisdom" within this Diamond Mind (Vajracitta), doubts have likely persisted for a long time. Though I, a fool, have traversed various [texts],...
In reality, there was no way to verify this through formal examination. One day, while reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, I came upon the "Chapter on the Ten Concentrations," which states:

"Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, by means of adamantine wisdom (*vajrajñāna*), universally enters the Dharma-realm. This passage specifically pertains to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samalaṃbuddhi*).

Since both [the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* and the *Avataṃsaka*] employ the term "adamantine wisdom," it can be known that this refers to the final mind of Equal Enlightenment. Furthermore, the Wu... [text ends]

The *Sūtra of the Adornment of the Mahāyāna* (*Mahāyāna-alaṃkāra-sūtra*), cited by Master Xing, states that within the nature of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) there is a person named Vajradhvaja-jñāna;

this is also the same as the present case. Furthermore, treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* state that after ascending the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), when the "diamond-like samādhi" (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, one suddenly severs the seeds of the subtle, innate obstacles and enters the stage of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
Is it not this that gives rise to delusion and eliminates attainment? Furthermore, the tenth fascicle of the present sutra states:

"From within mutual functioning, one can enter the Bodhisattva’s adamantine *ganhui* (dry wisdom). If this refers to the *ganhui* prior to the stage of faith (*śraddhā*), why would one enter from within mutual functioning?
Mutual functioning is precisely the *ganhui* of the stage of faith; how could it exist after the stage of faith? It further says: "In this way, one transcends..."

Since the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmana*), the ten grounds (*bhūmi*), and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) have already transcended all these positions, it can be known that the mind following Equal Enlightenment is designated as the "Vajra Dry Wisdom" (*vajra-śuṣka-prajñā*).

This is because it serves as the vanguard between the flames of Equal Enlightenment and the subtle perfection of Wondrous Enlightenment (*vimalā-saṃbodhi*). One should know that prior to the stages of faith, there is the drying up of desire and love; thus, "dry" (*śuṣka*) refers to this state.
"O Wisdom, now that ignorance has first been dried up, you possess two meanings of wisdom as vast as heaven and earth, yet people themselves fail to perceive this.
Someone might object: 'Previously, when desire was first dried up, it was not yet connected to the Tathāgata’s stream of Dharma, and thus it was called the Ground of Dry Wisdom;
but now that ignorance has first been dried up, how could it possibly not be connected to the Ocean of Wondrous Adornment?'"
The answer is: The Vajra-dry-wisdom (vajra-śuṣka-prajñā) is merely the initial manifestation of the exhaustion of ignorance.
Although it is contiguous with wondrous enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), one has not yet assumed its responsibility; thus, it may also be said that one has not yet attained it.

Nevertheless, while ordinary beings approach this with coarse minds, using many words and elaborate phrases, the sage’s realm of principle and their spiritual effort truly reside in a single thought-moment, as Qingliang [Chengguan] has stated.
The *Chao* (Commentary) cites the *Vyākhyāyukti* on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, stating:

"According to this treatise, within the single moment of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) following the ten stages, one is termed 'Equal Enlightenment' (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), and the second moment is termed 'Sublime Enlightenment' (*vimala-bodhi*). One can thus know with certainty that the profound mind of a single moment is beyond the reach of ordinary intellect.
Furthermore, regarding the sequence of practice, one must believe that the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) is the beginning and the Diamond-like Concentration is the end.

"Dry Wisdom" (*kandhī*) marks both the beginning and the end; since "Dry Wisdom" is thus indicated at both extremes, one must carefully contemplate its meaning to see that it must exist in every stage. Why is this?

It is because when the first grade of ignorance is initially dried up, wisdom is present; as one ascends to subsequent stages, this remains true for each and every one—how could these not be instances of "Dry Wisdom"?
Generally speaking, each succeeding stage is deeper than the preceding one, as is the case in the present text.
This is merely an abbreviation; therefore, only the beginning and the end are indicated to reflect what lies between them.

Those who exhaustively investigate the principle should contemplate this deeply and examine it with care. Thus, there are successive layers of concluding summaries that point to the wondrous enlightenment realized.

"Successive layers" refers to the various preceding stages. "Twelve, both single and multiple" means that regarding the first stage, it is "single," while regarding the ten stages, they are "multiple. "Multiple" refers to...

Regarding the meaning of "layered" (*chóngdié*): there are seven single stages and five layered groups. The "single" refers to the three progressive stages of *śuklavidarśana-bhūmi*, the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*), and *sambodhyanga*;
these are called the seven single [stages]. The "layered" refers to the ten stages each of faith (*śraddhā*), abiding (*sthiti*), practice (*caryā*), direction (*mukha*), and ground (*bhūmi*);
these are called the five layered [groups]. Furthermore, these twelve layered stages collectively encompass all positions; when encompassed collectively, they are not subject to comparison.
Regarding the "fifty-five stages" mentioned below: this excludes the aforementioned three progressive stages and the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśana-bhūmi*).

From the stage of Faith (*śraddhā*) up to Equal Enlightenment (*samayakīti*), there are fifty-five stages, at which point one finally reaches the destination. The final two lines serve as a formal conclusion, pointing to the realization of the fruit of the Way.
That which is called "Sublime Enlightenment" (*samyaksaṃbodhi*) refers to the ultimate nirvāṇa, in which one is forever separated from the parents of ignorance. This is the true reality.
At the limit where all dharmas are non-arising, Prajñā is non-arising;

this non-arising of non-arising is called Great Nirvāṇa, which constitutes the pure Dharmakāya abiding in the Land of Constant Quiescent Light—this is the mark of the Buddha of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). What is now termed the Unsurpassed Way is precisely Great Nirvāṇa.
The various [preceding] stages mentioned below are overturned to reveal that those prior positions were merely temporary halting places on the journey toward the ultimate source.
This meaning should not be considered as truly existent, nor should it be grasped as non-existent; therefore, it is illustrated by ten types of analogies, such as illusions and so forth.
Herein, "vajra" (diamond/thunderbolt) is used as a metaphor to signify that the wisdom of contemplation in these various stages can sever the afflictions;

thus, its meaning of "vajra" is not the same as that of the "Vajropama-samādhi" (Diamond-like Samādhi) occurring after the mind of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). That [latter] is the metaphor.
This is because these metaphors refer to the contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā*) at the stage of the cause (*hetu-bhūmi*). Regarding the ten kinds of metaphors, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"Like an illusion, like a mirage, like the moon in water, like space, like an echo, like a city of the *gandharvas*, like a dream, like a reflection in a mirror, and like a transformation—these are the ten.
Because they are what is contemplated at the stage of the fruition (*phala-bhūmi*), they are called "profound metaphors. *Śamatha* is the translated term [for the former].

The preceding term *vipaśyanā* is translated as "contemplation" (*guān*), which is a synonym for *samādhi*. Among the three meanings [of *samādhi*], the meaning of *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) is omitted;
logically, it should be fully present, for at each stage one employs these three contemplations to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Furthermore, the two characters "Tathāgata" refer directly to the three contemplations, as they are that which is possessed within the mind of a Tathāgata. Moreover, [this applies] both before and after...

All these texts clarify only the two meanings of *śamatha* (calm) and *vipaśyanā* (insight); *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) serves merely to harmonize and integrate them, as it has no separate essence of its own.
Therefore, they present only these two meanings. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* is likewise; this can be understood through careful study.
"Pure cultivation and realization" refers to not clinging to the two extremes and not abiding in the middle way, but being perfectly integrated and unimpeded.
"Because one cultivates and realizes [the path], one enters progressively deeper" means that one advances step by step through each stage without skipping over them;

this is the "gradual progression of the non-gradual. Ānanda, thus [it is said] below, to summarize from beginning to end and attribute the merit to the first step, it is like the principle of not forgetting the first basket of earth when building a mountain several *zhang* high. "Having done this," etc., refers to the world.
The Venerable One has repeatedly and earnestly instructed us to discern between the paths of the heterodox and the orthodox;

as observed through the three contemplations and ten metaphors above, that which is neither "existent" nor "non-existent," yet remains biased in its mind, is called heterodox contemplation. This concludes the section on the "Realization" (Skt. *adhigama*);
hereafter begins the section on the "Concluding Scripture" (*sūtra-paryavasāna*).
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince... (up to)... "The Śūraṅgama Samādhi of the Ten Thousand Practices; you should uphold it.
This section concludes the three essentials of principle, practice, and realization as previously established.

Mañjuśrī then requests the naming of the sūtra to serve as a model for future generations, so that those who uphold it may have a basis for reference. Furthermore, this name of the sūtra [is derived] from Mañjuśrī.
The reason for this special invitation is that what is revealed here is the perfect principle, the perfect practice, and the perfect realization;
were it not for one of great wisdom and virtue, one could never definitively establish the names and summon the essence to serve as the structural framework for the principles and applications.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī undertook these matters from beginning to end: first, he went to provide protection by holding mantras; next, he clarified the assembly’s realization of their own nature.
This selection of the perfect penetration follows next. Now, I again request that the title of this sutra be finalized.

One can truly know that the profound and subtle mysteries of this scripture lie precisely in these words. Mañjuśrī’s mastery of translation was evident before us; he is truly foremost in realized wisdom.

Is he not one who possesses great wisdom and great virtue? Furthermore, considering the intent behind Mañjuśrī’s inquiry regarding the name, it must surely encompass the request for the five [perfections].

"Chapters" refers to the name (nāman), essence (svabhāva), thesis (artha), function (kriyā), and the characteristics of the teaching (śāsana-lakṣaṇa). To say "receiving and upholding" means to resolutely uphold these five chapters; how could it refer to the name alone?
One must understand that when a name is established, beneath the name there must be its essence;

the essence must have its thesis; and since there is a thesis, there must be its function. Apart from these, there are no further characteristics of the teaching; they are simply the distinctions among the name and the others.

The four chapters constitute the aspect of the teaching (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*). Therefore, having raised the names [of the five chapters] as a request, the subsequent four chapters necessarily follow them.

Thus, one should know that "receiving and upholding" refers precisely to receiving and upholding these five chapters. Nevertheless, the five chapters of the present sutra are assigned to their respective categories as previously divided;
these are the five things answered in the following text, which are called "names," and what is revealed by these names is the eternally abiding reality.

The true mind is the essence; the three—wondrous generosity and so forth—are the thesis, for one proceeds toward the wondrous fruit by means of the wondrous cause. To shatter the false and reveal the true is its function. When harmonizing with the times and establishing the teachings, the "fresh butter" (navanīta) is taken as the characteristic of the teaching. These constitute the meaning of the five chapters of this present sutra, established according to ancient precedents rather than being a product of arbitrary speculation.
