Question: Why is it that before [the teaching] is complete, you immediately ask for the name of the sutra? Answer: This is because the previous sutra has already fully demonstrated the three meanings of principle (*li*), practice (*xing*), and realization (*zheng*).
Since the primary purpose of this sutra has already been accomplished, this question establishes the title of the preceding section of the teaching.

Although the subsequent text contains the "Seven Refinements" (*qīngyán*) and detailed expositions on the various *māras*, these also pertain to the matters of practice and realization; they serve solely as the practice.
These are merely the remnants of the realization; therefore, Wēn-líng’s designation of them as "aids to the Way" is precisely in accord with this.
Furthermore, the seven destinies are the objects of focus within the stage of practice (*caryā*), while the various māras are the obstructions to the stage of realization (*siddhi*).

This was skillfully compiled by the sūtra-recorder, who appended these remnants after the conclusion of the sūtra, intending to provide a systematic arrangement between the stages of practice and realization.

The *Guàn* (Commentary) is neither overly complex nor too simple, being easy to understand; therefore, those who read this scripture should master its underlying intent, for then there will be no further room for doubt.

Regarding the passage beginning with "The Buddha told," the World-Honored One here provides the formal response to the five names. First, he answers the first name, "Great Buddha-Crown" (*Mahā-uṣṇīṣa*), which has already been explained in the preface to the title.

Now, taking advantage of this opportunity, I shall briefly explain it according to the text. As for the title, I have previously provided a detailed explanation in accordance with the principles of the meaning.
Since principle can harmonize phenomena, all phenomena reside within principle; now, relying again upon phenomena to clarify that they have a source, we speak of the "Great Buddha-Crown.
This refers to the phenomenon of the Buddha’s crown emitting light, wherein emanated Buddhas proclaim the mantra.
It is called "non-action" (wuwei) and "non-seeing" (wujian), yet it reveals all forms of seeing. Among all phenomena, the Buddha-crown is most honored and unsurpassed; it proceeds from non-action.

In its practice, principle and phenomenon are unified; it elucidates the ultimate principle, which culminates in the perfect and ultimate state, for there is nothing that does not emerge from full enlightenment (saṃbuddha). Thus, it is called the "Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa. *Siddhārthapāṇḍarā* is a transliterated term as seen previously, which is the name of the Heart-Mantra. Regarding the "Unsurpassed Jewel Seal," it explains both the Exoteric and Esoteric meanings. The "Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa" refers to the Exoteric meaning. *Siddhārtha*... [text continues] ...is the Esoteric meaning. *Pāṇḍarā* means white, referring to the white silk cord. *Mudrā* means seal, signifying the binding of the hands. It is called "Unsurpassed" because it is the most supreme among all mantras and seals. It is called a "Jewel" because it is the most precious among all dharmas. It is called a "Seal" because it is the most efficacious among all methods. It is called "Unsurpassed Jewel Seal" because it is the most supreme, precious, and efficacious among all dharmas. It is called "Heart-Mantra" because it is the essence of all dharmas. It is called "Dharani" because it can sustain and maintain all dharmas. It is called "Great Dharani" because it can sustain and maintain all dharmas universally. It is called "Great Uṣṇīṣa" because it is the crown of the head of all Buddhas. It is called "Great White Canopy" because it can cover and protect all sentient beings. It is called "Great Compassionate Mother" because it gives birth to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. It is called "Great Sun" because it illuminates all darkness. It is called "Great Moon" because it cools all heat. It is called "Great Fire" because it burns away all afflictions. It is called "Great Wind" because it sweeps away all obstructions. It is called "Great Water" because it washes away all defilements. It is called "Great Earth" because it supports all worlds. It is called "Great Void" because it encompasses all phenomena. It is called "Great Wisdom" because it realizes all truths. It is called "Great Liberation" because it transcends all bonds. It is called "Great Bliss" because it bestows all happiness. It is called "Great Peace" because it removes all suffering. It is called "Great Nirvana" because it reaches the ultimate end. It is called "Great Samadhi" because it stabilizes the mind. It is called "Great Dhyana" because it concentrates the spirit. It is called "Great Prajna" because it discerns all things. It is called "Great Upaya" because it adapts to all capacities. It is called "Great Karuna" because it pities all beings. It is called "Great Maitri" because it loves all beings. It is called "Great Vajra" because it is indestructible. It is called "Great Padma" because it is unstained. It is called "Great Karma" because it accomplishes all deeds. The term *tathāgata* carries the meaning of "esoteric significance," for this single name encompasses both the exoteric and the esoteric.

The "Jewel Seal" (*ratnamudrā*) signifies the rectification of heterodoxy and the definitive establishment [of truth]. It is like the official seal of a magistrate established to prevent fraud and forgery;

by means of this metaphor, it indicates that these two scriptures—exoteric and esoteric—seal all phenomena so that they are in profound accord with the Buddha-mind, ensuring that no heterodox elements can disturb the truth. Thus, it is worthy of veneration.

Because it is weighty, it is called the "Precious Seal" (*ratnamudrā*). As the Sūtra says: "The three—aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)—are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
This is precisely the meaning of the seal, namely, the Seal of the Single Reality (*ekadharmamudrā*).

The two lines beginning with "In the ten directions" also apply to both Exoteric and Esoteric teachings; that is to say, these two types of sūtras, Exoteric and Esoteric, are the very eyes by which all Buddhas attain *bodhi*.
The eye is pure because it is unimpeded; regarding the five eyes, it is explained through both metaphorical and literal designations.

Because the eye encompasses all things without omission, it is likened to the "ocean eye. Among these five eyes, the *dharmacakṣus* (dharma-eye) illuminates the conventional, the *prajñācakṣus* (wisdom-eye) realizes the ultimate truth, and the *buddhacakṣus* (Buddha-eye) perfectly contemplates the three truths.
As for the remaining two—the *māṃsacakṣus* (flesh-eye) and the *divyacakṣus* (heavenly-eye)—they are subsumed within the category of superior nature.
Now, because the meaning of the five eyes is complete, it is called the "Ocean Eye. This is the second name for the protection and salvation of those below.
Regarding "the immediate cause for protection and salvation," this refers to present circumstances. "Immediate" (*qin*) refers to Ānanda; "cause" (*yin*) refers to Ḍākinī.

It can be understood that Ānanda was the Buddha’s own cousin, sharing the same paternal lineage, and is thus called "immediate. As for Ḍākinī, she has had a connection with Ānanda throughout successive kalpas.

Because the karmic conditions of husband and wife still entangle them even now, they are referred to as "causing rescue and protection" and "granting deliverance," spoken of collectively for both individuals;
thus, the word "and" (及) is used. The bhikṣuṇī Śīlabhadrikā is none other than Ḍākinī; the meaning is seen in the preceding text.

Regarding *bodhi* and *samyaksaṃbuddha*, these are explained according to the sense of perfection (*yuan*). Although Ānanda and Ḍākinī have realized the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle, this is merely their [attainment].

"Traces" refers to the fact that [the teachings] have now been dedicated toward the Noble Vehicle (āryayāna) to lead all ordinary beings and followers of the Small Vehicle (hīnayāna) into the ocean of universal knowledge and to cause them to ascend to Great Bodhi;
thus, "Tathāgata" concludes the third name. "Great Square" concludes the fourth name;
herein, "Square" (fang) signifies reality, as it is one of the twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna sūtras.

The Dharma is the method; its "greatness" (*mahat*) refers to the magnitude of the Dharma, and its "extensiveness" (*vistara*) refers to its broad significance. This interpretation is evident from the title itself.

"Greatness" carries the sense of being eternal and pervasive, while "extensiveness" carries the sense of universal entry. These two meanings mutually support one another: that which is eternal and pervasive extends outward, while that which universally enters penetrates inward.
Not only do they coexist, but they are also able to interpenetrate. Furthermore, "method" (*upāya*) maintains both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*), and is fully endowed with them.
The two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) thus clarify the meaning of the four dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*) in the *Avataṃsaka*.
Since the present sutra is subsumed within the Vaipulya section, it belongs to the Mahāyāna class. The "King of the Wondrous Lotus" is spoken of by way of analogy;
that which is signified by this analogy is the eternally abiding true mind. For while the lotus dwells in the mud yet remains unstained, my own mind is turbid.
Though surrounded by worldly desires, it remains ever-luminous; thus, the lotus is the king of all flowers, and the mind is the mother of all dharmas.

These phenomena and their metaphors correspond in profound harmony; this is merely a brief illustration. Therefore, a poet said: "Behold the purity of the lotus, and you shall know the unstained mind"—this is the intended meaning.
A detailed explanation may be found in the fifth scripture, *The Sutra of the Inconceivable King of Wondrous Names*.

The meaning of "possessing the eight masteries" is understood through mental realization. Furthermore, regarding the lower section on the ten directions, the name *dhāraṇī* is translated as "total retention" (*zongchi*).
This is because it retains in its entirety all mundane and supramundane names, meanings, dharmas, and practices;
thus, it refers to the meaning of the mantra. Consequently, the name of the mantra is used [for the scripture], as the Sūtra says: "It gives birth to all Buddhas. Thus, the mantra is the Buddha.
The term "Mother" (*mǔ*) is also a concise metaphorical expression taken in the sense of "giving birth.

Thus, the upper half of this name, "Lotus," is explained according to the manifest meaning (*khyāta-artha*), while the lower half, "Dhāraṇī," is explained according to the secret meaning (*guhya-artha*); it is named by combining both the manifest and the secret.

The phrase "Consecration" (*guàn dǐng*) below concludes the fifth name. The explanation is found in the title; however, [the specific focus here is] the four characters "Guanding Zhangju" (Chapter on Consecration).

Regarding the points in the title that have not yet been explained, they shall now be elucidated. According to Changshui’s Commentary (*Sū*), this scripture flows forth from the *Abhiṣeka* section of India.
In India, all mantra chapters are collected into one category called the *Abhiṣeka* section.
"Abhiṣeka" takes its meaning from the conferral of office through consecration at the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*); it is so named because it is honored as supreme among the families of mantras.
Furthermore, in all the sūtras, whatever is named a mantra is designated as having the supreme, secret meaning of empowerment (*abhiṣeka*);
therefore, at the end of the passage, the World-Honored One commands that these five preceding names be upheld as his response.
Having spoken these words, Ānanda immediately [realized] the six grades of subtle afflictions in the cultivation of the mind.

This section of the sutra is Ānanda’s comprehensive summary of the stages of sagehood (*āryabhūmi*). It explains the title and meaning of the scripture, how liberation is attained through the arising of understanding, and how delusions are eliminated by it.
As for the "secret seals" (*guhyamudrā*), their meaning is seen in the previous explanation; furthermore, having heard the subsequent [teachings], he summarizes the five names mentioned above.
Because it represents the perfect meaning of the Mahāyāna, it is called "Complete" (Liao); this is the meaning of the title itself.

Regarding "Sudden Enlightenment" (*dunwu*) below, this correctly clarifies the sense of awakening to understanding so as to give rise to and eliminate delusions; "Dhyāna" (*channa*) here refers to the combined meanings of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, citing one to encompass all three.
"Holy Stages" (*shengwei*) refers to the fifty-five stages, meaning that one has received and realized the aforementioned holy stages and all the various sages therein.
Each [of these] is fully endowed with the three contemplations of *dhyāna*; their profound observation is perfectly integrated, which is called the "superior and wondrous principle.

That "the mind and its deliberations are void and coagulated" is due to the removal of delusions; thus, the mind attains a state of void coagulation, which is precisely the meaning of the perfect integration of contemplative wisdom.
This section clarifies the limits of severing delusions: regarding the six grades of cultivation within the three realms, the "three realms" refers to...
There are nine stages (*bhūmi*), and each stage contains nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned through mental cultivation; this constitutes the stage of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
From the second fruit up to the third fruit, all are termed those on the Path of Cultivation. These "six grades" refer to the first six grades of afflictions within one stage of the lower realm;
because one realizes the second fruit by abandoning these six grades, they are called the "six grades of the mind cultivated. Ānanda, at the beginning...
The fruit [of the path] belongs to those at the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*); what is now called "cultivating the mind" refers to the subsequent realization.

This is because the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) are spoken of in contrast to the afflictions of seeing (*darśana-heya-kleśa*), and thus they are described as "subtle. This refers to Ānanda’s actual limit of realization.

Furthermore, if this is discussed according to the Mahāyāna treatises on the Four Reliances (*catvāraḥ pratisaraṇāḥ*) and so forth, it should be understood as explained in the *Sijiao yi* (Outline of the Four Teachings). Someone may ask: "In the text..."

Question: Regarding the sudden awakening to *dhyāna* and the cultivation of progress toward the holy stages (*āryabhūmi*), as well as the supreme subtle principle—how can it be said that the severing of delusions refers to the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle?
Answer: As the subsequent scripture states: "In principle, there is sudden awakening, and through this awakening, [delusions] are eliminated all at once;

yet phenomena are not suddenly removed, for they are exhausted only through gradual stages. Therefore, this interpretation is made based on the actual facts. Having concluded the naming [of the stages], the explanation is finished.
The following section concerns the remnants of the practice and realization [of the preceding].
That is to say, from "rising from his seat and prostrating at the Buddha’s feet" up to "for these sentient beings,
false habits arise," this passage of the sutra has Ānanda cite the all-pervading perfection of the true mind to deeply investigate where these false habits originate.

This can be understood from the following passage where the sūtra-narrator provides the account. The first two phrases of Ānanda’s own speech at the beginning of the section on "Great Power" (*mahāvega*) are explained as before.
The phrase "skillfully opening up subtle, submerged delusions" appears to connect with the preceding meaning regarding "subtle afflictions.
This is because the translator and the editor have integrated the previous context; here, it is treated according to the general perspective of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*).
The treatise points to the subtle states of both the pervasive and specific delusions to provide proof of their varying degrees of depth;

this is explained in general terms. "Sinking" (chen) carries the meaning of being deep and hidden. Regarding the three phrases beginning with "I": "I" is Ānanda’s self-designation as he articulates his intent for the sake of the entire assembly.
Thus, the two words "joyfully" and "beneficially" apply universally to the gathering. This is based on the primary evidence of the assembly.
Regarding the depth of severing delusions, the World-Honored One provides scriptural evidence below to address the objection:
Ānanda says that since the wondrously luminous, truly pure mind is fundamentally all-pervasive among all sentient beings, there is none who is not complete.
This is just as the grasses and trees of the great earth, though insentient, also manifest from within the nature of True Suchness; how much more so for those with sentience?
Even the most minute and wriggling sentient beings manifest from the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Although there is a distinction between those sentient beings and the insentient, their fundamental, originally pure nature is precisely the true body of the Tathāgata’s Buddhahood.
If one asks: "If living beings and Buddhas are of one essence, why is it that only the Buddhas realize the eternally true and constant, while sentient beings do not?"

"Are there indeed seven distinct destinies, World-Honored One? Below this, the objection is concluded by asking whether these paths, such as the hells, exist inherently, or whether they arise from the deluded habitual tendencies of sentient beings. In the current text, only the six destinies are indicated;
however, since the answer below separately lists the path of the *ṛṣis*, they constitute seven destinies. Generally, the word "etc. (*ādi*) is used to encompass them all.
"World-Honored One, as for the Bhikṣuṇī Ratnapadmagandhā... [up to] ...rejoicing, receiving it upon her head, and maintaining it with purity and without transgression.
This section of the sutra follows the previous discussion on deluded habits to further cite a present event, specifically investigating the private and fixed locations of the various hells.
Regarding "World-Honored One" and below, which cite evidence through a present event, the matter of the Bhikṣuṇī Ratnapadmagandhā is not yet fully detailed.
Regarding the observance of the Bodhisattva precepts, one must restrain both body and mind, maintaining them with unwavering resolve; how much more so for those who practice them authentically?
According to the forty-first precept of the Brahma Net Sūtra: "If one violates any of the ten precepts, one should be taught to repent.

These ten precepts must refer to the ten grave offenses (*daśa-guruka-āpatti*), as they admit of repentance. If one were further to falsely claim that sexual misconduct is not killing, [it would be a grave error].
To commit no theft yet harbor no sense of enmity toward one’s victims constitutes a most grievous false view that denies cause and effect;
such a great lie leads to falling into the Avīci Hell, which is the ultimate extreme of severity. This explains the immediate retribution (*vipāka-phala*).
As for the female organ being the path of birth: if one commits sexual misconduct through this, the fire of retribution likewise issues forth from it, burning limb by limb starting from below.

"Having burned the hundred joints, his entire body is consumed by fire until it becomes ash and embers; this is the provisional retribution (*hua-bao*), while the ultimate fruit lies in the Vaidūrya Hell.
Furthermore, two matters—killing out of anger and false speech—are cited to demonstrate how individual karma (*bie-ye*) enters into collective retribution (*tong-fen-bao*).
In the first two lines, 'first' refers to the name [of the person] being executed, and 'next' refers to the two specific acts; *Gautama* is the specific [name] of Śākyamuni."
The explanation of the surname is as seen previously. Vairāṭya (Líulí) was the illegitimate son of King Prasenajit of Śrāvastī;
the account of his slaughter of the Gautamas is found in detail in the *Vairāṭya-rāja-sūtra* (also known as the *Vaiḍūrya-rāja-sūtra*).
At the time of his birth, a precious lapis lazuli gem appeared, and thus he was named accordingly. He was born of Queen Mallikā and was her younger brother.

The son went to visit Śākyamuni’s maternal kinsmen; there, five hundred Kṣatriyas of the Śākya clan had jointly constructed a lecture hall and invited the Buddha, forbidding all other people from entering this hall first.
Unaware of this prohibition, Vimalakīrti (Liu-li) mistakenly ascended the high seat and was rebuked and expelled by the Śākyas.
It was for the sake of vowing to avenge this grievance that he [attacked the Buddha]. As for Sunakṣatra, he is mentioned in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 30.
The *Sang-kia-she-pin* (Sāṃkṛtyāyanīya-parivarta) states that the World-Honored One himself said:
"If I had not permitted Sunakṣatra to leave the household life, since Rāhula has already done so, Sunakṣatra would next have succeeded to the ancestral royal throne;

his power being unrestrained, he would surely have destroyed the Buddha-dharma. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śu* (Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra) states: "Sunakṣatra was the Buddha’s illegitimate son [庶子], [the elder brother] of Rāhula..."
The Buddha is the mirror of human relations; therefore, he permitted [his] elder brother to leave the household life.

Yet, because [the brother] heard the True Dharma but did not believe or accept it, he severed all roots of goodness and was named an icchantika. He falsely preached that dharmas are empty and denied the Two Truths;
because he slandered the Buddha by means of the doctrine of emptiness, Bao-lianxiang committed sexual misconduct and Liu-li committed killing. Both were good [in their intent].

Xingzao, Wangju, and Sheng all fell into Avīci because they committed their acts together; Ānanda cites these three cases to clarify the principle that while those who act together receive the same retribution, this does not negate the fact that each individual’s original karma brings its own private retribution.
Now, there are two points to consider in this inquiry:

first, although individuals may enter the same portion of hell due to their collective actions, the fundamental karma originally generated by each person is not lost, and thus it will still bring about a private retribution for that individual—just as sexual misconduct invites the iron stake.
The copper pillars on the beds and the false name of the "tongue-pulling plow" signify that each person generates their own karma and experiences its results individually;

this is because it refers to the specific locations of fixed karma. Having finished the inquiry regarding the nature of the hells—asking whether they are naturally formed by Heaven or created by human beings—the text concludes by expressing the intent of the request, saying: "I only pray... and so forth. [End of] Section on the Child.
"Those who are like children" refers to those of the Lesser Vehicle whose wisdom is shallow; because they have not yet reached the perfect realm, they remain stuck in biased views.

Whether they cling to existence or deny it, both constitute grave transgressions. Therefore, this request is made to reveal the reason [for these prohibitions], so that they may maintain the purity of their original resolve and commit no offense.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "How excellent is this question! [This continues] until: "...spontaneously transcending these is called the external division.

This section of the sutra is the Buddha’s response to the preceding question; it is intended to reveal to sentient beings the traces of the ascent and descent of internal and external emotional conceptions, thereby initiating the beginning of the seven destinies.
From "The Buddha told" onwards, before responding to the intent of the question, he first praises the question itself.

[The Buddha] extensively benefits Ānanda by providing a general response to the [notion of] false existence and true non-existence, as well as by designating the two divisions of internal and external.

Regarding Ānanda’s initial inquiry in the first section—asking how the fundamental reality of all Buddhas and sentient beings could have the distinctions of the six realms of rebirth—he now provides a general answer:
all sentient beings are in truth fundamentally true and pure, yet they arise from that delusion.
When one perceives the existence of false perfuming, once this false habituation has arisen, there are then the two divisions of internal and external.
The internal division is the sentiment of desire and attachment; because sentient beings are driven by desire and attachment, they transmigrate through the cycle of birth and death.

Since birth and death are matters pertaining to the internal sphere of sentient beings, they are called the "internal-external" division. This is the superior conception of sentient beings, their transcendent vital energy. By means of this—

Because it transcends the ordinary, it is a matter beyond the scope of sentient beings; therefore, it is called "external. Ānanda, regarding the internal, the following provides a detailed explanation.
Within this explanation, first the "internal" is explained. The first two phrases explain the name of the internal; the subsequent section beginning with "due to various...

explains the meaning of the internal. The initial explanation of the name is clear. As for the explanation of the meaning: it means that because of various forms of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), the emotion of craving is aroused.
Because craving has many varieties, it is called "various" (*nānā*); once these various sentiments have been aroused, they accumulate incessantly and are able to produce the water of craving.

Because craving can provide nourishment, it produces this water of craving. Water is a material thing belonging to the category of form (*rūpa-dharma*), whereas the sentiment of craving arises from deluded thought and belongs to the category of mind (*citta-dharma*).
This is truly because the deluded mind is able to melt deluded form. Below...
The Sūtra says that "interfused delusive thoughts" refers to this very state. Therefore, the following passage concludes by clarifying the characteristics of water produced from thought:
when one thinks of delicious food, saliva flows down the throat; when one recalls a sexual encounter, tears fill the eyes. All these instances of water are produced because of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Regarding "pity" (*anukampā*) and "resentment" (*dveṣa*): pity means to cherish and protect, referring to the cherishing of a loved one upon remembering their departure.
The resentment of this [resentment] refers to the memory of various feelings; when these are thin, resentment and hatred both cause tears to flow.

That which causes the secretion of "love-saliva" through greed for wealth means that greed arises from within, and the love-saliva nourishes the body so that the entire frame becomes lustrous and smooth.
When the mind is attached to sexual matters, the resulting discharge can be known. Ānanda, the lower bonds of all forms of craving are thus summarized above.
Although the causes of craving differ, the flowing liquid is the same. The two terms "flowing" (*liú*) and "binding" (*jié*) each carry a specific meaning:
"flowing" refers to the flowing liquid, while "binding" refers to the fetters. Because emotional craving flows by means of these fetters, they are called "flowing-fetters.

Being heavy and dense, one does not ascend but naturally falls downward; being moist and settling below, this clarifies that craving gives rise to water, thereby manifesting the sense of sinking and falling.
The final phrase concludes the definition of the internal bases (*ādhyātmika-āyatana*). Next, Ānanda, the external bases (*bāhya-āyatana*) are explained.
First, the initial two phrases explain the name of the external bases; "from the various... below explains their meaning. "Thirsting and yearning" refers to longing for superior objects.
"Thirst" is used metaphorically to describe the thought of external longing, just as one who thirsts thinks of drinking; because it is induced by such yearning, it is so called.
The phrase "thirsting and yearning for the Dharma" is an expression that employs both metaphor and literal meaning. Because one admires it from without, empty conceptions arise.

As for "empty conceptions," because the essence of such conceptions is light and buoyant, they are called "empty. When these conceptions accumulate without ceasing, they can generate a superior vital energy (*vāyu*).
This energy necessarily moves upward from below, transcending the ordinary; this can clearly be seen. Therefore, the following conclusion clarifies its superiority.
The signs of transcending the vital energy (*prāṇa*) are as follows: one who maintains the precepts eliminates the turbidity of breaking them, and thus their body becomes light and pure;
one who recites mantras possesses upright righteousness and courageous vigor, being free from flattery and sycophancy, and thus their gaze is majestic and resolute;

because the mantra can destroy what is heterodox, it is called a "mantra-seal" (*dhāraṇīmudrā*); and those who wish to be born in heaven constantly aspire to ascend, and thus they frequently fly upward at night.
Dreams arise from conceptualization; thus they are called "dream-thoughts. When one maintains the Buddha-land in mind, the sacred realm appears according to that recollection.
It can be seen that the meaning of *samādhi* as "mind-only" lies in the fact that external objects are but divisions of the mind.

Because one accumulates superior energy within and yearns for it with intense longing without, one is able to disregard even body and life in serving a teacher—all of this is brought about by superior conceptualization. Ānanda, all such thoughts...

The lower section concludes with the contemplation of the upper realms; although the causes differ, the lightness of their ascent and their soaring motion are the same, as they fly upward without sinking and naturally transcend [the lower realms].

The final phrase concludes by defining the names and meanings of the two external divisions. However, what is clarified by these two internal and external divisions is merely the two terms "sentiment" (*qing*) and "conception" (*xiang*).

This is because the retribution of the seven destinies is formed through the influence of sentiment and conception: since the cause of sentiment leads to moistening and falling, it belongs to the three miserable paths.
The perception of the evil realms arises from the cause of levity and thus belongs to the four wholesome paths.
In the following text, the distinctions between the seven realms are discussed through the gravity of emotional perceptions; this can be understood in general terms.
"Ānanda, all the worlds of birth and death continue in succession... (up to)... within the commonality of beings, there are also the original lands."

This section of the sutra follows the preceding discussion on the distinctions between good and evil destinies based on emotional and conceptual thought, thereby answering Ānanda’s question regarding the fixed locations [of rebirth].
Previously, Ānanda had asked about both the fixed locations and the principle of spontaneity; however, the Buddha now answers only regarding the fixed locations.
This is because the fixed locations constitute the primary inquiry, whereas spontaneity was a secondary inquiry. Thus it is.
Therefore, the World-Honored One first answers the primary question; only after the six subsequent mutual retributions are exhausted does he conclude with the answer, saying:
"All these arise from deluded karma and do not exist from the beginning. This phrase "not existing from the beginning" is the answer to the secondary question regarding spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
It means that while things appear falsely, they are truly non-existent; they do not exist spontaneously. Thus, the text says: "All worldly... [and so forth].
Question: First, it clarifies the initial signs of the ascent and descent of emotional perceptions (*saṃjñā*) at the intersection of the two habits of birth and death.
"All worlds" refers to the seven destinies (*sapta-gati*); birth is "forward" and death is "reverse," which all people can know.

"Transforming flow" refers to the transition of the marks of death and the shifting of the physical form; the consciousness-nature that transmigrates is called the "dead person. At the moment of the end of life, the warmth—
When contact has not yet dispersed, the realms of good and evil suddenly appear before one;
the two boundaries of birth and death confront each other, and from this point, the ascent or descent of one’s thoughts and feelings diverges. Therefore, first we clarify these "pure thoughts.
First, we clarify the heavenly realms: if the deceased’s consciousness, during their lifetime, was purely of thought and devoid of emotion, because those thoughts were light...
If one’s pure thoughts soar upward and ascend, they will necessarily be reborn in the heavens; thus, the heavens are the destination for those of purely conceptual thought.

Furthermore, if within the mind of such soaring thoughts there is either mundane or supramundane merit and wisdom, along with the arousal of pure vows, then at the time of death, the mind and eyes will naturally become clear and enlightened, and one will see various Buddha-lands, being reborn therein according to one's vows. This, moreover, is not the realm of the heavenly destinies.

This clarifies that those who surpass the superior perceptions of the external constituents (*bāhya-bhāga*) among sentient beings have diminished passions. Next, it clarifies the destinies of the *ṛṣis*, ghosts, and so forth.

If one were to contrast this with the textual passages concerning the seven or nine grades of passion, then within these perceptions (*saṃjñā*) there should likewise be a distinction between the seven and nine types of perception-based destinies.
That they are not mentioned here is due to brevity. As for the statement that "passions are few and perceptions are many," it is likely...
These six perceptions and four passions arise because their perceptions are manifold; thus they are buoyant, yet because of the four passions they fall.
They are said to be "buoyant but not far" to indicate that they do not rise high.
Whether they become flying immortals or powerful ghosts, they can traverse the four continents without obstruction, yet because they cannot ascend to heaven, it is said they are "not [far]."

If one follows Yuan’s classification of the four categories—devas, ghosts, yakṣas, and rākṣasas—it would seem more appropriate to assign them to the nine, eight, seven, or six classes of "perceptual destinies" (*saṃjñā-gati*) according to their relative gravity. Why is this so?

It is because when comparing yakṣas and rākṣasas with devas and ghosts, the former certainly do not belong to the destinies of the six types of perception or the four types of feeling (*vedanā*). Furthermore, regarding the destinies of the devas and others:
There are supramundane wholesome vows and wholesome minds capable of protecting the Buddha-dharma, or protecting the precepts, protecting mantras, or protecting meditative concentration;
according to what is being protected, one dwells intimately beneath the seat of the Tathāgata, not limited by the realms of rebirth. "Sui" (綏) has the meaning of "peace";

"dharmakṣānti" (法忍) refers to the correct reception (*samādhi*) attained within meditative concentration, or it may refer to the "patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) which is acceptable to the mind.

This is called the "patience regarding phenomena" (*dharmakṣānti*). Regarding the section on "the clarity of perception" (*saṃjñā-prasāda*), the first three phrases clarify the meaning of the three types of persons in the human realm;

the final two phrases specifically demonstrate the causes for the distinction between the sharp and the dull. Indeed, the sharpness or dullness of a person is also brought about by their perceptions and thoughts (*saṃjñā-vitarka*);
for although these may be equal, if they fluctuate like the rising and falling of a scale, one can predict in advance whether one will be wise or foolish.
If thought (*saṃjñā*) predominates, one is clear-sighted and intelligent; if emotion (*vedanā*) predominates, one is obscure, dull, and ignorant.
When emotion is excessive, one falls into the four lower realms of animals (*tiryagyoni*). When thought is predominant and emotion is slight, this refers to what is described as the seven emotions.

Although these six emotions and four thoughts are slightly biased toward either lightness or heaviness, the fall is not yet profound; thus, they constitute the animal realm, the flock of hairy beings.
Because they walk upon the earth and do not fly, the feathered species are heavy; because they travel through the air and have not yet fallen, they are light.

Regarding the heaviness of those in the five realms of desire and the ghost realm: because their afflictions are many, they are heavy; because their perceptions are fewer, they sink deeper and deeper into the water wheel. As the *Mūlasūtra* states:
"This great earth is four hundred and eighty thousand yojanas thick and rests upon the water wheel; the thickness of the water is..."
Six hundred thousand yojanas below this realm of hungry ghosts, one sinks beneath the water wheel (*āpa-maṇḍala*) to the boundary where it meets the fire wheel (*tejo-maṇḍala*).
This refers to those who dwell beneath the water wheel relying upon the fire wheel; they take the vapors of fierce fire as their bodies.
Therefore, this is the primary retribution (*vipāka*) of hungry ghosts, being constantly incinerated by the fires of karma. By the power of karma, even water [cannot extinguish them].
"Self-harming" means that water turns into fire, so that one cannot obtain food or drink; thus it is called self-harming.

Because they have neither food nor drink for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they are named *preta* (hungry ghosts). Regarding the "six [realms] below the nine feelings," this clarifies the realm of hell (*naraka*).
As for "the fiery wheel at the bottom of the abyss": "abyss" means to penetrate through; it is submerged deeper than the fires below and intersects with the wind-wheel (*vāyu-maṇḍala*).
Because the fires at the boundary rest upon the wind, the bodies of those in this hell enter a place where wind and fire intersect.

Since they have not yet exhausted the slight power of a single thought, they do not fall to the very bottom; thus the Buddha taught that those who take life lightly are reborn in the *Avīci* (Abyak) hell, while those who take life heavily are reborn in the *Mahā-avīci* (Mowon) hell.
Compared to those of purely passionate nature, these are slightly lighter. There are five types of *Avīci*; as the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:

1. Uninterruptedness of the single course to the fruit (*eka-yāna-phala-anantara*): This refers to not remaining in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), but entering directly like an arrow shot from a bow.

2. Uninterruptedness of suffering (*duḥkha-anantara*): This refers to the manifestation of retribution for evil deeds, wherein there is never any pleasure. 3. Uninterruptedness of time (*kāla-anantara*): This refers to the full duration of one great eon (*mahākalpa*).
4. Uninterruptedness of life (*jīvita-anantara*): This refers to the moments of sustaining life through being crushed, burned, pounded, ground, or pierced by sharp winds.

Because there is no interval between ten thousand deaths and ten thousand births, the five forms are "uninterrupted" (Avīci); that is to say, whether one person or many people, their forms completely fill the prison without obstructing one another.
For this reason it is called "Uninterrupted. As for the designation "Hell" (Naraka), the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states:

"The name 'Hell' is established according to its meaning; because it is a prison beneath the earth, it is called a 'Earth-Hell. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says... [The text continues with the description of Jambudvīpa].
Five hundred *yojana*s beneath the continent [Jambudvīpa] lie the hells;

since *yojana* is translated here as "hundred million," and because there are both large and small hells, the present text refers to them as "with interval" (*sāntara*) and "without interval" (*nirantara*), which is to say the large and the small.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the eight cold and eight hot hells are called the "great hells," while there are sixteen smaller ones.
The hells are its retinue, known as the minor hells (*kṣudranaraka*). Pure emotion being heavy and intense clarifies that this is the retribution of the most evil destinies.
As for pure emotion facing superior pure thought, one rises and one sinks; such is the force of their nature. Those who sink to the very bottom fall into the Avīci Hell.
*Avīci* is a Sanskrit term translated as "Without Interval" (*mūrdhānantarya*). The *Buddhabhāṣita-samādhi-sūtra* states: "Avīci..."

The term "a" means "no," and "bi" means "to obstruct" (*vāraṇa*); alternatively, "a" means "no," and "bi" means "to rescue" (*trāṇa*). Combined, they signify "without obstruction and without rescue," which is the name for the Avīci Hell.
Although this etymological explanation of "obstruction" and "rescue" is used here, in all the various sūtras and śāstras, it is universally designated by the general name "Uninterrupted" (*Avīci*).
Furthermore, it is said that the Avīci Hell is three million two hundred thousand *li* in length and breadth.
The intermediate extreme suffering is explained in detail as it is taught in the various sūtras and śāstras.

If one harbors within the mind such evils as slandering the Dharma or violating the precepts, one will be reborn in the Avīci Hell of the ten directions; this should be understood as the opposite of the aforementioned pure thought and the protection of the Dharma, etc.
Following the construction of the lower fetters, the question regarding the fixed locations is answered. "Following" (xún) has the meaning of "according to" (suí), which means:
According to whatever various evil karmas one has created, one receives retribution in accordance with those karmas.

As for the "homogeneous class" (*nikāya-sabhāga*), it refers to the hells as a general designation, so called because they are produced by the collective karma of sentient beings; thus, they are termed a "homogeneous class.

Nevertheless, although the karmic actions of individual sentient beings differ, the retribution they attract inevitably leads them into this realm, for their fundamental karma is fundamentally neither extinguished nor exhausted.

Therefore, it is said that they also possess their original grounds; thus, within the hells, each transgression—whether lust, killing, stealing, or lying—is represented by specific manifestations, such as the appearance of iron beds, copper pillars, having one's tongue pulled out, or being ploughed with an ox.
"Ānanda, all these [beings]... (up to) receive the sixfold mutual retribution.

Regarding the question "What are the ten causes?"—this section of the sutra follows from the preceding discussion on the retribution induced by one's own karma; it first clarifies that there are ten kinds of *vāsanā-hetu* (habitual causes).

In the text, the passage beginning with "Ānanda" serves as a transition to conclude the previous topic and introduce the subsequent one. As for the three phrases beginning with "these": "these" refers to...
The phrase "pointing to the mental conceptions above" means that the good and evil of all realms of existence are all produced through the retribution of one's own karma;

this is the meaning of concluding the preceding section. The phrase "committing the ten [evil deeds] below" is the commencement of the subsequent section, which first clarifies evil karma and its retribution to demonstrate birth in the realm of hell.

Regarding the "ten causes of habitual practice," "habitual practice" (xi) refers to perfuming (vāsanā); it is because the seeds within the inner mind are perfumed by these practices that they come into being.
Karma is the cause for birth in the evil realms and that which summons future retribution;
this karma is created by the mind, yet the resulting retribution emerges from the six sense faculties, as will be explained in detail below.

However, the "causes of habituation" (*vāsanā-hetu*) are specified as only ten because, within the two categories of fundamental afflictions (*anuśaya*), these represent a broad enumeration that subsumes all others. This concludes the general summary above.
The heading "What are the enumerated [defilements]? introduces the subsequent detailed interrogation and explanation.
Ānanda, first is the habit of sexual desire (*maithuna-vāsanā*), from the point of mutual union... up to: "When a Bodhisattva sees desire, they avoid it as if it were a pit of fire."
First, to explain the habit-energy of lust (*kāma-vāsanā*) first: the phrase "intercourse" refers to the two habits; the subsequent sections are all to be understood in this manner.

Because the mutual intercourse between self and other precisely clarifies the moment of lust, it is said that "it arises from mutual grinding. This means that self and other first grind against one another with a lustful mind;
because it arises through this grinding, it is called "arising from mutual grinding. This is due to the lust of self and other.
When the mental states rub against one another without ceasing, the fire of desire is ignited within; it blazes intensely in the inner mind because at the time of death, the fires of karma manifest.
Thus it is said that a great, fierce fire is set ablaze therein. Regarding the "inner mind," this is explained through a metaphor:
the rubbing together of two palms illustrates the mutual friction of the lustful minds of two people, while the sensation of warmth illustrates [the arising of desire].

The fire of desire arises from two habitual tendencies; the following clarifies that retribution manifests from karma. This means that because one is mutually drawn to and embraces another through the karma of sexual misconduct, one incurs the retribution of the iron bed and the copper pillar.
The iron bed is the retribution for the place of sexual misconduct, while the copper pillar is the retribution for the person with whom one has sexual intercourse.
Therefore, the following concludes by indicating the names of these karmas: "name and form" (*nāmarūpa*) refers to the designation of name and form. The Buddhas designate this as "sexual misconduct."
Because they are said to represent the same thing—desire-fire—they are called by the same name.
When those who practice the path of the bodhisattva see desire as a pit of fire, it is because they say it burns and sinks one in, making it difficult to escape.
Second, the habit-energy of greed manifests through mutual scheming and mutual attraction. (Up to: "The Bodhisattva views greed as avoiding a sea of miasma.
Second, this clarifies the habit-energy of greed. "Mutual scheming" means that both parties engage in reciprocal plotting.
This greed of plotting arises from "attraction" (*xi*). "Attraction" is explained by way of a metaphor: it refers to drawing air into the mouth.
Internally, "sucking" (xi) is a metaphor for greed for external objects, like the mouth sucking in air.

If one continues to suck in and grasp without ceasing, then at the moment of death, one will see accumulated cold and solid ice emerging from the very source [of the breath], freezing and chilling. This is because greed belongs to craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and craving can produce water;
thus, one experiences the realm of cold ice. Just as with the lower analogy, the meaning of this metaphor can be understood through its illustration.

Inhalation and contraction represent greed; the wind represents the objects craved. To crave those objects perversely—objects that others do not desire—and to take them by force despite their unwillingness is like the sensation of cold.
There is a popular proverb which says that a person who seeks much invites much contempt;
"contempt" here carries the sense of "cold. Thus, we know that the retribution of freezing ice is no idle talk. [End of] Section Two on Habits.
The *Mingbao* states that the three sounds such as "ta-ta" manifested from the karma of the offenders are the cries of those suffering from the cold.
Those [colors] such as blue and red refer to the flesh cracking from freezing, appearing like the four colors of a lotus flower; therefore, it concludes below by indicating the names of the karmas.
As for "greedy water," it is like the ocean’s Wozhao and Weilu, which never tire of swallowing water; thus, it is called a "miasmic sea."
"Miasma" refers to pestilential vapors; like the pervasive sea mist, it is full of poisonous mists.
Third, the habit of pride intermingles and overcomes others, arising from mutual reliance... [as stated in the text] ...the Bodhisattva views pride as he would avoid a great flood.
Third, the lower section clarifies the habit-energy of pride (*māna*). "Pride" refers to exalting oneself and degrading others;
because this involves mutual contempt between self and other, it is called "mutual disparagement. "Reliance" means relying on one's own strengths, which gives rise to much arrogance;

because each relies on their own particular qualities, it is said to "originate from mutual reliance. Regarding "galloping flow," this is explained through metaphor: "flow" refers to a river current, and "rapid galloping" describes its swift rushing.
Not returning [to the source], one uses this as a metaphor for the habit of pride (*māna*). Its rushing is like the force of a river's current;

if the flow of pride does not cease, then at the time of death, one will perceive a realm of surging and racing waves where accumulated ripples form water. This turbulent flooding appears before the deceased, just as when a person descends a precipice—this metaphor is used to clarify the meaning of the two types of pride racing together.

(The mouth and... *Note: The final characters "口與" appear to be a scribal error or fragment; they do not form a coherent part of the preceding philosophical exposition on pride and the river metaphor.*
Because the tongue consists of two substances, there are two types of habitual tendencies; the following section clarifies how retribution manifests from karma.
This means that because the two aspects of pride strike against one another like drums, they induce retributions within hell, such as the Blood River and the Ash River. Regarding these rivers:

pride belongs to delusion (*moha*), and delusion is a state of turbid, dull energy subsumed under the five dull afflictions (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*). Therefore, it induces appearances in the form of blood, ash, and so forth.

Therefore, the concluding summary below identifies the name of the karma as "the water of delusion" (*moha*). This means that pride (*māna*) is generated by delusion; because one clings to a self due to delusion, it is called "self-pride" (*asmimāna*).

Just as there is water in the world that, when drunk, causes people to become deluded, so too is the "greed-quenching spring" (*tṛṣṇā-udapāna*), which, when drunk, causes people to give rise to greed—it is the same.
"Great drowning" refers to the ocean, described as surging and boundless, difficult to escape and easy to fall into.
Because of being submerged [in delusion].
Fourth, the habit of anger manifests as mutual conflict and opposition; (up to: when a Bodhisattva sees anger, they avoid it as they would an execution.
Fourth, this clarifies the habit of anger. Regarding "mutual conflict": *chong* (conflict) refers to a violent clash, and *wu* (opposition) refers to contrariness. Because of these...
When mutual feelings clash and provoke anger, and one harbors resentment without ceasing, the mind becomes feverish and ignites fire.
This fiery affliction generates wind; when this wind is forged by fire, it solidifies into metal.

Since metal belongs to the category of weapons, its external manifestation involves mutual cutting and grinding, while internally it manifests as the sight of mountains of blades and iron spikes at the time of death.
"Equal objects" (等境) is like a person; below, this explains it through a metaphor so that it may be understood. "The two habits" (二習) and below clarify that retribution manifests from karma.

Regarding the phrase "the palace appears," Zheng Xuan’s commentary states: "A man removes his virility. The rest is understandable. "Therefore" and below concludes by indicating the name of the karma.
Fifth, the habit of deceit arises from mutual enticement and playful banter; (up to: when a Bodhisattva sees deceit, it is like fearing a jackal or a wolf.
Fifth, this clarifies the habit of deceit. "Mutual enticement" means using words to toy with others, which is called "enticement";
because such mutual toying and mutual deception give rise to the habit of deceit, it is termed "mutual enticement. If this playful leading does not cease, then at the time of death—
At that time, one perceives objects such as ropes and wooden stocks;

"ropes" refers to cords twisted together that can be untied, while "stocks" (*jiao*) belong to the category of shackles—what is commonly called "binding the feet" (*xie jiao*) is this. "Shackling the ears" (*he jiao*) refers to the cangue. Because one entices, seduces, and leads others astray, one experiences these objects.
This is illustrated by the metaphor of water being confined beneath a dam; "water" serves as a simile for the habituation to deceit.
The field is a metaphor for the mind-field; the grasses and trees are metaphors for the ceaseless cultivation and guidance [of afflictions]. Thus it is said they "grow.

This is because the human heart is largely debased and defiled, with a pervasive habit of deceit. The water of human [affliction] moistens the mind, causing this cultivation to spread and entwine like the incessant growth of grasses and trees.
Second, the lower section clarifies that the retribution resulting from karma manifests as the experienced realms of shackles, fetters, and so forth.

The manner of its taming and guiding serves as a cause by which the fruit may be verified; the manifestation of its characteristics is clear. That which is struck is a mallet belonging to this category, shaped like a human hand.
Therefore, the conclusion below indicates the name of the karma: it is called "calumny" (*piśuna*) because it traps people;

it is "private intrigue" (*sāhasa*) because it is secretly treacherous and deceitful; it is like a thief, a jackal, or a wolf; it resembles a dog but is larger, with a sharp head, and moves in packs, injuring people upon seeing them.
Those whose nature is full of deceit, once captured by others, can feign death to escape because they do not expect to be guarded against;
thus their deception is like that of a jackal or a wolf.
Sixth, the habit of delusion leads to mutual cheating, arising from the intent to ensnare one another; (until) the Bodhisattva views such delusion as treading upon a snake or a viper.
Sixth, the following clarifies the habituation to deception (*māyā*). Regarding deception, the *Śata-dharma-śāstra* states: "For the sake of profit, one feigns the possession of virtue;

its nature is guile and fraud, and it is subsumed under the categories of greed and delusion. It arises from mutual cheating and deluding one another, employing flattering words and artificial appearances to deceive.
"Deluding" (*wang*) refers to the intent to deceive; when this deluding does not cease, the mind soars forth to create [further illusions].
"Those with a 'flying mind' of wickedness" refers to those who, mounting poison upon the void, ensnare others while the victims remain unaware; this is termed "creating wickedness with a flying mind.

It is like the common proverb that speaks of "calamities that fly in," which is precisely what is meant here. Thus, when one approaches death, they perceive visions of dust, excrement, urine, and the like.
The dust is blown about by the wind, arising from the resonance of the flying mind; as for the excrement and urine, [they likewise arise from the same source].
Filth and impurity arise from the influence of deception, fraud, and guile; this may be understood by the analogy of dust falling downward.

Regarding the two types of habituation (*vāsanā*) below, it clarifies that retribution manifests from karma: retributions such as drowning, being submerged, or being tossed about are all induced by a soaring mind of fraud and guile.
Therefore, the following section concludes by indicating the names of these karmas; "killing during a kalpa" refers to bandits and thieves.
Because there is the fear of cities being slaughtered and towns destroyed, and because snakes and vipers possess many venomous stings, one treads upon them with a sense of startled wonder;
likewise, when the path of the Way-man is beset by such treachery and falsehood, he must avoid it.
Seventh, regarding the habituation to resentment and mutual suspicion arising from harbored hatred: (until) the Bodhisattva views an enemy as if drinking poisoned wine.
Seventh, the lower section clarifies the habit-energy of enmity (*vaira-vāsanā*). Because mutual resentment arises between self and other, it is called "enmity. This manifests as harboring a grudge;
when this grudge is not relinquished, at the time of death one perceives such phenomena as flying stones and hurling potsherds.

These arise from the harbored grudge. "Lò" (礰) refers to broken tiles or shards; those stored in a box are like the caskets or beds found within a worldly prison. "Chējiàn" (車檻) refers to a carriage cage or enclosure.
Regarding "those who were imprisoned and strangled," this refers to the case of the First Emperor of Qin strangling his two younger brothers.

As for "the metaphor of the agreement beneath the shade," it can be understood through its clarification. Regarding the second section on "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*), it clarifies that retribution manifests from karma;

such retributions as being thrown down, seized, and captured are all induced by harboring resentment. By tracing the cause and verifying the fruit, this can be understood. Therefore, the final section concludes by demonstrating the nature of karma.
The "Viheṭhaka" (Violent Harasser) ghost is so named because "vi" means opposition or contrariety and "heṭhaka" means harm; thus, it refers to a hostile spirit that causes injury.
For example, when Śāriputra was struck by such a Viheṭhaka ghost, he was of this very class. As for the "zhen" (poisonous fowl), "zhen" is the name of a bird whose feathers are poisonous;
if one uses these feathers to stir wine and drinks it, one will die.

Eighth, regarding the mutual illumination of the habit-energy of views: it is like the *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (the view of a self-identity), which universally clings to what is false, as if one were standing on the brink of a precipice filled with poison.

Eighth, this clarifies the habit-energy of views from below. "Views" refers to perspectives; "mutual illumination" means that each possesses their own view, which they clarify and manifest to one another;
hence it is called "mutual illumination. As for "like the *satkāya*" and so forth, it cites the actual term *satkāyadṛṣṭi*, which is translated as "view of a self-identity" (*shenjian*).

Because of grasping at "self" and "what belongs to self," the views of "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and "clinging to precepts and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) carry the meaning of "grasping.

Regarding these: clinging to views refers to grasping at the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism; clinging to precepts and observances refers, for example, to grasping at the precepts of cattle or dogs as the cause for rebirth in heaven.
These five sharp afflictions (*tīkṣṇa-kleśa*) are merely summarized here by three. As for those actions resulting from false awakening:

This comprehensively includes all other views; for among the ninety-five kinds of heterodox views, each clings to its own position as correct and refutes that of others, thus it is said they "arise from opposition.

Consequently, at the time of death, objects such as kings, messengers, and officials appear—all arising from the conflict between the internal and external luminosity. This is explained through an analogy below.
This is like those who each cling to what they deem right, engaging in mutual contest and seizure with no room for concealment;
thus it is as when travelers meet on a road and see one another. Second, the "two habits" below clarify that retribution manifests from karma:
because of this mutual debate and refutation, one incurs retribution in hell involving interrogation, deception, and the like. "Deception" refers to weighing the offender.
The deceptions herein can be understood as follows: the diagrams currently found in temples depict them in great detail, so one may identify them with certainty.

Therefore, the concluding summary indicates the names of the karmas: "seeing-pits" refers to the various views of false awakening, which are like pits because they cause one to fall in and be difficult to extricate.
"Poisonous ravines" is as explained previously; "miasmic seas" has the same meaning, referring to bodies of water that collect and pool together to form a ravine.
Therefore, the name "Great Abyss" refers generally to the pervasive false attachments of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Ninth, the habit-energy of injustice intermingles and gives rise to slander: [from] "the Bodhisattva views injustice as encountering a thunderbolt."
Ninth, this clarifies the habit of resentment (*wang*). To suffer injustice through no fault of one's own is called "resentment" (*wang*);

to be "mutually entangled" means that both parties inflict harm upon each other. This arises from slander and calumny. In the past, when others inflicted such injustice upon me, I harbored it in my heart;
yet those who inflict injustice remain complacent and show no remorse. If this bitterness is not expressed, then both parties will become slanderous and treacherous toward one another.
Therefore, at the time of death, one sees such phenomena as mountains closing in or rocks converging;

these are all manifestations of being falsely accused and oppressed, which can be understood through the metaphors used below. Regarding the second section on "the two habits," it clarifies that retribution arises from karma:

because the two types of false accusations and oppressions clash, they induce retribution within hell, consisting of events such as being crushed, pressed down, beaten, and pummeled. As for the term *cu-lu* (蹙漉), it means...
It compresses the body and drains the blood; thus, "measuring" (*heng*) refers to weighing the light and heavy, while "measuring" (*du*)—pronounced *duo*—refers to deliberating the long and short.
This is what Mencius meant when he said, "Only after weighing can one know lightness and heaviness; only after measuring can one know length and shortness.
The interpretation of "horizontal impact" (*heng-chong*) by Wenceng is incorrect; it is as depicted in the diagrams of modern temples.
The meaning of "weighing the limbs of the sinner" is precisely this. Therefore, the concluding summary below identifies the names of the karmas:

"Slanderous Tiger" refers to slandering and wrongfully biting others like a tiger; "Thunderbolt" refers to slandering and wrongfully inflicting harm based on falsehoods and delusions, much like what is called a "thunderbolt from a clear blue sky," which strikes people with terror.

Tenth: The habit of litigation (*sòng*) and mutual clamor arise from concealment (*zàngfù*). (This continues until: "It is like wearing a high mountain upon one's head while treading upon a vast ocean.
Tenth: This below clarifies the habit of litigation. Litigation has the meaning of exposing; clamor refers to noisy uproar.
Because it exposes what is hidden, it is said to "arise from concealment. Due to this exposure, both parties engage in mutual clamor; that which is concealed must not be [exposed].
What is heard from others leads to doubt and regret, which are difficult to dispel;

therefore, at the time of death, one perceives visions such as mirrors and illuminating lights, all of which arise from a mind of doubt and regret. This can be understood by means of the following analogies.
Below, it is explained that retributions manifest from karma: retributions such as evil associates and the karmic mirror all arise from concealment, doubt, and regret.
The resulting causes and effects are clearly intelligible; therefore, the conclusion below identifies the name of the karma as "the hidden thief. "Hidden" (*yin*) means to conceal;

it conceals grave transgressions that will inevitably lead to rebirth in the evil realms, which is what practitioners fear. Thus, it is metaphorically likened to carrying a mountain on one's head while treading through the sea.
"What are the six retributions? From "Ānanda, all sentient beings" (up to) "how do the evil retributions emerge from the six faculties.
This section of the sutra follows the previous discussion on retribution induced by one's own karma; it now clarifies the six types of reciprocal retribution (*jiaobao*).

At the beginning of the text, the phrase "What are... serves as a general inquiry. Following this, Ānanda [responds] below with a brief explanation of the meaning of retribution based on the preceding context. Next, it says:
What follows is a further inquiry and explanation of the underlying meaning.

First, regarding how the retribution of views invites evil fruits (extending to) being able to produce sparks that scatter and flare up, fanning the void. First, below, the preceding general explanation is expanded upon with a specific analysis;

here, we first clarify the "retribution of views. In the initial phrase, the character for "retribution" (*bao*)— *Note: The provided text appears to be a commentary on a Buddhist technical passage. The final segment is a philological note identifying the character "bao" (retribution) within the opening phrase.*
When one views this as the "karma of seeing," the meaning becomes very clear. This is because seeing karma that summons retribution gives rise to evil fruits;

this phrase specifically clarifies the "seeing of retribution. The subsequent section provides a separate explanation of the "crossing of retribution" (*jiaobao*), which means that the retribution of the karma of seeing and the retribution of other karmas manifest in alternation. As for "seeing a great, fierce fire at the time of death":
Because the eye belongs to the fire element, seeing a fierce fire is precisely the karmic retribution of the eye-faculty; this is called "retribution in the present life.
Below, the signs of the initial arising of "retribution upon rebirth" for the deceased are clarified:

once the deceased's spirit-consciousness has departed from the body, it rides upon the smoke and flames of the fire of karma, falling from above into the Avīci Hell. At that moment, [the following] arises:
This clarifies the two characteristics. What is perceived by these two characteristics is not fixed; one may perceive light or one may perceive darkness.
The deceased’s spirit-consciousness perceives one of these two characteristics to manifest the initial retribution of falling into hell. The following sections should be understood accordingly.

Since the eye takes light and darkness as its objects, this is explained in terms of light and darkness; the same applies to the other sense organs in the subsequent text, each according to its own respective object.

This explains that the meaning is the same as what is intended here. As for the "various evil things," these refer to the ox-headed *āpāpas*, fire-snakes, fire-dogs, the pouring and swallowing of molten copper, and so forth—things which one sees and feels fear toward.

"To see nothing at all" means that while walking through a vast wilderness or deep darkness, the mind becomes timid and gives rise to terror; this "fear" (*bhaya*) refers to the complete state of a fearful mind, whereas "terror" (*bhīti*) is the specific dread itself.

To be startled, doubtful, and fearful is the nature of the original mind. Thus, the following section correctly clarifies how the retribution of seeing and the retribution of being seen interact to produce fire.
According to medical treatises, the eyes preside over the heart, and the heart fundamentally belongs to the element of fire; since the eyes are the external orifices of the heart, one sees fire.
As for the subsequent passage, the ears preside over the kidneys, and the kidneys belong to the element of water; since the ears are the external orifices of the kidneys, [one hears water].

This is explained by way of water. Now, although this discourse on the five elements (pañca-mahābhūta) is superficial, it has not yet departed from the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), as these [aggregates] still belong to the five elements.
Since the hells possess the five aggregates of the hells, what is clarified here does not depart from the explanation of water and fire.
However, within the five sense-faculties (pañcendriya) discussed below, there is an exposition that reveals [the nature of the faculties] based on their original objective spheres (viṣaya).

Regarding the Five Elements, they generally manifest according to one's accumulated karma; their essential characteristics must be understood through their underlying categories, and thus they are not restricted to a single modality.
Now, when we observe fire interacting with hearing, water and fire strike one another to form shapes;

therefore, there are manifestations such as boiling cauldrons and molten copper. This interaction occurs within the breath; since breath is qi, and qi is the locus where fire interacts, [these phenomena arise].
It forms things such as black smoke and purple flames, which intersect with the taste;

because the cause of taste is manifested through eating, and because it is the intersection of fire, it becomes things such as scorched balls and molten iron porridge—“molten iron porridge” (*mici*) refers to melted iron that resembles congee, hence the name *mici*.

It intersects with the tangible (*spraṣṭavya*); because the tangible is manifested through conjunction, it carries the sense of obstructive physical form and substance; thus, the tangible is the intersection of fire.
It becomes like a hot ash pit or burning coals intersecting within the mind;

the mind is inherently filled with wandering discursive thoughts, and since the mind belongs to the element of fire, it is further intersected by the perception of fire, thereby forming sparks that scatter and spray.

These sparks manifest from the proliferation of wandering discursive thoughts, fanning and stirring the expanse of space; this refers to the inner and outer fires igniting one another, their flames becoming ever more intense.
Thus, it is like a fan that fanning the wind.
Second, hearing the retribution invites and draws forth evil fruits (extending to) becoming lightning and hail that shatter the heart and soul.
Second, the following clarifies hearing the retribution. The first phrase means "hearing that karma invites retribution," which restates the general meaning previously mentioned.
"Upon hearing this, [the text] correctly explains the reciprocal retribution: since the ear belongs to the water element, one sees billowing waves at the time of death.
However, as the retributions of the six sense organs manifest interchangeably, the characteristics of these six retributions are all present;

yet because the current text specifically manifests only one retribution at a time, it says 'first sees,' using the word 'first' to distinguish it from the subsequent stage where they all appear simultaneously. "The deceased," etc., refers to the departed.
Once the divine consciousness has departed from the body, it descends accordingly into the Avīci Hell.

At that moment, two appearances manifest; what is seen in these two appearances is as previously described. As for "hearing through movement and stillness," opening and closing constitute movement and stillness.
The various forms of clamor refer precisely to being hacked, burned, pounded, ground, flayed, and torn apart, resulting in agonizing pain.
The sound of this is clamorous; because it is clamorous, it disturbs the spirit. That which is silent and unheard is like being in a vast, empty space;
because it is profound and still, the soul and spirit have no place to lodge, and thus it is called "sinking. This section below correctly clarifies the mutual hearing of waves as explained above.
The commentary states that hearing issues from the fundamental root; therefore, the previous perception of fire did not arise from the fundamental root.
This is an abbreviation. "Reproaching" and "interrogating" belong to the category of the sound-constituent (*śabda-dhātu*);

because they are produced by the karma of hearing, when the waves of hearing intersect with the visual faculty, fire and water strike one another, giving rise to thunder and roars. Because fire is poured over by water, it transforms into poisonous vapors.
When these intersect with the breath, the breath carries the water and disperses it as rain and mist; furthermore, the breath...
Through conjunction with water, it undergoes transformation and becomes worms that fill the bodies of those who have committed sins; this is caused by the retribution for evil deeds.
When conjoined with taste, taste is infused by water and transforms into pus, blood, and the like. When conjoined with touch, touch possesses form and substance and is infused by water;
through the union of yin and yang energies, it becomes animals or ghosts. All such filth and excrement arise from the waves of auditory perception.
When the eyes interact with the mind, it is likewise like water and fire striking one another; riding upon the arising and ceasing of the mental consciousness, they manifest as lightning and hail.
Because thorns arise from the flickering stirrings of the human heart, one receives the retribution of being crushed and shattered.
Third, the retribution for smelling leads to the invitation of evil fruits, [extending] to having one’s body smashed by flying sand and gravel.
Third, the following clarifies the retribution for smelling. The first phrase—“the retribution for smelling karma”—restates the general meaning previously mentioned.

The subsequent section, “this smelling,” is the formal explanation of the mutual retribution; since smelling pertains to the sense of smell (air), at the moment of death one perceives air. This refers to the meaning of what was seen previously.
As previously stated regarding the deceased, there are two meanings for the phrase "the consciousness of the deceased surges forth from the earth":
first, inhalation is called "smelling the air," and because it necessarily proceeds from below upward, it is said to "surge forth from the earth" to clarify the retribution of smelling;
second, the contact of the olfactory faculty is not separate from the two objects of penetration and obstruction, just as nasal breath persists for a long time.
If one suddenly clears a blockage, the breath from within the nose issues forth like a gushing spring;
for these two reasons, it is said that [the breath] surges up from the earth to characterize one's prior karma.

Regarding the two signs perceived as previously described, "the breath fumes the heart and disturbs it" means that it is like a person who has been exposed to smoke compounded with poisonous gas, becoming extremely dazed, distressed, and agitated; thus, the breath overwhelms [the mind].

"Stupefied" (*mènjué*) means "obstructed," which refers to the nasal breath being blocked for a long time; because the internal and external passages are not permeable and the qi fills the interior, one becomes stupefied and on the verge of collapse.
Thus, the following clarifies their mutual interaction: "impact" (*chōng*) refers to the impact of the qi as it surges forth;
"impacting the breath" (*chōngxī*) refers to its emergence from the original root; "substance" (*zhì*) refers to the physical form, and "practice" (*lǐ*) refers to conduct, both arising from the qi.
Because it coagulates into form, when the retribution of olfaction interacts with vision, the qi is constrained by fire; this principle can be understood.
When it interacts with hearing, the qi overwhelms water and becomes pervasive, which causes one to be submerged and drowned.

As for "boiling" and "overflowing," these are further manifestations of the qi riding upon water and fire in a state of seething and parching. When it interacts with taste, the flavor is transformed by the qi.

Therefore, "nǎi" (putrefaction) refers to hunger, and "shuǎng" (stale) refers to spoiled fish; a spoiled soup is called "shuǎng. When these interact with sensory contact (*chù*), and that contact combines with noxious vapors, the resulting putrefaction and decay can be known.
The splitting of flesh is called "zhàn" (bursting); furthermore, when vapors attack the body, they form great mountains of flesh, which is caused by the contact of retribution for evil deeds.
As for those who interact through thought (*sī*), people cause one another to become muddled and agitated.
Furthermore, because the mind is permeated and steamed by the breath of the nose, it becomes ash and miasma; both this ash and the miasma are caused by confusion and agitation.
As for flying sand striking the body, it is brought about by deceitful schemes.
Fourth, the retribution for craving flavors invites and draws forth evil fruits (extending to) flying red-hot iron raining down from the sky.
Fourth, the following clarifies the retribution for flavors. The first phrase restates the general meaning mentioned previously.

"This flavor" and below is the actual explanation of the mutual retribution, specifically the intent behind what was previously described regarding the deceased. The subsequent mention of "passing through," "hanging in nets," and so forth refers to these matters.

The retribution for capturing [beings] with nets out of a craving for their flavor leads one to descend into the Avīci Hell in this very form. Regarding the two signs seen, they are also as previously described.
