As for "inhaling breath turns it into ice," this means that because one inhales external cold air, one experiences the retribution of freezing cold, as explained previously in the section on the habitual tendencies of craving.
As for "flying as a fierce fire," this is likewise due to cooking [beings] out of a craving for their flavor.
The retribution for roasting [meat] is as follows: what is explained below clearly demonstrates that those who experience mutual tasting do so because it originates from the fundamental root.
"Accepting and enduring" refers to how, due to craving for flavor, karmic adversaries testify against one another; thus, one accepts and endures while being interrogated and examined by King Yama.
The retribution for flavors manifests in the present life as burning iron and stone; this is because flavors undergo transformation when subjected to fire.
This refers to such things as molten bronze and glowing iron. When encountered by the faculty of hearing, they become sharp weapons;
when flavors are cast into water, they turn into broth, yet their physical form changes into sharp weapons—this is brought about by the retribution of craving for flavor.
When encountered by the faculty of respiration, they become iron cages; when flavors encounter the breath, the breath coagulates and transforms into iron nets and cages used for capturing.
The retribution can be seen: when one encounters touch and taste, these combine with touch;

the bow, arrow, and crossbow are all lethal instruments for craving flavors, manifested through the conjunction of touch. When one encounters volition, the "flying iron" is the retribution for a flying mind that creates evil.
Fifth, the retribution of touch invites and draws forth evil fruits—[ranging from] being cast down, to being flown away, to being boiled, and to being roasted.

Fifth, this clarifies the retribution of touch. The first phrase restates the general meaning of the preceding section; the phrase "this touch" and following provides the formal explanation of the mutual retribution, specifically the intent regarding what was previously seen.
As explained before, when at the time of death one sees a great mountain closing in, the "touch" is manifested through that closing.

Therefore, as for the statement that the deceased, experiencing this retribution, sees below an iron city and so forth, this is also what is perceived through the two aspects induced by the karma of contact (*spraṣṭavya-karma*).

It is as previously explained: the mountains closing in to press against the body is the meaning of the preceding passage. Furthermore, the alternation of contact and separation clarifies the nature of contact;
that they become swords and blades to slaughter and tear one apart can be understood accordingly. Thus, the following section correctly explains their mutual and successive contact.
This arises from the fundamental root. The Way is the path leading to the hells; the rest may be understood.
This is what is felt when karma is divided into segments and physical form is induced. "Intersecting with sight" may be understood accordingly. "Intersecting with hearing" refers to striking;

this is the instrument for the union of touch and sound. "Stabbing" (pronounced *zhù*): to insert a blade into flesh is called stabbing. "Intersecting with breath" refers to the throat and the bag [of the lungs].
"Collecting the vital energies" refers to the matter of examination and binding; "meeting at the touch" refers to the process of cultivating flavors, which is also called "plowing with the tongue.
"Pincers" are clamping tools, and "severing" means dismemberment;
these are all instances where the contact with flavors and the union with greed intersect within thought. As for "falling" and "flying," they refer to how one's karma follows from such contact.
The mind ascends and descends; "frying" and "roasting" refer to karmic contact entering the mind, where the fire of mental anguish is like being roasted.
Sixth, by contemplating the retribution that invites evil fruits, one undergoes ten thousand births and ten thousand deaths, turning face down and face up.
Sixth, the following clarifies the retribution of volition (*cetanā*). The first phrase restates the general meaning of what preceded;

"this volition" and below provide the formal explanation of the mutual retribution (*kṣipra-vipāka*) previously mentioned regarding the initial visions. As for the phrase "evil winds blowing and destroying," etc., it is because the arising and ceasing of the mind is as unstable as the wind that suddenly arises and ceases.
Since the retribution of karmic volition does not transcend the realm of mind and objects, one experiences these evils.

Regarding the retribution of being blown away by wind and the destruction of the land: those who fall downward, being blown up by the wind and then spinning back down, manifest due to the arising and ceasing of the mind.
This is because when one in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) falls into hell, they must necessarily fall headlong from above, just as fallen leaves are carried by the wind and then drop again.
The appearances seen in these two cases are as previously described; this pertains to delusion and awakening.
When the mental faculty (manas) does not perceive the objects of the mind (dharmas), this is delusion; it is the height of delusion.
Because the mind is thus desolate, one runs on without ceasing, like a child traveling in a foreign land who is lost on the road; the mind is desolate and its movements are chaotic.
Not to be deluded is awakening. When one awakens, everything seen and experienced within the prison is nothing but suffering, as described throughout the *Sūtra on Universal Suffering*.

The sensations of burning and intense pain that are difficult to endure are all characteristics of suffering; thus, the following section correctly clarifies the "mutually entangled thoughts," which arise from the fundamental root.
As for the term "entanglement" (*jiejie*), it means that the mental faculty (*manas*) becomes obstructed and bound by greed, anger, and delusion within the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*);
hence it is called "entanglement. Regarding "directions and locations," directions and locations are what the mental faculty calculates and conceptualizes.

The locations [of the hells] are places induced by karma; the spatial directions within the hells are formed by the convergence of visual perception, which can illuminate and discern, thus inducing the phenomena of reflection and verification.
The convergence of auditory perception forms the "greatly joined stones," which are produced by the binding of thoughts through the waves of hearing, like stones in a midstream.
Ice and frost may be dissolved, but earth and mist are the binding of thoughts through turbid confusion.

Because moisture is volatile and ascendant, it interacts with the breath (*āśvāsa*); because thought and spirit are concentrated and belong to the element of fire, one consequently experiences retributions such as the fiery chariot.
The "fiery cage" (*huo jian*) is an instrument for prisoners within the prison of the supervising vehicle.

As for the crying, wailing, and weeping that arise from tasting, these result from the mind giving rise to greed and seizing upon flavors; thus, they are the retribution for killing and craving flavors.

"Interacting with touch" means that touch is a provisional convergence of things; whether large or small, all are material objects. That "ten thousand beings undergo birth and death" arises from the arising and ceasing of the mind.
This "convergence with touch" is what is experienced: to speak in general terms, one undergoes ten thousand births and deaths in a single day.

However, since there are immeasurable births and cessations in every *kṣaṇa*, how could it be limited to ten thousand? "Lying prostrate or reclining" refers to bodily karma; because the mind converges with touch, [these postures arise].
The manner in which one lies prostrate and receives punishment is depicted in the current diagrams of the monasteries, which were produced by following this text.
Ānanda, these are called the ten causes and six fruits of hell (up to: "arising from false imagination, they do not exist inherently").

This section of the sutra concludes the discussion on the ten causes and six effects of the hells while simultaneously answering the question regarding individual karma and private retribution, as there exists the fundamental ground (*mūla-bhūmi*).
"Ānanda," and so forth, concludes the preceding [section] as may be understood; "If there are," and so forth, answers and demonstrates the fundamental ground.
Within this text, the names, numbers, and severity of the hells, as well as the principles of whether karmic offenses are shared or not, are [explained] of their own accord.
From antiquity to the present, the source of this [text] has not been clearly established; although various masters each champion their own strengths, none have seen its definitive authority.

Therefore, I do not dare to affirm or deny anything therein, but shall briefly provide a commentary and resolution following the text according to traditional interpretations, awaiting the discovery of its origin so that it may be appended as a supplement.
Furthermore, upon examining the twentieth fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, it says:
The sinful karma committed by all sentient beings is of two kinds: first, light; second, heavy.
If it is performed by mind and speech, it is called light; if it is performed by body, speech, and mind, it is called heavy.

This means that if one conceives it in the mind and speaks it with the mouth, but does not perform it with the body, the retribution received will be light. This is based on the scriptural evidence that the three karmas do not necessarily operate in combination.
This can be clarified by analogy: "collective creation" (*sādhāraṇa-karman*) means "complete creation.
As in the previous section on the ten causes and six fruits, "complete creation" refers to those who enter the Avīci hell and undergo immeasurable kalpas of extreme suffering.

Following this, the "individual creation" (*pratyeka-karman*)—the "separate creation"—is explained for those whose offenses are slightly less grave than the former; it is contrasted with the aforementioned collective creation, such that the former constitutes the complete [set of karmic conditions].

The statement that those who have committed the full set of evils and those who have committed them individually refer to the meaning of "sequential commission. Regarding the six sense faculties, there may be times when they function concurrently and times when they do not;

this refers to the sequential mind, which, because it is successively grave, enters the eight *ānantarya* (immediate) hells—namely, the eight [offenses] mentioned in the preceding text that are either with or without interval.
Because these are slightly lighter than the great Avīci hell, the Wēnlíng commentary states:
Since each act is committed with its own sequence, interval, and degree of gravity, the "successive" (anu-anu) and "immediate" (ānantarya) [offenses] refer to the eight hot hells.

If one possesses the intent but fails to commit the transgression, the object (*viṣaya*) is not included; if one lacks the intent but commits the offense by mistake, the basis (*mūla*) is not included.

Therefore, it is said that the intentional maintenance and the commission of the offense both involve these two aspects. Regarding the body and speech below, the next category of gravity is explained as follows:

Among the ten non-virtuous actions possessed by body, speech, and mind, if this person commits only the acts of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, and does not commit the remaining seven, they should enter the eighteen subsidiary hells (*upapāduka-naraka*).
Wēnlíng says: "Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct committed through body, speech, and mind are grave offenses;
because they are neither exclusive to six [of the ten] nor complete in all ten, they are also ranked below the preceding [major hells]."
In the hells, there are only the eight cold and eight hot hells, along with eighty-four thousand subsidiary hells, all of which are branches of the great hells.
The third section clarifies those whose karma is slightly lighter; that is, those who commit the three karmas of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, though not necessarily all three together.
Among these three karmas, if a person commits only one—either killing or stealing—they will enter the thirty-six [subsidiary hells].
These thirty-six hells are merely further subdivisions of the eighteen. Regarding "seeing" (*jien*):
the upper "seeing" character refers to the faculty of seeing (*darśana-indriya*), while the lower "seeing" character refers to the object seen (*dṛśya-viṣaya*).

This precisely conveys the meaning of the simultaneous engagement of both object and faculty; that is to say, this person has committed an offense involving only a single faculty and a single object within the domain of the eye.
Because one does not transgress against either the remaining faculties or objects within this karma, it is called "one karma. Such a person enters the hundred-and-eight hells;
furthermore, this is a subdivision from among the thirty-six [hells], as the power of the hell is divided and the suffering experienced is lighter.
Master Wuxing’s explanation regarding the single object and single faculty of the seer and the seen is also the same as this. For this reason:
The following section concludes the answer to the preceding question. Originally, Ānanda asked whether hell has fixed locations or whether it arises spontaneously;
therefore, the Buddha answered: "The various realms of hell each have their own fundamental ground, which constitutes their fixed location.
They arise from deluded conceptualization and do not exist inherently; thus, the answer is that they are not spontaneous."
Furthermore, Ānanda, as for these sentient beings (up to) "then this wondrous, perfect clarity fundamentally has nothing at all":
this section of the sutra follows the previous inquiry regarding the seven destinies and now responds to the question concerning the destiny of hungry ghosts (*preta*).

The phrase "Furthermore" below serves as a general heading indicating the causes for undergoing this destiny; it is also a transitional expression that concludes the preceding and introduces the following, rather than refuting the five subsequent sentences.
This bond [of ignorance] precedes and subsequently descends upon this birth; it is not that which destroys the three lower realms.

These three phrases clarify that extremely heavy evil karma does not refer to the denial and repudiation of cause and effect—namely, claiming there is no ethical discipline (*saṃvara*) to be maintained—which constitutes the destruction of discipline and the transgression of the Bodhisattva precepts.
To revile *nirvāṇa* is the conduct of an icchantika, severing the very root of goodness. Now, as for the transgression of the precepts...

If one can repent but does not refrain from slandering, it is difficult to redeem oneself; furthermore, having committed both primary and secondary karmas, as well as miscellaneous deeds, throughout their entirety, one will be scorched for kalpas—this can surely be known.
This concludes the preceding section on the fundamental karma of the hells;

what follows below correctly clarifies the subsequent transition to rebirth in the realm of hungry ghosts. This occurs because the waters of pure emotion and craving are both consumed by the fires of karma.
Because their transgressions have been exhausted, they attain liberation; yet, as residual habits have not yet perished, they undergo rebirth in the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).

If one were to distinguish the ten different classes of hungry ghosts below, it corresponds to the ten causes mentioned above. "Original cause" refers to the causal basis of the original habits among the ten [causes] mentioned previously.
"Coveting objects" refers to the habit of greed; because other forms of greed have not yet perished, as soon as they encounter objects, [they are seized by craving].
Because they manifest as monsters by attaching themselves to objects, they are called *guàiguǐ* (monster ghosts). "Those who crave beauty" refers to the habit of lust;
since beauty is the wind of lust, their residual habits still take form by attaching to that wind, and are thus called *hànbiébì* (drought-demon ghosts).

When these demons arise with the wind, they can suppress timely rain, causing the harvests of the year not to ripen; hence they are named drought-demons. "Those who crave delusion" refers to the habit of deceit.
Deceit can delude many people, manifesting the appearance of a fox-spirit; thus, its residual habits attach to animals to take form, which are called *mei*-ghosts (*mèiguǐ*).

"Those with greed and resentment" refers to the habituation of enmity; because the residual habits of hatred and resentment have not yet perished, they attach to insects or parasites to take form, which are called *gu*-poison ghosts (*gùdúguǐ*).
When such things happen in the homes of families in remote villages or lowly towns of this region, such as those in the two provinces of Guangxi and Guangdong:
The *gǔ* spirits who poison people belong to this class. "Greedy recollection" (*tānyì*) refers to the habit of anger (*dveṣa*).

Anger is called "recollection" because it harbors hatred and stores resentment; furthermore, it carries the sense of being cowardly, violent, overbearing, or declining. Therefore, its remaining habits take form when encountering decline and arise to cause calamity.
They seek food because they have no sacrifices offered to them, and thus they are called *lì*. Today, prefectures and counties establish shrines for the *lì*.
"Tán" (壇) refers to this [state]. "Greed and arrogance" points to the habit of pride (*māna*). Pride uses empty arrogance to insult others;

since empty arrogance is a form of vital energy (*qi*), its residual habits take shape according to that energy and constantly suffer from hunger. This is caused by empty arrogance, and thus they are called *preta* (hungry ghosts).
"Greed and deception" points to the habit of falsehood (*māyā*). Deception takes the act of misrepresentation as its core intention; it is a state of profound isolation.
Because of these habitual practices, their residual traces encounter the obscure and take form;
originally intended to deceive and ensnare others, they still manifest through the power of old habits as "suffocating ghosts" (*yàngguǐ*). Those who crave clarity refer to the habit of seeing;

having previously used right and wrong to discern and analyze principles while seeking the refined, their residual traces still persist, and when encountering the refined, they take form—these are called "wandering spirits" (*wǎng*).
The *liàngguǐ* (demon) encountered tonight in the mountain forests, manifesting its form upon wood or stone to a height of about one *zhàng*, belongs to this class.
"Accomplishing through greed" (*tānchéng*) refers to the habituation of injustice. Changshui’s commentary states:

"To rely on the void to point toward reality, to harass the innocent and perversely establish their guilt—this is called 'accomplishing through greed. It is like Qin Hui’s wrongful persecution of Yue Fei."
Wu Mu completed the matter by means of the three characters "Mo Xu You" (it must be so); this is of that same category.
Yet, because his residual habits still longed for such "completing through artifice," whenever he encountered clarity, it manifested as a form;

thus, he was content to be employed by other luminous spirits and ghosts, like a river or stream in which sand is piled up or boulders thrust in, causing the source of the current to be breached for their sake.
"Those who are mostly employed [in such tasks] are this class of greedy partisans," which refers to the habit of litigation. The *Changshui* commentary states:

"To side with oneself and conceal [one's faults], resulting in being sued by others. However, according to the present text, "partisan" (*dǎng*) should be explained as being adjacent to "litigation" (*sòng*).

Therefore, the remaining habit is that of associating with others to form names and transmit them; "transmitting to ghosts" is precisely the intent of litigation, like the modern practice of spirit-writing (*fújī*) to summon [spirits].
Immortals report the good and bad fortune of people and point out the reality of human affairs; furthermore, among the people of Wu, those called Taibao Duan-gong are mostly of this kind.
"This person" refers to Ānanda, who at the end of the passage answers the questions asked, clarifying the reason for his descent into the realm of ghosts.
"This person" points back to the ten aforementioned classes. "Pure emotion" refers to past karma; "the fire of karma having burned it dry" means that pure emotion is... [karma].
The water of craving is dried up by the fire of karma; once those who were heavy have completely fallen away, they emerge above as ghosts due to residual habits.
This is the direct answer to the question: it means that these are summoned by one's own delusions and thus falsely appear, while in truth they do not exist.
Therefore it is said: "If one awakens to Bodhi, one returns to the fundamental wondrous, perfect, and luminous state where nothing at all exists."
There is not a single phrase that provides a dual response, for both the fixed locus and spontaneity are equally unattainable.
Furthermore, Ānanda, once the karmic retribution of the ghosts has been exhausted, [all things] are merely the congealing of empty, false conceptualizations.
This section of the sutra follows the previous inquiry regarding the seven realms of existence; now, it provides the third response concerning the realm of animals.

First, from the passage beginning with "Ānanda," the text concludes the discussion on the realm of hungry ghosts and establishes the causes for the arising of the animal realm. It states that once the karma of the hungry ghosts is exhausted, their emotional attachments and conceptual thoughts (*saṃjñā*) from past kalpas become entirely empty.
The preceding text used the term "thought" (*saṃjñā*) to refer generally to emotion, while "sinking" (*chén*) primarily indicated those of purely emotional nature.
Having fallen [into the realm of ghosts], why does the current text further describe them in terms of "perception" (*saṃjñā*)?
It is because emotion is formed by perception; without perception, how could there be sentient beings? Because emotion is so intense, perception is shrouded by emotion.

Thus it is said that "pure emotion is consumed by the fire of karma until it dries up. Once the emotion has dried up, perception manifests; therefore, those who emerge above become ghosts, and these ghosts ride upon [that perception].

Other perceptions merely act as its instruments; now, the emptiness of emotion indicates that the karma of hell is exhausted, and the emptiness of thought indicates that the karma of ghosts is exhausted.
This section below correctly clarifies the realm of animals; however, one must know that animal retribution is not merely a destination, but comes specifically to repay past debts.
Now, only when the offenses of the hells and ghosts are exhausted does one then settle their original debt. The passage beginning with "The strange things" below clarifies the ten classes of beings.

This differs from the ten types of habitual practice mentioned previously; whereas above greed was treated as a singular anomaly, here it is categorized among the "other anomalies" such as the owl that adopts a clod of earth as its offspring.
Generally, those who are greedy and lustful act unrighteously, and thus the owl exhibits the cruelty of devouring its own mother.

Regarding the phrase "when the material basis is exhausted and the retribution ends": this means that once the physical object upon which the spirit depends has perished, the retribution of the dependent ghost also comes to an end.

A single lifetime cannot exhaust [the retribution]; other sutras clarify that the movement of retribution spans across *saṃkhyeya* kalpas, and one does not know how many hundreds of thousands of births a single retribution may undergo before one finally attains liberation.
The present text speaks in terms of the final birth; all subsequent passages follow this principle.

When it says "many," it does not necessarily mean that greed must manifest as an owl, but rather speaks in terms of the majority of cases. Above, [the text] addressed the custom of sexual misconduct...
The *pó* (drought-demon) is the presiding spirit of drought and calamity; even now, when it takes the form of a beast, it still serves as an omen of misfortune.
This "residual habit" refers to the fault (*guò*), while the "omen of misfortune" (*zhēng*) refers to the manifest verification (*yìngyàn*), a portent of impending disaster.

As it is said: "On Mount Taihua there is a serpent named Feiwei, with six feet and four wings; when it appears, a great drought occurs throughout the world. This is also mentioned regarding Mount Xiaoci.
There is a beast whose appearance is like that of a monkey, with a white head and red feet; it is named Zhuyān. When it is seen, there will be great military conflict throughout the world.
It is also like the *shāngyáng* bird that dances before rain, or the *jiāngtún* porpoise that blows before the wind; most beasts of ill omen are of this kind.
Because people habitually practice deception, they now transform into *hú* foxes; the nature of the *hú* is full of guile, and thus it arises.

The seduction of people by spirits is merely their residual habit (*vāsanā*). Previously, they took the habit of resentment as a *gū* (a malevolent spirit that causes illness); now it has transformed into poison, which is its residual habit.
[Creatures such as] those that shoot with sand, the *śagong* (crabs that shoot with poison), those that sting the hand, and those that block roads—all belong to this category.

Previously, they took the habit of anger as a *lì* (a pestilential spirit); a *lì* clings to decay to seek food. Now, having been reborn as intestinal worms (*kṛmi*), they likewise lurk in filth and impurity.
To consume vegetables is to retreat from cultivation and remain stubbornly vulgar. Above, one was constrained by the habit of arrogance amidst hunger and emptiness;
now, by providing foodstuffs to fill the kitchen and satisfy others, this is the most manifest repayment of debt. Above, one used the deception of solitary seclusion as a nightmare;
now, one turns to taming and serving others. The *I Ching* says: "To harness oxen and ride horses is to carry heavy loads and travel great distances."
This refers to that very thing; "mian" (綿) means both density and the sense of profound solitude. Above, it shows the habituation of harmony and refinement;

now, riding upon residual habits, one acts as a responsive category. "Responsive" (*ying*) means responding to the sequence of time, such as the swallow returning for the community festival, the wild goose arriving as a guest, the rooster heralding dawn, or the changing of summer—these are examples.
Above, through the habituation of being set aside, one attaches to clarity and willingly accepts service. Now...
To act as an auspicious omen and transmit good fortune to others is a residual habit. As the *Xijing zajiji* says:
"When the dry magpies shriek, a traveler arrives; when the spiders gather, all affairs are auspicious.
The above describes how those who were ghosts transmitting [messages] based on human habits have now been transformed into animals, yet they still follow and conform to humans.

This refers to cases such as domesticating animals like cats and dogs; however, since these creatures originally come to repay debts—much like owls, *gū* spirits, foxes, and intestinal worms—how can one reconcile this with those that have no debt to repay?

It is because when creatures such as owls and worms encounter those to whom they owe a karmic debt, their very capture or killing constitutes the repayment. As for foxes and *gū* spirits, their repayment may be... [text ends]
"By means of the mind, one attains [the state of] Ānanda. These concluding remarks are as previously stated; the current text is detailed and complete.

Regarding "animals" (*tiryag-yoni*), they are so called because their birth is not upright. The phrase "as you [have said]" below refers back to the objection based on manifest phenomena. The first four lines directly address the matter of that objection.
The phrase "in this way" below expresses the intent of the response, meaning that these three matters originally arise from oneself and are not caused by a creator god (*īśvara*).
Neither the earth nor humans bestow these [retributions]; they are summoned by one's own delusions and thus one receives the retribution oneself—there is no one who can act as a substitute.
Within the mind of Bodhi, such things have never existed from the beginning; therefore, it is said that "floating thoughts" refer to what is solidified by thoughts.
This means that through the solidification of wholesome and unwholesome thoughts, the seven realms of existence are formed; they are not inherently existent.
Furthermore, Ānanda, from these animals [until] the appearance of a Buddha, one cannot cease this [debt].

This section of the sūtra follows the preceding discussion on the human realm; it now first demonstrates that debt and service must be balanced so as to avoid the calamity of being pursued in return, thereby introducing the subsequent text.
From "From these... onwards, the Buddha means that animals are indeed [beings] who must repay their debts.
If they come as creditors and that creditor takes from them an excessive amount beyond what was owed, then these beings will, upon returning to human form, reclaim that remaining balance;
or they may kill those who should not be killed and eat those who should not be eaten—this constitutes taking more than what was owed. If...
If one possesses the power of merit, one will not forfeit the human body to repay what remains; yet, how can one repay it among humans?

Or perhaps the creditor instead pursues them as an animal to give to the original debtor as an unworthy son—one who ruins his household and squanders his wealth, even to the point of severing affection and love, causing their tender hearts to break ten times over while they gasp for breath.
Furthermore, there may be those who, as evil friends or enemies, come to cause harm and distress, squandering one's wealth or ensnaring one with false accusations;
these are those against whom one has the power to retaliate. Regarding the simultaneous possession of both merit (*puṇya*) and virtue (*guṇa*):
in this world, there are those who possess merit but lack virtue, and those who possess virtue but lack merit. If, however, one possesses both merit and virtue...
If one possesses [merit], it is easy to repay them among human beings; if one lacks such merit, the text can be explained as follows:
"Ānanda, you should know that the distinction between the excellence and deficiency of those who overstep [their bounds] below cannot but be treated with great care.
The text can be explained as follows: the final three lines speak by way of analogy; excluding *śamatha*, the Buddha appeared.

"Worldly" refers to those who wish to resolve such enmity; they should cultivate *śamatha*, as in the three types of cessation taught by Tiantai, ceasing evil and preventing transgression so that, by realizing the true nature, the enmity naturally vanishes.

Alternatively, when a Buddha appears in the world, he is able to uproot the suffering of sentient beings; therefore, apart from these two means, one cannot surely suppress the retribution of mutual devouring and mutual slaughter.
Furthermore, you should now know that those of the owl class—[omitted]—this group is called "those who are to be pitied.
This section of the sutra follows the previous inquiry regarding the seven destinies; here, it is the fourth response concerning the human destiny. You should now...

To know that a single phrase inherits the meaning of the preceding text clarifies that within the human realm there are likewise ten categories, all of which exist because past habits have not been forgotten.
First, there are those who were animals of strange appearance, such as owls, who, having fulfilled their karmic debts from previous lives, return to human form.

Because they recover what was previously lost and now return to it, they are called "Fù" (Recoverers). The character "Zú" (Sufficient) contained within this term carries profound significance; for indeed...
It is not that one life alone is sufficient; rather, it must necessarily repay [karma] over several hundred thousand lifetimes before it is fully satisfied.

Because the nature of the *xiāo* (owl) is ignorant, it belongs to the class of the stubborn. "Stubborn" refers to those who are dull-witted and do not follow ethical principles; their innate nature does not avoid its habitual tendencies.

Regarding the character "參合" (*cánhé*), it should be understood as "should" (*yīngdāng*). This is a judgment by the Buddha, meaning that having performed such-and-such karma, one "should" [experience such-and-such a result].
It is said that one should "investigate" (can) because it is certain that such a category [of phenomena] is not erroneous; thus it says "to investigate and harmonize," and so forth.

As for the character "bian" (change/deviate) appearing in the text, this was due to the translators' oversight and lack of thorough investigation. Second, the calamitous omens were provoked by lewd demons (*yinpó*);
for lustful desire is fundamentally a dull affliction (*dùnshǐ*), yet these omens further harbor the sprouts of a craving for misfortune—this is nothing other than folly.
For what reason is the third [category] associated with the "deluded"? Regarding the character "deluded" (*yú*) in this context, some editions read it as "different" (*yì*);
however, most masters such as Changshui have interpreted it as "deluded," and I follow the majority.

Third, because it is permitted that a *mèi* (possessing spirit) provokes the kindred of foxes, and because fox-spirits and slanderous thieves arise from deceit, and since deceit is fundamentally a vulgar and base practice, it is combined with the category of the "vulgar. Fourth, because...
1. Through resentment and malevolent sorcery, one is moved by poisonous karmic affinity; for all things that contain poison, people feel fear upon seeing them.
Because residual habits are difficult to eliminate, one thus joins the class of the fierce and violent—this fifth type arises from the intensity of anger and is caused by the decline of the noble.
Thus, it is fitting that one now joins the class of the minute; "minute" refers to those who are lowly, base, and insignificant. 6. This sixth type arises from emptiness and arrogance.
Because of pride, one receives the retribution of a hungry ghost (*preta*), and as an animal (*tiryagyoni*), one further serves as food for others;
how can such arrogance be so cruel in its transgression? That those who now participate in softness are still merely the remnants of the lingering hunger [of that state] is clear.

Seventh, because of deception, one is bound by the deep obscurity of a nightmare and undergoes retribution involving servitude; that those who now participate in toil are still merely the labor of being yoked and ridden is clear.

8. Because of the harmony and refinement resulting from the cultivation of views, greetings and inquiries accord with the proper sequence; thus, the present "Section on Literary Categories" (*Wenlei*) is also a remnant of the radiance of that sequence. 9.
Because of the attachment to and reliance upon the enlightened spirits, auspicious omens are foretold in advance;

since the traces of past habituation still persist, this is included within the "Section on Clarifying the Enlightened" (*Minglei*). 10. Because of factionalism and litigation based on personal influence, one first transmits [the matter] and only thereafter... [the text continues].

That the various classes of beings now being examined have their origins in this lies precisely in the fact that litigation, concealment, and the transmission of good and ill fortune all follow the patterns of worldly conduct;
thus, the emergence of these states is merely the manifestation of one's own intent.

Ānanda, these concluding remarks below demonstrate the causes of birth in order to clarify the falsity of cyclic existence. "These" refers to the various categories of karmic calculations and inverted views previously examined.

These karmas are deluded karma; this "reckoning" is a clinging attachment. Yet this karmic reckoning arises from a perverted mind, where mental states give rise to one another and destroy one another.
This retribution is suffering, arising from a perverted mind that gives rise to delusions and creates karma, resulting in the experience of various sufferings.
These three—delusion, karma, and suffering—have continued from beginningless time until now without being able to be halted. Upon meeting a Buddha, one extracts from suffering and hears [the Dharma].
The Dharma-principle clarifies that through truth one may avoid this drowning; had one not encountered or heard it, how could delusion ever be exhausted?
That which is "dharmatā" (the nature of things) means that the Dharma must be thus. "Giving forth and returning" implies that within the profound mystery there exists a presiding sovereign.
People truly cannot force themselves against it; hence it is said, "the wheel of turning is dharmatā," as stated in the final phrase.
The meaning is this: if the human mind does not return to the True Buddha, even the Buddha can hardly save them; he merely feels pity for them.
Ānanda, there are furthermore those who follow others and do not rely on Right Enlightenment (until their retribution is exhausted, they return and disperse into the various realms of existence).
This section of the sutra follows the previous inquiry regarding the seven destinies (*gati*) and now provides five responses concerning the destiny of the immortals (*ṛṣi*).

First, from the passage beginning with Ānanda, the World-Honored One intends to reveal the ten types of immortals and first points out that they do not follow the correct path but instead pursue a divergent one.

They are called "those who follow humans" because, although the immortals have not yet transcended the human realm, they are still subsumed within the category of the human destiny; furthermore, it is said that they do not rely upon the Tathāgata.
To cultivate right concentration after attaining true awakening is distinct [from worldly practice] because it does not involve deviant inclinations or outward wandering; thus it is called "distinct.

As for "deluded thoughts," this refers to suppressing those ten types of firm thoughts held by the immortals, as all such thoughts are delusive. The subsequent section clarifies the characteristics of distinct cultivation through visualization (*xiang*):
by means of that visualization, one harmonizes the essence, energy, and spirit (*jing qi shen*), thereby bringing the yin and yang into accord and nourishing the *rong* and *wei* channels.
Following the path of firmness to sustain their forms, they seek long life by roaming beyond the seas to famous mountains and great rivers in places where humans do not go;
there are ten kinds of immortals (*ṛṣi*). Gu Shan’s commentary explains: the *Shiming* says, "To grow old and yet not die is called *xian* (immortal).
*Xian* means 'to ascend' (*qiān*); because they ascend into the mountains, the character is composed of the radical for 'person' with 'mountain' on the side."
Next, Ānanda, following the general introduction, there is a specific explanation of the ten *ṛṣis*. First, it is indicated that all ten *ṛṣis* are "firmly established among sentient beings.

Regarding the first point, "the firmness of earth-based practices," this refers to the uninterrupted cultivation of mental visualization (*saṃjñā*). As for "ingesting elixirs" (*fu-er*), "elixir" (*fu*) is a sublime name for medicinal minerals;
it refers to the roasting and processing of mineral medicines, their harmonious blending for consumption, and the discernment of their benefits and harms in order to preserve [life].

Nourishing the vital essence and blood, consolidating the primal yang, and praying to Taiyi; through the practice of ingesting [substances], one’s merit and conduct are perfected, and thus one becomes a "Earth-Walking Immortal" (dìxíng xiān).
This term is pronounced with a departing tone (qùshēng) because it refers to the completion of merit and conduct; henceforth, it shall be understood accordingly.

These individuals merely achieve eternal life within the mountain forests and have not yet attained ascension, and for this reason they are called Earth-Walking Immortals. Second, regarding "flying among plants and trees," these refer to pine, cypress, lingzhi, and atractylodes.
There are various substances that can assist in extending one's lifespan; these may all be ingested.

Furthermore, by abstaining from grain (*pi-gu*) and ceasing the consumption of food, one may refine the body until it becomes as light as a crane, enabling one to ride the winds, traverse the heavens, and cross the seas—such individuals are called "Flying Immortals" (*fei-xing-xian*).

Those who "travel through metal and stone" (*san-ming-you-xing-jin-shi*) refer to those who cultivate the five metals and eight minerals, causing the divine sand (*shen-sha*) to undergo nine transformations within and without.
When the cinnabar is perfected, one transforms the physical form and transmutes the bones to roam the lakes and seas, traversing thousands and tens of thousands of *li* in an instant;

these are called the Wandering Immortals (*youxing xian*). As for those who move through the void of the Four Ming Mountains, observing the waxing and waning of time, calculating fullness and emptiness, unifying with the One Qi to achieve suppleness, gathering the Three Flowers to nourish their essential nature, and leaving the physical form behind to traverse the void, they are called the Void-Traveling Immortals (*kongxing xian*). Five.
Those who tomorrow shall circulate the vital fluids (jin-yi) are called "those who drum upon the Celestial Pond and enjoy the vital fluids. Their skin and flesh are like ice and snow;
they are elegant and pure like virgins, untouched by worldly desires and not eating the five grains. Riding upon clouds and vapors and driving flying dragons, they roam beyond the four seas.
Their practice is second only to that of Heaven, and they are named "Heaven-Walking Immortals" (Tian-xing-xian); this is the sixth stage of pervasive clarity and universal practice.

"Refined essence" (*jingse*) refers to the discourse on the solar essence and lunar radiance; it means inhaling the wind and drinking the dew, swallowing the five essences so that the refined purity penetrates in secret, which is called the practice of the Perfected Immortal.

"The Seven Clarities and Daoist Practice of Incantations" (*qiming daoxing zhujin*) means employing written talismans and dispatching incantations, treading the *dou* and pacing the *gang*, such as Kongming with disheveled hair wielding a sword, operating the celestial mechanism; this is called the Way (*dao*).

Regarding the ninth clarification, the practice of "Illuminating Contemplation" for the Immortal of Practice: this refers to gathering the mind within and looking back, whereby the male of the *kan* trigram and the female of the *li* trigram are brought into union.
By embracing the primal yang and guarding the yin, one causes the Valley Spirit not to die and the Celestial Gate to open;

this is what is meant by "recollection perfected as illumination," becoming an Illuminating Contemplating Immortal. Regarding the tenth clarification, the practice of "Essential Conduct" through sexual union: [as described in] the *Changshui*...
This refers to those in the world who employ the arts of Yin and Yang, known as "intercourse" (*jiaogou*), and after a long time achieve success;

they respond to one another's stimuli and inhale each other's vital essence (*jingqi*) to consolidate their own forms. This is called the "Transcendent of Refining Vital Essence" (*jingxing xian*). Regarding the "Transcendent of Severing Practice" (*juexing xian*), Wenling says:

"By maintaining mental visualization and transforming through principles, the mind follows perverse awakenings and is able to undergo great transformations; because its practice transcends the world, it is called 'severed' (*jue*)."
The practice of the immortals—Ānanda, this concludes the section below which demonstrates their error. "These" refers to the ten immortals mentioned above;
because they had not yet entered the human realm, it is said that although they refined their minds among humans, they did not cultivate right concentration and thus fell into deviant practices.

Therefore, it is said they "attained something else," meaning they failed to realize the principle of non-arising (anutpāda). As for "seeking the principle of longevity," this refers to the principle of attaining long life.
Even if one were to live for a thousand million years, when observed with the Buddha-eye, it would not equal a single snap of the fingers;

when Kāśyapa entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), he passed through hundreds of thousands of kalpas in that single snap of the fingers. Thus, a life of a thousand million years is regarded as nothing more than child’s play.
The following section explains his dwelling place on deep mountains and ocean islands; the *Bowuzhi* (Treatise on the Wonders of Nature) states: [text follows].
Upon the sea there are three divine mountains—Fangzhang, Penglai, and Yingzhou—where palaces of gold and silver stand as the dwellings of the immortals.
Zhuangzi further remarked that upon Mount Guoye lies a divine personage; these are all places where the transcendents reside.
Although their lifespans are indeed eternal and their joys are indeed great, they have not yet cultivated the Way.

Juesi also said: "Because one revolves in saṃsāra following the turning of deluded thoughts, when the retribution of the immortals is exhausted, one returns to be scattered and enter the various realms of existence.
Examining the preceding text in detail, since the three realms of ghosts, animals, and humans all take the ten habitual practices as their cause, they are listed as ten;
now, the realm of immortals is also listed in ten categories because ten is a perfect number, and perfection universally encompasses all things.
Regarding the classes of immortals (*xian*), as described in the Daoist tradition, there are three thousand "side-gates" (*pángmén*); how could they be limited to merely ten categories?
Thus, one should know that the present intention cites ten as a comprehensive summary; it does not mean that immortality is restricted to ten types.

Furthermore, these ten classes of immortals today are not the same as the ten meanings concerning ghosts, animals, and humans. Why is this? It is because the former are induced by the causes of past habituation (*xiyīn*).
This is because it now adopts the perspective of the Perfect [Teaching].
From "Ānanda, all people in the world do not seek the permanent" up until this point, it is called the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu).

This section of the sutra follows the previous inquiry regarding the seven destinies (*gati*) and now provides the sixth response concerning the heavenly destiny (*deva-gati*). First, from "Ānanda" onwards, it properly explains the heavenly destiny.
The first two sentences provide a general explanation of the error regarding the heavenly destiny, asserting that failing to seek the permanent and everlasting constitutes such an error.
From "has not yet been able" onwards, it first clarifies that the term "desire" (*kāma*) used for the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) does not refer exclusively to sexual desire.
It is said that each of the six heavens possesses three kinds of desire: first, food and drink; second, sleep; and third, sexual desire.

Because these three are present, they are called the "Desire Realm" (*kāmadhātu*). The reason this sutra refers specifically to sexual desire is because Ānanda’s accidental lapse served as the condition for the arising of this teaching;
therefore, it points specifically to sexual desire. Furthermore, it is because of [the cultivation of] this [virtue] that one is reborn in heaven.
The retribution is also not merely a thinning of desire; rather, one must necessarily personally cultivate the ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala*) to be born therein.
This "thinning of desire" is but one aspect of the ten wholesome actions.

It has not yet been explained below that the cause for being born in the first heaven is the inability to renounce attachment to wives and concubines, because while one has not yet abstained from sexual misconduct (*kāma-mithyācāra*), one merely prohibits it. Sexual misconduct refers to—
One who remains unmoved in the center is able to bring about rebirth in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
Generally, all external forms are termed sexual misconduct; because one is unmoved, a portion of right wisdom and clarity arises.

"Clarified" (*cheng*) refers to limpid stillness, and "polished" (*ying*) refers to the luster of gold, used here to manifest the purity of this wisdom and clarity. This wisdom and clarity is precisely what brings about rebirth.
Because the minds of the Four Heavenly Kings are the cause [for this], the subsequent phrase says, "after the end of life, they are adjacent to the sun and moon.
Being "adjacent to the sun and moon" refers to the place where they are reborn; it means that the Four Heavenly Kings dwell on the midpoint of Mount Sumeru.
Dwelling on the midpoint means they are forty-two thousand *yojanas* above the human realm, at a height level with the sun and moon.
Therefore, it is said that they "border the sun and moon. The meaning of the names of the four heavens has been explained previously.
Thus, the following concludes and indicates the name of the first heaven; below this, it clarifies the second heaven.

This means that if a person’s lustful attachment toward their own wife is slight, yet a sudden thought of desire arises while in a state of quietude, they are therefore unable to maintain that tranquility in its entirety.

In the passage above, it was stated that the Four Heavenly Kings do not indulge in sexual misconduct; now, even their engagement in sexual conduct is slight because their minds are superior to those [of the previous realm].
Consequently, they receive the retribution of the second heaven, which surpasses the brilliance of the sun and moon.
Regarding the radiance of the sun and moon, its extent is only eighty-four thousand *yojanas*: it illuminates forty-two thousand *yojanas* above and forty-two thousand *yojanas* below.
It is two thousand *yojanas* in width, and likewise on its sides; since the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven now dwells upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, it is said to surpass the brilliance of the sun and moon.
Furthermore, because Mount Sumeru rises high above the human realm, it is said to dwell at the "summit of the human world.

The meaning of "dwelling at the summit of the human world" is to clarify that the earth-dwelling heavens (*bhūmi-cara-deva*) have not yet attained the ability to dwell in the void; thus it is so described.
The following section indicates the name of the second heaven. In the Sanskrit language it is called *Trāyastriṃśa*, which translates as "Thirty-three"; the meaning was explained previously.

"Encountering desire" clarifies the third heaven. "Encountering desire and departing without recollection" clarifies that the mind of desire is even thinner than before, though one has not yet reached the point of forgetting it entirely;
thus, when objects of desire appear, they do not resist them but engage with them.
When departing, one does not think of desires; they are like drifting clouds lightly brushed away, for the mind truly does not dwell upon them, and thus [the attachment] is thin.
The two lines following "at people" mean that although this person dwells among humans, their minds are not greatly bound by the matters of the five desires;
therefore, stirring thoughts are few and quiet thoughts are many. This clarifies the mental cause for rebirth in the third desire heaven (*Tṛtīya-kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, this heaven is situated eighty-four thousand yojanas above the celestial abodes in the air;
because the deities therein each possess bodily radiance that illuminates everything, it is called "Lustrous" (Suyāma). Since the dimensions of the sun and moon cannot reach it, it is thus described.
This concludes the indication of the name of the third heaven: in the Sanskrit language it is Suyāma, translated as "Good Time."
This heaven is divided by day and night according to the opening and closing of lotuses; therefore, all those below it are considered to be in the fourth heaven.
"At all times" refers to the time of day and the time of night, or as some say, the time of waking and the time of sleeping.
If one constantly dwells in stillness at all times, one will naturally be free from desire; however, even if one is still, when sensory contacts arise, one may not yet be able [to remain so].
This is merely a provisional response to a contrary sentiment. "Contact" (*spraṣṭavya*) refers here to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
For this reason, at the end of life, one is reborn in the fourth heaven. Regarding the three phrases concerning ascending and descending:

it is said that this heaven is a celestial abode (*antarīkṣavāsin*), whereas the second [heaven] and the two terrestrial heavens (*bhūmivāsin*) of the lower realm, as well as the human world, are not in contact with one another; because they are far removed from all coarse impurities (*audārikakaluṣa*), it is so called.

The subtle and minute, down to the final two phrases—meaning that those not reached by the three calamities at the end of a kalpa—must refer specifically to Maitreya’s Inner Court (*abhyantara-maṇḍala*).
If it were the Outer Court, how could ordinary beings born there as a result of their retribution avoid the three calamities?

The Inner Court is the dwelling place of the Great Sage who is next to attain Buddhahood; thus, the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*) are utterly separated. Therefore, the kalpa calamities do not reach it.
"It is not equal," thus concluding the fourth heaven below. In the original Sanskrit, *Tuṣita* is translated as "Contentment" (*zhīzú*), because therein one knows contentment regarding all desires.
"I do not have... and so forth, clarifying the fifth heaven. The first two phrases state:
"Regarding the mind of desire and love, I do not possess it while they do; nor am I yet able to oppose it. If one were to engage in their activities, then I... [the text continues].

"Indulging in sexual intercourse without pleasure" means that I originally have no intention to engage in such matters; it is not merely a lack of intention, but rather that I actually loathe them and practice them only through forced effort.
Thus, it is called "indulging without pleasure. The phrase "its flavor is like chewing wax" is explained by way of a metaphor:
the nature of wax is inherently bland, and chewing it yields no taste; this serves as a metaphor for how the flavor of indulging in sensual desires is exceedingly thin.
Thus, by virtue of such a mind, one is reborn in the fifth heaven, the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*). "Mastery" (*vaśa*) means transcendence;
that is to say, while the various heavens of the lower realms each possess their own karmic reward-spheres, their merit is limited in thickness and they lack sovereignty over objects of desire.
Those born in this heaven, however, possess such abundant merit that they are able to spontaneously emanate objects of desire and enjoy them at will, thereby transcending [the lower realms].

Transcending the lower heaven of non-transformation, they dwell spontaneously in the ground of transformation; since "ground" (bhūmi) means "place," it is said that they transcend the ground of transformation.
Thus, the following concludes by indicating the name of the fifth heaven: because they delight in their own transformations, it is called the Heaven of Delight in Transformations (Nirmāṇarati).
Regarding the sixth heaven, the first two lines clarify that while they lack worldly minds, they share in worldly affairs. This means:
I am entirely free from desire, yet I have not yet transcended worldly etiquette; thus, the formal distinction between husband and wife still remains.
As for "interacting in conduct," it means that although the objects of desire appear before one, there are still traces of interaction;

yet, because the mind is unstained despite this interaction, it is said that one "clearly transcends" them. Through such a causal mind, one is reborn in the sixth heaven, emerging in a state of transformative transcendence.

"Without transformation" (*asaṃjñisattva*) refers to the Heaven of Transformation; "without non-transformation" (*asaṃjñisattvāsaṃjñisattva*) refers to the remaining heavens below. Both "transformation" and "without non-transformation" transcend these [lower realms].
This concludes the sixth heaven. As for the name "Mastery over Others' Transformations" (*paranirmitavaśavartin*):

it means that regarding all objects of desire, one does not need to labor at transforming them oneself, as they are transformed by others for one's own enjoyment; therefore, it is called Mastery over Others' Transformations.
Ānanda, this concludes the summary of the names for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Although their forms have emerged from movement, it is said that they move upward from below;
as their desire to move gradually lightens, they gradually emerge. Although their physical bodies are separated from movement, the traces of their minds have not yet been forgotten;

therefore, it is said they "still engage" (*saṃsarga*). As the verse in the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* says: "The six [classes] experience desire through embracing, holding hands, laughing, and gazing. This refers to sexual intercourse.
The Four Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa heavens embrace one another as humans do; in the Yāma heaven, they merely hold hands; in the Tuṣita heaven, they smile.
In the two higher heavens, gazing intently constitutes sexual desire; thus, the present text states that "the mind and its traces still intersect," which conveys this very meaning.
The final sentence provides a summary, which is easily understood.
Direct Explanation of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Cultivation and Realization and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas,
Volume Eight.
Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Cultivation and Realization and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas.
Direct Commentary, Volume Nine.
Explained by the junior monk Guangmo of Yunqi Temple in Ancient Hangzhou, and collated by the lay follower Yuan Yan of Wutang. Direct Commentary.
"Ānanda, when all those in the world who cultivate the mind [attain] a state where the various outflows (āsrava) do not move, this is called the First Dhyāna.

This section of the sutra follows the previous response regarding the heavenly realms and now proceeds to clarify the Form Realm (rūpadhātu); it first demonstrates the First Dhyāna. Regarding the three heavens of the First Dhyāna, it first clarifies the Brahmakāyika heaven.

The term "dhyāna" is a transliteration of the Sanskrit word *dhyāna*. (Note: The provided text fragment contains a partial explanation of the term "dhyāna" at the end; the translation reflects the full context as presented.)

"Dhyāna" (禪那) is translated as "cultivation through contemplation" (思惟修). This means that while in the lower Desire Realm there is no dhyāna, one cultivates meditative concentration (禪定) only upon being born in these heavens;
therefore, the heavens of the Form Realm are collectively called "Dhyāna Heavens. These Dhyāna Heavens are detached from desire because their concentration differs from the state of distraction.
First, regarding Ānanda’s downward observation, the first six phrases express the intent of suppressing distraction and exalting concentration; they also serve as a continuation...

The statement that "the former gives rise to the latter" refers to the six realms of desire (*ṣaḍ-kāmadhātu*) as being "scattered wholesome states" (*vikṣipta-kuśala*); thus, those who have not yet cultivated meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) remain immersed in the defilements of desire.
When it says "the mind cultivated by these persons," it specifically refers to the gods of the six desire heavens.

Since the desire heavens generally cultivate the ten grades of superior wholesome action (*daśa-kuśala-karma-patha*), and these ten wholesome actions are entirely conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and therefore scattered wholesome states, what is being cultivated here is indeed a conditioned mind.

The following two lines do not require [further explanation], as they precisely clarify the intent of suppressing distraction and uplifting concentration. "Not requiring" (*bu jia*) means not relying upon meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*);
thus, wisdom (*prajñā*) does not arise. This indicates that when the six desire realms (*ṣaḍ-kāma-dhātu*) are indulged in through passionate attachment, one becomes largely deluded;
because there is no *dhyāna*, there is no *prajñā*. This means that although such persons may be able to restrain their bodies and refrain from sexual misconduct, [they lack true wisdom].
"Desiring yet not having forgotten the traces of the mind"—these first four lines directly clarify the general outline of the mental cultivation of the desire-realm heavens (*kāmadhātu*).

If one proceeds to the section below, it clarifies the mental state that serves as the cause for birth in the Brahma realm (*brahmaloka*): namely, that among the four modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*), if even thoughts of various sensual defilements do not arise, then body and mind both vanish.

Because they both vanish, passionate attachment does not arise; this alone— (Note: The provided text appears to be an excerpt from a commentary on Buddhist practice, likely from a work such as the *Zongjing Lu* or similar Chan/Zen literature. The translation reflects the technical terminology of Chinese Buddhist scholasticism.)

The phrase "arising" contains many meanings. Why is this? In other sutras and treatises, it is said that when one cultivates the first dhyāna through various meditative practices (*vipaśyanā*), only upon entering and emerging from them does the mark of the first dhyāna manifest.
The present text is extremely concise, encompassing everything in a single sentence;
this is seen in detail in the Tiantai commentary on meditation. Here, it says that if desire and attachment do not arise, then one does not remain in desire.

The "realm" (*dhātu*) precisely refers to the signs of the arising of the first *dhyāna*. The following two phrases clarify that upon the end of life in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one is immediately reborn among the Brahmakāyika devas.
"In accordance with thought" (*yathāsaṃkalpa*) means that because thoughts of craving and defilement do not arise, one is born there.
Regarding "Brahma-companions" (*brahmakāyika*): "Brahma" is a foreign sound; in full it is *Brahmā*, translated as "pure conduct" (*śucicaryā*), or alternatively, "detachment."

Because one desires to be free from desire, one purifies oneself; because the name "Brahma" is preserved, those who are "companions" (varga) are his associates, and these associates constitute the assembly (*parṣad*).
Thus, the following concludes by indicating the name of the heaven: "The Brahma-assembly" refers to the subjects of the Brahma-world.

Regarding the phrase "having abandoned the practice of desire," this means that the coarse and heavy habitual tendencies of suffering within the lower Desire Realm have been eliminated. This is "separation."

The manifestation of the desire-mind refers to the emergence of the pure and wondrous [states] of the dhyāna heavens. Among all the lower [stages], it clarifies the ten wholesome precepts (śīla) of the external [lay practitioners];
because they accord with and delight in the dhyāna-mind, the commentary on dhyāna states:

"If one attains the first dhyāna, one is immediately endowed with the wholesome mental states of faith, ethical discipline (śīla), renunciation (tyāga), concentration (samādhi), learning (śruta), and wisdom (prajñā). Changshui’s sub-commentary states: "This correctly elucidates this point."

The gods of this heaven delight in and accord with the precepts coexistent with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahaja-śīla*); they achieve the holy life (*brahmacarya*), guard against wrongdoing, and do not lose it.

Thus, because they simultaneously protect the discipline (*vinaya*) and pure precepts (*śīla*) to perfect their virtues and assist the Brahmā King, they are called the "Brahma-Purohitas" (Ministers of Brahmā). Thus concludes the section identifying the name of this heaven.
Regarding the passage beginning with "body and mind," the first three lines clarify the third heaven of the First Dhyāna, while the first four lines constitute the formal exposition.
To say that the virtue of the Brahma King is "wondrously perfect" in both body and mind means that his external body upholds the precepts while his internal mind is free from desire;

this "wondrous perfection" is an epithet for supreme purity. It is described as "wondrously perfect" in contrast to the coarse obstructions of the lower realms, as both its interior and exterior are pure.
Furthermore, the addition of "clear awakening" serves as evidence that wisdom is generated through the provisional practice of *dhyāna*.
This person is also called "Brahmā" because he manifests the possession of Brahma-virtue and presides over the Brahma-multitude;

thus, "at the appropriate time" means at the time when his meditative concentration and wisdom are fully perfected. The following section concludes by indicating the name of the heaven, which can be understood.

Ānanda, these three [heavens] below summarize the meaning of the three heavens of the first dhyāna. As for "the superior stream," it serves as an indirect indication of the six heavens of the desire realm.
They are called "superior stream" (śreṣṭha-srotas) because they have attained meditative concentration and wisdom through the departure from desire.
Regarding the two phrases concerning "all suffering": it means that the coarse suffering of the defilements of desire in the lower realms cannot oppress them.

Although they do not belong to the lower world, the World-Honored One suppresses [their pride] and then exalts them; yet because they do not cultivate right awakening, their concentration is not true, and their antidote is merely a semblance.

It is taught that this is merely the mundane fundamental dhyāna (*laukika-maula-dhyāna*), a tainted semblance of meditative absorption (*sāsrava-ābhāsa-samādhi*) and not the supramundane, untainted true *samādhi*.

Therefore, after describing its purity, it further extols its excellence by stating that it is "pure" because one has attained freedom from desire regarding the coarse outflows (*āsrava*) of the lower realms.
"Immovable" (*āneñja*) means that these [outflows] have been suppressed and do not arise again. The final phrase summarizes the name of the first dhyāna.
Because one first attains dhyāna upon initially departing from the desire realm, there are sixteen factors of the dhyāna-branch forest (dhyānāṅga-vana), such as the contacts (*sparśa*) and so forth;
these are now abbreviated. For a detailed account, one should consult the Tiantai commentary on the *Pāramitās*, where they are presented together for study so that one may gain understanding.
Ānanda, next, the Brahmā Heaven governs the Brahmā people; having already subdued coarse outflows, it is called the Second Dhyāna.
This section of the sutra follows the previous response regarding the celestial realms to further clarify the Form Realm, and now specifically demonstrates the Second Dhyāna.

The phrase "next" (其) below clarifies that this is the first heaven of the Second Dhyāna; it is "next" because it follows the First Dhyāna mentioned previously, hence it "governs the Brahmā [Heaven]."
The person who perfects the holy life (*brahmacarya*) inherits the virtue of the previous Brahma-kings and further cultivates progress;

thus, the latter two lines, which describe the clarification of the mind, precisely represent the merit of this further cultivation. This is because that which is called "Brahma" by virtue of being free from desire refers to the meaning within the first dhyāna;
once one has distanced oneself from desire in the second dhyāna, the meaning of "Brahma" becomes even deeper, such that it can no longer be defined merely as freedom from desire.
Śakra and Brahmā. In Tiantai’s exegesis of dhyāna, this same teaching is also found;

therefore, the first dhyāna is called "joy and bliss born of seclusion" (*vivekaja-prītisukha*), and the second dhyāna is called "joy and bliss born of concentration" (*samādhija-prītisukha*)—this is precisely that meaning. "Brahma-conduct" (*brahmacarya*) is simply dhyāna.

When Brahma-conduct is fulfilled, one attains a tranquil mind that is unmoving. This "tranquil mind" is concentration (*samādhi*); its profound stillness is the tranquility of the mind, which is concentration.
Because the light produced from the objective realm is the efficacy of profound stillness, and the light of stillness manifests before one, it is called "Produced Light" (*Abhāsvara*).
Since this light has just arisen and is not yet fully perfected, it is named "Limited Light" (*Parīttābha*). Thus, the names of the heavens are concluded and indicated below; this may be understood.

Regarding "light upon light" (*ābhā-prabhā*) below, this clarifies the second heaven of the Second Dhyāna. "Light upon light mutually illuminating" (*ābhā-prabhā-saṃprabha*): "mutually illuminating" (*saṃprabha*) carries the meaning of responding through illumination. That is to say—
Because the meditative minds of this assembly of devas are serene and tranquil, and their light of concentration illuminates one another, they reflect each other endlessly;
thus it is said that "the illumination is inexhaustible. Because this internal clarity penetrates to the exterior, both the world-realm (*loka-dhātu*) and its inhabitants (*sattva*) are purified;

because both the environment and its beings are pure, it is said that "it is universally formed of lapis lazuli. Because the mutual illumination of these beings is inexhaustible, it is named "Immeasurable Light" (*Amitābha*).
The heavens are thus concluded below by indicating their names. "Sucking and Holding" (*Ābhāsvara*) below clarifies the third heaven of the second dhyāna.

The first two phrases, "sucking and holding," carry the meaning of "gathering and maintaining"; this is a skillful use of terminology. "Perfect Light" (*Prabhāsvara*) refers to "Immeasurable Light" (*Apramāṇābha*), which constitutes the substance of the teaching.
This is because in the second dhyāna, verbal teachings are not established; rather, one distinguishes excellence and deficiency through light to spur the mind forward.

Therefore, it is said that "upholding the light accomplishes the teaching. Because one urges practice forward by means of light, it is called the "body of the teaching" (*śāsana-tattva*). Regarding "manifesting transformation and purity":

"manifesting" (*fa*) refers to opening and developing (*kai-fa*), while "transforming" (*hua*) refers to changing and metamorphosing (*bian-hua*). This follows the meaning of the preceding two phrases, signifying that by means of the perfect light, one opens and develops the coarse and inferior, while transforming the sublime and wondrous.
This is like the explanation of *dhyāna* (meditation), which speaks to the meaning of internal defilement and internal purity.
Internal defilement is coarse; internal purity is sublime. Because of this internal purity, it is called "Pure. Regarding "its application is inexhaustible":

this means that through light, its function is manifested, and its responsive application is inexhaustible. Following the light, the teaching is formed; since the teaching is itself sound, it is therefore named the Heaven of Light-Sound (*Ābhāsvara*).
Thus, [the text] concludes below by indicating the name of the heaven. Ānanda, these three... [is the] general [conclusion].
Regarding the formation of the second dhyāna, this "superior stream" is even more excellent than the first dhyāna. As for "sorrowful anxiety," "anxiety" refers to the fetters;
it indicates that the *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) of the preceding first dhyāna constitute sorrowful anxiety.

Therefore, since this present second dhyāna is a samādhi without *vitarka* or *vicāra* and possesses internal purity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*), sorrowful anxiety cannot oppress it. Although it is not inferior, it is as previously explained.
The final sentence summarizes the names of the second dhyāna.
Ānanda, when the celestial beings thus possess the perfect radiance and the accomplishment of sound (up to) the complete presence of joy, it is called the third dhyāna.

This section of the sutra follows the previous response regarding the celestial realms (*deva-gati*) and now further clarifies the Form Realm (*rūpa-dhātu*), specifically indicating the first of the three dhyānas.

The phrase "Thus" (*rúshì*) below explains the first heaven of the third dhyāna. The single phrase "Spherical Radiance" (*yuánguāng*) connects to the merit of the previous "Heaven of Utmost Light-Sound" (*ābhāsvara*);

it refers to the intensification of effort through which the coarse is swept away and the subtle is revealed—meaning that by means of the prior light-sound, the coarse is cleared away and the wondrous is made manifest.
Relying on the excellence of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, one develops and achieves the refined practice of the third dhyāna.

Regarding this Ābhāsvara realm, what is coarse and what is subtle? It is because the great joy and vigorous movement of the second dhyāna are considered coarse, while the bliss of cessation (*śānti*) in the third dhyāna is considered subtle.
The term "cessation" is established by dispelling the preceding vigorous movement; the phrasing of the present text is thus ornate and elegant.
The true meaning is obscure; by carefully examining the Tiantai commentary on dhyāna, one gains insight.

"Pervading the bliss of cessation" (*sukha-nirodha*) means that before cessation, there is vigorous movement which pervades the bliss within cessation; because it momentarily pervades the bliss of cessation, it is called "pervasion.
Thus, the following concludes by indicating the name of the heaven: "Pure" (*śubha*) is the meaning of cessation, taking the preceding vigorous movement as [the basis].
The defilements have now attained quiescence and become pure; because this purity is only partial, it is called "Limited Purity" (Parīttasubha).
Regarding "Pure Space" (Subhakṛtsna) below, this clarifies the second heaven of the third dhyāna. "Pure space" refers back to what was said regarding Limited Purity:

"purity" is the spiritual effort (*abhyāsa*), while "space" is the actual result, namely the meditative state (*samādhi-viṣaya*). This means that by purifying the previously active defilements, one attains emptiness; thus, this is "emptiness."
When it manifests before one, it induces the vast expanse of quiescence; its merit is boundless, whereby body and mind attain pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
This pliancy and meditative concentration are also spoken of in contrast to joy, vigor, and heaviness (*dausthulya*);
because heaviness is extinguished, there is internal and external pliancy. While the previous [passage] spoke of "pervasion," this one speaks of "accomplishment"; the former is superior.
As previously stated, it is called "Immeasurable Purity" (*Apramāṇaśubha*) because it induces boundlessness; thus, the preceding section concludes by indicating the name of the heaven.
Below this, the "World-Sphere" (*Loka-dhātu*) clarifies the third heaven of the Third Dhyāna. Here, the "basis" (*āśraya*) refers to the body, and the "primary" (*adhiṣṭhāna*) refers to the mind.

This is "Universal Purity" (*Śubhakṛtsna*), meaning that both the basis and the primary are completely pure. Because both the basis and the primary are pure, it is termed "Universal" (*Kṛtsna*); that is, both the basis and the primary are equally perfected.
When the mind and its objects are fully tranquil and fused into a single state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one achieves virtue through this purity;
taking this very concentration as one’s supreme reliance, one returns entirely to tranquil bliss. "Returning" carries the meaning of abiding and maintaining.

Whereas previously it was merely said that [virtue] was accomplished, here one abides and maintains within it, such that the merit is doubled compared to before. Because both the environment and its inhabitants are pure, it is called "Universal Purity" (*Śubhakṛtsna*). Thus it is.

The following section concludes by indicating the name of the heaven, Ānanda. This final summary of the three dhyānas signifies that this "superior flow" is even more excellent than the second dhyāna.
"Possessing great conformity" means that it conforms to the state of cessation (*nirodha*), wherein mind and object are fused;
thus it is called "great. The final two phrases mean that within these three dhyānas, there is no joy (*prīti*).
Because it is free from movement, one attains peaceful and secure bliss. Both other sūtras and śāstras state that in the third dhyāna, one attains pervasive physical bliss;
therefore, it is said that body and mind are peaceful and secure, attaining immeasurable bliss.

Although this is not [the same as] what was previously described regarding "joy" (*prīti*), the term "joy" refers to the pervasiveness of bliss, and is not like the joy of vigorous agitation found in the second dhyāna. While the names are the same, their essential natures differ; they must not be conflated.

The phrasing [of the previous sections] obscures the intended meaning. In the "Explanation of Dhyāna," the concluding remarks for both the first and second dhyānas contain references to the "subduing of outflows" (*āsrava*).
Now, however, it concludes directly with the "characteristic of bliss. One can thus know with certainty that the tranquility and bliss herein are far superior to those of the preceding two;
