therefore, it is called "the stage of sublime bliss free from joy" (*prīti-virāga-praśrabdhi-sukha-bhūmi*).
Ānanda, furthermore, when gods and humans are not oppressed in body or mind... (up to) "the mastery of function is called the fourth dhyāna.
This section of the sutra follows the previous response regarding the heavenly realms and now further clarifies the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); it specifically indicates the fourth dhyāna.
The phrase "furthermore" below explains the initial stage of the four dhyānas; the first two phrases, "gods and humans are not oppressed," follow from the explanation of the third dhyāna.
Regarding the statement that "the cause of suffering is exhausted," this is because within the second dhyāna, the joy (*prīti*) and exultation (*saumanasya*) have been exhausted;
since joy and exultation are moving states and thus causes of suffering, and these characteristics do not exist within the third dhyāna, it is said that "there is no oppression.

These two phrases inherit from the preceding [discussion of] "pleasure" (*sukha*), while the following two phrases give rise to the subsequent [discussion of] "pleasure. As for the phrase "equal to that," it explains the state within dhyāna, referring to those devas.
Initially, when one desires to obtain pleasure, seeking it with single-minded diligence involves great hardship; once obtained, guarding it and becoming attached to it is likewise suffering;
and when it is suddenly lost or destroyed, there is yet further suffering. Therefore, the present text states: "Pleasure is not permanent; after a long time, it must inevitably lead to suffering.
These two lines give rise to the mind of renunciation (*upekṣā*). The four lines following "suffering and pleasure" constitute the main body [of the argument].
To clarify the characteristics of this divine state (*deva-caryā*): since these deities have realized the faults of both suffering and pleasure, they suddenly abandon these two states of mind.

Both the mind of suffering and the mind of pleasure are termed "coarse and heavy" (*dausthulya*); once suffering and pleasure are abandoned, the characteristics of coarseness and heaviness are extinguished.
"Pure merit" refers to the purity of equanimity and mindfulness; because the defilements of suffering and pleasure have been abandoned, it is attained.

Because the characteristics of pure merit and defilement are extinguished, the nature of pure merit arises; thus, by virtue of this arising of merit, it is named "Heaven. This concludes the explanation of the name of Heaven.
Regarding the "mind of equanimity" (*upekṣā-citta*) below, this clarifies the second dhyāna.

As for the "perfect fusion of the mind of equanimity": equanimity is the practitioner's causal mind; through equanimity, one attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Equanimity and concentration are the perfect fusion of subject and object.

Therefore, the *Bhūmivastu-śāstra* states: "This meditative absorption is called 'conjoined with equanimity' (*upekṣā-sahagata-dhyāna*). Its essence is free from both suffering and pleasure, and it arises together with a subtle and sublime feeling of equanimity.
Because this absorption is associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), it is named 'conjoined with equanimity.

The present text’s notion of 'perfect fusion' (*yuanrong*) refers precisely to the sense of 'association' (*saṃprayoga*) as explained in that treatise. Regarding 'purity of resolute conviction' (*adhimukti-viśuddhi*), it means that this deity attains the excellence within equanimity."
The wondrous vision maintains its resolve within the mind; it cannot be led astray by objects of suffering or pleasure, for it has forever severed the faults and afflictions of the third dhyāna.
Thus it is said that "resolute belief is pure. The *Changshui Shu* (Long Water Commentary) states:

"By the power of resolute belief, within this perfectly integrated and sublime samādhi, one feels love and accord, causing this sublime samādhi to become free from obstruction and to function according to the mind."
Because one enjoys mastery over inexhaustible [resources], it is said that one attains wondrous compliance (*anuloma*) that extends to the end of the future. Question:
Since this impure meditative absorption (*sāsrava-samādhi*) has a limited lifespan, why is it said to extend to the end of the future? Answer:

This refers to the long duration of the retributive lifespan obtained through the attainment of this concentration, which spans many kalpas; thus it is said to reach the end of the future. It does not refer to the period after the exhaustion of that retribution. Thus it is.
The concluding summary identifies the name of this heaven as "Loving Merit" (*Puṇyaprasava*). According to the text, "wondrous compliance" (*miāo suíshùn*) carries the meaning of "love" (*ài*);

thus it is named "Loving Merit. Since "merit" (*fú*) here refers to pure merit, and the first heaven is called "Birth of Merit" (*Puṇyaprasava*), how could this heaven—which possesses such superior and increasing pure merit—not possess love?
From this point downward, Ānanda clarifies that there are two branches; first, from "If one... downward, he clarifies...

Guangguo Qi said: "If one dwells in the realization and cultivation of the further perfection and clarity of pure light and pure merit within the unobstructed [sphere of] merit, this is called 'Vipulaphala' (Broad Fruit). 'Broad' means immeasurable;
since unobstructed pure merit is the cause and the perfect realization of clarity is the fruit, it is named Vipulaphala. One must know that Vipulaphala is the fourth dhyāna."
The correct path of the three heavens is the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi*); this is a divergent branch of the fourth dhyāna belonging to the heavens of external paths (*tīrthika*).
Therefore, the following section clarifies the branch of non-perception: "If, at a previous time, one simultaneously becomes weary of both suffering and pleasure—this refers to the first heaven.

Relying on this mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), one investigates and scrutinizes with intense precision, continuing from moment to moment until one perfectly and profoundly masters the Middle Way within equanimity."

When the principle of relinquishment reaches its ultimate limit, body and mind both perish and all mental deliberations are reduced to ashes. For five hundred kalpas, one remains motionless and unmoving;
yet the Buddha judges this person’s error, declaring that because they take arising and ceasing as their cause, they are unable to awaken to the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing.
It is said that during those five hundred kalpas, it is only after the first half has passed that they finally attain realization.
Having extinguished all perceptions until the final half-koṭi of five hundred koṭis of kalpas, perceptions arise once more;
these five hundred koṭis are merely the karmic reward of their lifespan. Thus, the conclusion below indicates the name of the heaven, which can be understood.
Ānanda, this section below summarizes the meaning of the four dhyānas; "all worlds" refers to the various heavens of the lower realms.
Regarding the objects of suffering and pleasure, they are as previously described: namely, the coarse and heavy states within the six desire realms and the first two or three dhyānas.

Because these various coarse and heavy states cannot disturb one’s equanimity (*upekṣā*), even though this is not yet the true immovable stage (*aniñjya-bhūmi*)—which is like the supramundane eighth stage—it constitutes the position of true immovability.
That which possesses the mind of attainment is the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
The mind that has attained [the fruits] appears as if it were unmoving. The World-Honored One suppresses and then elevates this, saying:
"These devas of the four dhyānas, having reached this state of relinquishment within the conditioned mind, have brought their cultivation to maturity; this is indeed worthy of joy.

The first part clarifies the various heavens born of retribution for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); the latter part clarifies the commonality of the mind of relinquishment among the three fruits of the noble ones (*ārya*). Fifth.
These are the Anāgāmin heavens.
Ānanda, herein there are further five Anāgāmin heavens... (omitted)... from this point downward, they are called the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).
This section of the sūtra follows the previous response regarding the heavenly destinies and now clarifies the Form Realm; it subsequently indicates the five [Anāgāmin heavens].
"Returning to the heavens" refers here to the fourth dhyāna heaven. Regarding the "five non-returners" (*pañca-anāgāmin*), the term "non-returner" is a name for the third fruit of the path.
In Sanskrit it is *anāgāmin*, translated as "non-returning" or "not coming," meaning that the nine grades of afflictions of the lower realms have been completely severed;
since these habitual tendencies are themselves the afflictions of volition (*cetanā*), when the afflictions are exhausted, suffering is ended.

Because both pleasure and pain are forgotten, there is no place for temporary residence in the lower stages; thus, one is called a "Non-returner" (*anāgāmin*) because they do not return to take birth in the lower stages.

Since suffering and pleasure have perished, they temporarily establish their dwelling within the equanimity (*upekṣā*) of the fourth dhyāna to await the exhaustion of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the higher stages.
Upon realizing the state of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), they then transcend the three realms. This...
The middle and lower sections provide a general indication of the overall meaning of the Non-returner (Anāgāmin). Next, from "Ānanda" onwards, the five heavens are distinguished individually;

although they are all equally non-returners, because their faculties vary between sharp and dull, there are distinctions of depth and shallowness among these five heavens. From "Ānanda’s suffering and pleasure" onwards, it clarifies the first heaven of the non-returners:
because the afflictions of the lower realms have been exhausted, both suffering and pleasure are extinguished; and because suffering and pleasure are extinguished, [the first heaven is established].
When the mind and its objects do not contend, there is no mutual engagement; thus it is said that "the contending mind does not engage. This concludes the first heaven, named *Avṛha* (No Affliction).
"Affliction" (*vṛha*) refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*). Because the realms of suffering and pleasure have ceased and external objects no longer disturb, the internal mind is free from affliction;
hence it is called the Heaven of No Affliction. The following section clarifies the second stage of the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
The "celestial mechanism" (*tian jiguā*) is a metaphor for the internal mind. Although the external objects of the previous day have perished, the internal mind has not yet vanished;

therefore, it is said that "the mechanism moves alone. This phrase inherits the meaning from the preceding text. The line "investigating their intersection finds no ground" precisely clarifies the characteristics of this celestial movement.
It means that because external objects have ceased, there is no place for them to intersect; "ground" (*di*) here refers to a location or locus.
Since there is no longer any ground for past associations, the internal mind is likewise extinguished.
Thus, the second heaven is concluded as being called "Without Heat" (*Atapa*). "Heat" is spoken of in contrast to "affliction" (*kleśa*);

because the external conditions of the previous heaven were not yet optimal, affliction did not cease and heat still remained within. Now, since the internal [mind] has also been extinguished, heat cannot be found; therefore, it is named "Without Heat."
"Next, the section 'Heating the Ten Directions' clarifies the third stage of the Non-returner (Anāgāmin). The world-spheres are the objects, and wondrous seeing is the faculty.
When the faculty does not grasp at objects, it is tranquil and unmoving; therefore, it is called 'perfectly clear. This wondrous seeing of perfect clarity is termed the 'faculty of wondrous seeing.
Because the faculty is pure, the images of sensory dust do not appear. When external images do not appear, internal defilements do not arise. Thus it is said.
The third heaven of the lower realm is named Sudṛśa, which means "Excellent Vision" (Sudṛśa), as "excellent" (*su*) also carries the sense of "wondrous.
Regarding "refined vision" (*sudarśana*), this refers to a subtle and refined vision;
it is said that this heaven further applies effort to the wondrous vision described above to refine and mold it. This "refining and molding" is also explained by way of metaphor.

By means of this metaphor, one contemplates the "Good Vision" (*Sudarśana*) mentioned previously: it merely involved not grasping at sensory objects and forgetting conditions to return [to the source].

Now, however, it further refines and molds that subtle vision so that it universally enters into sensory objects, manifesting unimpeded vision; therefore, it is called "Good Manifestation" (*Sudṛśa*). Previously, it was the revolving of vision to enter emptiness;
now, it is the revolving from emptiness to engage with the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), where diligent contemplation excels the former stage. Thus, it is named accordingly.
Subhūti, thus the fourth heaven below is named "Ultimate" (Kṛtsnāvaraṇa); this clarifies that the fifth heaven of the Non-returners (Anāgāmin) is the "Ultimate.
Regarding the term *kṛtsna*: *kṛ* has the meaning of "thorough investigation," and *sna* has the meaning of "completion.
*Kṛtsna* refers to the exhaustion of all forms (*rūpa*). *Kṛtsna-kṛtsna* means subtle and profound research until one reaches the ultimate nature of the nature of form.

The "upper nature" is the essential body of form (*rūpa*), while the "lower nature" is the true nature of the nature of form. This true nature is precisely the nature of the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
When one profoundly investigates the point where the nature of form is empty, the manifold conditions (*jī*) cease and the emptiness of nature manifests;
therefore, it is said that one "enters the boundless. The boundless is itself emptiness. Thus concludes the fifth section.
The heavens are called Akaniṣṭha (Ultimate Form) because they represent the ultimate limit where the nature of form is exhausted. Ānanda, this is not a summary of the heavens of the Non-returners;

it means that from the first dhyāna to the fourth dhyāna, the Heavenly Kings of these four stages alone have heard with reverence of the name of the five heavens of the Non-returners, yet they have never actually seen them.
This is because there is a separation between the holy and the ordinary, and [the former] is free from outflows (*āsrava*).
Because the untainted (*anāsrava*) states are not identical, as can be understood from the examples cited below.

The phrase "in this context" at the beginning of the text refers specifically to the state of relinquishing one's homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*), and does not imply that there are five distinct heavens for non-returners (*anāgāmin*). Therefore, this example is cited.

"Ānanda, these ten... and so forth serves as a general conclusion regarding the four dhyānas, which share the common name "the realm of form" (*rūpadhātu*). As for the term "solitary and unmixed," it refers to the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).

Because the merit of the heavens' exhaustion of form and cessation of form is superior, they are called "without intercourse. Yet, because the mind's longing for higher realms has not yet ceased, they are designated as "wandering alone.
From beginning to end, because the burden of the physical form remains unexhausted, they are collectively termed the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Furthermore, Ānanda, from this Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) down to what is called the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
This section of the sūtra follows the previous discussion to explain the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*) within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) among the celestial destinies.

The phrase "furthermore" below clarifies the beginning of entry into the formless realm. As for "the Peak of Existence," "existence" (*bhava*) is a synonym for form (*rūpa*), and "peak" (*agra*) refers to the limit.

The meaning of "limit" (*koti*) is that because one enters [the path] vertically, it is called the "summit" (*mūrdhan*). Thus, the Heaven of Ultimate Form (*Akaniṣṭha*) is the summit of existence (*bhava*).
Furthermore, this term "existence" is spoken in contrast to the aforementioned four formless realms (*ārūpya*), as that which possesses form is "existence" and that which is formless is "emptiness.
Within this heaven, there are two divergent paths; if we first clarify the path of horizontal emergence from below, it is as follows:
Within the state of equanimity, he illuminates the light of untainted, correct wisdom, which is perfectly penetrating and all-pervasive;

thus, what was tainted becomes untainted and is no longer constrained by the realm of dust. Therefore, by crossing directly and swiftly out of the mundane realm, he attains the status of a sharp-facultied Great Arhat.
He then breaks through ignorance for the first time outside the realms, immediately ascending to the First Abode and entering the ranks of the Bodhisattvas.
"Mounting [the vehicle] in this way" concludes the section on the Great Mind. To turn the mind of a Śrāvaka toward the Bodhisattva path is called "turning the mind," referring to the Great Arhats.
If one proceeds downward, it clarifies the vertical entry into the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).

Regarding those who achieve detachment through renunciation, they loathe form (*rūpa*) as if it were a prison; thus, the commentary on the dhyānas states: "The practitioner should deeply contemplate the faults of material phenomena."

The so-called fault is that as long as there is a body, there is hunger, thirst, disease, and so forth, up to the point where it says all material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) bind and entangle the mind, preventing it from attaining mastery.
This passage censures the faults of these material phenomena and praises the formless void (*ākāśa-arūpa*).

When this practice of censure and praise becomes mature, it is called the accomplishment of renunciation and aversion. The two phrases following "perceiving the body" constitute the destruction of matter.
The meaning of this passage can be explained as follows: One takes empty space as the object of wisdom and enters this meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Within this profound concentration, one perceives only empty space and no material forms (*rūpa*). It is like a bird in a cage; once the cage is broken, it emerges and soars with complete freedom.
Realizing the concentration of empty space is likewise so. This is the method for dissolving obstructions and entering emptiness.

The meaning is as follows. The subsequent section concludes by indicating the names of the heavens. Regarding the name "Sphere of Infinite Space" (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the commentary on the dhyānas states:
"Now, these four concentrations all rely upon formless dharmas (*ārūpya-dharma*) and derive their names from their objects.

Because within this state there is no shape and no substance, its meaning is identical to empty space; therefore, all four spheres are called 'Space Concentrations' (*ākāśa-samādhi*), taking the observed object as the 'sphere' (*āyatana*). Now, this...

When the physical substance of the heavens first dissolves and one enters space, one takes space as one’s dwelling; therefore, all obstructions subside. This clarifies the second heaven, the Formless Realm.
The first phrase of this section restates the meaning of the preceding heaven: since the obstruction of form has dissolved, even the "non-existence" of that obstruction is extinguished.

That which can be non-existent is space, and that which is non-existent is obstruction; now both the subject (the capacity for non-existence) and the object (the absence of obstruction) have been extinguished. This is...
The characteristic of the consciousness-deity’s cessation in emptiness is said to be the contemplation of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).

When the mind takes empty space as its object, if it lacks boundaries and becomes excessive, it scatters. Furthermore, since emptiness is an external phenomenon (*bāhyadharma*), entering meditative absorption by taking an external phenomenon as an object results in concentration arising from the outside;

because this fault is substantial, one abandons the external and relies on the internal. Thus, one enters absorption by taking internal consciousness as the object. The term "within" (*antaḥ*) refers to the internal.

Regarding the explanation of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*): it refers to the cessation of all coarse consciousnesses dependent upon the sense organs, leaving only the latter half of the subtle *manas* and the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna*.
Thus, the name of this heaven is concluded and indicated as "the Sphere of Consciousness" (*vijñānāyatana*), which should be understood accordingly.
*Manas* is translated as "mind," which is the seventh consciousness. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states that there are briefly several distinctions of this *manas*.
There are three types: first, that associated with the view of a self as a person (*pudgala-ātma-dṛṣṭi*); second, that associated with the view of a self in phenomena (*dharma-ātma-dṛṣṭi*);

and third, that associated with the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*). Among these three, the latter—the wisdom of equality—is the category of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that is transformed;
the former two are coarse and subsequently involve association with the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), whereas the latter wisdom of equality also encompasses both.
This accords with the current text; Changshui’s claim that it refers to the sixth consciousness is incorrect, for the sutra explicitly states it is the seventh *manas*.
*Ālaya* is translated as "containing and storing" (*hanzang*). Below, it clarifies the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*):

"empty space" (*ākāśa*) refers to the first dhyāna heaven, while "the cessation of consciousness" (*vijñānanirodha*) refers to the second dhyāna heaven; this means that prior to these two heavens, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) exists.

The two lines beginning with "The objects and the [perceiving] faculties are both destroyed" correctly clarify the mode of practice of this heaven. "The ten directions are tranquil" means that because both emptiness and consciousness have ceased, there is nothing at all remaining.
In the *Tiantai* commentary on the *Śrāmaṇera-śikṣā*, it says: "This heaven is named 'Sphere of Nothingness' (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
When one cultivates this concentration, one does not employ any internal or external objects. External objects are termed 'emptiness,' and internal..."

Regarding the objects [of these states]: because they are named according to the initial cultivation of the causes for abandoning these two objects, the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) is also called the Sphere of Little (*alpa-āyatana*), the Sphere of Non-existence (*akiṃcana-āyatana*), and the Sphere of Non-perception (*asaṃjñi-āyatana*).

Furthermore, it is said that in the passage above, entering meditative absorption by taking space as the object in the first heaven is called "external concentration" (*bāhya-samādhi*), while entering meditative absorption by taking consciousness as the object in the subsequent heaven is called "internal concentration" (*adhyātma-samādhi*). And...

If one relies on both the internal and external, neither of which is tranquil, and enters meditative absorption by taking the mind as the object of the internal mind, this absorption has already relied upon the minds of the three periods of time and is not the ultimate reality. Only when there is no place for consciousness and the mind has no support is it called "peaceful.
By cultivating based on nothingness, it is named the "Sphere of Nothingness" (Ākiṃcanyāyatana). That [sphere] and...

Because these are the same, this is cited briefly as proof. Thus, below, the names of the heavens are concluded and indicated; "the nature of consciousness" (*vijñāna-dhātu*) below clarifies the fourth heaven of the formless realm.
Regarding "the nature of consciousness is immovable," the two phrases below point to the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*);

it is called "immovable" because it is profoundly still and subtle. Because it is immovable, one employs cessation to exhaustively investigate it. "Exhaustively investigating through cessation" refers to ordinary beings and celestial beings.

When a person enters this samādhi, they mistakenly take it to be ultimate reality; because they do not perceive the arising and ceasing that is so profound and subtle, they claim it is an infinite investigation.
The *Shichan Zhong* (Explanations on the Middle of Dhyāna) states: "Those who enter this samādhi do not see the characteristics of existence or non-existence;
all things are obliterated and stilled, the mind is without fluctuation, and it is tranquil and pure like the state of nirvāṇa. This refers to [the experience of] this very state.
This concentration is subtle and exquisite; nothing within the three realms surpasses it. When non-Buddhists realize it, they call it the Middle Way and the True Mark (*dharmatā*).
Yet, becoming attached to this dharma, they no longer practice further, reckoning this very mind to be the *ātman*.

Therefore, the Buddha now judges that within the inexhaustible, they proclaim the nature of exhaustion; though it has never truly been exhausted, they mistakenly recognize it as already exhausted. It is for this reason that [he speaks] to the utmost.
Because it is subtle and minute, appearing as if existent yet as if non-existent, it is said to be "as if existing but not existing" and "if exhausted, yet not exhausted.

Thus, the following section concludes by indicating the name of this heaven: "Neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). This explains the state within dhyāna; there are differing interpretations of its name.
Some say that this concentration is named for the alternation between presence and absence. Regarding what is called "non-perception," it refers to the absence of coarse perception.
To conceive of this as being "beyond coarse perception" (asaṃjñā) is not to say it is "beyond non-subtle perception" (naivasaṃjñā); rather, this implies that subtle perception still persists.
Indeed, if one reads the preceding character "non" (fei) as "without" (wu), the meaning becomes clearer: it means that subtle perception is not absent.

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that while the previous contemplation of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana) involves perception, the Sphere of Nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) is without perception; now, both [aspects] are...

It is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" because it eliminates the two aforementioned perceptions and non-perceptions; it eliminates the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) and eliminates the non-perception of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Furthermore, another interpretation states that it is called "not having perception" because within this meditative absorption one does not perceive any objective images (*nimitta*);
it is called "not non-perception" because the practitioner might otherwise think that if there were [no perception], then—[if one were to hold] a single... [thought].

Regarding those who have entered the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*), they are like wood or stone, devoid of cognition; how then could they know that there is no perception? Therefore, it is said that it is "not non-perception.

This interpretation is based on the name as it applies when one is actually in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). However, if one follows the original meaning of the current sutra text, interpreting it solely through the sense of the latter two phrases—"neither perceiving" and "nor not perceiving"—seems more appropriate.
That is to say, it is "neither perception" because it does not seem to exist, yet it is "not non-perception" because it is not entirely absent.
Because it is neither perception nor is it as if perception exists— neither exhausted nor inexhaustible— it is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Those who exhaustively pursue emptiness yet do not fully realize the principle of emptiness fall into delusion and ignorance, lacking true hearing [of the Dharma], and thus enter the cycle of saṃsāra.
This section of the sutra follows up on the preceding four *ārūpya-dhyānas* to examine the differences between the noble and the ordinary, the sharp and the dull, and the heterodox and the orthodox;
it addresses how failing to exhaustively realize emptiness leads to the error of delusion.

The latter two phrases precisely constitute the analytical examination (*vicāra*), pointing out that while what was realized in the aforementioned four formless heavens is indeed correct, it has not yet exhausted the true essence of emptiness. True [emptiness]...
The principle of emptiness is that form is itself emptiness and emptiness is itself form; form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form.
That form and emptiness are non-dual is the meaning of the Middle Way. How could there be any fondness for or aversion toward that which lies between them?

Therefore, the Buddha did not exhaustively explain the principle of emptiness. From this point downward, he clarifies the Sage’s Path that culminates in emptiness, referring to those who have attained the stage of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
The noble path of the three fruits of the heavens culminates here; thus, they are called Śrāvakas of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*).

Because their faculties are dull, they do not turn toward the Great Mind, and as such they are the fruit of the small vehicle. Although their faculties are dull, they possess the untainted (*anāsrava*) noble path and will certainly not regress from the triple world;

furthermore, there is no prospect of further advancement. Therefore, they are termed "of fixed nature. This distinguishes them from those below, specifically from the [beings of] the Unconscious Heaven (*asaṃjñi-sattva*).

That which is exhausted within the heavens refers to those who are deluded by the outflows (*āsrava*) and yet mistake them for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); thus they weary of the realms of existence and seek the infinity of emptiness.
Since this is an error and they do not return, even the four formless heavens (*ārūpya-dhātu*) are not surpassed by the four heavens of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*).

How, then, could [the heavens] be considered empty? Therefore it is said that being "deluded by the outflows" refers to those of meager learning and shallow understanding; hence they are also called "those who have heard nothing. Since...
Because they take arising and ceasing as their cause, their retribution is exhausted and they enter the cycle of rebirth.
Ānanda, these various devas and each of the celestial beings (up to) the *pudgalas* each follow their own kind.
This section of the sutra concludes by separately designating the seven destinies within the three realms and collectively defining the names and meanings of the formless realm;

it demonstrates that while these are falsely existent, they are ultimately non-existent in truth. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "These various beings" summarizes the three realms, stating that the devas and humans of the three realms are all ordinary beings whose existence is induced by wholesome karma;
as the fruit repays the cause, once that retribution is exhausted, they return to revolve through the various destinies.

The following passage clarifies that the various heavenly kings are noble beings (*ārya*) and not ordinary (*pṛthagjana*). It states that these various Bodhisattvas, having entrusted their stations to them and directed their minds through them, manifest the bodies of heavenly kings;
as they progress sequentially upward, they turn their minds toward the noble path (*āryamārga*) and will necessarily enter the ranks of the noble ones.
This is not like the ordinary heavens, where all enter the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*). As in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, all ranks manifest heavenly bodies from the lower to the upper.
This means that these four [realms] are distinct from the lower [realms]; the designation "formless" (*ārūpya*) refers to the cessation of body and mind while the meditative state manifests.

This clarifies that while there is no matter resulting from karma (*karmaphala-rūpa*), there is matter resulting from meditative concentration (*samādhiphala-rūpa*). Regarding the commentary by Wu-xing, which states "there is no matter resulting from karma," this implies that matter resulting from concentration does exist.
Therefore, from this point until the end of the text, the character "this" (*cǐ*) should be read as "beginning" (*shǐ*); such was the correction made at the translation site.

This is a mistake; these are all general judgments regarding the various heavens of the three realms below who cling to conditioned existence and fail to realize the unconditioned wondrous enlightenment.

Because they have accumulated delusions over kalpas, there appear to be the three realms; yet when viewed through the lens of wondrous enlightenment, in reality, there are no such signs of ascending or sinking.
The term "intermediate" refers to those within the three realms, as they turn their backs on the Truth and pursue [delusion].
Because they are deluded, they revolve through the seven destinies, sinking into them and finding it difficult to escape; thus, *pudgala* is translated as "one who repeatedly takes up [existence].

The character for "repeatedly" (*shu*) is pronounced "shuo," meaning that one repeatedly undergoes birth and death, discarding this life to take up another, following each according to the nature of their karma—whether good or evil—into its respective category.
Furthermore, Ānanda, within these three realms... [up to] ...due to moisture there is inclusion in the realm of animals.
This section of the sūtra follows the previous inquiry regarding the seven destinies; these seven clarify the destiny of the asuras.
According to the sequence of the seven destinies, they should have been listed after the ten classes of rishis, but here they are erroneously placed later. Furthermore...
The last four phrases provide a general classification of the four types of asuras; their translated terminology was seen previously, but is presented again here for convenience.

They are translated as "Non-Gods" (*asura*) or "Those Without Wine. The *Fahua wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra) cites that when flowers were gathered from the four continents and fermented in the great ocean in an attempt to produce wine, the flavor could not be changed due to the karmic power of the fish and dragons; thus they swore an oath of anger and jealousy.
Because [the cause] has been severed, it is said that there is no alcohol. First, regarding the detailed explanation of the four types [of birth], the passage clarifying oviparous birth states:
"Those included within the realm of hungry ghosts dwell on the shores of the great ocean;

having taken refuge in the Buddha and protected the Dharma, through the power of protecting the Dharma and by means of their own innate supernatural faculties, they enter the void and go to protect the Buddha-dharma. This concludes the section below, clarifying what is [meant].
Furthermore, regarding those born from eggs, the *Buddha-darśana-samādhi-sūtra* states: At the beginning of the kalpa, beings from the Ābhāsvara Heaven were born upon this earth.
Desiring to touch their bodies, they entered the sea to wash away their impurities; however, they fell into the mud and were transformed into eggs.
After eight thousand years, a single girl was born with a thousand heads and twenty-three hands. This girl played in the water, and from the water-crystal [she produced]...
After entering the body for eight thousand years, a son was born with twenty-four heads and one hand short of a thousand;
this was the beginning of the asuras’ birth from eggs. Next, regarding those who are demoted from among the gods of womb-birth:
because they were prone to excessive anger, they contended with the gods for power, and because they lacked the virtues of a god, they were demoted. As for these demoted ones, observe:
The *Buddha-samādhi Sūtra* states: The Asura King Vemacitra had a daughter named Śacī, whose beauty was unsurpassed.
Śakra invited her to be his queen. The Asura said, "If you will dwell in my celestial palace, I shall grant your request.
When the Heavenly Emperor agreed to his terms, the daughter later slandered her father out of jealousy, and because of this, the war was instigated.
Because the Lord of Devas banished him by the power of the *prajñā* mantra, it is said that he was degraded and cast down from among the gods.
"Dwelling below, adjacent to the sun and moon" means he was degraded and cast down forty-two thousand *yojanas*, residing at the midpoint of Mount Sumeru and facing the sun and moon.
Therefore, this [passage] concludes the section on being encompassed by the light of cultivation; those who cultivate the lower light are born through transformation and sustain the world.
This clarifies the intent that his power is capable of moving mountains and shifting oceans;

therefore, the subsequent phrase states, "His power penetrates all things without fear," meaning that his power can thoroughly penetrate everything, being devoid of timidity or dread. Regarding the phrase "contending with the Brahma King," the Sūtra says:
when the Asuras first engage in battle, they first contend with the four deva-kings, then with the other scattered devas, and subsequently with the Four Great Kings.
The power of the Four Kings cannot withstand it, so they report to the Lord of Devas;
the power of the Lord of Devas cannot withstand it either, whereupon they successively beg for aid from Brahmā. This is categorized under the "transformative" (nirmāṇa) among the four types of birth.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Four, Ānanda," this clarifies moisture-born birth (*saṃsvedaja*); since moisture-born beings are fundamentally of a different class, they are classified as animals.

Among the four modes of birth, moisture-born beings are inferior to the first three categories; those moisture-born animals must belong to the class of fish and dragons, as they dwell at the bottom of the ocean.
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "There are asuras who dwell at the base of Mount Sumeru within the great ocean;
in the desire realm, they can manifest bodies of various sizes according to their will. They reside there.
In the City of Radiance (*Prabhāpurī*), the current character for "mind" (*xin*) refers to the "water-hole" (*yìshuǐxué*); this is the Tailgate (*wěijū*) hole at the bottom of the ocean.
The rest may be understood. This [section] concludes the summary of the *A* vowel.
"Ānanda, it is thus that the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals—[up to] if anyone else were to speak [of them], it would be the Māra speaking.

This section of the sūtra concludes the preceding discussion by summarizing the retributions of the seven destinies to clarify that they are falsely existent while the True is non-existent, and further exhorts those who seek the Truth to eliminate delusion.
The first part, beginning with "Ānanda," summarizes how all seven destinies are delusive.

"Lethargy" refers to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) in contrast to the wondrously bright and effortless (*anabhisaṃskāra*); from "such hells" up to "deluded thoughts follow karma" it clarifies that there is existence through delusion;
from "within the wondrous, perfect brightness" up to "there is no further root or thread" it clarifies that there is non-existence because of truth.
This means that within the wondrously bright, perfect mind—which is effortless and unconditioned—these seven realms of rebirth exist only as a dream; therefore, they are called "lethargic."

Conditioned phenomena are like flowers in the sky; because they are fundamentally non-existent, they are empty. The "sky" is a metaphor for the wondrous mind, and the "flowers" are a metaphor for the seven realms of rebirth.

Next, Ānanda, below this, it clarifies that the delusive causes of the seven realms are as follows: the phrase "those who do not recognize their original mind" refers to what was previously stated regarding the seven realms.
"Original mind" refers to the wondrous mind inherently possessed by every person; it means not recognizing the true mind that has existed from the beginning.
To mistakenly grasp at illusory reflections conditioned by delusion as being the mind, and to undergo arising and ceasing along with that mind—this very arising and ceasing is the cause of saṃsāra.
Because of this, one does not return to the truly pure essence for kalpas on end; all of this is due to the following: [the text] correctly clarifies the false causes of the seven destinies.
Following [the sequence of] killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are the causes of the three miserable paths. "Reversing" means to turn one's back on this.
The three matters such as killing and so forth are termed the "meaning of non-killing" and so on; these constitute the four auspicious destinies of humans and devas.

There are those called the "class of ghosts," whose speech is biased while their intent is comprehensive, referring to the three miserable realms. The names "non-killing" and so forth belong to the heavenly destiny.
Because the named and the nameless contend with one another, they give rise to the nature of ascending and sinking; thus, saṃsāra is metaphorically likened to ascending.
The meaning of "sinking" (immersion) is that when one attains the lower [level] and awakens to the truth, the delusions of existence and non-existence are finally eliminated.

This means that if all sentient beings possess the wondrous capacity to awaken to right concentration and rely internally upon the wondrous mind—which is concentrated, eternal, and quiescent—then both "having a name" and "having no name" will cease to exist.
When even this "non-duality of non-existence" is extinguished, such names as "non-killing" and so forth also vanish.

Furthermore, how could there be any further accordance with the actual facts of killing and so forth? Ānanda, the following section clarifies again that there is retribution according to karma, and there is individuality according to retribution;
this concludes the response to the original question.

It means that if one does not sever the three karmas of killing and so forth, then according to the individuality of those three karmas, there will be corresponding retributions of shared destiny (*sabhāga-vipāka*). "Individuality" refers to all sentient beings.
The karmas created in this life are each distinct: some are private acts of killing, some are private acts of stealing, and others involve private acts of sexual misconduct, lying, and so forth.

Because these karmic actions are each individually biased and private, one might think that although the evil karma is private, its retribution enters into a "common portion" (*sabhāgatā*), which is to say, hell.

Yet, within that common portion, the experiences of retribution differ; therefore, it is said that there is no lack of a fixed location, as was previously explained regarding the ten habitual tendencies.

This explanation of the "knots" is in response to Ānanda’s question regarding their fixed locations. From the phrase "arising from delusion" (*zì wàng*) downward, the knots are explained as being responses to the existence of delusion rather than being spontaneous;
that is, they arise from one's own delusion, and since they are produced from delusion, they originally have no cause. Because they lack a cause, there is nothing to be investigated;
because there is nothing to be investigated, no root or thread can be found. From the phrase "you must exert yourself" (*rǔ xù*) downward, the practitioner is encouraged and exhorted.
To attain true nature, one must eliminate delusive afflictions; these three afflictions are precisely killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.

This means that if one does not exhaust these three afflictions, even if one attains wondrous functions, they will all remain worldly phenomena involving conditioned effort, rather than the power of the supramundane, untainted path.

If habitual afflictions are not eliminated, one will inevitably fall into the way of demons. Once the mind has become perverse, if one wishes to remove delusions, one instead doubles the amount of emptiness.
Why is this so? Because it is fundamentally false; therefore, this is something created by the self-delusions of those who are objects of the Tathāgata’s compassion, and it is not the fault of Bodhi.

These four subsequent lines can be understood accordingly. Having thus completed the detailed investigation of the seven destinies (*sapta-gati*), what follows below further discriminates the delusions of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-māra*) as the final instruction left by the Tathāgata for the sake of posterity. Great! [The Tathāgata].
"Compassion" refers to that which is spoken spontaneously without being asked.
At that moment, as the Tathāgata was about to conclude his session on the Dharma seat— up until the point where it says, "I shall now distinguish these for you in detail"—
this sutra records how the World-Honored One, out of great compassion, was about to close the Dharma assembly when he again provided a detailed analysis of the demonic realms.
"Deeply guarding against error and delusion" refers to the two lines immediately following, which conclude that the current Dharma assembly is about to cease.
"Upon the Master... and so forth expresses the Buddha’s inexhaustible compassion as he again raises the intention to discern and refute demonic obstructions.

"Turning back the Purple Gold Mountain" means that the Tathāgata’s body, the color of purple-polished gold, is as majestic and lofty as a mountain; it was about to rise up, yet then turned back. "Universally proclaiming... and so forth.
This refers to those of the Two Vehicles who have already been extensively explained as being able to turn back from the Small toward the Great and having attained the methods for proceeding thereto;

however, because they have not yet clearly recognized the subtle demonic activities within meditative contemplation (*dhyāna*), this is now explained in detail. Regarding the phrase "true cultivation":
"true" (*zhen*) has the meaning of "perfect" (*yuan*). This perfect cultivation is the Mahayana method, which encompasses the principles and practices previously elucidated.

Realizing the three essentials constitutes the true method of practice. Because the practices cultivated by the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) in the past were partial and inferior, they were not the truth;
therefore, the mantra is added. *Śamatha* is translated as "stopping" (*zhi*) and *vipaśyanā* is translated as "contemplation" (*guan*).
Although three meanings were previously indicated, only these two are mentioned here, as explained in the previous section on the summary of names: the Vajrasamādhi is foremost.
The Sūtra says: "When a single thought-moment moves, the five aggregates arise together; within the arising of these five aggregates, fifty evils are present.
What we now analyze as the fifty māras of the aggregates are precisely those fifty evils. Therefore, one should maintain mindfulness of the Path and be cautious so as not to move;
for movement inevitably gives rise to māras. Thus, the Buddha has repeatedly and exhaustively demonstrated this as his final compassionate model for all practitioners.

One must guard against this deeply. If one is not clearly aware within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), mistaking a thief for a son, one’s merit and the wealth of the Dharma will be entirely plundered.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "to be satisfied with a small attainment," this specifically refers to the latter two types of persons fixed in their nature (*niyata-gotra*) concerning the ten matters of the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*);
the mention of the "demon of the aggregates" (*skandha-māra*) above applies generally to all five aggregates.

The work of Māra is finished. Regarding the six lines beginning with "false speech": it means that those non-conceptualizing bhikṣus, due to their deluded outflows, erroneously mistake the conditioned for the unconditioned;

having not realized [the truth], they claim realization. When the heavenly retribution is exhausted, subsequent existence manifests again, whereupon they give rise to slander and fall into the great hells.
One must certainly examine and distinguish this in detail.
"Ānanda rose together with those in the assembly... (until) how much more so for all worlds within empty space?

This section of the sutra records Ānanda’s attentive listening as the Buddha was about to reveal the works of Māra; he first clarifies that true awakening is fundamentally one, and that differences arise only through delusion.
"Ānanda... and below refers to the assembly of students listening as described in the text. "The Buddha said... and below follows.
First, it clarifies that true awakening is fundamentally one: although the twelve classes of beings in this world of outflows differ in their respective forms, their minds are the same.

Therefore, it is said that they are neither two nor different from the Buddhas of the ten directions. From the passage beginning "Because of you," it correctly clarifies how differences arise through delusion;
that taking the principle as an object of confusion constitutes a fault is because all sentient beings cling to those false thoughts.
Deluded regarding the True Principle, one takes this delusion as a fault, thereby giving rise to delusive craving. "Delusion" here refers to ignorance (*avidyā*); based on ignorance, craving arises.
Once delusive craving has arisen, there is nowhere that is not deluded. Delusion is the opposite of awakening;
since the nature of awakening (*bodhi*) is all-pervasive, when this nature of awakening is transformed into delusive emotion, delusion is likewise all-pervasive. This delusive emotion is ignorance.
Because of dullness, the spiritually awakened mind is transformed into a rigid void; this refers to the beginning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Emptiness is the beginning of delusion.
When delusive transformations do not cease, the void is transformed into existence, and the world is thereby established.

Thus, the following section concludes by clarifying that the world is established through false conceptualization (*vikalpa*); one should know that the subsequent section concludes by clarifying the void.
The small awakened mind is already smaller than the great void; how much more so are all worlds that exist within the void?

A fragment of cloud is used as a metaphor for the small, while the great clarity is used as a metaphor for the large. As the aforementioned sutra says: "The void arises within the Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the sea"—the meaning is the same.
"Among you, if even one person awakens their true resolve and returns to the source... (down to) they will tumble and fall away, beyond all hope of rescue.

This section of the sutra follows the preceding context to explain in detail the origins of demonic interference, warning practitioners to maintain profound vigilance and uphold the correct path so as not to fall into its grasp.
The phrase "Among you" and following carries forward the previous meaning, exhorting all practitioners to awaken [their resolve].
When one awakens to the Truth and returns to the primordial enlightenment, the emptiness of the ten directions naturally dissolves and vanishes.
Why is this? Because in the past, due to delusion, the wondrously luminous true awareness was transformed into this dull, inert, and stubborn emptiness;

today, through awakening, one again transforms this dull, inert, and stubborn emptiness back into the wondrously luminous true awareness. Delusion and awakening depend upon the person, yet the awakened mind remains unmoving.
However, when one person returns to the source, that one person’s emptiness perishes; yet this refers only to the emptiness within the practitioner's mind, not to the manifest empty space before you.
Emptiness is the supporting realm (*āśraya-dhātu*) and the self is what depends upon it (*āśrita*).
Now that the support has ceased, how could that which depends upon it not shatter? [The following section] clarifies the reason for the demonic disturbances.

Regarding "adorned samādhi": adornment refers to the embellishment of the mind. Since the Great Way is unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*), it is adorned by means of concentration and wisdom; thus it is called "adorned samādhi.

That which is cultivated by the Three Vehicles is a mind of refined purity that penetrates through to accord with true awakening. Wherever it touches, it is serene; right where it touches, it is touched.
When wherever it touches is serene, then emptiness and existence— *Note: The final phrase appears to be an incomplete or elliptical statement regarding the non-duality of emptiness and existence.*

Both vanish and return entirely to the Middle Way. All that is "below" refers to the disturbances caused by Māras and the like; whether they disturb you or not depends on your own mental aggregates (*skandha*).
If your mind is clouded by ignorance, then even the palaces of the Māras will be shattered by you, and the great earth itself will tremble and split apart—how much more so the palaces of the Māras?
For ordinary beings and the various devas also cling to worldly toil (*rajas*), and thus they come to cause such disturbances.
When the great earth trembles, all creatures moving on land, in water, or through the air are struck with alarm; "shè" (pronounced like "zhe") describes the state of a startled heart.
Ordinary people who do not perceive this are intoxicated by the seven emotions, and thus they fail to notice the shifting and upheavals of the world.
Even those creatures that dwell upon mountains and rivers or soar through the skies are terrified when the great earth quakes and splits asunder.
"How could they not know [this], yet they are startled and terrified—such a thing does exist.

Those classes of māras all possess the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), and because they have attained mastery over the five desires (*pañcakāmaguṇa*), they are attached to these worldly defilements; how then would they willingly allow you to shatter their domain?
Therefore, [the text] below correctly concludes the reasons for the māras' disturbances. *Qiān* (僉) means 'the multitude. All the ghosts and spirits..."
Because this belongs to Māra, it is thus; below, the text provides a detailed demonstration of the two paths of benefit and harm. First, to demonstrate the benefit:
although he may cause disturbance, he is himself obscured by the dust of afflictions (*kleśa*) and dwells in deep darkness. You, however, abide within the light of wondrous enlightenment;
thus, you occupy the great radiance. How could darkness invade this? This is the benefit. As for "like the wind," below it is explained in relation to the three...
An analogy clarifies that Māra cannot harm this light: it is the light of the sun and moon; this light has no substantial entity, so the wind cannot touch it.
Even if a whirlwind from the *svalana* mountain were to topple peaks, the light remains unmoved. Furthermore, the nature of water is without self; what injury can there be to its continuity?
Even if one were to cut, hack, chop, or slice it, the water is never diminished. The metaphors of wind and sword represent the disturbances of Māra.
The third analogy of hot water regarding the practitioner’s path-mind:

while the preceding two analogies clarify that the demonic mind cannot harm one's path-mind, this analogy of hot water illustrates the practitioner’s illuminating wisdom. The "ice" represents the demonic mind;
it signifies that right wisdom can destroy the demonic mind just as hot water melts ice. Therefore, to merely rely on supernatural powers is insufficient.
They are merely guests for the practitioner. "Guests" is a metaphor for external conditions; external conditions cannot invade my inner wisdom, just as a guest cannot harm the host.
Regarding the next section on "accomplishment," it shows what causes harm: why do practitioners encounter demons and those who cause disruption?
It is because of the "host" within your own mind—the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). If this host is upright...
They can do nothing to you; however, if the host is deluded, those guests—the demons—will find their opportunity.

If all practitioners maintain right concentration through *dhyāna* in every situation and remain awakened in every place so as not to be deluded, then those demonic activities will be powerless against them.
Once the five aggregates have dissolved and entered one's own fundamental luminosity, and...
When those dark hordes draw near, they will destroy themselves; how would they dare remain here to disturb your meditative concentration?
If you do not understand this, you will be deluded by the *skandhas*; those such as Ānanda were originally sons of the Buddha, yet for a long time they have been sons of Māra.

Having become followers of Māra, it will be difficult for them to emerge from this vast eon—should you not stand in awe? As for the "inferior" cited below, it is used to compare with the "superior" in order to ascend [to a higher understanding].
Kātyāyana, you have merely violated a single precept among the eighty thousand practices; furthermore, because your mind remains pure, its power has not yet been overwhelmed.
If you were to succumb to that Māra, your entire being would be lost, and all your merit and Dharma-wealth would be forfeited—this harm would be most severe.
The final four lines clarify the severity of this harm through a metaphor: it is like the total confiscation [of one's property].

"Zhe" (the one who) refers to having one's registered lineage (*jìguàn*) removed; this is what the *Hànshū* (Book of Han) means by "removing one from the clan register" (*chú qí shǔjí*). The meaning of the text is thus clear.
The above provides a general indication of how demonic disturbances arise; hereafter, their specific characteristics are detailed.
Within each of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), ten matters are presented, which precisely correspond to the fifty evils of the *Vajrasamādhi*.

"Ānanda, you should know that from 'you sit at the site of enlightenment' up to 'taking solid delusion as its basis,' this section of the sutra shows the ten demons of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

This first clarifies the boundaries of the aggregate of form and the signs of its exhaustion, so that people may penetrate the internal before they can resist the external. From 'Ānanda' onwards, it specifically demonstrates the aggregate of form."
What is the definition of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*)? Form is the essential substance that can obscure true emptiness; therefore, it is called the aggregate of form.
"Sitting at the site of enlightenment" means sitting within the site of the path of cultivation and advancing therein.

"Dissolving discursive thoughts" means that the practitioner, by means of the true wisdom of *prajñā*, empties all deluded thoughts; "dissolving" is the meaning of emptiness. Once deluded thoughts are empty, [the aggregate of form is likewise dissolved].
Thus, the characteristics of the departure from thought are, in all places, entirely lucid and penetrating, empty and hollow, without any trace;

therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* states that "the characteristic of the departure from thought is equal to the realm of empty space. This is precisely that meaning. This characteristic of the departure from thought is concentrated, tranquil, profound, and still;
it cannot be shifted by movement or stillness, or by recollection or forgetfulness. Therefore, it is said to be "like a single word" which is not affected by external objects.
"Movement" refers here specifically to abiding in the realm free from thought as the primary gateway for entering right concentration.
Furthermore, the limit of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is clarified through a metaphor: "like a person with clear vision situated in deep darkness.

This metaphor illustrates that although the practitioner's eye of wisdom is bright, it is obscured by the aggregate of form, and is thus like an eye situated in darkness. "The essential nature... [and so forth].
These two lines accord with the meaning of the Dharma. The first line specifically points to the nature of the practitioner’s contemplative observation:

although it is already wondrously pure, because it is shrouded by the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the mind has not yet emitted light. The first line corresponds to "bright clarity," while the second line corresponds to "gloomy darkness.
Thus, the following two lines conclude the scope of the aggregate of form; "district" (*qū*) refers to its boundaries, and "universe" (*yǔ*) refers to its covering.
The "dark recesses" clarify the boundaries of the *skandhas*, and the "luminous sphere" clarifies the meaning of the *skandhas*.

If it were previously stated that the eyes are in darkness when the *rūpa-skandha* is exhausted, yet now it says the eyes are luminous and clear, then the luminosity and clarity of the eyes means the mind emits light;

since the profound darkness has been removed, this is the sign of the exhaustion of the *rūpa-skandha*. "Transcending the turbidity of the kalpa" clarifies the actual efficacy of the exhaustion of form; once form is exhausted...
Regarding "transcending the turbidity of the kalpa": a kalpa refers to a period of time;

one must know that during the *apacayakalpa* (the aeon of decrease), the faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) of sentient beings become extremely dull and obscured. Now, when it is said that the eyes are bright and clear, the faculties are pure.
When the faculties are pure, the mind emits light; thus, as form is exhausted, one transcends the turbidity of the kalpa. This may be verified by consulting the Fourth Sūtra.
The three subsequent phrases point to the cause from which the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) arises:

form is the fundamental substance, which is constituted by the notion of grasping at solidity. As stated in the fourth sutra, "solidity, clarity, and obstructiveness" constitute the basis of the aggregate of form.
"Ānanda, you should within this state investigate the wondrous clarity" (up to) "if you take this as a holy realization, you will immediately be possessed by various demons.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding passage to correctly clarify the ten matters of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); it reveals the first sign.
"You should within this" refers to the aforementioned state of non-conceptual oneness; that is to say, one should proceed from this non-conceptual oneness.

One thoroughly investigates and exhaustively studies the locus [of the mind] to realize the wondrously luminous nature. Because of this thorough investigation, one suddenly attains the state where the four great elements do not interweave;
"not interweaving" means they are analyzed apart. To press down on the phrase "overflowing into the external objects," these "four great elements" refer to the six sense organs (*ṣaḍāyatana*);
it means the six sense organs do not interweave with the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). The term "suddenly" (*shaoxian*) refers to the momentary realization.
However, it is said that in an instant this body of the six faculties can emerge from the obstructions of the six objects;
this is called "emerging downward. This state of meditative concentration is so named because this function of brilliant clarity emerges from the obstructions of external objects.
What is called the "overflowing" of the brilliant clarity into the preceding realms refers to the fact that the faculties and their objects are merely states of dull stagnation.
When all things are penetrated by the power of wisdom’s illumination, they flow together without obstruction; this is what is meant by "the overflow of fame.

This is merely a warning for practitioners not to mistake this for the realization of sainthood. This is simply the point where the power of refined spirit reaches its peak and temporarily transcends worldly hindrances;
it is not the true certification of sainthood. If one does not mistake it for sainthood, it is called a "wholesome state"; if one mistakes it for sainthood, one will be possessed by various demons.
"Even if external demons do not enter your inner mind, your attachments and false views will remain inexhaustible;
this state is most superficial and must never be clung to.
Ānanda, if you again take this mind and investigate its wondrous clarity... (up to) ...if you treat it as a realization of holiness, you will immediately fall prey to the various devils."
This section of the sutra follows the preceding ten matters concerning the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) to clarify the second characteristic.
This "mind" refers to the mind that previously overflowed outward; "wondrous clarity" (*miao-ming*) refers to the wondrous mind being investigated, which penetrates through the body from within.

Because the four great elements do not interweave within the body, one is able to expel intestinal worms (*yao-hui*) from within the body. *Yao* and *hui* are two types of parasites; their collective name is "sun."

Sīmāo’s *Qīnjiān fāng* states: "Within the body there are nine types of parasites. The *jiàochóng* (ascariid worm) is as fine as a vegetable insect and dwells between the *gùcháng* (solid intestines);
when numerous, they cause hemorrhoids, and when severe, they cause leprosy. The *huíchóng* (long worm) is the one commonly seen today.
Now, because this practice penetrates inwardly, it extracts the *jiàochóng* and *huíchóng*; yet the bodily form remains undestroyed, which is why it is so described.
"Grasping the substance of the body without moving" is the name for exiting this samādhi; it refers to the name of this meditative state.
This means that the power of this refined spirit overflowed into the physical form: previously it overflowed into external objects, and now it overflows into the body itself.

Its efficacy is superior to before, as will be understood from the subsequent text which describes a doubling of excellence at each stage. This is merely a lower-level instruction to warn the practitioner not to mistake this for the realization of a sage.
As before.
Furthermore, "to investigate this mind internally and externally" (up to) "if one takes this as a realization of holiness, one will immediately succumb to various heterodoxies.
This section of the sūtra follows the ten matters of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and clarifies the third characteristic. "This mind" refers to...

The mind that penetrates inwardly applies its effort until both the internal and external are refined and pure through investigation. "Internal" refers to penetrating within; "external" refers to overflowing outward.

At the time of such investigation, among the six constituents—such as the *hun* spirits and so forth—within the body, with the exception of the physical body which remains unmoved due to its grasping nature, all others interpenetrate one another, acting as alternating guests and hosts.
When entering from the outside, they act as guests; when residing in their original store, they act as hosts. According to this principle:
In the thirty-fourth difficulty of *Bian Que’s Nan Jing* (The Difficult Classic of Bian Que), it is asked: "The five viscera have seven spirits; in which [viscera] do they each reside? The answer is:

"Indeed, 'residence' (*zang*) refers to that which contains and stores the human spirit and vital energy (*qi*). Thus, the liver resides the *hun* (soul); the lungs reside the *po* (corporeal soul); the heart resides the *shen* (spirit);
the spleen resides the *yi* (thought) and *zhi* (wisdom/intellect); and the kidneys reside the *jing* (essence) and *zhi* (will/determination). This is the current text.
It merely mentions the six objects while omitting "wisdom" (jñāna), meaning that these six objects interpenetrate one another to function as guest and host;
this is because their functional activity is internally pure, pervasive, and unimpeded, and because the various apertures are empty and numinous.

Thus, when suddenly hearing [the external sounds] below, it truly manifests the state of emptiness and numinosity: because the internal apertures are empty and numinous, one externally hears the sound of the wind and the cry of cranes.
All are fused into the esoteric meaning of the Dharma-sound, yet in reality they are neither Dharma nor meaning.
This is called "Emergence from this Samādhi," meaning that these are named the six substances, such as the *hun* spirit, which alternately separate and unite to form the seeds of goodness;

these seeds of goodness are precisely the empty and numinous [mind]. The phrase "temporarily attains" below serves as a warning to this practitioner not to form a realization of sainthood, as previously stated.
Furthermore, "with this mind clear, luminous, and transparently penetrating" (up to) "if one takes this as a realization of holiness, one will immediately succumb to various delusions.
This section of the sutra follows upon the ten matters of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and clarifies the fourth characteristic.

"This mind" refers to the mind previously described as investigating both the external and internal; through diligent and subtle inquiry, it first internally engages with the spiritual resonance (*vāk-śūnyatā*), and furthermore, it refines...
Because of this progress, one attains a state of profound stillness and clarity; it is revealed, bright, and penetrating, emitting light.

Since this inner light penetrates to the exterior, the ten directions appear golden, and Jambudvīpa is seen before one’s eyes. As for the explanation that "dāna" (giving) is the name of a tree, the details of its meaning are as previously explained.
That "everything is transformed into the Tathāgata" means that mountains, rivers, clouds, objects, plants, trees, and insects are all produced by the practitioner’s inner light.
Because that which is illuminated by spiritual awakening is imbued [with merit], it is transformed into the Tathāgata. Vairocana is translated as "Pervasive Radiance";

he is the Dharmakāya Buddha of this Sahā world. Regarding the "Terrace of Celestial Light," as stated in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, it is the majestic celestial light of the lion throne, which possesses radiance because it is adorned with celestial jewels.
This is the very seat upon which the Buddha sat; because the seat was high, it is called a "platform" (*tai*).

"A thousand Buddhas surrounding him" refers to the thousands of billions of transformation-Buddhas (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Śākyamuni. "Ten billion lands" refers to the *sāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu* (the great trichiliocosm) of the Sahā world;
"ten billion" is used to express "ten trillion," citing a large number for brevity. This name is established below based on the designation of this meditative state; that is to say, it is named thus.
The practitioner’s mind and spirit are permeated by spiritual awakening; this awakening arises from the inner radiance, which penetrates outward.
Thus, one perceives these realms. One should briefly receive this admonition: let the practitioner not form a conception of sainthood regarding them, as previously stated.
Furthermore, "with this mind, one minutely investigates the wondrous clarity" (up to) "if one takes this as a realization of sainthood, one will immediately be possessed by various demons.
This section of the sutra follows the ten matters of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and clarifies the fifth sign.

"This mind" refers to the mind of internal radiance mentioned above; because one applies effort to investigate it, penetrating deeply and making steady progress, one observes without ceasing—thus it is said.
Because its contemplative observation enters with diligence and does not abide, the following phrase precisely clarifies the characteristic of non-abiding:
if the mind is floating, one suppresses it to bring it to stillness; if the mind is sinking, one subdues it so that it neither floats nor sinks.
Conversely, by restraining the mind in this way, one must certainly ensure it neither floats nor sinks, thereby transcending the delusions of floating and sinking, or movement and stillness.
At the time of this observation, one suddenly sees that space becomes the color of a hundred jewels and so forth;
this is the sign that the coarse substance of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is gradually dissolving and its subtle characteristics are becoming manifest. This is called "descending below.
The name of this meditative absorption can be understood from this. The brief admonition regarding descending below is as previously stated.

Furthermore, with this mind one investigates until it becomes clear and transparent; yet if one takes this as a realization of sainthood (*ārya*), one will immediately fall prey to various heterodoxies.
This section of the sutra follows upon the ten matters of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and clarifies the sixth sign.

"This mind" refers to the mind of suppression and control mentioned above; by applying effort to investigate until it is clear, transparent, subtle, and refined, its essential radiance is kept from becoming disordered.
Suddenly, due to the effort applied below, one perceives the objective realm. "Night-closing" refers to the realm manifested at midnight, as described in the text.
This is called the "name emerging from this samādhi"; it means that the objective realm of this samādhi is termed "effortful application.

Because the mind is subtle, refined, and tranquil, one sees with clear eyes; that is to say, the nature of seeing is precise and subtle, and because the turbidity and coarseness have already been exhausted, one is thus able [to see].
What is perceived penetrates the profound darkness; one should briefly receive the admonition as stated before.

Furthermore, with this mind, enter completely into the state of voidity and fusion (until: if you form a conception of it as being the realization of a sage, you will immediately succumb to various delusions).
This section of the sutra follows upon the ten matters of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and clarifies the seventh characteristic.

This "mind" refers to the mind of unconfused, refined radiance; "adding effort" means entering through perfect cultivation. "Perfectly entering into emptiness and fusion" (*vṛta-praveśa-śūnya-saṃyoga*):

"perfect" (*vṛta*) means pervasive; "emptiness and fusion" is the realm of principle (*tattva-viṣaya*). It means to pervasively enter the ground of the principle of emptiness and fusion. Once one has entered this principle deeply, then...
Because the physical sense-faculties and the four great elements are suddenly cast off, his physical body and its four limbs become identical to grass and wood, like an insentient object;

therefore, even when burned by fire or cut by a blade, there is no sensation or cognition. This is entirely because the mind of meditative concentration has entered deeply, and body and mind are temporarily dissociated;
thus the body is like wood or stone. This is called "Emergence from Below" (*xiàchū*), and this meditative state is named "Dust" (*chén*).

"Conjoining" (*bing*) refers to merging; it means that when the sense-faculty of the body merges with the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) within the sensory object (*viṣaya*), the body becomes devoid of cognition.
Thus, even when cut by a blade or burned by fire, there is no sensation. "The sensory object conjoining" (*chen bing*) is explained by the following two lines:
"expelling the four great elements into the pure. Here, "pure" (*chun*) refers to the ultimate principle (*li*); it is pure, singular, and without admixture.

This refers to the aforementioned state of empty fusion. When the nature of the four elements is used to exclude phenomena and enter into principle, the mind becomes purely principle and forgets phenomena;
thus, there is no sensation regarding the body or sensory objects. The brief admonition that follows is as previously stated.
Furthermore, regarding this passage: "With this mind, one achieves purity... if one forms a holy understanding, one will immediately succumb to various heterodoxies.

This section of the sutra follows the ten matters of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and clarifies the eighth sign. "This mind" refers to the mind that has entered the perfect state (*pariniṣpanna*);
through the application of effort and investigation, one attains the pure, wondrous contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). When the power of this pure mind reaches its ultimate limit, [the eighth sign arises].

Regarding the passage "suddenly seeing the great earth," and so forth: this means that by contemplating the impure as pure, the five realms of mixed habitation immediately become the pure lands of the Buddhas.

This is not actually so; it arises merely from a mind of longing for the pure and loathing the impure. This is called the "Emergence from Below" (kha-adhaḥ-niṣkrānta), a name for this meditative absorption.
Because one delights in the pure and loathes the impure, the concentration on the pure image deepens daily, and through the power of the mind, transformations occur accordingly.
This constitutes a temporary attainment that is not a realization of the holy; the warning is as stated before.
Furthermore, if one uses this mind to investigate the profound and distant, yet interprets it as a holy realization, one will immediately fall under the influence of various heterodoxies.
This section of the sutra follows upon the ten matters of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and clarifies the ninth characteristic.
This "mind" refers to the aforementioned mind of ultimate purity; through the application of effort and investigation, it penetrates deeply into principle and reaches far into its function.

Suddenly, due to this lower causal application of effort, one perceives an objective realm. That which is able to see afar is the result of the function of reaching far, as stated in the text; this is its name.
