The reason for the designation "emerging downward from this meditative absorption" is that the object of this absorption is called "constricted.

When the pure mind is so intensely constricted, the mind temporarily departs from the body and flies out; therefore, it sees things at a distance. This is not a warning against going downward, as explained previously.

Furthermore, when this mind is investigated with such extreme refinement (reaching the point where it is about to become a sage), if one takes this for a realization of sainthood, one will immediately succumb to various heterodoxies.
This section of the sutra follows the ten matters of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and clarifies the tenth sign.

"This mind" refers to the mind that has reached its limit through exertion; "refined to the extreme" means that the application of effort has reached the pinnacle of purity. "Seeing goodness" and so forth refers to seeing [signs] due to the power of one's practice.
This state of extreme refinement is what is meant by the saying, "At the edge of the withered tree, there are many mistaken paths.
If a practitioner harbors even the slightest attachment toward this state of ultimate purity, external demons will seize the opportunity to enter;
thus, they perceive various false objects, and so forth. This is called "falling from this samādhi" and "the mind receiving the false. This is truly because...
The practitioner washes the mind, not to inwardly harbor improper influences so that they may enter from without;
yet, one may encounter inferior signs of external disturbance as described in the text. These are not, however, inferior warnings as previously mentioned.

Since the preceding nine matters mostly concern internal cultivation, they were all termed "auspicious states" (*sukha-viṣaya*); now, because external disturbances are being shown, they are not so termed.
Shanzhi said: "If one does not cling to demonic affairs (*māra-karman*), then even demonic affairs will not destroy one's wholesome state.

Furthermore, since the nine preceding matters have already examined this mind, why was external disturbance not mentioned? There are two reasons for this: first, one's prior practice was still shallow and demons were not yet capable of being resisted;
now, for those who have reached the pinnacle of refinement, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is about to be broken through. In all such cases..."
Since both form and substance are being torn asunder, Māra will inevitably strive to enter and cause disturbance. Regarding the first nine matters, external Māras can enter at various points;

however, because the scriptural text is still concise, these are omitted and not explicitly mentioned until the tenth matter is reached, where the external disturbances are then set forth to illustrate that such external disturbances were also present within the preceding nine matters.
Furthermore, my intention is that practitioners may understand the text and thereby guard against these states; thus, I have been brief.

Moreover, although the ten signs of this aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) represent the ultimate limit of pure cultivation, they merely serve to break through the aggregate of form. Therefore, all that manifests is a sign of the aggregate of form.

Upon reaching the subsequent aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha), the efficacy of the practice becomes increasingly subtle, yet the objects that manifest are external disturbances that become even more urgent.
"Externally disturbed" means that the adversary is even more formidable.
Ānanda, these ten kinds of meditative states (*dhyāna*) manifest as objects (up to the point where they) provide maintenance and protection, leading to the attainment of the Unsurpassed Way.

In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One summarizes the ten matters concerning the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) from the preceding discussion to admonish practitioners not to deceive themselves, thereby guarding their cultivation and entering realization.
The two phrases beginning with "Thus" (*evam*) formally conclude the preceding meaning;

the term "dhyāna" refers to the *dhyāna* among the three meanings previously mentioned. The terminology has been explained above; whenever one enters right concentration (*samādhi*), [the following occurs].
It must be that these three meanings are perfectly complete; what is mentioned here is one that encompasses the other three. The manifested objects are precisely the ten previously mentioned signs.
All these objective signs appear because the mind is interacting with the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
"The mind interacting" means that the practitioner’s mind of contemplation and the aggregate of form interact as subject and object, exactly as described above.
The aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) maintains its characteristics like two opposing armies engaged in combat. If the practitioner’s merit is superior, the aggregate of form is defeated by him;
if he falls into the ten realms of delusion, becoming confused and attached, then the aggregate of form prevails and the practitioner becomes perverse. Therefore, practitioners must be cautious.

Regarding the various sentient beings, the Buddha spoke of the final age: *Note: The term "伊十境" (yī shí jìng) refers to the "ten realms of delusion" (shí wàng jìng), which are states of ignorance and attachment that hinder spiritual progress.*

"Practitioners are deluded and fail to recognize themselves; they falsely identify with illusory phenomena, mistakenly believing that words regarding 'ascending to sainthood' or 'falling into hell' are literal.
This is truly terrifying! You must descend and issue a decree to Ānanda and others, enjoining them to remain in the Dharma-ending age to propagate this teaching.
Only by maintaining profound vigilance and upholding the correct method can one truly enter the Way."
"Ānanda, that good man cultivates samādhi... [up to] taking empty clarity and false conceptualization as its basis.
This section of the sutra next reveals the ten matters regarding the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

Here, the Buddha first clarifies the boundaries of the aggregate of sensation and the signs of its exhaustion, so that people may penetrate the internal before they can resist the external. "Ānanda," and so forth, reiterates what was previously stated.
Regarding the passage on the arising of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) following the exhaustion of form (*rūpa*):

whereas the preceding text merely indicated *dhyāna*, here both meanings appear together, from which one may discern the intent of perfect cultivation. "Citing" [the text] means that once the phenomena of form are exhausted, the mental phenomena manifest;
thus it says, "seeing the mind of all Buddhas," whereby the Buddhas' true emptiness and wondrous mind appear within the practitioner’s concentrated mind.

That which is called "the mind of all Buddhas" refers to my own original awakening (*prakṛti-āśraya-parāvṛtti*), the resultant essence that manifests within the causal mind of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*);
it is thus named the mind of all Buddhas. One must not conceive of it as existing externally to the mind as an object perceived by me.

As for the two lines following "As with clarity," they clarify this through analogy: the bright mirror represents the causal mind of the practitioner, and the image reflected in the mirror represents [the manifestation of the Buddha-mind].
"If the minds of all Buddhas were to have [defilements] below" correctly demonstrates the boundaries of the *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
To say that "there appears to be something attained yet it cannot be used" means that although the wondrous mind of all Buddhas has already been seen, its power has not yet been utilized;
that it cannot be utilized is precisely because it is oppressed by the *skandha* of sensation. This is further clarified by means of an analogy, as follows: "It is like..."

When a sleeping person is oppressed by a ghost, although they possess hands and feet and their sight and hearing are clear, they are unable to move or speak because they are possessed by the oppressive ghost and external malevolent spirits.
These "external malevolent spirits" (kṣetra-jña) do not remain for long before they depart;
likewise, the person oppressed by the ghost awakens before long. Being shrouded by the *vedanā-skandha* (the aggregate of sensation) is also like this. What is meant by "sensation"?

The *vedanā-skandha* (reception aggregate) takes the meaning of receiving external objects as its definition; because it receives these objects and holds them within the mind, thereby obscuring the wondrous nature of true emptiness, it is called the *vedanā-skandha*.
The metaphor of the nightmare-demon (*yāma-ghost*) refers to the reception aggregate;

the metaphor of a person whose hands and feet cannot move during a nightmare refers to seeing the Buddha-mind yet being unable to employ it. Nevertheless, within the *vedanā-skandha*, one perceives the Buddha-mind.
This [attainment] arises because the skandha of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has been exhausted; since the phenomena of form have been eliminated, the mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*) manifest.

Because the originally awakened mind (*mūla-bodhicitta*) does not exist apart from this, it is "seen. Although it is seen, it is still shrouded by sensation (*vedanā*), and thus one is unable yet to employ its power.
This concludes the section on the limits of the skandha of sensation; "district" (*qū*) refers to its boundaries, and "universe" (*yǔ*) carries the meaning of the *skandha* itself.
This refers to the meaning of "delimitation. The passage below, beginning with "if the curse of the nightmare ceases," illustrates the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
Because the aggregate of sensation is exhausted, the mind is able to transcend obstructions and manifest its function;

thus, one can depart from the body and observe it from afar, attaining mastery over going and staying, with the body and mind suspended in liberation—much like a Taoist priest (*huángguān*) who manifests a "yang-spirit" (*yángshén*).

This clarifies the efficacy of exhausting the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). The aggregate of sensation belongs to the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*); "view" refers to visual perception, and through this viewing, sensation arises.
Since all five sense-faculties possess the principle of sensation, it is here explained with reference to only a single faculty.

Thus, by exhausting the aggregate of sensation, one can transcend the turbidity of views; for the turbidity of views also extends to the other faculties. Therefore, the following passage explains the origin of the aggregate of sensation.
Because this mental dharma of sensation is comprised within the four aggregates that are non-material, it exists as a name without substance;
thus, it is called "empty and luminous delusion" and is the root of the aggregate of sensation.
Ānanda, when that good man is in this state—up until the point where he loses his right concentration—he shall fall into ruin.
This section of the sutra follows the preceding passage to correctly clarify the ten demons of the *vedanā-skandha* (aggregate of sensation); this demonstrates their initial manifestation.

"That good son" refers to the person mentioned in the previous text who was practicing within the *rūpa-skandha* (aggregate of form). "Should be among these" refers to the point where the *vedanā-skandha* is about to be exhausted.
"Attaining radiant brilliance" occurs because the coarse substance of the preceding *rūpa-skandha* has been exhausted, and thus the essence of the *vedanā-skandha* emerges.
The subtle essence belongs to the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*); it has a name but no substantiality, being formed by empty, luminous, and deluded thoughts. Therefore, it attains radiance.
Once the mind has manifested this radiance, one vigorously suppresses it within; yet if one exerts effort to an excess, an inexhaustible sorrow arises at the very point of internal suppression.
Thus, the following clarifies the object of this sorrow, as can be understood from the text.
This is called "descending"; the name of this meditative absorption can also be understood through awakening. Thus, the following admonition for the practitioner is:
do not become attached to this state. If one awakens, there is no fault; once awakened and no longer deluded by it, this state of compassion will naturally dissipate over time.
If one acts as described below—failing to awaken—one invites external māras to take advantage of the opening; the māras will then comply with their [delusions].
Because of compassion, the Mara of Sorrow enters; seeing people below, he displays the disturbances of Mara, which can cause the practitioner to lose the right concentration they have cultivated.
"Right reception" (正受) refers to the objects experienced within concentration;

since there is nothing to be received yet one receives, it is the experience of the Middle Way Truth that is called "right reception. Now, having already lost this, one further encounters immersion [in delusion].

One must be cautious regarding falling [into error]. Furthermore, if one carefully examines the sequence of the ten matters of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) as they were previously presented in vertical progression, and compares them with the ten matters of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) now presented in horizontal arrangement, one will see that when a practitioner adheres to a single state, they will immediately suffer retrogression;
this does not mean they must sequentially traverse all stages. Students, when encountering these texts, should clearly understand this point.
Ānanda, furthermore, those good sons within that samādhi (up to) shall lose their right concentration and fall into ruin.
This section of the sutra follows the ten matters regarding the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) mentioned previously; it clarifies the second sign.

"Within samādhi" refers to the samādhi of the aggregate of sensation. "Form dissolves and sensation becomes clear" means that once the coarse and turbid aggregate of form has dissolved, sensation [becomes manifest].
Because the emptiness and luminosity of the *skandhas* manifest before one, it is called "clarity" (*mingbai*); this refers to the meaning of the previously mentioned "attaining great brilliance.

This demonstrates the essential nature of meditative concentration. Regarding the two phrases below concerning "superior characteristics": because the clarity and refinement of the *vedanā-skandha* are not like the coarse, turbid, and dark obscurity of the *rūpa-skandha*, they are called "superior characteristics.
To be overly moved or excited beyond measure is precisely what constitutes a sickness; whether it is excessive or insufficient—[it is both a fault].
Because the illnesses are equal, one is suddenly negligent regarding the latter two lines, which correctly clarify the characteristics of the illness:

it refers to the sudden arising of a mind of joy and courage upon first attaining the supreme signs. Within this stirred heart, an infinite courageous resolve arises; the following two lines clarify the state of excessive courage.
As for the "three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas," the full term is *asaṃkhyeya*, translated as "innumerable"; these are great *kalpas*.
"Number" (*saṃkhyā*) is one of the sixteen great numbers in the *Avataṃsaka*.
In the Tripitaka Teaching of the Tiantai school, it is said that all Buddhas attain Buddhahood only after practicing the six perfections for three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
This is specifically stated with reference to Śākyamuni Buddha, meaning that from the time of the ancient Śākyamuni Buddha until the time of Śikhin Buddha, he encountered seventy thousand [Buddhas].
The first asaṃkhyeya kalpa consists of meeting five thousand Buddhas;
the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa, from Śikhin Buddha to Dīpaṃkara Buddha, consists of meeting seventy-six thousand Buddhas;
the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa, from Dīpaṃkara Buddha to Vipaśyin Buddha, consists of meeting seventy-seven thousand Buddhas. Now, it is said that one can transcend these in a single thought-moment.

Because the mind belongs to the realm of madness, it invites the mad demon to enter; this is what is meant by "descending from below. This name for the samādhi, "Overpowering and Leading" (Língshuài), is explained as follows:
"Overpowering" (líng) means to treat others with contempt in order to exalt oneself, thereby showing contempt for all Buddhas. "Leading" (shuài) means to lead according to one's own nature;

because one leads according to one's own superior nature, it is said that one can transcend [the three great kalpas] in a single thought-moment. The admonition regarding awakening is as stated previously.
If one performs the lower illumination and yet does not awaken, one will incur external insults; it can be understood that because the inner mind is frantic, it summons frantic demons.
This shows the matter of demonic disturbances to those below; the rest may be explained.
Furthermore, those good sons within that samādhi (up to) shall lose their correct reception and fall into ruin.
This section of the sūtra follows the ten matters regarding the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) and clarifies the third sign. "Within that samādhi" and so forth are as previously explained.
Regarding the two phrases "previously there was no... and so on: "previously" refers to the aggregate of sensation; although it was already clear, there had not yet been a new realization.
Having already dissolved the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), one loses the basis of the former abode;

because the power of wisdom is weak and unable to penetrate through to a perfect, subtle illumination, one falls into the "ground of collapse in the middle. This is a failure resulting from concentration (*samādhi*) surpassing wisdom (*prajñā*), for the power of wisdom cannot save itself.
As for the "ground of collapse in the middle," "collapse" means the destruction of what preceded—there is no realization before, and what followed has already been extinguished.
Within the center there is nothing seen; because there is no seeing within the center, it is called the "ground of the dissolution of the center.
Herein, one dissolves the mind, and suddenly a great parching thirst arises. This "parching thirst" occurs because one lacks the moisture of the water of wisdom.
"At all times" refers to day and night, movement and stillness, and so forth; during all such times, one should deeply and inwardly reflect and recollect.
"Neither scattering nor non-scattering" means that one concentrates the mind through focused contemplation (*ekāgratā*) so as not to allow it to be dissipated;
therefore, it is called "sinking recollection" (*laya-smṛti*). To take this sinking recollection as being "diligent application" (*vīrya*) is an error.

This is explained below. The name of this meditative absorption can be understood from what follows. If one awakens [to the truth], the subsequent admonition is as stated before. If one does not awaken, the following explains the consequences that will be incurred.
It can be understood that external insults are summoned by deep-seated recollection, and thus the demon of recollection manifests;
for one who concentrates the mind on a single point seizes the opportunity provided by that gathering of the mind, whereby this disturbance appears. The rest may be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, those good sons within that samādhi (up to) will lose their right concentration and fall into ruin.

This section of the sūtra follows upon the ten matters regarding the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) and clarifies the fourth sign. Regarding "within that samādhi" and so forth, it is as previously explained.
Regarding "the power of wisdom" and so forth, the preceding text states that because the samādhi exceeds wisdom, one's insight declines and one becomes established in a withered samādhi.

Now, because wisdom exceeds meditative concentration (*samādhi*), cognitive understanding arises in a distracted manner, and concentration is unable to sustain it. This failure results in the loss of sharpness and intensity;
"loss of sharpness and intensity" means that one does not strive for superior progress and is full of indolence.

"Those who harbor various superior natures within their minds" means that they maintain various resolute understandings (*adhimukti*) within their hearts; thus, they suspect themselves to be Vairocana. Lu... [text fragment]
Śīlāditya translates this as "Pure Fulfillment" (*viśuddhiparipūrṇa*); because it is perfected by pure light, it refers to the *saṃbhogakāya* Buddha.

This name appears below. Regarding the name of this samādhi, "losing constant scrutiny through mental application" means to be submerged in [erroneous] knowledge and views, thereby losing constant examination and failing to reflect upon oneself, resulting in much overweening pride.
If one realizes this, then as previously stated, one should issue a warning; if one acts [otherwise], [the fault remains].
The following clarifies that failing to awaken invites external contempt; because one is easily satisfied within, it summons external [afflictions].

"Easily satisfied within" means that while in the stage of clarity regarding the *vedanā-skandha* (feeling aggregate), one treats it as a definitive reality (*satya-viṣaya*). Thus, one fails to progress further, which is a grave error.
The rest is understandable.
Furthermore, those good sons within that state of concentration (up to) "shall fall away from right absorption.
This section of the sutra follows the ten matters concerning the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) and clarifies the fifth sign.

The phrase "within concentration" and so forth is as previously explained; the two phrases beginning with "newly realized" are verbally identical to the two phrases in the third sign mentioned previously.

The meaning is slightly different: previously, this was explained from the perspective of the *āśraya-skandha* (the aggregate as the basis), whereas now it is explained from the perspective of the *ālambana-citta* (the observing mind that relies upon it).
This can be understood through careful reflection. Furthermore, while the meditative object may appear similar, the "dhyāna-disease" (*dhyāna-vyādhi*) is entirely distinct.

Previously, dryness and thirst were taken as the disease; now, a sorrowful mind is taken as the cause of the disease. Because they are similar in name, they are distinguished here in detail, for the sorrow is profound.
Sitting like an iron bed and eating like poison, and so forth—all these are caused by anxiety. This is called "descending.

This samādhi is named "losing the skillful means" because it lacks the discernment provided by the skillful means of wisdom (*prajñā-upāya*). If one awakens [to this], then the admonitions for descending are as stated before.
If one does not awaken, then external insults will be invited; the demonic activities (*māra-karman*) are the same as those within, as previously described.
This can be understood.
Furthermore, regarding the passage from "those good sons within that samādhi" to "they shall lose their right concentration and fall into ruin":
this section of the sutra follows the ten matters concerning the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) and clarifies the sixth sign. [The phrase] "within samādhi," etc., [is as follows].
As previously stated, when the coarseness and turbidity of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) have been eliminated, one attains purity.
Because of this purity, the mind becomes stable; because of this stability, infinite joy (*prīti*) arises. If this joy is not restrained, it becomes an affliction.
This is called "descending from this concentration. It is so named because the heavy burden of the aggregate of form has already been extinguished.
Pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is a mental factor associated with meditative concentration; because it lacks the discernment of wisdom (*prajñā*), it suppresses this joy.

Therefore, upon awakening, one should apply the same admonitions as before. If one practices with inferior clarity and fails to awaken, one will incur external contempt. As with the internal, so too should the demonic activities (*mārakarman*) appearing externally be understood.
Furthermore, those good sons within that samādhi (up to) "will lose their correct reception and fall into ruin.

This section of the sutra follows the ten matters regarding the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) and clarifies the seventh sign. The phrase "within samādhi" and so forth is as previously explained;
the single phrase "claiming for themselves" is also identical to the fourth [sign]; "falling ill" differs from the illnesses mentioned previously.
It may still be remedied, yet now the illness is severe and without cause; "without cause" means it has no beginning and lacks any measure or standard.
As for "great conceit," it refers to relying on oneself to oppress others; thus it is called *māna* (conceit), meaning that one gives rise to arrogance by clinging to a self.
Even the Tathāgatas of the ten directions—who are most supreme, unsurpassed, and honored by the world—would still be slighted by such a person, let alone those of lower status.
Therefore, it is called "great conceit" (*mahāmāna*). Thus, the following seven types of conceit are enumerated; the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

First, "conceit" (*māna*) refers to being arrogant toward those of equal status, and is thus simply termed "conceit. Second, "excessive conceit" (*atimāna*) means that within a group of equals, one clings to the notion that oneself is superior to others.
Third, "conceit beyond conceit" (*mānātimāna*) [refers to being arrogant] toward those who are superior and pure...

1. *Śreyān-asmi-māna* (the pride of thinking "I am superior"): This refers to one who is actually inferior to others, yet through strong attachment, insists that they are superior to others; it is as explained above. 2. *Sadṛśo’smi-māna* (the pride of thinking "I am equal"): As explained above. 3.

*Hīno’smi-māna* (the pride of thinking "I am inferior"): As explained above. 4. *Abhimāna* (overweening pride): This refers to one who has not attained [realization] but claims to have attained it, or has not realized [the truth] but claims to have realized it;

because their stage of practice is fundamentally low, they forcefully consider themselves superior. 5. *Ūnamāna* (the pride of inferiority): Because one considers oneself inferior and thus does not seek further progress, one conversely...

Pride (*māna*) is so called because it holds itself to be superior. The seven types of false pride (*mithyāmāna*) refer to those who harbor wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), deny the Two Truths, do not prostrate before stūpas and temples, and do not revere the Triple Gem—as explained in the passage below.

In the present text, false pride is omitted because it will be clarified later; furthermore, among the seven prides, the pride of self (*asmimāna*) is primary, and if there were no self, these seven [prides] would not exist.
Pride and [the other afflictions] do not arise simultaneously; because of the existence of a self, the seven types of pride are established all at once.

The latter two lines specifically clarify the characteristics of "great pride" (mahāmāna). This name is derived from its specific definition: because one’s views and understanding are superior, it is similar to those previously described as being "sunk in knowledge and views.
Because one lacks the wisdom of discernment (*prajñā-vicaya*), one cannot save oneself; thus, it arises from [wrong] views.
To achieve victory and yet give rise to pride—there are many among those who study today who resemble this. If one attains awakening, the warning is as stated before;
if one fails to awaken, one will incur external contempt.

Regarding the statement that "the sutras are tree leaves and woolen cloth," this refers to how in the Western Regions (India), sutras were written either on palm leaves (*palāśa*) or on white felt (*karpāsa*). The rest is understandable.
Furthermore, those good sons within that samādhi (up to) "shall lose their right reception and fall into ruin.

This section of the sūtra follows the ten matters of the *vedanā-skandha* (aggregate of sensation) and clarifies the eighth sign. Regarding the phrase "within samādhi" and so forth, it is as previously explained.
The three phrases beginning with "in the essence" (*sāra*) precisely clarify the cause of the illness of dhyāna; that is to say, regarding the essence of the *vedanā-skandha*.
Within this clarity, Yuanwu mistook the principle of refined brightness for the true, wondrous principle of ultimate illumination;
this was premature calculation—like seeing an egg and demanding a rooster at dawn, or seeing a bowstring and demanding a roasted owl.
Because he was able to accord with this refined principle, he was called "Great"; it was due to his accordance with refined brightness that...
Suddenly, immeasurable pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) arises; yet, although one has attained pliancy, its root is already mistaken, and thus the pliancy itself becomes a disease.
To mistake this pliancy for a realization of holiness (*ārya-prativedha*) is to confuse the outflowing (*sāsrava*) with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) realization.
Therefore, it is said below that one acts as a "hearerless bhikṣu" (*aśrutavān bhikṣu*), which refers precisely to this. One takes a minor pliancy to be great.
The Master’s error was profound indeed. This name [of the samādhi] arises from below; this name of the concentration arises from below.

Because of this affliction, one discriminates with wisdom and becomes attached to that which is light and pure; therefore, upon awakening, the warning is as before. If one acts from below, it clarifies that if one does not awaken, one will incur external contempt.
The "unlearned bhikṣu" refers to the devas of the Realm of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*), for they exhaustively pursue emptiness and do not return to the solitary state.
Those of shallow learning and limited insight, with their tainted minds, mistakenly claim that upon the exhaustion of their lifespan they have attained sainthood and been reborn;
they thus give rise to doubt and slander, falling into the Avīci Hell. Since this present illness of meditation resembles that case, it is cited here as a corroborative proof.
Furthermore, those good sons within that samādhi (up to) "shall fall away from right reception.
This section of the sutra follows upon the ten matters of the *vedanā-skandha* (aggregate of sensation); it clarifies the ninth sign. The phrase "within samādhi" is as explained previously.
Regarding the phrase "in the clarity," this clearly explains the cause of the dhyāna-affliction; the preceding text pointed this out within the "clarity and essence."
The illness was previously contracted from the side of the perceived objects of sensation; now it is contracted from the side of the awakening mind that perceives.

Therefore, it is said that one attains the nature of empty luminosity within clear awakening. "Clear awakening" refers to the awakening mind, while "empty luminosity" refers to the aggregates (skandhas) which are the objects of awakening.
Because one awakens to empty luminosity, one contemplates non-attainment within the very nature of empty luminosity, for [the mind] has returned to its source.

Because there is no basis toward which to turn, it is said that one "returns to eternal extinction. Because of this eternal extinction, one then negates cause and effect and enters exclusively into emptiness.

When the mind of annihilation—the emptiness of what is grasped—manifests before one, then all observed phenomena, whether mental or physical, are entirely empty and ultimately reduced to total annihilation; therefore, it is said that "the mind eventually reaches annihilation."
"Extinguishing" (*mie*) means "understanding" (*jie*). The passage currently missing from the text refers to the phrase "generally speaking" (*da di*) and the following two sentences.
"Awakening" (*wu*) refers to the admonitory words as previously stated. Regarding the phrase "if one acts," this clarifies that failing to awaken invites external contempt;

however, because the inner mind is already empty while external demons further enter, their assault becomes increasingly fierce. Therefore, they slander the observance of the precepts as being merely the "Lesser Vehicle" (*xiǎochéng*).
The Way-Error states: "If a Bodhisattva has realized emptiness, how could there be observance or violation? This person’s inferior demonic signs can be understood. Furthermore, it says:
"Those good sons within that state of meditative concentration... shall lose their right reception and fall into ruin."
This section of the sutra follows the ten matters concerning the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) mentioned previously; it clarifies the tenth characteristic.
Regarding the phrase "within meditative concentration" and so forth, as explained before: "tasting its depths" correctly clarifies the cause of the maladies of dhyāna.

This is precisely because the practitioner fails to recognize the nature of the void clarity of the aggregate of sensation and mistakenly takes it for ultimate truth; consequently, they investigate and savor that realm of void clarity, becoming attached and immersed in it.
Because the penetration into the essence and the investigation of its flavor are profound, deep attachment arises from them; hence it is said that "limitless attachment arises.

Since this attachment reaches its extreme, the power of meditative concentration cannot overcome it, and thus madness is provoked. This madness is caused by attachment, and since attachment is the root of desire, it results in lustful craving.

This is called the "Emergence from Below" (xiàchū). As for the name of this samādhi, it is because these realms of the five aggregates are fundamentally empty and luminous; they are empty and luminous.
Because pliancy and suppleness have deeply permeated the mind, one gives rise to wild passion that lacks the restraint of wisdom, thereby falling into the entanglements of Māra.
If one awakens to this, one should issue a warning as before; if one fails to awaken through such lower clarifications, one will incur external contempt.

Regarding the "practice of desire with equanimity" mentioned among the deeds of Māra, it means that one does not distinguish between the monastic and the lay, nor between the path and what is not the path.
To act with such indifference that one has no sense of dread or restraint is called "equal conduct in desire.
Furthermore, because they are sustained by the power of demons and spirits, those foolish commoners do not perceive their transgressions;

thus, even if they reach the number of ten million, once the demonic influence has dissipated, both parties will fall into royal peril and descend into hell. Taking this as a mirror, how can one not be cautious?
"Ānanda, these ten kinds of visionary states appearing during *dhyāna* (up to) maintaining and protecting [the mind] to achieve the Unsurpassed Way.

This section of the sutra concludes the ten matters regarding the *vedanā-skandha* (feeling aggregate) mentioned previously, admonishing the practitioner not to err and to guard against obstacles while entering into realization.
The two phrases beginning with "Thus" (*evam*) formally conclude the preceding meaning concerning *dhyāna*.

The mutual relationship and other terms mentioned previously are also as explained in the section on the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); the citation of these prior proofs can be understood accordingly.
Ānanda, that good man who cultivates *samādhi*—[from here until] "takes the delusion of interpenetration as its basis."
In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One three times demonstrates the ten demons of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

This first clarifies the boundaries of the aggregate of perception and the characteristics of its exhaustion, so that people may master what is internal before they can guard against what is external. "Ānanda," and so forth, concludes the preceding section on the characteristics of the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) and introduces the following passage.
Although [the text] has not yet... it now correctly clarifies the characteristics of the manifestation of perception when sensation is exhausted.

"Although the outflows have not yet been exhausted," and so forth, means that because the afflictions of the upper realms within the three worlds have not yet been eliminated, one is temporarily able to detach from the physical form through the exhaustion of sensation (*vedanā*).
The text on the exhaustion of sensation states: "If the curse of a nightmare ceases, the mind leaves the body and looks back at its own face;
going and staying are then free. The present passage precisely accords with this former meaning. The phrase "escaping from the cage" is a metaphor for the aforementioned mind.

The analogy of the bird leaving its body illustrates the mind, while the cage illustrates the physical form; the intended meaning can thus be understood. Having explained this, the text now clarifies the efficacy of the mind that has left the form.
It means that this mind which has transcended form is already capable of accomplishing the *manomayakāya* (mind-made bodies) of the sixty stages from the ordinary person to the Sage;
all these sixty stages are realized by relying upon this mind that has transcended form.

From the third stage onward, there is the gradual progression of the Dry Wisdom (śuṣka-vipaśyanā); this belongs to the outer ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*). The ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*), ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), ten transferences (*daśa-pariṇāma*), and the four preparatory stages (*catasraḥ prayogabhūmayaḥ*) belong to the inner ordinary beings (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*).
The ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*), along with the two types of awakening—the wondrous and the sublime—are termed "sages" (*ārya*). These are called the sixty positions.

This correlation of the inner and outer ordinary beings is explained according to the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna*). As for the correlation of positions according to the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulyavyavasthāna*): *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the full sequence in the Perfect Teaching typically includes the five minor grounds, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten transferences, the ten stages, the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samantabhadra-bhūmi*), and the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*sudurjaya-bhūmi*).*"

Thus, from the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) upward, one is already a sage (*ārya*). Regarding the "mind-made body" (*manomaya-kāya*), according to the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, it is explained through metaphors:
it is called "mind-made" because it appears swiftly and without obstruction by mountains or walls, just like the movement of the mind.
It possesses three types [of analogies]. Below, these are explained through metaphors to clarify its departure from form and mind.
The sequence is as follows: it is like a person in deep sleep; the speech uttered during sleep is called somnambulism.

Although the sleeping person has such speech, they themselves do not clearly perceive it nor possess any distinct cognition of it. Yet, despite this lack of cognition, the words spoken in sleep have already formed a rhythmic sequence;
that is to say, the resonance of the somnolent speech is of the same category as the speech of one who is awake.
Because they are the same, those who were not asleep all awakened to his words. The metaphor of "sleep-talking" (somnia) illustrates the mind that is detached from form;
because this mind is "asleep," it is shrouded by the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), which forms a sequence of sounds and rhythms.

This illustrates how this mind detached from form can produce the various types of the "mind-made body" (*manomaya-kāya*). Those who were not asleep and awakened to his words represent those at the level of the Sages.
Because one has attained liberation from the functions of form and mind, the dharma and its metaphors are subtle and hidden; students should contemplate and realize them with a refined mind.
The various interpretations of Changshui all fail to grasp the intent of the sutra, resulting in reckless and forced exegesis;

only the *Yaojie* (Essential Explanations) of Wenling’s school accords well with the sutra. This concludes the clarification of the boundaries and scope of the *xiang-yin* (perception-aggregate), as previously described.
What is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*)? Perception is floating thought; because it can obscure the wondrous mind, it is called the aggregate of perception.

If movement subsides and perception is exhausted, this is the characteristic of the exhaustion of perception. To move one's thoughts is precisely floating thought. The first four lines refer to the subsiding of movement and the exhaustion of floating thought;
once these are removed, it is like clearing away dust and grime from the surface of the awakened, luminous mind. Dust and grime serve as a metaphor for floating thought.
The first section of the three lines below correctly clarifies the characteristics of the exhaustion of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and the manifestation of formations (*saṃskāra*).
"One period" (*i-lun*) refers to the entire duration of a single lifetime, beginning with birth and ending with old age and death; this beginning and end of birth and death is termed "one period.

Because the aggregate of perception is exhausted, the beginning and end of this one-period birth and death are suddenly revealed. This sudden revelation is precisely universal illumination (*yuanzhao*).
This "perfectly illuminating the beginning and end of birth and death" refers to the meaning of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) manifesting before one.

The final phrase concludes with the characteristics of the exhaustion of the *saṃjñā-skandha* (the aggregate of perception). The two subsequent lines clarify the efficacy of the exhaustion of perception:

since the *saṃjñā-skandha* belongs to the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), now that perception is exhausted, one transcends the turbidity of afflictions. This is because various floating perceptions greatly disturb the mind.

Afflictions (*kleśa*) are also the very essence of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); because afflictions are [identical to] perception, when perception is exhausted, one transcends the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).

This is explained in detail in the fourth scripture, within the "Explanation of the Five Turbidities. Observe the following for clarification regarding the causes from which the aggregate of perception arises.
As for "integration" (*yōtō*), it refers to the integration of the two dharmas of the void and the real, as in the end of the second scripture concerning vinegar.
The conceptualization of a plum is a mental image of a precipice; this is the "virtual. That it can cause water to flow from one's mouth and a tingling sensation in one's feet is the "real.

Because the virtual can move the real, it is called "interpenetrating delusive thought" (*yōngtōng wàngxiǎng*). Now, the aggregate of thought (*xiǎng-yīn*) takes this interpenetrating delusive thought as its basis.
"Ānanda, that son of good family, while the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is empty and subtle, [will fall] into delusion and ignorance and plummet into the Avīci Hell.
This section of the sutra follows the previous passage to correctly clarify the ten demons of the confusion of perception (*saṃjñā-vikṣepa*); this indicates the first sign [of such confusion].

"That son of good family" refers to the person mentioned in the preceding text who is practicing with respect to the aggregate of sensation. The aggregate of sensation is termed "empty and subtle" because sensation...
Because the *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is exhausted, it is called "void" (*śūnya*); because coarse characteristics are extinguished, it is called "sublime" (*miao*).

This is the general characteristic of the exhaustion of the *skandha* of sensation: because one no longer receives external objects, it is both void and sublime. Furthermore, because one does not receive external objects, one does not encounter perverse deliberations;
perverse deliberations are precisely floating thoughts. When "perfect concentration illuminates," this clearly demonstrates that floating thoughts are exhausted, and thus [the light] emerges.
Because this concentration is not mixed with various discursive thoughts, it is called "perfect concentration" (*pariniṣpanna-samādhi*). To illustrate the origin of the sickness of dhyāna:
one who loves the perfect and wondrous [state] takes "perfection" to mean "pervasiveness. Because they abide in perfect concentration, their mind desires to seek everywhere for clarity;
thus, they exert themselves with vigor in subtle reflection and greedily seek skillful understanding—this is "skillful understanding."
"Zhè" (者) refers to the understanding that is pure, wholesome, and expedient; "míng" (明) is itself understanding, thus "yuánmíng" (圓明) is perfect understanding.
However, to engage in meticulous contemplation within meditative concentration (*samādhi*) while seeking cleverness is a sickness of dhyāna. For this reason, the celestial Māras find an opportunity.
To "find an opportunity" means to wait for a lapse or opening to enter. As for the "celestial Māras," they refer to those who transform themselves from elsewhere.
Within the heavens there is a distinct class of celestial beings called the Māra-devas who dwell therein; these are known as the "celestial Māras.
When it is said that their flying essence (*fei-jing*) attaches to humans, it means that the essence of those Māras flies forth and separately attaches to another person.

The person so possessed does not realize they are possessed by a Māra, but claims to have attained Great Nirvāṇa and is able to preach the Dharma. They come to places where others seek skillful arts and—
A person who cultivates meditative concentration in pursuit of skillful means believes in its reality and prepares a seat for him, seeking the teaching of that skillful method.
His physical form appears upright and correct, demonstrating the skill of his bodily form; yet in an instant he undergoes transformations, feigning a state of skillful mastery.
As described in the text, such a person points to the seeker of skillful means as being obscured by Māra, their mind becoming even more deluded as they perceive that demonic teacher.

Their physical forms undergo constant transformations, deluding others with what they falsely claim to be true skill; they recognize themselves as bodhisattvas and people accept their teachings with increasing intimacy and attachment.
Their minds are so agitated that there is no limit to their deceptions;

they further employ verbal dexterity in their speech, using calamities and blessings as signs of good or bad fortune, and falsely claiming that the Tathāgata has appeared in such-and-such a place, using these clever transformations to feign auspiciousness.

Furthermore, the kalpa-fire, weapons of war, and so forth are the skillful transformations of calamities. The rest is as stated in the text. This section below indicates the names of the māras to which they are attached.
As for "strange ghosts" (*guǐkuài*), these are various spirits that manifest as anomalies by attaching themselves to objects; they are called strange ghosts.

Now, among the great mountains and rivers, there are things such as trees and stones thousands of years old that may transform their shapes and display wonders, bringing about blessings or misfortunes.
People who consume the essence of the *jing* leaves often encounter accounts in various texts describing them as "strange ghosts" or "companions of demons" who come to harass practitioners.
When disciples point out such individuals as being clever seekers, the masters are possessed by demons;
once the demonic essence has departed, both disciple and master alike fall into royal calamity. All subsequent cases follow this pattern.
Ānanda, furthermore, when the *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle for a good son (until) he is deluded and unaware, he falls into the Avīci Hell.

This section of the sutra follows upon the ten matters of the *skandha* of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and clarifies the second characteristic. "Furthermore, a good son" and so forth is as previously explained.
"The samādhi... and so forth indicates the cause of the sickness of dhyāna; those whose minds love wandering and dissipation are, regarding meditative concentration...
The interior is like the clear sky; if even a single thought arises, it is as if a fragment of cloud has appeared in the vast purity.
Now, these ten matters all arise falsely from within meditative concentration (*samādhi*); therefore, how could the demons of dhyāna, illness, and spirits not enter and become attached to this?
They roam about, arising from agitation (*auddhatya*), and their "flying essence" (*feijing*) manifests. Here, "flying" refers to the soaring and fluctuating nature of meditative power.
Because they cannot be restrained, their thoughts move falsely and fly about; as for "experiencing," this refers to descending into demonic realms.
This "experiencing" means traveling to distant lands and foreign customs to seek out the curious and search for the strange;
therefore, celestial Māras watch for such opportunities to enter. Regarding "flying spirits attaching themselves to people," it is as explained previously: their own forms do not [manifest].

Regarding "transformations and so forth," this means that the demonic teacher does not transform his own form, but causes the listeners to transform, appearing with bodies seated upon lotuses, golden in color, and so on; these are all merely summoned by the pursuit of curiosity through the play of desire. The text is clear. Regarding the phrase "in the mouth" and below, the demon again falsely utters words concerning strange and extraordinary experiences, which do not actually exist. Regarding the four lines beginning with "that person": [The four lines follow: If one hears such words, they will surely fall into the hands of demons. They will lose their lives and descend into the three evil realms. For ten thousand kalpas they shall never escape. How much more so for those who practice the Way! This means: if one hears such words, they will certainly fall into the hands of demons. They will lose their lives and descend into the three evil paths. For ten thousand kalpas they shall never be able to escape. How much more so for those who practice the Way! The seeds of the correct cause for wisdom are entirely extinguished by the secret taints of the perverse demons and heterodoxies of the seeker of wonders.
This is called "the Buddha below revealing the names of demons": *pó* (魃) is the ghost of the wind-demon;
since the lifespan of this ghost is already long, when it further encounters being subsumed by a demon, it becomes a member of the demonic faction. The remaining text may be understood.
Furthermore, if a good man, while the *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is empty and subtle, becomes confused and fails to recognize [the danger], he will fall into the Avīci Hell.
This section of the sutra follows the ten matters of the preceding *skandha* of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and clarifies the third sign.

"Furthermore, if a good man" and so forth is as previously explained. Regarding "three samādhis," this indicates the cause of the illness of dhyāna. As for "the mind loving the entanglement of *mian*": *mian* refers to cotton wool.

"Secretly merging" (*mimi*) means to merge with the principle and facts sought; it is "merging" because the upper part merges with the principle and the lower part merges with the capacity of the practitioner.
Regarding "clarifying refined thought": "clarifying" (*cheng*) means to clarify and purify. One seeks to merge with [the truth] by means of clarified and subtle thought.
While the previous phrase, "flying refined thought," was explained from the perspective of wisdom (*prajñā*), the present term "clarifying" is explained from the perspective of... [concentration].

Regarding the statement that "settling the mind" (*dingbian*) means to wrap it [in mindfulness]: when the will and the mind merge with the principle of reality, this belongs to concentration (*samādhi*).
For this reason, the subsequent passage states that the demonic realm first causes one to attain awakening; this is precisely the meaning of "wrapping.

If concentration or wisdom is pursued in isolation, neither attains its proper balance and thus becomes a sickness. Consequently, the celestial Māra finds an opportunity to enter and dispatch his flying spirits.

The "inferior" [level] is as previously explained; regarding "the identity of form and so forth," this refers to the teacher of Māra. This means that while the external forms of both speaker and listener have not yet changed, their internal minds have already attained union.

This is the "inferior" [level], which is the union with the capacity of the recipient (*yogya*). "Recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*) and so forth" refers to the "superior" [level], which is the union with principle (*tattva*).
Recollection of past lives and knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) are two of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*); seeing the hells and so forth is the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
To know the good and evil heard by others is the divine ear and the power of spiritual travel (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*);

that Māra causes listeners to obtain these five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) is because they are sustained by Māra’s magical power and are not truly attained. "Moment-to-moment shifting" means changing in an instant.
Furthermore, to be diffused among myriad affairs without exception is all a matter of false awakening; these are the works of Māra’s emissaries.

However, this is merely an auditory experience and not a true realization. Because the person’s lower faculties seek compliance with their own minds, they falsely produce empty and extravagant claims that are not actual facts.
Those below, who seek to conform to the practitioner, see these strange wonders and their hearts become inclined and thirsty;
thus, false views arise, and the fundamental, wondrously concentrated mind of the original cause is completely washed away by the saliva of that demon.
Because the fundamental mind is lost, one easily enters into deviant awakening; this "deviant awakening" refers precisely to the various matters previously awakened to.
This is called "showing the names of the demons to which one is attached"; "mèi" (魅) refers to the ghost of a fox-demon that forms a faction with other demons.
The rest is self-evident.
Furthermore, when the son of good family’s aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) becomes empty and subtle, [up to] he becomes deluded and unaware, falling into the Avīci Hell.
This section of the sutra follows the ten matters of the preceding aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) and clarifies the fourth characteristic. "Furthermore, when the son of good family...
and so on, as previously explained; "samādhi... indicates the cause of the dhyāna-affliction. Regarding "the root of mental craving," the "root" refers to...
It is the root of the myriad transformations; therefore, the following line says, "Examine the beginning and end of the nature of things' transformation.
This means first seeking the root and simultaneously clarifying the branches. "Beginning and end" carries the same meaning as "root and branches.

To thoroughly examine the transformations of things, one must achieve clarity through analytical discernment; by doing so, one refines and brightens the mind. "Refined and brightened" refers to a state of exhilaration and satisfaction.
However, in meditative concentration, whatever one becomes attached to is a sickness; for this reason, the celestial Māra finds an opportunity to enter.
His flying essence descends as previously described. "Seeking the Origin" means that the Origin is the Fundamental.

Because the Māra’s majesty subdues the multitude and causes them to follow him, he uses the seeking of objects to manifest throughout the beginning and end. Therefore, [he employs] the Buddha’s bodhi, pure and wondrous dharmas, and so forth.

To point out that the physical union of father and son, the mutual generation of lustful and lewd acts, is the root of phenomenal transformation—that is, to take these turbid and defiled laws of birth and death and call them the root of wondrously pure *nirvāṇa*—this is an investigation of the fundamental meaning with respect to the primary retribution (*sambhogakāya*).
Furthermore, as indicated below, it is an investigation of the fundamental meaning with respect to the environmental retribution (*bhājanaloka*), and thus it is said: "That is..."
This land of the five turbidities is itself the Buddha-land; there is no separate pure land of the Buddhas, nor is there a "golden-hued mark" apart from it.
The "golden-hued mark" refers to the Buddha’s body, meaning that this very physical body of mine before me is the true essence of Buddhahood;
there is no other body endowed with golden-colored marks and signs. The four lines following "that person" refer to this...

One who seeks the fundamental practice, yet believes in the delusions and fabrications of Māra, loses the mind that was previously in meditative concentration and entrusts their own life to the demonic teacher.
To investigate such a mind is to deliberate upon what the mind of Māra delights in and seeks to accomplish;
thus, the latter two lines describe the matter of fulfilling latent desires. One is held fast by the power of Māra and lacks the decisive wisdom [to discern it].
Because he selects from among these, he follows the mind that seeks the origin within the mouth;

thus, he points to the traces of defilement in the six sense organs and the male-female duality as the very origin of birth and life—this is precisely the true locus of Bodhi. This is called "below," indicating the place where [the teaching] is attached.

The name of the demon is "Gudu" (蠱毒), which can be understood through the practice of *yansheng* (厭勝). The character for *yan* (厭) is seen in the *Hanshu* (漢書) and is read with the third tone (*shēng*); this is merely a vulgar convention.
The term "yān-yāng" (厭殃) refers to practices such as those performed by earthwork or carpentry artisans who specialize in performing rites to suppress calamities for others;
all matters of misfortune, portents, decline, and depletion arise from the influence of malevolent spirits attached to these methods of "suppression and victory" (yànshèng). The rest is self-evident.

Furthermore, when the son of good family experiences the subtle emptiness of the *vedanā-skandha* (receiving aggregate), [up to] being deluded and ignorant such that he falls into the Avīci Hell—this section of the sutra follows the ten matters of the preceding *saṃjñā-skandha* (perception aggregate) and clarifies the fifth characteristic. "Furthermore, the son of good family" and so forth is as previously explained.
Regarding "the three samādhis," this indicates the cause of the dhyāna-affliction; "heart-love for a suspended response": "suspended" (*xuán*) means hanging.

To respond to that which is distant by being moved here is what is called a "remote response" (*xuanying*). Those who circulate and investigate with precision maintain that this occurs within the affairs of daily life;

they revolve and flow through these matters to precisely investigate the principle of resonance and response, seeking a hidden communion (*minggan*). Furthermore, when an action is performed now and the response arrives in the future, this too is a remote response.
As for what is termed "hidden communion," it means to silently accord with the principle, merging with it in a state of profound stillness.
Since the mechanism of resonance exists therein, it is said that there is "mysterious resonance.

When the mind in meditative concentration is still and unmoving, without a single aspiration or longing, its profound efficacy (*xuan-gong*) becomes manifest, and resonance occurs spontaneously as a dark correspondence.

If one gives rise to a thought to seek such a response, this immediately becomes a sickness; thus, the celestial Māras find their opportunity. The descent of flying spirits is as previously described.
The passage stating that it "causes the listener to see Māra as if he were a hundred thousand years old" correctly demonstrates a sign of a distant response;

the remainder of the text is easily understood. The subsequent section, which complies with the listener's desire for a response by habitually recounting matters of mystical resonance, consists entirely of the reckless and arrogant words of evil Māras, lacking any factual basis.
This is termed "Manifesting the Name of the Māra Attached," specifically identifying the Māra as *Lì* (厲).
These are the ghosts of decay and calamity; those like the sacrifices at the village altar that have no presiding lord are called *li* (hungry ghosts). The rest may be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, when a good man’s aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, he may become so deluded as not to know [his own state] and fall into the Avīci Hell.

This section of the sutra follows the ten matters concerning the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) previously mentioned; here it clarifies the sixth characteristic. Furthermore, "skillful" and so forth are as explained before.
Regarding "samādhi," this indicates the cause of meditative illness. "The mind loves to enter deeply" means to enter deeply into this concentration (*samādhi*).
Generally, while in concentration, one accords with the Middle Way, observing with clarity and attaining silent resonance, being neither lax nor hurried.
It is like tuning a lute: one does not force oneself to enter deeply, yet one enters deeply.

If one separately gives rise to a conceptual mind, praying to enter a place of deep joy, seeking hidden stillness and tranquility, this constitutes a great sickness. "Hidden stillness" (*yinji*) refers to a secluded and profound place;
"tranquility" (*mi*) also carries the meaning of calm. This means that while situated in such hidden stillness, amidst the sound of the wind, the cry of cranes, the moonlight, and the mountains—
If light, sound, and form are not empty, can they not be subject to movement? Therefore, attainment lies within the mind, while failure lies in seeking.
Thus, when the celestial Māras find an opportunity, it is of their own invitation. "The flying spirits descend" is as previously explained. The *Changshui Shu* states:
"Causing one to know one's past karma refers to matters of past lives; causing one to tread upon the tail refers to manifesting retribution in the future."
All of these are merely deceptions employed by Māra to subdue the minds of people; they are not actual realities. The *Shu* (Commentary) further states:

"To give rise to the mind that knows [others'] beginnings is the 'knowledge of others' minds' (*paracitta-jñāna*); to expose the affairs of others is the 'divine eye' (*divyacakṣus*) and 'divine ear' (*divyaśrotra*).

Because Māra has attained a perverted meditative concentration (*mithyā-samādhi*), he possesses such supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Who would not believe in and submit to such heterodoxies? To expose private matters is called "exposure" (*jue*). Or...
Question: One seeks supreme tranquility above, yet now Māra manifests supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and does not hinder that seeking;

why then does the mind submit? Answer: Māra seizes an opportunity to enter; the power of Māra is superior while the power of the Path is weak. The practitioner, being possessed by Māra, suddenly forgets their former resolve.
Furthermore, seeing various spiritual wonders, their mind becomes deluded. The false obscures the true, and the supernatural powers conceal this tranquility.
At that time, one must maintain composure and set aside all else to listen only to the Māra;

for the practitioner is like a seagull, and thus whether one remains still or moves about makes no difference. From the very beginning, the Māra utters pleasant words regarding future fortunes and calamities that will unfailingly come to pass at their appointed time;
this subdues the human mind. Therefore, [the text] below indicates the Māra upon whom he relies.
The names of the remaining [stages] can be understood.
Furthermore, when a son of good family, while the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is empty and subtle, falls into confusion and ignorance, he will descend into the Avīci Hell.
This section of the sutra follows the ten matters of the preceding aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and clarifies the seventh sign. "Furthermore, when a son of good family... and so forth.

As previously stated regarding the three samādhis, the cause of dhyāna-sickness arises from the mind’s attachment to knowledge and views. "Knowledge and views" refers to the past fundamental events and former births;
therefore, it is called "past-life recollection" (*pūrvanivāsa*). Past-life recollection is one of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
The *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm) states: "Past-life recollection means that within deep meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one gives rise to the wisdom of past lives."
One is thus able to know one’s own past lives—whether one, two, a hundred thousand, ten million, or even eighty-four thousand great kalpas—as well as the deeds performed therein;
furthermore, one develops the knowledge of the past lives and all the deeds of sentient beings within the six realms of existence.
This is the supernormal power of the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-abhijñā*). Wuxing’s commentary states: "Past lives."

Those who have cultivated the Lesser Vehicle and attained the Great Vehicle now advance; because they do not wait for further inspiration nor regress from their cultivation, yet seek it through mental effort, they invite demonic affairs.
As previously stated, "flying spirits descend" means that such people pointlessly claim to know and seek practitioners without cause—this is why it is called "without cause.
Regarding "obtaining precious jewels and the like," it is because they seek knowledge and views.
Therefore, let us first observe these anomalies; what is seen in the following text is similar to this. All that follows "the Māra" reveals anomalies intended to delude the masses.
As for "jian" (slips): in antiquity there was no paper, so bamboo was used to make slips (*jian*); writing matters upon them were called *jian-ce* (slips and tablets).
To deliberate on military and state affairs with such slips was called *ce* (deliberation). As for "fu" (talismans), these are the imperial mandates sent by the Son of Heaven.

Regarding the appointment of copper and tiger seals (*tongfu* and *hufu*), they were made either of copper or of bamboo. The imperial decree was inscribed upon them, and they were divided into two halves:

one half was given to the general, while the other half was retained within the palace. Thus, the character for "seal" (*fu*) is composed of the radicals for "bamboo" (*zhu*) and "to bestow" (*fu*). It is a tally;
because it involves the transmission of secret matters and requires the joining of the two halves for verification, it is called a "seal-tally" (*fuchi*). It is written upon a tablet (*du*).

This refers to using wood shavings (*piàn*) to construct [writing implements]; thus the character is derived from *piàn*. When there is lead and a writing board (*jiǎn*) upon it, it is called a *dú* (tablet).
As for "bright moon pearls," it means that the pearls possess a radiance like that of the bright moon; the rest is easily understood.

All of these are matters manifested by Māra within the sphere of false views and knowledge, intended to delude those practitioners seeking the Way, being boastful, deceptive, and devoid of reality. [The phrase] "beneath the mouth" [refers to] excellence.
As for the mention of "concealing strange events," "treasures," "sages," and so forth, these are all summoned by the seeking of knowledge within a single thought-moment.
This is designated as the name of the māra to which one is attached; the remainder is easily understood.
Furthermore, when the *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, the good son may become confused and fail to recognize this, thereby falling into the Avīci Hell.
This section of the sutra follows upon the ten matters of the preceding *skandha* of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and clarifies the eighth sign.

Regarding the phrase "furthermore, the good son" and so forth, as previously explained, the passage beginning with "samādhi" demonstrates the cause of the illness of dhyāna; those who love supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) generally practice this [path].

This refers to those whose minds aspire to the traces of this body’s appearing and disappearing, its concealment and manifestation, and its transformations within water and fire—traces that are attached to the phenomenal characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
Therefore, the subsequent phrase says, "various transformations," and so forth. The *Dharmadhātu-krama* states:

"Because natural wisdom (*prakṛti-prajñā*) penetrates and illuminates all things without obstruction, it is called supernatural power. This explains the meaning of supernatural power by way of its conformity with the nature (*dharmatā*).

Regarding the fact that the characteristics of phenomena have not yet manifested, the *Dharmadhātu-krama* (The Sequence of the Dharma Realm) further states that there are fourteen different types of transformations (*nirmāṇa*).
Specifically, the first dhyāna has two transformations, the second dhyāna has three, the third dhyāna has four, and the fourth dhyāna has five;
these together constitute the fourteen transformations. As for what is called "transformation," it refers to the ability to cause that which is non-existent to suddenly come into being.
To exist and then suddenly vanish, or to be great and yet able to become small, or small and yet able to become great—as manifested by the Māra below—is close to this.
Now, the various [transformations] mentioned in the text do not go beyond these fourteen transformations;

because they do not depart from fundamental dhyāna (*mūladhyāna*), the "source of transformation" (*huàyuán*) refers to the root of transformative power. According to the *Fǎjiè Cìdì* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm), it is said that by means of the out-flowing [outflows, *āsrava*] and the non-outflowing...
The profound and subtle meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) constitutes its true essence, while the various manifestations of transformation constitute its wondrous function;
this is because the various meditative concentrations and right samādhis serve as the foundation for these transformations.

If one now seeks them by deliberately stirring the mind without waiting for them to arise spontaneously, one falls into error, and thus the celestial Māras gain an opportunity. The descent of flying spirits is as previously described; they divide their hands... [as before].
Regarding "flames and so forth," this refers to the Māras manifesting supernatural transformations to entice those who seek them.
That they alone lack mastery over weapons clearly demonstrates their false, illusory, and unreal nature.

If it were as with the Buddha’s supernormal powers, all weapons would be transformed into lotuses, and flying spears and arrows would be suspended in mid-air; blades would break into pieces, unable to inflict harm.
How could there be anyone who is not subject to this? This is what is meant by "the names of the māras to which one is attached.
Regarding the phrase "heavenly realms and so forth," it refers to the māras in the heavens above, the ghosts and spirits in the earth below, mountain sprites, and so on; these are easily understood.
Furthermore, when the son of good family experiences the subtle emptiness of the *vedanā-skandha* (receiving aggregate), [up to] being deluded and unaware, he falls into the Avīci Hell.
This section of the sutra follows the ten matters of the preceding *saṃjñā-skandha* (perception aggregate) and clarifies the ninth sign.

"Furthermore, the son of good family" and so on is as previously explained. "The samādhi... indicates the cause of the dhyāna affliction; those whose minds crave entry into extinction are, in fact, practitioners of this [path].
Because such a person is addicted to the pleasure of quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*), they give rise to a mind that craves entry into extinction and seeks it;

yet this extinction is not true extinction. Since they do not attain it, the spirit of Māra first manifests. As for "profound emptiness" (*gambhīra-śūnyatā*), it means entering deeply into emptiness; this is also a denial of existence that enters into emptiness.
Because the meaning of emptiness is not real, Māra gains the opportunity to manifest. The descent of his flying essence is as previously described; thus Māra appears.
When one seeks the meaning of emptiness and the like, Māra—who possesses the five supernormal powers—arises and ceases within this very emptiness;
this is his constant modus operandi. Through false illusions and evil deeds, he deludes the world and deceives the people, which is truly to be feared.

With flattering words from his mouth, he denies the reality of eternal cessation and other such matters, thereby directly disturbing what one seeks. This is called "indicating the Māra to whom one is attached."

Regarding the term "eclipse of the sun and moon" (*rìyuè bósì*), the commentary by Xué of Wǔxīng states that while the *Jīng* and *Shǐ* classics all use the character for "eating" (*shí*), the *Shuōwén* uses the character for "corroding" (*shí*).

Jīngfáng’s *Yìchuán* says that when the sun and moon appear red or yellow, it is called a "thinning" (*bó*). Others say that an eclipse occurring without the conjunction of the nodes is called "thinning.

Wéizhāo states that when the solar or lunar vapors press against one another, it is called "thinning," while the physical damage and destruction is called "corroding" (*shí*). The *Chángshuǐ Shūsū* states that this is precisely...
Malevolent stars and spirits can cause eclipses and also act as demons and monsters; the rest is understandable.
Furthermore, good sons, when the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) becomes empty and subtle, they may become deluded and fail to realize this, thereby falling into the Avīci Hell.

This section of the sutra follows the ten matters concerning the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and clarifies the tenth characteristic. Furthermore, "Moreover, good... and so forth is as explained previously. "Samādhi...
indicates the cause of the sickness of dhyāna: because those who love long life possess a body of segmented birth (*pariṇāma-kāya*) with fixed limits, they seek eternal years;
desiring to cast off the segmented body, they hope for the transformed body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*). This is the division.
Birth by segments (*bhavopapatti*) refers to the coarse, outflowing physical form and life-span experienced by beings within the three realms;

because these have fixed and determinate limits, it is called "segmented birth. Birth by transformation (*pariṇāmikī upapatti*) occurs through the power of the compassionate vows of the Bodhisattvas, who transform their physical life so that it has no fixed limit;
they change their coarse bodies into subtle forms and exchange short lifespans for long ones.

Whether abiding for one kalpa or many kalpas, they come and go with sovereign ease; because the extraordinary and subtle fruit of maturation they induce is subtle in comparison to the coarse state of fragmented existence (*vibhava*), it is called "subtle.
Because they possess a definitive life and death in contrast to the former, it is called "permanent abiding" (as seen in detail in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*).
However, when this practitioner’s aspiration arises even once, external insults may take advantage of it, causing their refined essence to fly away.
The phrase "as previously explained" refers to such expressions as "going and returning to other realms," which signify the pursuit of transformation and change.
"In the mouth" (or "below the mouth") refers to addressing sentient beings as one's children; this is because the world arises from them.

This reflects the deluded attachment of the Māra of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven to the notion that he can produce human beings in the realm of men. *Cchanda* is translated as "the envious woman."
The *Vaiśya-kumāra* (Visheshi) is a *piśāca* ghost; translated as "one who devours vital essence," this class of ghosts is of two kinds:

those who have already generated a wholesome mind follow the Buddha and protect the Dharma, while those who have not yet generated a wholesome mind are inherently evil by nature and thus devour the vital essence of humans, harm the fetus in the womb, and consume the vital essence of the five grains. Therefore, [he is so named].
Those who profit from its empty clarity act in such a way that the practitioner attains the empty clarity of the *skandha* of sensation;

because they crave the energy of that empty clarity, their faction invades and disturbs him to devour him. "Speaking alone" means that the person before him does not understand, yet he alone is clear;
thus it is called "speaking alone. As for "listening," if it is a malevolent spirit or phantom, its meaning remains unclear.

Therefore, the rest may be understood. Among the ten types of māras mentioned above, the first refers to celestial māras (deva-māra), while the names subsequently indicated are all classes of ghosts, spirits, and monsters;
these are all merely the retinues, ministers, and subjects of the celestial māras.
This is seen in detail in the *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sāgara-sūtra*.
"Ānanda, you should know that these ten kinds of Māras [extend] to your following the Buddha’s words, which is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.

This section of the sūtra is the World-Honored One’s earnest admonition for the末法 (mofa, final dharma age), warning against Māras who attach themselves to the Buddha-dharma to destroy the correct and exalt the heterodox.
