He instructs them to practice correctly and to guard deeply against falling [into error]. Those who have been near [to Buddhahood] for nine lifetimes or many hundreds of kalpas are, according to the secular teachings, unified by one [principle].

To speak of "generations" (*shi*) as lasting for a single lifetime—as in the case of Qin Shi Huangdi’s succession to the second generation, and so on unto ten thousand myriad generations—is not the intent of the present scripture.
Here, "a generation" refers to the exhaustion of a single period of life; the character "life" (*sheng*) corresponds to the character "generation" (*shi*).

Life is also a "generation," for nine lives constitute ten generations. This literary artifice of "nine" specifically indicates that the True Dharma (*saddharma*) will endure for a thousand years, which constitutes one hundred generations in the distant future.

This refers to the teaching regarding the ten-thousand-year period of the Dharma-ending age (*mappō*). It means that these various demons will flourish within the periods of the True Dharma (*shōbō*), the Semblance Dharma (*zōbō*), and the Dharma-ending age;

they will prevail in the world in the near future and extend even to the distant end of the age. They will pass down lewdness from one to another, leading what is correct toward what is perverse, and shall become the followers of all such demons.
Practitioners of the correct path should guard against them deeply. "The One of Correct Universal Knowledge" (*Sambuddha*) correctly distinguishes between the correct and the perverse.
To distinguish thoroughly from the biased and the heterodox: "Māra" and "outsiders" refer to the biased; "provisional" and "lesser vehicles" refer to the partial.
Only the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is called "Right Universal Knowledge" (samyak-saṃbuddha-jñāna). Yet this Right Universal Knowledge is something that all people possess.

Once one becomes a partisan of Māra, one transforms the right into the heterodox, and for kalpas on end will be unable to return to it. Therefore, how can a person of integrity not be cautious? You, now—
The Buddha commanded Ānanda and his peers to remain in their vows and enter the period of the Final Dharma to save and deliver sentient beings; the rest is understandable.
Thus, Ānanda’s ten kinds of meditative states (*dhyāna*) manifesting as objects (up to the point of) maintaining and protecting [the teachings] so as to achieve the Unsurpassed Way.

In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One summarizes the ten demons of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) from the preceding discussion to admonish practitioners not to deceive themselves, so that they may guard their cultivation and enter realization.
The phrase "Thus it is" below formally concludes the preceding meaning;
as for *dhyāna* and the intermingling of mental applications, these are all as previously explained.

Direct Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra: The Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Volume Nine. Śūraṅgama Sūtra:
The Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas.
Direct Explanation, Volume Ten.
Clarified by the junior monk Guangmo of Yunqi Monastery in Ancient Hangzhou.
Directly explained and edited by the lay follower (upāsaka) Li Yulong of Mishui.
"Ānanda, when those good sons cultivate samādhi... [up to] ...taking obscure and hidden delusions as its basis.
This section of the sutra consists of the World-Honored One’s fourfold demonstration of ten matters regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Herein, he first clarifies the boundaries of the aggregate of formations and the characteristics of its exhaustion, so that people may attain correct understanding at the outset and be able to guard against deviance. "Ānanda," and so forth, concludes by restating the nature of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*).

The phrase "the arising of the mutual production of the exhaustion of the skandhas" refers to the following passage. "This person" refers to one who previously practiced the contemplation of the *skandha* of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
"Ordinary" means daily routine; during waking hours it constitutes perception, while during sleep it becomes a dream.
Since dreams are produced by perception, when the *skandha* of perception is exhausted, dreams and fantasies are extinguished. Thus, whether awake or asleep, the mind remains constant and unified.
"Because it is undisturbed, awakening becomes luminous"—the following twelve phrases clarify the efficacy of the exhaustion of discursive thought (*vikalpa*).

Awakening-luminosity (*jue-ming*) is the wondrously luminous mind of original awakening (*ben-ji*). Because floating thoughts have been exhausted, the mind of awakening-luminosity finally attains emptiness and stillness.
However, when thoughts have not yet been exhausted, the mind of awakening-luminosity is shrouded by those thoughts; thus, it is substantial rather than empty, and active rather than still.
Because the current thoughts have now been exhausted, one attains vacuity and stillness, just like a cloudless sky.

This single phrase uses a metaphor to reveal the meaning of the enlightened clarity (*jue-ming*) of vacuity and stillness: when thoughts have not yet been exhausted, the emptiness of enlightened clarity is overcast rather than clear;
although its empty substance does not move, it remains dark and dim, not yet bright. Now, because thoughts are exhausted, it is like a cloudless sky.
The simile of empty space illustrates the essence of awakening; the simile of the clear sky illustrates luminosity. The latter two lines of the verse explain the preceding [state]:

"vacuous stillness" refers to the conceptualization of mental images (*saṃjñā*), which constitutes a heavy veil. The nature of such conceptualization arises from cognitive perception, while its manifestations appear within the six sense-objects.
These are the shadowy phenomena resulting from the discrimination and calculation based on the reflected images of those six sense-objects. Now, these conceptualizations have been extinguished.
Therefore, it is said that there is "no further [discourse]," and so forth. Regarding the passage beginning with "observing all below":

this means that once the six internal perceptions (*saṃjñā*) have been exhausted, then although the external great earth, mountains, rivers, and the objects of the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) may appear before one, there is nothing internally grasped.
This is like a mirror reflecting clarity; "similarity" refers to the image, while "reflecting" refers to the illumination. That is to say, when the image comes, the mirror has no attachment to it.
Just as when an image leaves a mirror there is no trace, it merely receives the reflection in emptiness; the mind whose conceptualizations are exhausted is likewise so.
"Realizing nothingness" (*liǎowǎng*) is a subtle literary art, for "nothingness" here means the absence of habitual tendencies from the past.
Thus the next line says "only the singular, refined truth," where "only" serves as the counterpart to "singular."
"Ascending to non-being" is merely a linked verse; the two characters "essence" (*jing*) and "truth" (*zhen*) have not yet truly attained the state of essence and truth.

They are only temporarily granted the designation of "essence and truth" because floating and chaotic thoughts have been exhausted, even though the *xing-yin* (formative) aggregate has not yet been shattered.
Therefore, what follows—stating that "the root-source of birth and death is revealed from this"—has its meaning evident. "The root-source of birth and death" refers to...
Regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), it is said that all birth and death arise from this aggregate of formations;

therefore, the aggregate of formations is taken as the root source of birth and death. "Source" (*yuan*) means the fundamental basis. Now, when the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted, the aggregate of formations finally becomes revealed.
"The various [beings]" refers to the twelve classes of living beings, all of whom arise from the aggregate of formations; this means they are completely produced from it. That is to say:

The twelve categories of beings collectively refer to the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) as the basis for their shared birth; however, it is said that they have not yet understood the origins of their individual destinies.

"Individual origins of destiny" refers to the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna-svabhāva*); this means that the nature of consciousness is the source from which the twelve categories receive their life.
This is because the nature of consciousness transmits all life-force. Since the *saṃskāra-skandha* has not yet been shattered, [this state persists].
When one penetrates the consciousness that receives its mandate, one perceives only the common basis of birth. Regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the *Fajie Cidi* states:

"From ignorance arise karmas; these karmas are themselves formations (*saṃskāra*). Because wholesome and unwholesome karmas produce the fruits of the world, and because they obscure the luminosity of awakening, they are called the aggregate of formations.
This is further illustrated by means of an analogy to clarify the aggregate of formations.
The characteristics of these [phenomena] are like wild horses; they are the shimmering vapors of a mirage in the air. The *Changshui* commentary renders this as "flashing light.
Since it is called "flashing," it implies a state of intense brilliance; thus, it would not be termed "profoundly pure" (*youqing*).

Yet the sutra text explicitly states that they are "subtle and hidden delusions" (*youyin wangxiang*), and further refers to them as both "profoundly pure" and "clearly turbulent" (*qingrao*). All of these are indeed so.
How can one describe the characteristics of that which is hidden and subtle? They flicker like the phosphorescent glow of a firefly in the dark night, suddenly brightening and suddenly extinguishing;
this state of being hidden, subtle, profound, and remote is termed "flickering" (*yi yi*). This serves as an analogy for the subtle nature of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).
"Agitated clarity" refers to the *dharma* of the *saṃskāra-skandha*, while "a mirage" is the metaphor used to illustrate the hidden and obscure nature of the *saṃskāra-skandha*.
The appearance of movement arises from the subtle, pure, arising-and-ceasing agitation that disturbs the true essence of enlightened awareness; thus it is called "pure agitation.
Furthermore, this aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) constitutes the ultimate pivot-hole for the peripheral sense organs;

this means that the seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing of the six external sense organs mostly arise from the internal pivot-nexus of the aggregate of formations, and is therefore called the "ultimate pivot-hole."
The *Changshui Shu* states: "The pivot of the door is called the *shu*, and the socket of the door is called the *xue*;

these are used as metaphors for the *xing-yin* (the aggregate of formations) being the essential point for the opening and closing, and the turning, of the six sense organs. This concludes the section below by clarifying the boundaries of the *xing-yin*:

"qu" (district) refers to the realm, and "yu" (universe) refers to the meaning of the aggregates (*skandha*). What follows below clarifies the characteristics of the exhaustion of the *xing-yin*, where "original nature" (*yuan-xing*) points to the *xing-yin* itself as arising.
Because it is the root-source of the faculty of death, it is called the "root-nature" (*yuan-xing*). Yuan-cheng refers to the *vijñāna-skandha*;
it indicates that the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna*—being clear, tranquil, and immovable—is the foundation of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), and thus is called "root-clarity.

Yuan-xi refers to the habit-energy of the flux of the *saṃskāra-skandha*; because the *saṃskāra-skandha* is the basis of all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), it is called "root-habit. The first phrase restates [the subject].
The phrase "shining above, clear yet turbulent" clarifies the nature of the phenomenal marks (*lakṣaṇa*).

This means that if the fundamental nature of the root of birth and death enters into the primordial clarity of the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*), it will merge with that clarity; merging with the nature of consciousness, they become a single flow.
When the nature of consciousness is exhausted and clarified—like waves subsiding and all transforming into still water—the metaphor of the subsiding waves illustrates this.

The exhaustion of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) is likened to its transformation into clear water. This metaphor illustrates that the movement of the aggregate of formations is the torrential flow of the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛtti-vijñāna);
when these enter the profound nature (zhan-xing), they are separated from the water, yet the waves are nothing other than the water itself. Thus, it is said they "transform into clear water.

The transformation of the aggregate of formations into the nature of consciousness is likewise so. The phrase following "the aggregate of formations" (xing-xia) correctly concludes the exhaustion of the aggregate of formations.
"Exhausting practice to transcend the turbidity of sentient beings" means that all twelve classes of living beings take the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as their basis;

now, when this aggregate of formations is exhausted, one may know that they have transcended the turbidity of sentient beings. Observing what follows, which clarifies the origin of the aggregate of formations:
because its disturbances are profound, pure, subtle, and hidden, it takes these profound and obscure false thoughts as the aggregate of formations.
The root of this.

Ānanda, you should know that this "attaining correct knowledge" (up to) "the first heterodox teacher establishing the theory of no cause"—this section of the sutra follows the previous [section] to correctly clarify the ten matters of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations); this demonstrates its initial characteristic. This is "attaining."

"Right knowledge and so forth" refers to this very state. Right knowledge is identical to right universal knowledge (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Why was it not termed "right knowledge" within the previous aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*)?
It is because the aggregate of perception is floating, unstable, and coarse, and thus corresponds with external delusions;

for that reason, it was not termed "right. Now, as the aggregate of perception is exhausted, awareness is luminous, empty, and still; the mind is inwardly correct and external delusions are utterly removed.
The other quarters refer to "correct knowledge" (*samyag-jñāna*), which also encompasses the three meanings of *śamatha*; by citing one, all three may be understood through common application.

Now, within this aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), when a son of good family remains凝然 (tranquil and unmoving) and lucid, his state of correct knowledge is so profound that the ten classes of celestial Māras cannot perceive him; thus, they find no opportunity for interference. These ten classes—
The phrase "those" refers to all that was disturbed within the preceding state of perception; they are all part of the celestial māras.

Generally speaking, when the subtle and pure mind of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) accords with internal right wisdom, external māras are cut off. Yet, these ten matters now arise entirely from the inversion of one's own mind;
they are called "mental māras" rather than external intrusions. Therefore, it is said: "The concentrated clarity is the right mind."

The Māra shall find no opportunity. Now, once this practitioner has departed from external māras, they are able to internally investigate and exhaustively examine the root of sentient beings, which is precisely the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Regarding the manifestation of the characteristics at the very source where these classes of beings arise:
one observes that the place where that source of birth is revealed is inherently obscure and hidden, subtle and pervasive, yet it is agitated and restless. This—
The nature of circular agitation is the source of all movement. Immediately following the word "circular," [the text] correctly demonstrates the cause of inverted views.
Within this source of circular agitation and movement, those who give rise to conceptual calculations are declared by the Buddha to fall into the two theories of non-causality.
These two theories of non-causality refer to the absence of causality regarding both the fundamental and the derivative. The first phrase above provides a general heading for the first [theory].

The following is a detailed explanation; first, it clarifies the meaning of "primordial non-causality" (*mūla-abhāva-hetu*). "Primordial non-causality" refers to the initial point of arising of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as the root of all categories.
Because for eighty thousand kalpas prior to this, there was a profound darkness with nothing visible, they calculate this to be primordial non-causality.
Why? This is raised to interrogate and explain: since this person has completely shattered the vital mechanism of the continuous arising of the aggregate of formations.
The faculty of the eye possesses eight hundred merits, enabling it to perceive the past eighty thousand kalpas;

this is because the functional activity of the eye faculty is constituted by the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), and thus, by means of the eye faculty’s functional activity, one perceives many kalpas.

Regarding the phrase "the flow of karma meanders": "karma" refers to the *saṃskāra-skandha*, for the shifting and flowing of the *saṃskāra-skandha* is termed the "flow of karma"; "meandering" (*wān*) signifies whirling or circling.
The meaning of "revolving" (*vartana*) refers to the sense of a cycle; that is, the revolving cycle of following the flow of karma.
Therefore, the subsequent line states, "dying here and being born there," which expresses the intent of this flowing and circling.

The phrase "merely seeing sentient beings revolving in those places" refers to the intent of conceptualizing what is fundamentally without cause; it means that those who so conceptualize merely see the ten [realms].
Second, because sentient beings transmigrate within eighty thousand kalpas and there is no perception whatsoever beyond those eighty thousand kalpas, they form this interpretation.

This section below correctly clarifies "original non-existence as the cause" (benwu yin): it means that all sentient beings originally did not exist but now do, and are thus called "originally non-existent as the cause.
Because they calculate [existence] based on original non-existence, they lose sight of the nature of Perfectly Complete Knowledge (samyak-saṃbuddhatva).
Falling into the heterodox views of external paths and being deluded regarding true Bodhi—secondly, below this, the meaning of the "absence of cause" at the end is clarified.
First, the initial phrase sets forth the calculation; the words "What is it that... and so on, interrogate and explain. The Buddha said:

This person, having already perceived the fundamental basis within the phenomena of arising, sees that what was originally non-existent now exists; thus they know that its subsequent manifestations are likewise without cause and arise spontaneously.
As for "accomplishment," it means that because one knows humans naturally produce humans and birds naturally produce birds, things are accomplished spontaneously without any creator;
throughout eighty thousand kalpas, there has never been any alteration, and even after this present form perishes, it shall remain so through all future kalpas.
That one does not perceive bodhi is likewise due to the fact that there is no such thing beyond eighty thousand kalpas.

If that which is visible does not exist, then awakening (*bodhi*) likewise does not exist. Since the essential substance of awakening is non-existent, how could there be the attainment of the state of awakening?
If both the beginning and end of supramundane awakening are non-existent, then one should know that all mundane conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are likewise non-existent.
One should know that this concludes the refutation of their conceptualization; that is, to know that today’s [existence] is but one...

All phenomena and forms ultimately derive from causelessness; today’s words and phrases are contrasted with eighty thousand kalpas, taking the period before those eighty thousand kalpas as the root and today as the branch—all are fundamentally rooted in causelessness.
In this phrase, the word "root" (*ben*) does not refer to the "root" in the sense of a beginning versus an end;
rather, it is a skillful syntactic placement intended to convey the underlying meaning that all phenomena are rooted in causelessness.
This concludes the demonstration that those who cling to the secondary [factors] are in error;
it is thus a summary of how the first of the heterodox teachers' two theories of non-causality is established based on the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
"Ānanda, these good sons within *samādhi*... (up to) the second heterodox teacher who establishes the doctrine of pervasive permanence.
This section of the sutra follows the previous discussion of the ten matters regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), and here it clarifies the second characteristic.
"Ānanda, as explained previously... [The text continues: "...exhausting the arising of conceptualization within meditative concentration; observing that profound clarity and movement..."
The "original" (yuan) is also as previously explained; where it was previously called "round" (yuan), it is now called "constant" (chang).

Previously, "round" referred to horizontal pervasiveness, because what is round is pervasive. Now, "constant" refers to vertical exhaustiveness, because from eighty thousand kalpas ago until today, and extending infinitely into the future, it remains uninterrupted.
The simultaneous mention of both "round" and "constant" here is to explain constancy by combining the vertical and horizontal dimensions.

Furthermore, because it is pervasive, this doctrine of eternalism contains four distinct types of difficulties. While these four differ, the object of their calculation is the same: the theory of pervasive eternalism.
The phrase "this person" (referring to the proponent) below marks the total number of four; the section beginning with "firstly" provides a detailed explanation of the meaning of eternalism.
First, regarding the calculation of eternity based on the mind and its objects: this refers to the investigation of the two spheres of mind and object as being without cause, relying upon this mind.

Objects have no cause, yet through the power of cultivation, one is able to know that within twenty thousand kalpas, although all mental objects and states are fundamentally non-existent, they appear as if existent;
and that the sentient beings of the ten directions arise and perish of themselves in an uninterrupted cycle, never having been lost since those twenty thousand kalpas.
To reckon this as "permanent" is to regard continuity as permanence.

Second, regarding the calculation of permanence based on the four great elements (*mahābhūta*): although the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) of the four great elements circulates through the six realms of existence, its nature does not undergo change or alteration;

therefore, it is reckoned as permanent. Relying upon this permanent nature, one practices the vehicle. By virtue of the power of that practice, one contemplates the fundamental nature of the four great elements and thereby knows the events of forty thousand kalpas.
Since the world of sentient beings is constructed from the four great elements, although it is subject to arising and ceasing, [it is considered permanent].
Because its essence is eternal and non-dispersive, they establish the doctrine of permanence. Thirdly, they calculate permanence based on the eight consciousnesses:
they claim that the six [consciousnesses] are consciousnesses dependent on sense organs; *manas* is the seventh consciousness; and "grasping" (*upādāna*) is the eighth consciousness.

Because the eighth consciousness grasps the body with its sense organs and the seeds of beginningless good and evil, it is called "grasping" (*upādāna*). Thus, they refer to the mind and intellect as "grasping."

The "citta" (mind) is the eighth consciousness, because it accumulates and gives rise [to phenomena], and thus is called "mind. The "manas" (intellect/thought) is the seventh, because it constantly and deliberatively cogitates;
that which is thought is the "manas. The "vijñāna" (consciousness) refers to the first six consciousnesses, as they cognize what is to be known.
These—citta, manas, and vijñāna—are the fundamental origins from which they arise. Since the nature of consciousness is eternal, one should cultivate the vehicle based upon this eternal nature.
The power of cultivation of these eight consciousnesses enables one to know events within eighty thousand kalpas;

because all sentient beings who have existed since those eighty thousand kalpas circulating through birth and death have never been lost, the nature of the eight consciousnesses is reckoned as permanent.

Fourthly, regarding the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), one reckons it as permanent, thinking that once this person’s *saṃjñā-skandha* (the aggregate of perception) has fundamentally ceased, the principle of the *saṃskāra-skandha* will become subtle.

This profound stillness is the nature of the human mind; because coarse phenomena are no longer perceived and the coarse manifestations of the *saṃjñā-skandha* (aggregate of perception) have been exhausted due to its flickering movement, it is said that the principle of life is further devoid of flowing, ceasing, or circulating.

Furthermore, as the arising and ceasing of the *saṃjñā-citta* (mind of perception) has been eternally extinguished, one erroneously reckons the subtle characteristics of the principle of life within the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations) to be non-arising and non-ceasing, and thus reckons them as permanent. From this point downward, [the text] summarizes.

To summarize the error of the four [types of] permanence: this concludes the section on establishing the second discourse on "perfect permanence" based on the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations).
Furthermore, among those sons of good family within *samādhi*, [this leads to] the third type of externalist doctrine: the partial doctrine of permanence.

This section of the sutra follows the preceding ten matters regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); it clarifies the third characteristic. Furthermore, "the three" and below are as previously explained.

"Exhausting the lower" and below correctly clarifies those who give rise to conceptual calculations within meditative concentration; the observation of that single phrase is also as previously explained.
"In oneself" and below correctly clarifies those who now calculate themselves and others; such a person gives rise [to these views] based on self and other.
There are four types of distinctions, all of which are inverted views that falsely grasp at one as permanent and one as impermanent;
taking the permanent as self and the impermanent as other—this is the general heading. First, the specific explanation below:

regarding the arising of views of self and other based on the divine self (ātman) and sentient beings, the Buddha said that such a person contemplates their own wondrous mind as pervading the realms of the ten directions. This...
Because the mind is tranquil and still, its ultimate nature is taken to be the *puruṣa* (the divine self). However, this is a misconception;

they take the nature of the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) to be that tranquil and wondrous mind. Because it is extremely subtle and invisible, and because it cannot be measured due to its invisibility, it is called the "divine self" (*puruṣa*).
In contrast to sentient beings, this divine self is discussed in terms of permanence and impermanence, and as the self.
Because it is immovable, it is called "permanent"; yet because all sentient beings undergo birth and death within the self of the *puruṣa* (spirit), it is called "impermanent.
Second, next, regarding the discussion of permanence and impermanence in external objects:

this person does not contemplate the mind but contemplates objects; thus, they abandon the internal and grasp the external, calculating based on whether external objects are subject to destruction or not.
Regarding permanence and impermanence: generally, those who perceive the myriad things as having characteristics consider them subject to decay and thus calculate them as impermanent;
they consider space to be without characteristics and thus indestructible, calculating it as permanent. This is because they do not contemplate the mind but instead contemplate external objects.

Furthermore, below this, there is a sequential discussion on contemplating permanence and impermanence by distinguishing between body and mind; "distinct contemplation" refers to contemplating them separately.
Regarding the general summary above, which observed external objects as a whole, the present section is called "specific" because it observes solely one's own body and mind.
As for the statement that "the self is subtle like a mote of dust," the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) states:

"Non-Buddhists cling to a self whose substance is eternal and as subtle as a single atom, which secretly moves within the body to perform various activities. Thus, in the present text, it is likened to a mote of dust.
"Subtle and dense" has the same meaning as "flowing and circulating without change," because its nature as a latent activity is constant.
"The ten directions" refers to the six realms of existence, as the six realms pervade the ten directions.
The intent is that while my mind flows through the six realms, its nature has never changed; thus it is said below: "It can cause this very body..."
Arising is itself ceasing; through this arising and ceasing, the permanence [of the nature] is revealed.
Fourth, below, it further discusses permanence and impermanence by way of the three aggregates—form and so forth—and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

It states that because this person knows the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has ended while the aggregate of formations continues to flow, and because the flow of the aggregate of formations is uninterrupted, form and the other aggregates are termed "permanent."
The extinction of the three aggregates is termed "impermanence. From this point downward, the errors of the four views are summarized.
From "this then" downward, the name of the third theory—established based on the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) regarding self and other—is concluded.

Furthermore, regarding the section from "Again, among those good sons within samādhi" (至) to "The fourth heterodox school establishes the theory of existence with limits" (第四外道立有邊論), this passage follows the preceding discussion of the ten matters concerning the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), clarifying its fourth characteristic. The phrase "Furthermore, [from] below" is as previously explained;
"exhausting the arising of [inferior states]" (窮生下) correctly clarifies those who give rise to conceptual calculations within meditative concentration. One should also contemplate that single phrase.
As previously stated regarding the "parts" (*aṃśa*), here the current calculation of "stages" (*avasthā*) is clearly elucidated.
Wēn-líng’s commentary states: "There are four stages, namely: the stage of the three time-periods, the stage of seeing and hearing, the stage of self and other, and the stage of arising and ceasing.

This can be seen by entering the text. The phrase "having limits" (*antavat*) is an abbreviated expression; it should be stated as "four types: having limits, being limitless, both, and neither," as explained in the *Śāstra*.
To be able to see the limits of the boundaries is called "having limits" (*sānta*); not seeing the limits of the boundaries is called "having no limits" (*ananta*).
This is the general heading. First, the specific explanation follows. Regarding the "origin of birth throughout the three periods of time":
this refers to the origin of the arising of the *saṃskāra-skandha*. Since the stream of karma has wound and circled for eighty thousand kalpas, it has no end.
"Clouds flow and their function never ceases" means that because the past has already perished and the future has not yet arrived, each is seen only at its boundaries;

hence it is said they have "limits. The continuous mind (*saṃtāna-citta*) is precisely the present consciousness (*manas*), which is called "limitless" because this present continuity abides for a long duration.
This refers to the three periods of time (*traiyadhvika*) in terms of the sequence of a single lifetime (*ekajīvitakāla*), yet one does not realize [the nature of] this single lifetime.
First, because moments are constantly shifting and passing away, how could there be a "present"? Therefore it is said that the present does not abide;
how, then, can it be called "boundless"? Second, the following section explains the stages of seeing and hearing; the text is easily understood.

Third, the following three sections explain the stages of "self" and "other," meaning that this person conceives of their own *ātman* as universally knowing all things, and thus attains [the notion of] boundlessness.
Regarding the nature of those people who appear within my consciousness: it is held that the *puruṣa* (the self) is the knower and all people are the objects of knowledge.
Because those people, who are the objects of knowledge, appear within my consciousness as the knower, they are merely known by me;
they do not know that they themselves possess the nature of being a knower. Why is this? If they possessed the nature of knowing, then [they would likewise perceive me].
Since that which appears within your cognition lacks the nature of being cognizable, it is merely termed "finite" and cannot be called "infinite.
How can that which lacks the essence of cognition appear within your cognition? Furthermore, your own cognition cannot manifest it;
thus, that which appears within cognition should also be termed finite. How, then, could there be an infinite nature? This concludes the fourth [section], the four lower [points].
The explanation of the stages of arising and ceasing is as follows: this person, having exhausted the emptiness of the *saṃskāra-skandha*, perceives much;

because of what he perceives, his mental deliberations are likewise manifold. He reckons that within each individual body of all sentient beings, there is a state of being half-arisen and half-ceased.
He designates the point where the body and mind increase as "arising," such as when one passes from youth to maturity.
The examples of "being strong yet old" and so forth illustrate this; because they undergo momentary transition and cessation, they are termed "extinction.

Since birth and extinction each obtain only half [of the process], it is said that there is "half-birth and half-extinction. Furthermore, regarding all things within the world of dependent retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*), it is also considered to have "half-finitude and half-infinity.
This is because the locus of existence is called "finite" (*anta*) and the locus of non-existence is called "infinite" (*ananta*). This is based on the correct [principle].

The discourse on retribution (*vipāka*) concerns arising and ceasing (*utpāda-vyaya*), while the discourse on the environment (*bhājana-loka*) concerns having limits and being limitless (*anta-ananta*).
The meaning of "having limits and being limitless" subsumes arising and ceasing, and arising and ceasing also subsumes having limits and being limitless; thus, the texts mutually clarify one another.

Furthermore, the environment is described as having limits or being limitless in reference to the *paricchinna-bhava* (the realm of segmented existence), whereas the body and mind are described as arising and ceasing in reference to their transition and decay. — Wu-xing.

The commentary explains: This calculation takes the place where the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) ceases as being "empty space" (*ākāśa*), and because it is empty, it is "boundless.
Yet, when one uses the mind to deliberate upon it, one perceives that there is still arising; therefore, it is "bounded. The same principle applies to all meanings regarding the world.

From this point downward, the conclusion summarizes that these four theories of "having boundaries" are all erroneous calculations. Thus, the following section concludes by establishing the fourth [theory] based on the *saṃskāra-skandha*.
Regarding the name of the "Theory of Finite Existence" (*antavāda*):

furthermore, within the various states of *samādhi*, there are good sons (up to) those who engage in the "Evasive and Confused Discourse of Immortality" (*amarā-vikṣepa*) and formulate all manner of empty theories.
This section of the sutra follows the ten matters concerning the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and clarifies the fifth characteristic. Furthermore, from "Moreover... onwards...
As previously explained, this section clarifies how those who give rise to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) within meditative concentration investigate a single phrase;

this is also as explained before. Regarding the passage beginning with "In knowing," this section clarifies that those who now construct views based on knowledge do so because they investigate the fundamental nature of the categories of existence within concentration, thereby giving rise to conceptual construction regarding what is known and seen. Thus, "knowing" refers to knowing all things.
Regarding the mental factor of view (*dṛṣṭi*), it refers to the view that all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are eternal. The *Changshui shu* (Long Water Commentary) states:

"As for the term 'immortal' (*amara*), the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* explains that non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) conceive of the heavens as eternally abiding and thus name them 'immortal. They hold that by answering without confusion, one will be reborn in those heavens.
If one were to answer recklessly when actually lacking knowledge, there is fear that it would constitute equivocation (*vikuṭṭana*); therefore, when questioned, one should answer."
Regarding the statement that "secret matters should not all be explained" or that one should give an "indefinite answer," the Buddha’s critique was that this is truly evasive.

According to the original text, there are instances where [the teaching] is mutually present and instances where it is mutually absent; when one applies the mind to these distinct perspectives, there is no fixed response.
Thus, such indecisiveness is termed "immortality. The term "immortal" (amata) signifies that the intention is alive but remains unresolved. Therefore...
To answer "it exists," "it does not exist," or "it both exists and does not exist," and so forth, is to be indecisive and to distort one's speech;
therefore, it is called the "undying sophistry" (*amarā-vikṣepa*) of false discourse. Regarding the term "sophistry" (*jiao*):

according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to the shaft of an arrow which is naturally straight, yet bending that straightness into a curve is called "sophistry"; thus, the character is derived from the radical for "arrow" (*shi*). Furthermore—
According to the *Lunyu*, "is-jiao" (is-jiǎo) means the intention to force; "force" (*qiáng*) also refers to being perverse and contorted, arising from a distorted mind.
This is the general heading for the first [section]; below, it is explained in detail. Within this, there are four pairs of transformations.

"The primordial source" (*yuán*) refers to the fundamental source of the myriad transformations, which is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Because formation is the root of the myriad transformations, the subsequent passage beginning with "seeing change" (*jiàn qiān*) is as follows.
The pair of "change" (biàn) and "constancy" (héng): change refers to shifting transformation, while constancy refers to permanence.

Because the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) flows and shifts from moment to moment, the cessation of the preceding moment is taken as "change," and the continuous arising of the succeeding moment is taken as "constancy. The following pair is that of "arising" (shēng) and "ceasing" (miè):
this refers to seeing the locus of the seen aspect as "arising," and not seeing the locus of the seeing subject as "ceasing."

Continuing below is the pair of increase and decrease: the nature of the causal continuity being uninterrupted is "increase," while the fact that within this continuous succession the preceding moment ceases and thereby induces the subsequent moment to arise—such that the former and latter are separated by an interval—is "decrease.
Following each of these is the pair of existence and non-existence: the location where the subsequent moment arises is "existence," while the [location of] the preceding moment is... [non-existence].
The phrase "the place of cessation is non-existent for each" means that there is a prior, a subsequent, and a further subsequent;
because within each single moment there is a prior and a subsequent, it refers to the places where each subsequent [moment] arises as "each. "Mutually" (*hu-hu*) is equivalent to "each" (*ge-ge*);
it refers to the mutual presence of existence and non-existence, arising and ceasing, and so forth, by pointing to the places where each preceding [moment] perishes. Thus, "mutually" is used.

The final two lines of the principle section provide a general summary of the four preceding pairs; that is, because the principles of these four pairs are all observed through distinct modes of mental application, there arises the seeking [of further clarification].
Below this, the text correctly clarifies the meaning of the evasive response (*vāg-vibhrama*).

While the words of the evasive response in the text are easy to understand, the intent of the pair "the mutable and the constant" is subsumed within the category of "arising and ceasing. As for the phrasing of the four pairs, it is concise and complete.

Therefore, because the meaning of "change" and "constancy" is identical to that of "arising" and "ceasing," the first of the four lines below correctly concludes the intent of the deceptive confusion.

Second, below this, the Buddha says that such a person merely contemplates the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as being momentary and without a fixed locus, thereby attaining realization.
"Attaining realization" means that they have realized the principle of non-existence; thus, when someone comes to question them, they answer with what they have realized.

Aside from "non-existence," one’s words are exhausted and there is nothing further to say. Regarding the third point, "below" refers to this person who merely contemplates that within the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) there is a locus for every moment of thought.
To "attain realization" means to realize the principle that existence exists;

therefore, when someone comes to question him, he answers with what he has realized. He does not answer by saying "existence," but rather answers by saying "this is so. This is precisely the meaning of existence.
Because it exists, it is so; if it were non-existent, it would not be thus. Apart from these two, one’s arguments are exhausted and there is nothing further to say.
Fourth, "below" refers to this person who, regarding the arising and ceasing of the *saṃskāra-skandha*, perceives both existence and non-existence.

They differentiate the boundaries between the existing object and the non-existing object, and as the object becomes fragmented, the mind likewise follows into confusion, resulting in [the perception of] existence and non-existence.
Because the realms are in disorder, when people come to inquire, he answers according to what he perceives; thus he says "existence is precisely non-existence.
This is because they reckon that non-existence can give rise to existence, and therefore he says "existence is precisely non-existence.

Furthermore, "non-existence is not [simply] existence" means that the non-Buddhists reckon non-existence to be merely absolute nothingness, failing to realize that non-existence is precisely existence; therefore, he says "also non-existence."
There is nothing that is not so, yet their conceptualization intends to treat existence as if it could be made non-existent, while non-existence can never be made existent;
at all times and in all places, they distort and confuse their arguments, refusing to allow others to subject them to rigorous inquiry.

From this, the following concludes the errors of these four types of confusion; this then concludes the section based on the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) to establish the [fourth] stage.
The five types of evasive and confused discourse on immortality are called "pervasive conceptualization" (*parikalpa*).

Among the three natures, this refers to the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the nature of pervasive conceptual construction), because one universally conceptualizes various objects through various false imaginings, thereby constructing their respective natures; as seen in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.
Furthermore, regarding the section from "Moreover, among the good sons in samādhi" (up to) "the post-mortem existence of signs and the theory of inverted minds":
this passage follows the previous discussion of the ten matters concerning the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), and now clarifies the sixth sign.

The phrase "Moreover, [as explained] below" is as previously stated; "exhausting the lower [levels]" correctly clarifies those who give rise to conceptual calculations within meditative concentration. The observation of that single phrase is also [as follows].
As previously explained regarding the absence of a lower state, here we clarify the calculation of those who reckon within the inexhaustible flow.

This refers to the arising and ceasing of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), which has flowed and shifted without end since eighty thousand kalpas; thus, these people form conceptual calculations within this inexhaustible flow.

The Buddha prophesied that such individuals will fall into the category of externalists (*tīrthika*) after death, among those characterized by signs, and that the resolve they have generated [will lead them there].
Because these are inverted views, one either departs from oneself by means of those inverted perceptions of the signs of existence after death:
first, regarding the consolidation of the body, one reckons that the body of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is itself the self, and since there is no form outside the self, form is the self;
second, one perceives the mind of the self as complete and pervasive throughout the lands, and thus reckons that the self is capable [of such pervasion].

Regarding the statement "there is form, and form arises from the self": among these three [types of objects], the first refers to external objective forms, namely the external sense-objects such as visible form (*rūpa*).
"Turning according to the self" means turning in accordance with the rising and sinking of one's own mind through the three realms of existence and the six destinies of rebirth.
Therefore, to reckon that form belongs to the self is the superior [view] of reckoning that the self can produce it.

Regarding form (*rūpa*), one now reckons form as the object of the self; among the four [types of views], those who reckon that the self depends on the continuity of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) reckon that the self exists within form.
All these reckonings below collectively refer to the reckonings of the four types of persons regarding the "having signs" (*sanimitta*) after death.
This means that although the physical body dies, the self still persists; because form follows the movement of the self, it is called "having signs."
If the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is thus, then the three aggregates of sensation, perception, and formations (*vedanā-, saṃjñā-, and saṃskāraskandha*) are likewise so.
This "cycling" refers to the self following the four aggregates in a cycle, thereby forming sixteen aspects (four for each aggregate). In his commentary, Changshui poses the question:

"Since the first three aggregates have already been exhausted, and there now remain only the two aggregates of formations and consciousness (*saṃskāra- and vijñānaskandha*), how can one further cling to the first three?"

Furthermore, it is not said that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is not [negated]. The answer is: although the first three aggregates (*skandha*) were negated within the context of contemplation, this was done specifically because the method of contemplation was particularly effective in those cases;

thus, one was not deluded by the aggregates and skillfully attained patient endurance (*kṣānti*), so that no further faults arose. How could it be said that there was no negation simply because [the negation] was not extensive?

Now, when contemplating the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), one clings to the first three [aggregates] because they serve as its basis and continue in a state of flux. Therefore, one does not cling to the first three.

Regarding the term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*): because it is obscured by the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), one does not mention consciousness when referring back to what precedes this.
From here below, the text generally clarifies the faults of the conceptualizations; the two characters "from this" (*cong ci*) directly cite the four types of self-conceptualization.
Because of these conceptualizations of a self, one may hold that afflictions and bodhi do not obstruct one another, proceeding simultaneously without contradiction; hence it says "each."
The phrase "or not touching" (*bù xiāng chù*) uses the word "or" (*huò*) as an indefinite term, for it may be reckoned or not reckoned.

However, upon careful examination, the conceptual attachment that takes [the mind] to be a self gives rise to the afflictions (*kleśa*). Since the mark of self (*ātman*) exists, the afflictions likewise exist accordingly.
Afflictions are defilement (*saṃkleśa*), while Bodhi is purity (*viśuddhi*); because defilement does not obstruct purity, they are said to "drive side by side. This is the meaning.
This is the view of the non-Buddhist outsiders who reckon [the self] as permanent. From "By this" onwards, it summarizes the error of the four types of views regarding the self.
From "This is then" onwards, it concludes by naming the sixth discourse on the characteristics of existence after death, which relies upon the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).

Furthermore, the passage from "Again, among the good sons within samādhi" (extending to) "after death, they engage in inverted theories regarding the signless mind" is a section of the sutra that generally precedes the ten matters of the *xing-yin* (perception aggregate).
This clarifies the seventh characteristic. The portion beginning with "Furthermore, [the passage] below" is as previously explained.

The section beginning with "Exhausting the arising of birth" correctly clarifies those who give rise to conceptual calculations within meditative concentration; it also refers to the contemplation of that single phrase.
As previously stated, this section now clearly elucidates the current calculation regarding the Buddha’s view of such a person:

while in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they calculate that among the three aggregates (*skandha*) of form and so forth which were previously eliminated, there is "non-existence. Consequently, they will fall into the category of those non-Buddhist outsiders who hold to the view of non-existence after death.
Because the mind they have generated is a perverted view (*viparyāsa-dṛṣṭi*), the text reveals their inferiority by showing that their calculation of non-existence is inverted.
The reason for this is that, according to their reckoning, because form (*rūpa*) ceases, the physical body has no basis or cause;

furthermore, observing that perception (*saṃjñā*) ceases, the mind has nothing to which it is bound or attached; and knowing that feeling (*vedanā*) ceases, the internal mind no longer experiences [objects], and thus there is no further continuity.
"Continuity" (*zhuì*) here carries the sense of being held together and maintained without interruption. Such, then, is the essential nature of these three aggregates (*skandha*).

If it were to disperse, then even though the principle of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) might now still exist in isolation, since the natures of the three preceding aggregates upon which it depends no longer exist, your *saṃskāra-skandha* would have nothing to rely upon and would be identical to the insentience of grass and trees.
Thus you should know that the substance of the present life is formed by relying on form; once that form has perished, it cannot even be found while one is still alive, let alone after death.

Are there any marks? By comparing the cause with the effect, one must know that there are no marks. Read the character "yin" (因) as the character "zhi" (之) [in the phrase "yin zhi zhi zi"], and it will be easy to understand.
Thus, the following two lines refer collectively to the four aggregates (*skandhas*) beginning with form (*rūpa*);

since the present causes cannot be found, how could the effects after death exist? Because this is explained in terms of the cause and effect of the four aggregates, it establishes the eight non-marks (*animitta*).

From this point downward, the text generally clarifies the reckoning that there is no fault or transgression. The two characters "from this" (yǐcóng) cite the preceding eight aspects of signlessness (*animitta*).
This means that because of these eight aspects of signlessness, one may reckon that the causes and effects of supramundane *nirvāṇa* are all empty;
since the supramundane is empty, the mundane is likewise so, such that there are merely names in vain, and the reality beneath the name [is also absent].
Because they cannot be apprehended, they are ultimately and entirely extinguished; this is the nihilistic view (ucchedadṛṣṭi) held by the non-Buddhists (tīrthika).

From "thereby" below is the summary of the error of reckoning [the aggregates] as non-existent; from "this then" below is the conclusion regarding the establishment of the seventh and eighth "formless" treatises based on the *saṃskāra-skandha* (volitional formations aggregate);

and the phrase "referring to the five aggregates" concludes the discussion, as the preceding text had only treated the first four aggregates. This is because... [the previous section] was limited to the first four aggregates.
For example, because subsequent consciousness is also absent.

Furthermore, from the passage "Again, among the sons of good family in samādhi, until after death, they all fall into the delusion of neither-thought-nor-non-thought," this section of the sutra follows the ten matters of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) to clarify the eighth sign. From "Again, [three... onwards.

As previously stated, this concludes the section on those born in the lowest realms; now it correctly clarifies how those who give rise to conceptualization within meditative concentration contemplate that single phrase, also as explained before.

Regarding the section "at the end of formations" (*saṃskāra*), it correctly clarifies that those who currently reckon that formations persist mean that since the previous three aggregates have already perished, the aggregate of formations alone remains.
Thus, such a person not only contemplates the existence of the persisting formations, but also simultaneously contemplates what preceded them.

In the passage concerning the third [negation], it merely states "feeling and perception," omitting the aggregate of form; this can be understood by analogy with the subsequent phrase. Regarding the dual reckoning of existence and non-existence:

this means that one uses the characteristics of existence and non-existence to mutually refute one another, hence they are called the "characteristics of neither. The character "xiang" (相) is read with a level tone (*píngshēng*).

Furthermore, one uses the existence of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) to refute the non-existence of the preceding three [aggregates], and uses the non-existence of those preceding three to refute [the existence of the fourth].
Because this aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) exists, it is said that its own essential nature is undermined; because it is undermined, both existence and non-existence are negated.

This corresponds to the "neither existent nor non-existent" position among the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) imagined by these people. Therefore, after death, they fall into the perverted doctrine of "neither [existence nor non-existence].
Regarding the sections on form (*rūpa*) and sensation (*vedanā*), the following correctly clarifies the meaning of this "neither. Please consider the preceding three aggregates, such as form, etc.

At first one sees as if there were existence, but later one sees that it is non-existent; because it is said that what has already ceased no longer exists, one speaks of "seeing existence as non-existence.

Now, observing within the flux of the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the initial thought has not yet arisen and is thus non-existent, while the subsequent thought has already arisen and is thus existent;

therefore, one speaks of "observing non-existence as not non-existent. This is the meaning of existence and non-existence mutually subverting one another. Thus, the following summarizes [the preceding].
By means of the preceding four aggregates, one cycles through and thoroughly penetrates the boundaries of the four aggregates to clarify the characteristics of the eightfold "neither-nor" state.
Within these four aggregates, depending on whether [a characteristic] is present or absent, upon encountering a single object, one reckons that after death there is both a mark and no mark.
However, this person, for the most part, first reckons that there *is* a mark within the first of the four propositions.

Furthermore, because there is no subsequent awakening after the "neither-existence-nor-non-existence" phrase, one again reckons it as that phrase. The preceding text already clarified "neither [existence nor non-existence]" based on what was said regarding the time of another's awakening;
the following passage, however, specifically points to the arising of a conceptualization from a later awakening.

This means that when one further observes that the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) undergoes moment-to-moment transformation and distortion, one once again gives rise to a penetrating realization at the very point of that transformation and distortion.

The "gate of awakening" (wumen) refers to the realization that both existence and non-existence are unattainable; therefore, one reckons that both existence and non-existence are not [ultimately real].

"Losing one's bearings regarding the void and the real" means that the "void" is non-existence and the "real" is existence. To observe non-existence and find it not non-existent is to lose one's bearings within non-existence—this refers to the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).
To perceive existence and find it not existent is to lose one's bearings within existence—this refers to the preceding three aggregates (*rūpa*, *vedanā*, and *saṃjñā*).
In speaking of existence and non-existence, one loses the place where the mind should be applied; thus it is said that "the real and the unreal are misplaced.

The preceding passage’s calculation of whether there are marks or no marks after death constitutes the "both-and" (雙亦), intended to lead to the realization that existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended—this is the "neither-nor" (雙非).
From this point downward, the text concludes by summarizing the error of these dualistic calculations. "The obscurity of the future limit" (後際昏瞢) refers to the state after death.
The subsequent explanation states that because it is impossible to discern whether existence or non-existence persists after death, one is said to be "obscured and beyond description.

The word "description" (道) refers to verbal expression; since one is obscured and beyond verbal expression, this concludes the establishment of the eighth "neither-existence-nor-non-existence" theory regarding the state after death based on the *saṃskāra-skandha*.
This is named among the five aggregates as previously explained.

Furthermore, regarding the passage from "Moreover, among the good sons within *samādhi*" (up to) "the heterodox theory that [the self] is annihilated after death," this section of the sutra follows the previous discussion of the ten matters concerning the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and clarifies the ninth characteristic.

The phrase "Moreover, [as previously explained]" refers back to what was stated before; "exhausting the arising of birth" correctly clarifies those who give rise to conceptual calculations within meditative concentration (*samādhi*). One should also contemplate that single phrase.

As previously stated, the following section clarifies the current view regarding the non-existence of subsequent moments. This refers to a person whose contemplative practice observes that the aggregates (*skandhas*) perish moment by moment and are ultimately non-existent.
While the initial arising of a thought-moment is existence, its subsequent cessation is non-existence;

since this is the case for every successive moment, it is called "non-existence of the subsequent" (*paścāt-paścād-abhāva*). Because one clings to this notion of non-arising, one falls into the category of the seven types of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*).

This refers to the arising of inverted views within the intermediate state. Regarding the "extinction in seven locations," Gushan’s commentary states: the Desire Realm is divided into humans and the devas;
the Form Realm is divided into the four dhyānas; and the Formless Realm is combined as one. Counting these seven locations together, they are reckoned as the points of annihilation.

Alternatively, it is reckoned that below [the summit of existence], there are precisely these seven locations where the characteristics of extinction appear: the extinction of the body refers to the extinction of the human body, and the extinction of desire...
The cessation of this refers to the cessation of the heavens of the desire realm;

the cessation of suffering refers to the cessation of the first and second dhyānas, because in those two heavens, the coarse obstacles of suffering from the lower realms have ceased. Thus, it is "supreme bliss" (*paramasukha*);

in that heaven, one realizes the bliss of cessation, and since no bliss surpasses this, it is called supreme bliss. Yet, because this bliss is not permanent and will inevitably perish after a time, it is [still subject to change].

It is said that "extinction" (*nirodha*) refers to the ultimate relinquishment (*atyanta-utsarga*). This is because in the fourth dhyāna and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*), both pleasure and pain are relinquished;

thus, the four formless realms are termed "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), as they share this quality of relinquishment. Among the conditioned states (*saṃskṛta*) of the three realms, this heaven is the ultimate;
it is also called "the immovable" (*āneñjya*). "Immovable" conveys the sense of ultimate relinquishment. Because this [view] reckons relinquishment to be extinction, it is so designated.
"Ultimately abandoning and extinguishing" refers generally to the above seven points; because one circulates through and exhaustively investigates them, there is ultimate extinction.
"Extinction manifest before one" refers to the extinction of the cause. "Once extinguished, there is no further arising" refers to the extinction of the effect.
From "thereby" onwards is the summary of the errors regarding the seven extinctions; the text is intelligible. As stated previously, "neither [of the two]" (*ubhayānta-vinirmukta*) resides in both.
If one now claims that [the self] is annihilated between the pillars, this is entirely based on the calculation of non-existence; it is even more extreme than the previous view.
This concludes the ninth of the seven theories of annihilation established based on the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Furthermore, from "the various good sons within samādhi" (up to) "the inverted discourse on the mind manifesting nirvāṇa," this section of the sūtra follows the previous discussion of the ten matters regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and clarifies the tenth characteristic. The passage beginning with "Furthermore" is as explained previously;
"exhausting the arising of the inferior" correctly clarifies those who give rise to conceptual calculations within meditative concentration. One should also contemplate that single phrase.
As previously stated, following this, the text now clearly elucidates the current position regarding those who maintain that there is a succession of future existences (*paścāt-paścād-bhava*).

This person observes that the aggregates (*skandha*) arise moment by moment and that their locus of arising is ultimately existent, because these momentary arisings are inexhaustible; therefore, it is said that there is a succession of future existences.

As for the phrase "this subsequent [existence] shall become the preceding one," what does it mean? It refers to the previous passage which observed the non-existence of the subsequent [existence], intending to show that...

Cessation is the subsequent thought, while initial arising is the preceding; since we now observe that there is this initial arising of a thought, one should say that each preceding moment is preceded by another.

Generally speaking, scribes often err by following the momentum of the preceding words and thus mistakenly refer to "subsequent and subsequent," when in fact it is "preceding and preceding" that is correct.
By grasping the underlying meaning, one can understand that because there is a calculation regarding existence, the *Wu niepan lun* (Treatise on the Five Nirvanas) fell into error.

Furthermore, because that [view] reckons the five stages as secure and takes security to be *nirvāṇa*, or because it takes the lower right emergence as the characteristic of the security of the five stages—or alternatively, because it takes the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to be the true basis of transformation—Tiantai’s commentary on *dhyāna* states:

"In the desire realm there are two concentrations: the first is called the concentration of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*), and the second is called the 'not-yet-arrived' concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*). This...

In the two meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), the mind is perfectly clear and luminous; because one takes this luminous state of meditative absorption as a place of peace and security, it is said that when the mind is distracted it becomes deviant, whereas when it is concentrated it becomes correct.

By turning away from the five desires and their dark fluctuations, and relying upon the perfect clarity of these two absorptions, it is called "correct transformation of the basis" (*samyag-āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Thus, Changshui’s Commentary states: "By practicing contemplative cultivation, one gives rise to desire..."
In the *dhātu* and the *anāgamya-samādhi*, within the mind of contemplation, one perceives the sign of perfect luminosity, and so forth.
Second, some take the first dhyāna to be *nirvāṇa* because it is free from the coarse obstacles of suffering in the lower realms; they rejoice in the purity and subtlety of this celestial realm.
Because this state is initially free from the defilement of desire and its nature is without sorrow, they reckon it to be a secure place of *nirvāṇa*.
Third, because in the second dhyāna the mind is free from the suffering of vitarka and vicāra found in the first dhyāna, it is reckoned as a state of peace and security.
Fourth, because in the third dhyāna one attains bodily bliss that accords with supreme joy and is inseparable from it, there is delight within and bliss pervading without;
speaking in terms of the internal, it is called "supreme delight" (prīti). For this reason [it is so designated].

They recklessly consider these to be places of peace and security. Fifth, because within the four dhyānas there are the two pairs of suffering and pleasure, and because the mind of equanimity is unshakable, they falsely identify this state as being free from the birth and death of saṃsāra, reckoning it to be a place of peace and security.

Regarding the two lines below that concerning delusion regarding existence: the Buddha has collectively severed the delusions of the aforementioned five places; all are tainted heavenly retributions, and one is deluded by them.
Because those in the heavens with outflows (sāsrava) hold the view that it is unconditioned nirvāṇa, they reckon the five places of security as the basis for your supreme, pure nirvāṇa.
Thus, these five places are ultimately nothing but a cycle;
to mistake them for a place of ultimate security is an extreme delusion and a profound error. Below this, the conclusion summarizes the error of the five bases. This concludes [the section].
Based on the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the fifteenth discourse on Nirvāṇa is established, which speaks of "manifesting Nirvāṇa.
This means that within these five locations, one manifests birth and brings about peace and security, thereby effecting Nirvāṇa.
Ānanda, such ten kinds of deluded understandings regarding *dhyāna* (up to the point of) acting as the pure signpost for the Great Awakened King.

In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One, following the preceding [discussion], generally enumerates ten matters regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) to admonish practitioners not to deceive themselves, thereby guarding their cultivation and entering realization.

The phrase "Thus it is" and below formally concludes the previous meaning. The points concerning the interaction between *dhyāna* and the application of the mind, and so forth, are all as previously explained.
The concluding text for the preceding aggregates refers to the "manifesting objects" (*pratibhāsa*) within *dhyāna*; these manifesting objects...
This refers to the manifestation of demonic realms externally; the present text concludes by stating that this is the "madness of dhyāna.
This "madness of dhyāna" arises from inverted views within the inner mind; because it is neither right concentration nor right knowledge, it is termed "madness of dhyāna.

By knowing that the internal and external are thus utterly distinct, one's practice gradually deepens. Furthermore, while the previous "skandhas" referred to what was formerly manifest, this "matter" (vastu) points specifically to the external.
Because the demonic activities (*māra-karman*) are spoken of here by way of their names, this awakening (*bodha*) is manifested; "awakening" serves to distinguish it from external matters.

Since this awakening arises from the internal mind’s deluded understanding, it is not yet correct. It is spoken of as "internal" because those who mistake delusion for understanding—referring to the ten matters—take what is fundamentally delusive and false to be their calculations.
These ten matters are inherently delusive and illusory, yet they are called "understanding" because they are the mental demons (*citta-māra*).
The perverted views of the mind are themselves Māra; thus, "deeply perverse" (*shēnniè*)—where *niè* means a malevolent omen—is the perversion of Māra.
"Awakening to the true meaning" (*kāijué zhēnyì*) belongs to the category of enlightenment, meaning one awakens to the meaning of the Buddha’s true realization.

"Branching off into byways" (*zhīqí*)—where *zhī* refers to redundant branches and *qí* to many paths—means that redundant branches harm one's nature, while many paths cause one to lose the sheep of the mind.
Regarding "praying": to pray means to give rise to a mind of longing and hope, seeking in advance for the attainment of the fruit;

this very state of mind that awaits awakening is a great malady in the cultivation of dhyāna. Regarding "the pointing finger": this is explained by way of analogy, just as a finger points toward the moon;
herein, the verbal teachings are the pointing finger, and the ultimate meaning is the moon. The rest is easily understood.
"Ānanda, that son of good family who cultivates *samādhi* [up to] takes inverted deluded thoughts as its foundation.
This section of the sūtra consists of the World-Honored One’s fifth exposition on ten matters regarding the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

Herein, he first clarifies the boundaries of the aggregate of consciousness and the characteristics of its exhaustion, so that people may attain a correct beginning and be able to guard against the heterodox. "Ānanda," and so forth, concludes and restates the practice.

"Upon the exhaustion of the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the next [stage] arises. The phrase "that son of good family" refers back to the practitioner of the *skandhas* mentioned in the preceding text.
The subsequent section directly restates that prior meaning. Regarding the phrase "all worldly beings," "all worldly beings" refers to the twelve classes of living beings.
The character "nature" (*xing*) refers to the essential nature of the *skandha* of formations; for it is by virtue of the *skandha* of formations that these twelve classes [of beings] exist.
Because it arises, the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is pointed out as the nature of the world. From "profoundly pure" up to "the mechanism of arising," it is as previously explained.
The phrase "suddenly shattered and split apart" precisely clarifies the characteristic of the exhaustion of formations. "Suddenly" (*shu*) means instantaneous; "shattered" (*hui*) means destruction;
"split apart" (*lie*) means opening wide. This refers to the mechanism of the arising of that aggregate of formations, wherein mind and object suddenly undergo destruction and split apart.

Having opened it up, one exhausts it entirely. From the most subtle to the most extreme, the phrases clarify the signs of the exhaustion of the causal karma of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).
The "framework" (*gāng*) refers to the rope at the mouth of a net; if there were no framework, the net could not be spread out.
The "knot" (*niù*) refers to the binding knot, used as a metaphor for the causal karma of the arising and ceasing of the *saṃskāra-skandha*. All cycles of birth and death are like this.

All arise from the karmic causes of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). Because these karmic causes of the *saṃskāra-skandha* are profound and subtle, they are called "deep and subtle knots" (*chénxì guāngniù*).

The Sanskrit term *pudgala* is translated as "one who repeatedly undergoes rebirth" (*shǔqǔqù*). "Shǔ" (數) is pronounced like "shuò" (朔), and "qù" (趣) refers to the five destinies (*pañca-gati*), meaning that one repeatedly takes up the retribution of birth and death.
"Chóu" (酬) in "recompensing the deep channels of karma" means to repay or correspond to [past actions].
Repaying karmic causes is the cause, and the *pudgala* (the person) is the fruit; the *pudgala* as the fruit repays the karmic causes of past lives.
The character for "vein" (*mai*) is also explained by way of metaphor:

just as a single vein within a human body connects and sustains the entire organism, so too is the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) likened to the deep vein that repays karma as the fruit of all destinies of birth and death. Now, regarding this *saṃskāra-skandha*:
Once the pulse has been severed, the summoning of this response from that across all births and deaths is suspended and cut off. The syntax should be read as follows:

"The generative force of the homogeneous class suddenly shatters"—this single phrase is read continuously, while the four phrases from "sinking and becoming subtle" down to "suspended and cut off" are read together;
the meaning will then become self-evident. This section, following the character "niè" (nirvāṇa), precisely clarifies the boundaries of the consciousness aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Because both the principle (dharma) and the analogy (upamāna) are presented together, it is called "Nirvāṇa Heaven. Nirvāṇa is the principle; heaven is the analogy.
The following lines clarify that the character for "heaven" is the analogy and the character for "awakening" is the principle.

This means that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is adjacent to Nirvāṇa and is on the verge of awakening, just as when the sky is about to brighten, the rooster crows after the dawn. As the common proverb says: "When the rooster has crowed three times."
Because the east begins to turn white, it is said that one looks toward the east and already perceives a refined radiance;
this "refined radiance" is the appearance of the dawning light of the first principle of Nirvana, signifying that its color is about to illuminate the final limit of the *vijñāna-skandha*.

Below, regarding the six sense organs, the text clarifies the appearance of the manifestation of consciousness when karma is exhausted: because the internal and external are suspended and severed, [this state] is attained.

The six sense organs are empty and still, without wandering or dissipation. "Internally and externally lucid and bright" means that "internal" refers to the eighth consciousness and "external" refers to the six evolving consciousnesses.
When the six sense organs are active, there appears to be internal and external; now, being deeply settled, they enter into and merge with this profound stillness, becoming one as a single source.
Originally one delusion was divided into six; now, the external lucidity is precisely the internal lucidity, appearing as such.
