There is an entry, yet one enters where there is no entry. Because the practitioner follows their practice until consciousness (*vijñāna*) is fully manifested, they are able to deeply penetrate the fundamental source of the life-destiny of the twelve classes of beings throughout the ten directions.
This "fundamental source of the life-destiny" refers to the fact that all twelve classes receive their life-destiny through the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*);
this fundamental source is precisely the original cause, which is the aggregate of consciousness. [End of previous section]
The opening passage of the *Saṃskāra-skandha* states that "each life has its own source"; this refers precisely to the present text’s "original source of receiving life.

If a practitioner can contemplate this original source of receiving life and maintain the *mūla-vijñāna* (root consciousness) so as not to allow it to repay karma, then the various classes of existence will not summon one.
"Summoning" here carries the meaning of "responding," implying that one does not respond to what is induced by karma; thus, one attains [liberation] throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

That which is "identical" refers to attaining realization within the twelve classes throughout the entire world; this "identity" points specifically to consciousness (*vijñāna*), for it is by means of this consciousness that one receives life.
That the "essence and color do not sink" means that once the aggregate of consciousness has manifested, its subtle and refined nature becomes revealed;
hence it is said they do not sink. Because they do not sink, they remain profound, hidden, and secret.
The nature of these [phenomena] all manifests; this concludes the first phrase by clarifying the scope (*pramāṇa*) of the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*).
"District" (*qū*) refers to the meaning of boundaries (*sīmā*), which is the sense of "scope"; "universe" (*yǔ*) refers to the sense of covering the aggregates.

If one proceeds to the next section to correctly clarify the signs of the exhaustion of the consciousness-aggregate, "summoning the multitude" corresponds to the previous passage’s meaning of "not summoning the various classes"; here it means that all classes should respond.
If one can dissolve and polish the portals of the six sense organs, then one can achieve the "integration and opening.
To achieve integration and opening means that integration is the unification of the six into one, and opening is the differentiation of the one into six;
by being able to dissolve and polish the six gates, one attains mastery over this integration and opening, such that there is neither one nor six.

"Obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*) means "accomplishment. "Seeing and hearing penetrate the adjacent" means that the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*)—seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing—penetrate and reach their respective neighboring domains.
In this phrase, the two characters "sensing" (*jñāna*) and "cognizing" (*vijñāna*) are omitted for brevity. "Penetrating the adjacent" refers to the mutual functioning of these faculties.
Therefore, the subsequent line fulfills the meaning of the preceding one by stating: "Mutual functioning is pure," because this mutual functioning is unobstructed, it is called "pure. (10)

Now, to further clarify the meaning of the purity of the environment and its inhabitants: the ten directions of the world represent the environment (*āśraya*), and the body represents the inhabitant (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*).
Just as a *vaiḍūrya* gem is transparent both inside and out, this serves as a metaphor for the unimpeded transparency of the environment and its inhabitants;

this reveals the characteristic of the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Regarding the statement that "the exhaustion of consciousness transcends the turbidity of life-force": consciousness is indeed the fundamental basis for receiving life, precisely because it is the cessation of consciousness [that brings about such transcendence].
The three supports of warmth constitute life; if even one is lacking, death occurs. Therefore, it is called the turbidity of life (*āyuḥ-kāṣāya*).

Now, because [the practitioner] attains the exhaustion of these [supports], they transcend the turbidity of life. Examining what follows clarifies the origin of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*): taking the formless, the void, and deluded thought as the basis of the aggregate of consciousness.
"That which is the source" refers back to the fundamental state. "Formless and void" means that there is nothing to be perceived.
The "phantom" (wangxiang) appears and disappears momentarily; it seems real yet is not real. It is so subtle, minute, and dense that it is difficult to distinguish through existence or non-existence;
therefore, it is called the "phantom. "Voidness" (xuwu) conveys the meaning of being hazy and indistinct. It borders upon awakened clarity and leaves no trace of substantial obstruction.
Because its profound subtlety accords with the meaning of the "phantom," the two are mentioned together as "the phantom-void."
"Deluded thought.
Ānanda, you should know that these good sons (up to) turn their backs on the city of Nirvāṇa and give rise to the seeds of external paths.
This section of the sūtra follows the preceding part to correctly clarify the ten matters of the consciousness aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*); this indicates its first characteristic. This is "good."

The man then pointed to the person who had previously practiced the contemplation of the *skandhas*, citing his prior practice to introduce the following passage which correctly clarifies the present meaning.
"Consciousness returns to its source" means that from the *rūpa-skandha* up to this point, one has returned to the fundamental origin of the nature of consciousness;
therefore, it is called the "perfect source. "Having extinguished arising and ceasing" means that all the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) have ceased their production.
The cessation of these [coarse phenomena] all belongs to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); now that the aggregate of formations is exhausted, arising and ceasing have already ceased.

However, this merely refers to the exhaustion of the arising and ceasing of coarse characteristics; as for the arising and ceasing of the underlying flow (*pravāha*), which is profoundly deep and subtle, it has not yet been said to be exhausted.
Why is this? As the subsequent scripture states: "This stillness is not the True Suchness (*tathatā*); it is like a rapid current of water that appears tranquil on the surface while flowing beneath."
That one does not perceive [the truth] immediately does not mean that the outflow-free state is absent; this can be understood.

Thus, within the principle of Great Quiescent Extinction (mahāśānti), the subtle and wondrous [realization] is as yet not perfected. This principle of quiescent extinction is precisely what was previously called the Heaven of Nirvāṇa. It enables those below to receive from above;
when consciousness is exhausted and the mind speaks, although it is quiescent, it is not yet perfected. Once consciousness returns to its source, it can cause oneself [to realize it].

When the six sense organs of the body—through their conjunction, separation, opening, and closing—are perfected, they communicate with the enlightened nature possessed by the twelve classes of beings.

The nature of these six organs’ seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is fused and integrated; thus one is able to realize the fundamental source of the perfectly interfused consciousness-nature, because it is based upon these locations.
This section below correctly clarifies the arising [of delusion] within the fixed state of the consciousness aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*).
As for "resolute conviction" (*adhimukti*), it refers to the distinction between false and correct understanding. If one's understanding is correct, it will not obstruct meditative concentration;

rather, by following that understanding, one realizes the principle—what is called "flowing into the center of the center" and ascending to the heaven of Nirvana. This achievement depends upon understanding.

If, however, one erroneously gives rise to false understanding, one falls into the views of external paths and cannot escape the fault of the ten matters. Therefore, what is clarified here is entirely intended to demonstrate [the correct path].

This is indeed a fallacy; however, if this practitioner establishes a cause of true permanence within the fundamental nature of the consciousness that serves as the locus of refuge, they fall into the attachment to a "cause of causes.
While this fundamental consciousness is provisionally granted the status of "true" in contrast to the preceding false states of the sense organs and objects, this so-called reality is not truly real.
As the verse in the fifth fascicle of the Sutra says: "If the true were not true, one would fear delusion."
This refers precisely to this: constantly confronting the arising and ceasing of preceding moments, one provisionally allows for "permanence. This permanence is, in reality, not permanent.
Why? Because the flow has not yet ceased; thus, the cause is not a true cause.

If, regarding this point where permanence is provisionally allowed, one erroneously establishes a truly permanent cause, then one falls into the calculations of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). This is the clinging to causes and their objects.
This means: "Is it not erroneous to falsely reckon that which is inherently non-eternal as being an eternal cause?

This sentence is the Buddha’s judgment; all subsequent passages are to be understood in this manner. *Sāṃkhya* (in Sanskrit) is translated as "Yellow-Head" (*Huangtou*), the name of a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*) school characterized by yellow hair.
They reckon the *pradhāna* (the Unmanifest or Primordial Matter) to be the true, ultimate cause to which all things return, asserting it to be a single entity.
Since all phenomena arise from the *pradhāna* (the primal essence), the *pradhāna* is that which non-Buddhists reckon as the twenty-fifth principle (*tattva*).
Because they take the *pradhāna* to be the cause, they observe that for eighty thousand kalpas prior to this, there was a state of profound darkness and ignorance;

"primal" (*pra*) refers to this obscurity, and "essence" (*dhāna*) refers to its reality as such, hence it is called the *pradhāna*. After eighty thousand kalpas, all phenomena likewise emerge from this.
Because they arise, they are reckoned as causes. Now, because the practitioner’s own attachments are the same as those reckonings, he mistakenly falls into their category and becomes their companion.
Therefore, he is deluded regarding the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment and loses the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
This concludes the first section on the names of external paths. As for "the mind that is attained," this refers to establishing the mind that conceives of the imagined cause.

To achieve the true fruit to which one returns is to instead distance oneself from the Buddha’s perfect penetration; it is to turn one's back on Great Nirvāṇa and head toward the seeds of external paths.

The reason Nirvāṇa is metaphorically compared to a city is that within Great Nirvāṇa, all merit and the wealth of the Dharma are gathered together, just as all things are gathered within a worldly city;
therefore, it is likened to a city. Previously, the analogy of heaven was used to illustrate Nirvāṇa... [text truncated]

The city of *pāṇḍubhūmi* is a metaphor for *nirvāṇa*, while "virtue" (*guṇa*) refers to its qualities. Furthermore, the aforementioned scripture states that the ocean is a metaphor for the secret treasury of *nirvāṇa* and its vastness;
since each contains its own profound significance, the metaphors employed are not fixed.

Ānanda, furthermore, when a good man exhausts the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)—[continuing] until he gives rise to the seeds of the Great Brahmā Heaven’s universal pride (*māna*)—this section of the sutra follows upon the ten matters of the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) and clarifies its second characteristic. "Exhausts all...
and so forth is as previously explained. "If, regarding... correctly clarifies the present calculation; that is to say, if this practitioner, regarding the consciousness to which he has returned...

If one regards the nature as the self-substance and contemplates that all twelve classes of beings within the entirety of the empty realm are produced from flowing forth out of one's own body—such a resolute conviction falls into the grasping at the "capable" and the "incapable.

Regarding this grasping at the capable and the incapable, the Buddha judged that this conception is fundamentally not capable of producing [beings], yet it is falsely clung to as being capable. Maheśvara...
Rāhu possesses this attachment; thus, in the Sanskrit language he is called Maheśvara, translated as "Mahādeva" (Great Sovereign).

He is the Lord of the Heaven of Ultimate Form (*Akaniṣṭha*). This deity reckons himself as the progenitor of all phenomena, for he considers that all sentient beings emerge from him and that he is the sovereign of the great trichiliocosm;
therefore, he manifests boundless bodies. Now, this practitioner reckons himself to be identical with him, thereby achieving [his goal].
His followers are deluded regarding the Buddha, as previously stated; this is termed the second externalist school.
As for those who give rise to great pride in heaven, they refer to Maheśvara, who clings to the notion that "I" can produce all sentient beings.
Because all things arise from me, he conceives great *asmimāna* (the pride of "I am"). His mind pervades the ten directions and is reckoned to fully encompass all practitioners.
"Because they are identical, that seed is produced.
Furthermore, good son, [the mind] exhausts the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (up to) turning its back on the city of Nirvāṇa and producing the seed of inverted perfection.
This section of the sutra follows upon the ten matters concerning the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*); it clarifies the third characteristic. "Furthermore, good son," and so forth.
As previously stated, to now clarify the current position:

if this practitioner, regarding the nature of consciousness to which they have returned, clings to it as having real existence and perceives it as having a characteristic of a locus of refuge, yet fails to contemplate its emptiness, this is truly a perversion.

Because they cling to the real existence of that locus of refuge, they harbor doubts within themselves that their own body and mind flowed forth from that nature of consciousness; this is the former position.

If you regard that nature of consciousness as your own self-substance, yet now reckon it as not being yourself and instead suspect that your body flows forth from it, then you are treating the nature of consciousness as an external object.
Not only does your body flow forth from it, but the empty space of the ten directions all arises from it; and the worlds that exist within that space likewise arise from it.
Regarding the "other-birth" (tāra-janman), one calculates that the other can give rise to oneself;
thus, one takes the ground where the pervasive, flowing consciousness-nature arises as a truly eternal body, and clings to this as an understanding of being without birth or extinction.

The two characters "du-qi" (pervasive-arising) inherit the meaning from the preceding phrase regarding the arising of humans within the realm of beings, for all [phenomena] arise from that. This occurs in the section on "Birth" (Jie-sheng), following the Buddha.
Judging their delusion, it is said that because they are within the cycle of arising and ceasing, they do not realize arising and ceasing; they recklessly calculate it to be permanent.

Because they do not know the subtle flow of the nature of consciousness as it arises and ceases, they calculate it to be permanent. Being thus deluded regarding arising and ceasing, they likewise fail to recognize the eternally abiding.
Deluded at both ends, they fail to exert themselves toward superior progress and remain settled in this state of confusion.
To take delusion for liberation within this state is for such a person to fall into the attachment to permanence and impermanence.

"Permanence and impermanence" is a term used by the Buddha to describe those whose essence is not permanent yet who falsely cling to it as being so. This calculation arises from the same source as that of Maheśvara;
their calculations are identical, and they form a faction together. Now, this calculation and the previous one both originate from the Great [Self].

Regarding the fact that Maheśvara manifests two forms, since their respective calculations differ, the Buddha’s intention in marking them both is to indicate to practitioners that falling into a single calculation leads one to become part of its faction; he specifically issues this warning so that they may be cautious.
"Thus deluded regarding the Buddha" and so forth is as explained previously. This concludes the third section, the naming of the externalists.

Regarding "perverse perfection" (*āyatana-viparyāsa*): "perversion" refers to the inverted calculation that takes arising and ceasing to be permanent; because this very [notion] is the meaning of "perfection," it is called "perverse perfection.
If one gives rise to this understanding, one immediately produces that seed.
Furthermore, good son, having exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), [you have] turned your back on the city of Nirvāṇa and produced the seeds of perverse cognition.
This section of the sutra follows upon the ten matters concerning the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) and clarifies its fourth characteristic.
Furthermore, "if one is skillful" and so forth is as previously explained. "If, regarding... correctly clarifies the current calculation:

it means that if this practitioner, with respect to the nature of consciousness and its objects of knowledge, understands that the nature of knowing is pervasive and perfect, and because of this pervasive and perfect knowing, subsequently establishes a distinct [self] that is pervasive and perfect.
"Understanding understanding" means that once knowledge is pervasive and complete, then even the grasses and trees of the ten directions must all know the places they pervade;

thus they should be called sentient beings (*sattva*). Sentient beings are precisely those who possess knowledge. If one claims that grasses and trees lack knowledge, then the nature of knowledge would not be pervasive and complete.
Because knowledge is pervasive, grasses and trees all possess knowledge. If grasses and trees possess knowledge, then they are no different from humans.
There is no difference between grass, trees, and death; when they die, they become humans, and when humans die, they return to being grass and trees.
All know that among the myriad things, there is nothing to be distinguished or selected. If a practitioner gives rise to such a view, they fall into the attachment of "knowing non-knowing";
the Pāṭa and Sainika are examples of this class. Pāṭa and Sainika are the names of two non-Buddhist outsiders; in the Sanskrit language, *pāṭa* [means...]

Some say *Vatsa* is translated as "Avoidance"; [he was] once a cowherd who was stepped upon by the King of Vaiśālī, and his parents instructed him to avoid such things, hence the name was established.
*Sāṇavāsī* is translated as "Having an Army," though the meaning of the name is not fully detailed.
This is seen in the *Suvarṣa-vinaya* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. As for *Sarvabuddhika*, "buddha" (覺) means "to know."
The practitioner’s understanding of identity constitutes their faction; their delusion regarding the Buddha is as previously explained.
This is called the fourth externalist school, "Perfectly Knowing the Mind. That which was previously calculated is taken as this mind, serving as the cause to produce false and erroneous effects.
It is said that both cause and effect are erroneous. Because they calculate what is not-knowing as being known, it is called the inversion of knowledge.

Furthermore, the passage from "Moreover, the good man [realizes] the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena" up to "turning their back on the city of Nirvana, they give birth to the seeds of perverted transformations" constitutes this fifth characteristic, following upon the ten matters concerning the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) mentioned previously. The section beginning with "Moreover, the good man" is as explained before;
the section beginning with "If, regarding... correctly clarifies the current calculation. That is to say, if this practitioner, regarding the nature of consciousness, [perceives it as] perfect...

Within the mutual functioning [of these consciousnesses], one has already attained compliance with their subtlety; this is indeed fortunate. One must not give rise to conceptual calculations regarding this;
for if such calculations arise, one immediately falls into the various heterodoxies. To clarify these heterodox calculations below:

"Perfect Transformation" (yuánhuà) refers to the fact that the nature of this consciousness is fundamentally perfect and complete, and because it is capable of transforming all things, it is called "perfect transformation."
Once this practitioner has clarified the principle of the perfect transformation, they may give rise to various false interpretations within it:

seeking fire to emerge from below; harboring false calculations regarding appearances; falsely venerating the nature of transformation; seeking the luminosity of fire, the purity of water, the circulation of wind, and the accomplishment of earth;
and regarding "dust" as referring to the earth—describing the coarse as the great earth and the subtle as minute particles.
When the various particles (*rajas*) combine, they constitute the great earth; because this is a skillful literary device for moistening the text, it speaks of "particles" rather than "earth.
As for "accomplishment," it means that all things arise from the earth, hence it is called "accomplishment.

"The multitude of particles" refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), for all four elements belong to the category of particles. Thus, it refers to what they venerate and calculate as these four great elements.
If one takes the manifestation of virtue and activity as the cause for veneration and establishes a view of permanence, one falls into the attachment to birth or non-birth;

those such as the Kāśyapas are of this class. The three brothers of the Kāśyapa clan and others of that same lineage all venerate the four great elements (mahābhūta), and are thus called the "Kāśyapa Brahmins"—the translation of their name is as seen previously.

The Buddha’s definitive teaching on "arising from non-arising" means that the four great elements are not permanent or substantial realities and thus cannot produce an eternally abiding, wondrous fruit;
yet people falsely hope they can. To "exert the mind and labor the body" means to forget one's own toil within;
to "serve fire and revere water" means to follow external objects. The phrase "a deluded mind following the words of objects" refers precisely to this kind of delusion regarding the Buddha.
The passage below is as previously explained; this is termed the fifth "externalist's false attachment.

To abandon the original awakening and instead revere external objects—such as falsely seeking through fire-worship, water-reverence, and so forth—is the cause of deluded seeking. To hope for liberation from birth and death through these means is the fruit of such deluded hoping.

Regarding the term "perversion" (*diānhuà*): "perversion" (*diān*) refers to inversion (*dào*); it is not that there is originally no transformation, but rather that one falsely acts where there is none.
Because it is a transformation, it is called "perverted transformation.

Furthermore, the passage from "Moreover, good son, [he] exhausts the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena" up to "turning his back on the city of Nirvāṇa and giving rise to the seed of annihilationism" constitutes this sixth characteristic, following the ten matters concerning the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). From "Furthermore" onwards...

As previously stated, to clarify the current misconception: if this practitioner, regarding the sphere of the perfect luminosity of the nature of consciousness, reckons that within the essence of this perfect luminosity there is originally nothing but void stillness and no dharma to be found, they thereby claim that the myriad transformations are not extinguished and that the principle of "shattering" does not apply.
They falsely reckon that since the perfect luminosity is fundamentally empty, how could there be myriad transformations? Thus, they negate them.

Because they engage in manifold transformations while striving for emptiness and silence, it is said that "manifold transformations are not extinguished. To take this perpetual extinction as one's refuge logically constitutes the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).
Those who form such an understanding fall into the attachment of "taking what is no refuge as a refuge.

This "taking what is no refuge as a refuge" is a term used by the Buddha to describe the state of the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*), where one falsely calculates a non-existent state to be true refuge.
Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is of that same category; *Śūnyatā* is translated as "empty emptiness," which refers to annihilationism.
Thus, they form a faction that deludes the Buddha, as explained previously. This concludes the sixth externalist school. Regarding the name "Perfectly Vacuous Mind" (*yuan xū wú xīn*):
it means taking perfect investigation into vacuity as its causal mind; this "vacuous mind" carries the meaning of annihilationism as its cause.
Since they perceive that results are both void and non-existent, and that actions are likewise empty and lost, they give rise to the seeds of annihilationism.

Furthermore, son of good family, by exhausting all conditioned phenomena to their emptiness (and so forth), they turn their backs on the city of Nirvana and give rise to the seeds of delusive prolongation.

This section of the sutra follows upon the ten matters concerning the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) to clarify the seventh characteristic. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Moreover" is as previously explained;
the passage beginning with "If one" correctly clarifies the present calculation.

That is to say, if this practitioner, within the meaning of the perfect and eternal nature of consciousness, gives rise to an understanding based on its eternity and clings to all things as being eternal, they will falsely and stubbornly fixate upon the physical body, seeking to make it eternal.
Abiding by means of this physical body, which is identical in nature to consciousness—perfect, eternal, and long-enduring within the world—one does not allow it to decline or pass away.

One who gives rise to such an understanding falls into the attachment of either craving or non-craving. That which the Buddha designated as "craving" or "non-craving" refers to this illusory body being impermanent;
yet, because one falsely calculates it to be solid and permanent, one generates craving and attachment. Therefore, it is said: [as follows].
Greed is not greed; the various *ṛṣis* (Asis) belong to this class.

*Asita* is translated as "Incomparable" (*Abhūta*) or "Long-lived," for among those with life in the world, he is long-lived because he has not undergone transformation. Regarding the delusion concerning the Buddha, it is as previously explained.
This concludes the seventh category of externalists: those who cling to the source of life, maintaining that consciousness, breath, and warmth are the three things that sustain existence.
Among these three dharmas that constitute life, consciousness is the fundamental source, as previously stated: "The primary cause of receiving life is this.

It establishes the causes for the solidification of delusion and leads to the fruit of long-term toil. That the fruit is called "long-term toil" means that one is attached to worldly afflictions for a long duration, making them the ultimate fruit.
As for the prolongation of delusion, it is as the ancient saying goes: "Even if you have eight..."
After ten thousand kalpas, one will ultimately fall into emptiness and ruin; is this not a futile prolongation?

Furthermore, good man, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena to the point of realizing their emptiness (up to) turning one's back on the city of Nirvana and being born into the race of celestial Māras.

This section of the sutra follows upon the ten matters concerning the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*); here, the eighth characteristic is clarified. Furthermore, "skillfully" and below are as previously explained.
Regarding "observing life-force" and below, this correctly clarifies the current calculation.

As for "observing life-force and mutual penetration," it means that when this person, within the meditative concentration of the aggregate of consciousness, observes the nature of consciousness as the fundamental source of life-force, it mutually penetrates the twelve classes of living beings; thus, that [consciousness]...

Because these are mutually interpenetrating, they are said to be "mutually interpenetrating. Wénlǐng’s commentary, which states that this refers to the mutual interpenetration of the three periods of time, is incorrect.
If it were referring to the three periods, how could they be mutually interpenetrating? The past has already ceased and the future has not yet arrived;

life is restricted solely to the present, where it maintains the physical body. As for "life-of-life" (*jīvitendriya*), it cannot extend into the past, nor can the past life [extend into the present].
Since they have already ceased, how can they be mutually interpenetrated? The preceding passage clearly explained that the twelve sources of life have already attained their commonality;
the word "common" (*tong*) is precisely the meaning of mutual interpenetration. Now, this practitioner, while contemplating the source of life, thinks:

"If the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted, my life will also be exhausted. Who then will witness the true permanence? Fearing that the consciousness might be extinguished, he [hesitates].

Because they remain attached to the defilements of worldly toil, their aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) does not reach its end; thus, within the fundamental limit of the nature of consciousness, there manifest lotus palaces.
Describing their adornment as supremely magnificent and beautiful, they become immersed in the realms of the five desires.

Furthermore, they extensively transform themselves into seven-jeweled treasures and wealth, greatly increasing their "jeweled ladies"—"jeweled ladies" being women of exquisite beauty—to whom they give rein and abandon all restraint.
To indulge one’s mind in such views and form this kind of understanding is to fall into the attachment to "true non-truth.
"True non-truth" is a term used by the Buddha to describe those things that are fundamentally not true yet are falsely reckoned as true; thus it is called "true non-truth.
Takṣaka is of this class. Regarding Takṣaka, the fourth scripture states: "Takṣaka..."
The Luo translation calls it "Wheel Mountain" (*Cakravāṇa*); the current [translation] calls it *Takṣaka-giri*.

This name is derived from the fact that practitioners cultivate the Way (immortality) based on this mountain; thus it is named accordingly. Regarding "deluded by the Buddha," as explained previously, this concludes the eighth heterodox school.
As for "fervent dust of perverse thoughts," as clarified above, these are all the thoughts of demonic heretics which serve as the causal mind.
To establish the blazing afflictions as the fruit—such a practice and understanding is the seed of the celestial Māras.

Furthermore, son of good family, to exhaust all conditioned phenomena into emptiness (and so forth) until one turns one’s back on the city of Nirvāṇa gives rise to the seed of entanglement in emptiness.
This section of the sutra follows the ten matters concerning the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) previously discussed; it clarifies the ninth characteristic.
Furthermore, "Moreover, [it is] as explained before" refers to the preceding discourse. Regarding "At the end of life," this correctly elucidates the current calculation:

that is to say, this practitioner, within the fundamentally luminous aspect of the nature and life of consciousness, discriminates the reception of life—its good and evil, its refinement and coarseness—and decisively resolves the causes and effects of karmic actions, reaching the truth.

With a false intention, one regards that which is produced by tainted (*sāsrava*) karmic formations as coarse and false, and that which is produced by untainted (*anāsrava*) karmic formations as refined and true.
Taking such causes to yield such effects, this person makes the seeking of causal correspondence their primary practice;
this is precisely the meaning of "knowing suffering and abandoning its origin," which refers to the principle of causal correspondence.
If one seeks these as causes, they become utterly confused and chaotic, turning their backs on the path of the primary truth—purity and quiescence.
What is called "suffering" (duḥkha) refers to the present fruit of suffering;
what is called "origination" (samudaya) refers to the causal karma of the past, so named because it has accumulated over vast eons; and what is called "cessation" (nirodha) refers to its extinction.

Because one attains the realization of *nirvāṇa* through the cessation of suffering and its origin, these are termed "Cessation" and the "Path. This path consists of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), which are the practices that assist the path.
This constitutes the doctrinal characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) of the Four Truths of the Hīnayāna. When one attains abiding in the Truth of Cessation, the mind immediately rests;
those practitioners who give rise to such a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) fall into the category of the Śrāvaka of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*) and do not proceed further.
Among those in the heavens of non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), those such as bhikṣus who have not heard the Dharma and those of overweening pride (*adhimāna*) become their companions.

The meaning of "fixed nature" (*niyata-dhātu*) and "those who have not heard and are overweeningly proud" is as explained previously. Regarding the phrase "deluded by the Buddha," it is as stated before.
This concludes the ninth name of the practitioner. As for "the mind of perfect, refined practice" (*yuanjing xingxin*), it refers to its perfection.

Exhausting the distinctions between the refined and the coarse, the true and the false, they take this as the cause for their minds to advance toward the fruit of the Small Vehicle’s withered and silent state;
those "entangled in emptiness" refer to followers of the Small Vehicle who are entangled in and belong to the category of partial emptiness.
Furthermore, "the good man exhausts the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena" (up to) "giving rise to a perfectly clear awakening, not transforming the perfect seed.

This section of the sutra follows the ten matters of the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) and clarifies its tenth characteristic. The passage beginning with "furthermore, the good man" is as previously explained;
the passage beginning with "if, regarding... correctly clarifies the present calculation. That is to say, if this practitioner, regarding the nature of consciousness, is perfect...
To develop and investigate the profound and subtle principles within the ground of fused, pure, awakened clarity, one establishes the path of nirvāṇa therein and does not proceed further.
However, this pure, awakened clarity is merely the ultimate limit of the nature of consciousness—a partial truth that is an awakening to mere emptiness;
it is by no means the awakened clarity of the primary truth (paramārtha-satya). This is because...
To establish the principle of nirvana based on a state where quiescence is not yet perfected is to fall into the category of those with fixed nature (niyata-gotra) who are pratyekabuddhas.
To these *pratyekabuddhas*, the word "Buddha" (*buddha*) should be added; they are translated as "Conditioned Awakening" (*yuanjue*) or "Solitary Awakening" (*dudiao*).

Because they are attached to meditative concentration and do not initiate the practice of transforming others, they are called those of "fixed nature. Having become such companions, they have not yet [perfected] the Path.

Furthermore, as for the statement in the preceding text regarding "having causes and what is caused," such as "attachment and non-attachment," the reason these terms are not mentioned here within the context of the two fixed natures (*niyata-gotra*) is that those of a fixed nature merely indulge in the shallow and superficial; they do not turn toward the Great Way, and thus [for them] there is neither "correct" nor "erroneous.
Consequently, no such words are used. As with the eight matters previously discussed, all belong to erroneous understanding; therefore, the Buddha judged them to be mistaken.
The ear is deluded regarding the Buddha, as explained previously; this is called the conclusion of the tenth practitioner.

"The practitioner of Perfect Enlightenment" (*yuanjue xingzhe*) refers to one who has thoroughly and perfectly exhausted enlightened clarity (*jue ming*), merging it with the True Principle (*zhengli*) to form the causal mind;
thus, they achieve the minor fruit of serene and tranquil enlightened clarity. Regarding "the ear not transforming into perfection": "not transforming" refers to a fixed nature (*dingxing*).
Because the intention to transform others does not arise, but rather one perfects one's own practice through a settled mind, it is said that "perfection does not involve transformation.

Someone may ask: "If the point where the nature of consciousness is exhausted is identical to the awakening of a Buddha, then by cultivating the functions of the aggregate of consciousness, one would transcend the three realms and enter the vehicle of the Bodhisattvas.
Why, then, does the text state that the first eight matters still belong to the distinctions within the realm?"

How is this to be reconciled? The answer is: if one relies on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, it is true that prior to the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), one has merely abandoned the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), and after the Vajra Path, the emptiness of the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is realized; this is indeed as you have asked.

However, what is being clarified here concerns the period when the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is about to be destroyed but has not yet been destroyed. Furthermore, the meaning of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) applies throughout both the preceding and succeeding stages; therefore, other sutras and śāstras [speak accordingly].

It is said that while the Lesser Vehicle regards the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as *nirvāṇa*, and non-Buddhists reckon it as the *ātman*, this present scripture has not yet reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception among the first eight matters;

therefore, it merely clarifies that by giving rise to various false interpretations regarding the nature of consciousness, one falls into the calculations of the non-Buddhists. Hereafter follow the latter two matters.
This still pertains to those of the two vehicles who have transcended the world; they remain attached to the nature of this consciousness, halting at its shallow and proximate ultimate limit.
This discussion is generally situated within the refutation of errors on the side of the dualistic clinging to a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*).

However, once one ascends to the First Stage (*prathamabhūmi*), departing from the point of destroying the innate (*sahaja*) clinging to a self and phenomena, such divergent views no longer exist. Therefore, the present text stops with these two.

Those of fixed nature have profound reason for this. However, although the previous discourse on the "mutual functioning of the six sense organs" belongs to the stage of "similar realization" of a Bodhisattva—situated within the level of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*)—its severing of afflictions is identical to that of the Two Vehicles;
therefore, the text does not mention the word "Bodhisattva. By grasping the underlying intent, it can be understood. Furthermore, these five aggregates are exhausted in sequence.
This is because the Buddha has laid it out and expounded it in this sequential manner to accommodate those of the three capacities (*trividha-indriya*).
As for those of the perfect capacity (*paripūrṇa-indriya*), who sever everything in one stroke and realize everything in one realization—how could they be restricted by this?

Thus, one should know that while the detailed exposition (*khyāpana*) is comprehensive, the perfect fusion (*yuanrong*) allows for entry at any point. This is what is meant by the saying: "For example, the great ocean does not refuse even the smallest stream."
This is what is meant.
Ānanda, within these ten kinds of *dhyāna*, from the beginning until their completion, one shall not encounter byways [of deviation].
This section of the sutra concludes the ten matters concerning the *vijñānakāya* (consciousness aggregate) so as to admonish practitioners not to deceive themselves.
The guarding, cultivation, entry, and realization are thus. Below, the main body concludes the preceding meaning.

Those who become deranged midway are as previously explained regarding the ten matters: none have yet fully realized the limit (*jì*). Midway, they give rise to various delusory understandings, each relying on their own respective delusions;
taking what is insufficient to be sufficient, it is all as previously stated, and thus they are born into this state.
Regarding the term "stage" (*wei*): it follows from the previous discussion on the "knots of the aggregates" (*skandha-granthi*), where it was said that one gives rise to this awakening.

The previous mention of "awakening" referred to the side of the subject who awakens; the current mention of "stage" refers to the stage of realization attained by the object. Thus, the preceding and succeeding terms are mutually inclusive.
However, this realized stage is precisely that stage of delusory realization regarding the ten matters; it is not the true stage. As for the "multitudes of beings," it is as explained previously.

Regarding the statement "each according to what they themselves love" and so forth: this means that among the ten types of persons mentioned previously, each takes their own preferred object as the basis for prior cultivation;
with minds deluded, they grasp at that delusion as liberation and rest therein.
Each regards the place where they have found rest as the ground of ultimate refuge and peace, and each individually claims to have attained unsurpassed *bodhi*.
By committing a great falsehood, one receives demonic blessings that, once exhausted, lead inevitably to the Avīci Hell. "External heterodoxy" refers to the preceding seven matters;

"the demon" refers to the eighth matter. Regarding the final two types of those fixed in their nature (*niyata-gotra*), because they are attached to the bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and fail to achieve further progress, they are distinguished from those who fall away;
thus, they are separately identified and demonstrated. "You all," and so forth—this is the Buddha’s command to Ānanda and his peers to remain and fulfill their vows.
Entering the age of the Final Dharma (*mappō*), one transmits this teaching with the intent that people shall deeply guard and maintain the correct method; only then can they enter into realization.
As for "beholding demons," this refers to the demon of the mind within the preceding stage of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Because it arises from a perverted mind, now, through the extinction of the mind of birth-and-death, only views and interpretations remain. Since these views have become deviant, one takes these very views and interpretations as demons. This is the Great [Demon].
Reaching into the *vijñānaskandha* (consciousness-aggregate) and resolving it is similar to what was previously described as "profound. Regarding "entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision":

in the ten matters mentioned above, each adhered to the knowledge and vision of external paths or the two vehicles, thereby losing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; now, by teaching them to turn away from error and return to correctness, they enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
"This Dharma-gate, from the past through to the perfection of Bodhi, ultimately returns to non-attainment.

This section of the sutra summarizes the preceding discourse to demonstrate that, from beginning to end, all Buddhas rely upon this Dharma-gate to reach the ultimate, perfect state and return to the ground of non-attainment. "This Dharma-gate" refers to...
Regarding the two meanings previously mentioned: if referring broadly, the entire sūtra is [the subject]; if referring narrowly, it is the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
The Buddha stated that this dharma-gate is not something that only Śākyamuni Buddha himself could cultivate;
rather, all the Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have all relied upon this dharma to realize *bodhi*. This is as in the fifth sūtra.
This refers to what is called "the single path to nirvana for the Bhagavans of the ten directions.

Regarding the section on the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate) below, it follows the preceding by generally indicating the sequence of stages from beginning to end, as well as their names and meanings: if the *vijñāna-skandha* is exhausted, one attains the mutual functioning of all sense organs (*indriya*).
This mutual functioning belongs to the stage of the Ten Faiths; this cites its beginning. The "Vajra Dry Wisdom" (*vajra-śuṣka-prajñā*) refers to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samāpatti-bodhi*).
The phrase "the final mind" indicates its conclusion. The four lines beginning with "perfectly bright" (yuanming) clarify the Dharma by means of metaphors:

the first two lines represent the Dharma, and the latter two lines represent the metaphor. "Perfectly bright and refined mind" refers to the ultimate fruit-awareness manifesting at the point where the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) is exhausted, within the mutual functioning of the sense organs;
therefore, it says "it develops and transforms therein. The word "therein" (zhong) specifically points to this state.
The mutual application [of the two] is like the analogy of pure lapis lazuli; the mutual application of the mind is like the analogy of the moon, representing the perfect clarity of the mind.
The correspondence between the Dharma and these analogies can be understood as above; this is merely a general summary that briefly indicates the beginning and the end.
Below, the various stages are again set forth in sequence from the beginning to the end; therefore, it says, "Thus, one transcends... and so forth. Bodhi.
Regarding "the ten stages of the vajra practiced by the Bodhisattva": these vajra syllables metaphorically represent the contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) of the ten stages.

As the preceding sutra states, "These ten stages are all observed through ten kinds of profound vajra metaphors," which refers to the sense that the contemplative wisdom—taking metaphors such as an illusion—is firm and solid.
The phrase "entering into" below concludes and demonstrates the meaning of the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood, the wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Furthermore, "the ocean of wondrous adornment" (*miao zhuangyan hai*) reveals both the dharma and its metaphor simultaneously.
This refers to ultimate, perfect bodhi, which is inherently tranquil and quiescent, beyond the reach of thought and speculation, like the great void where not a single dharma can be found.
Because it is adorned by the two powers of meditative concentration and wisdom—adorned in a manner that is itself unadornable—it is called "wondrous."
This refers precisely to the fifty-five stages adorned with the wondrous power of inconceivable samādhi and wisdom.
The "ocean" is a metaphor used to illustrate that this perfected Bodhi is as vast and deep as the great ocean; yet it is not merely deep and vast.
The ocean possesses ten qualities, as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which serve as metaphors for this wondrously adorned ocean of enlightenment.

Because it possesses nature-endowed virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it is likened to the ocean. "Returning to that which is non-attainable" means that although one is endowed with nature-endowed virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, these very virtues are non-existent;
this is the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the ground of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
It does not admit even a single speck of dust; it is precisely the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, the ultimate perfection, which serves as the refuge.
"This is the final instruction left behind by the past Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, [up to] the ultimate cultivation and progress.

This section of the sutra records how the World-Honored One, having reversed the demonic activities of the five aggregates, earnestly instructed and exhorted [the disciples] to maintain deep vigilance and uphold the correct path as his final legacy.
The phrase "This is" and below clarifies that this Dharma-gate is [the teaching of] the past.
Regarding the three meanings—*śamatha*, *vipaśyanā*, and so forth—which were practiced and transmitted by previous Buddhas, the term "dhyāna" (*chan-na*) is currently omitted;
this is due to a brevity of expression. As for the phrase "within *śamatha* there is *vipaśyanā*," the character "in" (*zhong*, *madhya*) contains a profound meaning.
Why is this? *Śama* is translated as "cessation" (*zhi*), and *vipa* is translated as "contemplation" (*guan*); the meaning of the character "in" clarifies this point.

Within *śamatha* (calm abiding) the meaning of *vipaśyanā* (insight) is fully present, and within *vipaśyanā* the meaning of *śamatha* is likewise fully present. They are perfectly interfused and mutually inclusive; though they have different names, they share the same essence.

However, this is not a case of sequential or distinct *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, but rather the perfectly interfused Middle Way. Therefore, one must not treat the character "zhong" (middle) lightly or overlook it.

Furthermore, the reason only the two dharmas of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are mentioned here is that *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*— [...are] the basis for all phenomena. Thus, by means of these two, one can exhaustively encompass all dharmas. This is why only these two are cited. (Note: The bracketed section is an inferred continuation based on the context of the original Chinese text regarding the function of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.)
Because this is the ultimate meaning, the harmonious fusion of two dharmas constitutes three meanings; although three names are mentioned, two meanings are sufficient, and thus only two are cited.
This meaning is contained within the *Nirvāṇa*, *Yogācāra*, and other sūtras and śāstras, which scholars must not fail to understand.
As for "the analysis of enlightened clarity" (*jue-ming fen-xi*), "enlightened clarity" refers to contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*).
This means that based on the wisdom of contemplation arising from meditative concentration, one analyzes all demons to instruct those who have not yet learned.
When you say, "You are able to recognize them," you are referring to Ānanda and the assembly present here;

it can be known that because you have personally received the Buddha's teaching and your mental defilements are already purified, you do not fall into false views, and thus the demons cannot emerge from within.
The two external [māras] are the mind and the internal are the *skandha-māra*, as stated in the preceding text: "the two māras of mind and vision.
The external [māras] are those such as devas, ghosts, and spirits; as for the *skandha-māra* mentioned here as being "dissolved and extinguished," it may be understood from the preceding text.
Regarding the *deva-māra* being "crushed and shattered," this refers to what was previously called: "when one person develops the truth and returns to the source, that locus is torn asunder."
"Is this so? "To have one's soul stripped away" (*tīpò*)—*tī* means to lose; it refers to losing one's *po* and *huó*, thereby fleeing and departing.

"Inferior progress" (*xiàliè zēngjìn*) refers to those of the two types of fixed-nature individuals (*niyati-gotra*). Because they indulge in and savor meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), this is their inferior progress;
their minds are the result of the practice described in the preceding sutra. As for those who are inferior to the Buddhas, the Buddha commanded Ānanda and his peers to [turn]...

The teaching also includes the bestowal of methods for protection: it is said that in the final age, practitioners will be dull-witted and fail to recognize right concentration, while their preceptors and monks will not understand how to preach the Dharma.
Consequently, these practitioners will not distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox;

since they do not recognize the correct path, those who delight in practicing meditation must fear falling into the same category as heterodox outsiders. Therefore, you should exhort them to single-mindedly uphold the Buddha’s heart-mantra.
Whether by reciting, writing, or wearing [this mantra], one may provide protection; thus, Māras will be unable to disturb them.
This constitutes the Great Compassionate One’s earnest instruction and serves as his final model for posterity. The remaining text is easily understood.
"Ānanda immediately rose from his seat upon hearing the Buddha’s instruction... (until) all sentient beings shall serve as eyes for the future.

This section of the sutra describes how Ānanda, having heard of the demonic affairs concerning the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), again based himself on the five aggregates and formulated three points of inquiry.
The phrase "Ānanda [immediately]" and so forth is the narrative commentary provided by the compiler of the sutra; "immediately rose from his seat" refers to the first point.
The phrase should be placed under "Hearing the Buddha’s instruction" to accord with the current wording; it is slightly inverted here.

Just as "the Buddha below" refers to Ānanda’s question, the three phrases following "the five aggregates" state that Ānanda, based on what he previously heard regarding the five aggregates, takes the five kinds of deluded thoughts as their root;
thus he says, "These five kinds of false and illusory [thoughts] serve as the fundamental basis for the thinking mind. I... [text ends].

The three subsequent phrases below describe the intention of not having heard [the teaching] before. Furthermore, from "Moreover" (*kō*) onwards, the three points are formally presented as questions, which together resolve the meaning of the "sudden" (*ton*) and the meaning of the "gradual" (*zoku*).
"To what does one arrive as a realm? (*ki*) asks about the boundaries of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*);
these constitute the three questions. "I only pray... and so forth is the concluding phrase of the inquiry. "Clarifying the mind and eyes" (*shōmei kokumin*) refers to the Buddha.
"Reveal to us these three meanings so that our minds and eyes may become clear and bright; only then shall we be capable of serving as the true eye for that future age.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "From 'the refined, true, wondrous, and luminous' (up to) 'how much more so those who do not know and yet push the blame onto nature.'"
In this section of the sutra, the World-Honored One answers the question by first designating the True to clarify that the realm of emptiness arises falsely;
he then reveals that the two natures are fundamentally non-existent based on that falsity. The passage beginning with "Essential Truth" (jing zhen) formally designates the essence of the True:
it means that true awakening is originally perfect and pure, such that all defilements of birth and death cannot remain within it, for emptiness is like [space].
Because the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) does not receive even a single speck of dust, [the text] proceeds downward to demonstrate that the realm of space (*ākāśa-dhātu*) arises falsely;
from the word "even" (*nai-zhi*) onward, it connects with the aforementioned discussion of various defilements, which cannot be fully enumerated and is therefore spoken of by leaping over them.

That is to say, even empty space is produced by deluded thought (*vikalpa*), let alone anything else. As the Fourth Sūtra says: "Due to ignorance (*avidyā*), it transforms and gives rise to insentient matter..."
That "empty ignorance" is precisely deluded thought (*vikalpa*). These latter two lines further explain the return of the deluded to the True:

this empty space is originally the essence-body of the true quintessence of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). Because sentient beings momentarily give rise to deluded minds, they transform the True into the deluded;
thus, they undergo the transformation into stubborn emptiness. When delusion does not cease, one relies on this emptiness with firm attachment, and the false world-receptacle (*bhājana-loka*) arises.
The section "The Elements" (Dhātu) cites an example below to clarify that delusion has no cause.

In the fourth sutra, it uses the case of *Evayūṣmat* (*Yanruo Dada*), who mistook his own head for the reflection in a mirror, as an analogy for the present situation where one is deluded regarding the True and pursues various delusions.

Delusion originally has no cause; it arises from delusion based upon delusion. Therefore, the natures of being caused by conditions or being spontaneous are themselves delusory. Since causes and conditions are already delusory...

Furthermore, to be deluded regarding causes and conditions and to reckon them as being spontaneous (*svabhāva*)—since these two natures, cause-and-condition and spontaneity, arise based on the conceptualization of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)—is illustrated by taking the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) space as an analogy.

It is said that even space, an unconditioned phenomenon, still belongs to the realm of illusory arising; how much more so must conditioned phenomena be illusory? Therefore, it is directly shown: they are causes and conditions.
That which is "spontaneous" (svabhāva) is entirely the conceptual construction of the deluded minds of sentient beings. Ānanda, below I shall clarify that delusion is fundamentally non-existent:

if one knows where delusion arises, one may speak of the causes and conditions of that delusion; but if one realizes that delusion is fundamentally non-existent, one will know that causes and conditions are originally nothing at all.
If causes and conditions themselves do not exist, how much less can one claim to be ignorant of them while further postulating spontaneity?

It is indeed as if Yajñadatta were deluded regarding his own head and falsely pursued its external reflection; while his original head remained unmoving, his delusion and error had no cause whatsoever.
Therefore, the Tathāgata has explained this for you [up to] what is called "the first solid false imagination."

This section of the sutra concludes the preceding [discussion] and properly answers the question regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), perceptions (*saṃjñā*), and mind (*citta*). The text consists of five segments;

this first part clarifies the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*). The initial portion, beginning with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*), concludes the preceding discussion on the causes of delusion and how it arises.

The Buddha states that the fundamental cause of the five aggregates is likewise constituted by false conceptualization (*vikalpa*); because they are deluded regarding the Truth (*tattva*), they pursue various delusions.

[The Buddha] agreed. Although the original intent regarding the first five aggregates had already been clarified, Ānanda now asks about them again so that sentient beings of the future age may easily understand.
Because of this question, the World-Honored One provides a further summary and demonstration. From the words "Your body... onwards, he begins the subsequent text;
first, he demonstrates the original intent regarding the aggregate of form. He addresses Ānanda specifically to represent all Buddhas, saying: "As for you..."
The physical body is first produced by the desire-thoughts of the parents; it is formed through the union of the vital essence and blood during the parents' sexual intercourse.

This section of the sutra again emphasizes that the merit of reciting this sutra for even a single thought-moment surpasses the most evil and grave offenses of the Avīci hell over long kalpas;

The Buddha spoke these words below because he wished to compare evil with merit; fearing that people might not believe him, he first clarified that the Buddha’s words are without falsehood to alert them and inspire faith.
"If again... and so forth is the formal comparison of extreme evil with the ability to transcend it;

The Verse of Dedication says:
I take refuge in the Honored One of Ten Powers, In the Buddha-Usnīṣa Samādhi, And in the Bodhisattvas and Śrāvaka Saṅgha.
May they bestow their compassion upon me, That I may understand this most profound meaning; I vow to dedicate [this merit] to the three spheres.
The Buddhas and Bodhi, the ten types of ordinary beings— In their essential nature and characteristics, they are ultimately non-dual and without discrimination.
May I, in all future lives, never lose sight of the three kinds of giving as I relieve the suffering of the multitudes;
Through the accumulation of kalpas, may my generosity be inexhaustible, And through right practice, may I give rise to the true cause.

Whether following or opposing, both accomplish transformation; Self-benefit and benefiting others, The two virtuous paths of coming and going, and the ability to adapt to the seven realms of existence;
Through seeing and hearing, beings are subdued as they encounter them; Supported by what belongs to them, they achieve the capacity to attain Buddha-wisdom;
Transformation follows transformation, with vows arising together; Practice after practice, the *pāramitā* of infinite crossing.
Pointing to the Pure Land as Mind-Only, I realize that my original nature is the Buddha. The Four Great Vows pervade every mote of dust and hair;
there is nothing to be done, yet there is no end to what is done. My heart’s aspiration is rooted in Śākyamuni;
may the Bhagavāns of all lands and that Amitāyus pour their intermingled light upon the crown of my head. I pray that you extend your broad and long tongue.
Bestowing upon me the prediction of Bodhi, you act as the supreme banner for all beings.
Expounding the primary truth, we shall ascend together the mountain of Nirvana and forever part from the Mother of Ignorance.
